A useful analogy is that of a tree, with a trunk, major branches, minor branches, twigs, and ultimately, leaves ( Fig. 0.1 ). Instead of memorizing thousands of leaves, a logical, progressive differential diagnosis. Inflammatory versus neoplastic An early and major “branch point” in classifying skin diseases is deciding if a skin condition is “neoplastic” (either benign or malignant) or “inflammatory” (either infectious or non-infectious) (see Fig. 0.1 ). However, an experienced clinician knows that one must consider possible diagnoses along multiple limbs before narrowing the differ- ential diagnosis, because overlap and mimicry can occur. For example, mycosis fungoides, the most common form of cutaneous T cell lymphoma, is a clonal lymphoproliferative disorder (a “neoplasm”), yet its clinical presentation resembles an inflammatory disorder ( Fig. 0.2 ), particularly in its early stages. Conversely, sarcoidosis is an inflam- matory condition, yet it may present as an isolated infiltrated plaque or nodule that may mimic a neoplasm ( Fig. 0.3 ). Morphology To an engineer or material scientist, the word “ morphology ” refers to the structure and appearance of a material without regard to function. In dermatology, the term refers to the general appearance of a skin lesion, irrespective of the etiology or underlying pathophysiology. The average adult has 1.75 m 2 (18.5 ft 2 ­ adnexal structures, including hair follicles, nails, glands, and specialized sensory structures, all of which function in protection, homeostasis, and the transmission of sensation. Dermatology is the field of medicine that deals with the macroscopic study of skin, adjacent mucosa (oral and genital), and cutaneous adnexa, while dermatopathology deals with the microscopic study of these same structures. The two fields are Multiple studies have shown that dermatologists are the most effective diagnosticians of skin disease 1,2 . This enhanced acumen reflects experience in recognizing distribution patterns and configura- tions, as well as subtle variations in morphology and colors, in addition to appreciating associated histopathologic findings. This chapter serves as an introduction to classification schemas and to descriptive termi- nologies and diagnostic tools utilized in dermatology. It also highlights additional means for studying skin, including dermoscopy (derma- toscopy), artificial intelligence, and dermatopathology, with clinico- pathologic correlation between macroscopic and microscopic findings. Proper use of morphologic terms establishes a structural framework for grouping skin diseases based upon their macroscopic appearances 3 . In essence, morphologic terms form a “native language” by which dermatologists, and other health professionals, communicate with each other to describe skin lesions. As such, they are key elements of our shared lexicon. Without a working knowledge of morphology, it is impossible to describe cutaneous observations in a consistent manner. Ergo, one of the initial steps in studying dermatology is to learn the basic morphologic definitions inherent to the specialty. There exist both primary morphologic terms ( Table 0.1 ), which refer to the most characteristic, representative, or native appearance of skin lesions (e.g. a “papule”), as well as secondary morphologic terms ( Table 0.2 ), which augment or supplant primary morphologic terms. Secondary morphologic terms often reflect the effects of exogenous factors or temporal changes (e.g. “scales”, “crusts”) that evolve during the course of a skin disease. Secondary features must be considered when performing, or examining histologically, a biopsy of a skin lesion. An astute clinician will biopsy a lesion that is both “fresh” and well-developed as it most aptly demon- strates the primary pathologic process. Lesions with confounding secondary changes such as erosions, excoriations, and lichenification are avoided, if possible, as this allows the dermatopathologist the oppor- tunity to evaluate the histologic features in their native state. Lastly, the skin is a three-dimensional structure, and like cartog- raphers who construct maps, there are accepted descriptors used by dermatologists to describe the topography of individual skin lesions. Examples include flat-topped (lichenoid), dome-shaped, verrucous, umbilicated, filiform, and pedunculated 3 . Palpation and appreciation of textural changes Any discussion of morphology must include textural change, and palpating a lesion often provides diagnostic clues. In dermatology, palpation can prove useful in several ways. Firstly, it helps in making a distinction amongst various morphologies (see Table 0.1 ). For example, the key difference between macules and papules, or patches versus plaques, is that macules and patches are flush with the surrounding skin and cannot be appreciated by palpation. On the other hand, papules and plaques, by definition, must be palpable ( Table 0.3 ). Secondly, palpation may augment understanding of a disease process that is otherwise unimpressive or nonspecific. Lastly, purpura is often classified as palpable or non-palpable, and this division can imply different underlying etiologies (e.g. small vessel vasculitis is aligned more with palpable purpura). Examples of useful distinctions that can be gleaned via palpation are outlined in Table 0.4 . Color The color of skin lesions provides clues as to the nature of the disease process. Sometimes the perception of color may be modified by palpation (see Table 0.4 ). For example, while many dermatologic processes appear erythematous (red to purple) in color, it is important to ascertain whether this color is “blanchable” (i.e. disappears with pressure), which suggests it is due to vasodilation, or “non-blanchable,” which suggests it is due to extravasation of erythrocytes into the skin. Exogenous sources of pigment, such as topical medicaments, oral drugs, and other ingestants, can also lead to skin discoloration. Variations in skin color are a result of differences in the amount and distribution of melanin within epidermal melanocytes and keratino- cytes 6 , rather than the number of melanocytes (see Ch. 65 ). The ratio of eumelanin (brown–black) to pheomelanin (yellow–red) also influ- ences skin color, with pheomelanin the predominant pigment in those with freckles and red hair. Exposure to ultraviolet radiation also impacts melanin production (tanning). Mucocutaneous pigmentation influences the prevalence of certain cutaneous findings and disorders. For example, individuals with darker skin phototypes are more likely to develop longitudinal melanonychia (see Ch. 71 ) 7,8 , pigmentation of the oral mucosa 9 , persistent postin- flammatory hyperpigmentation (see Ch. 67 ), and pigmentary demar- cation lines 10 (Futcher lines or Voigt lines; see Fig. 67.12 ). Whether postinflammatory hypopigmentation 11 is more common or simply more apparent is a matter of debate. In addition, discoid lupus erythe- matosus, sarcoidosis, and keloids are seen more often in patients with darkly pigmented skin and African ancestry, but there is no known relationship of these disorders to melanocyte function. There can also be differences in the physiologic properties of the skin. For example, the stratum corneum of black skin often retains more layers and is more compact and cohesive than that of white skin. In addition, darker skin produces less vitamin D 3 in response to equiv- alent amounts of sunlight, and this is postulated to have been a driving force in the evolution of more lightly pigmented skin as early humans migrated away from the equator 12 . Perhaps the most important point to remember is that erythema (redness) can be difficult to appreciate in darkly pigmented skin. Erythema is caused by vasodilation and/or increased blood flow within the dermis, and if the epidermis is deeply pigmented, the red hues of oxyhemoglobin may be less apparent. For this reason, diseases often described as decidedly erythematous (e.g. cellulitis) or violaceous (e.g. lichen planus) may have a different hue in darker skin types ( Fig. 0.6 ) 13 . For this reason, diseases often described as decidedly erythematous (e.g. cellulitis) or violaceous (e.g. lichen planus) may have a different hue in darker skin types ( Fig. 0.6 ) 13 . When performing diagnostic procedures that depend upon the devel- opment of overt erythema, such as patch testing for the evaluation of allergic contact dermatitis, appreciation of the influence of epidermal pigment is important. Lastly, cyanosis (blue hues indicative of poor oxygenation and a critical clinical sign) may be more difficult to appre- ciate when the skin is darkly pigmented. Configuration and Distribution After carefully considering the morphology and color of skin lesions, the dermatologist must analyze two closely related properties – ­configuration and distribution – in order to generate a differential diagnosis. For example, pruritic and fragile vesicles on the elbows and knees prompt consideration of dermatitis herpetiformis, whereas grouped vesicles on an erythematous base, confined to a single dermatome, mandate consideration of herpes zoster (see Fig. 0.4A ) or zosteriform herpes simplex. Configuration The configuration or arrangement of skin lesions can provide important diagnostic clues. Examples include annular (e.g. tinea corporis, granuloma annulare; see Ch. 19 ), serpiginous (e.g. cutaneous larva migrans), clustered/grouped (e.g. piloleiomyomas, herpetiform vesicles), reticulated (e.g. erythema ab igne), and retiform (e.g. purpura fulminans, purpura due to calciphylaxis [ Fig. 0.7 ]; see Ch. 23 ). The latter pattern reflects occlusion of cutaneous vasculature 14 . It is important to determine if the lesions have a linear configu- ration ( Fig. 0.8 ). They may follow the lines of Blaschko, which reflect patterns of embryonic development (see Fig. 62.1 ) 15 , or lesions may be confined to a dermatome, which represents an area of skin innervated by a single spinal nerve (see Fig. 80.13 ). Irrespective of whether lesions are along the lines of Blaschko (e.g. epidermal nevi) or are in a derma- tomal pattern (e.g. herpes zoster [see Fig. 0.4A ]), there is often charac- teristic midline demarcation. A linear arrangement can also result from trauma-induced Koebner phenomenon (an isomorphic response [ Table 0.7 ]), as in vitiligo, lichen planus ( Fig. 0.9 ), and psoriasis 16,17 , or trauma-induced autoinoculation, as in verrucae vulgares or verrucae planae. lines of Blaschko (e.g. epidermal nevi) or are in a derma- tomal pattern (e.g. herpes zoster [see Fig. 0.4A ]), there is often charac- teristic midline demarcation. A linear arrangement can also result from trauma-induced Koebner phenomenon (an isomorphic response [ Table 0.7 ]), as in vitiligo, lichen planus ( Fig. 0.9 ), and psoriasis 16,17 , or trauma-induced autoinoculation, as in verrucae vulgares or verrucae planae. Linear lesions are often seen in acute allergic contact derma- titis due to plants (e.g. poison ivy), reflecting a brushing of branches and leaves against skin. Lastly, papulonodules due to a range of infec- tious agents can align along lymphatic vessels in a sporotrichoid pattern (see Ch. 77 ). On occasion, cutaneous lesions have an unusual, even “unnatural”, shape that corresponds to an external (exogenous) insult, such as allergic or irritant contact dermatitis ( Fig. 0.10 ), an accidental or purposeful injury (see Ch. 90 ) 18 , or even ritualistic medicinal practices (e.g. “cupping” or “coining”; see Ch. 133 ). Distribution Stepping back and observing the anatomic distribution of skin lesions can also prove useful. Photodermatoses include polymorphic light eruption, phototoxic drug reactions (e.g. to doxycycline), and subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus. Of note, sometimes a disorder will display a combination of distribution patterns; for example, in dermatomyo- sitis, lesions can be photodistributed and involve extensor surfaces (e.g. elbows, knees). In addition to differences in the color of inflammatory lesions, individuals with darkly pigmented skin also have an increased frequency of several cutaneous disorders (see section on Color) and certain types of reaction and distribution patterns 20 . Examples of these reaction patterns include papular eczema and a follicular accentuation of atopic dermatitis and pityriasis versicolor, as well as an annular configuration of seborrheic dermatitis and facial secondary syphilis. With regard to distribution, pityriasis rosea often assumes an “inverse” pattern, in which lesions occur primarily in the axillae and groin rather than on the trunk. Although underlying pathomechanisms are not known, it is important to be aware of their occurrence 20 . Sometimes a distribution pattern is better explained by the phenomenon of locus minoris resistentiae , in which certain anatomic sites are more vulnerable than others to a particular disease process 21 . Examples would be cutaneous infections in a lymphedematous limb or asteatotic eczema within a skin graft site. There is also the poorly understood phenomenon of Wolf isotopic response , in which a second condition, such as granulomatous dermatitis or leukemia cutis, occurs preferentially in the site of a prior healed process (often herpes zoster; see Table 80.7 ) 22 . Dermoscopy is discussed in detail later in this chapter. Temporal Course Central to any medical history, including that of cutaneous disorders, is the temporal course. The patient should be queried as to duration and relative change in intensity and/or distribution over time. For example, there are some dermatoses that have a cephalocaudal progression over time, such as measles and pityriasis rubra pilaris. Of course, the time course is more prolonged in the latter as compared to the former. The dermatologist is at an advantage because the skin is so acces- sible. Information provided by the patient can be readily compared to the physical examination. With experience, a dermatologist can usually determine by observation if cutaneous lesions are acute, subacute, or chronic. As an example, scale (not to be confused with crust) reflects parakeratosis, and due to epidermal transit time, it requires 2 weeks to develop. Intact tense bullae are rarely more than a week old. Lichenification, i.e. thickening of the skin with accentuation of normal skin markings, takes weeks to months to develop. If lichenification is present, the lesion has not appeared acutely, despite what the patient may believe. In otherwise healthy individuals, there are several diseases whose cutaneous manifestations are often acute in nature, in particular urticaria, morbilliform drug eruption, viral exanthem, acute allergic or irritant contact dermatitis, and pityriasis rosea. This does not mean these skin diseases require emergent management, but rather that the rashes appear abruptly and are distinguished, particularly from neoplasms or chronic dermatoses, by temporal acuity. Of note, sometimes a more serious and potentially life-threatening cutaneous disease may present with skin findings that mimic a more common and less serious disorder, especially early on. Basic Principles of Dermatology Finally, while emergencies in dermatology are uncommon, there are a few illnesses, particularly those that present with a rash and fever, which are true emergencies and must be recognized promptly and treated accordingly. Examples include Stevens–Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, Kawasaki disease, meningococcemia (including purpura fulminans), Rocky Mountain spotted fever, necrotizing fasciitis, and endocarditis with cutaneous manifestations. OVERVIEW OF BASIC SCIENCE The next two sections of this introductory chapter focus upon basic principles of dermatopathology and dermoscopy, respectively. It is important to remember all diagnostic techniques (unaided clinical examination, histologic examination, dermatoscopy, confocal microscopy, and imaging, including ultrasound [ Fig. 0.12 ]) are comple- mentary. In other words, synergistic strength and clinicopathologic correlation are achieved when the techniques are used in combination. As a corollary, using any one technique, to the exclusion of the others, may be misleading and result in misdiagnosis. THE ROLE OF DERMATOPATHOLOGY IN CLINICOPATHOLOGIC CORRELATION Dermatopathology, the study of skin under the microscope, is uniquely related to the study of clinical dermatology, for few other medical specialties place so much emphasis on both the clinical and the histo- logic features of diseases within their realm 25 . However, this union exists not only because of overlapping subject matter, but because derma- tology and dermatopathology both rely heavily upon careful observation and pattern recognition. In addition, clinical dermatology represents the “gross macroscopy” of dermatopathology, as clinical examination can be regarded akin to gross examination of biopsy specimens in other organs. Experienced clinicians may anticipate associated histologic findings as they examine a cutaneous lesion or eruption (e.g. hyperkeratosis and/ or parakeratosis when scale is present clinically, or dermal hemorrhage when there is purpura clinically). As a result, a sophisticated differential diagnosis often accompanies a skin biopsy performed by a dermatol- ogist. Moreover, when the microscopic features are clearly delineated in a histopathology report, an experienced dermatologist can utilize clinicopathologic correlation to arrive at a final diagnosis. In a similar fashion, an experienced dermatopathologist can utilize clinical pictures to arrive at a final pathological diagnosis. The Skin Biopsy In no other field of medicine is the tissue of interest so readily acces- sible for histologic analysis. As a result, performing a skin biopsy is an integral component of medical decision-making in dermatology. A skin biopsy may be performed for a multitude of reasons, including: another, or disease. Regardless of the rationale for performing a skin biopsy, the securing of appropriate tissue involves more than the mere mechanical procurement. Instead, a multistep process is executed, with forethought, precision and care, in order to maximize diagnostic utility 26 . Also, because a skin biopsy is often just a small sampling of a larger process, it may not always be representative of the entire disease state. Inappropriate technique or poor tissue handling may seriously limit the diagnostic yield of a skin biopsy; accordingly, clinicians must have an appreciation of the principles of histologic examination. Site selection Often, the first step in performing a biopsy is to identify an unadul- terated primary lesion . Lesions with obfuscating secondary features, such as those resulting from rubbing or traumatic injury (e.g. lichenifi- cation, excoriations) or other superimposed processes (e.g. crusting and impetiginization), should be avoided, unless the purpose of the biopsy is to prove existence of such confounders. A well-developed, “fresh” lesion is typically chosen for biopsy. Such sampling is premised on an assumption that it will demonstrate the most diagnostic histopathology. Immature lesions may not yet manifest characteristic histopathologic changes, and older lesions may be compromised by secondary features. Of course, there are exceptions to this general principle, such as the sampling of early lesions of cutaneous small vessel vasculitis ( < 24 hours old) or immunobullous diseases, especially when performing direct immunofluorescence. While specimens are often taken from the center of a primary lesion, exceptions to this guideline exist, particularly in the case of bullae (see relative to uninvolved skin. For example, in atrophoderma an incisional biopsy should include both affected and unaffected skin and be sectioned longitudinally, so that subtle differences can be detected (see Ch. 99 ). In ulcers, nonspecific inflammation of vessels underneath the wound may be misinterpreted as a primary vasculitis, but in a biopsy specimen that includes the surrounding skin, the “vasculitis” disappears a few milli- meters away from the ulcer. Biopsying the border of suspected porokera- tosis is also recommended in order to best detect the diagnostic cornoid lamella. In sum, selection of a proper biopsy site will always be influ- enced by knowledge of the suspected underlying pathology. Common punches range from 1.5 to 8.0 mm in diameter, with 4 mm being the most commonly used size for inflammatory diseases. Optimal biopsy techniques based upon the suspected cutaneous disease are outlined in Table 0.10 . Handling of the specimen after biopsy Skin specimens must be handled carefully upon extirpation. For example, excessive lateral pressure by forceps on small punch biopsy specimens can distort cellular infiltrates, particularly lymphomas and Merkel cell carcinoma, creating so-called “crush” artifact. This type of artifact may compromise the diagnostic utility of a biopsy. These two cell types are also subject to desiccation artifact when the biopsy specimen is placed onto gauze rather than into formalin solution. For routine histologic analysis, tissue specimens are usually fixed in 10% neutral buffered formalin (NBF) solution, with a volume 10- to 20-fold that of the tissue itself. When culturing for microorganisms, the tissue specimen cannot be placed in 10% NBF; instead it must be placed in a sterile container with a small amount of non-bacteriostatic saline. For direct immunofluorescence (DIF) studies, specimens must be flash-frozen, placed in normal saline (for no more than 24–48 hours), or placed in specialized transport medium (Michel’s solution). Recently, honey was shown to be an excellent transport medium for DIF studies 29 . Fixation in paraformaldehyde and glutaraldehyde in a cacodylate buffer is required for electron microscopy. To obtain the most accurate histopathologic assessment, all biopsy specimens sent to a dermatopathologist should be accompanied by relevant clinical data such as: age and sex of the patient, anatomic site(s) involved, pertinent physical findings, and suspected clinical differ- ential diagnosis. Prior treatments that might impact upon the histo- logic findings should be disclosed. Any special instructions or requests should be detailed (e.g. inking of an area of special concern in a melano- cytic neoplasm, longitudinal sectioning to detect subtle changes in atrophoderma). Inclusion of drawings or clinical photographs (favored) may prove very useful, especially in difficult or complex cases. text: cases. Classification of Inflammatory Skin Diseases by Pattern Analysis First conceived by Dr Hermann Pinkus, but more firmly established by Dr A. Bernard Ackerman 30,31 , histopathologic assessment by pattern analysis has emerged as the principal means of classifying inflam- matory skin diseases ( Fig. 0.14 ). The number of patterns and the precise descriptors assigned may vary among examiners, but the core principle remains the same – a major pattern is first identified, then additional histologic features are used to further subcategorize the disease process until a final diagnosis is rendered. The algorithmic approach of pattern analysis is reproducible, and it minimizes subjectivity. However, the method has two important limita- tions, namely, it is based on artificial disease categories and it cannot include every possible pattern. Furthermore, while pattern analysis clearly narrows the differential diagnosis, a final assessment may require clinical correlation and/or ancillary laboratory testing, imaging, or genetic testing 32 . The histopathologic appearance of skin disease may also vary based upon the age of the lesion, reflecting the “life of a lesion”. As noted previously, histologic findings may be altered by previous treatment(s) or by secondary changes such as rubbing, scratching, or infection. Lastly, pattern analysis is not only applicable to inflammatory skin diseases, but is also used for neoplasms, primarily to distinguish benign from malignant. Ten major patterns defined Over the past several decades, different classification schema based upon pattern analysis have emerged. The number of patterns in any schema has varied from 9 to 28 or more, but in this introductory chapter, 10 major patterns will be discussed. Perivascular dermatitis Perivascular dermatitis is defined and recognized by the presence of an inflammatory infiltrate that is arranged chiefly around dermal blood vessels ( Fig. 0.15 ). Traditionally, perivascular dermatitis has been subdi- vided into “superficial” and “superficial and deep” variants, and while this division has some diagnostic value, considerable overlap exists. In addition, inflammatory skin diseases can exhibit a spectrum of findings, depending in part upon severity, as well as the duration of an individual lesion (acute vs chronic). Because this pattern is shared by the majority of inflammatory skin diseases, there is a wide range of potential diagnoses. Because this pattern is shared by the majority of inflammatory skin diseases, there is a wide range of potential diagnoses. Once a perivascular pattern is identified (see Fig. 0.14A ), the next step is to: (1) determine if there are associated epidermal changes; and (2) characterize the types of inflammatory cell(s) that are present in the infiltrate (e.g. lymphocytes, neutrophils, eosinophils, plasma cells). There are disorders without detectable changes within the epidermis, such as deep gyrate erythemas (see Ch. 19 ), and when an inflammatory process is beginning or resolving, epidermal changes may be subtle. To further refine the diagnosis, a search is performed to detect subtle spongiosis (intercellular edema of the epidermis), subtle parakeratosis (aberrant retention of nuclei in the stratum corneum), subtle interface and vacuolar changes at the dermal–epidermal junction, or extrava- sated erythrocytes. Interface dermatitis This pattern is characterized by inflammation and/or degener- ative change(s) at the dermal–epidermal junction (see Fig. 0.14B ). Morphologically, this pattern may be further subdivided into primarily vacuolar (vacuoles between two adjacent basal cells or between basal cells and the underlying basement membrane with mild or no inflam- mation; Fig. 0.16 ) or primarily lichenoid (lymphocytes fill the papillary dermis in a band-like fashion and often obscure the dermal–epidermal junction; Fig. 0.17 ), but there is overlap between these two groups. It is important to remember that even though an entity has lichenoid features under the microscope (e.g. fixed drug eruption), clinically, it does not have to resemble lichen planus. Also, some degree of lichenoid inflammation may be associated with a variety of benign and malignant neoplasms, such as lichenoid keratoses and melanoma. In these instances, the lichenoid inflammation represents an immunological response to the tumor. Spongiotic dermatitis Spongiosis (intercellular edema) is a nonspecific morphologic alteration that is observed in a variety of skin conditions. It manifests as widened spaces between keratinocytes, with elongation of intercellular bridges (see Fig. 0.14C ). The degree of spongiosis may vary from microscopic foci to grossly visible vesicles or intraepidermal bullae. There is often associated exocytosis of inflammatory cells, with migration from the vasculature into the epidermis. There is often associated exocytosis of inflammatory cells, with migration from the vasculature into the epidermis. It is important to note that even those spongiotic dermatitides that characteristically develop vesicles, for example acute allergic contact dermatitis, may not do so, i.e. patients have only macules and papules throughout the entire course of their disease. Spongiotic dermatoses may be further subdivided into acute, subacute, and chronic forms. In acute spongiotic dermatitis, the spongiosis is often severe, sometimes resulting in microvesicles within the epidermis ( Fig. 0.18 ). Parakeratosis, a histologic equivalent of scale, often overlies subacute spongiotic dermatitis. In chronic spongiotic dermatitis, the spongiosis may be more difficult to appreciate, being instead OVERVIEW OF BASIC SCIENCE overshadowed by epidermal acanthosis (thickening of the epidermis). Also, a predominance of certain inflammatory cells in association with spongiosis, such as eosinophils or neutrophils, may serve as a clue to a hypersensitivity component or infectious process, respectively. Lastly, it is important to recognize that multiple cutaneous disorders with eczematous features, such as allergic contact dermatitis, atopic dermatitis, nummular dermatitis and seborrheic dermatitis, may have histologic evidence of spongiosis, but this pattern is not exclusive to those diseases. In other words, spongiosis may also be seen as a reactive epidermal component of other disorders better classified under another pattern. Pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia represents a related benign condition due primarily to hyperplasia of adnexal epithelium. It may occur in response to a range of insults to the skin, such as chronic rubbing or scratching (e.g. lichen simplex chronicus, prurigo nodularis), or it may appear in inflammatory, neoplastic, and infectious skin diseases (e.g. hypertrophic lupus erythematosus, halogenodermas, chromoblastomycosis). In early pustule formation, neutrophils are scattered within the lower portion of the epidermis, whereas later, accumulation is noted in the upper epidermis and/or beneath the stratum corneum ( Fig. 0.21 ). In a resolving pustule, the neutrophils or their remnants may even appear within a scale-crust in the cornified layer. In both vesiculobullous and pustular dermatoses, autoimmune and non-autoimmune mechanisms (e.g. subcorneal pustular dermatosis versus IgA pemphigus) may be histopathologically indistinguishable. As a result, direct and indirect immunofluorescence studies are of utility in determining the precise etiology. Subepidermal vesiculation (see Fig. 0.14F ) In this subcategory of disease, vesicles or bullae form at the junction between the epidermis and dermis ( Fig. 0.22 ), or between the mucosa and submucosa of mucous membranes. While such clefting can be the result of autoantibodies that target specific components of the dermal– epidermal junction (e.g. collagen XVII in bullous pemphigoid, linear IgA bullous dermatosis), it may be the result of an inflammatory or toxic/metabolic insult (e.g. bullous erysipelas or porphyria cutanea tarda, respectively). The number of inflammatory cells varies within subepidermal blisters, and this variance influences the differential diagnosis. For example, some diseases such as porphyria cutanea tarda are classically pauci- inflammatory, while the majority of cases of bullous pemphigoid contain a significant number of inflammatory cells, particularly eosinophils. However, because there is histologic overlap among blistering disorders, the final diagnosis must depend upon cumulative infor- mation, including direct and indirect immunofluorescence microscopy, ELISA, and, of course, clinicopathologic correlation. Vasculitis/pseudovasculitis Vasculitis refers to inflammatory damage to and destruction of blood vessels, which leads ultimately to the deposition of fibrin and/or thrombus formation (see Fig. 0.14G ). The histopathologic classifi- cation of vasculitis is based upon the size of the vessel involved (small, medium-sized, or large vessel vasculitis; see Ch. 24 ) as well as the predominant inflammatory cell type that is mediating the damage (neutrophils, lymphocytes, eosinophils, or histiocytes). The most common form of cutaneous vasculitis is leukocyto- clastic vasculitis ( Fig. 0.23 ), a process that is mediated by neutrophils and affects chiefly the postcapillary venule. Leukocytoclastic vascu- litis begins with deposition of circulating immune complexes in and around blood vessel walls, with neutrophils recruited to these sites of deposition; this ultimately leads to leukocytoclasia (nuclear fragmen- tation) and vessel destruction, with resultant fibrin deposition. In the few longstanding disorders that are mediated by leukocytoclastic vascu- litis, such as erythema elevatum diutinum, concentric fibrosis may develop over time. The concept of lymphocytic vasculitis is less well defined and is even a controversial pattern for some authors. It is postulated as a mechanism in disorders such as pernio, Sneddon syndrome, and pityriasis lichen- oides et varioliformis acuta (PLEVA), although the latter lacks fibrinoid necrosis (see Table 24.2 ). Granulomatous vasculitis is defined by the presence of histiocytes within and around blood vessel walls, in association with fibrin and/ or degenerative and necrotic changes. Like lymphocytic vasculitis, granulomatous vasculitis is a pattern that is observed in a restricted group of diseases which includes granulomatosis with polyangiitis (formerly Wegener granulomatosis), eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg–Strauss syndrome), and giant cell arteritis (formerly temporal arteritis). Occasionally, it may also represent a later evolu- tionary stage of another form of vasculitis, either leukocytoclastic or lymphocytic in nature. In medium-sized vessel cutaneous vasculitis , there is involvement of the blood vessels at the dermal–subcutaneous junction and/or within the septa of the subcutaneous fat ( Fig. 0.24 ). For dermatopathologists, cutaneous arteritis (formerly cutaneous polyarteritis nodosa) is the most commonly encountered entity in this disease category. Giant cell arteritis represents a form of large vessel vasculitis, but biopsies of this disorder are rarely performed by dermatologists. Pseudovasculitis refers to a group of heterogeneous, non-inflam- matory conditions that are broadly classified into non-inflammatory purpura (disorders that primarily cause hemorrhage) and occlusive vasculopathies (conditions that primarily occlude vessels) (see Chs. 22 & 23 ). Many of these latter disorders involve occlusion of vessels due to emboli, thrombi, vasospasm, intimal–medial hyperplasia secondary to vessel trauma, or non-inflammatory vessel wall pathology. The latter includes calcification, cholesterol emboli, and amyloid deposition. Nodular and diffuse dermatitis Nodular dermatitis is somewhat similar to perivascular dermatitis, but the inflammatory infiltrate has enlarged and has coalesced to form one or multiple nodules within the dermis (see Fig. 0.14H ). Further expansion of these nodules can fill nearly the entirety of the dermis, yielding a diffuse pattern ( Fig. 0.25 ). The nodular and diffuse pattern of dermatitis may be further subdi- vided based upon the predominant inflammatory cell present. When histiocytes predominate in one or more foci, the pattern is designated granulomatous . This can be observed in a large family of chronic inflam- matory diseases due to a wide variety of immunogenic stimuli, including infectious and non-infectious agents. If the granulomatous response is sustained, histiocytes become “epithelioid”, i.e. the cells have abundant pink cytoplasm with indistinct borders and plump ovoid nuclei and they appear to touch one another reminiscent of the cells in an epithelium. Granulomas may contain other cells, including neutrophils, eosino- phils, plasma cells, lymphocytes, and giant cells. Giant cells form via the fusion of histiocytes and are typically large and multinucleated. There are three major types of multinucleated giant cells whose morphologies differ: Langhans giant cells, foreign body giant cells, and Touton giant cells. None of these giant cells are exclusive to a singular disease, but some disorders are characterized by the conspicuous presence of one or more type(s) (e.g. Touton giant cells in juvenile xanthogranuloma). OVERVIEW OF BASIC SCIENCE All granulomatous infiltrates, but particularly tuberculoid, sarcoidal and suppurative granulomas, require exclusion of infectious agents and/ or foreign material by means of special stains, immunohistochemical stains, tissue culture, PCR, and/or polarization microscopy. Nodular and diffuse infiltrates comprised chiefly of histiocytes may also be further subcategorized into Langerhans cell and non-Langerhans cell histiocytoses (see Ch. 91 ). In Langerhans cell histiocytosis, the cells of interest have reniform (kidney bean-shaped) nuclei and a charac- teristic immunohistochemical staining pattern (i.e. S100 protein + , CD207 + , and CD1a + ). Non-Langerhans histiocytes, on the other hand, have a range of cytologic features (vacuolated, spindle-shaped, foamy, scalloped, oncocytic) as well as multiple admixed multinucleated giant cells (Touton type, Langhans type, foreign body type). Sometimes, the histiocytes and giant cells display a homogeneous “ground glass” cytoplasm; these cells are generally S100 protein − , CD1a − , CD68 + , and CD163 + . The varying histopathologic features of the non-Langerhans histiocytoses may possibly be related to the actual physiologic function of histiocytes within the granuloma 33 . Lastly, xanthomas are characterized by the accumulation of lipophages (foamy histiocytes filled with lipid) within the dermis (see Ch. 92 ). The lipid content may impart a yellowish hue to the lesions ( Fig. 0.27 ). Cutaneous xanthomas can take various forms, including widespread papules ( eruptive ), nodules ( tuberous or tendinous ), and plaques ( xanthelasma , palmar ). Folliculitis/perifolliculitis Folliculitis (inflammation of a hair follicle) is defined by the presence of inflammatory cells in the wall and lumen of a hair follicle (see adjacent dermis. Folliculitis may be due to infections (bacterial, fungal, viral, Demodex mites), drugs, occlusion, or unknown etiologies (e.g. eosinophilic folliculitis). The classification of folliculitis (and perifolliculitis) can be made on the basis of the primary inflammatory cell (lymphocytes, neutrophils, or eosinophils), the nature of the underlying pathologic process (e.g. derma- tophyte infection), the temporal course (acute versus chronic), and the site of involvement along the length of the hair follicle. If the inflam- matory process is severe and/or if it irreversibly damages epithelial stem cells, located in the bulge region of the follicle, permanent “scarring alopecia” may result ( Fig. 0.28 ). Fibrosing/sclerosing conditions Fibrosing conditions include a wide spectrum of disorders that result from altered production of collagen, typically related to injury or an autoimmune connective tissue disease (see Fig. 0.14J ). Histopathologically, the pattern is characterized by either: (1) abnormal fibrous dermal (and sometimes subcutaneous) tissue with an increased number of fibroblasts and increased, but rather unremarkable, collagen B A B A infiltrate surrounding a hair follicle, with vacuolar alteration of basilar outer root sheath epithelium. An example of the former is nephrogenic systemic fibrosis, while an example of the latter is morphea ( Fig. 0.29 ) or systemic sclerosis. These two patterns represent the ends of the spectrum and overlap can occur. Panniculitis Panniculitis represents inflammation of the subcutis (see Fig. 0.14K,L ) and it encompasses a wide range of disease processes (see Ch. 100 ). The diagnosis of panniculitides is difficult for clinicians and for dermatopa- thologists because the clinical presentation is often nonspecific and the histopathologic changes may vary over time and/or the changes may be nonspecific. Adding to the challenge, biopsy specimens are often inade- quate, due to their being too superficial in nature, too narrow in breadth or too badly crushed by forceps, to render a definitive diagnosis. An important first step in the subdivision of panniculitides is determi- nation of the predominant location of the cellular infiltrate ( Figs. 0.30 & 0.31 ). That is, does it chiefly affect the fat lobules or the septa between the fat lobules? Second, there should be an assessment as to whether a coexisting vasculitis is present or absent. If a coexisting vasculitis is detected, the size and type of the vessels affected must be determined. With panniculitides, it is important to note the type and quality of the inflammatory infiltrate, as well as peculiarities in the pattern of fat necrosis. Early in the course of erythema nodosum, the most common panniculitis, the infiltrate may include acute inflammatory cells (neutrophils in particular), but in later stages, the infiltrate is com­posed primarily of chronic inflammatory cells (lymphocytes, histiocytes; see of cytologic atypia should be assessed, as subcutaneous panniculitis- like T cell lymphoma may mimic an inflammatory panniculitis. Lastly, peculiarities of fat necrosis, such as the hyaline changes in lupus panniculitis, the basophilic saponification in pancreatic panniculitis (see Fig. 0.31 ), or the pseudomembranous degeneration in lipodermato- sclerosis, should be appreciated. As is the case for granulomatous infiltrates, panniculitis requires a low threshold for performing special stains to exclude an infectious etiology and polarized light examination to identify foreign material. Invisible dermatoses Occasionally, one encounters a dermatosis that lacks an immediately recognizable pattern, and these types of cases are collectively referred to as “invisible dermatoses” ( Table 0.11 ). From the perspective of the dermatopathologist, these invisible dermatoses represent cases where disease appears to exist clinically, but the histologic examination is rather unremarkable with conventional hematoxylin–eosin staining (i.e. the microscopic findings differ minimally from those of normal skin) 34 . Among the “invisible dermatoses” are: (1) diseases with subtle patho- logic changes and diseases that require special stains to visualize the diagnostic pathology (e.g. disorders of elastic and collagen tissue without significant fibrosis or sclerosis) ( Fig. 0.32 ); (2) diseases with focal patho- logic processes requiring serial tissue levels to identify diagnostic features (e.g. cutaneous arteritis); and (3) diseases that require precise clinical information and/or strict clinical correlation to make the diagnosis (e.g. vitiligo, melasma, telangiectasia macularis eruptiva perstans). OVERVIEW OF BASIC SCIENCE Because the histopathologic changes in “invisible dermatoses” are subtle and vexing, careful analysis is recommended. This includes careful searching for diagnostic pathology at all levels of the skin (cornified layer, epidermis, papillary dermis, reticular dermis, hypodermis, adnexa) and the use of special stains or immunohistochemical stains. Lastly, it should be remembered that causes of a seemingly invisible dermatosis may include poor selection of the biopsy site. text: Materials within the Skin Occasionally, materials not normally present in the skin are deposited, either by exogenous or metabolic insult, and this can be appreciated histologically. In some patients, there is aberrant deposition of endog- enously produced materials, such as uric acid in gouty tophi or light chain-derived amyloid due to an underlying plasma cell dyscrasia, whereas in others, exogenous material has been purposefully or accidentally inoculated into the skin (e.g. cosmetic filler material, tattoo pigment). These materials may accumulate within the dermis, the subcutaneous fat, or both. Deposits of some materials, such as the silver in patients with argyria, may be limited to cutaneous adnexa. Use of polarized light or darkfield microscopy (where light enters tissue at an angle that is not perpendicular to the slide) may be of use in identi- fying foreign material. Some deposits engender a granulomatous inflammatory reaction (see Ch. 94 ), while others evoke no appreciable reaction at all. Deposited material is usually visualized during microscopic examination, but it may be removed during processing (e.g. siliconosis), leaving only characteristic “empty spaces” to suggest its clinical presence. Special stains may be helpful for precise identification, depending upon the suspected nature of the material. Sometimes mass spectrometry is required. Histologic Stains The various stains are characterized by their affinity to different pH values within tissues or to different chemical structures. The standard stain in dermatopathology is hematoxylin and eosin , referred to as “H&E”. This stain yields a predictable pattern, with hematoxylin marking basophilic structures a blue–purple color (cellular nuclei and the granular layer of the epidermis) and eosin marking eosinophilic structures a pink–red (cytoplasm, collagen, muscle, nerve, and fibrin). H&E staining alone enables the histopathologic diagnosis of many skin diseases, but some disorders require additional special stains to facilitate a diagnosis 35 . For example, elastic tissue, unless significantly altered by ultraviolet radiation or calcium deposits, does not stain with H&E, and special stains such as orcein or Verhoeff–van Gieson are required to identify alterations in these fibers (e.g. in anetoderma; see Fig. 0.32C,I ). Similarly, special stains exist to screen for the presence of infectious agents, such as the Brown–Brenn stain (a modified tissue Gram stain) for bacteria, the periodic acid Schiff (PAS) or Grocott methe- namine silver stain for fungus, and the Ziehl–Neelsen or Fite-Faraco stain for mycobacteria (see Fig. 0.32F,G ). Most commonly, the tissue to be examined is incubated with antibodies conjugated with an enzyme that catalyzes a color-producing reaction when the antibody– enzyme conjugate is bound to the appropriate antigen within tissue; the enzyme is often peroxidase, hence the older terminology, immuno- peroxidase technique. While IHC is most often used to characterize the cellular lineage of neoplasms, it is also helpful in assessing the biological behavior of tumors and in identifying specific infectious agents that are not discernible or are difficult to detect in routine H&E-stained sections ( Fig. 0.33 ) 36,37 . IHC is also used as a research tool to determine the distribution and localization of specific biomarkers and proteins within biological tissue. Finally, more recently, IHC has been used to verify the presence of antigens targeted by specific drugs (e.g. PD-L1). When used rationally and appropriately, IHC is a formidable tool in diagnostic dermatopathology, but if used without insight or used excessively, it can be misleading and economically wasteful. Important factors to consider when utilizing IHC include the following: (1) almost no antibody is specific for a certain cell type, therefore a panel of antibodies should be employed to avoid premature, incomplete, or erroneous conclusions; (2) a differential diagnosis must be constructed prior to ordering an antibody panel so that the antibodies requested are appropriate; and (3) no antibody can differentiate irrefutably between a benign and malignant neoplasm (although, on occasion, evidence of an increased proliferative index or the aberrant expression of certain proteins may support such a conclusion). We now turn to an increasingly utilized ancillary examination technique known as dermoscopy (dermatoscopy). It is a non-invasive diagnostic technique that allows one to observe the morphologic features that are not visible to the naked eye, thus forming a link between macroscopic clinical dermatology and microscopic derma- topathology. This “sub-macroscopic” observation of colors and struc- tures ( Figs. 0.34–0.39 ) enhances clinical assessment by providing new diagnostic criteria for the differentiation of melanoma from other benign and malignant neoplasms, both melanocytic and non-melanocytic 38–40 . The technique of dermoscopy classically involves applying a liquid or gel to the skin surface and then inspecting the lesion using a hand-held, illuminated microscope (also called a dermatoscope), a stereomicro- scope, a camera, or a digital imaging system. The magnification of these instruments ranges from 6 × to 40 × and even up to 100 × . The widely used dermatoscope has a 10-fold magnification, suffi- cient for routine assessment of skin tumors. The technique of dermoscopy classically involves applying a liquid or gel to the skin surface and then inspecting the lesion using a hand-held, illuminated microscope (also called a dermatoscope), a stereomicro- scope, a camera, or a digital imaging system. The magnification of these instruments ranges from 6 × to 40 × and even up to 100 × . The widely used dermatoscope has a 10-fold magnification, suffi- cient for routine assessment of skin tumors. When fluid is placed on the lesion this eliminates surface reflection and renders the cornified layer translucent, thus allowing a better visualization of pigmented structures within the epidermis, the dermal–epidermal junction, and the superficial dermis. Moreover, the size and shape of vessels within the superficial vascular plexus are better visualized with this procedure ( Fig. 0.40 ; see Figs. 0.38 & 0.39 ) 41 . Subsequently, hand-held devices were introduced that utilize polarized light, which renders the epidermis translucent. With these latter devices, the use of a liquid medium is no longer required in order to visualize subsurface structures. The intro- duction of polarized light dermatoscopes definitively improved the dermoscopic examination of skin lesions by speeding up the process. In addition, this light mode allows the visualization of new features, such as shiny white structures, which were proved to be an additional important clue for the diagnosis of melanoma. Nowadays, the dermatoscope is increasingly being used by derma- tologists as a stethoscope equivalent. This is because it not only facili- tates the diagnosis of pigmented and non-pigmented skin tumors, but it also improves recognition of a growing number of non-pigmented skin conditions. For example, dermoscopy can facilitate the diagnosis of scabies due to the presence of the pathognomonic “jet with contrail” sign 42 (see Fig. 0.40D ). Additional skin infections and infestations that may be differentiated with increased confidence include pedicu- losis, phthiriasis, tungiasis, tinea nigra, and molluscum contagiosum (see Fig. 0.40A ). For two of the more common inflammatory skin disorders – psoriasis and lichen planus – the use of dermoscopy allows the visualization of specific sub-macroscopic features, including “red dots” pattern in psoriasis and “whitish striae” pattern in lichen planus (see Fig. 0.40E,F ). Scalp psoriasis and seborrheic dermatitis may also be differentiated via dermoscopy. Basic Principles of Dermatology of this technique is trichoscopy, namely the dermoscopic observation of the scalp, which can prove helpful in the differential diagnosis of hair and scalp diseases 44 (see Fig. 0.40G ; see Fig. 69.7 ). With regard to melanoma screening, the aim of dermoscopy is to maximize early detection while minimizing the unnecessary excision of benign skin tumors. Over the past several years, three meta-analyses and two randomized studies have proven definitively that dermoscopy improves the sensitivity for melanoma detection as compared to just the naked eye 45–49 . In a meta-analysis of dermoscopic studies performed in a clinical setting, the relative odds ratio for dermoscopic diagnosis of cutaneous melanoma (compared to naked eye examination) was 15.6 (p = 0.016). The average sensitivities for melanoma detection by naked eye versus dermoscopic examinations were 74% and 90%, respec- tively. Furthermore, this improved sensitivity came about without a decrease in specificity, suggesting that better melanoma detection (16% improvement) occurred without increasing the number of unnecessary excisions of benign lesions 49 . A randomized study found that combining eye and dermoscopic examinations led to a significant reduction in the percentage of patients referred for biopsy (9% vs 15.6%; p = 0.013) 47 . In summary, the use of dermoscopy is associated with a significant increase in the number of excised melanomas, as well as a significant reduction in the number of excised benign pigmented skin lesions 50,51 . Pattern analysis is the most well-known and reliable method for differen- tiating pigmented skin tumors. This is based on a two-step algorithm, where first there is recognition of basic criteria for melanocytic and non-melano- cytic tumors (first step; Table 0.14 ) and then benign and malignant features of melanocytic nevi and melanoma, respectively (second step; Tables 0.15 & 0.16 ) 38 . Attempts to simplify the dermoscopic approach to diagnosing melanocytic nevi and melanoma include the ABCD rule, the Menzies method, and the 7-point checklist 38 ( Tables 0.17–0.19 ). Attempts to simplify the dermoscopic approach to diagnosing melanocytic nevi and melanoma include the ABCD rule, the Menzies method, and the 7-point checklist 38 ( Tables 0.17–0.19 ). In a virtual “Consensus Net Meeting on Dermoscopy” 38 , 40 experts were able to correctly classify more than 95% of melanocytic lesions and more than 90% of non-melanocytic lesions, with pattern analysis producing the best diagnostic performance. The alternative algorithms (ABCD rule, Menzies method, and 7-point checklist) revealed similar sensitivities as compared to pattern analysis but ~10% less specificity. The favorable results of pattern analysis were not unexpected, as this method probably reflects the human brain’s approach to categorizing morphologic images and is similar to the pattern analysis utilized in general clinical dermatology and dermatopathology (see above). That is, there is a subjective perception of the “gestalt” of a given lesion and its integration into an internalized knowledge base, which is the result of expertise on the subject; in contrast, “simplified” algorithms were designed to keep non-experts from failing to detect melanomas, even at the cost of decreased specificity. Results of the virtual consensus study showed that three criteria (asymmetry, atypical network, and blue–white structures) were especially important in distinguishing malignant from benign pigmented skin tumors ( Table 0.20 ). Using this 3-point dermoscopy rule as a screening test, general physicians with no prior experience in the use of dermoscopy were able to better classify skin lesions suggestive of skin cancer as compared to examination with the naked eye (referral sensi- tivity of 79% and 54%, respectively), without increasing the number of unnecessary expert consultations 48 . While the continued, skilled use of dermoscopy will undoubtedly aid in the early recognition of melanoma as well as the diagnosis of inflam- matory disorders and other cutaneous neoplasms, there are additional technologies that may also have a significant impact on our specialty over the next decade, including confocal microscopy 52 and artificial intelligence. Dermoscopy of pigmented skin lesions: results of a consensus Basic Principles of Dermatology INTRODUCTION TO CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY Reflectance confocal microscopy (RCM) is a non-invasive imaging technique that enables a microscopic, horizontal view of the epidermis and papillary dermis. RCM provides a “virtual” skin biopsy that allows assessment of different layers of the skin at a cellular level 53 . In clinical settings, RCM can be used for the pre-histologic diagnosis of skin tumors as a way of improving patient management. Most commonly, RCM is employed as a second-level analysis to support clinical and dermoscopic evaluation, especially when biopsies are a concern because of anatomic location (e.g. face, genitalia) or the clinical condition of the patient 54 . By increasing specificity and sensitivity, RCM improves the diagnostic accuracy of skin cancers, especially melanocytic tumors. It also reduces the number of unnecessary biopsies and excisions, guides biopsy selection in a suspicious lesion so as to provide a more accurate diagnostic specimen, and helps to define the margins of large tumors to ensure an adequate surgical excision. In addition, RCM is used to monitor and longitudinally evaluate the clinical and therapeutic evolution of neoplastic and inflammatory skin diseases 55 . Adapted from OVERVIEW OF BASIC SCIENCE RCM Principals, Technology, and Limitations In RCM, the basic principle is to have a point source of light focused on a specific point within tissue. Due to the different refractive indices in the skin, the light is scattered back by various tissue structures. Only light reflected from the tissue focus point can pass through a pinhole-sized spatial filter into the RCM detector; it is then processed by dedicated software. The contrast in confocal images is due to differ- ences in the reflectance index between cellular structures, subcellular structures, and their surroundings. Melanin and keratin have a high reflectance index, as do white blood cells, chromatin, and dermal fibers, but to a lesser extent. Therefore, they appear brighter than surrounding structures in RCM images 54–57 . RCM provides cellular details similar to those seen by histopathology at low magnification. Commercially available RCM devices often use a near-infrared (830 nm) laser with low power (up to 35 mW) at the tissue level. Immersion oil or water must be applied to the skin lesion to obtain a refractive index close to that of the stratum corneum. The immersion lens is used with water/gels placed between the window and the objective lens and has a refractive index close to that of the epidermis. The laser scans a two-dimensional grid over the skin to obtain a thin horizontal optical section, and back-scattered photons from the illumi- nated living tissue are detected. Processed data are usually displayed as a grayscale image (“single RCM image”: 500 × 500 microns field-of- view) with a lateral resolution of ~0.5 microns and an axial resolution of ~3.5 microns. For most lesions and anatomical sites, RCM exami- nation is feasible, but there are limitations, e.g. hyperkeratotic, acral, or ulcerated lesions ( Table 0.21 ) 54 . Currently, two different RCM instruments are commercially available. They are designed for different indications, based primarily on the clinical lesion and its anatomical site. Inc.) usually employs an automated stepper in order to obtain up to 64 sequential images for a mosaic grid of 16 × 16 contiguous images in the horizontal plane (8 × 8 mm field- of-view 54,57 ; termed “Vivablock”). By adjusting the focal length of the laser beam, a series of consecutive RCM single images can be stacked vertically (termed “Vivastack”), from the skin surface to the superficial dermis. A dermoscopic picture usually serves as a gross map to guide RCM imaging so as to examine the site of interest within the lesion. The handheld RCM device (Vivascope ® 3000, Caliber I.D. Inc.) allows one to investigate anatomic sites that are curved or difficult to reach, such as the nose, ears, eyelids, or mucosa. The technical charac- teristics are similar, but the field-of-view is smaller and limited to 0.5 × 0.5 mm 54 . The most common application of this device is examination of pigmented macules and patches in photodamaged facial skin. In addition, this handheld device can be moved easily on the skin and allows for analysis of multiple lesions in different body sites, which is particularly useful when studying inflammatory skin diseases. RCM Applications Cutaneous tumors The RCM criteria for melanocytic and keratinocytic skin tumors have been extensively described in the literature ( Table 0.22 ). RCM is particularly useful for flat pigmented lesions, especially when the differential diagnosis is atypical nevus versus melanoma. It has been shown to significantly reduce the number of unnecessary skin biopsies and excisions. In the case of nodular lesions, RCM does not allow assessment of the deep cellular component, but assessment of the superficial confocal features that reflect the melanocytic proliferation is often sufficient to define the nature of the lesion. INTRODUCTION TO ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE Reports of the potential benefits of artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare, including dermatology, are rapidly increasing. This section is intended as a guide to basic AI concepts, available technologies, and current and potential future application of computer-aided derma- tology. Technical concepts, which are described on an abstract level, are accompanied by instructive schematic illustrations. Clinicians should become familiar with these basic concepts, as they are similar across most models and when understood allow for critical evaluation of current and emerging clinical studies. Gather and prepare both training data and test data for a specified problem that are completely independent , e.g. from different study centers. If obtaining independent test data is not possible, ~20% of the original data are initially split off in a random, but usually stratified, fashion as this ensures that cases or patients do not overlap. Test data obtained in this manner must not be touched or examined until the very end; otherwise, the data will have lost their quality as true test data. Only the remaining 80% of the data are used as training data in steps 2 to 4. 2. Train the model with training data for the target task (e.g. proba- bility of melanoma, correct specific diagnosis, affected body surface area); this step utilizes ~80% of the training dataset. 3. Validation: Measure performance of the model based on the remaining ~20% of the training data. 4. Repeat steps 2 and 3 while changing training approaches and parameters until a satisfactory performance in the “validation” step is attained. 5. Lock the model parameters and proceed to the test phase. 6. Test : Measure the model performance on the test data once and report these results. This sequence is somewhat simplified, as there are more advanced methodologies such as using k-fold cross-validation instead of a fixed, single 20% validation split. However, the steps should reflect the essential concept of strict data handling and experimental workflow in order to avoid negligence or errors that can lead to misinterpretation of results. Unfortunately, the lack of a truly independent test set is not uncommon in machine learning and has measurable consequences when generalized, i.e., inferior performance in the real world. A meta- analysis found that studies without an independent test set had system- atically different performance results 64 . Image-Based Tasks Solved with Neural Networks What kind of tasks can a machine learning model potentially solve? Conceptually, anything where there are enough data and the perfor- mance can be parameterized as a numeric value, e.g. accuracies of diagnoses in percentages. Classification ( Fig. 0.45A ) is the most well-known technique for a visual specialty such as dermatology. The concept is to predict a diagnosis or a list of differential diagnoses from a single image or a sequence of images. This technique can be performed on clinical 65 , dermatoscopic 66 , or histopathologic images. Utilizing modern neural networks together with large public image datasets 67 , experimental, large-scale international studies 68 have shown that the models are equal or superior to dermatologists in classification tasks. Although skin cancer recognition is the most common topic in the literature, one can also automatically grade inflammatory skin diseases or predict diagnoses in general dermatology 65,69 . In addition, tedious tasks such as organizing image databases can be enhanced via classification 67 . Measurements for classification performance are usually chosen for the task at hand and are usually classic diagnostic values such as sensitivity or specificity, crude accuracy, Youden’s J, area under the ROC (receiver operating characteristic) curve, or mean sensitivity across multiple diagnoses. Segmentation ( Fig. 0.45B ) allows the automatic highlighting and measurement of areas of interest, e.g. affected body area with psoriasis or visual dermatoscopic patterns. In histopathology, semi-automatic and interactive segmentation could enhance the annotation speed of researchers. Well-known measurements for segmentation perfor- mance are Intersection-over-Union (IoU, “Jaccard” index) or the Dice coefficient. Detection ( Fig. 0.45C ) provides one or multiple marks on an image where an object-of-interest was recognized, as well as the predicted area (“bounding box”). Relevant applications of this technique are detecting skin lesions in full-body images or detecting nuclei in histopatho- logic images. The detection of skin lesions in full-body images can be combined with a change-detection algorithm to automatically assess whether a lesion has changed over time. The standard measurements for performance is Intersection-over-Union and average precision at prespecified cutoffs of IoU percentages. Annotation ( Fig. 0.45D )

Annotation ( Fig. 0.45D ) is similar to classification, but there is the potential for multiple elements, rather than a single prediction, to be returned. A non-medical analogy would be providing multiple descriptive terms (“hashtags”) for an image on social media, e.g. providing all these terms – “scenic”, “mountains”, “dawn”, “alps” – instead of just “mountains”. Metrics can be the ones employed in the field of information retrieval such as precision@k, mean reciprocal rank, or average precision. Retrieval ( Fig. 0.45E ) of similar cases can be achieved by a technique called content-based image retrieval (CBIR), in which a neural network recognizes patterns, structures, and colors from an image, encodes them, and compares them to images in a database. Retrieved similar images can be used for education or for explaining a machine learning model. Although metrics of information retrieval can theoretically be applied to CBIR, the highly subjective nature of visual similarity makes it difficult to evaluate this technique objectively. Generation ( Fig. 0.45F ) of artificial images is a more experimental technique. Special types of neural networks, such as GANs (generative adversarial networks) 70 , can learn the ability to create artificial images. This application can generate high quality artificial facial and derma- toscopic images, and in the future, it may create genuinely anonymous images for clinical training and reference. Inputs and results of the techniques mentioned above are basically straightforward, but there are, of course, more advanced applica- tions that use other image material or combinations of data. An example would be automated analysis of histopathologic images to predict genetic changes, prognosis, or treatment efficacy. OVERVIEW OF BASIC SCIENCE of convolutional neural networks (CNNs), image-based machine learning has largely moved from manually crafted “computer vision” techniques to “deep learning”, i.e. the application of multilayered neural networks. While there is extensive literature on improvements of CNN models, a detailed discussion is beyond the scope of this section; therefore, they are simply referred to as “neural networks”. At the time of this writing, the most well-known modern CNN-based architectures are EfficientNet-, ResNet-, ResNeXt-, SqueezeNet-, MobileNet-, and Inception-type networks for classification and Mask R-CNN, DeepLab, YOLO, SSD, U-Net, and RetinaNet for object detection and/or segmentation. Although dermatology is a visual domain, it is important to mention other subfields of machine learning that are not image-based but may be helpful to dermatologists. One example is natural language processing (NLP), a field in which texts can be analyzed, predicted, or even created. In the future, NLP could automate initial patient interviews through chat-bots, automatically extract ICD-coding from free text, provide diagnosis or management suggestions from patient summaries, automate report generation from a few keywords, or retrieve study patients from electronic health records. AI does not need to be based on neural networks entirely. For example, another approach that uses classic logic and rule-based systems, in conjunction with a knowledge database, can generate meaningful sets of differential diagnoses from listing clinical descriptions 72 . Shortcomings and Limitations of AI Convolutional neural networks may learn image-based pattern recognition at a similar pace compared to humans 73 , but are inher- ently limited to the knowledge they can extract from training data. Thus, to achieve a clinically useful and robust performance, CNNs require large, diverse, comprehensive, well-curated training datasets. While such large datasets are available for images of general objects, they are mostly unavailable in dermatology. The nearly exhaustive list of usable public datasets at the time of this writing are derma- toscopic images from PH2, the ISIC archive (including HAM10000 and ISIC challenge datasets), and derm7pt, as well as clinical images from the SD-198 dataset. Except for melanoma in the TCGA, there is basically no relevant public, reusable dataset for dermatopathology at the time of this writing. This limited list highlights that clini- cians and clinical researchers are in need of more published useful datasets. What are the specific impacts of too little data? When only a few datasets are available, the rule of strict test set splitting (see above) may become impossible. Test sets will then originate from the same source as training images, skewing estimates of diagnostic performance 64 . Fewer examples of diagnoses in datasets introduce dataset bias . If image examples of one of the diagnoses are mostly from one single center and photographed there with one specific camera or lighting conditions, a CNN will learn to recognize this camera and lighting conditions rather than the diagnosis itself. Another example is that melanomas are often photographed with skin markings or rulers to document their size, resulting in CNNs predicting “melanoma” at a higher rate when skin markings or rulers are included in an image 74 . With techniques to control biases, such as illumination color, de-biasing images is theoretically possible but difficult to implement in practice. Lastly, academic skin cancer centers usually have more expensive equipment to document diseases and well-trained staff to provide high-quality images, both of which may not be available in future point-of-care settings where CNNs will later be deployed. When predicting diagnoses from clinical images, there is a wide range of possible diagnoses in dermatology. CNNs will perform well on common, well-documented diagnoses such as psoriasis or melanoma, but may fail on the “long tail” diagnoses, which are numerous but rare, because there are fewer or even missing training examples. Another problem is not machine learning itself, but the way it is being studied, measured, and compared to physicians. Often, ensembles of several large CNNs require large computational resources and a lot of time to make predictions. Compared to single human participants (physicians) who make decisions almost instantly, these large ensembles are rarely used in real-life situations. This is because the computing is too expensive, not feasible on smaller devices such as smartphones, or simply too time-consuming. Target metrics to evaluate performance were briefly mentioned above but are sometimes inadequately chosen in the clinical context. For example, experimental studies measuring the area under the ROC curve for differentiating malignant from benign skin tumors may allow for comparison of differences in performance in general. However, the resulting models may not be useful for clinical applications because no specific cut-off is chosen and measured in a clinically meaningful way. The quality of clinical endpoints is also difficult to measure. In studies of CNNs that diagnose melanocytic tumors, “ground truth” for comparisons is problematic. Even for experts, interrater reliability in histologic discrimination of melanoma from nevi is far from perfect, and this issue may only be solved by integrating clinical information and dermatoscopic evaluation. The fact that the targeted “ground truth” may not even be true is often not considered in technically focused CNN studies. As a result, standalone applications in which patients receive an automated diagnosis directly from an AI model have not gained traction in dermatology. Instead, collaborative models involving the interaction of physicians and CNNs seem much more promising. The successful use of AI depends not only on its experimental

Possible Clinical Implementations of AI The application of automated predictions carries tremendous opportu- nities, but also significant risks and liability as malignant diseases may be misdiagnosed. As a result, standalone applications in which patients receive an automated diagnosis directly from an AI model have not gained traction in dermatology. Instead, collaborative models involving the interaction of physicians and CNNs seem much more promising. The successful use of AI depends not only on its experimental accuracy, but even more importantly on where, how, and by whom it is used. The different implementation scenarios of AI will depend on the task at hand. Autonomous predictions ( Fig. 0.46A ) aimed directly at the patients are currently best suited for low-risk tasks and monitoring, such as calculating the PASI (Psoriasis Area and Severity Index) or monitoring the severity of acne. In the field of skin cancer, direct patient education has been successfully tested, but applications for skin cancer diagnosis have been found to lack accuracy 75 . Although modern CNNs will probably be more accurate in the future, appropriately controlled prospective clinical trials demonstrating utility and safety are lacking at the time of writing. ? + ? ? www + ? ? It has been shown that triage using teledermatology can reduce wait times for skin cancer patients. Patients at high risk for skin cancer can perform self-monitoring to automatically detect skin cancer with reasonable specificity; however, such applications should not be used to avoid in-person screening altogether but rather to increase screening intervals. Cai et al. 77 have shown that histologic case retrieval can be improved by interactive use of a machine learning model. Other groups have successfully generated diagnosis lists with a logic-based algorithm as an education tool for building clinical differential diagnoses 72 . Future of AI In summary, machine learning and AI will almost certainly guide and help physicians in clinical practice in the future. Maybe it will not be necessary to calculate scores like PASI by hand anymore or it will be easier to narrow down diagnostic gray areas in melanocytic lesions, conduct population-wide skin cancer screenings, and perform semi- automated telemedicine/triage. Automated predictive staging systems may replace TNM staging systems. However, what will become a reality depends on physicians and researchers, technical advances, patients, politics, companies, ethical considerations, and regulatory agencies. There are also many other applications and techniques that are not or only briefly covered here, given limitations on content. Finally, the field of machine learning is fast-paced, and critical review of relevant literature is paramount in understanding new concepts and possibilities of AI. Keratinocytes , the major population, are epithelial cells that originate pool then differentiate as they migrate upward, ultimately forming the laminated stratum corneum. The human epidermis has an average thickness of 50 microns and a surface density of ~50 000 nucleated cells/mm 2 . Under normal conditions, differentiated keratinocytes require about two weeks to exit the nucleated compartment and another two weeks to move through the stratum corneum 2 . When stimulated by injury, inflammation or disease, keratinocytes can significantly increase their proliferation and maturation rates ( Ch. 8 ). Melanocytes , as noted in a DOPA-stained whole mount of the epidermis, manufacture the light-absorbing pigment melanin, which plays a major role in protecting the skin from the harmful effects of ultra- violet (UV) radiation ( Ch. 86 ). Melanosomes, with their complement of melanin, are produced by melanocytes and then transferred to nearby keratinocytes, where their preferred location is above the nucleus, providing protection for genetic material (see Fig. 65.5 ) 3 . Langerhans cells metabolize complex antigens into peptides, some of which are immunogenic. After activation, these cells migrate from the epidermis to regional lymph nodes, where they play a critical role in antigen presentation during the induction and regulation of immunity (see Fig. 4.13 ). Merkel cells contain neuroendocrine peptides and are found in the basal layer of the epidermis, although they may not be apparent in routine histologic sections. Although these cells are thought to play a role in mechanoreceptor responses, their precise physiologic role remains an area of inquiry. Since each of these topics is covered in subsequent sections of the textbook, this chapter will briefly introduce the cells and struc- tures, with references to the appropriate chapters for further details. We will reverse the conventional approach by examining diseases that illustrate the function of the skin in the context of the cells and struc- tures that sustain it. This method is derived from the assertion that the structure and function of the skin are best illustrated by disease. The strength of this alternative approach may be seen in clinical vignettes easily recognized by those who care for patients with skin disease: develops a lentigo maligna melanoma of the face heatstroke while competing in outdoor athletics in Texas develops in a 40-year-old woman, leading to dehydration and sepsis forearms of a renal transplant recipient with significant cumulative sun exposure develops on the left flank of a young man with HIV infection These patients and their diseases illustrate at least four of the functions immunologic protection. THE BASIC STRUCTURE OF SKIN The skin is divided into three major layers: the epidermis, dermis, and subcutaneous fat ( Fig. 1.1 ). The anatomic structures observed by light microscopy are fairly similar in most body regions ( Fig. 1.2 ). However, specialized skin regions such as the palms, soles, genitalia, and scalp have modified forms that address regional functional requirements ( ). The composition of cutaneous infiltrates differs depending on the disease entity, providing useful diagnostic clues ( Fig. 1.6 ). Dermal–Epidermal Interface The boundary between the epidermis and dermis consists of a specialized aggregation of attachment molecules and associated matrix, collectively known as the basement membrane 4 ( Ch. 28 ). This structure is of considerable interest because various diseases originate from genetic defects in the composition of the basement membrane or from auto­antibodies, which render individual components dysfunctional.
