text: Clinical features HIT usually occurs between days 5 and 10 of heparin therapy 1 . In patients exposed to heparin within the past 90–100 days, HIT may develop within hours after re-exposure. Occasionally, there is an anaphy- lactoid reaction within 30 minutes of a heparin bolus 1 . A delayed-onset form of heparin-induced skin necrosis has been described in which lesions can occur up to 3 weeks after exposure to heparin, including short chain variants 3,4 . Of note, heparin-dependent antibodies usually do not reappear if subsequent heparin use is after 100 days. There are additional unusual clinical scenarios in which HIT can develop. In patients receiving chronic heparin, e.g. for renal dialysis, major surgery may trigger HIT within 5–10 days. Even in the absence of exposure to heparin, major surgery or bacterial infections can trigger a spontaneous or autoimmune HIT syndrome (see above). Cutaneous lesions are usually tender, sharply demarcated, non-inflam- matory, and purpuric or necrotic, often with a retiform morphology. Large necrotic areas with or without branching margins can also be seen. Lesions may occur at the site of subcutaneous injections ( Fig. 23.2 ) or may develop at sites distant to the heparin infusion (see Fig. 21.22 ) 3,4 . Although consumption of platelets is part of this syndrome, absolute thrombocytopenia is often not present in patients with significant vascular occlusion. A decline in the platelet count of > 50% from the most recent highest value prior to the administration of heparin (preferably from the day heparin is begun) should prompt consideration of HIT. All limbs and organs are at risk for vascular occlusion, including the CNS. Heparin may also induce bullous hemorrhagic dermatosis that lacks necrosis (see Ch. 21 ). This adverse reaction is unrelated to HIT and is not associated with an increased risk of thrombosis 5 . Pathology In HIT-associated thrombosis, there is non-inflammatory occlusion of blood vessels and ischemic necrosis. Microvascular as well as venous or arterial occlusion can be seen, both in the skin and internal organs. Differential diagnosis A recent history of heparin administration should prompt consideration of this diagnosis in any patient who develops retiform purpura or bland necrosis, whether or not the patient is thrombocytopenic. However, a decrease in the platelet count is a common incidental finding in patients who are ill and coincidently receiving heparin and so it can be unrelated to the development of this syndrome. Differential diagnosis A recent history of heparin administration should prompt consideration of this diagnosis in any patient who develops retiform purpura or bland necrosis, whether or not the patient is thrombocytopenic. However, a decrease in the platelet count is a common incidental finding in patients who are ill and coincidently receiving heparin and so it can be unrelated to the development of this syndrome. Conversely, a normal platelet count does not exclude the diagnosis. Other cutaneous occlusion syndromes associated with thrombocytopenia include antiphospholipid antibody syndrome, purpura fulminans secondary to sepsis, and throm- botic thrombocytopenic purpura (although skin lesions due to micro- vascular occlusion are rare in the latter syndrome). Detection of anti-PF4–heparin complex antibodies by ELISA has a 98%–99% negative predictive value but low positive predictive value 1 . While specialized testing can confirm the presence of anti-PF4–heparin complex antibodies, a clinical diagnosis is often needed before the results of this test are known. The 4Ts score based upon acute t hrombocytopenia, t iming of onset, t hrombosis, and absence of other causes of t hrombocyto- penia is often used to estimate the likelihood of HIT syndrome. This score can be combined with functional assays (e.g. C-serotonin release assay, PF4-enhanced platelet activation assay) to greatly improve accuracy 6,7 . Treatment Treatment requires cessation of heparin therapy and initiation of thera- peutic anticoagulation. Argatroban and bivalirudin, direct thrombin inhibitors, are FDA-approved for the treatment of HIT and for patients with HIT undergoing cardiovascular procedures, respectively. Although not FDA-approved for these indications, subcutaneous fondaparinux is also effective. Whereas patients with HIT and thrombosis require thera- peutic anticoagulation for at least three months, treatment duration for patients with only HIT has not been standardized. Vitamin K antagonists (e.g. warfarin) are contraindicated during the acute phase because of an increased risk of developing venous limb gangrene secondary to decreased protein C levels 8 . Patients with delayed or spontaneous HIT should be anticoagulated with non-heparin agents (e.g. argatroban, bivalirudin). Based upon observational studies, direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) may also be effective, although isolated cases of heparin necrosis-like skin lesions have been reported with rivaroxaban and apixaban 9 . For refractory and autoimmune HIT, IVIg and plasma exchange have been used 1,2 . text: Key features  Philadelphia chromosome-negative myeloproliferative neoplasms include essential thrombocythemia (ET), polycythemia vera (PV), and primary myelofibrosis (PMF)  90% of patients have somatic phenotypic driver mutations in JAK2 (V617F), CALR , or MPL  Thrombosis, vascular events (e.g. stroke), and bleeding can occur in all three disorders Introduction Myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs) are clonal hematopoietic disorders whose manifestations depend on the type of stem cell affected, with some patients eventually developing myelodysplastic syndrome or acute myelogenous leukemia. The Philadelphia chromosome-negative MPNs (which exclude most chronic myelogenous leukemias) are clonal disorders driven by mutations in JAK2 , CALR , or MPL in all but the 10% of patients who are “triple-negative”. These genes encode a tyrosine kinase, calreticulin, and the thrombopoietin receptor, respec- tively. Thrombosis, vascular events (e.g. stroke, pulmonary emboli), and hemorrhage are the most common causes of morbidity and mortality in PV and ET. The frequency of thrombosis is highest in PV, followed by PMF and ET, while bleeding complications are highest in PMF followed by ET and PV. The JAK2 V617F, mutation is associated with an increased risk of thrombotic complications whereas CALR mutations have a lower risk. Pathogenesis In that thrombosis in ET has been attributed to platelet dysfunction/ number and platelet-driven events appear important in patients with ET and other MPNs, these disorders are discussed under platelet- related thrombopathies. However, the degree of thrombocytosis does not correlate with thrombotic and vascular complications. For example, patients with ET and extreme thrombocytosis are at greater risk of bleeding than thrombosis 10 . In both myeloproliferative and myelodysplastic disorders, platelets can function abnormally, leading to occlusion and/or hemorrhage. When the platelet count is 400–1000 × 10 9 /L, thromboembolism is common, whereas both thrombosis and bleeding may occur with a platelet count of 1000–2000 × 10 9 /L; bleeding predominates when the platelet count is > 2000 × 10 9 /L 11 . Acquired von Willebrand syndrome may develop when the platelet count is > 1000 × 10 9 /L, providing an explanation for the associated hemorrhage. When the platelet count is within the normal range in the setting of an MPD, the risk of thrombosis is uncertain. Of the three most frequently associated genes (see Introduction), mutations in MPL and CALR occur more commonly in ET and PMF and only rarely in PV. Of the three most frequently associated genes (see Introduction), mutations in MPL and CALR occur more commonly in ET and PMF and only rarely in PV. A single mutation, JAK2 V617F, is present in 90%–95% of PV patients and 50%–70% of those with ET and PMF. The JAK2 mutations lead to activation of the JAK–STAT pathway (see Fig. 128.11 ) 10 . Epidemiology Both PV and ET occur more often in women. They are uncommon before the age of 50 years, but the incidence increases almost exponen- tially after age 60 years. Clinical features Cutaneous lesions occur in ~20% of patients with ET, including purpura, hematomas, livedo reticularis and racemosa, erythromelalgia, Raynaud phenomenon, urticaria, cutaneous small vessel vasculitis, leg ulcers, gangrene, and recurrent superficial thrombophlebitis. An important subset of these cutaneous lesions is due to microvascular occlusion. Erythromelalgia is a syndrome that can occur as a primary (idiopathic) or a secondary phenomenon (see Ch. 106 ). It is characterized by intense burning and paroxysmal bright erythema of the distal extremities. Most closely associated with ET, and less often with PV, erythromel­ algia can occur with any myeloproliferative or myelodysplastic disorder if the platelet count is sufficiently elevated 12,13 . Because this form of secondary erythromelalgia is caused by platelet-mediated acral vasodi- lation, inflammation, and microvascular occlusion, patients can also develop discrete areas of purpura or necrosis, often retiform, as a unique manifestation. This version of erythromelalgia typically responds dramatically to aspirin administration, whereas idiopathic and other secondary forms generally show minimal or no benefit from aspirin. Other clinical features of patients with MPNs depend on the diagnosis, e.g. PV patients may have a ruddy cyanosis and experience severe pruritus following exposure to warm water 14 , while neutrophilic dermatoses (pyoderma gangrenosum, Sweet syndrome) have been reported with MPNs. Pathology Microvascular occlusion of dermal vessels or subcutaneous arterioles is found in biopsy specimens from retiform purpura or necrotic lesions. Cutaneous Manifestations of Microvascular Occlusion Syndromes Differential diagnosis Useful findings which suggest an MPN include anemia or elevated hematocrit, an abnormal white blood cell count or differential, and an abnormal platelet count or platelet morphology. The differential diagnosis of reactive thrombocytosis, especially due to iron deficiency, post-splenectomy, infection or malignancy, must be considered when assessing the significance of an elevated platelet count. Treatment Low-risk patients with PV and ET may be treated with low-dose aspirin. Traditionally administered once daily, more recent data suggests 100 mg twice daily may be more beneficial 15 . In PV, control of the hematocrit is usually achieved via phlebotomy. In higher risk patients, options include cytoreductive therapy (typically hydroxyurea), pegylated interferon- α , or JAK inhibitors such as ruxolitinib 14,16 . Prompt and lasting relief of burning pain by low-dose aspirin is a characteristic finding in thrombo- cythemic ET while refractory pruritus in PV may respond to paroxetine (20 mg/day), interferon- α , UVB phototherapy, or ruxolitinib 14 . Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria Key features  Coombs-negative intravascular and extravascular hemolytic anemia due to PIG-A mutations  Cytopenias and thrombosis  Cutaneous lesions are uncommon, but may be extensive Introduction Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) is a rare hematopoietic stem cell disorder that is associated with an increased risk of thrombosis. Pathogenesis This disease is due to a somatic mutation in PIG-A ( p hosphatidyl i nositol g lycan class A ) in hematopoietic stem cells. This X-linked gene encodes a glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored protein that is required for the cell membrane attachment of several important membrane proteins. Some of these proteins are responsible for protecting blood cells and platelets from complement-mediated injury. The alternate complement pathway is part of the innate immune system, with chronic low-level activation of complement by a process termed C3 tickover. This results in C3 and C5 convertase amplifi- cation (involving Factors B and D) and formation of membrane attack complex (MAC) on the antigen. Normal red cells are protected from this attack by the presence of both CD55 (decay decelerating factor), which stabilizes these convertases, and CD59 (membrane inhibitor of reactive lysis), which inhibits MAC formation. These protective proteins are unable to anchor to cells lacking the GPI anchor protein 17 . The lack

Normal red cells are protected from this attack by the presence of both CD55 (decay decelerating factor), which stabilizes these convertases, and CD59 (membrane inhibitor of reactive lysis), which inhibits MAC formation. These protective proteins are unable to anchor to cells lacking the GPI anchor protein 17 . The lack of protection leads to red cell lysis and activation of platelets. The cause of venous thrombosis is multifactorial and is due in part to microparticle formation from platelets and other blood component membranes as well as depletion of nitric oxide related to hemolytic release of free hemoglobin. Clinical features This acquired clonal hematologic disorder classically presents with intravascular hemolysis, deficient hematopoiesis, and a thrombotic tendency. It may also occur in the setting of hematologic disorders such as aplastic anemia and myelodysplastic syndrome where it is often subclinical because of a limited number of mutated clones 17,18 . Thrombotic events are the most common cause of death, and venous thromboses (e.g. Budd–Chiari syndrome) are more common than arterial. Depletion of nitric oxide related to chronic hemolysis can lead to smooth muscle dystonia with dysphagia, abdominal pain, and erectile dysfunction 17 . There is also a six-fold increased risk of chronic kidney disease. A variety of cutaneous findings have been reported in PNH, including hemorrhagic bullae, petechiae, leg ulcers, non-inflammatory retiform purpura, and a purpura fulminans-like presentation 19 . Pathology Biopsy specimens reveal microvascular occlusion, typically fibrin thrombi. Detection of an absence or severe deficiency of GPI-anchored protein in ≥ 2 cell lineages (e.g. WBCs, RBCs) by flow cytometry of peripheral blood is diagnostic of PNH. Differential diagnosis The differential diagnosis of the various skin lesions that can occur in PNH is broad. The presence of hemolytic anemia plus pancytopenia should suggest the diagnosis. Treatment In the past, treatment was largely supportive, consisting of transfusions, iron and folic acid supplementation, and anticoagulation when needed. Nowadays, patients can receive life-long IV therapy with eculizumab or ravulizumab which inhibit the terminal phase of the complement cascade at the C5 stage and can reduce intravascular hemolysis and venous thrombosis 20 . Crovalimab, a C5 inhibitor which can be admin- istered subcutaneously, has shown noninferiority to eculizumab; its prolonged half-life, as well as that of ravulizumab, is based upon SMART-Ig technology which allows prolonged recirculation. Because C5 inhibition does not prevent extravascular hemolysis 21 , agents that inhibit C3 activation (e.g. pegcetacoplan) have been FDA approved for PNH or are in clinical trials (e.g. danicopan, iptacopan) 20,21 . Since complement inhibitors can increase the risk of meningococ- cemia via C5 inhibition, patients under 45 years of age should ideally receive the meningococcal vaccine at least 2 weeks before instituting therapy. However, patients still have a > 1000-fold increased risk of Neisseria infections, leading to consideration of prophylactic chronic penicillin administration 20 . Primary Thrombotic Microangiopathy Key features  Thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) is characterized by micro­ angiopathic hemolytic anemia (RBC fragmentation with schistocyte formation) and thrombocytopenia  The focus here will be the three primary TMAs: thrombotic throm- bocytopenic purpura (TTP), Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli hemolytic uremic syndrome (STEC-HUS), and complement- mediated HUS (CM-HUS)  Round, macular petechiae are seen in inherited or acquired ADAMTS13-related TMA (i.e. TTP), most likely due to simple hemorrhage  Skin lesions are not observed in STEC-HUS while patients with CM-HUS occasionally develop distal necrosis or purpuric/necrotic lesions Introduction TMA is a syndrome characterized by microangiopathic hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia and it can be primary or secondary. The differential diagnosis can be challenging, especially since most of these syndromes evolve rapidly, leading to significant morbidity and mortality 22–24 . Within the larger spectrum of all TMAs, primary TMA includes three entities: TTP, HUS-STEC, and CM-HUS. The latter is also referred to as atypical HUS. Pathogenesis Hereditary TTP (Upshaw–Schulman syndrome) is due to biallelic mutations of ADAMTS13 . Its protein product is an enzyme respon- sible for cleaving ultra-large multimers of von Willebrand factor (vWF). However, for 90% of patients, TTP is an acquired disorder that develops during adulthood and is immune-related with antibodies that reduce the function of ADAMTS to < 10% of normal 25 . Complement activation is thought to contribute

Its protein product is an enzyme respon- sible for cleaving ultra-large multimers of von Willebrand factor (vWF). However, for 90% of patients, TTP is an acquired disorder that develops during adulthood and is immune-related with antibodies that reduce the function of ADAMTS to < 10% of normal 25 . Complement activation is thought to contribute to acute TTP, with vWF multimers possibly acting as scaffolding to support alternative pathway activation. In acute TTP, complement activation has been associated with increased mortality 25 . HUS was initially recognized in association with Shigella dysentery, but can also be caused by Shiga toxin-producing enterohemorrhagic E. coli ; STEC-HUS includes both etiologies. Historically, CM-HUS was referred URTICARIAS, ERYTHEMAS, AND PURPURAS to as atypical HUS because of the absence of diarrhea. However, mutations that lead to complement dysfunction (e.g. increased complement activation due to deficiencies of alternate complement pathway inhibitory molecules) have been detected in at least 50% of patients with CM-HUS 25,26 . Clinical features The complete syndrome of classic TTP is characterized by fever, petechiae, thrombocytopenia, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (schistocytes or fragmented red cells prominent on peripheral smear), renal disease, and neurologic symptoms (most commonly headache and confusion). The macular petechiae usually reflect simple hemorrhage, but occasionally may be attributed to platelet plugging. While platelet occlusion occurs primarily in visceral organs, very few papers have addressed the histology of cutaneous lesions. Currently, the classic syndrome of TTP would be classified as within the spectrum of ADAMTS13 deficiency-mediated TMA, either inherited or acquired/immune 25 . The HUS syndromes may mimic the findings in TTP, but hemolysis and renal involvement predominate. STEC-HUS is typically associated with diarrhea in children, less so in adults, and is not associated with skin hemorrhage. The fatality rate in children is < 3%, rising to 15%–30% in frail or elderly adults. Long-term sequelae are seen in a third of children and up to 50% of adults 26 . CM-HUS rarely leads to digital necrosis or scattered necrotic skin lesions 27 . Pathology Microvascular occlusion of visceral terminal arterioles and capillaries is expected but is rare in the cutaneous microvasculature. Petechial (cutaneous) hemorrhage is most likely due to simple hemorrhage, but documentation is limited. In the rare lesions of CM-HUS, microvas- cular occlusion may be seen.

Immunofluorescent staining of normal skin in patients with CM-HUS may be positive for MAC factors C5–9 in vessels, supporting but not confirming the diagnosis of CM-HUS 28 . Differential diagnosis Traditionally, primary TMA requires exclusion of other causes of TMA, such as disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), sepsis, or other infections; pre-eclampsia, eclampsia, scleroderma renal crisis, or malignant hypertension; catastrophic antiphospholipid antibody syndrome; and HELLP syndrome of pregnancy ( h emolysis, e levated l iver enzymes, l ow p latelet count) 22–25 . Both toxic and immune drug-induced TTP-HUS also need to be excluded, e.g. cyclosporine, tacrolimus, VEGF inhibitors, gemcitabine, oxaliplatin, and quinine can trigger TMA 24 . In addition, an HUS-like syndrome that involves a VEGFR2 pathway can occur in infants with diacylglycerol kinase epsilon deficiency 24,29 . DIC is characterized by evidence of clot activation (prolonged prothrombin time [PT] and partial thromboplastin time [PTT]) as well as clot lysis (significant elevation of fibrin split products or D-dimers; marked decrease of plasma fibrinogen). Such findings are absent in the primary TMAs. A normal or minimally elevated PT plus profound thrombocytopenia strongly favors primary TMA over DIC. Treatment Since TTP is usually due to acquired antibodies to ADAMTS13, total plasma exchange represents first-line therapy, leading to a reduction in mortality of up to 90%. Corticosteroids are also helpful in reducing antibody production and in refractory cases, rituximab has been used. For patients with severe disease poorly responsive to plasma exchange, chronic relapsing disease, or congenital disease with absence of ADAMTS13, caplacizumab – a humanized anti-vWF antibody that interferes with platelet–vWF interactions – can reduce thromboembolic complications 25,30–32 . However, initial use of standard first-line therapy may lead to a more rapid response 33 . Treatment of hereditary TTP has traditionally been plasma infusions during flares and then routine prophylactic infusions in patients with frequent recurrences or serious complications 34 . DISORDERS OF CRYOPRECIPITATION OR CRYOAGGLUTINATION Key features  Retiform purpura most often in an acral location  Due to cryoglobulins and rarely cryofibrinogens or cold agglutinins  Cold-induced cryoprecipitation and vascular occlusion most commonly associated with type I cryoglobulins  In acute lesions, eosinophilic hyaline deposits occluding blood vessels may be present Introduction Cryoglobulins are immunoglobulins that are present in both serum and plasma and reversibly precipitate with cold exposure 37 . Cryofibrinogens are fibrinogens which precipitate in the cold, are consumed in clotting, and are therefore detectable only in plasma samples 38 . Cold agglutinins are antibodies which promote agglutination of red cells on exposure to cold, often leading to a brisk hemolytic anemia 39 . All three groups can cause occlusive syndromes in the skin that are triggered by cold exposure. While cryofibrinogens and cold agglutinins can be detected in many patients in association with a variety of illnesses, they are rarely the cause of cold-related occlusion syndromes directly due to cryopre- cipitation or cryoagglutination. Pathogenesis Cryoglobulins cause disease via two mechanisms: occlusion (usually type I) or immune complex-mediated vasculitis (usually types II, III; see Table 24.6 ) 37 . Type I cryoglobulin is a monoclonal antibody, most often IgM, less often IgG, and rarely IgA. Because type I cryoglobulins are not part of an immune complex, they typically affect vessels via induction of hyperviscosity or precipitation in the cold. Type I cryoglobulin is a monoclonal antibody, most often IgM, less often IgG, and rarely IgA. Because type I cryoglobulins are not part of an immune complex, they typically affect vessels via induction of hyperviscosity or precipitation in the cold. The possibility of secondary vasculitic changes in older occlusive lesions (see Fig. 22.4 ) needs to be considered in any reports of type 1 cryoglobulin-induced vasculitis 40 . Cryoglobulins change their configuration in the cold and become water-insoluble, but plasma proteins, pH, and salt concentrations (e.g. in renal glomeruli) can also induce conformational changes 37 as many of these proteins transform only at refrigerator temperatures, not at skin temperatures typically seen with cold exposure of acral areas. Simple occlusion with minimal early inflammation and often retiform purpura/ necrosis develops when cryoproteins precipitate upon cold exposure. Intravascular deposits of type 1 cryoglobulins are subdivided into: (1) amorphous deposits – account for most cryo-occlusive syndromes; (2) gelatinous forms – lead to hyperviscosity; and (3) cryocrystals – rarest form with dense linear or herringbone-like arrays 41 . The presence of monoclonal immunoglobulins (IgG, IgM ≫ IgA, light chains), including type I cryoglobulins, points to an underlying plasma cell dyscrasia or lymphoproliferative disorder 37,42,43 . Cryofibrinogen precipitates are composed of fibrinogen, fibrin, fibro- nectin, and occasionally albumin, immunoglobulins, or other plasma proteins. Cold agglutinins bind to red cells in the cold, often triggering complement activation and red cell lysis. Because of their ability to bind multiple red blood cells, pentameric IgM antibodies more readily agglu- tinate these cells, leading to occlusion. Epidemiology The prevalence of cryofibrinogenemia varies from 2% to 9% in healthy individuals and from 8% to 13% in hospitalized patients 38 . Its female : male ratio is 1.4 : 1. Cryofibrinogenemia may be essential or secondary to a wide spectrum of disorders including infections, autoimmune diseases, and carcinomas. When a cryopathy has been suspected, cryofibrinogenemia was observed in 10%–50% of patients, although usually not in isolation. Clinical features The cardinal sign of cold occlusion, including that due to cryoglobu­ linemia , is purpuric or necrotic lesions, often retiform, at sites of cold exposure that are typically acral ( Fig. 23.3 ). Other cutaneous findings include acral cyanosis, Raynaud phenomenon, and livedo reticularis. Cutaneous Manifestations of Microvascular Occlusion Syndromes Although some reports describe cutaneous small vessel vasculitis in patients with type I cryoglobulins, it is likely that this finding is often a secondary leukocytoclastic vasculitis that occurs following occlusive necrosis or ulceration (see Fig. 22.4 ). Mixed (types II and III) cryoglobulins may cause occlusion if they are unstable at close to body temperature, but more frequently they induce lesions via immune complex mechanisms, with clustering of classic palpable purpura in dependent areas. Because of the prevalence of cryofibrinogenemia (see above), clinical correlation is critical in judging the significance of its presence. Cutaneous findings are similar to those induced by cryoglobulins and include both venous and arterial occlusion. Cold agglutinins are frequently asymptomatic incidental findings, as in Mycoplasma infections. When symptomatic, cold agglutinins lead to hemolysis post cold exposure, which can be severe 39,44 . Very rarely, cold exposure in patients with cold agglutinins can induce red cell aggluti- nation, sludging, and vascular occlusion in cold-exposed sites 45 . Lesions may develop at infusion sites following administration of cold blood products. Although skin lesions due to vascular occlusion are unusual, in one study 90% of patients with primary cold agglutinin disease had symptoms, ranging from moderate acrocyanosis to severe Raynaud phenomenon precipitated by even slight cold exposure 44 . Pathology In type I cryoglobulinemia, occlusion of small dermal vessels is a typical finding ( Fig. 23.4 ). Types II and III cryoglobulinemia show features of an acute cutaneous small vessel vasculitis and are only rarely associated with intraluminal thrombi. Treatment Management of cryoglobulin occlusion is primarily directed at minimizing cold exposure and controlling the underlying plasma cell dyscrasia or lymphoproliferative disorder in order to reduce the titer of monoclonal cryoglobulin. Plasmapheresis or plasma exchange provides only short-term improvement. Patients with Waldenström macro- globulinemia and symptomatic hyperviscosity syndrome should not be treated with rituximab until the hyperviscosity is addressed, usually by plasmapheresis and other systemic therapy (e.g. ibrutinib) 46 . Treatment of cryofibrinogenemia also includes minimizing cold exposure. Beyond that, there is little evidence to guide treatment of cutaneous disease. Stanozolol, low-dose aspirin, corticosteroids, fibri- nolytics, and immunosuppressives have been suggested, although a rationale for their use is not clear 38,47 . Anticoagulants are only recommended for patients with arterial or venous thrombosis. For secondary cryofibrinogenemia, therapy is aimed at the associated disease. Over time, some patients with “essential” cryofibrinogenemia may develop a lymphoma 47 . In cold agglutinin disease, cold avoidance is recommended but often ineffective. When no secondary cause is identified (e.g. Epstein–Barr virus), most patients are assumed to have a low-grade lymphoprolifer- ative disorder and are treated with rituximab therapy. Clinical features/pathology Ecthyma gangrenosum is the syndrome of occlusion by organisms (usually bacterial) proliferating in the adventitia of subcutaneous blood vessels. The classic organism is Pseudomonas aeruginosa , but ecthyma gangrenosum-like skin lesions have also been described with other organisms, including other Pseudomonas spp. ( P. cepacia, P. maltophilia), Serratia marcescens, Aeromonas hydrophila, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Vibrio vulnificus, Moraxella spp ., Morganella morganii, Escherichia coli , and Staphylococcus aureus ; these lesions may also be due to fungal organisms, e.g. Candida albicans, Mucor spp ., Aspergillus fumigatus, Fusarium spp., and Neoscytalidium dimidiatum 48,49 . Ecthyma gangrenosum begins as erythematous, painless macules, but typically progresses to purpuric or escharotic lesions which may be bullous or pustular, and frequently show retiform or branching features. There is extensive bacillary infiltration of the media, adven- titia, and perivascular regions of blood vessels, typically with sparing of the lumen and intima. As the bacteria proliferate, gradual compression of the vessel wall narrows and then ultimately occludes the lumen of a subcutaneous arteriole that supplies an overlying cone of skin. This is followed by clot formation within many blood vessels in that skin zone. In diabetic patients, mucormycosis may present in the central face with cutaneous necrosis, presumably originating from a sinus cavity infection. Opportunistic fungi that produce retiform purpura tend to proliferate and invade from within the lumen into the vessel wall and into vascular branches. Thrombus develops around the hyphal elements within the vessels and presumably also on the altered endothelium. Disseminated strongyloidiasis can occur in patients infected with the human nematode Strongyloides stercoralis . In autopsy studies, cholesterol embolism was observed in 15%–20% of patients older than 60 who had a history of atherosclerotic disease, and in up to 3% of unselected autopsies 53,54 . Given the relatively low frequency rate of the clinical diagnosis of cholesterol embolus, this figure suggests that cholesterol emboli are frequently undiagnosed or asymptomatic. Pathogenesis Since fragmentation of ulcerated atheromatous plaques is the cause of cholesterol emboli, affected patients usually have severe (but often unrecognized) atherosclerotic disease. Although spontaneous fragmen- tation of plaques can occur, there are three, possibly four, clinical settings known to prompt embolization. The first is arterial or coronary catheterization , which may disrupt a plaque, leading to emboli within hours to days of catheterization. The second is acute thrombolytic therapy given for myocardial infarction or stroke. Embolization may occur within hours to days of lytic therapy but a true causal relationship has been questioned. A third recently described trigger for cholesterol embolus is the Heimlich maneuver 55 . The fourth, prolonged antico- agulation , which typically occurs after 1 to 2 months of therapy, is also a matter of debate. Theoretically, anticoagulation slowly lyses the clot which may be reinforcing a friable plaque, leaving exposed areas of the plaque subject to the shear stress of arterial flow. This “warfarin blue toe syndrome” is not restricted to warfarin anticoagulation and should not be confused with warfarin necrosis 56 . Of note, ~20% of patients with cholesterol emboli have no known inciting event 54 . Clinical features Clinical findings include fever, weight loss, myalgias, altered mental status, and a sudden onset of arterial hypertension. Transient ischemic attacks, strokes, renal failure, gastrointestinal ulcerations, and hemorrhagic pancreatitis may also occur. Patients with multisystem involvement can have significant morbidity and occasionally may die from embolic complications. Cutaneous findings are reported in 35%–90% of patients with cholesterol embolization and they include: livedo reticularis (50%–75%), cyanosis/ blue toes (30%–75%), ulceration (15%–40%), multiple sites of peripheral gangrene (0–35%), nodules (~10%), and purpura (~10%) ( Fig. 23.5A–D ) 57 . Because retiform purpura represents a purpuric accentuation of the livedo reticularis pattern, it may be described as livedo reticularis in some reports. Oxalate Embolus Introduction Oxalate embolism is a rare event, usually occurring in association with primary hyperoxaluria. Three types of primary hyperoxaluria result from rare enzyme deficiencies in which there is increased hepatic production of oxalic acid 59 . This leads to hyperoxalemia and calcium oxalate deposition within tissues 59,60 . Secondary hyperoxaluria, and occasionally hyperoxalemia, usually reflects increased gut absorption of oxalate due to: (1) increased dietary intake of oxalate (e.g. rhubarb, spinach and green smoothies, almonds) or oxalate precursors (e.g. ascorbic acid, ethylene glycol, naftidrofuryl oxalate); (2) fat malab- sorption leading to calcium binding by fatty acids in the gut and increased absorption of free oxalate; or (3) decreased intestinal oxalate degradation due to a change in gut microbiota 59 . Clinical features Type 1 primary hyperoxaluria (oxalosis) is the most common and most severe form, usually presenting during childhood with recurrent urolithiasis. The kidney is the major site of oxalate deposition until progressive renal insufficiency develops, at which time clinical signs of deposition in other organs become evident. Pathology Skin biopsy specimens demonstrate yellow–brown, birefringent crystals in a rectangular or radial pattern within and around vessels in the deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue. Crystals are yellow to golden-brown in routinely stained sections and birefringent under polarized light 61 . They also stain with alizarin red S at pH 7.0 but not at pH 4.2. Foreign body giant cells may be present. Although clinical lesions may mimic those of cutaneous calciphylaxis, calcium deposition in vessels is not a characteristic finding in cutaneous oxalate emboli. Differential diagnosis This disorder is most likely to be confused with cholesterol embolus or cutaneous calciphylaxis in a patient with renal failure, but the differential diagnosis includes other causes of retiform purpura and livedo reticularis. A history of renal calculi in a patient with sudden-onset livedo reticularis or retiform purpura suggests hyperoxaluria as a prime diagnostic possi- bility. Brawny, woody fibrosis of the distal upper and lower extremities, suggestive of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis, has also been described 60 . Treatment In patients with primary hyperoxaluria without renal failure, therapeutic options include massive fluid intake and calcium oxalate crystallization inhibitors 59 . Oral pyridoxine may be helpful in type 1 oxalosis. Liver transplantation is the only “curative” treatment 59 . Renal transplan- tation is contraindicated without correction of the underlying abnor- mality, since the transplanted kidney will be damaged by continued oxalate deposition. Lumasiran, a small interfering RNA (siRNA), is approved for type 1 hyperoxaluria 59 . Emboli from these disorders may produce retiform purpura, but cutaneous findings are diverse. Atrial myxomas are rare, typically present between the third and sixth decades of life, and may be associated with symptoms or signs secondary to: (1) intracardiac obstruction – dyspnea, chest pain, syncope; (2) cytokine release by the tumor – fever, myalgias, arthralgias; and (3) extracardiac embolism – most often to the CNS but occasionally to skin 62 . Cutaneous findings of myxomatous emboli include acral papules (with claudication), purpuric, serpiginous or annular viola- ceous fingertip lesions, splinter hemorrhages, livedo reticularis, Raynaud phenomenon, toe necrosis, a red–violet malar flush, and distal petechiae 48,53,62 . Carney complex (NAME/LAMB syndromes) is associated with multiple, early-onset cardiac myxomas and may have other cutaneous findings such as lentigines and blue nevi, unrelated to the emboli. Treatment of atrial myxoma consists of surgical removal. Portions of these loose sterile deposits may occasionally embolize. Vegetations of infective endocarditis may also embolize. Emboli are more likely to occur with acute bacterial endocarditis, whereas cutaneous lesions in subacute bacterial endocarditis are more likely to result from immune complex disease, not embolization, despite frequent localization to hands. Warfarin necrosis usually develops within 2–5 days of warfarin initiation in the absence of heparin, and it is much more likely to occur if loading doses of warfarin are used 8,68,69 . This coincides with the expected early drop of protein C function. Reversal of warfarin necrosis via replacement with protein C concentrates and laboratory confirmation of very low functional levels of protein C in this setting support this pathomech- anism. The incidence of warfarin necrosis is four times higher in women, with a peak incidence in the sixth and seventh decades of life. Although up to one-third of cases of warfarin necrosis may involve inherited partial deficiency of protein C, the disorder occurs more commonly in individuals without inherited defects in protein C. Late-onset warfarin necrosis, occurring up to 6 months after initiating therapy, has been attributed to poor compliance or inappropriate dosing, alterations in the synthetic function of the liver, or drug–drug interactions 69 . Affected sites usually overlie areas of abundant subcutaneous fat, such as the breast, hip, buttock, or thigh. Pain is often the presenting sign, followed by well-demarcated erythema, which rapidly becomes hemorrhagic and then necrotic ( Fig. 23.7 ). Partial retiform or branching purpura typically can be seen within or at the margin of the cutaneous lesions. Biopsy specimens reveal bland (non-inflammatory) thrombosis of most of the dermal vessels 53 . Treatment consists of warfarin discon- tinuation and administration of vitamin K and heparin. Use of protein C replacement, if available, should also be strongly considered. Warfarin-associated venous limb gangrene Synonym:  Warfarin-induced venous limb ischemia/gangrene Severe venous limb ischemia and gangrene is a catastrophic compli- cation of warfarin therapy and there are two predisposing clinical settings – malignancy (often occult) and HIT syndrome (see above) 8 . In patients with a malignancy, there is platelet consumption and ongoing consumptive coagulopathy; administration of heparin leads to an increase in platelet counts while discontinuation of heparin leads to a decline. There is also evidence of persistent thrombin generation despite anticoagulation. Another characteristic finding is warfarin-associated supratherapeutic international normalized ratios (INRs). However, it can also occur in association with sepsis from a variety of bacteria, including S. aureus , groups A and B β -hemolytic streptococci, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae , and H. aegyptius 70,71 . In neonates, it is most often due to group B streptococcus. In a septic patient with DIC, development of retiform purpura can be the first sign of microvascular thrombosis, possibly due to an inability of the protein C–thrombomodulin pathway to prevent propagation of clot 72 . Support for this hypothesis comes from a study in pediatric patients with purpura fulminans in whom early use of protein C corre- lated with improved survival 73 . However, in adults with septic shock, use of activated protein C did not confer survival benefit and increased the risk of bleeding 74 . While some authors support the use of protein C (as well as antithrombin) for sepsis with purpura fulminins 75 , to date definitive studies in which native or activated protein C supplemen- tation is administered to patients with new-onset retiform purpura in the setting of sepsis and DIC have not been done. Some of these antibodies were subsequently associated with thrombotic and obstetric syndromes. Despite their designation as aPL antibodies, it wasn’t until the 1990s that co-binding of aPL antibodies to a protein was recognized as essential for pathogenicity 80 . Epidemiology Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome (APS) is estimated to affect 0.3%–1% of the population 81 . In a 1000-patient cohort of individuals with APS, there was a strong female predominance (82%) and the mean age was 42 ± 14 years at study entry. Fifty-three percent of the patients had primary APS, 36% had APS secondary to systemic lupus erythe- matosus (SLE), and the remaining 11% had other associated diseases 82 . Thrombosis occurred in a third of patients, most commonly cerebro- vascular accidents, transient ischemic attacks, DVTs, and PE. The most frequent obstetric and fetal complications were early pregnancy loss (~15% of pregnancies), premature birth (~50%), and intrauterine growth restriction (~25% of total live births). Mortality was ~10%, usually due to thrombosis (35%) or infection (30%). Catastrophic APS (CAPS) occurred in 0.9% of this 1000-patient cohort and 55% of those affected died 82 . In a study of 500 patients with CAPS and thrombosis of multiple small vessels, the majority were female (70%), the mean age was 38 years, and the mortality was ~35% 83 . Autoimmune disease was present in 40%, primarily SLE (75%). Organs involved were kidneys (70%), lungs (60%), brain (55%), heart (50%), and skin (50%). Malignancy was a trigger primarily in older patients, whereas infection was a common trigger in younger patients. Lupus patients with CAPS were more likely to have severe cardiac and brain involvement, resulting in a higher mortality (50%). The latter is most strongly associated with thrombosis and adverse pregnancy outcomes 85 . Antibodies against β 2 GPI bind directly to

The three APS criteria antibody groups are: (1) IgM and IgG anti- β 2 - glycoprotein I ( β 2 GPI) antibodies; (2) anti-cardiolipin (aCL) antibodies; and (3) lupus anticoagulant (LA) (see Table 23.3 ). The latter is most strongly associated with thrombosis and adverse pregnancy outcomes 85 . Antibodies against β 2 GPI bind directly to this protein, which is not a phospholipid, and then may bind to phospholipids on cell membranes. β 2 GPI is a unique five domain protein with anticoagulant, antiplatelet, and procoagulant actions (see Table 23.3 ). β 2 GPI, along with C-reactive protein and thrombomodulin, are the only three proteins that have the dual capability of regulating the complement and coagulation systems both up and down depending on external stimuli 8 . Anticardiolipin antibodies are not pathogenic unless their binding is dependent on co-binding to a protein (usually β 2 GPI). Likewise, LA is not pathogenic (prothrombotic) unless its binding is co-dependent on either β 2 GPI or prothrombin 85 . Of note, pediatric patients with LA that targets prothrombin can rarely develop hypoprothrombinemia and present with bleeding rather than thrombosis. In addition, some forms of LA can punch holes in the annexin 5 shield, leading to phospholipid exposure and thrombosis vulnerability, including in placental vessels. Different molecular mechanisms may underlie the obstetric versus thrombotic APS subsets 81,85 . Purified IgG from patients with obstetric, but not thrombotic, manifestations of APS were capable of inhibiting trophoblast invasion, while in thrombotic APS, neutrophils produced spontaneous neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) which incorpo- rated into thrombi 81,85 . Of note, aPL antibodies can also bind to β 2 GPI receptors on platelets leading to platelet activation and aggregation, resulting in thrombocytopenia in roughly a third of patients with APS 85 . Vascular findings such as prominent and persistent livedo racemosa or reticularis are unlikely to be due solely to thrombotic mechanisms; they may be related in part to aPL antibodies binding to receptors on endothelial cells with inhibition of endothelial nitric oxide synthase. This would lead to impairment of nitric oxide production and release, inducing endothelial dysfunction and potentially endothelial cell prolif- eration and intimal hyperplasia 84,85 . Adapted from Cutaneous Manifestations of Microvascular Occlusion Syndromes In addition to the skin, many other organ systems may be involved, with DVT/PE and CNS disease the most common extracutaneous manifestations. CAPS is uncommon and precipitating factors include infection (often younger patients), surgical procedures, drugs (e.g. sulfur-containing diuretics, captopril, oral contraceptives), discontinu- ation of anticoagulant therapy, and malignancy, especially in older individuals. These patients often present with multi-organ failure; the majority present with renal involvement as well as evidence of acute respiratory distress syndrome. In a series of 65 patients with CAPS and skin involvement, the cutaneous findings included livedo racemosa (45%), necrotic or ulcerated lesions (42%), splinter hemorrhages (29%), apparent distal inflammatory edema (hands, feet, face; 23%), and purpura (14%) 86a . Complement activation appears to play a role in CAPS and up to 60% of patients with CAPS have germline mutations in complement regulatory genes 87 . Histologic features of early lesions typically reveal non-inflammatory thrombosis of small dermal vessels; later lesions may show inflam- mation following necrosis or with wound healing. In CAPS, there can be arterial and venous occlusion as well as microvascular occlusion in multiple organs including the skin. Complement activation and NETosis can lead to inflammation of blood vessels. Differential diagnosis The differential diagnosis of APS includes many of the syndromes discussed in this chapter plus the diseases or syndromes associated with the cutaneous findings in Table 23.4 . The presence of persistent or widespread livedo reticularis or livedo racemosa, especially in associ- ation with SLE, points to Sneddon syndrome or APS. Complement- mediated HUS (CM-HUS) and sepsis-associated purpura fulminans/ DIC can mimic CAPS, but the latter does not typically result in prolonged PT/PTT or elevated fibrinolysis, as in DIC. Treatment Therapy for APS normally consists of heparin followed by a vitamin K antagonist to maintain an INR = 2.0–3.0 85,89 . In CAPS, treatment options include heparin, methylprednisolone, IVIg, plasmapheresis, and more recently C5 inhibitors (e.g. eculizumab) 85,90 . Rituximab, cyclophosphamide, and other immunosuppressive agents have been used for both refractory APS and for CAPS 85,91 . In general, direct-acting oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are not recommended 85,89 . Controversy surrounds the use of low-dose aspirin; while multiple lupus trials showed no benefit except for arterial thrombosis 85 , it may have a role as preventive therapy in asymptomatic non-lupus patients with aPL antibodies. Hydroxychloroquine, HMG CoA reductase inhibitors (“statins”), and vitamin D replacement may be considered as adjunctive therapies. Underlying risk factors include aPL antibodies, mutations in the NOTCH3 signaling pathway, and adenosine deaminase 2 deficiency ( Table 23.5 ) 91–95 . Cutaneous Manifestations of Microvascular Occlusion Syndromes Key features  Favors the distal lower extremities, especially the ankles  Female predominance  Painful, punched-out ulcers  White, round, or stellate scars with peripheral telangiectasias  Livedo reticularis or racemosa in some patients Introduction Livedoid vasculopathy is an unusual disorder characterized by small, punctate, painful ulcers that sometimes cluster, are usually on the lower extremities near the ankles, and may be surrounded by reticu- lated erythema or hemorrhage 99,100 . Resolution classically results in small atrophic white macules with surrounding telangiectasias, referred to as atrophie blanche (see Fig. 105.7 ). Unfortunately, this term has also been used to describe similar lesions that can arise in the setting of venous insufficiency but are not preceded by small painful ulcerations, leading to variable analyses of etiologies and treatment outcomes. Epidemiology Based upon four retrospective series from different countries with a total of just over 200 patients 99–102 , the ratio of women : men ranged from 2 : 1 to 5.2 : 1. Although most patients were middle-aged at disease onset, there was a wide range (6 to 67 years) 100 . In one study, flares were reported during the spring and summer in ~80% of patients, supporting previous reports of seasonal variation 102 . Pathogenesis The precise pathogenesis of livedoid vasculopathy is not known, but it is thought to involve an alteration in endothelial function and/or in coagulation with formation of fibrin thrombi focally within super- ficial dermal blood vessels. Pathogenesis The precise pathogenesis of livedoid vasculopathy is not known, but it is thought to involve an alteration in endothelial function and/or in coagulation with formation of fibrin thrombi focally within super- ficial dermal blood vessels. A number of prothrombotic factors have been associated with this syndrome, including hyperhomocysteinemia, elevated lipoprotein (a), aPL antibodies, protein C and S abnormal- ities, factor V Leiden and prothrombin mutations, antithrombin III deficiency, sticky platelet syndrome, and excess plasminogen activator inhibitor (PAI-1; see Table 105.9 ) 99–102 . Because data from age-matched controls are frequently lacking and genetic polymorphisms for some of these thrombotic factors are relatively common (e.g. PAI-1), determi- nation of their pathogenic role can be challenging. Clinical features Painful, persistent, and often punched-out ulcerations on the legs, especially over the malleoli and in women, should suggest this diagnosis ( Fig. 23.10A ), as should atrophic white scars with peripheral telangiectasias. Some patients, particularly those with prominent livedo surrounding these ulcers, may develop retiform or stellate purpura or ulcer extension. In one study, peripheral neuropathy was documented in 10 of 20 evaluated patients, a finding which had been previously noted in the literature 100 . In all four retrospective series from different countries, a spectrum of associated prothrombotic laboratory findings were detected but they neither affected response to treatment nor predicted devel- opment of thrombotic complications such as venous thrombosis 99–102 . Of note, even in patients with DVTs/PE, routine screening for coagu- lation disorders may not be beneficial in directing therapy or predicting risk of recurrence 103 . Pathology The characteristic histologic findings in livedoid vasculopathy are mild perivascular lymphocytic infiltrates and extravasated red cells surrounding superficial dermal vessels with hyalinized walls and luminal fibrin deposition 99–102 ( Fig. 23.10B ). Immunofluorescence findings are frequently positive (40%–100%), most often C3 and IgM deposits in blood vessel walls 102 . In a recent study of 62 patients, 95% had positive findings, usually for a combination of immunoreactants (C3 and IgM > IgA > IgG) 102a . Benign and Malignant Atrophic Papulosis Synonyms:  Degos disease  Kohlmeier–Degos disease Introduction Described by Kohlmeier in 1941 and Degos in 1942 as malignant atrophic papulosis, this disorder typically occurs between the second and fourth decades of life and has a slight female predominance. In some patients, it may be familial. Pathogenesis There are two forms of atrophic papulosis – benign (skin-limited; BAP) and malignant (systemic; MAP). Risk factors or triggers of this small vessel vasculopathy include genetic predisposition (especially with the benign form), coagulation disorders, viral infections, and autoim- munity 118–121 . In addition to lymphocytic vasculitis and endothelial dysfunction, there is some evidence to support a role for dysregulated interferon- α and the C5–9 membrane attack complex in the underlying endothelial injury 122 . Clinical features Atrophic papulosis is a rare vasculopathy that may affect only the skin (benign) versus other organs (malignant). The latter occurs more often, with the gastrointestinal tract (~70%) and CNS (~45%) the most commonly involved sites, and less often the lungs or eyes. In a recent systematic review (n = 347 patients), the mean age of onset was 34 years, 64% had systemic findings, and the mortality rate was 57% in the “malignant” form 118 . Cutaneous lesions are usually asymptomatic and begin as scattered crops of small erythematous papules (2–10 mm) on the trunk (~60%) or extremities (~60%) 118–120 . These evolve over 2 to 4 weeks, with the development of a central depression and ultimately a porcelain white scar ( Fig. 23.11 ), often with a rim of telangiectasias and an appearance similar to atrophie blanche. These evolve over 2 to 4 weeks, with the development of a central depression and ultimately a porcelain white scar ( Fig. 23.11 ), often with a rim of telangiectasias and an appearance similar to atrophie blanche. Cutaneous findings typically precede systemic manifestations by 2 years, but this may range from 0 to 28 years 118 . Gastrointestinal lesions can lead to bowel perforation, and, along with CNS manifestations (e.g. CVAs), are the leading causes of death 118,120 . Pathology Skin lesions are characterized histologically by a wedge-shaped area of ischemic dermis with a sparse perivascular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate at the edge of the ischemic area and an atrophic but slightly hyperkera- totic overlying epidermis. Edema and mucin deposition are found within the ischemic dermis, and in later stages sclerosis may be observed. The base of the lesion shows vascular damage with thrombosis, but exami- nation of deeper tissue sections may be required for detection 123,124 . Differential diagnosis It is important to consider other systemic diseases, especially SLE, dermatomyositis and APS, as possible causes of malignant atrophic papulosis-like lesions ( Fig. 23.11 , inset ) 118,121 . Localized lesions can occur when due to interferon- α injections. Treatment Some studies recommend semi-annual evaluations for the first 7 years after diagnosis and then annually 120 . This is based on the observation that the likelihood of the benign variant increases to > 95% after 7 years of skin-limited disease 120 . In the systematic review, surgery (especially bowel resection) was the most commonly reported intervention for MAP, but the therapeutic goal should be to prevent serious events requiring surgery 118 . Antiplatelet monotherapy was the most common pharmacologic treatment for BAP and MAP, with complete response rates of 42% and 20%, respectively. These results support an underlying coagulopathy. When antiplatelet agents were combined with other therapies, the complete response rate in BAP was similar to that achieved with antiplatelet monotherapy while the complete response rate in MAP was halved (9%). This suggests that antiplatelet monotherapy was more often prescribed for milder cases, whereas patients with more aggressive disease received multiple therapies that were unable to achieve complete resolution. Approximately 20%–30% of patients have fever and arthralgias, with myalgias, acute renal failure, and pulmonary involvement in ~10% of patients. Pathology and laboratory findings Laboratory findings include leukopenia and/or neutropenia (40%–50% of patients), agranulocytosis (10%), ANCAs (95%), and both anti- myeloperoxidase and anti-proteinase antibodies in half of those with ANCAs; < 5% of patients have only cANCA positivity. In addition, aPL antibodies are present in ~70% of patients and an ANA titer > 1 : 80 in ~50%. Autoantibodies resolve after discontinuation of levamisole. Histologically, both leukocytoclastic vasculitis (~50%) and throm- botic vasculopathy (~40%) can be seen. Sometimes there is an angio- centric neutrophil-rich infiltrate in the superficial and deep plexus 53 . Variation in the age of the thrombi, ranging from a fibrinous plug to organized fibrotic thrombi with focal recanalization, may be a clue to recurrent use of levamisole-adulterated cocaine. Direct immunofluo- rescence may show immune complexes and complement deposition in the vessel walls 53 . Differential diagnosis The lesions of levamisole-induced vasculopathy tend to be more widespread than the acral lesions of cryoprotein-induced disorders. In the setting of sepsis and hypotension, purpura fulminans is a more likely diagnosis. Given the high incidence of ANCAs, aPL antibodies and ANAs, in concert with cytopenias, ANCA-associated vasculi- tides, systemic lupus, and APS need to be considered, especially in the presence of renal or pulmonary involvement. Since cANCA positivity is rare in this syndrome 124 , its singular presence requires strong consider- ation of a primary ANCA-associated vasculitis. Of note, this syndrome is distinct from cocaine-induced vasculitis. Treatment In a review of 151 patients, 28 improved with drug cessation alone while 85 improved following additional interventions, most often prednisone at a median dose of 60 mg/day. Less often, cyclophos- phamide, rituximab, methotrexate, thalidomide, and plasmapheresis are employed. Occasionally, surgery is required to remove necrotic tissue 124 . Calciphylaxis Synonyms:  Calcific arteriolopathy  Calcific uremic arteriolopathy The cutaneous manifestations of calciphylaxis are reviewed in Chapters 50 and 106 . This section focuses on the mechanisms that underlie the associated thrombotic vasculopathy. While calcification in vessels or peri-eccrine areas within the subcutis is considered the gold standard for the diagnosis of cutaneous calciphylaxis, identical calcifi- cation has been demonstrated in normal skin in ~40% of patients with end-stage and chronic renal disease without calciphylaxis as well as in 18% of a small sample of control patients without renal disease under- going elective surgery 126 . In one study, patients whose skin biopsies fulfilled the histologic criteria for calciphylaxis also had areas of thrombosis within vessels without evidence of calcification 127 . This raised the question of whether calcification is a driver of occlusion, an incidental factor, or a conse- quence of an underlying vascular dysfunction distinct from calcification (subcutaneous thrombotic vasculopathy). More recently, at least half of patients with uremic and non-uremic calciphylaxis were found to have lupus anticoagulant, offering an explanation for vascular dysfunction 128 . The elevated calcium × phosphate product, association of calciphy- laxis with administration of vitamin D, and calciphylaxis in individuals without chronic kidney disease treated with teriparatide (PTH agonist for osteoporosis), suggests that calcium plays a triggering or synergistic role in this disease 129 . Vitamin K is thought, at least in part, to play a role in the pathogenesis of the vascular calcification. There are two forms of vitamin K: (1) K1 (phylloquinone), stored primarily in the liver, is an essential cofactor for synthesis of the procoagulant factors II, VII, IX, and X as well as the anticoagulant proteins C and S; and (2) K2 (metaquinone), stored primarily in vessels and bones, is essential for carboxylation of multiple inhibitors of vascular calcification, especially Gas6 (growth arrest-specific 6) and MGP (matrix Gla) proteins 130 . Chronic renal disease leads to depletion of vascular stores of vitamin K2, resulting in accelerated atherogenesis with arterial calcification and presumably increases the risk of cutaneous vessel calcification 130 . DISORDERS OF CELL-RELATED VASCULAR OCCLUSION Red Blood Cell (RBC) Vascular Occlusion: Sickle Cell Disease (SCD) Introduction and pathogenesis Cell-free hemoglobin, arginase-1, and RBC metabolites interfere with nitric oxide availability and contribute to vasculopathy in SCD 131 . Slow flow results in local hypoxemia, triggering further sickling, providing an explanation for lower extremity ulcerations 131 . In addition, cell-free hemoglobin and heme serve as danger signals, prime the innate immune system, and trigger a proinflammatory endothelial environment 131 . Adherent neutrophils often undergo NETosis which increases RBC entrapment as do activated platelets 131–133 . Damaged RBC-derived microparticles, which are found in large numbers in patients with SCD, also trigger a proinflammatory phenotype on endothelial cells 134 . Lastly, coagulation activation may play a role as inhibitors of thrombin or factor Xa improve microvascular stasis in a mouse model 135,136 . Clinical features In SCD, the overall incidence of leg ulcers is 8%–10% and they most frequently develop during the second decade of life 137 . The incidence does vary widely by geographic location, from 1% in Saudi Arabia to 25% in the US to up to 75% in Jamaica. Ulcers may be triggered by trauma or edema, are frequently punched-out in appearance, and usually measure < 10 cm 2 (see Fig. 105.20C ) 137 . Treatment Hydroxyurea reduces hemolysis and lowers exposure to phosphati- dylserines on damaged RBC-derived microparticles, abolishing their proinflammatory properties 134 . There is a reduction in vaso-occlusive crises (VOCs) and presumably the risk of ulceration, but as noted previ- ously hydroxyurea can independently cause ulcerations 137 . Additional potential therapies include L-glutamine (reduces oxidative stress), voxelotor (stabilizes oxygenated hemoglobin S) 133 , and crizanlizumab (reduces VOCs via binding to P-selectin on endothelial cells and platelets) 133 . Red Blood Cell (RBC) Vascular Occlusion/Ischemia: Thalassemia Approximately half of patients with severe β -thalassemia, particularly those in Southeast Asia, have hemoglobin E (HbE). Leg ulcers occur in ~20% patients with HbE β -thalassemia 139 . Ulcers are usually located on the medial or lateral malleoli and often follow minor trauma. They are thought to be due to tissue hypoxia, tend to become chronic, and are severely painful. RBC transfusions, zinc supplementation, and hydroxyurea, either alone or in combination with recombinant human erythropoietin, can accelerate healing. Hyperbaric oxygen and platelet- rich plasma may lead to improvement 139 . Red Blood Cell (RBC) Vascular Occlusion/ Ischemia: Other Occasionally, other severe hemolytic anemias such as hereditary spherocytosis have been associated with leg ulcers 140 . Splenectomy, which reduces hemolysis and results in normalization of the reticu- locyte count, may lead to ulcer resolution. Intravascular Cellular Occlusion Although chronic lymphocytic leukemia is the most common cause of a marked elevation of circulating atypical leukocytes, these cells are fragile and do not lead to vascular occlusion syndromes. Reduced perfusion of various organ systems may accompany high blast counts, nearly always of myelogenous origin. Cutaneous bland leukemic occlusion syndromes have not been reported, although repeated arterial occlusion from myeloblasts has been described (e.g. retinal artery, cerebral arteries) 141 . Leukemic vasculitis in the skin has been described 142 , as has a case of T cell prolymphocytic leukemia with a cutaneous presentation that mimicked livedoid vasculopathy 143 . Intravascular lymphoma (B cell > T cell) is a very rare syndrome which is frequently diagnosed post mortem , usually because of vague clinical findings. CNS involvement is often the most severe clinical manifes- tation. Skin lesions are commonly observed (40% of patients) but nonspe- cific and include erythematous, sometimes painful plaques or nodules and macular or telangiectatic lesions 144 . The lower extremities are the most common location (often in association with edema), followed by the trunk. Occasionally, it may present as retiform purpura ( Fig. 23.12 ). The histopathologic finding of intraluminal occlusion by atypical lympho- cytes can be missed on initial interpretation (see Fig. 119.14 ). Cutaneous intralymphatic histiocytosis is characterized by dilated lymphatic vessels filled with histiocytes, leading to overlying erythem- atous patches without purpura (see Fig. 121.6 ). This entity was previ- ously referred to as cutaneous intravascular histiocytosis, until it was recognized that only lymphatic vessels are involved. It is often associated with chronic inflammation, rheumatoid arthritis, joint replacements, or metal implants 145 . DISORDERS OF OCCLUSION, MISCELLANEOUS Loxosceles Spider Bites Clinical and histologic features as well pathogenesis and treatment options are discussed in Chapter 85 . At the site of the bite, edema, erythema, and a painful reddish blister develop that is surrounded by a cyanotic bluish discoloration with ischemic borders and then intensely erythematous halo. This results in a characteristic blue–white–red concentric pattern 146 . The cyanotic area can darken and enlarge over a few days, sometimes becoming geographic or retiform in appearance with central necrosis. Systemic symptoms include fever, nausea, headache, shivering, weakness, myalgias, and arthralgias. Rarely, patients can develop hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, disseminated intravascular coagulation, hemoglobinuria, myoglobinuria, acute renal failure, and gangrene 146 . Hematoma-Associated Retiform Purpura Retiform purpura with necrosis, best explained by compression of subcutaneous arterioles by large trauma-induced hematomas, may rarely occur, including in patients with hemophilia 147 . SARS-CoV-2 Purpuric Syndromes Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) is associated with a diminished type I interferon response during its early phase 148,149 . Resultant viral replication contributes significantly to septal capillary compromise within the lung as well as extrapulmonary pseudovirion dissemination with extrapulmonary vascular sequelae 148 . Spike glycoprotein and other viral capsid proteins localize to micro- vasculature expressing angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2), the receptor utilized by spike glycoprotein 148 . The primary localizations of viral capsid/spike protein and its ACE2 receptor are the septal capillaries of the lung, deeper dermal and subcutaneous capillaries and venules of both diseased and normal-appearing skin, and the microvessels of the brain 148 . There is little evidence to support viral proliferation in tissues beyond the nasal epithelium and lung; evidence instead suggests that pseudovirions or spike proteins that disseminate from the lung and localize to sites of ACE2 receptors are important in disease expression. Differently modulated immune responses appear to correlate with observed patterns of vascular inflammation and coagulopathy. Pernio/chilblains-like disease (“COVID toes”) Individuals with this disorder, more often children, are usually antibody- and PCR-negative for SARS-CoV-2, leading many authors to question whether there is a true association. Patients typically present with tender or pruritic red–purple papules on the toes > fingers which may blister or ulcerate 148,149 . Although the overall histologic features are similar to those of idiopathic pernio (see Ch. 88 ), a distinguishing feature is the presence of occlusion of some blood vessels within the reticular dermis. By immunostaining, there is increased MxA expression in the epidermis, eccrine coils, endothelia, T cells, and plasmacytoid dendritic cells, pointing to a robust type I interferon response 148,149 . One theory advanced in support of a true association is that a very brisk innate immune type I interferon response clears the virus quickly, without enough viral proliferation to trigger a humoral antibody response to SARS-CoV-2. Retiform thrombotic purpura A hypercoagulable state and organ failure, particularly progressive acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and acute renal insuffi- ciency, qualify as critical SARS-CoV-2 infection. In both affected and normal skin of patients with critical infections, there is evidence of complement activation in the ACE2-positive microvascular beds that have bound viral capsid protein (but not active viral replication) 148 . The mannan-binding lectin (MBL) pathway has been implicated as the driver of vascular damage that leads to thrombosis and coagulopathy, with possible augmentation by the alternate complement activation pathway. C5b-9 deposition and vascular injury are similar to that seen in CM-HUS. The MBL pathway is also implicated as an inducer of the overproduction of various cytokines (e.g. tumor necrosis factor, inter- leukin-6) by activated endothelium. Histologically, there is a pauci-inflammatory thrombogenic vascu- lopathy affecting dermal capillaries and venules, and in half of the patients with retiform purpura, the arterioles and small arteries are also involved. This finding is associated with a higher risk of stroke and death. Degenerative endothelial cell changes with sloughing is more conspicuous in the deeper dermis and subcutaneous fat, along with secondary ischemic necrosis of eccrine coils 148 . SARS-CoV-2-related systemic coagulopathy Malignancy-associated DIC frequently leads to bleeding with signif- icant fibrinolysis while sepsis tends to suppress fibrinolysis and favor thrombosis, termed sepsis-induced coagulopathy (SIC) 156,157 . The coagulopathy of SARS-CoV-2 infection resembles SIC, but because it manifests in a distinct manner, the term COVID-19-associated coagu- lopathy (CAC) is often employed 156–158 . For example, a decreased platelet count and prolonged PT, hallmarks of SIC, are uncommon in the early phase of CAC. Symmetrical peripheral gangrene can occur due to microthromboses, and acute hepatic dysfunction (shock liver) appears to predispose to this complication 157 . Systemic thromboembolic events include PE, DVT, ischemic stroke, myocardial infarction, and systemic arterial embolism 159 . SARS-CoV-2 infection-associated DIC is an unusual but potentially lethal compli- cation, reported in ~2% of hospitalized patients. VITT is specifically due to anti-platelet factor 4 (anti-PF4) antibodies that are induced primarily by adenoviral vector vaccines and, very rarely, SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccines. VITT strongly resembles spontaneous “heparin- induced” thrombocytopenia or classic HIT (see above). Unlike classic HIT, spontaneous HIT results from an anti-PF4 antibody that does not require co-binding to a long chain polyanion such as heparin and occurs in the absence of exposure to heparin. The rate of this complication from SARS-CoV-2 viral vector vaccines is 3.83 per million doses versus 0.00855 per million with the mRNA vaccines, a 450-fold difference in frequency. The possibility exists that the rate in the mRNA vaccine group represents the background incidence of spontaneous HIT in the US. Compared to HIT, VITT appears to target a different antigenic site on PF4, which is shared with neutrophil activating peptide-2 (NAP2). NAP2 is one of the most abundant chemokines released from activated platelets and is known to be involved in the initiation and propagation of the immunothrombotic response 162 . Clinical features include cerebral venous (sinus) thrombosis (55%), PE (40%), extremity DVT (40%), and abdominal vein thrombosis (30%), with one sixth of the patients developing arterial thrombosis, mirroring the frequency seen in spontaneous HIT 160,161 . Characteristic laboratory findings include a moderate-to-severe thrombocytopenia and evidence of DIC with D-dimer elevation and hypofibrinogenemia. CLASSIFICATION The 2012 revised International Chapel Hill Consensus Conference Nomenclature, which is based upon expert consensus, provides of vasculitis 2 . A 2018 dermatologic addendum to the Chapel Hill Nomenclature further classifies cutaneous vasculitides 1 . In addition, the Diagnostic and Classification Criteria in Vasculitis Study (DCVAS), a large, multinational observational study that utilized patient data, aims to develop and validate evidence-based diagnostic and classi- fication criteria for use in practice and clinical trials. These data are the basis of revised ACR-EULAR classification criteria for large vessel vasculitis and ANCA-associated vasculitis 3 . Because a system based upon the predominant size of the involved blood vessels is conceptually useful and helps to predict the clinical presentation and corresponding histopathologic findings, this type of classification scheme will be employed in this chapter (see Table 24.1 ). Additional features that aid in classifying cutaneous vasculitis are systemic manifestations, direct immunofluorescence studies, and the presence or absence of pertinent laboratory findings, e.g. anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCAs) (see Fig. 24.16 ). Despite descriptions of distinct vasculitic syndromes, unique diagnostic criteria are often lacking and clinicopathologic correlation is always required. EPIDEMIOLOGY The annual population-based incidence of biopsy-proven LCV is ~45 per million. Of note, this figure includes various subtypes such as urticarial vasculitis, cryoglobulinemic vasculitis, and ANCA-associated vasculitis, any of which may demonstrate LCV histologically 4 . Cutaneous vascu- litis occurs in all age groups (mean age in adults, 47 years; mean age in children, 7 years), has a slight female predominance 5,6 , and is much more common in adults than in children. The most common type of vasculitis in children is IgA vasculitis (Henoch–Schönlein purpura). Any organ system can be affected, and clinical manifestations correlate with the size of affected blood vessels, such that disorders are generally classified according to vessel size. Cutaneous vasculitis may represent: (1) a manifestation of a systemic vasculitis; (2) a skin-limited or skin- predominant variant of a systemic vasculitis; or (3) a single-organ vasculitis with no detectable systemic involvement 1 . Vasculitis can affect small, medium-sized, or large vessels of the arterial and/or venous systems ( Table 24.1 ). Small vessels include arterioles, capillaries, and postcapillary venules, which are found in the superficial and mid dermis of the skin. Medium-sized vessels refer to the small arteries and veins that reside within the deep dermis or subcutis. In general, the lesions are asymptomatic, but they may itch, burn, or sting. In medium-sized vessel vasculitis, the affected blood vessels reside within the reticular dermis or subcutis. As a result, it typically presents with livedo racemosa, retiform purpura, ulcers, subcutaneous nodules, and/or digital necrosis. In general, the presence of larger ulcerations or necrosis suggests deeper arterial involvement. The combination of purpuric macules and papules plus features of medium-sized vessel disease points to a “mixed” pattern of vasculitis with involvement of both small and medium-sized vessels, as in cryoglobulinemic vasculitis and ANCA-associated vasculitis (see Table 24.1 ). Common manifestations of systemic vasculitis include inflammatory arthritis as well as constitutional symptoms, such as fever, weight loss, and malaise. These common findings can be seen in virtually any type of systemic vasculitis, whereas other signs and symptoms (e.g. motor neuropathy, sinusitis) are more often associated with specific disease states. As in the skin, systemic manifestations tend to correlate with the size of the affected blood vessels; for example, glomerulonephritis is a manifestation of small vessel disease, while renal artery aneurysms and renovascular hypertension are features of medium-sized vessel vasculitis 6 . PATHOLOGY Timing and appropriate sampling of the most likely involved vessels increase the diagnostic yield of a skin biopsy. Ideally, lesions should be biopsied for routine processing within the first 24 to 48 hours of appearance. When small vessel vasculitis is suspected, a biopsy specimen for direct immunofluorescence (DIF) should be obtained, as the presence of certain immunoglobulins (e.g. IgA) may suggest a particular diagnosis and prognosis. Biopsies for DIF should also be obtained from lesions of recent onset, ideally those that are only hours old. In general, punch biopsies are adequate for the diagnosis of small vessel vasculitis, while an incisional deep biopsy may be required to diagnose vasculitis of larger vessels. In cutaneous vasculitis, the histologic findings vary depending upon the type and age of the sampled lesion in addition to the size of the affected vessel. The classic histopathologic features of CSVV are referred to as LCV and consist of transmural infiltration of the walls of small vessels (primarily postcapillary venules) by neutrophils undergoing karyorrhexis of their nuclei, as well as fibrinoid necrosis of the vessel walls ( Fig. 24.4 ). Other findings include leukocytoclasia (degranulation and fragmentation of neutrophils, leading to the production of nuclear dust), extravasated erythrocytes, and signs of endothelial cell damage. However, lesions present for greater than 48 to 72 hours may have a predominantly mononuclear rather than neutrophilic infiltrate. Binding of antibodies to circulating antigens creates immune complexes. Immune complex deposition within postcapillary venules activates complement and subsequently leads to an increase in adhesion molecule expression on the endothelium. Complement split products (C3a and C5a) induce mast cell degranulation and neutrophil chemotaxis. Mast cell degranulation leads to increased vascular dilation and permeability, enhancing immune complex deposition and leukocyte tethering to endothelium. Increased adhesion between inflammatory cells (especially neutrophils) and the endothelium is mediated by elevated expression of selectins (E-selectin, P-selectin) and members of the immunoglobulin superfamily (ICAM-1, VCAM-1, PECAM-1) on endothelial cells in concert with the upregulation of their corresponding ligands and receptors/adhesion molecules on leukocytes (e.g. P-selectin glycoprotein ligand-1, LFA-1, Mac-1) (see Ch. 102 for details).
