Differential Diagnosis The boundary between dry skin (xerosis) and mild ichthyosis vulgaris is not always clear-cut. In male patients, X-linked ichthyosis may be differentiated by larger, darker scales and involvement of the neck and other flexures; cryptorchidism, a maternal history of delayed or prolonged labor, and the inheritance pattern can represent additional clues. Chromosomal microarray or fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) testing can exclude steroid sulfatase deficiency. A rare mild form of autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis that presents with gener- alized fine, whitish scaling similar to ichthyosis vulgaris results from mutations in CASP14 (caspase 14), which is involved in the proteo- lytic degradation of profilaggrin. Acquired ichthyosis is distinguished by its development later in life and association with conditions such as malnutrition, infections (e.g. leprosy), neoplasms (e.g. lymphoma), inflammatory disorders (e.g. sarcoidosis), and medications (e.g. statins, ponatinib, immune checkpoint inhibitors) 15a . Some individuals with other heritable forms of ichthyosis also have a partial or complete filaggrin deficiency, which may result in a more severe phenotype than is usually observed for those ichthyoses. Treatment The mainstay of treatment is application of emollients, humectants, and keratolytic agents to reduce scaling. Preparations that contain urea and/or glycolic, lactic, or salicylic acid are usually beneficial; with the latter, care must be taken to prevent salicylate toxicity (see Ch. 129 ). Skin irritation from topical retinoids limits their use for ichthyosis vulgaris, and vitamin D analogues are typically ineffective. Systemic treatment with acitretin or isotretinoin is rarely indicated. The use of moisturizing cleansers and humidifiers may also be helpful. Research is underway to identify compounds that could upregulate filaggrin expression and, for those patients with nonsense mutations, modify protein translation 13 . STEROID SULFATASE DEFICIENCY Synonym:  X-linked recessive ichthyosis Ichthyoses, Erythrokeratodermas, and Related Disorders History A type of ichthyosis occurring only in boys and men was first reported in the early nineteenth century, and its X-linked recessive inheritance was clearly recognized in the 1920s. In 1966, the clinical features of this entity were distinguished from those of ichthyosis vulgaris 5 . The underlying steroid sulfatase deficiency was identified in the late 1970s 6 . Epidemiology The worldwide incidence is between 1 in 2000 and 1 in 9500 male births. It is an X-linked recessive disorder that is transmitted by asymp- tomatic female carriers and almost exclusively affects boys and men. Pathogenesis Diminution or complete absence of steroid sulfatase activity is caused by a deletion of the entire STS gene on chromosome Xp22.31 in ~90% of patients and inactivating mutations in others 16 . Steroid sulfatase deficiency results in impaired hydrolysis of cholesterol sulfate and dehydroepiandros- terone sulfate (DHEAS), with subsequent accumulation of cholesterol 3-sulfate in the epidermis. High levels of this metabolite can inhibit trans- glutaminase-1, explaining the partial overlap with lamellar ichthyosis. In women pregnant with an affected fetus, steroid sulfatase deficiency in the fetal placenta causes low or absent levels of estrogen in the urine and amniotic fluid because of inadequate deconjugation of DHEAS, which is necessary for estrogen synthesis. As a result, labor often fails to initiate spontaneously or progress, due to insufficient dilation of the cervix. This can only be partially overcome by oxytocin administration, often necessitating cesarean delivery. Clinical Features In ~90% of affected boys, steroid sulfatase deficiency presents during the neonatal period with mild erythroderma and generalized peeling, often with exfoliation of large, translucent scales. The typical polygonal, dark-brown, adherent scales develop later during infancy or childhood and are distributed symmetrically on the extremities, trunk, and neck ( Fig. 57.5 ). The scales are occasionally grayish or white, and they tend to be larger on the lower extremities. Involvement of the preauricular area and neck is highly characteristic, which has resulted in the descriptive term “dirty neck disease” (see Fig. 57.5D ); however, other skin folds are often not affected. The palms, soles, and remainder of the face are typically spared. Fine scaling of the scalp is frequently seen during early childhood but diminishes over time. Because the STS gene at least partially escapes X-chromosome inactivation, mosaic ichthyotic changes are not seen. Pathology Histopathologic findings include hyperkeratosis or parakeratosis overlying a normal or slightly thickened granular layer. Follicular hyper- keratosis may be present. Other diagnostic tests Underlying deletions can be identified by chromosomal microarray analysis or FISH, and molecular testing of STS is available. Prenatal diagnosis can also be performed (see Introduction) 10 . However, non-invasive prenatal diagnosis may be accomplished by identifying decreased maternal serum estriol levels or the presence of non-hydro- lyzed sulfated steroids in maternal urine. Accumulation of (hydroxy) cholesterol sulfate can be detected indirectly by increased migration of the β -fraction in serum lipoprotein electrophoresis, or measured directly by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) of serum, epidermal scale, placental tissue, or amniotic fluid. In addition, steroid sulfatase enzymatic activity can be measured in leukocytes, fibroblasts, keratinocytes, or placental tissue. Differential Diagnosis Clinically, ichthyosis vulgaris is distinguished by its sparing of the neck and other flexural areas as well as the presence of hyperlinear palms and keratosis pilaris. As discussed above, an identical ichthyosis phenotype can be associated with extracutaneous findings in patients with larger contiguous gene deletions. Chromosomal microarray analysis, refined karyotyping, or FISH can be utilized to detect Xp deletions and X;Y translocations in patients who present with these additional findings. Autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis due to defective cholesterol sulfotransferase ( SULT2B1 mutations) has a phenotype similar to that of steroid sulfatase deficiency, with lamellar scaling that spares the central face and skin folds 18 . Treatment Topical humectants (especially propylene glycol), keratolytics, and retinoids are helpful alone or in combination. In contrast, vitamin D Ichthyoses, Erythrokeratodermas, and Related Disorders analogues are less effective and cause significant irritation. Systemic retinoids are rarely necessary. Based on the distinctive histopathologic features of the epidermis, Frost and Van Scott 3 introduced the name “epidermolytic hyperkeratosis” for this autosomal dominant blistering form of congenital ichthyosis in 1966. In 1937, Siemens 19 first recog- nized a superficial form of epidermolytic ichthyosis as a distinct entity (“ichthyosis bullosa of Siemens”). Epidemiology Epidermolytic ichthyosis (EI), which includes the superficial subtype (SEI), has an estimated worldwide prevalence of 1 in 200 000 20 . It is generally an autosomal dominant disorder with complete penetrance, with rare reports of autosomal recessive inheritance. Both sexes are affected equally. At least 50% of all cases occur sporadically due to new mutations. Pathogenesis EI is caused by heterozygous mutations in the genes encoding keratin 1 (KRT1) , keratin 10 (KRT10) , and (for SEI) keratin 2 ( KRT2 ) 21 . There are rare reports in consanguineous families of a severe autosomal recessive form of EI due to biallelic loss-of-function mutations 22 . Keratins 1 and 10 are coexpressed in the differentiated spinous and granular layers of the epidermis, whereas keratin 2 is found in the uppermost spinous and granular layers; these represent the sites of disease pathology in classic EI and SEI, respectively. KRT1 mutations are usually associated with palmoplantar keratoderma (PPK), which may be severe, while most KRT10 mutations result in sparing of the palms and soles because there is less expression of KRT10 in these locations 23 . Pathogenic mutations alter highly conserved amino acid residues located at the boundaries of the α -helical rod region; these sites represent mutational “hot spots” that impact the helix initiation and termination motifs (see Fig. 56.5 ) 21 . GENODERMATOSES Clinical Features Classic epidermolytic ichthyosis and variants Classic EI presents at birth with erythroderma ( Fig. 57.6A ), peeling, erosions, and often widespread areas of denuded skin (see Fig. 34.16 ). Hyperkeratosis may be present, but it usually develops later during infancy. Skin fragility, blistering, and erythema decrease over time, and severe hyperkeratosis prevails ( Fig. 57.6B–E ). However, patients may still periodically shed large plates of superficial epidermis, revealing a tender, erythematous base. Ridges along skin lines are common in flexures (see Fig. 57.6C,D ), while hyperkeratosis over the extensor surfaces of the joints often forms a cobblestone pattern (see Fig. 57.6E ). When present, PPK may be severe and associated with digital contrac- tures ( Fig. 57.6F ). The clinical presentation of EI varies considerably, and six charac- teristic clinical patterns with or without PPK have been described 23 . Unusual clinical variants of EI include “cyclic ichthyosis with epider- molytic hyperkeratosis” and “annular epidermolytic ichthyosis”, which are caused by distinct mutations outside the helix boundaries of KRT1 and KRT10 , respectively 21 . EI is disfiguring and has tremendous impact on patients’ quality of life and social interactions. Sepsis as well as fluid and electrolyte imbalances can be life threatening in the neonatal period. Episodes of blistering and secondary skin infections are also problematic later in life.

Episodes of blistering and secondary skin infections are also problematic later in life. The disorder is accompanied by a pungent body odor, and it is occasionally associated with posture and gait abnormalities. Angular cheilitis and severe scalp involvement leading to encasement of hair shafts and hair loss are additional associated findings. Superficial epidermolytic ichthyosis (SEI) SEI is less severe than classic EI. At birth, the skin may appear normal or have mild blistering. Trauma-induced vesicles on the extremities occur during infancy but usually subside by early childhood, as hyper- keratosis develops. The skin overlying the joints, the flexures, and the dorsa of the hands and feet ( Fig. 57.7 ) are sites of predilection, whereas the palms and soles are spared. Involved skin may appear ridged, shiny, or lichenified. A characteristic feature is superficially denuded areas with collarette-like borders, described as “molting” or “Mauserung”, which develop due to superficial blistering and shedding of the stratum corneum 21 . Epidermolytic epidermal nevi (mosaic epidermolytic ichthyosis) The mosaic form of EI is characterized by unilateral or bilateral streaks of hyperkeratosis that follow the lines of Blaschko 24 . Extensive involvement with marked hyperkeratosis leading to protruding, porcupine-like spines has been referred to as “ichthyosis hystrix”, but this is a descriptive term rather than the name of a distinct disorder. Epidermolytic epidermal nevi are caused by a postzygotic mutation in KRT1, KRT10 , or rarely KRT2 that arises during embryogenesis. If this mutation involves gonadal cells, it can potentially be transmitted to the patient’s offspring, resulting in full-blown, generalized disease 24 . Examination of both parents of a child with sporadic EI and genetic counseling are therefore recommended. Key features of EI on routine histologic examination are dense orthokeratotic hyperkeratosis, prominent acanthosis, hypergranulosis, and cytolysis of the suprabasal and granular layers leading to small intraepidermal blisters ( Fig. 57.8 ). Key features of EI on routine histologic examination are dense orthokeratotic hyperkeratosis, prominent acanthosis, hypergranulosis, and cytolysis of the suprabasal and granular layers leading to small intraepidermal blisters ( Fig. 57.8 ). In SEI, cytolysis is limited to the granular cell layers and can occasionally lead to superficial intraepidermal separation. Keratinocytes within the affected cell layers exhibit marked intracellular vacuolization and dense clumps of keratin intermediate filaments (KIFs). A mild perivascular lymphohis- tiocytic infiltrate is usually present in the upper dermis. Ultrastructural analysis of EI reveals fragmented, clumped KIFs in the lower epidermis and perinuclear KIF shells in the upper epidermis, while SEI has tonofil- ament clumping in the upper spinous and granular cell layers. Other diagnostic tests Mutation screening and complete sequencing of KRT1, KRT10 , and KRT2 are available. Prenatal diagnosis can be performed when the underlying mutation has been identified in affected family members. GENODERMATOSES Treatment Treatment is symptomatic and depends on the age of the patient, disease severity, and clinical issues. In the neonatal period, infants with classic EI typically require management in an intensive care nursery to provide protective isolation and prevent or treat dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, and cutaneous superinfection. Sepsis should be treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics. When the neonate is handled carefully and protective padding and lubricants are used, erosions and denuded skin usually heal rapidly. In children and adults with classic EI, therapy is aimed at reducing hyperkeratosis, removing scale, and softening the skin. Topical products containing urea, salicylic acid, α -hydroxy acids, and N-acetylcysteine can be effective but are often not well tolerated, especially in children, because of burning and stinging. Widespread topical application of higher-concentration salicylic acid preparations should be avoided because of the risk of systemic salicylism. Topical tretinoin and vitamin D may be beneficial but often cause skin irritation. Topical tretinoin and vitamin D may be beneficial but often cause skin irritation. Frequent use of emollients and humectants can be combined with hydration (e.g. soaking of the skin during bathing) and mechanical abrasion of keratotic skin via gentle scrubbing with a soft brush or sponge. Bacterial skin infections are common in patients with classic EI and often trigger blistering; they require topical or systemic antibiotic treatment. Use of antiseptics such as antibacterial soaps, chlorhex- idine, or dilute sodium hypochlorite baths may help to control bacterial colonization. Continuous use of oral or topical antibiotics should be avoided due to the risk of developing antibiotic resistance. Because of the increased skin fragility, it is also important to prevent mechanical trauma, e.g. by wearing comfortable clothing and shoes. Oral retinoids may drastically reduce hyperkeratosis and the frequency of infections in patients with generalized EI, but they also increase epidermal fragility and blistering. Low initial doses with gradual increase and careful monitoring are advisable, with use of the lowest effective maintenance dose 11,25 . Responses to topical and systemic retinoids tend to be better in patients with EI due to KRT10 mutations than in those with KRT1 mutations; the latter individuals are vulnerable to retinoid-related down-regulated expression of KRT2, which can function as a substitute for KRT1 20 . Promising therapeutic approaches utilizing gene editing technologies to inactivate keratin genes with dominant-negative mutations are under development (e.g. ex vivo use of a transcription activator-like effector nuclease [TALEN]) 26 . ICHTHYOSIS HYSTRIX CURTH–MACKLIN Synonyms:  Ichthyosis hystrix  “Porcupine man”  Ichthyosis hystrix gravior type Lambert  Systematized verrucous nevus Introduction Ichthyosis hystrix is a descriptive term for massive hyperkeratosis that leads to a verrucous surface or protruding porcupine-like spines. Of note, it does not represent a distinct clinical entity. This phenotype is most commonly observed in patients with EI, but can also be seen in clinically and genetically heterogeneous disorders ranging from ichthyosis hystrix Curth–Macklin to verrucous epidermolytic nevi to hystrix-like ichthyosis with deafness (HID) syndrome. The latter is a variant of keratitis–ichthyosis–deafness (KID) syndrome and is due to mutations in GJB2 29 . History In 1954, Ollendorff-Curth and Macklin 30 described a family with hystrix-like spiky hyperkeratosis and PPK. Electron microscopic exami- nations by Anton-Lamprecht et al. 31 revealed binucleated keratinocytes and peculiar ultrastructural abnormalities of the cytoskeleton. Since the initial description, several large families with autosomal dominant inheritance have been reported as have sporadic cases. A well-known example of the ichthyosis hystrix phenotype is the “porcupine men” of the Lambert family from Suffolk, England 32 . Since no blister formation was mentioned in the records of this kindred, it remains unclear if they had ichthyosis hystrix Curth–Macklin or a form of EI. Pathogenesis In several unrelated patients with ichthyosis hystrix Curth–Macklin, heterozygous mutations in the keratin 1 ( KRT1 ) or keratin 10 ( KRT10 ) genes have been demonstrated. In contrast to EI, the mutations were small nucleotide deletions/insertions that mostly led to a frameshift and produced a keratin protein with an aberrant tail. Because the latter lacks the usual glycine loop motifs, protein–protein interactions are altered 33 . Clinical expression varies even within families, ranging from isolated PPK (which may be severe and mutilating) to localized keratotic verrucous plaques to generalized hystrix-like hyperkeratosis with horny rigid spikes. Hyperkeratosis is present at birth or develops during early childhood. It has a cobble- stone-like or ridged surface over large joints and in skin folds. Circular constriction bands (pseudoainhum), starfish-like keratoses, knuckle pads, digital flexion contractures, and secondary bacterial infections have been described. Pathology Most histopathologic features, including orthokeratotic hyperkeratosis, hypergranulosis, acanthosis, and church spire-like papillomatosis, are nonspecific. Cells in the differentiated cell layers may be vacuolated or binucleated. Ultrastructural abnormalities in the upper epidermis are diagnostic, with a shell-like, interspersed network of tangled KIFs, often associated with perinuclear vacuolization and formation of binucleated cells. In contrast to EI, there is no epidermolysis or keratin clumping. Differential Diagnosis Ichthyosis hystrix Curth–Macklin can be differentiated from EI by the absence of blistering and skin fragility as well as by electron microscopic findings. Treatment The most effective treatments are systemic retinoids and topical kerato- lytic agents (see EI above). Approximately one-third of patients with ARCI are born preterm, and the most common presentation at birth is a collodion membrane ( ∼ 70%; see below) 7,34 . Ectropion (eversion of the eyelids) occurs in ∼ 50% of neonates and may persist, while eclabium (eversion of the lips), observed in ∼ 25% of neonates, often resolves 34 . The spectrum of fully developed ARCI phenotypes ranges from large, dark, plate-like scales with no or minimal erythema in lamellar ichthyosis (LI) to fine white scales and pronounced erythroderma in congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma (CIE). The spectrum of fully developed ARCI phenotypes ranges from large, dark, plate-like scales with no or minimal erythema in lamellar ichthyosis (LI) to fine white scales and pronounced erythroderma in congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma (CIE). In addition, there are many intermediate phenotypes with variable degrees of erythema as well as size and quality of the scales. Other frequent accompanying features include PPK, hypohidrosis, heat intolerance, scarring alopecia, and conductive hearing loss. Patients may also develop recurrent infec- tions, arthritis or arthralgia, anemia, and vitamin D deficiency. ARCI is caused by pathogenic variants in at least 13 genes which encode proteins that contribute to the structure and function of lipid and cornified cell envelopes, in particular via their roles in epidermal lipid processing and transport (see Chs. 56 and 124 ). As a result, affected individuals have perturbed homeostasis of the stratum corneum and abnormal skin barrier function. History In 1966, Frost and Van Scott 3 coined the term “lamellar ichthyosis” for all autosomal recessive forms of non-bullous congenital ichthyosis. Williams and Elias 35 further separated this group into two distinct phenotypes, lamellar ichthyosis (LI) and (non-bullous) congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma (CIE), which now have been recognized to reside along a continuum with intermediate phenotypes. In the current classification system, the LI–CIE spectrum as well as harlequin ichthyosis (HI) and ichthyosis–prematurity syndrome (IPS) fall within the nonsyndromic ARCI category 7,36 . GENODERMATOSES Epidemiology ARCI occurs worldwide with an estimated overall prevalence of 1 in 100 000 to 200 000 live births. It is more common in certain regions such as Norway (1 in 90 000) and Spain (1 in 60 000) as well as in highly consanguineous populations 12 . The various forms of ARCI are inherited as autosomal recessive traits. Ichthyoses, Erythrokeratodermas, and Related Disorders COLLODION BABY Synonyms:  Collodion fetus Self-improving collodion ichthyosis/baby:  Self-healing collodion baby  Lamellar exfoliation of the newborn Epidemiology The collodion baby is a shared presentation of several congenital ichthyoses, most with autosomal recessive inheritance. It is not a distinct disorder. Pathogenesis The pathomechanisms leading to formation of a collodion membrane are not completely understood, but this presentation points to disturbed adaptation of the fetal epidermis to postnatal life. The most common causes of collodion ichthyosis are deficiencies of the crucial cross- linking enzyme TGM1 64 or various lipid-processing enzymes and lipid transporters. This includes ALOX12B ( > ALOXE3 ), CERS3 , PNPLA1 , and SULT2B1 (see ARCI). Less common etiologies are fatty aldehyde dehydrogenase deficiency in Sjögren–Larsson syndrome, deficiency of an activator of the adipose triglyceride lipase in neutral lipid storage disease, and β -glucocerebrosidase deficiency in Gaucher disease (see Fig. 56.2 ). In ~10% of collodion babies 12 , a milder “self-healing” phenotype known as self-improving collodion ichthyosis occurs. This has been reported in association with TGM1, ALOX12B, ALOXE3 , NIPAL4 , or CYP4F22 mutations that fully inactivate the encoded protein in utero but not after birth 46,65 . It has been postulated that this “dynamic” phenotype is dependent on environmental conditions, which influence the stability of the mutant protein. A form of self-improving collodion ichthyosis in which membranes are localized to acral areas due to compound heterozygous TGM1 mutations has also been described 66 . At birth, the neonate is covered with a taut, shiny, transparent membrane formed by the thickened stratum corneum, which resembles a plastic wrap ( Fig. 57.10 ). At birth, the neonate is covered with a taut, shiny, transparent membrane formed by the thickened stratum corneum, which resembles a plastic wrap ( Fig. 57.10 ). Its tautness often leads to ectropion, eclabium, and hypoplasia of nasal and auricular cartilage. Sucking and pulmonary ventilation may also be impaired, resulting in dehydration, malnu- trition, hypoxia, and pneumonia. After birth, the parchment-like membrane gradually dries, cracks, and breaks up. In the process, fissures develop that impair epidermal barrier function, which can lead to percutaneous loss of water and permit the entry of microor- ganisms; fluid and electrolyte imbalances, skin infections, and sepsis may follow. In addition, circular bands of hardened skin can lead to vascular constriction, ischemia, and distal edema. Growth hormone resistance and an increased prevalence of hypothyroidism have also been described. Within two to four weeks after birth, the membrane peels off in sheets and a transition to the underlying disease phenotype takes place. Most commonly, CIE or LI ensues. Other ichthyoses may rarely present as a collodion baby ( Table 57.4 ). In self-improving collodion ichthyosis, desquamation of the collodion membrane leaves normal skin or variable clinical findings including xerosis, fine or focal scaling, palmar hyperlin- earity, mild PPK, red cheeks, and hypohidrosis 65 . In situ assays of transglutaminase activity can also be performed on skin biopsy sections and allow rapid identification of patients with TGM1 deficiency, even as a collodion baby 67 . However, interpretation of the transglutaminase activity assay requires experience, and this test is not widely available. Differential Diagnosis The phenotype of harlequin ichthyosis is much more severe and so striking that a clinical distinction between the two disorders is, in most circumstances, not difficult. Treatment Collodion babies are at risk for thermoinstability, hypernatremic dehydration, skin infections, and sepsis. It is therefore essential to keep them in a controlled environment and to carefully monitor for fluid and electrolyte imbalances. Collodion babies are also at risk for pneumonia secondary to restricted ventilation and aspiration of amniotic fluid containing scales. To facilitate gradual desquamation of the collodion membrane, it is generally recommended that infants be placed in a humidified incubator and the skin treated with wet compresses and light emollients to increase its elasticity and pliability. Manual removal of the collodion membrane and use of topical keratolytic agents are not advisable because of the increased risk of infections and percu- taneous absorption. Distal constriction bands occasionally require surgical release. Systemic retinoid therapy is rarely necessary but may be of benefit in selected cases of delayed membrane shedding or severe underlying ichthyosis 11 . Most affected neonates are encased in a collodion membrane that is gradually replaced over the first few weeks of life by large scales in a generalized distribution. These large, brown, plate-like scales form a mosaic or bark-like pattern, and there is minimal to no associated erythroderma ( Fig. 57.11A,B ). The scales are centrally attached and have raised borders, often leading to superficial fissures. “Bathing suit ichthyosis”, which is caused by temperature-sensitive TGM1 mutations, affects primarily the trunk and scalp; it was first reported in South Africans and subsequently described in individuals from around the world 68 . Tautness of facial skin commonly results in ectropion ( Fig. 57.11C ), eclabium, and hypoplasia of nasal and auricular cartilage. Severe ectropion may lead to lagophthalmos, madarosis, conjunctivitis, and ensuing corneal exposure and keratitis. Traction and compression exerted by the taut skin can cause scarring alopecia, especially at the periphery of the scalp. Although hair shafts are normal, they are often encased by the thickened stratum corneum. At least half of individuals with LI have PPK, which can range from accentuated skin markings to severe thickening with cracking and fissuring. Secondary nail dystrophy with thickened nail plates and ridging sometimes develops. Intraepidermal constriction of sweat ducts often results in severe heat intolerance, while accumulation of scale in the external ear canals can lead to occlusion, bacterial colonization, and recurrent infections. In contrast to CIE, the epidermal proliferation rate is normal or only slightly elevated. While characteristic of CIE, these findings overlap with those seen in LI and other hyperprolif- erative epidermal disorders 79 . Epidemiology This rare disorder has an estimated incidence of 1 in 300 000 births and is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. HI has been reported in patients with a wide variety of ethnic backgrounds 80 . Clinical Features Individuals with HI are usually born prematurely (mean gestational age, 35 weeks) and may die within a few days or weeks because of respi- ratory insufficiency or sepsis 80 . Affected neonates are encased in a hard, armor-like, tremendously thickened stratum corneum that results in severe immobilization and restricts ventilation. Shortly after birth, the hyperkeratotic cast cracks and forms large, yellow, adherent plates separated by broad, deep, intensely red fissures ( Fig. 57.13 ). Increased transcutaneous loss of water and heat results in dehydration, electrolyte imbalances (e.g. hypernatremia), and temperature instability. The latter may impede recognition of skin infections or sepsis, which are promoted by the large fissures. The tautness of the skin results in marked eversion of the eyelids (ectropion) and lips (eclabium), rudimentary development of ear and nasal cartilage, and sometimes microcephaly, giving the face an extremely distorted appearance. The hands and feet are edematous and swollen, often covered by a mitten-like casing. Although the digits are well developed, autoamputation due to constricting skin bands occasionally occurs. Eyelashes and eyebrows are usually missing, while scalp hair may be present. Eclabium and taut facial skin prohibit effective suckling by the infant. Over the past two decades, improved postnatal care and oral retinoid therapy have led to prolonged survival in an increasing number of HI patients. More than half of affected individuals now live beyond the neonatal period, with the oldest HI patient to date being > 25 years of age 80 . All survivors develop a severe, exfoliative ichthyosiform eryth- roderma, and half have a painful PPK; dystrophic nails (e.g. small, thickened) and poor hair growth are also common. Complications in these patients include recurrent skin infections, reduced sweating with heat intolerance, ocular problems related to persistent ectropion, chronic constipation, vitamin D deficiency, anemia, arthralgias, arthritis, and joint contractures 80 . Hair follicles and sweat ducts have prominent hyperkeratotic plugging. Ultrastructural features include abnormal or missing lamellar bodies in the granular layer, absent extracellular lipid lamellae, and the presence of lipid inclusions or remnant organelles in the stratum corneum 44 . Netherton, an American dermatologist, subsequently discovered a hair shaft abnormality that he termed “bamboo hair” in a child with a CIE phenotype. Wilkinson et al. 83 delineated the triad of congenital ichthyosis, trichorrhexis invaginata, and atopy as “Netherton syndrome” in 1964. It was later recognized that this disorder encompasses different cutaneous presen- tations including ichthyosiform erythroderma, localized ichthyosis linearis circumflexa, and continuous skin peeling 84 . Epidemiology Netherton syndrome (NTS) is an autosomal recessive disorder that occurs worldwide, with a higher prevalence in inbred populations. Considering the phenotypic variability and clinical overlap with atopic dermatitis as well as other forms of ichthyosis, it has been estimated that the incidence of NTS might be as high as 1 in 50 000 84 . In one series, 18% of patients who presented with erythroderma during the neonatal period had NTS 85 . 18% of patients who presented with erythroderma during the neonatal period had NTS 85 . Pathogenesis NTS is caused by biallelic mutations in the serine protease inhibitor Kazal type 5 gene ( SPINK5 ) 86,87 . Approximately 100 SPINK5 mutations have been identified to date, with functional null alleles in ~65% of cases and missense mutations that compromise enzyme function in the remainder. SPINK5 encodes the multi-domain serine protease inhibitor LEKTI that is expressed in the lamellar granules of epithelia and lymphoid tissues. A lack of functional LEKTI leads to uncontrolled activity of serine proteases, and NTS patients have an up to five-fold increase of trypsin-like proteolytic activity in their stratum corneum 88 . This disturbs the regulation of lipid-processing enzymes, which are critical to proper formation of the lamellar lipid bilayer system in the stratum corneum. Hastened degradation of desmoglein 1 results in disinte- gration and shedding of horny cells, ultimately producing superficial clefts within the stratum corneum and severely disrupted skin barrier function 89 . In addition, LEKTI deficiency leads to a loss of crucial anti- inflammatory and antimicrobial mechanisms in the skin. Histochemical analysis of hair shafts in NTS demonstrates a reduced number of disulfide bonds, which is suggestive of diminished cross- linkage of hair keratin structures and a weaker coherence of cortical cells. Such focal softening of the hair shaft may allow intussusception of the distal shaft into the dilated proximal cup. Clinical Features NTS presents in most (but not all) patients at or soon after birth with CIE-like generalized erythroderma and scaling or with continuous peeling of the skin ( Fig. 57.14A ). A collodion membrane is not a feature of NTS. Approximately 20% of neonates develop potentially fatal complications such as hypernatremic dehydration, electrolyte imbalances, perturbed thermoregulation, failure to thrive, pneumonia, and sepsis. In patients with severe disease, generalized ichthyosis and erythroderma persist throughout life ( Fig. 57.14B–D ). The plaques are usually distributed on the trunk and extremities and change over time in size, shape, and location, reflecting the undulating course of NTS. The lesions are pruritic, and many patients develop eczematous plaques and/or lichenification in flexural sites, especially the wrists and antecubital and popliteal fossae. Scalp

There are often dense, almost band-like, lymphohistiocytic perivascular infiltrates in the papillary dermis. Subcorneal clefting, spongiosis, exocytosis, and Munro micro- abscesses can occur. Trichorrhexis invaginata, in which the distal hair shaft is telescoped into the proximal segment, is a highly character- istic light microscopic finding in clipped hairs; other hair shaft abnor- malities may also be evident (see above). A band-like pattern in hairs with polarized microscopy has also been described 95 . Trichoscopy of eyelashes and eyebrow hair may also reveal a “matchstick” or “golf tee” appearance. Ultrastructural abnormalities in the epidermal lipid system that are not present in other erythrodermic disorders have historically assisted in differentiating NTS from CIE and erythrodermic psoriasis. Premature secretion of lamellar body contents in the upper epidermis as well as the presence of intercellular electron-dense accumulations and abnormal splitting in the superficial stratum corneum are specific for NTS and represent indicators of accelerated desquamation 89,96 . Other variable ultrastructural abnormalities include round cytoplasmic inclusion bodies in the upper cell layers, a decreased tonofilament–desmosome system, and a lack of lamellar bodies. Other diagnostic tests Molecular testing of SPINK5 can facilitate diagnosis of NTS, and prenatal diagnosis may be performed in families with known SPINK5 mutations 87 . In addition, immunostaining of skin biopsy specimens with anti-LEKTI antibodies can be used to determine absence or aberrant distribution of LEKTI protein in the epidermis 97 . Differential Diagnosis During infancy, NTS often presents a diagnostic challenge due to its clinical overlap with CIE, erythrodermic psoriasis, and other primary immunodeficiencies. Although the presence of trichorrhexis invaginata and other hair shaft abnormalities can distinguish NTS from these conditions, characteristic hair shaft abnormalities may not be present at birth or in early infancy, and their detection requires repeated analysis of many hairs from different locations (e.g. scalp, eyebrows). Elevated serum IgE levels can also help to differentiate NTS from CIE and psoriasis. Autosomal dominant hyper-IgE syndrome (AD-HIES) also features elevated serum IgE levels in association with atopic-like derma- titis and recurrent skin and respiratory tract infections. However, AD-HIES presents with a neonatal papulopustular eruption rather than erythroderma, and eventually characteristic facial, dental, and skeletal anomalies that are not seen in NTS develop. Other primary immunodeficiencies characterized by erythematous, scaly skin and elevated IgE levels include Wiskott–Aldrich, Omenn, and IPEX ( i mmune dysregulation, p olyendocrinopathy, e nteropathy, X -linked) syndromes (see Ch. 60 ). In 1988, Rizzo et al. 104 discovered an underlying deficiency in the oxidation of long-chain fatty acids due to malfunction of the fatty alcohol ­dehydrogenase : fatty aldehyde dehydrogenase enzyme complex. Subsequently, De Laurenzi et al. 105 identified the underlying defect in the fatty aldehyde dehydro- genase gene ( ALDH3A2/FALDH ). It is most common in northern Sweden, where the carrier frequency is estimated to be 1.3% 103 . Pathogenesis SLS is caused by a deficiency of the microsomal fatty aldehyde dehydro- genase enzyme (FALDH) due to mutations in ALDH3A2 105 . More than 140 distinct mutations, including whole gene deletions, have been identified to date. Mutation analysis of ALDH3A2 has an almost 100% sensitivity in patients with a clinical diagnosis of SLS. A few mutations have a high allelic frequency in northern European and Middle Eastern populations due to a founder effect 106 . Clinical Features The hallmark of classic EKV is the coexistence of transient erythem- atous patches and more stable keratotic plaques, with one of these features frequently predominating. The erythematous component is most prevalent during childhood, but it later slowly subsides and can be absent in adults. More than 50% of patients present at birth or in the neonatal period, and 90% within the first year of life, with transient erythematous patches that have a random distribution. These lesions are well demarcated with a geographic, circinate, or target-like appearance, and they can coalesce into large figurate patches ( Fig. 57.20A ). Circinate or gyrate erythematous patches have been associated primarily with mutations in GJB4 , and this variant might be identical to the previously described “erythrokeratodermia en cocarde”. The erythema is of variable intensity and is sometimes surrounded by a blanched halo. Individual lesions usually persist for only minutes to hours, although they may last for days. In about 35% of patients, the erythema is preceded or accompanied by a burning sensation, which may cause discomfort. The remarkable variability in number, size, shape, location, and duration of erythematous patches is reflected in the name of the disease. Hyperkeratosis evolves simultaneously with or following the appearance of transient erythematous lesions. Sharply demarcated, yellow–brown to pink–brown thickened plaques with geographic borders progressively develop on the limbs, buttocks, and trunk in an almost symmetric distribution, descriptively termed progressive symmetric erythrokeratoderma (PSEK) ( Figs. 57.20B–D & 57.21 ). In approximately half of all patients, the thickening of the skin extends onto the palms and soles, while the flexures, face, and scalp tend to be spared. The surface can be ridged, verrucous, or velvety, and it may have collarette-like peeling or fine, adherent scales. Topical management with keratolytic agents (e.g. α -hydroxy acids, salicylic acid), urea, and/or retinoids (e.g. tretinoin, tazarotene) may be sufficient for mild disease. Systemic retinoids such as acitretin and isotretinoin are the treatment of choice for more extensive or severe EKVP. These agents often produce dramatic improvement or complete clearing of hyper- keratosis and significant reduction in the development of erythematous lesions, although the latter cannot be completely suppressed. The minimal maintenance dose for patients with EKVP is usually consid- erably lower than that required for other disorders of cornification 134 . Nevertheless, the use of retinoids should always be considered carefully, since chronic therapy is necessary to avoid relapse and long-term side effects, especially in children, may ensue. Of note, other forms of PSEK do not tend to respond as well to systemic retinoids. The red patches in EKVP often result in cosmetic concerns, which can be limited by using camouflaging makeup. Avoidance of sudden temperature changes, friction, and irritation may be beneficial. Subsequently, several case reports emerged in the literature using different names to describe the skin involvement, such as “atypical erythrokeratodermia with deafness”, “atypical ichthyosiform erythroderma”, and “ichthyosiform derma- tosis”. In 1981, Skinner summarized the previous reports and coined the acronym “KID” (keratitis–ichthyosis–deafness) syndrome 135 . Although several authors argued that the skin findings represent erythrokerato- derma rather than ichthyosis 84,136 , the widely-used acronym prevailed. KID syndrome presents an overlap between disorders of cornification and ectodermal dysplasias. Hystrix-like ichthyosis with deafness (HID) syndrome, which was first described as ichthyosis hystrix gravior type Rheydt, was originally considered to represent a distinct entity but is now classified as a clinical subtype of KID syndrome with more severe skin

and coined the acronym “KID” (keratitis–ichthyosis–deafness) syndrome 135 . Although several authors argued that the skin findings represent erythrokerato- derma rather than ichthyosis 84,136 , the widely-used acronym prevailed. KID syndrome presents an overlap between disorders of cornification and ectodermal dysplasias. Hystrix-like ichthyosis with deafness (HID) syndrome, which was first described as ichthyosis hystrix gravior type Rheydt, was originally considered to represent a distinct entity but is now classified as a clinical subtype of KID syndrome with more severe skin findings but less severe keratitis 29 . Epidemiology KID syndrome is a rare disorder, with ~300 published cases. Although it is primarily inherited in an autosomal dominant manner, > 90% of reported cases have been sporadic. Pathogenesis The vast majority of KID syndrome patients harbor mutations in GJB2 , which encodes connexin 26 (Cx26), a β -type gap junction protein 137 . In a single patient with features of KID syndrome and congenital atrichia, a causative mutation was identified in GJB6 (encoding connexin 30) 138 . All pathogenic GJB2 variants identified to date have been heterozygous missense substitutions; D50N is particularly common and is detected in > 80% of KID patients 137,139 . This latter mutation can also underlie KID syndrome associated with the follicular occlusion triad and hystrix- like-ichthyosis–deafness (HID) syndrome 29,139a . Other GJB2 mutations affecting the amino terminus or transmembrane domains of Cx26 have been associated with atypical clinical features such as a lack of PPK or corneal involvement, generalized spiny or verrucous keratoses, mucosal involvement, and the follicular occlusion triad. Two GJB2 mutations, G45E and A88V, cause a very severe neonatal form of KID syndrome that is typically fatal during infancy or early childhood 140 . In vivo and in vitro functional studies have shown that GJB2 mutations increase connexin hemichannel permeability, leading to ATP release, Ca 2 + overload, and cell death. Mutations altering the Cx26 amino terminus may also allow the formation of constitutively active heteromeric Cx43/Cx26 hemichannels, whereas gap junction channels are not functional 141 . Cx26 hemichannels containing the substitutions N14K, N14Y, A40V, and A88V were shown in vitro to abolish the sensi- tivity of Cx26 to CO 2 , providing a possible explanation for breathing abnormalities in patients with fatal KID syndrome 142 . Of note, somatic heterozygous GJB2 mutations have been identified in porokeratotic eccrine ostial and dermal duct nevi (PEODDN), nevoid spiny hyperkeratosis, and other epidermal nevus variants, which

Cx26 hemichannels containing the substitutions N14K, N14Y, A40V, and A88V were shown in vitro to abolish the sensi- tivity of Cx26 to CO 2 , providing a possible explanation for breathing abnormalities in patients with fatal KID syndrome 142 . Of note, somatic heterozygous GJB2 mutations have been identified in porokeratotic eccrine ostial and dermal duct nevi (PEODDN), nevoid spiny hyperkeratosis, and other epidermal nevus variants, which could be considered to represent mosaic forms of KID syndrome. If these mutations involve the gonads, their transmission to the offspring of such individuals can result in KID syndrome 143 . Revertant mosaicism has also been documented in a KID syndrome patient with progressive development of normal-appearing spots within erythrokeratodermic lesions 144 . Clinical Features There is considerable variability in the type, extent, and severity of cutaneous features in patients with KID syndrome ( Table 57.5 ). The first manifestation is often transient erythroderma at birth or during infancy. Later, most patients develop symmetrically distributed, well- demarcated, hyperkeratotic plaques with an erythematous base and a rough, ridged, or verrucous surface (i.e. erythrokeratoderma); psoria- siform plaques may also occur. The plaques favor the knees, elbows, and face, often with radial furrows around the mouth ( Fig. 57.22A,B ). The helices, scalp, groin, other skin folds, extremities, and, less often, trunk may be affected. A plaque-like or diffuse PPK with a grainy, reticulated, or stippled surface (reminiscent of Vohwinkel syndrome) is almost always present ( Fig. 57.22C,D ). Prominent follicular keratoses and cheilitis (especially perlèche) are common. Some patients develop diffuse thickening of the skin with a coarse, grainy appearance, which may also lead to deep facial furrows (see Fig. 57.22A ). Nails may be dystrophic and show leukonychia. Although most patients have normal hair, some affected individuals have lusterless hair or alopecia of the scalp, eyelashes, and eyebrows. Heat intolerance occasionally occurs. Another serious compli- cation is the development of SCC of the skin and oral mucosa, which occurs in 10%–20% of patients at a median age of 25 years, but as early as the first decade of life 136 . KID syndrome is also associated with increased susceptibility to mucocutaneous bacterial, viral, and fungal infections, in particular with Candida albicans . All KID patients have congenital sensorineural hearing impairment that (in contrast to the keratitis) is not progressive. Hearing loss is generally severe and bilateral, although some patients have unilateral or moderate hearing impairment. Approximately 95% of patients have ocular involvement, which typically presents at birth, during infancy, or in early childhood with photophobia and blepharitis. Vascularizing keratitis and conjunctivitis develop and worsen with age. Scarring and neovascularization often cause a progressive decline in visual acuity and may eventuate in blindness. Dental abnormalities may include small or absent teeth, delayed eruption, or excessive caries. The Dandy–Walker malformation of the cerebellar vermis and fourth ventricle, short heel cords, other joint contractures, facial dysmorphism, and developmental abnormalities have also been reported. A rare severe form of KID syndrome with a fatal outcome during infancy or early childhood presents with erythroderma and areas of massive, fissured hyperkeratosis on the scalp, periorificial skin, and extremities 140 . These patients also have a grainy PPK, atrichia, and nail dystrophy. Pathology Histology is not specific. Acanthosis and papillomatosis of the epidermis with basket-weave hyperkeratosis and follicular plugging are the most frequent features. Vacuolization of the cells in the granular layer has also been described. The corneal epithelium may be dyskeratotic, atrophic, or absent centrally, and Bowman’s membrane may be absent. The eccrine glands may be diminished in number and atrophic. In the inner ear, the organ of Corti is immature or atrophic. Other diagnostic tests Molecular genetic testing is available. A rapid molecular diagnosis can provide important prognostic information in infants with the severe fatal form of KID syndrome. Differential Diagnosis Autosomal recessive keratitis–ichthyosis–deafness syndrome results from biallelic mutations in AP1B1 (see Table 57.7 ). It encodes adaptor related protein complex 1 subunit β 1, which is involved in intracellular vesicular trafficking. Patients present by early infancy with ichthyo- siform erythroderma accompanied by ectropion, pruritus, sensorineural hearing loss, and failure to thrive. Photophobia and PPK develop over time, and additional features distinct from those of classic KID syndrome include chronic diarrhea, hepatomegaly, thrombocytopenia, low plasma levels of copper and ceruloplasmin, and large numbers of basophilic vesicles within the epidermis 145,146 . Autosomal recessive keratoderma–ichthyosis–deafness (ARKID) syndrome features diffuse PPK, mild generalized ichthyosis, intellectual disability, microcephaly, short stature, and occasionally hip dislocation, pancreatic insufficiency, or copper overload. Both ARKID and the more severe arthrogryposis– renal dysfunction–cholestasis (ARC) syndrome are caused by biallelic mutations in VPS33B (see Table 57.7 ). Treatment Skin treatment includes use of emollients and keratolytics; topical retinoids may be beneficial. Oral retinoid therapy (e.g. acitretin) yields mixed results: the hyperkeratosis may or may not respond, the PPK is recalcitrant, and ocular side effects may aggravate keratitis and neovas- cularization in some patients. Successful use of oral alitretinoin (not available in the US; see Ch. 126 ) for patients with recalcitrant disease has also been described 149 . Use of allele-specific small interfering RNA (siRNA) to inhibit expression of mutant GJB2 is under investigation in a human–murine chimeric skin graft model 150 . Gas-permeable contact lenses can improve vision in KID patients, while corneal transplants may have limited efficacy because of revas- cularization 136,151 . Hearing aids and cochlear implants have been used successfully. Mucocutaneous infections often require prolonged systemic therapy. Surveillance for the development of SCC and other tumors via periodic examination of the mucous membranes as well as the skin (including the scalp) is required. X-LINKED DOMINANT ICHTHYOSIFORM DISORDERS CHILD SYNDROME Synonyms:  Congenital hemidysplasia with ichthyosiform erythro- derma (or nevus) and limb defects  CHILD nevus History The first description of this condition in 1948 was followed by 17 case reports before Happle delineated the key features and proposed the acronym CHILD syndrome in 1980 152 . Epidemiology This is a rare X-linked dominant disorder that occurs primarily in girls and women, as it is generally lethal in affected male embryos. Very few affected boys have been reported, one of whom had a normal karyotype and a mosaic NSDHL mutation 153 . Pathogenesis CHILD syndrome is a disorder of lipid metabolism that results in disturbed cholesterol biosynthesis. Inactivating mutations in NSDHL , which encodes the enzyme 3 β -hydroxysteroid-dehydrogenase, were initially identified in five families with right-sided skin and skeletal involvement 154 ; such mutations were subsequently described in additional patients with left-sided involvement. The striking hemilateral phenotype is postulated to result from skewed X-inactivation and deficient sonic hedgehog signaling in the cells expressing the X-chromosome with an NSDHL mutation, resulting in selection against these cells on one side of the body. This hypothesis reflects the role hedgehog signaling plays in conferring left–right asymmetry during embryogenesis. Cholesterol has critical functions during mammalian development, including hedgehog signaling, and inborn errors in cholesterol biosynthesis cause several other malfor- mation syndromes. Clinical Features CHILD syndrome classically presents at birth or in the neonatal period with a striking unilateral distribution of erythema and thickened skin with a waxy surface or yellowish adherent scale ( Fig. 57.23A ). The erythema most often involves the right side of the body and is sharply demarcated at the anterior and posterior midline of the trunk. The face is typically spared. Occasionally, there is partial spontaneous resolution or periodic exacerbation of the cutaneous inflammation 152 . Parakeratotic nuclei characteristically retain a round shape 155 , and numerous vacuoles are present within the cells of the lower stratum corneum. Ultrastructural abnormalities include abundant pale-staining mitochondria, cytoplasmic glycogen, lipid retention in the stratum corneum, and altered intracellular and intercellular lamellar granule content. CONRADI–HÜNERMANN–HAPPLE SYNDROME Synonyms:  X-linked dominant chondrodysplasia punctata  Chondrodysplasia punctata type 2 (CDPX2)  Conradi–Hünermann syndrome  Happle syndrome History In 1971, the dominant Conradi–Hünermann type of chondrodysplasia was differentiated from the autosomal recessive rhizomelic form. Happle subsequently reviewed the literature and established that the Conradi– Hünermann type has an X-linked dominant mode of inheritance 160 . Epidemiology Conradi–Hünermann–Happle (CHH) syndrome is a rare X-linked dominant disorder that occurs primarily in girls and women. It is lethal in male embryos outside the setting of an XXY karyotype or mosaicism due to a postzygotic mutation in EBP . However, an X-linked recessive multiple congenital anomaly syndrome (MEND – male EBP disorder with neurologic defects) in which male patients often die by early childhood and female carriers are unaffected has been described with less severe germline mutations in EBP 161 . Pathogenesis Conradi–Hünermann–Happle syndrome results from a cholesterol biosynthesis defect caused by mutations in EBP , which encodes emopamil-binding protein (EBP) 162,163 . The resulting deficiency of EBP, a widely expressed integral membrane protein with Δ 8- Δ 7-sterol isomerase activity, leads to accumulation of 8-dehydrocholesterol and 8(9)cholestenol 163 , which can be detected in plasma, scales, and cultured fibroblasts. However, levels of the end product cholesterol sulfate are normal in plasma and fibroblasts because of X-inactivation 162,163 . Impaired cholesterol synthesis during a critical period of mammalian development is thought to be responsible for the phenotype. Hemizygous missense mutations affecting the first transmembrane domain of EBP, presumably with less deleterious effects on enzyme function, have been identified in boys with MEND syndrome 161 . Clinical Features CHH is a multisystem disorder that involves primarily the skin, eyes, and skeletal system. Clinical presentations in female patients are variable as they depend on the pattern of X-chromosome inactivation in relevant tissues. At birth, most CHH syndrome patients have generalized erythema with thick, adherent, feathery scale; streaks and whorls of hyperkeratosis following the lines of Blaschko are often observed ( Fig. 57.24A ). Molecular analysis of EBP is available. Differential Diagnosis Stippled epiphyses during infancy and asymmetric limb shortening are also seen in girls with CHILD syndrome, but the skin involvement usually shows striking lateralization and does not fade completely. However, some overlap in the clinical findings of CHILD and CHH syndromes is not surprising, since both represent disorders of choles- terol biosynthesis (see Table 57.6 ). Ichthyosis linearis circumflexa in NTS is readily distinguished by its double-edged scale, and the lesions do not follow the lines of Blaschko. Cutaneous manifestations in CIE are more generalized. Hyper- and hypopigmentation in “pigmentary mosaicism”, incontinentia pigmenti, and epidermal nevi (including epidermolytic variants) follow the lines of Blaschko but lack follicular atrophoderma. Treatment Although the erythema gradually resolves, residual mild scaling may benefit from application of emollients and products containing urea or a keratolytic agent. Orthopedic and ophthalmologic care are essential. In older children, hyperkeratosis is largely replaced by linear or patchy follicular atrophoderma with dilated follicular openings, ice-pick-like scars, and mild residual scaling. The atrophoderma is most pronounced on the forearms and dorsal hands, whereas the palms and soles are usually spared. Hyper- or hypopigmentation along the lines of Blaschko may coexist separately from atrophodermic areas 160 . Scalp involvement results in patchy scarring alopecia. In addition, hair may be sparse, coarse, or lusterless. Nail changes include onychoschizia and flattening of the nail plate, while teeth are normal. Skeletal anomalies include asymmetric shortening of the proximal limbs, kyphoscoliosis, frontal bossing, malar hypoplasia, a flat nasal bridge, and a short neck. Widespread premature calcifications manifest as stippling (chondrodysplasia punctata) of the long bone epiphyses, tracheal cartilage, and vertebrae. These can be detected by fetal ultrasound in severe cases or postnatally in radiographs during infancy ( Fig. 57.24B ), but they are not apparent once bone maturation progresses (after ~9 months of age). Unilateral, asymmetric, and/or sectorial cataracts, which are present at birth or develop within the first months of life, are the most common ocular abnormality and may be accompanied by microphthalmia or microcornea. Less common features include congenital heart defects, sensorineural hearing loss, CNS malformations, and congenital renal anomalies. Attenuated cases with characteristic skin findings but mild or no associated systemic anomalies have been observed 164 . Psychomotor development and life expectancy are normal. Boys with the allelic X-linked recessive MEND syndrome have a collodion-like presentation at birth and evolution to a variable ichthyosis phenotype 161 . Additional features include cardiovascular, craniofacial, and skeletal anomalies as well as the Dandy–Walker malformation, hydrocephalus, cataracts, and cryptorchidism. Pathology Hyperkeratosis with focal parakeratosis is common and most prominent in follicular ostia, where dystrophic calcification may be observed within keratotic plugs. The granular layer is diminished and keratinocytes contain small vacuoles with needle-like calcium inclusions on electron microscopy. Many hereditary forms of PPK do not develop until the first months or years of life. This was followed by Unna’s description of a clinically identical, autosomal dominant PPK in two families. Although “Unna–Thost type” has been used to designate non-epidermolytic PPK (NEPPK), in 1992, Küster et al. 7 reviewed the family described by Thost and found the histologic features of epidermolytic hyperkeratosis, which characterize the “Vörner type” of PPK. Subsequently, after keratin mutations were reported in epidermolytic PPK (EPPK), identical mutations were found in the descendants of the family studied by Thost 8 . This confusion underscores the need for careful histologic examination and sometimes multiple biopsy specimens to identify epidermolytic hyperkeratosis. Epidemiology EPPK is likely the most common form of diffuse keratoderma, with an estimated incidence of ≥ 4.4 per 100 000 in Northern Ireland 9 . Pathogenesis Mutations in KRT1 and KRT9 (encoding keratins 1 and 9) underlie diffuse EPPK. The expression of keratin 9 is limited to the suprabasal cell layers of palmar and plantar skin. Such mutations are highly disruptive to keratin filament assembly, causing tonofilament clumping and cytolysis that result in blistering as well as hyperkeratosis. Within palmoplantar skin, keratin 9 is thought to partner with keratin 1. Of note, mutations in KRT1 and KRT10 are associated with epidermolytic ichthyosis (EI), in which epidermolytic hyperkeratosis is seen histologically (see Ch. 57 ). PPK in EI is predictive of a mutation in KRT1 , which is the only type II keratin expressed in palmoplantar skin. In contrast, EI due to KRT10 mutations rarely has involvement of palmoplantar skin, likely reflecting compensation by keratin 9, which is also a type I keratin. The majority of mutations in EI patients are in the critical 1 A and 2B domains of the keratin molecule 10 . However, when keratin 1 defects underlie diffuse EPPK alone, including the “tono­tubular“ subtype, the mutations are typically in the beginning of the 1B domain 11 . Although KRT1 mutations have been reported in some families with the Greither type of EPPK, other Greither variants with NEPPK not associated with KRT1 mutations have also been described. Of note, KRT1 mutations have also been identified in patients with focal PPK (see below). Clinical features The palmoplantar skin is initially red, followed by the appearance of thick, yellow hyperkeratosis by 3–4 years of age. In adults, there is confluent hyperkeratosis with a smooth, waxy surface and sharply demarcated erythematous border, sparing the dorsal aspects of the palms and soles ( Fig. 58.5 ). Blistering and fissuring are not common but may occur during childhood or during oral retinoid therapy. Knuckle pads and thickened nails are occasionally present 2,12 , and digital or palmar constriction has been described 13 . Disabling pain, especially of the palms, can occur in the “tonotubular” EPPK subtype 11 . The Greither type (PPK transgrediens and progrediens) presents with limited trans- gredient lesions, e.g. overlying the Achilles tendon, elbows, and knees. Pathology EPPK shows the typical pattern of epidermolytic hyperkeratosis, which is characterized by vacuolated suprabasal keratinocytes with round or ovoid eosinophilic inclusions that represent large tonofil- ament aggregates at an ultrastructural level 14 . In the “tonotubular” subtype, electron microscopy shows whorls of keratin containing tubular structures 11 . Histologic findings also include coarse kerato- hyalin granules, acanthosis, and marked orthohyperkeratosis. Intraepidermal blistering and a mild superficial dermal inflammatory infiltrate may result from keratinocyte cytolysis ( Fig. 58.6A ). The findings of epidermolytic hyperkeratosis are often subtle and patchy, requiring a careful search and often multiple biopsy specimens to enable their identification. Connexin Connexon Homomeric Heteromeric Homomeric Heterotypic Homotypic Heteromeric Homotypic Gap junction channels Gap junction plaque Intercellular gap Cell 1 Cell 2 CONNEXIN CHANNELS AND GAP JUNCTION PLAQUE Intercellular channel plaque. Gap junctions are specialized transmem- brane channels that connect the cytoplasm of neighboring cells, facilitating cell-to-cell communi- cation. The status of the channels (i.e. open or closed) is controlled by mechanisms, including voltage, calcium concentration, pH, and phosphorylation. Each gap junction channel is composed of integral membrane proteins called connexins. The half-life of each connexin is short (i.e. hours), which results in a constant state of assembly and degradation of channels. Different connexins are expressed in a tissue- and differentiation-specific manner as well as in response to stimuli. Six connexin molecules oligomerize to form a connexon hemichannel with a central pore that has a maximum diameter of 2 nm. Connexons may be homomeric if all the participating molecules are of the same connexin species, or heteromeric if they differ. Connexons of adjacent cells dock in the intercellular gap to form a complete gap junction intercellular channel. Mechanical debridement can be performed with a blade, foot file, or pumice stone and followed by application of a keratolytic agent to help avoid fissure formation. Options for keratolytic therapy include 50% propylene glycol in water under plastic occlusion several nights per week, lactic acid- and urea-containing creams and lotions, and salicylic acid 4%–6% in petrolatum; the latter should not be applied to large areas in young children to avoid salicylism from systemic absorption (see Ch. 129 ). Oral retinoids may improve the hyperkeratosis, but even low doses can lead to excessive peeling and increased fragility of volar skin in EPPK 15 . Topical calcipotriene (calcipotriol) has reportedly been helpful 16 . Genome editing utilizing CRISPR/Cas9 technology was shown to decrease expression of mutant keratin 9 and lead to pheno- typic improvement in an EPPK-like transgenic mouse model 17 . Epidemiology and pathogenesis An autosomal dominant form of NEPPK that was initially described in families from Bothnia in Northern Sweden and the United Kingdom is due to heterozygous missense mutations in AQP5 , which encodes aquaporin 5. Aquaporins are transmembrane proteins that allow the osmotic movement of water across the cell membrane. Aquaporin 5 is expressed by keratinocytes in the granular layer, and the gain-of- function mutations that cause Bothnian-type NEPPK lead to increased keratinocyte water uptake rather than transepidermal water loss 18 . The form of NEPPK described by Kimonis is caused by a heterozygous mutation in a highly conserved lysine residue in the V1 domain of keratin 1 that does not result in epidermolytic hyperkeratosis 19 . Nagashima -type NEPPK, an autosomal recessive disorder most commonly observed in Asians and also described in Finns, is caused by biallelic nonsense mutations in SERPINB7 . More recently, biallelic mutations in SERPINA12 were found to underlie another autosomal recessive form of NEPPK. These genes encode ser ine p rotease in hibitor family B member 7 and family A member 12, respectively, which are thought to regulate proteolytic activity in the skin 25,26 . Mal de Meleda is an autosomal recessive condition that was first described in inhabitants of the island of Mljet (Meleda) off the Dalmatian coast. It is caused by biallelic mutations in SLURP1 ( s ecreted l eukocyte antigen-6/ u rokinase-type plasminogen activator related p rotein 1 ), which is expressed in the granular layer of the epidermis 27 . SLURP1 acts as a ligand of the α 7-nicotinic acetylcholine receptor and plays a role in epidermal differentiation. Heterozygous female carriers may have a mild clinical phenotype. Clinical features The clinical findings and time course of the different types of NEPPK are overall similar to those of EPPK (see above). The hyperkeratosis is variably thick and hyperhidrosis is common, with frequent dermatophyte infec- tions and pitted keratolysis. The Bothnian, Nagashima, and SERPINA12 - related types feature transgrediens and a white spongy appearance upon exposure to water 18,28 . Acrokeratoelastoidosis-like papules have been reported in Bothnian-type PPK as has acral melanoma in Japanese patients with Nagashima-type PPK; the latter is also characterized by “soft” hyper- keratosis, prominent erythema, and a nonprogressive course 28 . Fungal superinfection is common, and hyper- keratosis of the fingers may lead to sclerodactyly and digital constric- tions (pseudoainhum). The elbows, knees, wrists, and ankles as well as the dorsal surfaces of the hands and feet can be involved, and the nails show thickening, koilonychia, and subungual hyperkeratosis. Angular cheilitis and involvement of the lips and perioral skin may be observed 21,29 . Hyperpigmented macules, melanoma, and Bowen disease within the keratotic areas have been reported 30 . Differential diagnosis In addition to diffuse EPPK, diagnostic considerations may include aquagenic PPK, acral peeling skin syndrome, and keratolytic winter erythema. Pathology Histologically, palmoplantar skin shows orthohyperkeratosis, hyper- granulosis or normogranulosis, and acanthosis ( Fig. 58.6B ). A moderate perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate may be present. In Mal de Meleda, papillomatosis is a characteristic finding. PAS staining should be performed to exclude infection by dermatophytes. Management Keratolytic therapy may be helpful, such as 5%–10% salicylic acid in white soft paraffin, or 5%–6% salicylic acid in 70% propylene glycol gel; occlusion for a few nights per week enhances efficacy, and mechanical debridement can also be performed. However, salicylic acid should not be applied to large areas in young children. Low-dose acitretin (0.2–0.5 mg/kg daily) may be considered, especially for patients with functional impairment. Fungal superinfection and bacterial overgrowth should be treated. Responses to oral erythromycin and topical tacro- limus have been described in the Bothnian and Nagashima types, respec- tively 31,32 . Nonsense-suppression (readthrough) therapy with topical gentamicin has been shown to reduce hyperkeratosis in Nagashima-type PPK 33 . Excision of hyperkeratotic skin with split-thickness skin grafting represents an option to relieve functional impairment. Keratolytic winter erythema (KWE) is an autosomal dominant disorder of cornification characterized by recurrent erythema followed by centrifugal peeling on the palms ( Fig. 58.8 ), soles, occasionally the extremities, and rarely elsewhere; episodes typically occur during the winter (see Table 57.8 ). The term “Oudtshoorn disease” derives from a town in South Africa, where the condition was first described and is common due to a founder effect. KWE is caused by genomic duplica- tions in a noncoding region containing an enhancer element for the cathepsin B gene ( CTSB ), which lead to upregulation of this cysteine protease that functions in keratinocyte homeostasis 34 . In addition, a missense gain-of-function CTSB mutation was found to underlie an autosomal dominant form of diffuse transgredient PPK with an erythematous border and associated peeling 35 . Histologically, KWE demonstrates ballooning degeneration in the upper epidermis associated with eosinophilic granular material, absence of the granular layer, parakeratosis, and variable spongiosis 34 . Regenerative basal cell hyperplasia may be evident. In CTSB -related PPK, orthohyperkeratosis and areas of intra- and subcorneal separation have been described 35 . Other features include flexion deformity of the fingers with associated sclerosis and parallel linear arrays of keratotic papules in the flexural areas of the extremities. Huriez Syndrome Synonyms:  Palmoplantar keratoderma with scleroatrophy  Sclerotylosis This rare autosomal dominant disease is caused by mutations in SMARCAD1 ( S WI/SNF-related, m atrix-associated a ctin-dependent r egulator of c hromatin, subfamily a , containing D EAD/H box 1 ) that lead to haploinsufficiency for a skin-specific isoform with a role in the repair of double-strand DNA breaks 59 . Diffuse scleroatrophy of the hands typically becomes evident during infancy, and there is eventual development of sclerodactyly and absent dermatoglyphs. The mild PPK presents as diffuse parchment-like skin on the palms and, to a lesser degree, the soles; circumscribed hyperkeratosis over pressure points may develop during adulthood. Hypoplastic nail changes (e.g. thinning, longi- tudinal ridging, fissuring) are also seen 60 . The risk of developing SCC in areas of atrophic skin is increased by ≥ 100-fold, and early metastasis often occurs 61 . The differential diagnosis may include Kindler epidermolysis bullosa, PPK with sex reversal and SCC, and dyskeratosis congenita. Histologic features of the keratoderma include orthohyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and hypergranulosis. A characteristic finding is almost complete absence of Langerhans cells in the affected skin. Palmoplantar Keratoderma With Sex Reversal and Squamous Cell Carcinoma This rare autosomal recessive syndrome, initially described in several consanguineous Italian kindreds, is due to mutations in the R-spondin 1 gene ( RSPO1 ), which encodes a protein that activates β -catenin signaling and has an important role in gonadal development 62,63 . In addition to a diffuse NEPPK that develops during infancy, there is a marked predisposition to the development of acral SCC. Affected individuals with a 46,XX genotype have either: (1) a male phenotype (i.e. female-to-male sex reversal), often associated with hypospadias and hypogonadism; or (2) ambiguous genitalia, sometimes with hermaph- roditism (existence of both male and female gonadal structures). Other manifestations include sclerodactyly with variable cutaneous atrophy resembling Huriez syndrome, ichthyosiform scale on the lower legs, nail dystrophy (e.g. hypoplasia, longitudinal ridging, skin growth over the nail plate), periodontitis leading to early loss of teeth, ocular anomalies (e.g. cataracts, colobomas), and microcephaly 62,63 . Clouston Syndrome Synonym:  Hidrotic ectodermal dysplasia 2 Clouston syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by missense mutations in the gap junction β 6 gene ( GJB6 ), which encodes connexin 30 64 . The dysfunctional connexin 30 disturbs cell–cell communication in epithelial cells. Although first reported in a large French-Canadian kindred, Clouston syndrome has also been described in a variety of other ethnic groups. This condition features diffuse PPK in conjunction with hypotrichosis and nail dystrophy 65 , thereby qualifying as an ectodermal dysplasia (see Ch. 63 ). The PPK initially develops over pressure points and then becomes diffuse, increasing in severity with age. In addition, thickened skin with a “pebbled” appearance is often evident on the dorsal aspects of the digits, knees, and elbows ( Fig. 58.11 ). Small papules in a grid-like array that corresponds to eccrine acrosyringia may be seen, especially on the distal digits where the dermatoglyphs are most prominent. Progressive hypotrichosis that can eventuate in complete alopecia affects the scalp, eyebrows, eyelashes, and axillary and genital regions; the hair is typically wiry, brittle, and pale. The nails, which may be normal or milky white at birth, gradually become thickened and dystrophic, displaying short nail plates that are easily shed (see Fig. 58.11 ). The nail abnormalities may mimic those of pachyonychia congenita or other syndromes of “hair–nail hypoplasia” 66 . Histologic evaluation of thickened palms and soles shows ortho­ hyperkeratosis with a normal granular layer. Papular lesions may demonstrate proliferation of eccrine ductal structures within a fibro- vascular stroma (eccrine syringofibroadenomas). Ultrastructural exami- nation of the hair shows disorganization of the hair fibers, with a loss of the hair shaft cuticle. GENODERMATOSES Odonto-onycho-dermal dysplasia encompasses a diverse group of autosomal recessive disorders caused by mutations in WNT10A , which encodes a signaling molecule with a critical role in the devel- opment of ectodermal appendages 67 (see Fig. 55.6 ). The clinical features include various combinations of diffuse PPK, facial telangiectasias or reticulate erythema, dental anomalies (e.g. hypodontia, small teeth), nail dystrophy, and hypotrichosis (see Table 63.13 ) 68 . Patients with Schöpf–Schulz–Passarge syndrome also develop hidrocystomas of the eyelids and other adnexal tumors (e.g. poromas, tumors of the follicular infundibulum) during adulthood 69 . Histologic examination of the PPK demonstrates eccrine syringofibroadenomas. Olmsted Syndrome Synonym:  Mutilating PPK with periorificial keratotic plaques Autosomal dominant and the less common autosomal recessive variants of Olmsted syndrome are caused by different gain-of- function mutations in the t ransient r eceptor p otential v anilloid 3 gene ( TRPV3 ) 70,71 . TRP cation-selective ion channels are involved in epidermal differentiation, hair growth, and the modulation of inflammation, pain, and pruritus. The X-linked recessive variant of Olmsted syndrome, which presents with total alopecia and severe nail dystrophy, results from specific mutations in the m embrane- b ound t ranscription factor p eptidase s ite 2 gene ( MBTPS2 ). The zinc metal- loprotease encoded by this gene is essential for cholesterol homeostasis and endoplasmatic reticulum stress response 72 . MBTPS2 mutations also underlie IFAP syndrome (ichthyosis follicularis with atrichia and photophobia) and KFSD (keratosis follicularis spinulosa decalvans) (see Chs. 38 and 57 ). In addition, heterozygous mutations in PERP (p53 effector related to PMP22), a component of desmosomes, underlie an autosomal dominant form of Olmsted syndrome 73 . Olmsted syndrome features a sharply defined, diffuse PPK with an erythematous border, and progression over time leads to flexion contrac- tures and digital constriction or autoamputation. Erythema and warty hyperkeratosis develop in the perioral and perianal regions as well as in other intertriginous sites 74 , resulting in pain and pruritus 75 . Keratoses in linear streaks and with a perifollicular distribution also appear in the flexures of the extremities 76 . Additional findings may include alopecia, blonde curly hair ( PERP -related form), nail dystrophy, oral involvement (e.g. keratotic plaques, periodontal disease), corneal dysplasia, eryth- romelalgia, deafness, and joint laxity 76 . Keratoses in linear streaks and with a perifollicular distribution also appear in the flexures of the extremities 76 . Additional findings may include alopecia, blonde curly hair ( PERP -related form), nail dystrophy, oral involvement (e.g. keratotic plaques, periodontal disease), corneal dysplasia, eryth- romelalgia, deafness, and joint laxity 76 . Recurrent skin infections are common, and the development of SCC and melanoma within areas of keratoderma has been reported 77,78 . The differential diagnosis may include Mal de Meleda, Vohwinkel syndrome, KDSR -related erythrokeratoderma (see Ch. 57 ), pachyo- nychia congenita, acrodermatitis enteropathica, chronic mucocuta- neous candidiasis, and (early on or in milder cases) psoriasis. Histology of affected skin demonstrates acanthosis with orthohyperkeratosis and parakeratosis, papillomatosis, and a perivascular inflammatory infil- trate; an increased number of mast cells has also been observed 79 . There are reports of dramatic improvement of the PPK in patients with gain-of-function mutations in TRPV3 following administration of the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) inhibitor erlotinib 80 . This targeted therapy is based upon the observation that EGFR activation can lead to enhanced TRPV3 activity. Systemic treatment with a retinoid or sirolimus and excision of hyperkeratotic areas with skin grafting may also be of benefit 81 . Papillon–Lefèvre and Haim–Munk Syndromes Papillon–Lefèvre syndrome is an autosomal recessive condition caused by mutations in CTSC which encodes cathepsin C, a lysosomal cysteine protease that activates serine proteases found in inflammatory cells as well as the skin 82,83 . This disorder is characterized by a diffuse, trans- gredient PPK with associated erythema. Pseudoainhum and hyper- keratotic psoriasiform plaques on the elbows and knees often develop. An additional feature is periodontitis with onset during childhood, which leads to premature loss of teeth. There is a predisposition to pyogenic infections of the skin and internal organs, including hepatic abscesses 84 .
