Laboratory Findings and Pathology HIES patients have markedly elevated serum levels of polyclonal IgE, usually peaking at > 2000 IU/ml and sometimes declining during adulthood. Patients develop particularly high levels of anti-staphylo- coccal and anti-candidal IgE antibodies and often have immediate wheal- and-flare reactions to a variety of foods and environmental allergens. Many affected individuals also have eosinophilia of the peripheral blood and sputum. Cell-mediated immunity is often abnormal, as manifested by anergy to skin testing and impaired in vitro lymphoproliferative responses to specific antigens. Serum levels of IgG, IgA and IgM are usually normal in STAT3-HIES, as are lymphocyte subsets. In contrast, DOCK8 deficiency represents a combined immunodeficiency that is characterized by lymphopenia with a paucity of CD4 + T cells > CD8 + T cells > B cells, low IgM levels, and variable IgG levels as well as elevated IgE levels and peripheral eosinophilia 91,92 . The infantile papulopustular eruption of STAT3-HIES is charac- terized histologically by eosinophilic folliculitis, eosinophilic spongiosis, and a superficial and deep perivascular infiltrate with abundant eosinophils 101,102 . Diagnosis Current diagnostic criteria for STAT3-HIES include an IgE level > 1000 IU/ml and a weighted score of five clinical features ( Table 60.14 ) 105 ; these characteristics plus a lack of Th17 cells or the detection of a heterozygous STAT3 mutation allow for a probable or definitive diagnosis, respectively. HIES must be differentiated from a number of other disorders that can feature elevated IgE levels and a cutaneous eruption, including atopic dermatitis, Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome, Netherton syndrome, Omenn syndrome, DiGeorge syndrome, IPEX syndrome, ARPC1B (actin-related protein 2/3 complex subunit 1B) deficiency, Loeys– Dietz syndrome, and GVHD. Atopic dermatitis and Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome are most easily confused with HIES because they present with eczematous dermatitis and staphylococcal infections. However, the development of cold abscesses, recurrent pneumonia, coarse facial features, and osteopenia help to differentiate STAT3-HIES from these disorders, and platelet abnormalities distinguish Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome as well as ARPC1B syndrome. In a series of pediatric patients who had a serum IgE level of > 2000 IU/ml, 69% (48/70) had atopic dermatitis and only 8% (6/70) had HIES; no correlation was observed between the IgE level and diagnosis of HIES 106 . Panhypogammaglobulinemia has a prevalence of 1 in 25 000, with X-linked agammaglobulinemia 102 (affecting primarily boys) and common variable immunodeficiency 108 (CVID; no sexual predilection) representing the most frequent forms. CVID has its clinical onset at a mean age of 30 years whereas X-linked agammaglobulinemia often manifests during the first few years of life, after levels of maternal antibodies wane at ~6 months of age. Approximately 15% of patients with CVID have family members with selective IgA deficiency. The pathogenesis and clinical features of immunoglobulin deficiencies are presented in Fig. 60.10 and Table 60.15 108–115 . The treatment of hypogammaglobulinemia is antibody replacement by IVIg or subcutaneous immunoglobulins and antibiotic therapy for infec- tions 116 . However, IVIg and other blood products containing IgA should be avoided in individuals with profound IgA deficiency, who may develop anti-IgA antibodies; fatal anaphylactic reactions have been reported. Recalcitrant non-infectious cutaneous and extracutaneous granulomas in patients with CVID may respond to treatment with TNF inhibitors. Female carriers of X-linked agammaglobulinemia may be detected via examination of B cell X-inactivation patterns, which show skewing towards cells with inactivation of the mutated X chromosome. DNA-based prenatal diagnosis is possible when the genetic defect in affected family members has been identified. This β 2 -subunit can be linked to different α -chains to form distinct cell surface glycoproteins including: (1) lymphocyte function antigen 1 (LFA-1 – CD18 paired with CD11a); (2) complement receptor type 3 (CR3/iC3 b receptor/Mac-1 – CD18 paired with CD11b); and (3) p150,95 (complement receptor type 4 – CD18 paired with CD11c). It is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the fermitin family member 3 gene ( FERMT3 ) that encodes kindlin-3, an effector of integrin activation in hematopoietic cells 124 . Clinical Features The most common manifestation of LAD is gingivitis with periodon- titis, which often leads to tooth loss and alveolar bone resorption and is thought to be related to excessive production of interleukin-17. Minor injuries to the skin may rapidly expand to form large, chronic ulcerations that can resemble “burnt out” pyoderma gangrenosum ( Fig. 60.13 ). Poor wound healing also results in paper-thin, atrophic scars. A history of delayed separation of the umbilical stump represents a clue to the diagnosis. Patients with LAD develop recurrent otitis media, pneumonia, and cutaneous infections caused by pyogenic bacteria. The latter often present as cellulitis and necrotic abscesses with relatively little production of purulent material, typically located in the perianal area or on the face. Life-threatening bacterial, fungal, or (less frequently) viral infections may also occur. More than three-quarters of patients with severe LAD-I ( < 1% of normal CD18 levels) die within the first 5 years of life, whereas approximately half of patients with moderate disease (1%–10% of normal CD18 levels) live to age 30 years 122 . Additional clinical manifestations of LAD-II include intellectual disability, microcephaly, hypotonia, short stature, and facial dysmor- phism 123 . Patients with LAD-III often present with a bleeding tendency as well as variable osteopetrosis and hepatosplenomegaly. Dermal hematopoiesis with a “blueberry muffin” appearance secondary to myelodysplastic syndrome has been described in infants and children with LAD-III 125 . Pathology Individuals with LAD have marked peripheral blood neutrophilia (5–20 times normal levels). Although cutaneous ulcerations may resemble pyoderma gangrenosum clinically, histologic examination reveals a relative paucity of tissue neutrophils . Flow cytometric analysis reveals markedly decreased leukocyte CD18 expression in individuals with LAD-I. Patients with LAD-II have the Bombay red blood cell type due to a lack of the H blood group antigen, and those with LAD-III have abnormal platelet aggregation due to defective activation of β 3 -integrin and less often have anemia. Meticulous dental hygiene is important in reducing the severity of the periodontitis. Granulocyte transfusions have potential benefit in LAD-I and -III, and oral administration of fucose may improve immune function in patients with LAD-II 123 . SEVERE COMBINED IMMUNODEFICIENCY AND OMENN SYNDROME Synonyms:  Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) syndrome  Severe mixed immunodeficiency syndrome  Glanzmann–Riniker syndrome  Alymphocytosis  Thymic alymphoplasia Key features  Group of conditions characterized by defective function of both cell-mediated and humoral immunity  Recurrent infections, diarrhea, and failure to thrive within the first 3–6 months of life  Risk of GVHD, especially from unirradiated blood products  Lack of lymphoid tissue Introduction Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) is a heterogeneous group of disorders that share clinical manifestations related to defective function of both cell-mediated and humoral immunity 128–130 ( Table 60.16 ). Epidemiology SCID occurs in ~1 in 50 000 live births 131 , and three-quarters of affected patients are boys. Approximately 40% of cases have X-linked recessive inheritance, primarily due to defects in the gene encoding the common γ ( γ c ) chain of the IL-2 receptor, while the remainder are autosomal recessive. Other relatively frequent causes of autosomal recessive SCID include deficiencies of adenosine deaminase (ADA), the IL-7 receptor, or JAK3, each accounting for 5%–15% of cases 131 . Cutaneous findings may also resemble lichen planus, acrodermatitis enteropathica, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, ichthyosiform erythro- derma, and systemic sclerosis. Extensive eczematous dermatitis or exfoli- ative erythroderma, often associated with diffuse alopecia, may also occur in infants with Omenn syndrome (RAG1 or RAG2) , which also features lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, chronic diarrhea, peripheral eosinophilia, leukocytosis, and elevated IgE levels in the setting of SCID (see Tables 10.2 and 60.16 ). Of note, extensive cutaneous and extracuta- neous granulomas (including destructive midfacial lesions) can develop in children with hypomorphic RAG1 or RAG2 mutations ( Fig. 60.14 ). Recurrent infections, chronic diarrhea, and failure to thrive are apparent within the first few months of life. Recurrent infections, chronic diarrhea, and failure to thrive are apparent within the first few months of life. Common early infections include mucocutaneous candidiasis, persistent viral gastroenteritis, and pneumonias due to bacteria, viruses, or P. jirovecii . Cutaneous infections are most often caused by C. albicans, S. aureus , and Str. pyogenes . Despite recurrent infections, patients with SCID typically lack tonsillar buds and palpable lymphoid tissue. SCID due to ADA deficiency is associated with an increased risk of developing dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans, often multiple and morpheaform, during the first two decades of life 130 . Laboratory Findings and Pathology Nearly all patients with SCID have a profound T cell deficiency and a low absolute lymphocyte count. Patients are further classified by the results of fluorescent activated cell sorter (FACS) analysis into those with and without B lymphocytes and NK cells. The laboratory abnor- malities observed in different types of SCID are noted in Table 60.16 . Certain forms of SCID show distinctive radiographic manifestations; for example, patients with ADA deficiency demonstrate cupping and flaring of the costochondral junction on chest radiographs. Flow cytometric analysis of peripheral blood mononuclear cells with antibodies directed against a particular protein that is missing from the cell surface (e.g. γ c , JAK3) as well as genetic testing (e.g. a multigene panel) can help to establish a specific diagnosis. Maternal T cell engraftment accounting for ≥ 1% of peripheral blood leukocytes is present in approximately half of infants with SCID. The presence of maternal T cells is often asymptomatic, but a third of patients have mild changes such as cutaneous erythema and scale, a morbilliform eruption, elevated hepatic transaminases, and eosinophilia. Skin biopsy specimens show the histopathologic features of GVHD (see Ch. 52 ). Maternofetal GVHD is typically less severe than that resulting from postnatal inoculation of allogeneic lymphocytes, such as from unirradiated blood product transfusions, which can be fatal. Histologically, the erythroderma of Omenn syndrome shares some features with GVHD such as necrotic keratinocytes but also has epidermal acanthosis, parakeratosis, and a dense dermal infiltrate composed primarily of T cells. Differential Diagnosis SCID must be differentiated from other immunodeficiency disorders, especially HIV infection. The latter is distinguished by normal to increased immunoglobulin levels, a relative decrease in CD4 + T cells, and the presence of anti-HIV antibodies and HIV RNA. Treatment Without intervention, the outcome for SCID patients is death by 1 year of age. Early diagnosis of SCID is critical, preferably before the admin- istration of live vaccines or unirradiated blood products. Newborn screening for SCID is performed in the US and several other countries. Infants with SCID should be kept in protective isolation and monitored for the development of infections, which should be treated aggressively; administration of IVIg and prophylaxis for P. jirovecii pneumonia are also recommended. Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) during infancy is currently the first-line treatment for SCID. Because the patient’s immune system is unable to reject the transplanted cells, myeloab- lative therapy is not required. The result is engraftment of donor T and NK cells, but usually not B cells. With an HLA-identical sibling donor, T cell reconstitution typically occurs within 3–4 months, GVHD is uncommon, and the long-term survival rate is > 90%. Transplantation of haploidentical parental stem cells, which can be depleted of post- thymic T cells to reduce the risk of GVHD, often requires some chemo- therapeutic conditioning to facilitate engraftment and results in ≤ 80% survival. In utero injection of haploidentical CD34 + cells has also been used to treat X-linked SCID. SCID patients often require IVIg replacement therapy for persistent B cell deficiency following HSCT, and T cell function may decline over time. Administration of virus- specific T cells from their stem cell donor or a third-party donor may be useful for the treatment and prevention of viral infections (e.g. with EBV or cytomegalovirus) in HSCT recipients with SCID 132 . Enzyme replacement via injection of polyethylene glycol-conjugated ADA can lead to improved immune function in children with ADA deficiency. WISKOTT–ALDRICH SYNDROME Synonyms:  Wiskott–Aldrich–Huntley syndrome  Eczema–thrombo- cytopenia–immunodeficiency syndrome Key features  X-linked recessive immunodeficiency disorder characterized by the classic triad of atopic-like dermatitis, a bleeding tendency due to microthrombocytopenia, and recurrent sinopulmonary infections  Onset of bacterial infections is early in life, with later development of viral and P. jirovecii infections  Patients are also at risk of autoimmune diseases and lymphomas Introduction Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome (WAS) is characterized by recurrent pyogenic infections, bleeding due to thrombocytopenia and platelet dysfunction, and recalcitrant eczematous dermatitis 140,141 . The full triad develops in a minority of patients, with platelet abnormalities representing the most constant feature. Epidemiology Most patients with this X-linked recessive immunodeficiency are boys, but girls are occasionally affected in the setting of non-random X-chromosome inactivation or homozygosity for a mild mutation. WAS has an incidence of ~1 in 250 000 live male births in European popula- tions; it is less common in Black individuals and Asians. Pathogenesis WAS is caused by loss-of-function mutations in WASP , which is consti- tutively expressed in hematopoietic cell lineages. The WAS protein (WASP) controls the assembly of actin filaments, which are required for microvesicle and pro-platelet formation as well as T cell activation and polarization toward antigen-presenting cells 142 . Loss-of-function WASP mutations also cause isolated X-linked recessive thrombocytopenia, while gain-of-function WASP mutations can lead to X-linked congenital neutropenia. Abnormal T cell function is central to the immunologic defect in WAS, with resultant diminution of both cell-mediated and humoral responses 142 . Although the number of T cells in WAS patients has been observed to decrease with age, affected infants also have reduced numbers of T cells (especially naive T cells) and B cells 143 . This suggests that impaired lymphocyte maturation and output from the thymus are central to the immunodeficiency of WAS. WASP

Although the number of T cells in WAS patients has been observed to decrease with age, affected infants also have reduced numbers of T cells (especially naive T cells) and B cells 143 . This suggests that impaired lymphocyte maturation and output from the thymus are central to the immunodeficiency of WAS. WASP function is required for the activation of regulatory T cells, helping to explain the autoimmune manifestations of WAS. Defects in B cell migration, differentiation, and organization into germinal centers have roles in the impaired humoral immunity of WAS, with reduced expression of the CD21 and CD35 complement receptors involved in antigen capture and presentation also potentially contributing to autoimmunity 143,144 . Although NK cells are not decreased in number, their cytolytic activity is abnormal in WAS. Lastly, small, structurally abnormal platelets with a reduced half-life (due in part to splenic destruction) account for the thrombocy- topenia of WAS 142 . Clinical Features Because thrombocytopenia and platelet dysfunction are present from birth, the first clinical signs of WAS are usually petechiae and ecchy- moses of the skin and oral mucosa. Spontaneous bleeding from the oral cavity, epistaxis, hematemesis, melena, and hematuria are commonly observed. The dermatitis of WAS typically develops during the first few months of life, and it fulfills the diagnostic criteria for atopic dermatitis (see although patients often have widespread involvement with progressive lichenification. Exfoliative dermatitis occasionally develops. Excoriated areas frequently have serosanguineous crusts and petechiae ( Fig. 60.15 ). Secondary bacterial infections are common, as are eczema herpeticum and molluscum contagiosum. Recurrent bacterial infections begin during the first 3 months of life, coincident with diminishing levels of placentally transmitted maternal antibodies. These infections include otitis externa and media, pneumonia, sinusitis, conjunctivitis, furunculosis, meningitis, and septicemia. Encapsulated bacteria such as Str. pneumoniae, H. influenza , and Neisseria meningitidis are the predominant organisms. With advancing age, there is increased susceptibility to infections with viruses (e.g. herpes simplex) and P. jirovecii . Most children with WAS develop at least one autoimmune disease, most commonly cutaneous small vessel vasculitis (often associated with painful edema), autoimmune cytopenias, arthritis, inflam- matory bowel disease, and cerebral vasculitis 145 . Primary Immunodeficiencies Laboratory Findings and Pathology The most frequent laboratory abnormalities in WAS are persistent thrombocytopenia (platelet counts < 70 000/mm 3 ) and low mean platelet volume ( < 5.0 fl). WAS patients may also have lymphopenia and eosino- philia. Serum IgM and IgG 2 levels are typically low, while IgA, IgE, and IgD levels tend to be elevated. Antibody responses to polysaccharide antigens are markedly diminished. Delayed-type hypersensitivity skin test reactions are usually absent, and responses to mitogens are often depressed, especially in older patients. Monocyte and neutrophil chemotaxis may also be defective. Assessment of WASP expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells by flow cytometry-based assays or immunoblot analysis can be performed in patients suspected to have WAS prior to mutational analysis. Patients with a complete lack of WASP expression in circu- lating cells tend to have a more severe phenotype. Full engraft­ment results in normal platelet numbers and function, resto- ration of immunologic status, and clearance of the dermatitis. Affected children who receive a HSCT have an overall survival rate of > 90%, with lower rates in those transplanted at > 5 years of age with an unrelated donor 147,148 . Gene therapy using lentivirally transduced, WASP-reconstituted, autologous CD34 + cells can lead to sustained resolution of the dermatitis and susceptibility to infection as well as improvement in the bleeding diathesis and autoimmunity, without the high risk of leukemic transformation that was observed with utilization of a retroviral vector 149–151 . Prophylactic use of antibiotics can decrease the risk of fatal infec- tions in WAS patients 152 . IVIg therapy also helps to prevent infections and may potentially improve the dermatitis. Topical corticosteroids remain a mainstay of treatment for the latter. Although splenectomy may reduce bleeding complications in patients with recurrent severe hemorrhage, it further increases the risk of infections with encapsu- lated organisms. Platelet transfusions may be given prior to surgery and in the setting of life-threatening hemorrhage. Systemic corticosteroids, rituximab, and other immunosuppressive agents may be utilized for autoimmune disorders. In the mid twentieth century, Crowe, Schull, and Neel compiled a landmark monograph with a comprehensive description of the manifestations of this disease 4 . Epidemiology NF1 occurs worldwide. Its incidence is ~1 in 2000 to 3000 births ­ . Pathogenesis NF1 is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. Most large series have found that 30%–50% of patients have no affected relatives and thus likely harbor new spontaneous mutations 4,8,9 . There is also the possi­ bility of germline mosaicism in a parent, especially when two siblings develop NF1 in the absence of a prior family history. The penetrance of NF1 approaches 100% in carefully examined adults 10 , but expressivity is variable. A wide range of clinical findings and complications can develop among individuals with the same underlying mutation. The specific NF1 mutation is therefore not the only factor that determines phenotype. In 1987, an international consortium found evidence of linkage to the pericentromeric region of chromosome 17 in families with NF1 11 . Subsequent descriptions of two NF1 patients with balanced translo­ cations involving the long arm of chromosome 17 (17q11.2) further refined the position of the NF1 locus 12,13 . The localization data derived from these studies led to the cloning of the NF1 gene 14–16 . NF1 encodes neurofibromin, a 327 kDa protein composed of 2818 amino acids, and consists of at least 59 exons ( Fig. 61.1 ) 17 . Over 80% of NF1 patients have a mutation that predicts truncation of the neuro­ fibromin protein, and ~5% of patients have a large deletion (“micro­ deletion”) that encompasses the entire NF1 gene plus variable flanking genes 18 . Clinical Features The clinical features of NF1 ( Table 61.1 ) are myriad and vary in frequency 4,8,9,30–40 . Almost every organ system has been found to be involved in NF1, which can lead to a wide range of morbidities and mortality 7 . The cutaneous manifestations of NF1 represent particularly important clinical features that have a central role in its diagnosis 41 . Oculocutaneous manifestations Café-au-lait macules (CALMs) are tan to dark brown (depending on the degree of constitutive pigmentation), uniformly pigmented macules and patches that are randomly distributed on the body, with the exception of the scalp, palms, and soles. The CALMs of NF1 are sharply demar­ cated with regular borders and often have an oval shape ( Fig. 61.3 ); the diameter can vary from a few millimeters to > 4 cm. CALMs may not be apparent at birth and frequently become more noticeable during the first year of life; fading of these lesions during later adulthood has also been described 42 . When located within areas of dermal melanocy­ tosis, CALMs may be surrounded by a rim of normally pigmented skin (see Ch. 112 ). Larger CALMs, especially those with associated hyper­ trichosis, should be palpated to exclude the possibility of an underlying plexiform neurofibroma (see below). Plexiform neurofibromas (PNFs; Fig. 61.6 ) may track along nerves to create tender, firm nodules or masses in the subcutaneous tissue with a “bag of worms” consistency upon palpation, or they can infil­ trate diffusely to involve various layers of the skin, fascia, muscle, or even internal structures. Approximately 25% of NF1 patients have clinically apparent PNFs. Larger lesions may cause soft tissue and bony hypertrophy, and massive distortion of the head and neck or extremities occasionally develops. Impingement upon nerves can lead to neurologic deficits, and (peri)orbital PNFs may result in visual loss as well as facial deformity 48 . Unlike other neurofibromas, PNFs are probably all congenital in origin. Superficial and/or diffuse lesions usually become clinically apparent by the age of 4 or 5 years 30 , while deep/internal nodular lesions may remain undetected even in adulthood unless full-body magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is performed 49 . Older children without evidence of soft tissue overgrowth related to a PNF are unlikely to develop this finding later in life. Both hyperpigmentation and hyper­ trichosis can overlie PNFs 50 , sometimes leading to the misdiagnosis of congenital melanocytic nevus (see Fig. 61.6 ). The transformation of PNFs into malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors (MPNSTs, also known as “neurofibrosarcomas”) occurs in 8%–15% of patients with NF1 9,44,51 , with a peak incidence in young adults. The onset of rapid growth, increased firmness, or persistent pain within an established PNF or the development of a new neurologic deficit may herald malignant degeneration ( Table 61.4 ; see Management section). MPNSTs can be very aggressive and are often fatal 52 . Young children with NF1 also have a 200- to 500-fold greater risk of developing juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia (JMML; incidence 1/2000–1/5000) than does the general pediatric population. Although a “triple association” between NF1, JMML, and JXG has been described 56 , the magnitude of additional risk of JMML in children with NF1 plus JXGs compared to NF1 alone remains to be determined. Neurofibromin is known to regulate the proliferation of myeloid cells, but the exact etiopathogenesis of the “triple association” remains unclear. Vascular anomalies that have been recognized as manifestations of NF1 include nevus anemicus and glomus tumors 54,57,58 . In two prospective studies, a nevus anemicus was identified in a total of 55% (92/166) of children and 36% (19/53) of adults with NF1, compared to only 2% (6/302) of age- and sex-matched controls 57,58 . These lesions favor the trunk, especially the mid chest, and become more evident after rubbing the skin. Because nevus anemicus is prevalent in NF1 patients and apparent by early childhood, its use as a diagnostic criterion has been proposed but not yet adopted 54,57,58 . Biallelic inactivation of NF1 has been documented within glomus tumors in NF1 patients 59 . The tumors are often multiple and develop on the fingers > toes; like their sporadic counterpart, they can present with paroxysmal pain and sensitivity to cold (see Ch. 114 ). Focal swelling, ill-defined reddish discoloration (often of the nail bed), and nail dystrophy may be observed. Pigmented iris hamartomas, or Lisch nodules, begin to develop at about 3 years of age and are found in ~90% of NF1 patients by 20 years of age 36,44,60,61 . These 1–2 mm, dome-shaped, yellow–brown papules are best seen on slit-lamp examination ( Fig. 61.7 ). Lisch nodules rarely lead to symptoms or complications. Asymptomatic choroidal nodules are also present in 80%–100% of adults and 60%–70% of children with NF1, and this finding has been added to the recently published revised diagnostic criteria 62 . The behavior of these CNS neoplasms is variable, ranging from spontaneous regression to progressive visual compromise and proptosis due to tumor expansion 5 . Precocious puberty occurs in about 3% of children with NF1, typically in association with an optic pathway glioma 67,68 . Non-optic CNS tumors occur in ~5% 45 and pheochromocytomas in ~1% of NF1 patients 30,69 . Hyperintense lesions on T2-weighted MRI of the brain (T2 hyper­ intensities; “unidentified bright objects”) can be observed in 50%–75% of children with NF1 70 . These are most commonly seen in the basal ganglia, brainstem, and cerebellum. T2 hyperintensities have been shown to evolve over time 71 , and they may contribute to cognitive impairment via thalamocortical dysfunction 72 . Although severe intellectual impairment is uncommon, learning difficulties occur in 30%–50% of affected children 44,73 ; there is also an increased likelihood of attention deficit disorder, headaches, and sleep disturbances. Seizures develop in about 5% of NF1 patients, although no specific cortical lesions have been linked to the abnormal EEG activity 35 . Skeletal manifestations Macrocephaly 31,74 , hypertelorism, and scoliosis 39,73 are common cranio­ skeletal abnormalities in individuals with NF1. Osteopenia is another frequent finding, with potential pathogenic factors including vitamin D deficiency and increased bone turnover 75 . A highly distinctive but less common manifestation is pseudarthrosis of the long bones, most often the tibia. This congenital defect begins as bowing and eventually results in erosion of the bone cortex, leading to pathologic fractures and false joint formation (pseudarthrosis) 30,44 . Sphenoid wing dysplasia is a congenital, typically unilateral bony defect in the posterior wall of the orbit that may present as pulsating exophthalmos 44 . Cardiovascular manifestations Hypertension is a common finding in NF1 patients. Although essential hypertension is most frequent, renovascular stenosis 76 (especially in children) and unsuspected pheochromocytomas 77 may be the cause in some patients. PNFs and skeletal defects are probably congenital, while CALMs and nevus anemicus may be evident at birth or become apparent during the first few years of life. Pathology The CALMs, CNFs, and MPNSTs associated with NF1 are histo­ logically similar to their sporadic counterparts. CALMs from affected individuals are characterized primarily by increased epidermal melanin; other nonspecific findings may include giant melanosomes and a higher number of melanocytes compared to the surrounding skin 78 . CNFs feature a well-circumscribed but unencapsulated dermal collection of small nerve fibers and loosely arranged spindle cells; the latter have scanty pale cytoplasm and elongated wavy nuclei (see Ch. 115 ). These spindle cells represent a mixture of fibroblasts, Schwann cells, and perineural cells all set in a collagenous stroma with varying amounts of mucin and scattered mast cells. The nuclei are bland and mitotic activity should raise a suspicion of malignancy. PNFs are specific to NF1. Histologically, they are composed of large, hypertrophied nerves surrounded by spindle-shaped fibroblasts and Schwann cells embedded in a myxoid matrix and growing in a plexiform pattern (see Ch. 115 ). In some PNFs, neurofibromatous changes extend diffusely into the papillary and reticular dermis. The stroma may be more collagenous than myxoid and organoid differentiation may occur, forming structures resembling Meissner corpuscles. MPNSTs are characterized by tight intersecting bundles of spindle cells. There are often alternating cellular and myxoid areas. The cells (as in neurofibromas)

Differential Diagnosis In an affected individual with complete expression of NF1, classic clinical criteria 79 are met and the diagnosis is usually straightforward. In infants, establishing the diagnosis can sometimes be difficult because age-dependent features have not yet developed 80 . Recently published revised diagnostic criteria for NF1 developed by an international consensus group incorporate genetic testing, update the clinical features (primarily the addition of choroidal abnormalities), and emphasize distinction from mosaic NF1 and conditions with overlapping findings (e.g. Legius syndrome) (see Table 61.2 ) 62 . An approach to children with multiple CALMs (NF1 suspect) 81 is outlined in Figure 61.10 . In a series of 110 children (median age 3 years; range, 1 month to 17 years) who presented to an NF1 clinic with CALMs but no other features of NF1, 34/44 (77%) of those with ≥ 6 “typical” CALMs (distinct regular borders, uniform pigmentation) eventually met criteria for NF1 (almost all before age 6 years), compared to 2/15 (15%) of those with ≥ 6 “atypical” CALMs (smudgy irregular borders, non-homogeneous pigmentation) and 0/51 of those with < 6 CALMs 82 . Comprehensive, highly sensitive analysis of NF1 is available, with methods including targeted massively parallel/next-generation sequencing (NGS), multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification (MLPA; assesses copy number variation), and RNA-based testing 83 . GENODERMATOSES These techniques can identify the underlying pathogenic variant in ≥ 95%–98% of non-founder patients who fulfill classic clinical diagnostic criteria 79 . This is because they can detect low-level mosaicism (down to 3%–5% variant allele frequency with NGS) as well as deep intronic splice variants and deletions that are missed by conventional genomic DNA-based sequencing. Molecular testing allows for more accurate diagnoses in young children and individuals with atypical clinical presentations. It also makes prenatal or preimplantation diagnosis an option for affected families. In addition to mosaic NF1 (see above), unilateral lentigines in the axilla or groin may be seen in patients with partial unilateral lentigi­ nosis (PUL) or a large speckled lentiginous nevus (nevus spilus) 84 . These segmental conditions are characteristically sharply demarcated at the midline, but bilateral involvement occasionally occurs. The presence of CALMs in addition to lentigines increases the likelihood of NF1. When individuals suspected of having mosaic NF1 do not have a detectable mutation in the peripheral blood, the diagnosis can be confirmed by analyzing NF1 in melanocytes or Schwann cells cultured from a lesional skin biopsy specimen (e.g. of a CALM or neurofibroma, respectively). Management Management of NF1 patients requires a multidisciplinary approach 79,90 ; if available, a multispecialty NF clinic can help to optimize care. Dermatologists are often consulted to assist in establishing the diagnosis in affected children. Evaluation of individuals newly diagnosed with NF1 should include a thorough history (personal and family) and physical examination, with particular attention to signs and symptoms of disease manifestations (see Table 61.1 ). As part of the initial care of NF1 patients, an in-depth educational discussion should include the natural history of the condition, possible medical complications and neurodevelopmental sequelae, and psychosocial considerations; genetic counseling should also be provided. Table 61.4 summarizes recommen­ dations for the evaluation and management of NF1 patients 92–95 . Goals of longitudinal care include early recognition and treatment of compli­ cations, maximization of academic and vocational achievement, and minimization of the disease’s psychosocial impact. As with NF1, cutaneous lesions are often the initial clinical features, and derma­ tologists are routinely called upon to assist in the diagnosis of TSC. History During the mid-1800s, Virchow recognized scleromas in the brain and von Recklinghausen described a similar patient with both scleromas and myomata in the heart 44 . Between 1880 and 1900, Bourneville provided the first systematic descriptions of the disease, including neural and cutaneous findings. Vogt posited the classic triad of epilepsy, low intelligence, and angiofibromas (termed the Vogt triad) in 1908, and Sherlock coined the term “epiloia” a few years later. Vogt posited the classic triad of epilepsy, low intelligence, and angiofibromas (termed the Vogt triad) in 1908, and Sherlock coined the term “epiloia” a few years later. In 1920, van der Hoeve described the significance of retinal hamartomas, which he termed “phakomas” (hence the designation “phakomatosis”) 106 . At that time, examination of the ocular fundi was the only external access to the CNS before death. Epidemiology TSC has an incidence of ~1 in 10 000 births, and the overall prevalence is estimated to be between 1 in 10 000 and 1 in 30 000 107,108 . Pathogenesis TSC is a hamartomatous condition characterized by disordered cellular proliferation, migration, and differentiation. It has an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance. However, the majority of affected individuals have new spontaneous mutations. In the 1980s, TSC kindreds from around the world were analyzed and the disease locus was mapped to chromosome 9q34 in a subset of affected families. Further study led to the discovery of a second disease locus on chromosome 16p13 109 . In 1994, Povey et al. 110 studied 32 TSC families and found that about half demonstrated linkage to chromosome 9q34 ( TSC1 ), whereas the other half showed linkage to chromosome 16p13 ( TSC2) . In 1993, the TSC2 gene on chromosome 16 was identified and found to be deleted or mutated in the subset of TSC families linked to this region 111 . TSC2 is composed of 41 exons that encode an 1807 amino acid, 200 kDa protein referred to as tuberin . Like neurofibromin, tuberin contains a GAP domain ( Fig. 61.12 ). Tuberin stimulates the GTPase activities of RAB5, a protein involved in endocytosis 112 , and RHEB, a RAS-related protein that activates the mTOR pathway. By “turning off” RHEB, tuberin inhibits the cell growth and proliferation that result from mTOR signaling. The latter is a central regulator of cellular responses to nutrition, energy levels, and a variety of growth factors. The TSC1 gene, which was identified in 1997, consists of 23 exons that encode a 130 kDa protein termed hamartin 113 . Hamartin shares no sequence homology with tuberin or other known tumor suppressor genes. However, hamartin interacts with tuberin 114 and other cytoskeletal components, and it functions together

The TSC1 gene, which was identified in 1997, consists of 23 exons that encode a 130 kDa protein termed hamartin 113 . Hamartin shares no sequence homology with tuberin or other known tumor suppressor genes. However, hamartin interacts with tuberin 114 and other cytoskeletal components, and it functions together with tuberin to negatively regulate mTOR signaling 115,116 . In patients with TSC, mTOR inhibition by sirolimus (rapamycin) and related agents can have therapeutic benefit (see Fig. 61.12 and Management section). In large series of TSC patients, TSC2 mutations have been identified more frequently than TSC1 mutations, with an overall ratio of approx­ imately 3 : 1 117,118 . However, in familial cases, there is a more equal proportion of TSC2 and TSC1 mutations. Of note, individuals with TSC2 mutations tend to have a more severe phenotype than those with TSC1 mutations. Familial TSC due to TSC2 mutations tends to have a milder phenotype than de novo cases 117,118 , which likely reflects a decreased likelihood of reproduction in more severely affected individuals. Some patients with mild sporadic TSC are mosaics for a mutation in TSC1 or TSC2 ; if there is gonadal involvement, they may pass on generalized disease to their offspring. In mouse models, heterozygous TSC1 mutant ( Tsc1 + / − ) mice develop renal and extrarenal tumors such as hepatic hemangiomas with loss of the wild-type Tsc1 allele. Heterozygous TSC2 mice ( Tsc2 + / − ) display a high incidence of multiple bilateral renal cystadenomas, liver hemangiomas, and lung adenomas. Progression to renal carcinoma, fatal bleeding from the liver hemangiomas, and angiosarcomas are occasionally observed 119 . These mice also have abnormalities in learning and memory associated with hyperactive hippocampal mTOR signaling. Treatment of adult mice with the mTOR inhibitor sirolimus resulted in improved cognitive function 120 . Neurofibromatosis and Tuberous Sclerosis Complex Clinical Features As with NF1, the diagnosis of TSC often involves a dermatologist, as some of the earliest findings of TSC are cutaneous ( Table 61.6 ). Oculocutaneous manifestations The time course for developing the cutaneous findings of TSC is shown in Fig. 61.13 . The hypomelanotic macules are not depigmented, as in vitiligo, but instead are hypopigmented ( Fig. 61.14 ). A Wood’s lamp can help to detect these lesions, which may be very subtle in children with lightly pigmented skin. The macules are usually present at birth or within the first few months of life, although their appearance is sometimes delayed until early childhood in individuals with fair skin. They may adopt several configurations, and small ( < 2 cm) polygonal or “thumbprint”-shaped macules are most common 121 . The lance-ovate hypopigmented macule or “ash leaf spot” (named after the Eastern Mountain ash tree) is rounded at one end and tapered at the other, and it can range from 1 to 12 cm in size. Although less frequent than polygonal macules, ash leaf spots are characteristic of TSC. Over 90% of TSC patients have more than one hypomelanotic macule 122 , and some have > 100 lesions. Scores of 1–2 mm, “guttate” hypopigmented macules (also known as “white freckles” or “confetti” macules) may also be seen, especially on the extremities ( Fig. 61.15 ). Although these guttate lesions occur in < 5% of affected infants, they are probably the most specific pigmentary manifestation of TSC 121,122 . Approximately 1%–4% of healthy infants and children have a circum­ scribed hypopigmented macule or patch, i.e. a nevus depigmentosus (see Ch. 66 ) 121,123,124 . Debard and Richardet 123 examined the skin of 9737 infants aged 1–18 months and found that 0.7% had one or two white spots that were larger than 1 cm; however, no unaffected infant had more than three spots. Thus, the presence of three or more hypomela­ notic macules ( ≥ 5 mm in diameter) was chosen as a major criterion for diagnosis of TSC 125,126 ( Table 61.7 ). Clusters of scalp hair, eyebrows, or eyelashes may be lighter or white (poliosis) when the underlying skin is affected. Café-au-lait macules (CALMs) have been reported in up to 30% of patients with TSC and are usually evident within the first few months of life 121,122 . Most TSC patients, however, have fewer than the six CALMs required to diagnose NF1. Angiofibromas, previously referred to as “adenoma sebaceum”, are not typically present at birth. They begin to appear in the centrofacial area as early as the first 2 years of life, and by adolescence angiofibromas are present in ~80% of TSC patients. A high frequency of somatic second-hit CC > TT “UV signature” mutations has been identified in TSC-related facial angiofibromas, suggesting a role for UV light in their pathogenesis 127 . The lesions may begin as erythematous macules on the cheeks and forehead and then mature into pink to red or red– brown papules or papulonodules, which may coalesce into plaques. The papules are often dome-shaped and have a smooth, shiny surface ( Fig. 61.16A,B ). With the exception of mosaic TSC, facial angiofi­ bromas have a bilateral and symmetric distribution. Because one or two angiofibromas (fibrous papules) are relatively common in the general population, the presence of at least 3 angiofibromas is required as a diagnostic criterion for TSC 125 . The fibrous cephalic plaque represents a larger variant of an angiofi­ broma that develops on the face or scalp in ~20% of TSC patients 122,125 . These plaques favor the forehead and are usually firm and yellow–brown to pink–tan in color ( Fig. 61.16C ). They may slowly enlarge over time and when on the scalp typically lack hair. A characteristic truncal lesion is the shagreen (“leather”) patch, which represents a type of collagenoma (see Ch. 116 ). Shagreen patches occur most commonly in the lumbosacral area and typically begin to develop at around 2 years of age, although occasionally they are apparent earlier. Eventually these lesions are observed in approximately half of TSC patients 122 . Clinically, they typically appear as skin-colored to hyper­ pigmented plaques that can reach up to 10 cm in diameter and

Most ocular lesions in TSC patients do not lead to visual loss. Neurologic manifestations Infantile spasms occur in ~70% of infants with TSC. These seizures last for several minutes and are characterized by massive flexion or extension of the limbs, trunk, and head for < 1–3 seconds, occurring in series separated by intervals of a few seconds. These spasms typically begin at about 3 months of age, as opposed to other types of TSC-associated seizures, which usually develop after 1 year of age 134 . The EEG changes that characterize infantile spasms are termed hypsarrhythmia 134,135 . Intellectual disabilities of varying degrees occur with a high frequency in children and adults with TSC 134,135 . The spectrum of T SC- a ssociated n europsychiatric d isorders (TAND) also includes autism, attention deficit disorder, aggressive behaviors, and psychiatric conditions 136–138 . Multiple subependymal nodules along the ventricular surface can be seen on MRI (more sensitive) or CT scan in > 80% of TSC patients by 2 years of age. These nodules progressively calcify and are found in almost all patients by puberty 139 . Subependymal giant cell astrocy­ tomas (SEGAs), which affect 5%–15% of patients with TSC, usually develop during childhood 140 . Unlike subependymal nodules, SEGAs tend to enlarge over time, which may

Arrhythmias, especially Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome, appear to be more common in affected individuals 143 . Renal manifestations Multiple bilateral angiomyolipomas are frequently noted on routine renal ultrasounds of TSC patients. Most of these lesions are asymp­ tomatic, especially during childhood and when they measure < 4 cm in diameter 142 . However, angiomyolipomas tend to enlarge and increase in number with age, and they may lead to life-threatening hemor­ rhage 144 . Children with TSC who develop severe renal cysts often have a contiguous gene syndrome in which both TSC2 and the polycystic kidney disease ( PKD ) genes are lost in a single large chromosomal deletion 145 . Occasionally, renal cell carcinomas develop in TSC patients. Other manifestations Pulmonary lymphangioleiomyomatosis is often asymptomatic and occurs in at least 30%–40% of women with TSC. On high-resolution CT scan, these lesions appear as cysts. Men rarely develop this manifes­ tation of TSC 146 , and estrogen is suspected to be involved in stimulating growth of smooth muscle cells in the lung 147 . Of note, lymphangio­ leiomyomatosis can occur sporadically due to biallelic somatic TSC2 mutations, and renal angiomyolipomas also develop in a subset of these patients. Multifocal micronodular pneumonocyte hyperplasia, hamar­ tomatous gastrointestinal polyps, congenital segmental lymphedema, other vascular anomalies, segmental lipomatosis, and hemihypertrophy have also been reported in individuals with TSC 129,148–150 . Pathology Hypopigmented macules have a reduction in the amount of epidermal melanin but a normal number of melanocytes. The melanocytes have poorly developed dendrites 151 . On electron microscopy, small, immature melanosomes are seen whose number, degree of melanization, and transfer to keratinocytes are reduced 151–153 . Angiofibromas consist of an irregular proliferation of fibrous tissue and blood vessels. Expansion of the hamartomatous process can lead to compression of adnexae. The dermis is replaced by thick bundles of collagen, and elastin fibers are typically absent. The fibroblasts may be large and morphologically atypical. It is thought that the various fibrous lesions seen in TSC belong to the same histopathologic spectrum, with perifol­ licular fibrosis representing a characteristic feature; a cystic component is occasionally evident, as observed in FCCH 154,155 . Differential Diagnosis The diagnostic criteria for TSC were revised in 1998 and then updated in 2012 (see Table 61.7 ) 125,126,141 . Four of the major features are cutaneous, and a thorough dermatologic examination frequently helps to establish the diagnosis. Although seizures occur in the majority of affected infants, the possibility of TSC is often considered in asymp­ tomatic infants with multiple hypomelanotic macules. An approach to this clinical situation is outlined in Fig. 61.21 . Echocardiography can be helpful in establishing the diagnosis in infants and is easier to perform in this age group than is a brain MRI to detect CNS lesions. Conventional genetic testing, including sequencing and deletion/ duplication analysis, identifies a pathogenic variant in TSC1 or TSC2 in ~85% of individuals who meet the clinical criteria for TSC. Use of targeted next-generation sequencing (including deletion/dupli­ cation analysis) can increase the yield to ~95%, enabling detection of intronic splice site

Conventional genetic testing, including sequencing and deletion/ duplication analysis, identifies a pathogenic variant in TSC1 or TSC2 in ~85% of individuals who meet the clinical criteria for TSC. Use of targeted next-generation sequencing (including deletion/dupli­ cation analysis) can increase the yield to ~95%, enabling detection of intronic splice site and mosaic pathogenic variants that tend to result in relatively mild disease 156,157 . Analysis of DNA from a lesional skin biopsy specimen (e.g. angiofibroma) may be necessary for mosaic TSC with more limited involvement 156 . Multiple facial angiofibromas, collagenomas, gingival papules, and confetti-like hypomelanotic macules can occur in patients with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN 1; see Ch. 63 ). Multiple facial angiofibromas and collagenomas have also been observed in adults with Birt–Hogg–Dubé syndrome (see Ch. 111 ), whereas multiple collagenomas can occur in Cowden syndrome (storiform variant, also referred to as sclerotic fibromas; see Ch. 63 ), Buschke–Ollendorf syndrome (dermatofibrosis lenticularis disseminata; see Ch. 116 ), and familial cutaneous collagenoma. The clinical differential diagnosis for facial angiofibromas may include acne vulgaris and trichoepitheliomas, but individual acneiform lesions should resolve over a period of weeks. Trichoepitheliomas are usually less red in color, although a biopsy is often required to establish the diagnosis. Additional causes of multiple facial papules are listed in Table 36.2 and Figure 111.5 . As discussed above, a nevus depigmentosus represents a common cause of a congenital hypopigmented macule or patch, and some infants have more than one of these lesions. A larger nevus depigmentosus that has a segmental distribution (segmental pigmentation disorder) or follows the lines of Blaschko may be composed of multiple hypopig­ mented macules and patches within the affected areas. Features that distinguish the hypopigmented lesions of TSC from postinflammatory hypopigmentation (e.g. due to atopic or seborrheic dermatitis) and the amelanosis of piebaldism or vitiligo are presented in Figure 61.21 . Idiopathic guttate hypomelanosis (IGH) may resemble the confetti-like leukoderma of TS; however, IGH is an acquired condition that favors the shins and extensor forearms of older adults. A congenital smooth muscle hamartoma can present during infancy as a firm, skin-colored to hyperpigmented plaque that may resemble a shagreen patch; however, it accentuates with rubbing (pseudo-Darier sign), contains follicular papules due

(e.g. due to atopic or seborrheic dermatitis) and the amelanosis of piebaldism or vitiligo are presented in Figure 61.21 . Idiopathic guttate hypomelanosis (IGH) may resemble the confetti-like leukoderma of TS; however, IGH is an acquired condition that favors the shins and extensor forearms of older adults. A congenital smooth muscle hamartoma can present during infancy as a firm, skin-colored to hyperpigmented plaque that may resemble a shagreen patch; however, it accentuates with rubbing (pseudo-Darier sign), contains follicular papules due to hyperplastic arrector pili muscles, and has associated hypertrichosis rather than prominent but depressed follicular orifices. Histologically, smooth muscle hamartomas feature intradermal bundles of smooth muscle rather than collagen. Management Nearly every organ can be affected by TSC, and clinical findings vary tremendously even within families. Certain signs and complications typically appear at birth, whereas others develop much later in life. The 2012 International TSC Consensus Conference Recommendations and 2019 United Kingdom Guidelines for the evaluation and management of individuals with TSC are summarized in Table 61.8 142,158–160 . Investigations in TSC patients should focus on detecting disease manifestations and complications that are potentially significant and treatable, and it is important to provide genetic counseling to affected individuals and families. In clinical trials involving TSC patients, systemic therapy with the mTOR inhibitors sirolimus and evero­ limus has led to regression of SEGAs, control of recalcitrant seizures, reduction in the size of renal angiomyolipomas, and improvement of lung function in women with lymphangioleiomyomatosis 161–163 . Considering the UV-induced mutations implicated in facial angio­ fibromas, sun protective measures may be of utility 127 . Use of electro­ surgery, dermabrasion, and ablative fractional or pulsed dye lasers has led to variable results. Topical sirolimus (rapamycin) has been employed to treat angiofi­ bromas as well as fibrous plaques and hypomelanotic macules, with limited systemic absorption. More irritation is produced by topical appli­ cation of the commercially available 0.1% solution (Rapamune ® 1 mg/ ml) than with compounded 0.1%–1% ointment, cream, and gel formu­ lations 164–167 . Reduced erythema and flattening of the angiofibromas are typically seen within 3 months of initiating daily topical therapy, especially if treatment is initiated at ≤ 10 years of age. In randomized placebo-controlled studies in adults and children with TSC, angiofi­ bromas improved in 60% (18/30) of patients treated topically with sirolimus 0.2% gel twice daily for 3 months and 82% (45/55) of those treated with sirolimus 1% daily

Schaffer * Mosaicism and Linear Lesions SECTION 9 GENODERMATOSES on the X chromosome reflected two populations of cells, one expressing the maternal X chromosome and one the paternal X chromosome. She hypothesized that all women are functional mosaics with regard to the X chromosome. In 1965, Curth and Warburton 2 used the Lyon hypothesis incontinentia pigmenti. A decade later, Happle recognized lyonization as the reason that skin lesions follow the lines of Blaschko in heterozygous female patients with other X-linked genodermatoses 3,4 . We now recognize that mosaicism affecting autosomes as well as X chromosomes may result from either: (1) changes in the DNA sequence due to mutations or chromosomal alterations ( genetic or genomic mosaicism); or (2) changes in gene expression ( epigenetic or functional mosaicism) as in lyonization 4 ( Table 62.1 ). Autosomal mosaic conditions usually result from de novo postzygotic mutations and are not inherited. However, the clinical manifestations of some autosomal dominant disorders reflect a mosaic “second hit” in affected tissues, such as the skin lesions of neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1). The unusual familial occurrences of autosomal mosaic disorders may be explained by inheritance of either an unstable “premutation” or a transposon (“jumping gene”) of retroviral origin that can modulate the expression of other genes when the disorder has a genetic versus epigenetic etiology, respectively 5 . The idea that the lines of Blaschko represent the embryonic migration pathways of skin cells was first expressed in English by Douglass Montgomery, who proposed that the linear patterns of epidermal nevi “may be due to the streams or trend of growth of the tissues” 6 . Although both Montgomery and Blaschko presented their findings in May 1901, Montgomery’s contribution was eclipsed by that of his German contem- porary. In fact, the now widely held theory that the lines of Blaschko reflect routes of embryonic cell migration did not surface again until the late 1970s 3,7 . PATTERNS AND PATHOGENESIS OF CUTANEOUS MOSAICISM Blaschko’s original diagram (see Fig. 62.1A ) omitted the midface, scalp, in these areas have now been established 8 ( Fig. 62.1B–E ), as have analogous patterns in the eyes, teeth, and oral mucosa. Considerable - tions of lines on the face; the posterior midline may be shifted to the left or right, but the anterior midline tends to be sharply centered from the upper sternum to the pubis. Mosaic skin conditions do not always follow the lines of Blaschko ( Fig. 62.1F-H ). Happle categorized patterns of cutaneous mosaicism into seven types 8a : (1,2) narrow or broad bands along the lines of Blaschko; (3) checkerboard (block- or flag-like); (4) lateralization, i.e. one side of the body only; (5) phylloid (leaf- or flower-like); (6) patchy without midline separation; and (7) sash. To date, all patterns, except for sash, have been shown to be mosaic at the molecular level in at least one condition. Other patterns have also been described in genetically proven mosaic conditions, such as multiple small, relatively circular congenital melanocytic nevi. Assuming that the pattern is determined by cell migration, it depends on both the timing of the genetic alteration ( Table 62.2 ) and the cell type affected. These two factors also contribute to other aspects of the mosaic phenotype. A mutation occurring early in embryonic development tends to affect a higher proportion of that individual’s cells and a greater number of tissue types. Likewise, the identical mutation in a keratinocyte, melanocyte or pluripotent precursor cell can result in a nevus sebaceus, nevus spilus, or both of these birthmarks, respectively. The classic pattern defined by Blaschko is seen in disorders of epidermal cells 9 , which is not surprising since Blaschko based his diagrams on epidermal nevi. Investigation of patterns in congenital pigmentary disorders led to the proposal that narrow bands following Blaschko’s lines reflect mosaicism involving keratinocytes, but not melanocytes 9a . For example, KITLG mutations in keratinocytes can result in narrow hyperpigmented bands 9b . Embryonic keratinocytes move via directional proliferation, in more-or-less continuous lines that are affected by the complex interplay between cell migration and surface remodeling. In contrast, melanoblasts migrate from the neural crest to the skin, where they then proliferate antenatally. This as well as other characteristics of the aberrant cells and the timing of the genetic alteration may explain the broad bands along Blaschko’s lines as well as checkerboard and phylloid patterns seen in mosaic pigmentary condi- tions and the patchy or garment-like distribution of larger congenital melanocytic nevi. For melanocytic mosaic disorders, two major patterns have been proposed: (1) segmental - characterized by quadrilateral shapes with midline demarcation, encompassing broad Blaschko-linear and checkerboard patterns; and (2) non-segmental - characterized by circular shapes without midline demarcation 9a (see Fig. 62.1G and H ). The phenotypic consequences of mosaicism also vary according to: (1) whether the trait is dominant or recessive; (2) whether the mutation is “forward” (pathogenic; gain- or loss-of-function) or revertant (correcting; “backward”/“back”); and (3) whether the individual’s background germline genome is “normal” or contains an autosomal dominant or autosomal recessive mutation ( Fig. 62.2 ). In individuals with a “normal” germline genome, the postzygotic mutation can result in simple segmental mosaicism . Such mutations are further categorized as either lethal or compatible with life if in the germline. When compatible with life, this has been referred to as type 1 mosaicism , defined as a postzygotic mutation in one allele of a gene that underlies an autosomal dominant disorder (e.g. epidermolytic ichthyosis) resulting in one or more regions of affected skin ( Fig. 62.2A ). The latter may have a linear distribution, e.g. an epidermolytic epidermal nevus. On the other hand, if the postzygotic mutation is lethal when in the germline (e.g. Proteus syndrome), there is no correlate of generalized disease. Sometimes, a more severe segmental lesion is superimposed upon the background of a generalized autosomal dominant disease. Superimposed (type 2) mosaicism has been proven on a molecular level in Hailey–Hailey disease, Darier disease 10 , PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome 11 , NF1, and basal cell nevus syndrome. Clonal loss of heterozygosity leading to clinical manifestations may also occur in carriers of autosomal recessive skin conditions such as epidermal dysplasia-skin fragility syndrome and autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis 12,12a ( Fig. 62.2D ). The opposite phenomenon – regional absence of skin disease attributed to a correcting mutation (revertant mosaicism) – can occur in both autosomal recessive and autosomal dominant conditions, including ichthyosis with confetti and several forms of epidermolysis bullosa (EB) 13,14 ( Fig. 62.2C, E ). Revertant mosaicism has therapeutic potential and has been employed to create pluripotent stem cells and autologous grafts for patients with recessive dystrophic EB 15,16 . Mosaic skin conditions can also be categorized based upon the nature of the corresponding generalized condition ( Table 62.3 ). When assessing a linear skin disorder, it is helpful to consider what the most likely diagnosis would be were the condition to affect the entire skin surface. While the lesional morphology and histology of the mosaic condition are typically similar to the generalized form, the connection may not be immediately obvious due to differences in distribution and overall appearance. If no generalized disorder exists to match the linear lesions, then the patient could have a dominant mutation (autosomal or X-linked) that is only survivable in the mosaic form. Mosaicism for autosomal dominant disorders can arise after fertil- ization (postzygotic/somatic mutation) or less often during gameto- genesis (half-chromatid mutation). Although a simple segmental (type 1) mosaic condition itself is not heritable, there is a risk of passing on the full-blown disorder to the next generation if mutant cells are present not just in the skin but also in the gonads (gonadal mosaicism). APPROACH TO MOLECULAR TESTING FOR GENOMIC MOSAICISM Although mosaic mutations are sometimes present in the peripheral blood (especially when findings are widespread), a sample of affected tissue (e.g. skin biopsy specimen) is more likely to contain mutant cells. In addition to the skin biopsy, it is often recommended that a blood sample be sent for comparative analysis. For DNA-based tests (including whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing, multi-gene panels, and arrays), DNA can be extracted directly from the skin biopsy, which is typically used in its entirety if it is not known with certainty which cell type is affected (e.g. keratinocytes vs melanocytes). Many phenotypically distinct mosaic diseases have been found to have the same genetic basis and therefore have been grouped together as part of a spectrum. For example, depending on the cell type(s) affected, manifestations of the PIK3CA -related overgrowth spectrum (PROS) can include vascular malformations, lipomatosis, and epidermal nevi. This enables genotype-driven targeted therapies, such as treatment of PROS with phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) inhibitors, when the genetic etiology has been identified 17a . Sons who inherit the abnormal X chromosome carry and express the mutation in all cells; if “recessive”, the disorder is generally compatible with survival (e.g. hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia), but if “dominant”, the disorder is typically so severe that males die before birth (e.g. incontinentia pigmenti, Goltz syndrome). Occasionally, male patients present with skin lesions following the lines of Blaschko because they themselves are mosaic for an X-linked dominant disorder, and therefore, protected by the presence of some normal X chromosomes. X-chromosome mosaicism in boys and men can result from Klinefelter syndrome (where the extra X chromosome permits lyonization) or a postzygotic or half-chromatid mutation (see Tables 62.1 and 62.4 ). Lyonization occurs synchronously in all cells at about the 1000-cell stage, so the two clones are intimately mixed from the beginning. Female patients with X-linked genodermatoses typically have numerous skin lesions that follow the lines of Blaschko in narrow bands. A curious exception is CHILD ( c ongenital h emidysplasia with i chthyosiform nevus and l imb d efects) syndrome, which characteristically shows large unilateral blocks of abnormal skin. This lateralization pattern may reflect the effects of expression of the mutant versus normal X-chromosome in organizer cells that control large developmental fields. Alternatively, a deficiency in sonic hedgehog signaling (which normally helps to confer left–right asymmetry) in cells expressing the NSDHL mutation may result in selection against these cells on one side of the body. Genodermatoses History Although Garrod probably first described IP in 1906, Bloch’s 1926 report of a “previously unreported pigment disorder” and that 2 years later by Sulzberger are remembered eponymously. In 2000, the International Incontinentia Pigmenti Consortium established that IP is caused by mutations in IKBKG , which encodes inhibitor of nuclear factor κ B kinase regulatory subunit γ , also known as NEMO ( N F- κ B e ssential mo dulator). Genetics IP is an X-linked dominant disorder, usually antenatally lethal in boys, that is caused by mutations in IKBKG located at Xq28 18 . Approximately 80% of patients have a common large deletion of exons 4–10 that tends to arise during paternal meiosis (male gametogenesis). Occasional occur- rences of clinically typical IP in boys are attributed to Klinefelter syndrome (~10% of male patients) or to genomic mosaicism due to a half-chromatid or postzygotic NEMO mutation ( Table 62.4 ) 19

Pathogenesis The NEMO protein is a subunit of a kinase that activates NF- κ B, a transcription factor that protects against TNF- α -induced apoptosis ( Fig. 62.4 ). Defective linear ubiquitination has been described in association with a truncated NEMO protein 19b . The idea of IP as a pro-apoptotic state explains male lethality, destruction of epidermal cells, and progressive replacement of cells expressing the mutant X chromosome by those expressing the normal allele 18 . In one report, a liveborn boy whose mother had classic IP died hours after birth due to lethal hematopoietic and immunologic disturbances 20 . Milder hypomorphic NEMO mutations are responsible for hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia with immune deficiency (HED-ID) in boys, whose mothers often have relatively subtle features of IP (see Table 62.4 and Ch. 63 ) 21 . Milder hypomorphic NEMO mutations are responsible for hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia with immune deficiency (HED-ID) in boys, whose mothers often have relatively subtle features of IP (see Table 62.4 and Ch. 63 ) 21 . Clinical features IP typically presents with linear erythema and vesicles (stage 1) during the first few weeks to months of life in an otherwise healthy baby girl (see Fig. 34.13 ) 22 . Vesiculobullous lesions are most common on the limbs and scalp, frequent on the trunk, and rare on the face ( Fig. 62.5A ). They resolve within days to weeks and are often replaced by verrucous linear plaques (stage 2) that favor the extremities ( Fig. 62.5B ) and usually disappear later in infancy. Streaks and swirls of reticulate grayish-brown hyperpigmentation (stage 3) develop next and have a predilection for the trunk and intertriginous sites, with scalloped edges that are thought to reflect the growth of normal keratinocytes into affected skin ( Fig. 62.5B, C ). Gray-brown dots in a linear array represent a characteristic dermoscopic finding of stage 3 IP. The inflammatory sequence sometimes recurs within pigmented areas during later infancy or childhood together with intercurrent febrile illnesses. In addition, acral keratotic nodules (including subungual lesions) occasionally arise after puberty ( Fig. 62.5D ). The hyperpigmented streaks tend to fade by adolescence, although a few areas of slate-gray pigmentation may persist lifelong. From puberty onward, linear hypopigmented bands lacking hair and sweat glands (stage 4) appear on the posterior aspects of the limbs (especially the calves; Fig. 62.5E ) and may be the only stigmata of the disease during adulthood 23 . Individual stages of IP may be absent or overlap. Extracutaneous manifestations of this condition are listed in Table 62.5 . Pathology The early inflammatory phase of IP demonstrates eosinophilic spongiosis and scattered dyskeratotic keratinocytes. The epidermis of verrucous lesions is acanthotic with hyperkeratosis and foci of dyskeratosis. In stage 3, there is pigmentary incontinence as well as variable vacuolization of basal keratinocytes, whereas stage 4 is charac- terized by a thinned epidermis and dermis devoid of adnexa 23 . Differential diagnosis Neonatal IP can usually be distinguished from infectious conditions (e.g. herpes zoster, varicella, herpes simplex viral infections) by the wellbeing of the child and characteristic patterning of the skin lesions. Genodermatoses Treatment Baseline and longitudinal ophthalmologic (especially during infancy) and neurologic evaluations represent the most important aspects of IP management early in life 17b . Prompt laser therapy can reduce the likelihood of visual sequelae in patients with retinal vasculopathy 23a . MRI and electroencephalogram are indicated for infants with neuro- logic symptoms, and European consensus guidelines also recommend a brain MRI at ~2 years of age in children without neurologic manifes- tations 17b . Initial dental assessment is recommended at 2-3 years of age, with further intervention by specialists as indicated. The mother should be examined for subtle atrophic streaks, usually most visible on the calves, and genetic testing can assist with family planning. Rare cases of transmission from a mosaic father to a daughter have been reported 23b . Hypohidrotic Ectodermal Dysplasia With Immune Deficiency This condition is discussed in detail in Chapter 63 . Mosaicism and Linear Lesions Genetics Goltz syndrome is an X-linked dominant condition caused by mutations in PORCN , with the mosaic distribution of skin lesions in female patients reflecting lyonization. Although Goltz syndrome is antenatally lethal in boys with non-mosaic hemizygous mutations (as in IP; see Table 62.4 ), male patients with genomic (e.g. due to a postzy- gotic mutation) or functional (in the setting of Klinefelter syndrome) mosaicism account for ~10% of affected individuals. Approximately 95% of all Goltz syndrome cases are sporadic, which likely reflects both a decreased likelihood of reproduction by severely affected women and the lethality of PORCN mutations with widespread expression. Some authors have postulated that either preferential inactivation of the mutant X chromosome or a postzygotic mutation is required for survival of affected female fetuses 24 . Rare familial cases often show anticipation, with the offspring being more severely affected than the parent and having a higher proportion of cells expressing the mutant X chromosome. The possibility that an apparently normal mother is a carrier must therefore be considered. Pathogenesis PORCN belongs to the evolutionarily conserved porcupine gene family and is expressed in the skin, craniofacial and long bones, tooth buds, and eyes – structures affected in Goltz syndrome. PORCN is an endoplasmic reticulum protein with multiple transmembrane domains. It functions as an O-acyltransferase involved in palmitoylation and secretion of Wnt, a morphogen important in ectomesodermal tissue development 24,25 . Wnt signaling stimulates fibroblast proliferation, inhibits adipogenesis, and induces osteogenesis, explaining the dermal hypoplasia, fat “herniations”, and osteopathia striata (streaks of decreased bone density) observed in Goltz syndrome. Wnt also has key roles in early limb patterning and tooth formation. Although the primary cutaneous abnormality in Goltz syndrome is in the dermis, the

It functions as an O-acyltransferase involved in palmitoylation and secretion of Wnt, a morphogen important in ectomesodermal tissue development 24,25 . Wnt signaling stimulates fibroblast proliferation, inhibits adipogenesis, and induces osteogenesis, explaining the dermal hypoplasia, fat “herniations”, and osteopathia striata (streaks of decreased bone density) observed in Goltz syndrome. Wnt also has key roles in early limb patterning and tooth formation. Although the primary cutaneous abnormality in Goltz syndrome is in the dermis, the distribution of skin lesions along the lines of Blaschko reflects embryonic migration pathways of epidermal cells. Ectoderm-specific deletion of PORCN in mice has shown that expression of this gene in the epidermis and resultant Wnt signaling regulate development of the underlying dermis and fat 26 . Of note, patients with Goltz syndrome have a thin epidermis and abnormal adnexal structures. This is not surprising considering that Wnt signaling, including β -catenin-dependent pathways, is known to have critical roles in epidermal regeneration and adnexal morphogenesis/ maintenance (see Fig. 55.6 ). In 3 of 24 patients in one series, a microdeletion affected both PORCN and the adjacent EBP gene responsible for Conradi–Hünermann–Happle syndrome (see below). Curiously, however, these patients showed no features of the latter disorder. This implies that the PORCN -related hypoplastic skin phenotype predominates over the ichthyosis and follicular changes of Conradi–Hünermann–Happle syndrome 24 . Clinical features The phenotype of Goltz syndrome is highly variable, depending on the proportion and distribution of cells expressing the mutant X chromosome 25,27 . Streaks of vermiculate dermal atrophy and/or telan- giectasias are often present from birth ( Fig. 62.6A–C ). Later, hypo- and hyperpigmentation as well as “herniations” of fat develop. Although “raspberry-like” papillomas with a verrucous surface and fibrovascular core may appear in any location, they favor the anogenital region as well as the lips ( Fig. 62.6D ), larynx, and acral sites. Limb malformations affect > 80% of patients and include ectrodactyly (split hand/foot malformation), asymmetric syndactyly, oligodactyly, and long bone reduction defects. Radiographs of the midportion of the lower extremities characteristically show osteopathia striata. Eye abnormalities, often unilateral, include iritic and chorioretinal colobomas, microphthalmia, anophthalmia, and cataracts. Dystrophic nails (e.g. longitudinal fissures, hypoplasia), sparse hair, abnormal teeth (e.g. vertical grooving, hypodontia), and dysmorphic facies (e.g. notched nasal alae, pointed chin, large malformed ears) may be observed. Eye abnormalities, often unilateral, include iritic and chorioretinal colobomas, microphthalmia, anophthalmia, and cataracts. Dystrophic nails (e.g. longitudinal fissures, hypoplasia), sparse hair, abnormal teeth (e.g. vertical grooving, hypodontia), and dysmorphic facies (e.g. notched nasal alae, pointed chin, large malformed ears) may be observed. Other reported features include aplasia cutis congenita, ventral body wall defects, cleft lip/palate, obstructive sleep apnea, gastro- intestinal dysfunction, impaired hearing, intellectual impairment, and anomalies of the CNS, spine, urinary tract, or uterus. Pathology Affected skin shows a marked reduction in the thickness of the dermis, with fewer adnexal structures 25 . As a consequence of the decreased dermal thickness, adipose tissue may be found just below the epidermis. An increase in papillary dermal blood vessels may also be seen. Differential diagnosis The distinctive cutaneous and extracutaneous findings of Goltz syndrome, especially dermal atrophy/fat “herniations” and osteopathia striata, distinguish it from other X-linked dominant genodermatoses. Examples of such conditions include MIDAS (which does not involve the distal extremities), Conradi–Hünermann–Happle, and oral–facial– digital type 1 syndromes. Although an inflammatory component is occasionally observed, the skin lesions of Goltz syndrome are relatively static compared to the evolving lesions of IP. Treatment Treatment is supportive, with appropriate subspecialist referral based on the associated abnormalities. The telangiectasias may be improved by pulsed dye laser treatment. Troublesome exophytic papillomas can be treated with curettage or photodynamic therapy. Conradi–Hünermann–Happle Syndrome (X-Linked Dominant Chondrodysplasia Punctata) This rare X-linked dominant disorder presents in female neonates with ichthyosiform erythroderma characterized by feathery, adherent scale distributed along the lines of Blaschko (see Ch. 57 ). Characteristic extracutaneous findings include asymmetric shortening of the proximal limbs with epiphyseal stippling (chondrodysplasia punctata) and ocular anomalies such as cataracts and microphthalmia 28 . Patients often have swirled cicatricial alopecia and coarse, lusterless hair. After infancy, the skin changes evolve into follicular atrophoderma. Conradi– Hünermann–Happle syndrome is caused by mutations in the emopamil binding protein ( EBP ) gene 29 , which lies on the X chromosome adjacent to PORCN and encodes an isomerase essential for cholesterol biosyn- thesis. The cardinal biochemical abnormality is increased plasma 8(9)-cholestenol and 8-dehydrocholesterol 28 . Linear Skin Defects With Multiple Congenital Anomalies (Including MIDAS Syndrome) Linear skin defects with multiple congenital anomalies (LSDMCA) represents a group of X-linked dominant conditions that are antena- tally lethal in males and characterized by mi crophthalmia, d ermal a plasia, and s clerocornea (MIDAS syndrome; see Table 64.4 ) 32 . Aplastic linear skin lesions with stellate borders are usually confined to the face and neck. Other reported features include agenesis of the corpus callosum, developmental delay, short stature, cardiac anomalies, and genital malformations. LSDMCA can be caused by mutations in several genes that encode mitochondrial enzymes – HCCS (holocyto- chrome c synthase), COX7B (cytochrome c oxidase), and NDUFB11 (NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase subunit B11) 33 .
