Oral–Facial–Digital Syndrome Type I Oral–facial–digital syndrome type I is an X-linked dominant condition characterized by cleft (or pseudocleft) lip/palate, lobulations and hamartomas of the tongue, hypertrophic oral frenula associated with alveolar clefts, digital malformations, structural brain abnormalities, intellectual disability, polycystic kidneys, facial milia (primarily during infancy), and patchy alopecia that is typically whorled at the vertex. It is caused by mutations in OFD1 , which encodes a centrosomal protein located at the base of primary (non-motile) cilia 34 . The latter structures are present on most cells and mediate signaling pathways such as Hedgehog and Wnt during embryonic development. X-linked Etiologies of Blaschko-Linear Hypo- and Hyperpigmentation Several X-linked disorders can present with hypo- or hyperpigmentation along the lines of Blaschko in affected girls and women. Börjeson- Forssman-Lehmann syndrome , due to germline mutations in PHF6 , presents with Blaschko-linear hyperpigmentation that favors the axillae; additional features include dental and digital anomalies, hypoplastic nails, intellectual disability, and facial features such as prominent supraorbital ridges and frontotemporal hypotrichosis 34a . TFE3-associated neurodevelopmental disorder is characterized by linear hypopigmentation or (less often) hyperpigmentation as well as lysosomal storage disorder-like findings such as skeletal anomalies, intellectual disability, seizures, and coarse facial features. Although most affected individuals are female, there are reports of male patients with this disorder, some of whom were shown to be mosaic 34b . The TFE3 transcription factor functions in mTOR signaling and has roles in lysosomal biogenesis and embryonic stem cell differentiation 34b . Female-restricted X-linked syndromic intellectual development disorder-99 due to germline mutations in USP9X (encodes ubiquitin- specific peptidase 9) is associated with pigmentary alteration (hypopig- mentation documented) along the lines of Blaschko in the majority of patients 34c . Other features include structural brain abnormalities, facial dysmorphism, cleft palate, short stature, polydactyly, cardiac defects, breast underdevelopment, and scoliosis 34c . Lesions EPIDERMAL NEVI AND RELATED SYNDROMES Classification and Clinical Features of Epidermal Nevi Epidermal nevi represent a heterogeneous group of mosaic lesions that are typically distributed along the lines of Blaschko, although those with a later developmental origin may be smaller with a round to oval shape. They may be warty, smooth, or barely palpable; brown, pink, yellow, tan, or hypopigmented ( Fig. 62.7 ); localized or extensive; unilateral or widespread; and isolated or (for more extensive lesions) associated with extracutaneous abnormalities. The appearance is affected by both the age of the patient and the site of the lesion. Epidermal nevi are often whitish or pink in color and macerated at birth. Sometimes they first become evident later in infancy or seem to extend over time, a phenomenon parents find worrisome and difficult to reconcile with the term “birthmark”. Epidermal nevi may be purely keratinocytic or demonstrate organoid differentiation (see Chs. 109 & 111 ). Organoid subtypes include nevus sebaceus, Munro acne nevus, nevus comedonicus, woolly (or rarely straight) hair nevus, linear syringocystadenoma papilliferum, and porokeratotic adnexal ostial nevus ( Table 62.6 and Fig. 62.8 ). A nevus sebaceus typically presents as a congenital hairless plaque on the scalp or face, with a characteristic yellowish-pink to orange-brown color and waxy texture (see Fig. 62.8A ). These lesions tend to thicken after puberty and can become verrucous. In a patient with widespread epidermal nevi, it is not uncommon for lesions to be keratinocytic on the trunk and extremities but have sebaceous differentiation when they involve the head and neck region. In general, epidermal nevi on the scalp tend to have overlying alopecia or hair with an abnormal (e.g. woolly) texture (see Fig. 62.8B ). Keratinocytic epidermal nevi can be divided clinically into inflam- matory (e.g. inflammatory linear verrucous epidermal nevi [ILVEN]) (see below and Ch. 109 ) and noninflammatory categories. The latter may be further classified histologically into non-epidermolytic and epidermolytic variants ( Fig. 62.9 ), although this is not an absolute distinction and even organoid nevi occasionally display epidermolysis. Keratinocytic epidermal nevi are often thicker and more pronounced within skin folds (see Fig. 62.7B ), where they can have an appearance similar to acanthosis nigricans; softening and decreased hyperkeratosis may also be observed in intertriginous sites. RAVEN, also referred to as nevoid acanthosis nigricans, is characterized by lesions with a distinctive rounded outline arranged in a linear pattern 34d . Patients with PENS present with congenital skin-colored or pinkish hyperkeratotic papules or small plaques that are typically circular/ovoid or polygonal in shape, with only one report to date of a lesion following the lines of Blaschko 34e,34f . Although usually sporadic, familial cases have been reported as have associated neurodevelopmental abnormalities 34e,34f . Characteristic histopatho- logic findings include basal cells with palisaded nuclei in a pattern reminiscent of a city skyline 34e . Genetics of Epidermal Nevi The genetic bases of multiple types of epidermal nevi have been estab- lished 35–49 (see Table 62.6 ). Several variants as well as their syndromic associations (see below) are caused by activating postzygotic mutations in genes that encode proteins in two major signaling pathways: (1) RAS/MAPK (mitogen-activated protein kinase), resulting in mosaic RASopathies (see Fig. 55.4 ); and (2) FGFR (fibroblast growth factor receptor)/PIK3CA (phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase catalytic subunit α )/AKT1, which is negatively regulated by PTEN (phosphatase and tensin homolog) (see Fig. 55.3 ). For example, mosaic HRAS or KRAS mutations account for ~ 40% of noninflammatory, non-epidermolytic keratinocytic epidermal nevi, with FGFR2/3 or PIK3CA mutations in another ~ 50% of these lesions 35,36 ( Fig. 62.10 ). subset of keratinocytic epidermal nevi that includes RAVEN, which can also result from FGFR3 mutations 43 . Mutations in either HRAS or BRAF , whose protein product is also in the RAS/MAPK pathway, have been identified in woolly hair nevi 49 ( see Fig. 62.8B ), and BRAF mutations can result in linear syringocystadenoma papilliferum. Epidermal Nevus Syndromes Introduction “Epidermal nevus syndromes” (ENSs) represent a group of heteroge- neous disorders in which keratinocytic and organoid epidermal nevi are associated with ocular, neurologic, and/or musculoskeletal abnor- malities 50–53 . Schimmelpenning syndrome can be caused by somatic mutations in HRAS or KRAS 52 , and the genetic etiologies of other ENSs are presented in Table 62.6 . Overgrowth syndromes resulting from activation of the PIK3CA/AKT1 pathway include Proteus syndrome, PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome (PHTS), and the PIK3CA -related overgrowth spectrum (PROS). These disorders, which are discussed below and summarized in Table 104.5 can have cutaneous manifes- tations including lipomatosis and vascular malformations as well as epidermal nevi. Additional skin findings that have been described in association with epidermal nevi include hypo- or hyperpigmentation (e.g. café-au-lait macules [CALMs]) in a mosaic distribution, melano- cytic nevi (e.g. in phakomatosis pigmentokeratotica; see below), and aplasia cutis congenita. History and terminology Reports of epidermal nevi occurring in conjunction with abnormalities in other organ systems date back over a century. Various authors are credited with descriptions of these associations, including Jadassohn, Schimmelpenning, Feuerstein, and Mims. Solomon and Esterly reviewed epidermal nevi and related extracutaneous findings in 1973 50 , and Solomon is often credited with the term “epidermal nevus syndrome”. Happle later extended ENSs to encompass multiple additional mosaic entities such as Proteus and CHILD syndromes 51 , while others limited the term to the Schimmelpenning phenotype classically associated with sebaceous nevi 53 . Phakomatosis Pigmentokeratotica, Schimmelpenning Syndrome, and Cutaneous Skeletal Hypophosphatemia Syndrome Phakomatosis pigmentokeratotica ( phakomatosis spilosebacea ) is defined as the association of a nevus spilus (see below and Ch. 112 ) with a nevus sebaceus, while Schimmelpenning syndrome is the term classically used for the association of extracutaneous findings with a nevus sebaceus. These clinical diagnoses exist on a spectrum, as they result from mosaic HRAS or, for a small subset of Schimmelpenning syndrome, mosaic KRAS mutations 34,57 . Additional cutaneous features may include keratinocytic epidermal nevi and CALMs, with the latter potentially representing a nevus spilus prior to the appearance of super- imposed

spilus (see below and Ch. 112 ) with a nevus sebaceus, while Schimmelpenning syndrome is the term classically used for the association of extracutaneous findings with a nevus sebaceus. These clinical diagnoses exist on a spectrum, as they result from mosaic HRAS or, for a small subset of Schimmelpenning syndrome, mosaic KRAS mutations 34,57 . Additional cutaneous features may include keratinocytic epidermal nevi and CALMs, with the latter potentially representing a nevus spilus prior to the appearance of super- imposed nevi. The distributions of the various skin findings can be overlapping or distinct. Extracutaneous manifestations of these mosaic RASopathies most often involve the CNS (e.g. hemimegalencephaly, seizures, hemipa- resis, intellectual impairment) 53 , eye (e.g. [lipo]dermoids, colobomata, choristomas), and skeleton (e.g. hemihypertrophy, scoliosis). Epidermal nevi involving the head are thought to be more likely to have associated cerebral defects than those in other sites, although this has not been systematically evaluated. Neurologic abnormalities are also more likely when sebaceous nevi on the scalp are linear rather than round, presumably reflecting their earlier origin and the consequent wider tissue dissemination (see Table 62.2 ). Epidermal nevi due to RAS mutations have also been associated with extracutaneous malignancies, in particular rhabdomyosarcoma and urothelial carcinoma, which occur at increased frequency in patients with Costello syndrome due to germline HRAS mutations (see Table 97.7 ). The cutaneous skeletal hypophosphatemia syndrome may occur in patients with an extensive keratinocytic and/or sebaceous nevus caused by particular HRAS and NRAS mutations 48 . Affected individuals develop vitamin D-resistant rickets due to overproduction of fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF-23), which is normally secreted by osteocytes to regulate vitamin D and phosphate homeostasis. There are reports of successful treatment with the FGF23 inhibitor burosumab or the MEK inhibitor trametinib, with the latter also leading to improvement of the patient’s nevus sebaceus 48a,48b . PIK3CA-Related Overgrowth Spectrum (PROS) PROS encompasses a variety of mosaic conditions with dermatologic manifestations, including: CLOVE(S) syndrome ( c ongenital l ipomatous o vergrowth, v ascular malformations, e pidermal nevi, s coliosis/skeletal/ spinal anomalies); megalencephaly-capillary malformation; CLAPO syndrome ( c apillary and l ymphatic malformations of the tongue/neck with a symmetry and p artial o vergrowth); Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome; fibroadipose hyperplasia/overgrowth; and hemihyperplasia multiple lipomatosis 53a,53b . Depending on the tissue(s) involved, characteristic findings in addition to epidermal nevi (which are present in a subset of patients) include asymmetric overgrowth, lipomatosis, and vascular malformations (see Table 104.5

syndrome ( c ongenital l ipomatous o vergrowth, v ascular malformations, e pidermal nevi, s coliosis/skeletal/ spinal anomalies); megalencephaly-capillary malformation; CLAPO syndrome ( c apillary and l ymphatic malformations of the tongue/neck with a symmetry and p artial o vergrowth); Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome; fibroadipose hyperplasia/overgrowth; and hemihyperplasia multiple lipomatosis 53a,53b . Depending on the tissue(s) involved, characteristic findings in addition to epidermal nevi (which are present in a subset of patients) include asymmetric overgrowth, lipomatosis, and vascular malformations (see Table 104.5 ). Proposed diagnostic criteria require documentation of a mosaic PIK3CA mutation, which can be done via genetic analysis (e.g. an overgrowth syndrome panel) of DNA extracted from a biopsy of affected skin 53a . Although there is some clinical overlap with Proteus syndrome (see below), PROS is distinguished by congenital, less progressive overgrowth, and the cerebriform connective tissue nevi that charac- terize Proteus syndrome are typically absent 53a,53b . Management of PROS depends on the types and distribution of the clinical manifestations. Patients with PROS have an increased risk of venous thromboembolism, with potential contributing factors including venous malformations, impaired mobility, decreased anticoagulant proteins, and effects of the underlying mutation on the vascular endothe- lium 53c . There is debate regarding whether routine screening for Wilms tumor via serial abdominal ultrasounds until age 8 years is indicated, as only a few Wilms tumors have been reported in PROS patients 53b . Targeted therapy with the PI3K inhibitor alpelisib is FDA-approved for patients ≥ 2 years of age with severe manifestations of PROS. In a retrospective study (n = 32 patients), administration of alpelisib for 24 weeks improved vascular malformations and overgrowth in ~ 75% of PROS patients. A 6-month course of low-dose oral sirolimus was also found to result in a small reduction in the bulk of affected tissues in PROS patients, but adverse effects (e.g. infections, cytopenias) were common. Proteus Syndrome Proteus syndrome is a rare mosaic disorder characterized by overgrowth of a variety of tissues due to activating mutations in AKT1 . The 1999 diagnostic criteria were revised in 2019 to include the genotype as well as clinical manifestations 54 . A hallmark of Proteus syndrome is progressive and disproportionate postnatal overgrowth, which is distinct from the relatively stable congenital overgrowth seen in PROS. Manifestations of overgrowth in Proteus syndrome include asymmetric macrodactyly or limb gigantism, typically with abnormal bones and soft tissue in the affected areas, as

by overgrowth of a variety of tissues due to activating mutations in AKT1 . The 1999 diagnostic criteria were revised in 2019 to include the genotype as well as clinical manifestations 54 . A hallmark of Proteus syndrome is progressive and disproportionate postnatal overgrowth, which is distinct from the relatively stable congenital overgrowth seen in PROS. Manifestations of overgrowth in Proteus syndrome include asymmetric macrodactyly or limb gigantism, typically with abnormal bones and soft tissue in the affected areas, as well as scoliosis related to megaspon- dylodysplasia. Another characteristic feature is cerebriform palmar or plantar connective tissue nevi, which tend to expand and thicken during childhood and adolescence 55,56 . EN in patients with Proteus syndrome are often “soft” but have variable clinical morphologies 56 . Other cutaneous manifestations include slow-flow vascular malfor- mations, papulonodular connective tissue nevi on the face and digits, patchy dermal hypoplasia, hyper- and hypopigmented macules/patches, asymmetric hypertrichosis, and abnormal fat deposition resulting in lipomas and/or lipoatrophy 56,56a . Management of Proteus syndrome includes genetic analysis (e.g. an overgrowth syndrome panel) of DNA from affected tissue and radio- logic evaluation to assess and monitor bony and soft tissue disease. Similar to PROS, patients with Proteus syndrome have an elevated risk of venous thromboembolism, which represents the leading cause of death in this condition and requires individualized surveillance and management 56b . Targeted therapy with the AKT inhibitor miransertib has shown promising results in early clinical studies 56c . Mosaicism and Linear Lesions Superimposed (Type 2) Mosaic PTEN Hamartoma Tumor Syndrome The growth-promoting PIK3CA/AKT pathway that is activated in the affected tissues of Proteus syndrome patients is negatively regulated by PTEN (see Fig. 55.3 ). In the autosomal dominant PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome (PHTS, including Cowden syndrome; see Ch. 63 ), patients have a heterozygous germline PTEN mutation, and the hamar- tomas/tumors result from a “second hit” causing loss of heterozygosity. The same mechanism, occurring earlier during embryogenesis, can lead to a “Proteus-like” phenotype distinguished from true Proteus syndrome by macrocephaly, thicker and more verrucous epidermal nevi, vascular anomalies with a fast-flow component, and a lack of cerebriform palmo- plantar connective tissue nevi. PTEN negatively regulates mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) signaling downstream of AKT1. The mTOR inhibitor sirolimus has been anecdotally reported to slow overgrowth in superimposed mosaic PHTS 56 , and further investigation of this agent in PHTS is in progress. ILVEN (Inflammatory Linear Verrucous Epidermal Nevus) ILVEN represents a spectrum of inflammatory mosaic disorders that manifest as linear, erythematous, scaly plaques that follow the lines of Blaschko and are characteristically pruritic 57 ( Fig. 62.12 ; see Ch. 109 ). While occasionally present at birth, ILVEN usually appears during childhood (or, less often, adult life) and extends over months to years. It responds temporarily, if at all, to topical anti-inflammatory agents and rarely remits spontaneously. Reported genetic etiologies of ILVEN include heterozygous postzygotic mutations in GJA1 (encoding connexin 43; mosaic erythrokeratodermia variabilis et progressiva) and CARD14 as well as germline plus postzy- gotic mutations in ABCA12 (mosaic autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis) 57,57a,57b . The differential diagnosis of ILVEN includes linear psoriasis (see Fig. 62.15 ), which may be difficult to distinguish but tends to be less recalcitrant to therapy, and secondary inflammation within an epidermal nevus (e.g. with an underlying postzygotic HRAS or KRT10 mutation). Linear porokeratosis (e.g. due to germline plus super- imposed somatic PMVK mutations) can mimic ILVEN clinically and histologically, with potential misinterpretation of the cornoid lamella as alternating ortho- and parakeratosis 57 . In addition, some patients presenting with an ILVEN phenotype actually have a forme fruste of CHILD syndrome due to a germline NHDSL mutation. An alternative acronym for this variant is PEN/PENCIL ( p soriasiform e pidermal n evus ± c ongenital i psilateral l imb defects) 58 . Knowing the genetic basis of these lesions can direct targeted therapies such as topical statin/choles- terol ( PMVK or NSDHL ) and ustekinumab ( CARD14 ). MOSAICISM IN OTHER AUTOSOMAL DOMINANT DISORDERS Mosaicism for other autosomal dominant disorders may present with a linear or segmental distribution of cutaneous findings that are usually generalized.

Linear Darier Disease (Acantholytic Dyskeratotic Epidermal Nevus) Linear and segmental presentations of Darier disease are usually mor­phologically identical to the generalized form ( Fig. 62.13 ). Heterozygous mutations in ATP2A2 have been found in lesional but not normal-appearing skin, documenting simple segmental (type 1) mosaic Darier disease on a molecular level 59 . Genodermatoses increased severity due to a “second hit” in ATP2A2 are found in patients with generalized Darier disease, reflecting superimposed (type 2) mosaicism. Linear Hailey–Hailey Disease (Relapsing Linear Acantholytic Dermatosis) Linear Hailey–Hailey disease is characterized by relapsing erosions and crusting within a segmental area; histologically, acantholysis resem- bling a “dilapidated brick wall” is observed (see Ch. 59 ). Heterozygous postzygotic ATP2C1 mutations reflecting type 1 mosaicism have been identified in such patients. Inactivation of the second ATP2C1 allele (loss of heterozygosity) has also been found in linear regions with earlier and more severe involvement in patients with generalized Hailey–Hailey disease, confirming superimposed (type 2) mosaicism 60 . Linear Porokeratosis Linear porokeratosis is composed of multiple plaques with keratotic borders that represent cornoid lamellae. These plaques are usually congenital and persistent, with a higher risk of developing squamous cell carcinoma than other porokeratosis variants 61 . Linear porokera- tosis sometimes coexists with familial forms of porokeratosis such as disseminated superficial actinic porokeratosis (DSAP), which result from germline heterozygous mutations in genes encoding various enzymes in the mevalonate biosynthesis pathway such as MVD (meval- onate diphosphate decarboxylase; see Fig. 109.8 ). Mosaic “second hit” mutations in MVD and PMVK (phosphomevalonate kinase) have been found

lamellae. These plaques are usually congenital and persistent, with a higher risk of developing squamous cell carcinoma than other porokeratosis variants 61 . Linear porokera- tosis sometimes coexists with familial forms of porokeratosis such as disseminated superficial actinic porokeratosis (DSAP), which result from germline heterozygous mutations in genes encoding various enzymes in the mevalonate biosynthesis pathway such as MVD (meval- onate diphosphate decarboxylase; see Fig. 109.8 ). Mosaic “second hit” mutations in MVD and PMVK (phosphomevalonate kinase) have been found to underlie linear porokeratosis 61a . Pathogenesis-directed topical treatment of linear porokeratosis with cholesterol 2%/lovastatin 2% cream or ointment has been reported 61b . Porokeratotic Adnexal Ostial Nevus (PAON) PAON, which includes the porokeratotic eccrine ostial and dermal duct nevus (PEODDN), features keratotic spines and/or punctate pits with keratotic plugs (see Fig. 111.40 ). Histologically, parakeratotic columns arise from the eccrine ducts and/or hair follicles. PAON is caused by postzygotic mutations in GJB2 , which encodes connexin 26, and therefore represents the mosaic form of the autosomal dominant keratitis–ichthyosis–deafness (KID) syndrome 62 (see Ch. 57 ). Erosions during the neonatal period, development of SCC, and psoriasiform lesions have been described in association with PAON, but extracuta- neous features of KID syndrome have not yet been reported. Linear Basal Cell Nevus Syndrome Superimposed mosaic manifestations of basal cell nevus syndrome can include congenital basaloid skin tumors and palmoplantar pits in a linear pattern. This has been confirmed on a molecular level, with identification of a germline PTCH1 mutation in addition to a “second hit” mutation in affected skin 63 . A heterozygous mosaic PTCH1 mutation has also been identified within multiple superficial BCCs in a Blaschko-linear distribution pattern 63a . Curry-Jones and Happle-Tinschert Syndromes Curry-Jones and Happle–Tinschert syndromes, which were described in 1995 and 2008, respectively, represent mosaic disorders with genotypic and phenotypic overlap 64,65 . Both conditions are caused by postzy- gotic activating mutations in the gene encoding Smoothened (SMO), which is inhibited by Patched in the Hedgehog signaling pathway (see of basaloid follicular hamartomas that are variably accompanied by hyperpigmentation, hypopigmentation, atrophoderma, hypertrichosis, and hypotrichosis. Extracutaneous manifestations can include dental, digital, cranial, cerebral, and gastrointestinal anomalies 64–66 . Extracutaneous manifestations can include dental, digital, cranial, cerebral, and gastrointestinal anomalies 64–66 . Mosaic Neurofibromatosis Type 1 and Legius Syndrome Patients with café-au-lait macules (CALMs) and/or neurofibromas limited to a segmental distribution may have a type 1 mosaic form of NF1 or (for CALMs) Legius syndrome due to a postzygotic mutation in the gene encoding neurofibromin or SPRED1 ( sp routy- r elated E VH1 d omain- 1 ), respectively 67,68 (see Ch. 61 ). The distribution of the CALMs, which are often accompanied by lentigines, may be block-like or rarely in a broad Blaschko-linear distribution, sometimes with subtle relative hyperpig- mentation of the background skin. In contrast, neurofibromas usually occur in a segmental pattern. Like other simple segmental (type 1) mosaic conditions with nonlethal underlying mutations, offspring may have full- blown NF1 69 . In addition, plexiform neurofibromas and CALMs represent manifestations of superimposed (type 2) mosaicism (i.e. due to a postzy- gotic “second hit”) in patients with NF1 and (for CALMs) Legius syndrome. Linear or Segmental Angiofibromas and Mosaicism in Tuberous Sclerosis Complex Mosaicism accounts for ~ 5–10% of patients diagnosed with tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) based on clinical criteria, many of whom have relatively mild clinical manifestations but not an obvious segmental distribution of skin lesions 70 . However, mosaic TSC can also present with an asymmetric distribution of facial angiofibromas 70a . Of note, “second hit” mutations have been identified within angiofibromas, fibrous cephalic plaques, and shagreen patches in patients with TSC 70b . Linear or Segmental Benign Tumors Trichoepitheliomas, spiradenomas, and/or cylindromas occasionally occur in a linear distribution. These may represent mosaic forms of autosomal dominant CYLD cutaneous syndrome caused by hetero- zygous germline CYLD mutations, and heterozygous postzygotic CYLD mutations have been identified in clustered cylindromas 71 . A somatic BRAF V600E mutation has been associated with linear syringocystad- enoma papilliferum. Leiomyomas can occur in a segmental pattern as a manifestation of autosomal dominant hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer due to fumarate hydratase mutations, most often representing superim- posed (type 2) mosaicism (i.e. with a germline mutation plus “second hit” in the affected segment). Leiomyomas can occur in a segmental pattern as a manifestation of autosomal dominant hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer due to fumarate hydratase mutations, most often representing superim- posed (type 2) mosaicism (i.e. with a germline mutation plus “second hit” in the affected segment). An autosomal dominant tendency to develop seborrheic keratoses is recognized, although no gene has yet been implicated. An adult onset of seborrheic keratoses distributed along the lines of Blaschko has also been described (see Fig. 62.10B ); in one patient, activating FGFR3 and/ or PIK3CA mutations were variably present within the lesions, some of which showed keratinocytic atypia histologically, but were not found in the background skin 72 . Encephalocraniocutaneous Lipomatosis (Haberland Syndrome) Encephalocraniocutaneous lipomatosis (ECCL) is a rare mosaic condition caused by postzygotic activating mutations in FGFR1 or KRAS 73,74 . Patients present with cerebral malformations, ipsilateral eye abnormalities (usually choristomas), and papulonodular skin lesions including lipomas, fibromas, fibrolipomas, and angiolipomas. These lesions favor the eyelids and scalp, and alopecia overlying scalp lipomas, referred to as nevus psiloliparus , is occasionally associated with aplasia cutis congenita. The cranial and eye lesions are usually unilateral, but lipomas may be found on both sides of the scalp. Of note, germline activating FGFR1 mutations lead to autosomal dominant craniosyn- ostosis and skeletal dysplasia syndromes. Oculocerebrocutaneous (Delleman–Oorthuys) syndrome has similar clinical features and is thought to exist on a spectrum with ECCL 74 . VASCULAR MALFORMATIONS Mosaic mutations have been identified as the cause of multiple types of sporadic and familial vascular malformations (see Ch. 104 ). In addition to the entities discussed below, mosaic mutations underlying lymphatic ( PIK3CA ) and arteriovenous ( MAP2K1, BRAF, KRAS, HRAS ) malforma- tions have also been identified (see Table 104.2 ). Venous and Glomuvenous Malformations Heterozygous somatic activating mutations in TEK , which encodes the TIE-2 endothelial cell tyrosine kinase receptor, or PIK3CA are frequently Mosaicism and Linear Lesions found in sporadic venous malformations . A subset of these lesions therefore represents a simple segmental (type 1) mosaic form of the autosomal dominant multiple cutaneous and mucosal venous malfor- mation syndrome caused by germline TEK mutations 75 . Verrucous venous malformations (“verrucous hemangiomas”) result from hetero- zygous somatic mutations in MAP3K3 (MAPK kinase kinase 3) 76 . Large segmental plaque-type glomuvenous malformations , which are typically congenital, can

A subset of these lesions therefore represents a simple segmental (type 1) mosaic form of the autosomal dominant multiple cutaneous and mucosal venous malfor- mation syndrome caused by germline TEK mutations 75 . Verrucous venous malformations (“verrucous hemangiomas”) result from hetero- zygous somatic mutations in MAP3K3 (MAPK kinase kinase 3) 76 . Large segmental plaque-type glomuvenous malformations , which are typically congenital, can occur as a superimposed (type 2) mosaic manifestation of hereditary glomuvenous malformations due to heterozygous germline GLMN (glomulin) mutations. Capillary Malformations (Port-Wine Birthmarks) Somatic activating mutations in GNAQ are found within affected tissues in most patients with Sturge–Weber syndrome and non-syndromic port- wine birthmarks 77 . This gene encodes a Q-class G protein α -subunit, activation of which increases MAPK signaling. Somatic mutations in GNAQ and the related GNA11 are also found in blue nevi and nevus of Ota. It is therefore not surprising that patients with phakomatosis pigmentovascularis type II have the same activating GNAQ or GNA11 mutation in both their port-wine stain and dermal melanocytosis 78 ( Fig. 62.14 ). Of note, somatic activating mutations in GNAQ , GNA11, GNA14 , and RAS have been identified in congenital hemangiomas (noninvoluting and rapidly involuting variants), pyogenic granu- lomas ( RAS ), and other vascular tumors. GNAQ , GNA11 , and GNA14 mutations have only been reported in mosaic form and are likely otherwise lethal. RASA1 and EPHB4 mutations are responsible for the autosomal dominant capillary malformation–arteriovenous malfor- mation syndrome, in which lesions have been shown to demonstrate loss of heterozygosity 79 . PIGMENTED LESIONS WITH A MOSAIC DISTRIBUTION PATTERN Congenital Melanocytic Nevi (CMN) CMN have more recently been viewed as forms of mosaicism and are discussed in Chapter 112 . In addition to classic CMN , which are categorized based upon their size, the nevus spilus-type CMN is characterized by multiple small to medium-sized CMN superim- posed on a CALM-like background. A single, small classic CMN is the most common presentation. Rarely, numerous widespread classic CMN are seen. Such patients, who sometimes also have a large or giant CMN in a “cape”- or “bathing trunk”-like distribution pattern, are at risk of neurocutaneous melanocytosis and other involvement beyond the skin. The macular background hyperpigmentation is often subtle and may not be evident at birth. McCune–Albright Syndrome McCune–Albright syndrome features large blocks of café-au-lait pigmentation, demarcated at the midline and sometimes following the lines of Blaschko in broad bands, together with polyostotic fibrous dysplasia of the bone and/or endocrine hyperfunction (classically preco- cious puberty). It is due to particular postzygotic activating mutations in GNAS , the gene encoding the α -subunit of the G protein that stimu- lates adenylate cyclase activity. This results in increased signaling in pathways where cyclic AMP acts as a “second messenger”, explaining endocrine overactivities and increased pigmentation due to stimulation of tyrosinase. Associated bone involvement can be asymptomatic or present with manifestations such as pain, a limp, pathologic fractures, facial asymmetry, and FGF23-related phosphate wasting. Evaluation may include X-rays of the long bones, bone scintigraphy, and laboratory assessment of phosphate homeostasis 83b . LINEAR INFLAMMATORY DISORDERS Several inflammatory skin conditions are occasionally distributed along the lines of Blaschko. When generalized, these disorders are multifac- torial, typically with both a genetic susceptibility and environmental contributions. Linear presentations likely result from mosaicism for a “susceptibility” mutation. In some cases, a streak of more severe disease is superimposed on a generalized background of the same condition, perhaps reflecting clonal loss of heterozygosity 85 . Such conditions provide an opportunity to identify the genes involved in multifactorial cutaneous diseases. Lichen Striatus This self-limited linear inflammatory condition usually occurs during childhood, most commonly on an extremity in an atopic individual (see Ch. 11 ) 89 . The condition is not particularly pruritic, but it has histologic features similar to those of both eczema and lichen planus. Although both lichen striatus and linear lichen planus can be associated with nail dystrophy, postinflammatory hypopigmentation points to the diagnosis of lichen striatus. “Blaschkitis” “Blaschkitis” refers to a rare inflammatory dermatosis that typically presents as pruritic papules and vesicles along multiple lines of Blaschko, particularly on the trunk. More common in adults than children, it follows a relapsing course, with episodes often resolving spontaneously within days. Although the histology is more eczematous and less lichenoid than in lichen striatus, they may represent variants of the same condition 90 . Other Linear Inflammatory Disorders Several other inflammatory disorders occasionally occur in a distri- bution along the lines of Blaschko. These conditions include atopic dermatitis, lupus erythematosus (with morphea-like/“sclerodermiform” features in one variant) 91,92 , dermatomyositis, lichenoid and fixed drug eruptions 93,94 , lichenoid GVHD 95 , morphea 96 , and atrophoderma of Pasini and Pierini (linear atrophoderma of Moulin 97 ; Fig. 62.16 ). Traditionally, such presentations have been split into the disorders described below, but there is consid- erable overlap between these heterogeneous conditions, and distinc- tions can become blurred. Linear and Block-Like Hypo- and Hyperpigmentation Synonyms/variants:  Linear nevoid hypo- and hyperpigmentation  Blaschkoid dyspigmentation  Pigmentary mosaicism  Hypomelanosis of Ito (becoming historical)  Linear and whorled nevoid hypermelanosis  Segmental pigmentation disorder  Incontinentia pigmenti achromians (historical) Key features  Descriptive terms rather than specific diagnoses, with a variety of genetic etiologies  Hypo- or hyperpigmentation following the lines of Blaschko or in a block-like pattern can be evident at birth or appear later  Variable extracutaneous involvement, which can include CNS, musculoskeletal, and ocular abnormalities Introduction Hypo- or hyperpigmentation following the lines of Blaschko reflects epidermal mosaicism and has a wide variety of genetic etiologies 98 . Block-like hypo- or hyperpigmentation, which has been referred to as “ segmental pigmentation disorder” 99 , is also presumed to result from mosaicism. Associated extracutaneous findings are found in a minority of affected individuals with either distribution pattern 99–101 . History The first published description of hypopigmentation along Blaschko’s lines was by Ito in 1951, resulting in the eponym “hypomelanosis of Ito.” This term is becoming historical and should be reserved for patients with extracutaneous manifestations due to the presence of the mosaic abnormality in tissues other than the skin 98,100,101 . Epidemiology Linear and block-like pigmentary alterations affect both sexes and are typically easier to see in darkly pigmented skin. The areas of patterned hypo- or hyperpigmentation may be apparent at birth or become evident during childhood, especially in those with lightly pigmented skin. Genetics and pathogenesis Blaschko-linear hypo- or hyperpigmentation can have a variety of genetic etiologies, which range from mosaic chromosomal alterations (up to 50% of cases; e.g. trisomy 18 or 20) or point mutations (e.g. MTOR ) to germline X-linked conditions (e.g. Börjeson-Forssman- Lehmann syndrome; see above) and rarely chimerism (see below) 102,103 . Clinical features Streaks and swirls of hypo- or hyperpigmentation along the lines of Blaschko can occur anywhere on the cutaneous surface, with unilateral or bilateral involvement. Superimposed lentigines, hypertrichosis, and alopecia are occasionally observed. Only a small proportion ( < 15–30%) of children with Blaschko-linear hypo- or hyperpigmentation who present to a pediatric dermatologist at a tertiary referral center have extracutaneous abnormalities, which generally became apparent during infancy 100,101 . The extracutaneous abnormalities are highly variable, depending on the genetic etiology and tissues affected; they most often involve the CNS, eyes, and musculoskeletal system. In a recent series, neurodevelopmental abnormalities were significantly more common in children with Blaschko-linear hypopigmentation affecting ≥ 4 vs < 3 of 5 body areas 101a . Block-like hypo- or hyperpigmentation favors the trunk, but any site can be affected. Midline demarcation is more often present ventrally than dorsally, and the lateral borders tend to be less distinct. Segmental hyperpigmentation occasionally coexists with a light red-pink capillary malformation (“phakomatosis melanorosea”). Associated extracuta- neous findings are uncommon, affecting < 2–5% of patients 99 . Some patients have linear streaks of both hypo- and hyperpigmen- tation or a combination of linear and block-like hypopigmentation. When involvement is extensive, it may be difficult to determine whether the lighter or darker skin represents the background color. Associated syndromes The most common known single-gene cause of Blaschko-linear hypopigmentation is mosaic activating MTOR mutations. In a recent French series of 71 patients with “hypomelanosis of Ito”, 15 (21%) had an underlying mosaic MTOR

< 2–5% of patients 99 . Some patients have linear streaks of both hypo- and hyperpigmen- tation or a combination of linear and block-like hypopigmentation. When involvement is extensive, it may be difficult to determine whether the lighter or darker skin represents the background color. Associated syndromes The most common known single-gene cause of Blaschko-linear hypopigmentation is mosaic activating MTOR mutations. In a recent French series of 71 patients with “hypomelanosis of Ito”, 15 (21%) had an underlying mosaic MTOR mutation 103a . Additional findings in affected individuals can include macrocephaly, (hemi)megalencephaly, intellectual disability, seizures, facial dysmorphism, ocular anomalies, and asymmetric overgrowth 103b . RHOA-related neuroectodermal syndrome results from mosaic mutations that lead to inactivation of a RAS-related Rho GTPase. Clinical features include Blaschko-linear hypopigmentation ( Fig. 62.17 ), scarring alopecia, leukoencephalopathy (usually asymptomatic), facial dysmorphism, and hemihypoplasia as well as digital, dental, and ocular anomalies 103c . X-linked syndromes that present with Blaschko-linear hypo- or hyperpigmentation are discussed above. Pallister-Killian syndrome due to mosaic tetrasomy 12p, which usually results from gonadal mosaicism in a parent, is a distinct disorder that presents with hypopigmentation following the lines of Blaschko or in an irregular pattern. Frontotemporal alopecia and hypohidrosis represent additional cutaneous manifestations. Extracutaneous features include facial dysmorphism, intellectual disability, and broad first digits in addition to cardiac, renal, genitourinary, and gastrointestinal abnormalities 104 . Phylloid hypomelanosis in a pattern of leaf-like and floral shapes represents a distinct entity due to mosaic copy number variation involving chromosome 13 105 . Additional features may include telangi- ectatic macules, thick eyebrows, long eyelashes, intellectual disability, agenesis of the corpus callosum, conductive hearing loss, colobomas, and digital anomalies. A few patients with phylloid hypermelanosis have also been reported, with variable extracutaneous manifestations and underlying mosaic chromosomal aberrations (e.g. involving 5p) 105 . Diagnostic consider- ations for block-like hyperpigmentation may include McCune–Albright syndrome, which tends to have darker, sharply demarcated lesions that follow the broad lines of Blaschko, as well as a large CALM, Becker nevus, and early nevus spilus. Evaluation and management A thorough history and physical examination should be performed to assess for extracutaneous involvement, with further evaluation directed by abnormal findings and/or recognition of distinct syndromes (see above). Growth and development should be followed in conjunction with the child’s pediatrician. In patients with extracutaneous abnormalities, identification of the underlying genetic alteration may provide better understanding of the overall diagnosis, help direct further evaluation, and potentially impact future family planning. For example, mosaic MTOR mutations involving the gonads have been implicated in transmission of Smith-Kingsmore syndrome, which presents with megalencephaly, seizures, and intel- lectual disability due to heterozygous germline MTOR mutations. In addition, recognizing the genetic etiology can provide the basis for targeted therapies such as sirolimus or other mTOR inhibitors. Although mosaic mutations are sometimes present in the peripheral blood, a sample of affected tissue (e.g. a skin biopsy specimen) is more likely to contain mutant cells. If no specific single-gene disorder is suspected, genetic testing should start with an assessment for chromo- somal mosaicism, which can be performed via microarray-based tests, e.g. single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) array or array comparative genomic hybridization (CGH). If initial evaluation of DNA from a blood sample is not diagnostic, the test can be repeated on DNA extracted from a 4 mm punch skin biopsy of affected skin. The latter is generally of higher yield than the fibroblast cultures routinely performed by cytogenetics laboratories, as the mutation may not be present in that cell type. Keratinocyte cultures may be of utility when available 102 , and whole exome or whole genome sequencing represents an additional testing option. Nevus Depigmentosus A nevus depigmentosus is another hypopigmented skin lesion that is thought to reflect cutaneous mosaicism. However, it is limited in extent and generally lacks extracutaneous associations. The most common presentation is a localized patch that breaks apart into smaller macules with a mosaic RHOA mutation. CHIMERISM Block-Like Hyper- and Hypopigmentation Due to Chimerism Chimerism differs from mosaicism in that the different clones originate from different organisms. Human chimeras can result from fusion of two zygotes (i.e. fused dizygotic twins) or fertilization of one egg by two sperm. Usually detected by hematologists as anomalous blood groups, or by endocrinologists as ambiguous sexual differentiation, chimerism is exceedingly rare. Findlay and Moores 106 studied more than a million routine blood samples and found evidence of chimerism in only two. Pigmentary variation in chimerism typically presents in a checkerboard pattern; however, streaks along the lines of Blaschko and mixtures of light and dark skin that do not correspond to recognized patterns of mosaicism have also been described 107 . In cases of XX/XY chimerism, the karyotype of dermal fibroblasts does not necessarily correspond to the overlying skin color, probably reflecting the different embryonic migration routes in the dermis and epidermis 9 . text: Susan J. Bayliss, Monique G. Kumar, Ángela Hernández-Martín, Bernard A. Cohen, Teresa Martínez-Menchón, Encarna Guillén-Navarro and Virginia P. Sybert Other Genodermatoses 63 SECTION 9 GENODERMATOSES Three major MEN syndromes with mucocutaneous findings – termed types 1, 2A, and 2B – have been clinically and genetically defined and are described in Table 63.2 1,2 . Mucocutaneous features are most prominent in MEN types 1 and 2B. In MEN1, multiple facial angiofibromas and collagenomas are present another common finding 3,4 . Compared to those in tuberous sclerosis, facial angiofibromas in MEN1 tend to be smaller and fewer in number, and they are more likely to arise on the upper lip and its vermilion border in addition to the nose and medial cheeks. Although melanoma has been reported in patients with MEN1 and there is evidence that MEN1 expression is frequently lost in sporadic melanomas 5,6 , it remains unclear whether individuals with this syndrome have an increased risk of melanoma. MEN2B is notable for multiple mucosal neuromas, especially of the conjunctivae, lips, and anterior tongue ( Fig. 63.2 ). These lesions, which may be evident at birth or develop during early childhood, represent a relatively specific marker that can enable timely diagnosis and thyroidectomy, as medullary thyroid cancer typically develops during the first few years of life in patients with MEN2B 7,8 . However, mucosal neuromas are also occasionally observed in patients with the PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome (PHTS; see below). Cutaneous neuromas are rare in MEN2B and when present are usually in a perinasal location. Macrocephaly and mucocutaneous lesions (e.g. tricholemmomas, acral keratoses, oral papillomas) are the most constant and characteristic features 9 . Up to 85% of CS patients develop at least one malignant neoplasm, most often of the breast, thyroid, or endometrium 10 . Introduction In this chapter, a number of genodermatoses are discussed that are not covered in other chapters of this textbook ( Table 63.1 ). Disorders characterized by cutaneous or mucosal tumors in conjunction with a variety of extracutaneous neoplasias, both benign and malignant, as well as endocrine abnormalities are the focus of the first section. It includes multiple endocrine neoplasia types 1, 2 A, and 2B in addition to PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome (including Cowden syndrome), Gardner syndrome, and Muir–Torre syndrome. This is followed by sections on: enzyme deficiencies; premature aging syndromes and poikilodermas; and ectodermal dysplasias. They named the disorder “Cowden disease” after their first patient. Epidemiology PHTS is probably more common than is reflected by the number of cases reported, because the clinical findings can be subtle. It is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait with variable expressivity; a female predominance has been noted in some series 11 . Most of the reported patients have been White, and it is estimated to affect 1 in 200 000 individuals 12 . Pathogenesis The PTEN protein is a lipid and protein phosphatase that plays a role in cell-cycle regulation and apoptosis 13,14 . In particular, PTEN downregu- lates the PI3K (phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase)/AKT/mTOR (mechanistic target of rapamycin) pathway that promotes cellular proliferation and survival (see Fig. 55.3 ). Like other autosomal dominant disorders caused by a defective tumor suppressor gene, PHTS is caused by a heterozygous germline PTEN mutation, with hamartomas and neoplasms resulting from a “second-hit” somatic mutation that inactivates the remaining allele of the gene (loss of heterozygosity). Lack of PTEN function leads to excessive mTOR signaling in affected tissues, in particular those with physiologic proliferation, such as the epidermis, oral and

text: target of rapamycin) pathway that promotes cellular proliferation and survival (see Fig. 55.3 ). Like other autosomal dominant disorders caused by a defective tumor suppressor gene, PHTS is caused by a heterozygous germline PTEN mutation, with hamartomas and neoplasms resulting from a “second-hit” somatic mutation that inactivates the remaining allele of the gene (loss of heterozygosity). Lack of PTEN function leads to excessive mTOR signaling in affected tissues, in particular those with physiologic proliferation, such as the epidermis, oral and gastro- intestinal mucosa, and thyroid and breast epithelium. PTEN also has phosphatase-independent activities and nuclear functions independent of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway 14 . Clinical presentations of PHTS vary substantially even among patients with the same germline PTEN mutation, and in some families both CS and BRRS phenotypes are observed. Although genotype/phenotype correlations have not been established, mutations leading to an inactive protein may produce a more severe phenotype than those resulting in partially retained protein function 15 . Mosaicism due to a very early postzygotic initial mutation may produce a phenotype with dissemi- nated findings clinically similar to germline disease 16 . Manifestations such as vascular anomalies and epidermal nevi with segmental distri- bution patterns can reflect an early postzygotic second-hit mutation (type 2 mosaicism; see Ch. 62 ) in a patient with a germline mutation, with different clinical findings depending on the tissue type affected. Clinical Features The 2013 revised clinical diagnostic criteria for PHTS are outlined in Mucocutaneous manifestations Cutaneous involvement occurs in > 80% of patients with PHTS and often serves as an early sign of the disorder. Characteristic mucocutaneous lesions usually begin to appear during the second to third decades of life (average, 22 years; range, birth to 75 years). Facial tricholemmomas present as multiple skin-colored to yellowish-tan, verrucous, or keratotic papules that resemble common warts 18 ( Fig. 63.3A ; see Ch. 111 ). Other Genodermatoses Both tricholemmomas and nonspecific cutaneous papules show a predi- lection for the central face, and they may coalesce around facial orifices (especially the nostrils) and on the ears. Papules on the head and neck of PHTS patients may also represent inverted follicular keratoses or acrochordons. Multiple sclerotic fibromas of the skin are a relatively specific cutaneous marker of CS 19 . These lesions present as sharply circum- scribed, firm dermal papules that display a strikingly uniform storiform pattern of collagen bundles on histologic examination (see Ch. 116 ). Punctate palmoplantar keratoses, often translucent with a central depression, are present in more than half of patients 20 ( Fig. 63.4 ). Keratotic papules can also be seen on the heels, the dorsal aspects of the hands and feet, and the extensor surfaces of the forearms and lower legs. Punctate palmoplantar keratoses, often translucent with a central depression, are present in more than half of patients 20 ( Fig. 63.4 ). Keratotic papules can also be seen on the heels, the dorsal aspects of the hands and feet, and the extensor surfaces of the forearms and lower legs. Other skin and soft tissue manifestations include lipomas (especially testicular lipomatosis), angiolipomas, and vascular anomalies. The cutaneous vascular anomalies tend to be fast-flow lesions with intra- muscular involvement and associated ectopic fat 21 . A distinctive “PTEN hamartoma of soft tissue” that presents as a subcutaneous and intra- muscular mass with adipocytic, fibrous, and vascular (arterial, venous) components and sometimes lymphoid, bony, and neural elements has also been described 22 . Lastly, PHTS patients may have a slightly increased risk of melanoma, with a lifetime incidence of ~5% 10 . Oral lesions of PHTS appear as 1–3 mm, asymptomatic, mucosa- colored papules that often lead to a cobblestone appearance ( Fig. 63.3B ). They have a predilection for the lips and tongue, but extensive involvement of the entire oral cavity can occur 20 . Other Genodermatoses Extracutaneous manifestations Multinodular goiter or thyroid adenomas occur in more than two-thirds of patients with PHTS, and the lifetime risk of thyroid carcinoma is estimated to be 10% to > 30%. Fibrocystic disease and fibroadenomas of the breast affect three-quarters of female patients. Breast carcinoma develops in up to 85% of female patients with PHTS and is diagnosed at a mean age of ~40 years 10,23 ; it has also been reported in affected men 24 . Multiple polyps may be found anywhere in the gastrointestinal tract but most frequently affect the colon ( ≥ 85% of patients). The lifetime risk of colon carcinoma is estimated to be ~10% 17,23 . Benign ovarian cysts and uterine leiomyomas commonly develop and endometrial carcinoma occurs in as many as 20%–30% of women with PHTS. The lifetime risk of renal carcinoma is estimated to be as high as ~30% 23 . Pathology Histologically, tricholemmomas are characterized by a lobular prolif- eration of pale keratinocytes, often in association with a hair follicle. Basal keratinocytes are oriented to form a palisade, and hyperkeratosis can lead to a cutaneous horn. Demonstration of complete loss of PTEN expression within a tricholemmoma via immunohistochemical staining is suggestive that the patient has PHTS 25 . Histologically, some facial papules in patients with PHTS may simply be squamous papillomas, while others show follicular infundibular hyperplasia. Oral lesions often represent fibromatous nodules with collagen fibers arranged in whorls. On biopsy, extrafacial and palmoplantar papules tend to be hyperkera- totic papillomas, and they may have changes reminiscent of verrucae or acrokeratosis verruciformis 26 . The clinical differential diagnosis of multiple facial tricholemmomas may include angiofibromas (as seen in tuberous sclerosis complex or MEN1), trichoepitheliomas, and fibrofolliculomas (Birt–Hogg–Dubé syndrome); in addition to their histologic features, the tendency of tricholemmomas to have a verrucous appearance clinically may help to distinguish them from these lesions. The differential diagnosis for SOLAMEN syndrome includes the PIK3CA - related overgrowth spectrum and Proteus syndrome (see Table 104.5 ). Treatment Although the recognition of PHTS is based upon clinical and histo- logic evaluation, genetic testing allows confirmation of the diagnosis and facilitates identification of affected family members. Due to the high risk of malignancy, cancer surveillance is a critical part of PHTS management (see Table 63.3 ). Agents that downregulate the mTOR pathway, such as sirolimus (rapamycin), can lead to improvement in vascular anomalies, lipoma- tosis, cutaneous papules, gastrointestinal polyps, and cerebellar function 27 . It is considered to represent a phenotypic variant of the familial adenomatous polyposis syndrome (FAP) with prominent extraintestinal involvement 28,29 . History In 1951, Gardner described a large family in which colonic polyps and carcinoma were associated with osteomas and “surface tumors”. This FAP phenotype with prominent extraintestinal manifestations continues to bear Gardner’s name. Epidemiology The prevalence of FAP is estimated to be 1 in 7000 to 1 in 30 000 live births. It is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait with high penetrance of the gastrointestinal manifestations but variable expres- sivity of extraintestinal findings, affecting men and women equally. Pathogenesis FAP (including Gardner syndrome) is caused by heterozygous germline mutations in the adenomatous polyposis coli ( APC ) tumor suppressor gene. APC encodes a protein that downregulates the Wnt/ β -catenin signaling pathway, which has important functions in cellular prolif- eration, differentiation, and adhesion (see Fig. 55.6 ). Extraintestinal manifestations (especially desmoid tumors) are more likely in patients with mutations in the distal portion of APC 30,31 . Clinical Features Cutaneous and soft tissue manifestations Skin lesions appear during childhood and adolescence, frequently preceding the onset of polyposis. Cutaneous epidermoid cysts affect ~50% of patients with FAP and are often multiple 31 . The cysts typically begin to appear before puberty and favor the face, scalp, and extrem- ities 31 . Multiple familial pilomatricomas have also been reported as a presentation of Gardner syndrome 32 . Gardner-associated fibromas may occur in the skin, subcuta- neous tissues, mesentery, or retroperitoneum. The fibromas typically arise during the first two decades of life, favor the back (especially the paraspinal region), and can serve as a desmoid tumor precursor. Lipomas, leiomyomas, trichoepitheliomas, and neurofibromas are less frequently observed. Desmoid tumors (also referred to as desmoid fibromatosis) are non-encapsulated, non-metastasizing, locally aggressive tumors that are usually rare but affect 10%–30% of patients with FAP. These lesions arise from musculoaponeurotic structures and can occur spontaneously or at surgical sites. In patients with APC, desmoid tumors most often develop within the abdominal wall or intra-abdominally following colectomy, with the latter location causing greater morbidity via obstruction of the small bowel and/or ureters. In patients with APC, desmoid tumors most often develop within the abdominal wall or intra-abdominally following colectomy, with the latter location causing greater morbidity via obstruction of the small bowel and/or ureters. Extra-abdominal lesions affecting the shoulder girdle, chest wall, or inguinal region can also occur. Although cytologically benign, desmoid tumors represent a potential cause of mortality in FAP, e.g. due to compression of vital organs. Other extraintestinal manifestations Retinal pigment epithelial hamartomas (RPEH) are evident in ~75%–80% of patients with FAP. These lesions may be present at birth, serving as an early and specific sign of the disorder 33,34 ( Fig. 63.5 ). Although often referred to as congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium (CHRPE), FAP-associated pigmented retinal lesions have irregular borders and a haphazard bilateral distribution that differ- entiate them from sporadic multifocal CHRPE 34 . Osteomas occur in ~65%–80% of patients with FAP and favor the frontal bone, mandible, and maxilla, although they can also develop in other bones of the skull and long bones. Seen in children as young as 8 years of age, osteomas are painless and can grow large enough to be clinically obvious or be detectable only by radiographic studies. Other skeletal lesions include exostoses, endostoses, and cortical thickening of the long bones. Dental anomalies are apparent in ~30% of patients with FAP and include supernumerary teeth, odontomas, unerupted teeth, and congenitally missing teeth. pigment epithelial hamartomas in Gardner syndrome. Other Genodermatoses Patients with FAP are at increased risk for the development of other tumors, including papillary carcinoma of the thyroid (particularly in women), hepatoblastoma (usually affecting children < 3 years of age), pancreatic and biliary tract carcinomas, nasal angiofibromas, adrenal adenomas (or occasionally carcinomas), and sarcomas (e.g. fibrosarcoma, osteosarcoma). The association of brain tumors (most often medullo- blastomas) with adenomatous polyposis in patients with heterozygous APC mutations has historically been referred to as Turcot syndrome type 2. The latter is distinct from the constitutional mismatch repair deficiency syndrome (previously referred to as Turcot syndrome type 1) that presents during childhood with brain tumors (primarily glioblas- tomas), colonic polyposis, hematologic malignancies, and multiple café-

The latter is distinct from the constitutional mismatch repair deficiency syndrome (previously referred to as Turcot syndrome type 1) that presents during childhood with brain tumors (primarily glioblas- tomas), colonic polyposis, hematologic malignancies, and multiple café- au-lait macules due to biallelic mutations in mismatch repair genes (see below and Table 61.3 ) 35 . Gastrointestinal manifestations In adults, the diagnosis of FAP is commonly made when the patient presents with gastrointestinal bleeding secondary to adenomatous polyps. Other findings may include anemia, abdominal pain, diarrhea or constipation, and weight loss. Premalignant adenomatous polyps most commonly occur in the colorectum but are also found in the small intestine and stomach in over half of patients. Polyps are typically < 1 cm in diameter and are rarely seen before the age of 10 years. By the age of 20 years, 50% of patients with FAP have demonstrable polyps. Without surgical intervention, colorectal carcinoma is inevitable; it usually develops before age 40 years and arises by early adolescence in ~5% of affected individuals 29,36 . Carcinomas of the small intestine (especially the duodenum) can also occur 29 . Pathology Histologically, intestinal polyps show adenomatous hyperplasia of the mucosa. Cutaneous cysts in patients with FAP usually demon- strate the same microscopic changes as ordinary epidermoid cysts, with a lining of keratinizing epithelium that includes a granular layer. Pilomatricoma-like changes, with characteristic basophilic and shadow cell populations, have also been noted. Differential Diagnosis Although epidermoid cysts represent a common sporadic finding, multiple lesions with onset during childhood should prompt a thorough family history and evaluation for other findings of Gardner syndrome (e.g. RPEH, osteomas). Of note, mutations in the MUTYH base excision repair gene can cause an autosomal recessive form of colorectal adeno- matous polyposis, with osteomas, RPEH, desmoid tumors, pilomatri- comas, and sebaceous neoplasms (see below) having been described in affected individuals 37 . Management The diagnosis of FAP is established by identifying a pathogenic variant in APC in an individual with multiple colorectal adenomatous polyps ( ≥ 100 for an adult pre-colectomy and without a relative with confirmed FAP). Genetic counseling is imperative, and family members should be evaluated for intestinal and extraintestinal signs of the disorder. Because of the inevitable development of colorectal carcinoma, prophylactic colectomy is recommended when polyp formation becomes evident, and it is usually performed between 15 and 25 years of age. Initially, children with FAP should be monitored with sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy every 1–2 years beginning at 10–12 years of age. Once polyps are detected, patients should undergo annual colonoscopy until a colectomy is done. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy is recommended every 6 months to 4 years (depending on polyp burden) beginning at 20–25 years of age, with careful inspection of the ampulla of Vater. Annual physical examination should include evaluation for neurologic deficits and other extraintestinal manifestations, including palpation of the abdomen (for desmoid tumors) and thyroid starting in the late teenage years. If there is a family history of desmoid tumors, abdominal CT or MRI beginning 1–3 years post colectomy and then every 5–10 years should be considered. Because of the increased risk of hepatoblastoma, some experts recommend abdominal ultrasound and measurement of serum α -fetoprotein every 3–6 months during the first 5 years of life. Symptomatic epidermoid cysts can be surgically excised. Desmoid tumors are also treated by surgical excision, although there tends to be a high recurrence rate. Preoperative MRI of the abdomen can demon- strate the origin of the tumor and the extent of involvement. If wide surgical excision fails, radiotherapy, hormonal therapy (e.g. tamoxifen, raloxifene), chemotherapy, or a combination thereof can be tried. The osteomas of FAP may or may not be amenable to surgical intervention. Medications that affect prostaglandin metabolism, such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), may reduce the risk of colorectal cancer and desmoids 38 . It is considered to represent a variant of Lynch syndrome, which is also known as hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC) syndrome 39 . History Muir in 1967 and Torre in 1968 independently reported the syndrome that bears their names. Their two patients had malignancies in several organs plus either keratoacanthoma-like lesions or multiple tumors of sebaceous origin. Epidemiology The male : female ratio in MTS is 3 : 2, and affected individuals present with cutaneous manifestations at a mean age of 55 years. The preva- lence of Lynch syndrome in the general population is estimated to be ~1 in 350. In a study of Lynch syndrome patients, MTS was observed in 28% (14/50) of families and 9% (14/152) of individuals with a confirmed germline mismatch repair gene mutation 40 . Pathogenesis MTS is caused by heterozygous germline mutations in one of several DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes, including MSH2 (90% of MTS cases), MLH1 , and rarely MSH6 or PMS2 . MMR proteins are respon- sible for detecting and repairing DNA replication errors. In patients with MTS, somatic inactivation of the other allele of the affected gene (loss of heterozygosity) results in microsatellite instability, i.e. increased variability in the lengths of repetitive “microsatellite” sequences in the genome, as well as mutations that lead to tumor formation 41 . The skin tumors sometimes appear decades before or after a visceral malig- nancy develops. Clinical Features Sebaceous tumors can present prior to (~30%), concurrently with (~10%), or after (~60%) the diagnosis of a visceral malignancy. The skin tumors sometimes appear decades before or after a visceral malig- nancy develops. In general, sebaceous tumors favor the head and neck region ( Fig. 63.6 ), and sporadic sebaceous carcinomas tend to affect the GENODERMATOSES periocular area. However, in patients with MTS, these neoplasms can occur in other locations (trunk > extremities) 42 . Sebaceous adenomas are the most common tumor type, and they present as slow-growing, yellow to pink papules or nodules, numbering from one to hundreds. Keratoacanthomas, which are keratotic skin-colored to erythematous papules or nodules that arise quickly, are seen in ~25% of patients with MTS and usually exhibit sebaceous differentiation. Fordyce granules (“free” sebaceous glands) on the vermilion lip and oral mucosa (especially the vestibule) are more common and prominent in patients with MTS than in the general population 43 . The most frequently observed malignancies in Lynch syndrome are colorectal (~50%–60% of patients with MSH2 or MLH1 mutations) and genitourinary (e.g. endometrium [15%–50% of women], ovary [10%–35% of women], urinary tract; highest risk with MSH2 mutations) carcinomas 44 . Colorectal carcinoma in Lynch syndrome most often involves the proximal colon and develops at a median age of 45 years, about one decade before it typically occurs in the general population. Lynch syndrome patients are also at increased risk of neoplasms of the small intestine, stomach, pancreas, hepatobiliary system, CNS, and perhaps breast 45,46 ; hematologic malignancies and sarcomas have also been reported. Diagnosis The diagnosis of MTS was traditionally based on the presence of at least one sebaceous tumor (or keratoacanthoma with sebaceous differ- entiation) and a visceral malignancy without another known predis- posing factor. In the absence of a sebaceous tumor, the diagnosis can be made in a patient with multiple keratoacanthomas, multiple visceral malignancies, and a family history of MTS 47 . Findings that suggest a higher or lower likelihood of MTS in patients with sebaceous neoplasms are summarized in Table 63.5 48 . Testing for a mismatch repair gene mutation is helpful in confirming the diagnosis and facilitating identi- fication and surveillance of affected family members. Pathology Skin tumors arising as part of MTS fall into two general categories: sebaceous neoplasms and keratoacanthomas. Sebaceous adenomas (with a predominance of mature sebocytes), sebaceomas (vertically oriented with a predominance of basaloid seboblastic cells), so-called sebaceous epitheliomas (inconsistently defined term used for various lesions with seboblastic differentiation), and sebaceous carcinomas may occur (see Ch. 111 ). A type of keratoacanthoma with sebaceous differentiation that may be specific to this syndrome has been called a sebo(kerato)acanthoma; it has the architecture of a keratoacanthoma but contains well-differentiated sebaceous lobules ( Fig. 63.7 ) 49 . In addition, cystic sebaceous tumors, which are well-circumscribed, deep sebaceous lesions with a cystic growth pattern, occur in some MTS patients and are a strong clue for the presence of the syndrome. Immunohistochemical (IHC) staining for MSH2, MSH6, MLH1, and PMS2 can be a valuable screening tool for MTS-associated tumors, which frequently show a lack of expression of one or more of these mismatch repair proteins (see Table 63.5 ) 43,45,50 . However, abnormal IHC staining is not diagnostic of MTS, as it is sometimes seen in sporadic sebaceous neoplasms, especially in immunocompromised patients; conversely, IHC staining may rarely be normal in lesions from patients with a mismatch repair gene mutation (see Ch. 111 ) 50,51 . PCR-based assays can also be used to demonstrate microsatellite instability (MSI) in tissue from MTS-associated neoplasms. Sebaceous adenomas and carcinomas as well as colorectal carcinomas have also been described in patients with autosomal recessive colorectal adenomatous polyposis caused by mutations in the MUTYH base excision repair gene 37,52 . This disorder accounts for some of the patients with sebaceous neoplasms and visceral malig- nancy who meet the traditional criteria for MTS, but whose tumors do not exhibit microsatellite instability. Some authors have referred to patients without evidence of microsatellite instability due to mismatch repair dysfunction as having MTS type 2 47 . Additional manifesta- tions of MUTYH -associated polyposis include other malignancies (e.g. small bowel, ovarian, bladder) and findings that overlap with Gardner syndrome, such as osteomas, RPEH, desmoid tumors, and pilomatricomas 53 . Multiple keratoacanthomas may occur as an isolated finding (i.e. without visceral malignancy), especially in patients with the Ferguson– Smith (multiple self-healing) or Grzybowski (generalized eruptive) types of keratoacanthomas. However, these patients should be evaluated to exclude the possibility of MTS. Treatment Patients with an internal malignancy require appropriate oncologic referral and management. Recommendations for surveillance of high-risk individuals are outlined in Table 63.6 . Long-term aspirin therapy may decrease the risk of colorectal carcinoma in patients with Lynch syndrome 39 . Treatment options for benign sebaceous tumors include curettage, excision, and cryosurgery. Sebaceous carcinomas have metastatic potential and require wide local excision or Mohs micrographic surgery, with the latter recommended for facial lesions. Oral retinoids with or without interferon- α may be useful in the prevention of new sebaceous neoplasms. disease Alkaptonuria is an autosomal recessive inborn error of metabolism in which homogentisic acid (HGA), an intermediate in phenylalanine and tyrosine metabolism, cannot be further metabolized and therefore accumu- lates in body fluids and tissues 54 . The disorder results from a deficiency of the enzyme homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase. It is estimated to have a prevalence of ~1 in 250 000 in most ethnic groups, but as high as 1 in 20 000 in Slovakia and the Dominican Republic due to founder effects. The cardinal clinical features of alkaptonuria include urine that turns dark on standing, discoloration of cartilage and other connective tissues, and arthritis ( Fig. 63.8 ). The arthritis often presents in the third or fourth decade of life with chronic back pain and stiffness, and radiographs show flattened and calcified intervertebral discs. Later involvement of large peripheral joints can resemble rheumatoid arthritis clinically but osteo- arthritis radiographically. Renal complications include an increased incidence of calculi and occasionally kidney failure. Aortic stenosis is common by the sixth or seventh decade of life and coronary artery calci- fications may also develop 54 . Life expectancy is normal. The dermatologic features of alkaptonuria are rarely noted prior to 10–15 years of age and typically become apparent during adulthood, often in the fourth decade of life. Axillary skin may be one of the initial sites to develop discoloration, which can range in color from blue to yellow to brown. The classic blue–grey color associated with this disorder is often first noted in the helices of the ear and sclerae (see Fig. 63.8 ). Later, it may affect the palmar and plantar surfaces as well as the entire face. Dermoscopy can show speckled white globular structures overlying a grayish-blue structureless area 55 . Collagenous and elastotic marginal plaques of the hand may also develop, typically during the fourth to sixth decades of life 56 . Classic Fabry disease presents in boys during childhood or adolescence with the cardinal clinical features of acral pain (episodic or chronic), acral paresthesias, hypohidrosis, and angiokeratomas ( Fig. 63.9 ). Angiokeratomas are one of the earliest signs of Fabry disease, typically beginning to appear during childhood or adolescence 63–65 . They develop in most male patients and ~30% of female heterozygotes. Angiokeratomas present as punctate, dark red to blue–black macules or papules ( Fig. 63.10 ). The lesions do not blanch with pressure and may become slightly keratotic as they enlarge. The angiokeratomas of Fabry disease, referred to as angiokeratoma corporis diffusum, tend to be concentrated between the umbilicus and the knees but can develop at any cutaneous site (see Fig. 63.10 ); oral and conjunctival lesions are also seen. Less frequent vascular findings include linear telangiectasias favoring the face, lips, and oral mucosa; episodic acral vasospasm resembling Raynaud phenomenon, typically accompanied by pain and paresthesias; and peripheral edema and lymphedema 64,65 . Hypohidrosis is an early and almost constant feature of Fabry disease that can result in heat intolerance. Decreased body hair has also been described. Histologically, angiokeratomas are composed of dilated capillaries in the uppermost dermis, partially enclosed by elongated rete ridges (see Ch. 114 ); hyperkeratosis may be seen in older lesions. In the skin, there is evidence of lipid storage in endothelial cells, pericytes, arteriolar smooth muscle, and arrector pili muscle. This can be detected by a lipid stain such as Sudan black B, or highlighted by periodic acid Schiff (PAS) staining. Lipid accumulation may also be observed in sweat gland epithelium (see Ch. 39 ) and perineural cells. Ultrastructural exami- nation demonstrates characteristic cytoplasmic inclusions in all of these cell types. The diagnosis of Fabry disease can be established by demonstration of deficient α -gal A activity in plasma, leukocytes, dried blood spots on filter paper, or cultures of amniocytes or chorionic villi obtained from prenatal testing. However, enzyme activity is within the normal range in up to a third of female heterozygotes. GENODERMATOSES Fucosidosis is a rare autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder resulting from pathogenic variants in FUCA1 , which encodes the enzyme α -fucosidase. In the past, patients were classified into two groups: type I, a more severe form with onset in the first year of life; and type II, a milder form with onset in the second year or later. However, a continuous spectrum of severity is now recognized. The extracuta- neous manifestations include coarse facial features, short stature, organomegaly, dysostosis multiplex, and neurologic deterioration with associated hypomyelination (see Fig. 63.9 ). Patients may also have corneal opacities, retinal vascular abnormalities, and frequent sinopul- monary infections 71 . Angiokeratomas virtually indistinguishable from those associated with Fabry disease are found in approximately one-third of fucosidosis patients < 10 years of age and 85% of those 10–19 years of age. The lesions are distributed primarily on the trunk and lower extremities but can also develop within the mouth. Other reported cutaneous findings include telangiectasias, acrocyanosis, nevus anemicus, xerosis, and elevated sweat chloride levels 72 . The light microscopy findings of the angiokeratomas are similar to those seen in Fabry disease. Electron microscopic examination of clinically normal skin may reveal empty- appearing storage vesicles in endothelial cells, melanocytes, eccrine glands, and fibroblasts.
