Within minutes to hours of sun exposure, pruritic, erythematous papules, papulovesicles, or rarely vesicles develop. In patients with darker skin phototypes, pinhead-sized papules represent the most common morphology. Lesions resolve within a few days without scarring. The eruption is generally most severe in the spring and early summer, especially in temperate climates. As summer progresses, PMLE becomes milder, a phenomenon known as “hardening”. PMLE was first described by Carl Rasch in 1900 and mentioned again by Haxthausen in 1918. Treatment PMLE in its milder forms can be managed by photoprotection, including the use of broad-spectrum, high SPF sunscreens and physical barriers. In patients with more severe disease, two-to-three times per week sessions of NB-UVB, usually for 15 sessions in the spring, can produce hardening and be effective for several months 12 . An initial starting dose of 30%–50% of the MED for NB-UVB is recommended, with the dose then increased by 10%–15% per treatment. Oral prednisone (0.5–1 mg/ kg) may be used during the initial seven to ten days of phototherapy to minimize photoexacerbation. Once hardening is achieved, it may be possible to maintain the effect by having patients expose themselves weekly to sunlight between 10 AM and 2 PM for 15–20 minutes (without sunscreen) for the remainder of the sunny season. Other therapeutic options for prevention of PMLE include oral prednisone ( < 0.5 mg/kg, usually given for 5–7 days during vacations to a sunny climate) 13 and less commonly, hydroxychloroquine 14,15 . Actinic prurigo Synonyms:  Hutchinson’s summer prurigo  Familial (or hereditary) polymorphous light eruption of American Indians  Hydroa aestivale Key features  Severe form common in Native Americans, often with cheilitis and conjunctivitis  Can occur in all races  Childhood onset; often resolution by adolescence, but can persist indefinitely  Intensely pruritic, crusted papules or nodules in sun-exposed sites  Strong association with HLA-DR4 (DRB1*0401) and subtype DRB1*0407  Primary management: photoprotection, NB-UVB, topical calcineurin inhibitors, and thalidomide Introduction and history Actinic prurigo is a fairly uncommon, sunlight-induced, pruritic and crusted, papular or nodular eruption involving uncovered and, to a lesser extent, covered skin 16 . It was first described in the 1960s and 1970s, and was noted to affect North, Central, and South Americans of indigenous or mixed race. Hutchinson first described this disorder in 1879, followed in 1918 by Haxthausen, who described it as a PMLE variant. In 1968, Londoño coined the term “actinic prurigo”. Epidemiology Actinic prurigo is particularly common in Native Americans, especially Mestizos (mixed American Indian and European ancestry) living at high altitudes. It also occurs, but much less commonly, in Europe and Asia. A familial form is relatively common. Pathogenesis Actinic prurigo is triggered by UVR exposure and therefore typically flares during the spring and summer, especially in temperate climates. Phototesting results are abnormal in approximately two-thirds of patients and cutaneous lesions can be provoked by UVB or UVA. The immunologic nature of actinic prurigo is supported by a study of Mexican Mestizo patients, where the remarkable therapeutic efficacy of thalidomide has been shown to be associated with an inhibition of TNF synthesis and the modulation of interferon- γ -producing CD3 + cells. The presence of a dense lymphocytic infiltrate and lymphoid follicles in lesional biopsy specimens from the lips provides further support for this concept 16 . Actinic prurigo may represent a persistent variant of PMLE, as clinical conversion between actinic prurigo and PMLE has been observed, and in family studies, the two disorders are closely linked 17 . There is also a strong association of actinic prurigo with HLA-DR4 (DRB1*0401) and subtype DRB1*0407 17 , and this may be the genetic factor that transforms PMLE into actinic prurigo. Indeed, the presence of this HLA ­subtype is strongly suggestive of the diagnosis. Clinical features Actinic prurigo usually appears during childhood and is more frequently seen in girls. Pathology In early lesions, there is epidermal spongiosis, acanthosis, and a dermal perivascular mononuclear cell infiltrate with occasional eosinophils, but, unlike in PMLE, papillary edema is usually absent 16 . Later, crusts, more pronounced acanthosis, variable lichenification, excoriations, focal dermal papillary fibrosis, and a heavier mononuclear cell infiltrate can be seen. These latter features are nonspecific and may resemble those of chronic dermatitis, prurigo nodularis, or, very rarely, cutaneous B cell lymphoma. Dermal lymphoid follicles have been observed in biopsy specimens taken from the lips 16 . Direct immunofluorescence microscopy is negative. Differential diagnosis The history and clinical features often suggest the diagnosis. Clinicopathologic correlation and laboratory evaluation aid in excluding LE and childhood porphyrias (see Table 87.3 ). Lesions of prurigo nodularis are not accentuated in sun-exposed skin. Patients with CARMIL2-related immunodeficiency can develop an actinic prurigo- like photosensitivity in addition to Epstein–Barr virus (EBV)-associated smooth muscle tumors and impaired T cell function 18 . Treatment Rigorous photoprotection is helpful. For milder disease, topical corti- costeroids and topical calcineurin inhibitors may be used. NB-UVB should be considered next, with protocols similar to those for PMLE (see above). Resistant disease is best treated with oral thalidomide (50–100 mg nightly) 16 , administered for several weeks until remission is achieved and then tapered to as low a maintenance dose as possible (e.g. 50 mg every second or third night). However, the risks of teratogenicity and peripheral neuropathy require very careful patient selection and supervision (see Ch. 130 ). Other possible systemic therapies include corticosteroids, azathioprine, cyclosporine, dupilumab, and lenalid- omide or pomalidomide. In comparison to thalidomide, the latter have significantly less neuropathy, fatigue, and constipation. Photodermatologic Disorders Introduction and history Classic hydroa vacciniforme (HV) is a rare, sunlight-induced, childhood- onset, intermittent but permanently scarring disorder. The condition was first reported by Bazin in 1862. Epidemiology HV is well recognized globally, including in the US, UK, Europe, Korea and Japan, and in these countries has been reported to have a predi- lection for lightly pigmented individuals. The condition typically has its onset during childhood, affecting boys slightly more often than girls and with more severe disease in boys. The disorder can resolve during adolescence or early adulthood 19 ; rare familial cases have been noted. The 2018 update of the WHO-EORTC classification of primary cutaneous lymphomas contains a new category in which patients have chronic active EBV infection. Of particular interest to dermatologists, this category includes HV-like LPD (usually CD8 + T cell phenotype) and severe mosquito bite allergy (usually NK cell phenotype) 20 . Per this classification scheme, the term HV-like LPD encompasses patients previously referred to as having HV as well as HV-like T cell or NK cell lymphoma.

Of particular interest to dermatologists, this category includes HV-like LPD (usually CD8 + T cell phenotype) and severe mosquito bite allergy (usually NK cell phenotype) 20 . Per this classification scheme, the term HV-like LPD encompasses patients previously referred to as having HV as well as HV-like T cell or NK cell lymphoma. However, inclusion of classic HV remains controversial. In patients with HV-like lesions, the development of facial edema, lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly points to the diagnosis of HV-like LPD or even lymphoma. The latter disorders have been observed primarily in Asians and indigenous populations of Latin America 21,22 . Pathogenesis Although tropical sunlight or summer sunlight in temperate regions is generally required to provoke the eruption, abnormal erythematous, or rarely vesicular, phototest responses to repeated monochromatic or broad-spectrum UVR exposure can be induced. The exact pathophysi- ology of the cutaneous reaction in HV is unknown. In a study from Japan, T cells positive for EBV RNA were detected in lesional skin infiltrates from 94% of children with clinically typical HV (17/18) and 11/11 patients with severe HV-like eruptions associated with systemic symptoms, but 0/32 skin biopsy samples from patients with various other dermatoses, including photodermatoses 21 . While the relationship between EBV infection and classic HV remains a matter of debate, it is likely that classic HV and HV-like LPD reside along a clinical spectrum 22 . Clinical features Within hours of summer sun exposure, symmetric, clustered, pruritic or stinging, erythematous macules develop in a photodistri- bution, especially on the face and dorsal aspects of the hands. Over the next several hours, the macules become tender papules or plaques surmounted by vesicles or bullae (often hemorrhagic), before umbili- cating and condensing into hemorrhagic crusts over a span of several days ( Fig. 87.9A,B ). Healing then occurs over a period of weeks, leaving individual or confluent, sometimes telangiectatic, varioliform scars ( Fig. 87.9C ). Generalized malaise with fever or headache rarely accompanies the attacks. However, quality of life in affected children is negatively impacted by their inability to play outdoors 19 . In addition to fevers, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and facial edema, the development of more severe HV-like papulonodules (including in sun-protected sites), oral and labial ulcerations, and panniculitis point to HV-like LPD

A high circu- lating EBV DNA load is generally detected by PCR. Pathology Progressive epidermal spongiosis precedes findings that are almost pathognomonic: prominent, reticular keratinocyte degeneration; the formation of intraepidermal vesicles containing fibrin and acute inflam- matory cells; and confluent epidermal and occasionally focal upper dermal necrosis ( Fig. 87.11 ). Early on, a variably dense perivascular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate admixed with neutrophils and occasionally a few eosinophils is seen; this is followed by epidermal necrosis. Direct immunofluorescence microscopy findings are nonspecific. In situ hybridization for EBV RNA shows positivity within the lymphoid infiltrate. Differential diagnosis LE and childhood porphyrias can be excluded by clinicopathologic corre- lation and laboratory evaluation (see Table 87.3 ), while herpes simplex is excluded by a negative PCR, DFA assay, or viral culture. Occasionally, other photodermatoses such as the vesicular form of PMLE and actinic prurigo may be considered. Treatment HV is almost always refractory to treatment. Rigorous photoprotection can be useful in mild to moderate disease. Anecdotally, the following have been reported to be helpful: broadband (BB)-UVB, NB-UVB, PUVA, β -carotene, antimalarials, azathioprine, thalidomide, cyclosporine, and dietary fish oil. Systemic therapies such as thalidomide and interferon are also used for HV-like LPD while treatment of EBV + T cell lymphoma includes systemic chemotherapy and allogeneic ­hematopoietic stem cell transplant. It is evoked by UVR and occasionally also visible light exposure. CAD probably represents a contact allergy-like DTH response against endogenous photoinduced antigen(s). Reference to a condition suggestive of CAD was first made in 1933 by Haxthausen, then in the 1960s by Wilkinson in the UK and Jillson and Baughman in the US, with the latter authors terming it “ persistent light reaction ”. In 1969, its severe form, actinic reticuloid , was described, followed shortly thereafter by reports of two milder variants, photo- sensitive eczema and photosensitivity dermatitis . In 1979, the current encompassing term, CAD, was introduced by Hawk and Magnus 24 . Epidemiology CAD has been regularly observed throughout the world. It occurs primarily in temperate zones and more commonly affects older men 2,23 . However, CAD has been increasingly recognized in younger women as well as in patients with darker skin phototypes. 3,25 Familial incidence has not been noted. Pathogenesis The action spectra for CAD include UVB, UVA and/or visible light, with UVB plus UVA being the most common. CAD has been regularly observed throughout the world. It occurs primarily in temperate zones and more commonly affects older men 2,23 . However, CAD has been increasingly recognized in younger women as well as in patients with darker skin phototypes. 3,25 Familial incidence has not been noted. Pathogenesis The action spectra for CAD include UVB, UVA and/or visible light, with UVB plus UVA being the most common. The eczematous clinical and histologic appearances of CAD, its dermal infiltrate of primarily CD8 + T lymphocytes, and its pattern of adhesion molecule activation all closely mimic the DTH response of allergic contact dermatitis. This strongly suggests that CAD is presumably a reaction against endog- enous, photoinduced, cutaneous antigen(s). CAD was initially described as most common among individuals who spent a lot of time outdoors. However, a significant number of patients, especially those with darker skin phototypes, do not have a history of frequent outdoor activities 23,25 . It is possible that in CAD chronic photodamage leads to a partial abrogation of normal cutaneous immunosuppression, thereby permitting enhanced cutaneous immune responsiveness against an otherwise weak endogenous photoantigen. It should be noted that positive patch testing to Compositae , commonly observed in the UK, has not been confirmed in the US and Japan. It is likely that nucleic acids may be involved as chromophores in the pathogenesis of CAD, in that the shape of the CAD induction spectrum resembles that of sunburn inflammation, for which UVR absorption by nucleic acids is known to be responsible 23 . Clinical features CAD may develop in previously normal skin, in patients with a prior history of dermatitis (in particular, photoallergic contact dermatitis, allergic contact dermatitis, and atopic dermatitis), or rarely following longstanding oral drug photosensitivity or PMLE. Coexistent allergic contact sensitivity to plant antigens, fragrances, or topical medica- tions is common. The eruption consists of pruritic papules and lichen- ified plaques in sun-exposed areas ( Fig. 87.12 ); during disease flares, involvement of sun-protected sites, albeit less severe, can be seen. Scattered or widespread, erythematous, shiny, infiltrated, pseudolympho- matous papules or plaques may be present in severely affected individuals. Lesions develop primarily within sun-exposed sites, frequently with a sharp cut-off at the lines of clothing, and often with sparing in the depths of skin furrows, upper eyelids, finger webs, nasolabial folds, or postauricular areas ( Figs. 87.13–87.15 ). Photodermatologic Disorders Differential diagnosis Photoaggravated dermatoses are differentiated by the characteristic clinical features of the underlying primary disorder and normal cutaneous irradiation responses. In drug- and chemical-induced photosensitivity, there is usually a history of exposure to a relevant drug or allergen or clinical evidence (e.g. positive photopatch testing results; see below). In contrast to CTCL, CAD infiltrates are predominantly CD8 + cells 23 and T cell receptor gene rearrangement studies are negative. Very rarely, primary CTCL may present with severe CAD features and should therefore be considered if apparent CAD is totally refractory to treatment 27 . Erythrodermic CAD must be differentiated from other causes of erythroderma (see Ch. 10 ), but histologic features may not allow discrimination so phototesting after the erythroderma has been controlled can assist in establishing the diagnosis. Treatment Strict photoprotection and the avoidance of relevant contact allergens are of primary importance. Of note, computer and video screens are safe. Commercially available films that block UVR can be placed on home and car windows. Topical or intermittent oral corticosteroids, along with emollients, are generally needed, and topical calcineurin inhibitors may also be helpful 23 . Therapy for refractory disease includes mycophenolate mofetil (1–2 g/day) cyclosporine (3.5–5 mg/kg/day), or azathioprine (1–2.5 mg/kg/day). Dupilumab has recently been reported to improve recalcitrant CAD 27 . DISORDERS DUE TO PHYSICAL AGENTS Clinical features Patients present with whealing limited to sun-exposed areas, particu- larly the upper chest and extensor arms, within 5 to 10 minutes of sun exposure. Occasionally, erythema without urtication may occur. The lesions then resolve over 1 to 2 hours. Patients almost invariably note an accompanying pruritus, burning sensation, or rarely pain, while severe attacks are rarely associated with malaise, light-headedness, nausea, bronchospasm and/or syncope. Although solar urticaria is oftentimes classified by its action spectrum, in an individual patient, the spectrum may gradually change over time 29 . Most commonly, visible light is responsible, but usually with extension into the UVA waveband. In some patients, the action spectrum may include UVB 30 . Occasionally, continued regular skin exposure to UVR may decrease the likelihood of attacks of solar urticaria, a phenomenon referred to as “hardening”. The probability of spontaneous resolution has been estimated as being 15% at 5 years and 25% at 10 years after onset 28 . There are several uncommon manifestations of this disorder. The probability of spontaneous resolution has been estimated as being 15% at 5 years and 25% at 10 years after onset 28 . There are several uncommon manifestations of this disorder. Fixed solar urticaria is limited to specific areas, presumably due to mast cell alterations just at those sites 30 . “Drug-induced” solar urticaria has been reported following exposure to chlorpromazine, tetracycline, or tar. Solar angioedema occurs 2-10 hours after exposure and takes days to resolve. Pathology The histologic findings are similar to those of other urticarias. There is mild dermal edema with a sparse perivascular mixed neutrophilic and eosinophilic infiltrate; mononuclear cells may also be seen. In addition, eosinophil major basic protein has been demonstrated within the dermis by immunofluorescence. Differential diagnosis The differential diagnosis includes other forms of urticaria, particularly heat urticaria, PMLE, and very rarely, EPP. A detailed history should differentiate solar urticaria from idiopathic urticaria and other physical urticarias. Phototesting of affected patients generally results in typical whealing within minutes ( Fig. 87.16 ), while the use of a water filter in front of the light source eliminates heat to exclude heat urticaria. Patients with EPP complain of a more deep-seated pain following sun exposure, and they have elevated free RBC protoporphyrin levels (see Ch. 49 ). The time course of PMLE is distinct from that of solar urticaria, and LE can be excluded via laboratory evaluation (see Fig 87.1 and Ch. 41 ). Treatment Oral non-sedating antihistamines, often in high doses and taken regularly or about an hour or so before expected sun exposure, are effective in ~50% of patients. Those with very mild disease may occasionally require only photoprotective measures; however, sunscreens do not generally provide sufficient protection against long-wavelength UVA and visible light to be effective 31 . Omalizumab is often effective 32 . Graduated exposures to UVA, UVA1 or PUVA are occasionally helpful 33 . Other treatment options, including methotrexate, cyclosporine, plasma- pheresis, or IVIg, 34 have been reported to be successful. The underlying pathogenesis is reviewed in greater detail in Chapter 86 . Five of the disorders are associated with defects in one of the nucleotide excision repair (NER) proteins: xeroderma pigmentosum, Cockayne syndrome, cerebro-oculo-facio-skeletal (COFS) syndrome, UV-sensitive syndrome, and the photosensitive form of trichothiodystrophy 35,36 . Xeroderma pigmentosum Introduction and history Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP) is an autosomal recessive condition associated with a marked increase in the development of malignancies, especially cutaneous. Eight complementation groups, corresponding to eight genotypes, have been identified. XP was first described by Hebra and Kaposi in 1874. Epidemiology XP has an estimated incidence of 2.3 per million live births in Western Europe, 1 in 20 000 in Japan, and 1 in 250 000 in the US 37 . Pathogenesis XP can result from defects in one of eight genes. The seven comple- mentation groups A through G are each associated with a different site of impairment in global genomic nucleotide excision repair (GG-NER), i.e. impairment in the removal of DNA damage from any part of the genome 37 ; the damaged DNA then accumulates, leading to mutations and cancer. XP-A through XP-G represent different proteins in the NER pathway (see Fig. 86.14 ). It should be noted that different mutations in ERCC3 ( XPB ) , ERCC4 ( XPF ), and ERCC5 ( XPG ) can be associated with different phenotypes – either XP or XP/Cockayne syndrome – and mutations in ERCC3 ( XPB ) and ERCC2 ( XPD ) can also be associated with photosensitive forms of trichothiodystrophy (see below). Mutations in an eighth gene, which encodes DNA polymerase- η , lead to the XP variant phenotype. This enzyme is responsible for bypassing unrepaired DNA photoproducts during DNA replication; mutations thus result in the insertion of erroneous residues during replication. Mutations in an eighth gene, which encodes DNA polymerase- η , lead to the XP variant phenotype. This enzyme is responsible for bypassing unrepaired DNA photoproducts during DNA replication; mutations thus result in the insertion of erroneous residues during replication. Phototesting in XP patients has shown the action spectrum for inflammatory erythema of the skin to be in the 290 to 340 nm range. The MEDs corresponding to those wavelengths are generally quite reduced, with the peak responses often vesicular and delayed by a day or two. Clinical features Fifty percent of patients have marked photosensitivity in addition to an early onset for all major types of skin cancer (see Table 87.4 ) 37 . From an early age, many patients easily develop sunburns with erythema, edema and vesicles following minimal sun exposure. By the age of 2 years, practically all patients have developed solar lentigines ( Fig. 87.17 ). With continued sun exposure, the skin gradually becomes xerotic, accounting for the term “xeroderma pigmentosum”. Actinic keratoses, basal cell carcinomas (BCCs), squamous cell carcinomas (SCCs), and less frequently, melanomas then develop in sun-exposed sites, also prematurely. In addition to the lips, SCCs of the distal tongue can also develop. Individuals with severe photosensitivity are less likely to develop skin cancers than those who are less photo- sensitive, presumably due to more rigorous photoprotective behaviors in the former group 38 . Ocular abnormalities are observed in ~40% of patients. Severe photo- phobia, keratitis, corneal opacification, and vascularization are common manifestations, while loss of eyelashes, ectropion, and SCC and melanoma of the UVR-exposed parts of the eyes are also frequently reported 38 . Approximately 20%–30% of XP patients develop neurologic degen- eration, especially those in the XP-D group. The most severe presen- tation is the DeSanctis–Cacchione syndrome, in which microcephaly, a progressive decline in intellectual capacity, delayed growth and sexual development, deafness, choreoathetosis, ataxia, and quadriparesis may all occur. However, some XP patients develop a limited number of clinical manifestations, such as isolated hyporeflexia and progressive deafness. XP variant patients usually have no neurologic problems. Deep tendon reflex testing and audiometry are good screening tests for the presence of neurologic involvement. It has been postulated that these neurologic abnormalities are due to defective DNA repair in nerve cells, resulting in neuronal death. Patients with

Cockayne syndrome Introduction and history Cockayne syndrome is a rare, progressive, multisystem disease with photosensitivity that is transmitted in an autosomal recessive fashion (see Table 87.4 ). 40,41 This entity was first described by Cockayne in 1936. Epidemiology Cockayne syndrome has been reported from the US, Europe and Japan, with over 120 genetically confirmed patients from Western Europe 39 . Pathogenesis The fundamental defect in NER in Cockayne syndrome is different from that of XP (see Fig. 86.14 ). In the former, there is defective transcription- coupled NER (TC-NER), a repair that specifically removes transcription- blocking lesions from the genome. This defect results in the inability to recover mRNA synthesis after exposure to UVR. Photodermatologic Disorders In contrast to XP, skin cancers on sun-exposed areas are not observed in patients with Cockayne syndrome, whose average lifespan is only 12 years (although there is considerable variation) 40 . One explanation is that cells with low-level damage due to defective TC-NER are elimi- nated, protecting the body from carcinogenesis, but at the expense of accelerated aging. Rigorous photoprotection may also play a role in reducing the formation of skin cancers 41 . Two-thirds of the patients have mutations in ERCC6 (also known as CSB ) while one-third have mutations in ERCC8 (also known as CSA ) (see Table 87.4 ) 41 . Clinical features Patients with Cockayne syndrome have been classified into three types based upon severity of symptoms and age of onset 41 . In the most severely affected individuals, there is a congenital onset and the clinical manifestations overlap with those of cerebro-oculo-facial-skeletal (COFS) syndrome (see Table 87.4 ). In a more recent series of 16 patients with Cockayne syndrome and COFS, patients were noted to have sensi- tivity to UVB and UVA, pigmented macules, stellate scars, clubbing of the nails, and acral edema 40 . Treatment This consists of photoprotection and symptomatic treatment only. UV-sensitive syndrome UV-sensitive syndrome (UV s S) is a rare, photosensitive, autosomal recessive disease. To date, fewer than 20 patients have been reported (Japan, France, Israel, Iran and Pakistan) 42,43 . Although it shares defective TC-NER with Cockayne syndrome (see above), clinically patients only have UV photosensitivity (see Table 87.4 ). However, the action spectrum is unknown. In addition to mutations in ERCC8 ( CSA ) and ERCC6 ( CSB ), mutations in a gene that encodes a UV-stimulated scaffold protein A ( UVSSA ) have been identified in these patients. The action spectrum for the photoexacerbated erythema remains unclear. Growth delay and short stature with a disproportionately small head are usually the most common reasons parents seek medical care (see Table 87.4 ) 47 . Exogenous photosensitivity Introduction and history Photosensitivity induced by exogenous agents can be divided into phototoxicity and photoallergy ( Table 87.5 ). Phototoxicity is the result of direct tissue and cellular injury following UVR-induced activation of a phototoxic agent; theoretically, phototoxicity can be induced in any individual. In contrast, photoallergy is a delayed-type hypersensitivity response consisting of a sensitization phase, an incubation period of 7 to 10 days (following the first exposure), and a clinical elicitation reaction with any subsequent challenge; only immunologically sensi- tized individuals can develop photoallergy. Phototoxic agents have been used as medications from as early as 4000 BCE, with the inhabitants of Mesopotamia (and later the Indians and Egyptians) employing plant-derived psoralens for the treatment of leukoderma. In 1913, Meyer-Betz demonstrated hematoporphyrin- induced phototoxicity on himself, while the current method of PUVA therapy was introduced in the 1970s. Photoallergy was first recognized in 1939 based on a classic study of sulfanilamide by Epstein. Epidemiology While the exact prevalences of phototoxicity and photoallergy in the general population are unknown, their frequency in photodermatology referral centers has ranged from 3% to 16% for phototoxicity and 1% to 8% for photoallergy. Both are more common in White as compared to Black individuals 3,53,54 . Pathogenesis The pathogenesis of phototoxicity involves the generation of free oxygen radicals, superoxide anions, hydroxyl radicals and singlet oxygen, which leads to a host of cytotoxic tissue effects. Other mechanisms of damage include the generation of stable photoproducts (e.g. chlorpromazine, tetracy- clines), the formation of photoadducts (e.g. psoralens), and the recruitment of inflammatory mediators (e.g. porphyrins, demeclocycline) 55 . The pathogenesis of photoallergy is identical to that of allergic contact dermatitis, with the exception of the requirement for the presence of UVR to induce photoallergen formation. Phototoxic reactions due to oral medications resemble an exaggerated sunburn. These reactions then resolve spontaneously with desquamation and hyperpigmentation once the photosensitizer or UVR is avoided 56 . In a systematic review of photo- toxicity due to oral agents, evidence was strongest for vemurafenib, NSAIDs, and antibiotics (fluoroquinolones and tetracylines) 57 . The medications most commonly associated with phototoxicity are listed in Table 87.5 . 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU), methotrexate, and retinoids, three commonly used medications in dermatology, have also been associated with photosensitivity reactions; however, none is typically associated with classic phototoxicity or photoallergy. Exacerbation of 5-FU-induced inflammation by UVR usually occurs in sites with actinic keratoses. The administration of methotrexate can cause a recurrence (“recall”) of previous UVR-induced erythema. However, phototesting in patients taking methotrexate has been normal, and the mechanism for this “recall” reaction remains unclear. Phototesting in patients taking isotretinoin or acitretin, or who apply topical tretinoin, is also usually normal. The propensity for these patients to develop UVR-induced erythema is most likely due to retinoid-induced thinning of the stratum corneum. Phytophotodermatitis is another phototoxic reaction, with linear streaks of erythema occurring a day or so after skin contact with plants containing furocoumarins plus subsequent exposure to UVA in sunlight. Linear postinflammatory hyperpigmentation is a classic finding. Plants capable of inducing phytophotodermatitis include yarrow, parsley, celery, lime, and fig (see Ch. 17 ). Therefore, this condition most commonly occurs in individuals whose outdoor activities expose them to such plants, such as vegetable harvesters and bartenders who mix drinks outdoors. Roofers and road workers occasionally develop phototoxicity secondary to exposure to tar and concomitant UVA from sunlight. St John’s wort ( Hypericum perforatum ), used in non-traditional medicine to treat a variety of ailments including depression, contains hypericin, another known phototoxic agent. Voriconazole is often prescribed for months or even years in immunocompromised hosts as a prophylactic systemic antifungal agent. Vemurafenib, a selective BRAF inhibitor, has been shown to be phototoxic with an action spectrum in the UVA range 58 . Photoallergy In previously sensitized individuals, exposure to photoallergens and sunlight results in the development of a pruritic eczematous eruption. In more severely affected patients, vesicles and bullae may develop, though less commonly than in phototoxic reactions. While phototoxic reactions usually resemble sunburns and photoallergic reactions often resemble allergic contact dermatitis, these two reaction patterns may not always be easily distinguishable by morphology alone 56 . In the UK and the US, sunscreen agents (especially benzophenone-3 [oxybenzone]) were the most common causes of photoallergy 59 . However, the overall prevalence of photoallergy amongst sunscreen users is very low. In Europe, topical NSAIDs, especially ketoprofen and etofenamate, were the most common cause (see Table 87.5 ) 60 . Photoallergy can generally be confirmed by photopatch testing, where duplicate sets of photoallergens are placed on the patient’s back and only one set is irradiated with UVA ( Table 87.6 ). The interpretation of results from such testing is shown in Fig. 87.19 . Pathology Phototoxicity is characterized by scattered necrotic keratinocytes (“sunburn cells”) and a superficial dermal infiltrate of primarily lymphocytes and neutrophils. In contrast, photoallergy is characterized by epidermal spongiosis plus a superficial dermal lymphohistiocytic infiltrate, indistinguishable from other causes of spongiotic dermatitis. Differential diagnosis Inflammatory phototoxic reactions should be distinguished from ordinary sunburn, which requires more UVR exposure, and LE (see Table 87.3 ). The differential diagnosis of photoallergic reactions includes all other forms of dermatitis that can involve sun-exposed areas, partic- ularly airborne contact dermatitis and atopic dermatitis. Treatment The identification and avoidance of the offending agent are of prime importance. Sometimes it is not possible to discontinue the culprit medication and strict photoprotection (UVB and UVA) is required. For phototoxic and photoallergic reactions, analgesia may be helpful. Topical corticosteroids, and, for severe flares, short courses of systemic corticosteroids, can be used for photoallergic dermatitis. Occasionally, evening dosing of a phototoxic drug can be implemented so that peak systemic levels occur during the night. Endogenous photosensitivity The cutaneous porphyrias, discussed in Chapter 49 , represent the most obvious examples of photosensitivity induced by endogenous agents. The mechanism of porphyrin-induced phototoxicity involves reactive oxygen species, the complement system, mast cells, and neutrophils ( Fig. 87.20 ). Smith–Lemli–Opitz syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder with an early onset of photosensitivity to UVA in 55% to 75% of patients 61 . Its frequency is 1 in 40 000 conceptions. Mutations in DHCR7 , which encodes 7-dehydrocholesterol reductase, result in an accumulation of 7-dehydrocholesterol. The mechanism of the photosensitivity is unknown. Pellagra, which is due to niacin deficiency, is also associated with photosensitivity but its pathogenesis remains unclear as well 62 . Otherwise, the typical delayed bright red appearance of a sunburn develops conflu- ently on all sufficiently exposed skin, beginning within 30 minutes to 8 hours, peaking at 12 to 24 hours and diminishing over hours to days in the case of UVB exposure. With exposure to UVA alone, however, the reaction is deeper red in color and is usually more persistent. After excessive exposure, edema and blistering may occur, which if widespread, may lead to systemic symptoms such as chills and malaise. Such reactions are generally followed by pruritus and desquamation over a period of days to weeks. In individuals with lighter skin phototypes, visible light has been shown to produce immediate erythema 64 . Photoprotection is the best preventive measure. In the case of excessive UVR exposure, symptomatic treatment is instituted as soon as possible after exposure. This includes increased fluid intake, emollient creams or lotions, topical corticosteroids, and oral nonsteroidal or steroidal anti- inflammatory agents. Of note, in a placebo-controlled trial involving 20 healthy adults, 200 000 IU of vitamin D 3 administered one hour after an experimental sunburn led to a reduced expression of proin- flammatory mediators (e.g. TNF), reduced skin redness, and increased expression of the anti-inflammatory mediator arginase-1 in those with higher serum vitamin D 3 levels 65 . Pigment darkening and delayed tanning Immediate, often grayish, darkening of irradiated skin that lasts for 10–20 minutes may occur within seconds of ~2–12 J/cm 2 of UVA irradiation; however, this response can last for up to 3 months 1 . In darkly pigmented individuals, the blue spectrum of visible light induces similar changes, possibly due to absorption of the blue light by opsin-3, a receptor on the surface of their melanocytes (see above) 66 . Transient pigmentary changes, known as immediate pigment darkening , result from photo-oxidative darkening and the cellular redistribution of melanin within epidermal melanocytes. Pigmentation that persists for more than 2 hours after irradiation is referred to as persistent pigment darkening ; it is brownish in color, lasts for up to 24 hours, and is also due to oxidation of pre-existing melanin. Persistent pigment darkening then blends with delayed pigmentation , or tanning , which develops in genetically competent individuals over hours to days and persists for weeks to months following ~40 mJ/cm 2 of broadband UVB (slightly higher than the MED, particularly in fair-skinned persons), and 15–20 J/ cm 2 of broadband UVA (a little less than the MED). As a result of delayed tanning, further sunburning sensitivity is mildly decreased by a factor of two to four. Epidermal hyperplasia Hyperplasia lasting a month or so occurs over a period of hours to days following UVB, but generally not UVA, exposure. This results from a markedly increased cellular mitotic rate and DNA, RNA and protein synthesis, following several initial hours of inactivity. Hyperplasia of the viable epidermis and thickening of the stratum corneum result in several-fold protection against later sunburning; this adds to, and may exceed, that simultaneously provided by delayed tanning, particularly in fair-skinned individuals. UV-induced epidermal hyperplasia is generally neither visible nor apparent by palpation. Immunologic changes Exposure to UVB and UVA radiation alters epidermal Langerhans cell function, generates suppressor T lymphocytes, and changes the cutaneous cytokine profile. This topic is discussed in greater detail in Chapter 86 . Vitamin D 3 synthesis UVB (maximum: 300 ± 5 nm) irradiation quickly converts epidermal 7-dehydrocholesterol into previtamin D 3 (see Fig. 51.11 ) 67 ; the latter then isomerizes to vitamin D 3 (cholecalciferol), which is then converted in the liver to 25-hydroxyvitamin D and subsequently in the kidneys to 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, its active form. UVR-induced vitamin D 3 synthesis is maximal at suberythemogenic doses. The action spectrum for vitamin D synthesis is similar to that for DNA damage. Ideally, vitamin D homeostasis is achieved by a combination of incidental outdoor daylight exposure and dietary sources rather than through intentional exposure to sunlight or tanning beds. Other changes Occasionally, otherwise healthy individuals who are not on any medica- tions may develop photo-onycholysis and increased skin fragility with blistering ( pseudoporphyria ) following intense exposure to sunlight or tanning beds. Mid-dermal elastolysis is characterized by patches of finely wrinkled skin and loss of elastic fibers in the mid-reticular dermis (see Ch. 99 ); its onset is frequently associated with intense UVR exposure. Brachioradial pruritus , characterized by primary pruritus of the outer arm, is associated with cervical radiculopathy; however, in many patients, UVR may act as a trigger of the symptoms (see Ch. 6 ). Chronic Effects Photoaging in fair-skinned patients Photoaging refers to cutaneous changes secondary to long-term exposure to sunlight ( Table 87.8 ). Characteristic clinical manifestations are outlined below. Solar (actinic) elastosis develops in chronically sun-exposed areas and presents as thickened skin with a yellow hue. It is most commonly seen on the face, neck, and extensor aspect of the mid arms ( Fig. 87.24A ). More widespread involvement can be seen in those from tropical climates, especially when there is minimal constitutive pigmentation ( Fig. 87.24B ). Histologically, a marked increase in abnormal, altered dermal elastic fibers is seen. Cutis rhomboidalis nuchae refers to similar changes occurring on the posterior neck ( Fig. 87.24C ); it is characterized by deep furrowing associated with a leathery texture. A solar lentigo is a light brown to dark brown, even-colored or reticu- lated macule or patch that occurs in sun-exposed areas, most often as multiple lentigines. The dorsal aspects of the hands, extensor forearms, upper trunk, and face are the most commonly affected sites (see Ch. 109 ). An ephelide , also known as a freckle, presents as a light red– brown to medium brown macule, usually < 6 mm in diameter. Such lesions occur primarily in sun-exposed areas, are usually clustered, and are more apparent after sun exposure (see Ch. 112 ). In Favre–Racouchot syndrome , multiple large open comedones develop on the lateral and inferior aspects of the periorbital area ( Fig. 87.24E ), in association with marked solar elastosis of the surrounding skin. In some patients, cigarette smoking may be a cofactor. Histologically, there are dilated pilosebaceous openings and cyst-like spaces filled with horny material in addition to marked solar elastosis. Solar purpura occurs in areas of cumulative photodamage that are subject to trauma, e.g. dorsal hands, extensor forearms, shins ( Fig. 87.24F,G ). As lesions resolve over weeks, a brown discoloration due to hemosiderin may appear. It is often accompanied by skin fragility ( Fig. 87.24H ). There are usually numerous, closely spaced lesions in chronically sun-exposed sites, especially the neck, face and dorsal hands. Histologically, homogeneous masses of PAS-positive, diastase-resistant colloid are present in the papillary dermis; positive staining with thioflavin T and Congo red has been reported in some cases. Erosive pustular dermatosis of the scalp classically presents as sterile pustules, keratotic crusts, erosions, and mild inflammation arising within the atrophic, photodamaged skin of a bald scalp 68 ( Fig. 87.24I ). However, similar clinical findings can occur in other sites with atrophic or fragile skin, e.g. the lower extremities of older patients with venous hypertension, sites of injury in neonates (see Ch. 25 ). Acquired elastotic hemangiomas present as erythematous plaques within actinically damaged skin, usually on the neck or upper extrem- ities. Histologically, there is a horizontal proliferation of capillaries in the upper reticular dermis and prominent solar elastosis. Photoaging in patients with dark skin phototypes Photoaging is much less pronounced and has a delayed onset in individuals with more darkly pigmented skin 69 ( Fig. 87.24K ). Small seborrheic keratoses, melasma, and mottled hyperpigmentation are common signs of photoaging in East Asians, such as Chinese, Japanese, Koreans, and Filipinas; in addition, any wrinkles are fine and do not usually appear before 50 years of age. South Asians, such as Indians, Pakistanis, Sri Lankans and Bangladeshis, often have darker skin than East Asians and dyspigmentation and fine wrinkles are the primary signs of photoaging. Lightly pigmented Latinos have changes similar to those seen in White individuals, while those with brown skin photoage in a manner similar to that seen in South Asians. Black-skinned individuals, including African-Americans, Afro-Caribbeans and people from Africa, have a wide range of skin phototypes, from III to VI. Dyspigmentation is common and fine wrinkles appear late in life. Photocarcinogenesis Chronic sun exposure has been associated with the development of actinic keratoses (AKs), SCC, BCC and melanoma, in particular lentigo maligna. Epidemiologic studies have shown that SCCs tend to develop within chronically sun-exposed areas in fair-skinned individuals; e.g. people who migrate to Australia early in life have a higher risk of developing SCC than immigrants who arrive when older. Photocarcinogenesis Chronic sun exposure has been associated with the development of actinic keratoses (AKs), SCC, BCC and melanoma, in particular lentigo maligna. Epidemiologic studies have shown that SCCs tend to develop within chronically sun-exposed areas in fair-skinned individuals; e.g. people who migrate to Australia early in life have a higher risk of developing SCC than immigrants who arrive when older. Furthermore, the incidence of BCC is higher in native-born Australians than immigrants, and a statistically significant associ- ation between intermittent sun exposure and the risk of BCC has also been reported. These findings are supported by the observation that the use of sunscreens led to a decrease in the development of AKs, SCC, melanoma, and to a lesser extent, BCC 70 . Exposure to tanning beds is associated with an increased risk for developing cutaneous melanoma as well as SCC and BCC. In studies of populations in which there was a greater proportion of individuals with darkly pigmented skin, a higher melanoma incidence associated with an increased UV index and lower latitude was only seen in non-Latino White populations, but not in Black or Latino populations 69,71 . Sarah Hannam and Michael L. Smith Environmental and Sports-Related Skin Diseases 88 SECTION 13 sensors send signals to the preoptic area of the anterior hypothalamus. Communication with the posterior hypothalamus sets up the subcon- scious thermoregulatory mechanisms of vasomotor control, sweating, and shivering. When prolonged exposure to a hot environment leads to an increase in core temperature, the subsequent decrease in sympathetic output results in peripheral vasodilation, allowing an increase in cutaneous These changes allow radiant, conductive, convective, and evaporative heat loss. In contrast, cold temperature exposure leads to increased sympathetic output with peripheral vasoconstriction. Countercurrent heat exchange between parallel arteries and veins further reduces heat loss to the skin, thereby conserving core heat. The behavioral response of shivering generates heat through muscular activity 1 . Pathologic conditions arise when the normal hypothalamic regulatory set point is overcome by extremes of temperature ( Table 88.1 ). The following discussion will explore heat-related illnesses and thermal burns. Heat-induced urticaria is covered in Chapter 18 . History It has been speculated that King Edward and his armored crusaders lost the final battle of the Holy Land because the Arab horsemen were adapted and dressed appropriately for the severe heat. Epidemiology The frequency of heat-related illnesses is unknown, since milder forms resolve with simple measures. Heat-related illness accounted for more than 8000 deaths in the US between 1979 and 1999, and is respon- sible for ~7% of wilderness deaths. The European heat wave of 2003 contributed to the deaths of about 14 800 individuals in France 1 . In US high school athletes, the incidence of heat-related illness is ~9000 cases annually, with the highest rates during football season and repre- senting the third leading cause of death in this cohort. From 2006 to 2010, five in 10 000 visits to the emergency department were for heat- related illnesses: 75% with heat exhaustion and 5% with heat stroke 2 . Risk factors are listed in Table 88.2 . Burn injuries are far more commonly reported, with more than half a million Americans presenting for medical treatment each year, resulting in 40 000 hospitalizations and > 3000 deaths, half of which occur in children 3–5 . The male to female ratio is ~2 : 1, and the major sources of burns in children are scald, flame, and electrical. Abuse or neglect may account for up to 20% of pediatric burns. The male to female ratio is ~2 : 1, and the major sources of burns in children are scald, flame, and electrical. Abuse or neglect may account for up to 20% of pediatric burns. Mortality rates have steadily declined due to improved resuscitative and surgical management. In the 1940s, burns in children involving 50% body surface area (BSA) had a 50% survival rate, A unique form of burn injury is that due to fireworks. In the US alone, there were at least 25 000 emergency department visits for injuries due to fireworks between 2006 and 2010. Half of the visits were by individuals ­ 20 years of age, with a predominance of male patients (~75%). The most common injuries were distal extremity burns, followed by ocular injury, open wounds of distal extremities, and ocular burns 6 . Pathogenesis Athletic activity can generate 800 to 1000 kcal/h of heat for prolonged periods. This results in a 1°C rise in core body temperature every 5 to 8 minutes. The normal thermoregulatory mechanisms dissipate this heat as it is generated. When these regulatory mechanisms fail, heat injury occurs. Heat illnesses are not defined by a specific temperature, but by the abnormal response to heat. Table 88.1 outlines the pathogenesis of heat-related disorders. At normal core temperature, cutaneous blood flow is about 4% of cardiac output or 250 ml/min. Modulation of cutaneous blood flow is performed by the hypothalamus via a delicate balancing act between heat retention and loss. Cutaneous, muscle, and spinal cord temperature DISORDERS DUE TO PHYSICAL AGENTS Thermal burns occur when skin is exposed to infrared radiation (800 to 170 000 nm) from an external heat source with a temperature exceeding 44°C (111°F). Time and temperature curves have been developed to determine maximum threshold thermal exposure times. Necrosis of the epidermis occurs in about 45 minutes at 47°C (117°F) but in only 1 second at 70°C (158°F). Denaturation and coagulation of cellular proteins occur in thermal injury. Interstitial edema develops from altered osmotic pressure and capillary permeability. Several chemical mediators with vasoactive and tissue-destructive properties are released, including prostaglandins, bradykinin, serotonin, histamine, lipid peroxides, and oxygen radicals 5 . Clinical features Although heat-related illnesses are not primary skin diseases, they can present with cutaneous findings. Their clinical features are summa- rized in Table 88.1 . Thermal burns of the skin differ in their clinical presentation, depending upon the depth of injury ( Table 88.3 ) 5,7,8 . Conventional nomenclature categorizes cutaneous burn wounds as first degree (super- ficial; limited to epidermis), second degree (partial-thickness), and third degree (full-thickness). Second-degree burns are further subdivided into superficial ( Fig. 88.1 ) and deep variants. Burns involving deeper struc- tures such as muscle are sometimes referred to as fourth-degree burns. However, a definitive determination of wound depth may not be possible for the first 24 to 72 hours because of vascular occlusive changes. At sites where the dermis is thinner (ears, volar forearms, medial thighs, perineum), burns may be deeper than the initial presentation might suggest; this is also the case in the comparatively thinner skin of children and the elderly. Wounds that appear dull red from entrapment of clot (denatured hemoglobin) imply full-thickness injury 7 . The severity of burn injuries is based upon depth and BSA involvement. BSA is estimated in adults by the “rule of nines” ( Fig. 88.2 ). This formula cannot be applied to children, since the head accounts for ~19% BSA in a 2-year-old, 15% in a 7-year-old, and 13% in a 12-year-old. Lund & Browder charts are useful for more accurate assessment of BSA involvement 5,7 . Initial evaluation should address airway and circulatory status; associated inhalation injury is seen in up to 25% of burn patients. Cardiovascular evaluation must address the issue of hypovolemic shock, regardless of burn severity. Urine output must be monitored because of the significant fluid loss and rhabdomy- olysis that may compromise renal function 4,5,7 . Pathology Pathologic features of thermal burns are summarized in Table 88.3 . Differential diagnosis The differential diagnosis of heat injury is listed in Table 88.1 . Although there is considerable overlap in clinical features, an important distinction is the degree of neurologic compromise. The most important diagnostic issue with thermal burns is the depth of the injury (see Table 88.3 ). Treatment Management of heat-related injuries involves removal from the hot environment, rest, rehydration, restoration of electrolyte balance, and evaluation of involved systems ( Table 88.1 ; see Atha 1 for more details). Initial management of burn victims includes assessment of cardiopul- monary status as well as the extent and depth of the burn. Information regarding resuscitation of burn victims is beyond the scope of this text, but can be found in references 4, 5, and 7 . For first- and second-degree burns, the burn wound itself should initially be rinsed with room temperature/cool running water for 20 minutes in order to ease pain, reduce heat, and reduce burn depth 5 . Then the wound should be gently cleansed to remove any foreign material. The next step is prevention of infection, followed by creation of a proper healing environment. Topical

Silver sulfadiazine has gained wide acceptance for both pediatric and adult burn treatment, but it is known to be cytotoxic and percutaneous absorption can lead to leukopenia. Silver sulfadiazine also produces a pseudoeschar that may interfere with burn depth assessment and prolonged application may lead to localized argyria. Some experts therefore prefer mafenide acetate. While superficial wounds may require minimal additional therapy 4,5,7 , deeper burn wounds need more aggressive therapy, with the standard approach being serial excision and autografting (if there are sufficient donor sites). Third-degree burns are excised early, with indeterminate and deep second-degree wounds delayed until maximum depth and extent are known. Biologic dressings (e.g. pig skin, human allograft) were popular for several years, but have been largely displaced due to higher infection risk and poorer healing. Skin substitutes such as acellular human dermal matrix (Alloderm ® ), bilaminar bovine collagen–shark chondroitin sulfate (Integra ® Dermal Regeneration Template), and cultured epithelial autografts are increasingly being utilized 7 (see Ch. 145 ). Although the advent of central heating in much of the industrialized world has led to a dramatic decline in incidence, creative cultural and therapeutic applications of various heating devices continue to induce EAI 9–11 . Epidemiology In the past, EAI was seen up to 10 times more frequently in women than in men. The vast majority of those affected were middle-aged or older. Risk factors include lack of central heating, occupations with close heat exposure, and medical conditions with symptoms relieved by heating or associated with decreased sensation. More recently, EAI has been associated with technologic advances such as heated car seats and recliners as well as laptop computers. The latter lead to EAI in a wide range of age groups and characteristically lead to an asymmetric distribution pattern 10,11 . Pathogenesis Long-term exposure to heat below the threshold for thermal burn is the primary etiologic factor in EAI. The precise pathophysiology is unknown, but the clinical pattern corresponds with the dermal venous plexus. Repeated exposure to heat below 47°C (116.6°F) produces retic- ulated erythema followed by hyperpigmentation in the same pattern 9 . Heat sources reported to cause EAI are found in Table 88.4 9–12 . Clinical features The initial presentation is transient macular erythema in a broad retic- ulated pattern that easily blanches. The overall size and shape often approximates that of the heat source. Clinical features The initial presentation is transient macular erythema in a broad retic- ulated pattern that easily blanches. The overall size and shape often approximates that of the heat source. With recurrent heat exposure, the erythema evolves into a dusky hyperpigmentation; lesions become fixed and are no longer blanchable ( Fig. 88.3 ). Epidermal atrophy may overlie the reticulated pigmentation. Later-stage lesions can become somewhat keratotic and bullae may appear. Lesions are characteristically asymptomatic, although a slight burning sensation is sometimes noted 9 . Once the heat source is identified, it is important to determine if it is being used to relieve pain and, if so, the cause of the pain. A lumbo- sacral location usually points to musculoskeletal disease or, less often, bone metastases. EAI of the abdomen, flank, or mid back may reflect an attempt to relieve pain from inflammation (e.g. pancreatitis, peptic ulcer disease) or malignancy (e.g. pancreatic, gastric). Symptoms of pain should prompt a thorough review of systems and consideration of a search for occult disease. An inquiry into occupation and hobbies is also important, as EAI can develop in exposed areas, e.g. the forearms of bakers, the face or arms of glass blowers and foundry workers, and the anterior thighs or abdomen in those with prolonged use of laptop computers 10,11,13 . The possible development of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) or Merkel cell carcinoma represents the major long-term risk. The latent period may be 30 years or more. The risk of developing SCC is reportedly highest with hydrocarbon-fueled heat exposure, e.g. “peat fire cancers” on the shins of women, Japanese “Kairo cancers” and “Kangri ulcers” in Kashmir due to coal-fired clothing warmers, and Chinese and Tibetan “Kang cancers” from sleeping on coal fire-heated bricks (“Kang beds”) 9,10 . Basal cell carcinoma and cutaneous marginal zone B cell lymphoproliferative disorder have also been reported in association with EAI 10,13 . Pathology The earliest histopathologic changes include epidermal atrophy, vasodi- lation, and dermal pigmentation (both melanin and hemosiderin) ( Fig. 88.4 ). As lesions progress, the epidermal atrophy becomes more pronounced, with flattening of the rete ridges. Basal cell vacuolization has been reported and the dermal–epidermal junction may exhibit interface dermatitis. The dermis appears thinned and sometimes edematous, with accumulation of abnormal elastic tissue and pigment as well as ectatic capillaries. Dermal capillaries may exhibit enlarged endothelial cells with hyperchromatic nuclei. Later lesions may also show basophilic degeneration of connective tissue. Hemosiderin deposition and prominent telangiectasias are seen most often in leg lesions. Focal hyperkeratosis and dyskeratosis may be noted, along with squamous atypia, in long-standing lesions. Ultrastructural evalu- ation also shows increased melanocyte dendritic processes, suggesting melanocyte activation 9 . Differential diagnosis EAI needs to be distinguished from livedo reticularis, which is a temperature-sensitive vasculopathy that favors the extremities and only occasionally develops associated hyperpigmentation (see Ch. 106 ). Cutis marmorata and cutis marmorata telangiectatica congenita are less commonly considered in the differential diagnosis of EAI. Burns and Cutaneous Radiation Injury Associated With Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) and Fluoroscopy Key features  MRI may produce first-, second-, or third-degree burns due to metal or wire contact with skin, creating a closed-loop conduction system  Fluoroscopy, particularly when repeatedly performed in patients with cardiovascular disease, may result in radiation-induced injury Introduction The radiologic literature is replete with reports of superficial to full- thickness thermal or electrical burns occurring during MRI. Risk factors for MRI burns are listed in Table 88.5 15 . In addition, there are reports in the radiologic and dermatologic literature of ulcerations, most commonly on the back, following repeated fluoroscopy 16–18 . Pathogenesis Although the precise cause of MRI burns is unknown, the presence of both pulsed radiofrequency and pulsed magnetic gradient fields is thought to play a role. If an electrically conductive loop is formed between the patient and an electrode, patient and wiring, or even small areas of skin–skin contact, current can be produced by the changing magnetic flux, causing a thermal or electrical burn. Resistance at the skin surface may create a thermal injury, while contact with wiring may create electrical injury via current induction. Alternatively, the burn may result from formation of a resonant conducting loop with an extended wire creating a resonant antenna, heating maximally at the antenna tip 15,19 . In addition to thermal burns, cutaneous complications of fluoroscopy include allergic drug reactions, irritant and allergic contact derma- titis, non-target embolization to the skin, intravascular catheter- related infections, and radiation dermatitis 17 . The mechanism behind fluoroscopy-induced radiodermatitis is related to the dose of radiation that is delivered, the interval between radiation exposures (dose fraction- ation), and the size of the irradiated area 16 . Repeated procedures are notorious for increasing the risk 18 .

The mechanism behind fluoroscopy-induced radiodermatitis is related to the dose of radiation that is delivered, the interval between radiation exposures (dose fraction- ation), and the size of the irradiated area 16 . Repeated procedures are notorious for increasing the risk 18 . Additional potential risk factors include smoking, diabetes mellitus, obesity with overlapping skin folds, autoimmune connective tissue diseases (e.g. systemic sclerosis), genetic DNA repair defects, and various drugs including chemothera- peutic agents 16,17 . Radiation recall, which can occur days to years after fluoroscopy, has been observed following the administration of drugs such as methotrexate 16 . Clinical features Thermal burns appear soon after MRI, and may be partial- to full- thickness (see Table 88.3 ). The shape and size of the burns are deter- mined by the conductor causing the injury (e.g. circular burns under ECG electrodes; figurate burns conforming to the shape of metallic wires or tattoo pigment deposition) 15,19 . Fluoroscopy-induced radiation dermatitis may be acute, but, as time passes and the acute injury resolves, the patient may continue to develop further changes, including epilation of hair, desquamation, telangiectasias, permanent erythema, and eventual ulceration due to dermal necrosis ( Fig. 88.5 ). The left upper back is a characteristic location for patients with cardiovascular disease who have had cardiac catheterizations with attempts at revascularization (e.g. angioplasty, stent placement) 18 . Although often referred to as cutaneous compli- cations, severe radiation injuries can extend into the subcutaneous fat and muscle 16 . Rarely, skin burns develop at the site of an indif- ferent electrode in those undergoing radiofrequency catheter ablation of cardiac arrhythmias 18a . Differential diagnosis Because of the proximity of the MRI event to the detection of a burn injury, the diagnosis is generally straightforward. However, in the case of a tattoo burn, allergic contact dermatitis or foreign body granuloma formation within the tattoo may be considered. Timing of the event plus the sensation of a burn rather than pruritus should allow a distinction. Although patented in 1953, US manufacturers only began installation of airbags in the mid-1970s. European airbag installation began in 1981. The US Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard 208 was amended in 1984, requiring that all vehicles made after 1989 have passive restraints. Further revisions in 1998 made dual front seat airbags mandatory. Despite the beneficial effect, numerous injuries have resulted from airbag deployment, including burns, abrasions, and lacerations 20,21 . Pathogenesis Airbag activation consists of detection, inflation, and deflation phases. The sudden deceleration caused by impact triggers sensors in the front bumper to fire a sodium azide canister inside the nylon rubber bag. The sodium azide ignites with an explosive release of hot nitrogen gas which inflates the bag in about 10 milliseconds at speeds exceeding 160 km/h. The hot nitrogen gas and other by-products are then vented out the upper sides of the bag away from the occupant, thus deflating the bag. Vented aerosol contains nitrogen, carbon mono- and dioxides, sodium hydroxide, ammonia, nitric oxide, metallic oxides and other trace gases, creating a corrosive environment. Friction and pressure from the bag, heat from the bag and gases, and contact with the corrosive aerosol may produce injury 20–22 . Clinical features The cutaneous injuries produced by airbag deployment are summarized in Table 88.6 . Chemical burns occur rarely, but appear to be a result of skin exposure to small amounts of the corrosive alkaline aerosol. The aerosolized particles need to dissolve in a water layer such as tears or sweat before creating a corrosive injury. Of note, alkali burns of the skin may continue to deepen and extend over time, unless all the corrosive chemical is washed away 20–22 . Differential diagnosis The pattern of injury and history of airbag deployment makes the diagnosis obvious. However, it is important to determine whether a burn injury is purely thermal or if it has a chemical component. Assessment of tissue pH and monitoring for continued extension of the burn help determine whether an alkali injury exists. Treatment Prevention is, of course, the most effective approach. Newer airbag designs include repositioning the exhaust vents in order to direct the escape of hot gases away from areas of potential skin contact. Seats should be positioned as far back from the airbag module as possible. Children too small to benefit from the adult three-point restraint should not be in the front passenger area. Children in any type of car seat or booster should never be put in the front seat. Prolonged exposure may lead to hypothermia, frost-nip, or frostbite. Hypothermia, i.e. a decline in core temperature below 35°C (95°F), is a systemic process with minor cutaneous features and therefore will not be discussed in detail. History Cold injury predates recorded history – the quest for clothing, shelter, and fire as protection from the elements must have preoccupied prehis- toric humans. Mass casualties from cold injury have historically been seen most often in military conflicts. However, as interest in outdoor activities and the number of homeless individuals have risen, there has been increased exposure to cold among the general population 23–25 . Epidemiology Environmental risk factors for the development of frostbite include prolonged duration of exposure, higher wind chill, and immersion. A history of psychiatric illness, alcohol and illicit drug use, or smoking are additional risk factors as are previous cold injury, peripheral arterial disease, and dehydration 23,25 . As extremities cool, the “hunting response of Lewis” (alternating vasoconstriction and vasodilation) occurs, ending with vasoconstriction. This tends to conserve the core temperature at the expense of the extremity, which shifts toward ambient temperature. The head does not exhibit a vasoconstrictor response, except for the nose and ears. The trunk surface may cool slightly, but the core temper- ature is maintained. Frostbite is therefore unusual on the trunk or head (except the nose and ears), unless there is direct contact with ice or a refrigerant. The pathophysiologic stages of frostbite are summarized in Clinical features Frostbite has been divided into four categories of severity, analogous to burn injuries. These are only recognizable upon rewarming. Frost- nip (first-degree frostbite) presents with erythema, edema, cutaneous anesthesia, and transient pain ( Fig. 88.6A ). Full recovery is expected, with only mild desquamation. Second-degree frostbite is characterized by marked hyperemia, edema and blistering, with clear fluid in the bullae ( Fig. 88.6B ). Healing occurs, but many patients have long-term sensory neuropathy, often with significant cold sensitivity. Third-degree frostbite consists of full-thickness dermal loss, with hemorrhagic bulla formation or development of waxy, dry, mummified skin. The latter features are poor prognostic indicators for tissue loss. In fourth-degree frostbite , there is full-thickness necrosis leading to skin, muscle, tendon, and bone damage and tissue loss. Injuries of this severity lead to amputation 23,24 . Some authors advocate a simpler classi- fication consisting of superficial or deep injury, citing better prognostic accuracy. Some authors advocate a simpler classi- fication consisting of superficial or deep injury, citing better prognostic accuracy. Pathology Superficial dermal edema and subepidermal bulla formation are typical findings in early frostbite. Vascular permeability leads to hemorrhage that is most pronounced in deep injury. The epidermis and involved dermis become necrotic, with an inflammatory infiltrate and granu- lation tissue at the junction with normal tissue 8 . Differential diagnosis Frostbite injuries should be readily recognizable, given an exposure history and typical presentation. A greater diagnostic challenge is deter- mining the depth of the injury (see above). One possible diagnosis in the differential is cold water immersion foot (see Table 88.9 ). Treatment Fundamental therapeutic goals in frostbite are rapid rewarming, prevention of further cold exposure, and restoration of circulation. Once the patient is in a setting in which re-freezing cannot occur, rapid water bath rewarming is indicated. The water bath temper- ature should be about 37–39°C (99–102°F), ideally a whirlpool is utilized so a steady temperature can be maintained. This process of rewarming may be painful, so appropriate analgesia should be provided. Rubbing the frozen extremity with ice, using dry heat, and slow rewarming are all contraindicated. In the hypothermic patient with frostbite injury, it is important to complete fluid resuscitation and core rewarming before limb rewarming, to prevent sudden hypotension and shock. Accurate clinical assessment of the degree of injury, routine wound care, protective dressings, monitoring for infection, and consideration of tetanus prophylaxis should then follow. Radiologic evaluation (e.g. MRI, bone scan, plain films) may help determine extent of injury and prognosis. Nowadays, angiog- raphy and triple-phase bone scans are considered the standard of care for assessing tissue viability and guiding care during the initial days following injury 23 . Additional therapeutic suggestions have been based on animal studies, case reports, or small series. Because of increased blood viscosity and sludging, thrombolytic therapy (e.g. heparin, tissue plasminogen activator, streptokinase) ± a vasodilator (e.g. iloprost, limaprost) has been suggested. Superficial non-hemorrhagic bullae may be aspirated or debrided to avoid prolonged exposure to prosta- glandins and thromboxanes within blister fluid. Aloe vera, a throm- boxane inhibitor, has been

Pentoxifylline has been found to be useful, as have anti-inflammatory agents such as methylprednisolone, methimazole, and aspirin. It is most common in areas without central heating. History Over a hundred years ago, pernio/chilblains was apparently common enough in Europe and the UK that the condition was well recognized. In 1881, Piffard 28 described it quite well: “This affection, so common in cold climates, affects, by preference, the face, hands, nose, and ears. It is characterized by redness, usually with a purplish tinge, together with more or less pain of a burning character giving little or no trouble during the summer, but causing inconvenience and suffering as cold weather sets in.” Epidemiology Exposure to cold, wet conditions is the major risk factor for pernio. This disorder has been reported most frequently in the UK and north- western Europe, particularly in those whose homes lack central heating. It also occurs more often in individuals whose work and leisure activ- ities are outdoors. Young women, children, and the elderly are most commonly affected, as well as those with a lower body mass index. Elderly patients may have a prolonged course, while younger patients improve spontaneously 29–31 . Pathogenesis Pernio can be either primary (idiopathic) or secondary, i.e. due to an underlying condition. The precise pathogenesis of idiopathic pernio is unknown, but it is thought to represent an abnormal inflammatory response to vascular ischemia caused by prolonged vasoconstriction in the setting of extended exposure to cold, damp environments 27 . In children and adults, it may be associated with cryoglobulins or cold agglutinins 31,32 . In severe cases, blistering and ulceration may be seen ( Fig. 88.7D ). Lesions are often symmetri- cally distributed on the distal toes and fingers, and less often on the heels, nose,

In addition to clinical features, e.g. retiform purpura, these entities can be further assessed by laboratory evaluation including: (1) complete blood count to exclude hemolytic anemia, myelogenous leukemia, or myelodysplastic syndrome; (2) cryoglobulin, cold agglutinin, and cryofibrinogen levels to eliminate cold-sensitive dysproteinemia; and (3) serum protein electropho- resis and immunofixation electrophoresis to exclude a monoclonal gammopathy. During the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic, an increased incidence of pernio has been reported (“COVID toes”), most often in children and teenagers. The vast majority of patients have been SARS-CoV-2 PCR-negative and did not develop anti-SARS-CoV-2 antibodies. As a result, there is an ongoing debate as to the relationship of pernio to SARS-CoV-2 infection. Nonetheless, patients with pernio should be questioned regarding symptoms of SARS-CoV-2 infection and possible contacts 34,35 . In general, those individuals who were infected had a mild clinical course. Treatment Adequate clothing and avoidance of cold, damp conditions are important preventive measures, as are keeping feet dry and avoidance of smoking. In a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, nifedipine (20 to 60 mg daily) was found to be efficacious for the treatment of pernio. None of the nifedipine-treated patients relapsed, while all of the placebo- treated patients developed new lesions 36 . It is effective in about 70% of patients with pernio. Medium- to high-potency topical corticosteroids are often prescribed, but supportive evidence is lacking. Other anecdotal remedies include topical 0.2% nitroglycerin, topical minoxidil, oral nicotinamide, pentoxifylline, phenoxybenzamine, sympathectomy, and erythemogenic UVB phototherapy 29 . Shelter foot  ­Paddy-field foot  Swamp foot  Jungle rot  Foxhole foot  Peripheral vasoneuropathy  Nonfreezing cold injury Key features  Injury occurs after continuous exposure of feet to moist, occluded conditions  Cold water, warm water, and tropical variants exist  The underlying pathologic process is overhydration of the stratum corneum  Nonfreezing cold injury can lead to peripheral vasoneuropathy  Neuropathy may persist indefinitely  Feet exposed to immersion injury are more sensitive to re-injury Introduction Immersion injury occurs in either cold or warm environments when the feet are exposed to continuous moisture with no opportunity for intermittent drying. Severe injury may produce permanent peripheral neuropathy and long-term morbidity. History Soldiers on the Western Front in World War I spent extended periods of time in the cold, wet, muddy conditions of trench warfare, leading to the death of ~75 000 British soldiers and the term trench foot . Immersion foot emerged during World War II, with shipwrecked troops spending days in partially submerged lifeboats. The Korean conflict and the Vietnam War led to more variations and tremendous numbers of casualties. Immersion foot also occurs outside armed conflicts, including in persons experiencing homelessness, fishermen, skiers, and revelers at music festivals 37–39 . Epidemiology Susceptibility to immersion foot is widely variable. Use of sandals or open shoes, constant activity, thinner plantar stratum corneum, and intermittent air drying seem somewhat protective. Risk factors for immersion foot include: prolonged occupational or recreational exposure to wet conditions, constrictive clothing, immobility or prolonged dependency of feet, dehydration, poor nutritional status, altered mental status, smoking, peripheral vascular disease, uncontrolled diabetes, tinea pedis, trauma, and experiencing homelessness 37,39 . Pathogenesis The underlying pathophysiology of all forms of immersion foot is overhy- dration of the stratum corneum. The permeability coefficient of plantar skin is ~10 times that of the dorsal foot skin, leading to increased water absorption. The plantar stratum corneum can absorb ~200% of its dry weight in water, with a proportionately higher absorption of fresh water than saline. Warm water immersion foot (WWIF) results from severe hyperhy- dration of the stratum corneum, with subsequent maceration. Plantar skin temperature reaches body core temperature after about an hour in an impervious boot with 19°C (66°F) water. As the injury continues, inflammatory changes develop and may progress to a lymphocytic vasculitis with vascular compromise and erythrocyte extravasation ( tropical immersion foot [TIF]).
