Non-infectious Granulomas Cutaneous Crohn disease is relatively rare with < 300 cases reported in the literature to date and < 100 cases in children. Two-thirds of the patients are women, and the mean age of onset is 35 years. Approximately 20% of the reported cases had skin disease that preceded the diagnosis of intestinal Crohn disease by 3 months to 8 years. Pathogenesis Cutaneous Crohn disease occurs in association with or precedes intestinal Crohn disease, reflecting a multisystem disease. A number of genetic abnormalities which can lead to an exaggerated T cell response to certain commensal enteric bacteria and defective microbial clearance, including after breaks in the mucosal barrier or an alter- ation in the balance in gut flora (dysbiosis), have been linked to Crohn disease. The protein products of these genes have several functions, including regulation of NF- κ B function (e.g. NOD2 [ CARD15 ]) and autophagy ( ATG16L1 , IRGM ). Patients with variants in TRAF3IP2 , a psoriasis susceptibility gene, may have a greater risk of cutaneous involvement 121 . Like psoriasis, Crohn disease is a predominantly Th1- and Th17-mediated disease, with elevated levels of IL-23 and IL-17 within involved tissues 122 . Clinical Features Cutaneous Crohn disease may be either genital or extragenital, with genital involvement found in approximately two-thirds of children and one-half of adults. Labial, penile, or scrotal erythema and/or lymphedema are common presenting signs and can be dramatic 123 ( Fig. 93.17A–C,F ). Linear or “knife-like” ulcerations that are within body folds (e.g. inguinal creases, perianal region, axillae) or involve the oral mucosa are relatively specific

disease, with elevated levels of IL-23 and IL-17 within involved tissues 122 . Clinical Features Cutaneous Crohn disease may be either genital or extragenital, with genital involvement found in approximately two-thirds of children and one-half of adults. Labial, penile, or scrotal erythema and/or lymphedema are common presenting signs and can be dramatic 123 ( Fig. 93.17A–C,F ). Linear or “knife-like” ulcerations that are within body folds (e.g. inguinal creases, perianal region, axillae) or involve the oral mucosa are relatively specific for mucocutaneous Crohn disease (see Figs. 53.28 and 72.25 ) 121 . Perianal involvement, which may extend to the adjacent perineum, buttocks or abdomen, consists of sinus tracts, fissures, ulcers, and vegetating plaques ( Fig. 93.17D,E ) 124 . These findings occur in approx- imately one-third of patients with intestinal Crohn disease. Perianal skin tags, thought to be secondary to lymphedema, are observed in up to 40% of patients; as with other sites of lymphedema, granulomatous inflammation may be present as well. Sites of abdominal surgery, e.g. laparotomies, colostomies, ileostomies, may also develop granulo- matous inflammation. For semantic purposes, the latter is considered to be “contiguous” rather than non-contiguous (“metastatic”) Crohn disease. Oral lesions occur in 5%–20% of patients with Crohn disease, and these may consist of cobblestoning of the buccal mucosa, tiny gingival nodules, gingival hyperplasia, aphthae-like ulcers ( Fig. 93.17G ), linear, knife-like ulcerations, pyostomatitis vegetans (see Fig. 25.9A ), angular cheilitis and ulceration, secondary orofacial granulomatosis ( Fig. 93.17I ), diffuse oral swelling, or indurated fissuring of the lower lip. Histologically, 90% of oral lesions associated with Crohn disease contain granulomas 124 . Non-genital disease presents with dusky erythematous plaques, often followed by the development of ulceration with undermined edges, draining sinuses and fistulas, and scarring ( Fig. 93.17H ). These lesions have been observed on the lower extremities and soles (40%), abdomen and trunk (25%), upper extremities and palms (15%), face and lips (10%), flexural areas (8%), and in a generalized distribution (4%) 116,125 . Other reactive cutaneous manifestations of Crohn disease include cutaneous arteritis (cutaneous polyarteritis nodosa), erythema nodosum, erythema multiforme, finger clubbing, cutaneous small vessel vasculitis, epidermolysis bullosa acquisita, vitiligo, palmar erythema, a pustular response to trauma (pathergy), Sweet syndrome, and pyoderma gangrenosum (see Ch. 53 ). Other reactive cutaneous manifestations of Crohn disease include cutaneous arteritis (cutaneous polyarteritis nodosa), erythema nodosum, erythema multiforme, finger clubbing, cutaneous small vessel vasculitis, epidermolysis bullosa acquisita, vitiligo, palmar erythema, a pustular response to trauma (pathergy), Sweet syndrome, and pyoderma gangrenosum (see Ch. 53 ). Zinc deficiency may cause an acrodermatitis enteropathica-like syndrome in patients with severe Crohn disease 116 . Based upon a large retrospective series, cutaneous involvement may be indicative of colonic, rather than ileal, involvement 117,118 . No consistent correlation exists between mucocutaneous disease activity and degree of gastrointestinal involvement. However, levels of fecal calprotectin can reflect the degree of intestinal inflammation. Pathology In both cutaneous and oral lesions of Crohn disease, small, nodular, non-caseating, epithelioid granulomas with surrounding lympho- cytes are found in the superficial and deep dermis, sometimes extending into the subcutaneous fat. There are a few scattered multinucleated Langhans-type giant cells and a sparse perivascular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate; overlying ulceration may be present. Of note, the combination of lichenoid and granulomatous inflam- mation plus granulomatous perivasculitis can serve as a histopatho- logic clue 126 . The walls of perianal sinuses and fistulas have similar granulomatous inflammation. However, the granulomatous foci may be subtle, requiring multiple sections to identify the granulomas, and clinicopathologic correlation as well as additional biopsies may be required. Differential Diagnosis Clinically, the differential diagnosis of cutaneous Crohn disease includes other granulomatous disorders such as cutaneous sarcoidosis, mycobacterial infections, deep fungal infections, and foreign body reactions. Other infections, such as actinomycosis or cellulitis, may mimic cutaneous Crohn disease. Ulcerated lesions may be mis- diagnosed as pyoderma gangrenosum. In the case of genital swelling and ulcerations, one must consider granuloma inguinale, schistoso- miasis, hidradenitis suppurativa, and chronic lymphedema due to obstruction 125 . The histopathologic picture of cutaneous Crohn disease can be indistinguishable from other granulomatous diseases with tuber- culoid features, including lupus vulgaris. In the latter, central necrosis within tubercles is a helpful distinguishing clue. Differentiating cutaneous Crohn disease from sarcoidosis can also be challenging, although Crohn disease usually has denser collections of lymphocytes and granulomatous perivasculitis as well as the features described above. Foreign body granulomas and infectious granulomas should be considered in the histologic differential diagnosis. Special stains for acid-fast bacilli and fungal organisms should be obtained, and all skin biopsies should be polarized to look for foreign bodies. Pyoderma gangrenosum and cutaneous

latter, central necrosis within tubercles is a helpful distinguishing clue. Differentiating cutaneous Crohn disease from sarcoidosis can also be challenging, although Crohn disease usually has denser collections of lymphocytes and granulomatous perivasculitis as well as the features described above. Foreign body granulomas and infectious granulomas should be considered in the histologic differential diagnosis. Special stains for acid-fast bacilli and fungal organisms should be obtained, and all skin biopsies should be polarized to look for foreign bodies. Pyoderma gangrenosum and cutaneous Crohn disease can sometimes have overlapping clinical and histopathologic features as neutrophilic inflammation may be present in both, but granulomas are absent in pyoderma gangrenosum. Treatment Cutaneous Crohn disease tends to be chronic, and its severity does not always correlate with the activity of the patient’s intestinal disease. For localized disease, topical or intralesional corticosteroids and/or topical calcineurin inhibitors may be utilized 127 . Oral metronidazole (250 mg TID for at least 4 months) can be an effective treatment. For more extensive disease, use of systemic medications including corticosteroids, sulfasalazine, azathioprine, 6-mercaptopurine, and thalidomide may lead to improvement. By targeting the underlying immunopathogenesis, TNF inhibitors (e.g. infliximab, adalimumab) 128 and ustekinumab have been reported to improve cutaneous disease. IL-17 inhibitors have been reported to exacerbate Crohn disease. Surgical excision of lesions is often complicated by wound dehiscence and disease recurrence, but can be considered for refractory disease. small foci of vasculitis also may be present Introduction Palisaded neutrophilic and granulomatous dermatitis (PNGD) and interstitial granulomatous dermatitis (IGD) with arthritis represent two patterns of granulomatous dermatitis that occur in patients with RA and other autoimmune disorders. Since these entities exhibit overlapping clinicopathologic features and may represent a disease spectrum, the overarching term reactive granulomatous dermatitis has been proposed 129 . History In 1994, Chu and colleagues 130 proposed the term “palisaded neutrophilic and granulomatous dermatitis” for the histologic reaction pattern that characterizes papular eruptions on the extensor extremities that present in the context of autoimmune connective tissue disease and other condi- tions characterized by immune complex generation. Such skin lesions were originally described in the setting of eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg–Strauss syndrome), and their association with a broad spectrum of autoimmune and inflammatory disorders was first recognized by Winkelmann in 1978 (cutaneous extravascular necrotizing granuloma). text: and other condi- tions characterized by immune complex generation. Such skin lesions were originally described in the setting of eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg–Strauss syndrome), and their association with a broad spectrum of autoimmune and inflammatory disorders was first recognized by Winkelmann in 1978 (cutaneous extravascular necrotizing granuloma). Some authors include “interstitial granulomatous dermatitis with arthritis”, a term coined by Ackerman in 1993, within the PNGD spectrum. Others argue that the former represents a separate entity with distinct clinical (annular plaques and cords favoring the lateral trunk and skin folds) and histologic (histiocytic rosettes without evidence of vascu- litis) features. More recently, the term reactive granulomatous dermatitis was introduced as an overarching term 129,131 . Pathogenesis It is thought that the initiating insult in reactive granulomatous derma- titis is immune complex deposition on or around the walls of small dermal blood vessels as a result of the underlying disease, which leads to a subacute or chronic neutrophil-rich small vessel vasculitis. This then impairs blood flow to the area in a smoldering fashion, as opposed to the abrupt vascular occlusion of classic vasculitis; consequently, there is degeneration of the local collagen rather than acute necrosis. The degenerated collagen incites an immune response resulting in a palisading lymphohistiocytic infiltrate. This cascade of events is likely aggravated or precipitated by exogenous trauma, which explains the predilection of lesions for the extensor surfaces. Variable sizes, amounts, and sites of immune complex deposition (e.g. dermal venules versus the interstitial dermis), chronicity of the process, and different triggers and underlying systemic inflammatory disorders may account for the spectrum of clinical and histologic features. Central umbilication with crusts or perforation (with extrusion of necrobiotic collagen) may be present (see Fig. 53.2 ), and ulceration occasionally occurs. Such papular lesions have been observed most commonly in patients with SLE, rheumatoid arthritis, or systemic vasculitis, particularly granulomatosis with polyangiitis. IGD with arthritis has been described as erythematous plaques, often with an annular configuration ( Fig. 93.18A ), or linear cords (the “rope sign”; Fig. 93.18B ) that favor the lateral trunk, axillae, and girdle area (see Fig. 53.1 ). Extensive areas of involvement can be seen ( Fig. 93.18C ). This presentation has been described most often in women with rheumatoid arthritis, seronegative arthritis, or polyarthralgias and it may be associated with autoimmune thyroiditis. However, in a large retrospective series, the rope sign was noted in only two patients with autoimmune disease-associated IGD 131 . When viewed as a disease spectrum, the skin findings in reactive granulomatous dermatitis consisted of plaques, often annular, as well as macules, papules, or nodules located primarily on the extremities and trunk 131 . Associated conditions were observed in 75% of patients, irrespective of whether they were classified histologically as having IGD versus PNGD; the majority of these underlying disorders were autoimmune diseases (54%), followed by malignancies (12%). In addition to myelodysplasia, PNGD can develop in patients with chronic myelomonocytic leukemia, including those with SRSF2 mutations. Reactive granulomatous dermatitis also encompasses interstitial granulomatous drug reactions. The most likely culprits are calcium channel blockers and HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors (“statins”; expand. Cutaneous lesions typically appear after months to years of exposure to the drug. Of note, in patients with rheumatoid arthritis and psoriatic arthritis, TNF inhibitors have led to the development of IGD- and PNGD-like lesions 132 . Pathology In that PNGD and IGD have overlapping clinical features, it follows that the histopathologic features of PNGD and IGD also constitute a spectrum, with features depending on the stage of evolution of the lesion that is biopsied. One series demonstrated overlapping histopathologic findings in 25% of cases, lending support for use of the overarching term reactive granulomatous dermatitis 131 . Early lesions of PNGD often show a pandermal infiltrate of neutro- phils, sometimes with focal leukocytoclastic vasculitis. Classic, fully developed lesions are characterized by zones of basophilic degen- erated collagen surrounded by palisades of histiocytes, neutrophils, and nuclear debris ( Fig. 93.19 ). “Incomplete” early lesions may display focal basophilic collagen necrosis and histiocytes without orderly palisading in association with prominent neutrophils. On the other hand, late lesions can exhibit well-developed palisading granu- lomas with only a sparse complement of neutrophils. Mucin is rare to absent. There is no evidence of vasculitis, and dermal mucin is usually absent. The histologic pattern of IGD features smaller “rosettes” of palisading histiocytes surrounding tiny, discrete foci of degenerated collagen (piecemeal fragmentation) within a dense, “bottom-heavy” dermal interstitial infiltrate that contains variable numbers of neutrophils and sometimes eosinophils. There is no evidence of vasculitis, and dermal mucin is usually absent. In interstitial granulomatous drug eruptions, histopathologic features overlap with both PNGD and IGD, but there may be more tissue eosin- ophilia, lymphocyte atypia, and interface vacuolar changes. Differential Diagnosis The clinical differential diagnosis is broad. For classic PNGD lesions, it includes perforating disorders, early rheumatoid nodules, accelerated DISORDERS OF LANGERHANS CELLS AND MACROPHAGES rheumatoid nodulosis, and papular granuloma annulare (GA). The clinical presentation of IGD with plaques may resemble patch-type GA, the inflammatory stage of morphea, erythema migrans, or mycosis fungoides. The histologic differential diagnosis includes other palisaded granulo- matous dermatitides such as GA, necrobiosis lipoidica, and rheumatoid nodules. GA is more likely to have a patchy infiltrate concentrated in the upper dermis (“top heavy”) and mucin deposition. A paucity of neutrophils and leukocytoclasis distinguishes GA from PNGD, whereas the presence of either larger palisades or a lack of palisades (e.g. in the interstitial pattern seen in patch-type GA) differentiates GA from IGD. Rheumatoid nodules can be recognized by their central eosinophilia (rather than basophilia) and predominantly subcutaneous location (see Fig. 45.10 ). All of these entities may show transepidermal elimination of degenerated collagen. Additional diagnostic considerations for an interstitial granulo- matous infiltrate with variable neutrophils may include dimorphic fungal or atypical mycobacterial infections, borreliosis, and leprosy. Histologic features that favor an interstitial granulomatous drug reaction over IGD include a vacuolar interface dermatitis, atypical lymphocytes, prominent eosinophils, a paucity of neutrophils, and minimal collagen degeneration. The relationship of PNGD and IGD with other dermatoses that have granulomatous, neutrophilic, or vasculitic components and affect this patient population are shown in Table 93.8 . Lastly, neonates with primary immunodeficiencies can develop perforating neutrophilic and granulomatous dermatitis associated with immunodeficiency in which papules develop into vesicles, pustules, crusts, and ulcers; histologically there is evidence of transepidermal elimination via hair follicles. Treatment Treatment of the underlying disorder or removal of the inciting medication can lead to resolution of existing lesions and prevent recur- rences. In addition, foreign body reactions have been observed in association with 2-octyl cyanoacrylate, a tissue adhesive used for small superficial wounds and lacerations, as well as a copolymer-containing lubricating agent used for liposuction 4 . Iatrogenic Foreign material implanted into the skin for the purpose of tissue augmentation, e.g. injectable soft tissue fillers, can induce reactions in some individuals ( Fig. 94.1 ). Paraffin is still being used illegally for tissue augmentation (see below), and a paraffin foreign body reaction can also occur after the application of paraffin-containing materials such as nasal packs 5 . Tattooing Tattooing is the introduction of an exogenous pigment into the dermis, either deliberately or accidentally, resulting in permanent discoloration of the skin. Topical application When applied to the skin surface, antiperspirant and antipruritic preparations that contain zirconium oxide or zirconium lactate were noted to cause foreign body reactions. As a result, zirconium lactate was generally banned in 1978 (see below). These zirconium compounds have subsequently been replaced by aluminum–zirconium complexes and while the latter are less sensitizing, they may occasionally lead to foreign body reactions 6 . Self-inflicted Self-administered intravenous and subcutaneous injections, a common practice among individuals with substance use disorder, may lead to the introduction of foreign material into the skin. An example is the injection of crushed talc-containing tablets. Pathogenesis The initial tissue response to most foreign substances involves an accumulation of neutrophils, which usually fail to properly deal with the foreign body. Its persistence attracts monocytes and local tissue macrophages that engulf the foreign material and become activated. Engulfed material may resist degradation and remain sequestered within the macrophages. Activated macrophages secrete a variety of specific biologically active substances, e.g. cytokines and chemokines, that attract additional macrophages and blood monocytes. The formation of a chronic granuloma represents an attempt by the body to sequester a persistent indigestible material. Individual macrophages may become larger (epithelioid histiocytes) or fuse to form multinucleated foreign body giant cells ( Fig. 94.2 ) 7 . The infiltrate also contains T lymphocytes and fibroblasts. The pathogenesis of other patterns of reactions, e.g. lichenoid, pyogenic granuloma-like, pseudolymphomatous, remains speculative. Clinical Features The host response and, consequently, the clinical presentations of foreign body implantation are variable ( Table 94.2 & 94.3 ). An acute inflammatory response occurs shortly after the entry of the foreign material. This may resolve, to be followed weeks, months, or even years later by a chronic inflammatory response. Although the latter may have a variety of clinical presentations, red to red–brown papules, nodules, and plaques (with or without ulceration) are most commonly observed. Over time, the lesions may become firmer due to fibrosis. Such a broad definition also includes infectious agents, but they are covered elsewhere (see Chs. 74–85 ). This chapter will focus on non-living materials that have been introduced into the dermis or subcutis 1–3 . They represent inorganic compounds or organic material of high molecular weight (or their products) that resist degradation by the body’s inflammatory cells. Although granulomatous reaction patterns are most commonly observed, there is a broad range of clinicopathologic presentations. Foreign bodies reported to elicit skin reactions are listed in Table 94.1 . Routes of Entry Accidental Inoculation with foreign bodies may occur unintentionally during various activities such as gardening (wood splinters, cactus spines) or swimming and diving (coelenterate envenomation, sea urchin spines), or it may result accidentally, such as in a blast injury (silica particles) or motor vehicle accident. Surgical procedures Contamination of wounds by talc or starch powders used for lubrication of surgical gloves may incite a foreign body reaction. Foreign Body Reactions (see Table 94.3 ). Granulomas that develop as a reaction to foreign bodies are of two major types: The allergic type is characterized by the presence of collections of individual epithelioid histiocytes associated with variable numbers of lymphocytes and fewer multinucleated Langhans-type giant cells 7 . In the non-immunologic type, the foreign body giant cell is the most conspicuous component of the infiltrate (see Fig. 94.2 ), which also contains histiocytes, lymphocytes, and other inflammatory cells 14 . A histologic decision as to whether a granuloma is of the foreign body type or of the allergic type is not always possible and different patterns may be seen in the same section. The foreign material inciting a reaction may be detected in conventional H&E-stained sections or may require special procedures for its identification (see Table 94.3 ). Diagnosis Foreign body reactions should be considered in the differential diagnosis of localized inflammatory nodules and plaques, especially when there is a persistent draining wound or sinus. Occasionally, these reactions present as pyogenic granulomas or localized lichenoid papules. Clinical morphology is usually not distinctive, but there may be a suggestive distribution pattern, and a thorough history is indispensable for arriving at the correct diagnosis. Histopathologic examination can confirm the granulomatous nature of a lesion and occasionally foreign bodies may show distinctive microscopic features in H&E-stained sections ( Fig. 94.3 ) 14 . Because some foreign bodies are better visualized via polarized microscopy, this is routinely performed ( Fig. 94.4 ). In addition to detecting radiolucent foreign bodies, high frequency ultrasound has been employed to assess the severity and depth of inflammatory reactions to tattoos and soft tissue fillers 14 . CT, MRI, and PET-CT have also been used to evaluate foreign body reactions but can have limitations with regard to detection of small cutaneous foreign bodies. Identification of the chemical nature of the foreign body requires sophisticated physicochemical procedures (e.g. energy-dispersive X-ray analysis, laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy) that are available in only a few research centers 15 . FOREIGN BODY REACTIONS TO INORGANIC AND METALLIC COMPOUNDS Tattoo A tattoo may occur accidentally or deliberately for cosmetic and decorative purposes. Accidental tattooing results from unintentional deposition of exogenous pigmented substances such as asphalt, carbon, or graphite (pencils) within injured skin ( Fig. 94.5 ). Automobile, bicycle, and skating accidents as well as puncture wounds are the most common causes of traumatic tattoos. In decorative tattooing, the pigment is introduced into the dermis via needles or a tattoo gun to create various designs, group- identity symbols, or writings. Cosmetic tattoos are also done to define the contours of lips and eyebrows, permanently replace eyeliner, make eyebrows appear fuller (via microblading), or camouflage an abnormality in skin color. An iatrogenic tattoo may remain after the use of ferrous subsulfate (Monsel’s solution) for hemostasis. Other hemostatic agents, e.g. aluminum chloride, may cause a foreign body reaction histologically (see below), but do not lead to discoloration of the skin. Decorative tattoos often contain a number of pigments that are combined to create different hues, but the composition of tattoo inks has not been standardized. In some patients, granulomatous papulonodules within a tattoo can be a manifestation of cutaneous or systemic sarcoidosis 17 . Rarely, a photoallergic reaction, presenting as pruritic, inflamed nodules, occurs in red or yellow tattoos containing cadmium sulfide following exposure to UV light 16 . Pathology Different patterns of an inflammatory response can be elicited, including sarcoidal, foreign body granulomatous, lichenoid, eczematous, and pseudolymphomatous 13 . The majority of tattoo pigments appear black in H&E-stained sections, regardless of the color of the pigment (see Fig. 72.23B ). Occasionally, colors other than black are seen (see below) 19 . The pigment is deposited in the upper and mid dermis, both extracellularly between collagen bundles and around blood vessels as well as a smaller amount within the cytoplasm of macrophages. The pigment deposits in professional tattoos are relatively small and homogeneous in size and shape, while in traumatic tattoos they are larger and vary in size and shape 14 . Coarse, granular brown pigment within macrophages and between collagen fibers are seen in iatrogenic tattoos due to ferrous subsulfate (Monsel’s solution; Diagnosis and differential diagnosis The presence of inflammatory lesions confined to the site of a tattoo suggests the diagnosis. Inoculation of certain infectious agents (e.g. atypical mycobacteria) may mimic pigment-induced inflammation within a tattoo ( Table 94.4 ). In addition to hypertrophic scars and keloids, unrelated benign and malignant tumors can also develop within tattoos. Identification of the causative pigment is generally unnecessary unless further tattooing is anticipated. Other causes of dermal pigmentation include melanin, hemosiderin, lipofuscin, exogenous ochronosis, silver, gold, minocycline, amiodarone, and chlorpromazine. Special stains to identify melanin and iron (hemosiderin) may be useful (see Ch. 0 ). Treatment Topical or intralesional corticosteroids can be used to treat inflamed tattoos. If injections do not lead to significant improvement, surgical excision, if feasible, to remove the inciting pigment is an option. Q-switched and picosecond lasers are commonly employed to remove the various pigments in tattoos (see Fig. 137.16 & Table 137.4 ) 18 , but it is recommended that laser therapy be limited to non-inflamed tattoos 20 . Paraffin Paraffin, being a mineral oil, is not hydrolyzed by tissue lipases and is treated by the body as a foreign substance. Augmentation of body contour by local injection of paraffin, although banned in most countries, is still performed in some regions of the world and is mostly done by non-medical personnel. Accidental paraffinoma of the orbit and palpebra has been reported following intraoperative placement of paraffin-impregnated gauze packs within the nasal cavity 5 . Clinical features In those cases due to injected paraffin, the genitalia, buttocks, and breast are the most common sites of involvement. Penile paraffinomas, also referred to as sclerosing lipogranulomas of the penis, can lead to significant deformity ( Fig. 94.9A ). Clinically, non-tender firm nodules and indurated plaques are seen, sometimes with ulceration or abscess formation and involvement of subcutaneous tissue (see Ch. 100 ). The interval between the time of injection and the development of lesions varies from weeks to decades. Pathology The dermis shows a characteristic “Swiss cheese” appearance due to the presence of numerous ovoid or round cavities where the paraffin resided prior to processing ( Fig. 94.9B ). Between the cavities, there is fibrotic connective tissue and a cellular infiltrate composed of macro- phages, variable numbers of multinucleated foreign body giant cells, and lymphocytes. Some of the macrophages have foamy cytoplasm. In specially processed tissue, the foreign material stains with fat stains 22 , although less intensely than neutral fats, helping to differentiate paraf- finoma from reactions to silicone, which also have numerous cavities but negative fat stains. Foreign Body Reactions Silicone Silicone (polydimethyl siloxane), in a liquid, gel, or solid form, is used for tissue augmentation. While silicone is generally regarded as an inert substance, in some patients its use has been followed by foreign body reactions. Clinical features Silicone gel-filled implants are widely used for breast augmentation as well as reconstruction after mastectomy and leakage due to perme- ability loss or rupture can occur. Silicone injections and implants have also been employed for body and facial contour augmentation, including correcting HIV-related lipoatrophy. When a cutaneous foreign body reaction occurs, nodules and plaques develop at the site of injection or placement after a period of months to years. Skin lesions also appear at distant sites, reflecting the tendency for silicone to migrate, including in a dependent, gravity-driven direction. With progression, sclerosis and ulcerations can be seen. Whether the immune system is recognizing the silicone itself versus additives or contaminants including microbes remains speculative 23 . In a recent systematic review, hypercalcemia with renal failure was noted in association with silicone-induced foreign body granu- lomas and, to lesser extent, polymethylmethacrylate-, paraffin-, and mineral oil-induced foreign body granulomas 24 . Agreement does exist that textured breast implants, both saline and silicone, are associated with anaplastic large cell lymphoma of the breast. Pathology A biopsy specimen is critical to establishing the diagnosis. Histologic sections have a multivacuolated appearance due to the presence of silicone-filled cavities surrounded by histiocytes, lymphocytes, and eosinophils. The histiocytes may be foamy or multinucleated. Fibrous tissue within the areas separating the cavities is also seen. In contrast to paraffinomas, the cavity contents do not stain with lipid stains. Occasionally, silicone granulomas can mimic a low-grade liposarcoma. Treatment Excision of persistent symptomatic lesions is recommended. Silica Wounds or penetrating injuries accidentally contaminated with silica (silicon dioxide) contained in sand, soil, rocks, and glass may be followed some years later by the formation of a foreign body reaction. The period between inoculation and development of a reaction may be as long as 25 years. This extended “incubation” period is due to the very slow release of colloidal silica (the only form capable of inciting a reaction) from the large particles of silica introduced into the body 26 . Reactions to silica are thought to be due to a delayed-type hypersensi- tivity response. Clinical features At first, the wound heals, but then papules, nodules, or indurated plaques develop within the scar years later. Multiple disseminated lesions may follow trauma produced by the explosion of land mines and bombs 26 . Patients with sarcoidosis may be at increased risk for immunologic responses to silica 27 . Pathology The dermis contains multiple nodular aggregates of granulomas, usually sarcoidal and less often foreign body, separated by strands of connective tissue. Langhans- and foreign body-type giant cells are usually numerous in both types of granuloma. Colorless crystals may be observed within the cytoplasm of the giant cells or lying free in the interstitium. These bodies are birefringent when examined with polarized microscopy. Differential diagnosis Granulomatous lesions occurring at the site of an old scar may mimic cutaneous sarcoidosis clinically and histologically 28 . However, the presence of foreign material within a sarcoidal granuloma does not exclude sarcoidosis, given the attraction of sarcoidosis to existing scars. Examination under polarized light will identify silica crystals. Treatment Excision of persistent symptomatic lesions is recommended. Spontaneous resolution of silica granulomas, although reported, is exceptional. Talc Talc (hydrous magnesium silicate) is a common cause of foreign body granulomas given its presence in dusting, antifungal, and antibiotic powders. In addition, it is still preferred by some surgeons as a lubricant for surgical gloves. Talc can therefore contaminate wounds, erosions, and umbilical stumps, or it may enter the skin via abrasions and fissures, particularly in intertriginous zones in obese individuals who apply talc powder liberally 29 . Individuals with substance use disorder who inject solutions intrave- nously or subcutaneously that contain crushed tablets may also develop foreign body reactions to talc as talc is a common filler in tablets. text: As with reactions to other forms of silica, the lesions usually take a long time to appear. The clinical appearance is varied: it may take the form of erythematous papules and nodules or simply thickening and erythema of an old scar, similar to the range of findings in sarcoidosis. Rarely lesions may resemble a pyogenic granuloma. Despite the long latency period, the diagnosis should be considered, especially when lesions appear in certain sites, e.g. the umbilicus in infants, inguinal area in patients with a history of intertrigo, injection sites in those with a history of intravenous drug use. Pathology The histologic features may be similar to those of sarcoidosis or non-caseating tuberculosis. Alternatively, there may be granulomatous inflammation consisting of histiocytes and foreign body giant cells. A few of these cells may contain clear, blue–green, or yellow–brown, needle-shaped or round crystals. Under polarized light, talc crystals are birefringent. A picture simulating a pyogenic granuloma plus giant cells has also been described 5 . Treatment Excision of persistent symptomatic lesions is recommended. Zirconium Some zirconium salts were once components of antiperspirant prepara- tions as well as over-the-counter preparations used in the treatment of allergic contact dermatitis. Sodium zirconium lactate was the first salt incriminated as a cause of foreign body reactions and while banned in the late 1970s, it was replaced by aluminum–zirconium complexes. Subsequently, zirconium oxide and aluminum–zirconium complex were shown to be capable of producing the same reaction. Development of foreign body granulomas represents a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction to zirconium 6 . In sensitized individuals, persistent, soft, red–brown papules appear in areas to which zirconium-containing preparations were applied. The axillary skin is the most frequently affected site. Histologically, non-caseating granulomas resembling a sarcoidal reaction are seen 6 . The small size of the zirconium particles does not allow their detection with polarized light microscopy; however, energy- dispersive X-ray analysis can prove their presence. Histologically, cutaneous lesions of systemic berylliosis are indistin- guishable from sarcoidosis. In the past, when beryllium was used in the manufacture of fluorescent light bulbs, local cutaneous berylliosis was noted to have a caseating tuberculoid pattern. In systemic berylliosis, bronchioalveolar lavage is recommended for diagnosis. Aluminum Rare hypersensitivity reactions to the aluminum adjuvant in vaccines and hyposensitization immunotherapy do occur. Persistent subcu- taneous granulomatous nodules can appear at the sites of injection several months after vaccination 32 . Histologically, a central zone of degenerated collagen is surrounded by a rim of both histiocytes, whose cytoplasm contains bluish-grey granules, and lymphoid aggregates, some of which form germinal centers 32,33 . There are also abundant eosinophils. Special stains (e.g. staining for aluminon in which the aluminum appears red) may make aluminum particles more evident. Of note, application of topical aluminum chloride for hemostasis can result in the presence of basophilic granules of varying size and shape within the cytoplasm of macrophages 34 . Zinc A zinc-induced granuloma at the site of an injection is a rare compli- cation of zinc-containing insulin 35 . Sterile furuncles develop at the injection sites and eventually heal with atrophic scars. Histologically, an initial stage characterized by a dense neutrophilic infiltrate is followed by granuloma formation that ends in fibrosis. By polarizing microscopy, birefringent rhomboid crystals are seen. Treatment Zirconium, beryllium, aluminum, and zinc granulomas may be surgi- cally excised if they are symptomatic. REACTIONS TO ORGANIC AND BIOLOGIC PRODUCTS Starch Granulomas may result from the contamination of wounds with starch used as a lubricant for surgical gloves. Pathology Foreign body granulomas with multinucleated giant cells are seen. Starch granules appear as ovoid basophilic structures. They stain positively with periodic acid Schiff (PAS) and with polarized light are birefringent with a characteristic “Maltese cross”-like appearance 36 . Cactus Spines Accidental implantation of cactus spines into the skin results from contact with cacti in gardens and fields. Occupational exposure occurs in persons peeling and selling prickly pear fruit, especially in the Middle East and Latin America. Most of the reported cases are due to contact with the genus Opuntia 37 . At the time of injury, acute inflammation occurs and then, in some patients, eventually evolves into a typical foreign body reaction. The lesions occur primarily on the hands and fingers as clusters of dome- shaped, skin-colored papules with a central black dot, sometimes called “Sabra dermatitis” (see Ch. 17 ). This may resemble scabies or fiberglass dermatitis. Pathology Foreign body granulomas occupy the entire dermis and surround the spine fragments, which stain intensely red with PAS stain 14,37 . Wood splinters and thorns of other plant origin have a similar suppurative or granulomatous reaction. However, most splinters appear brown with a geometric pattern of cell walls. Fungal hyphae may be present within the plant material, but they seldom invade the surrounding dermis in a healthy host. Cnidaria (Coelenterata) – Jellyfish, Corals Members of the phylum Cnidaria (Coelenterata) include jellyfish, corals, and sea anemones (see Ch. 85 ). Almost all cnidarians possess nematocysts which contain highly coiled, hollow harpoon-like struc- tures that inject a toxin into the skin upon contact. Clinical features Jellyfish and coral stings elicit similar cutaneous reactions: an early primary irritant toxic reaction in all exposed persons, and a delayed- type hypersensitivity reaction in a small percentage. A sharp burning pain is felt and, within minutes, the affected area becomes erythem- atous and edematous and may form blisters (see Fig. 85.20 ). The acute response may be accompanied by an immediate-type hypersensitivity reaction including urticaria, angioedema, and even anaphylaxis. The lesions resolve, leaving postinflammatory hyperpigmentation in a streaky flagellate fashion corresponding to where the coral or jellyfish brushed the skin. The acute response may be accompanied by an immediate-type hypersensitivity reaction including urticaria, angioedema, and even anaphylaxis. The lesions resolve, leaving postinflammatory hyperpigmentation in a streaky flagellate fashion corresponding to where the coral or jellyfish brushed the skin. In some individuals, new lesions appear a Foreign Body Reactions few weeks later at previously involved sites (average 3 weeks) 8 . The latter are severely pruritic, shiny, lichenoid papules and plaques and are arranged in a number of patterns, including linear, zig-zag, and whip-like. Pathology The lesions that comprise the delayed response have a lichenoid tissue reaction. Treatment First aid includes soaking the site in hot, but not scalding, water (denatures proteins). Subsequent use of topical potent corticosteroids, antihistamines, and systemic corticosteroids is controversial. Treatment of acute reactions is reviewed in Chapter 85 . Intralesional corticoste- roids are the most effective therapy for delayed-type hypersensitivity reactions. Keratin Keratin, normally sequestered from the body’s immune surveillance by the surrounding epithelium, is treated as foreign if it directly contacts the dermis. This may occur as a result of the rupture of hair follicles, epidermoid cysts, or acne lesions as well as from external keratin sources such as ingrown nails or ingrown hairs; the latter occur in pseudofolliculitis and in pilonidal sinuses. Another source is accidental entry of hairs into interdigital skin, especially in barbers, hairdressers, and dog groomers. Pseudofolliculitis barbae In pseudofolliculitis barbae, there is a foreign body inflammatory reaction surrounding a hair that has been previously shaved or plucked (see Ch. 38 ). This condition affects mainly those with curly hair, with an incidence of more than 50% amongst Black individuals. Certain inherent properties of the hairs in affected individuals, in particular a curled flattened elliptical shape, play an important pathogenic role. Because the shaft is curved, it grows back toward the skin surface. When shaved, the flattened elliptical hair shaft develops a pointed tip, which facilitates re-entry of the hair into the skin (extrafollicular penetration). Transfollicular penetration can also occur (see Fig. 38.10 ). A foreign body reaction to keratin results in the development of inflammatory papules and pustules that are often followed by hyperpigmentation or small keloidal scars (see Fig. 38.11 ) 11 . Pseudofolliculitis also affects women or men who

Transfollicular penetration can also occur (see Fig. 38.10 ). A foreign body reaction to keratin results in the development of inflammatory papules and pustules that are often followed by hyperpigmentation or small keloidal scars (see Fig. 38.11 ) 11 . Pseudofolliculitis also affects women or men who regularly remove hair from the pubic region, axillae, and legs by plucking or shaving. Papules containing embedded hairs, pustules, and crusted papules develop in affected areas, often resolving with significant postinflam- matory hyperpigmentation. Treatment Apart from cessation of shaving or laser epilation of the affected areas, nearly all therapeutic modalities are unrewarding. For further details, see Chapters 38 and 137 . Pilonidal sinus Most cases of pilonidal sinus occur in the sacrococcygeal region (see Ch. 38 ). Much less often, it is seen in the umbilical region 38 , and, rarely, interdigitally in barbers 39 . Sacrococcygeal pilonidal sinuses may be asymptomatic (debris-filled pit) or present as a draining sinus or an acute abscess. The condition is more common in young men. There is often an underlying cyst with associated granulation tissue, fibrosis, and frequently tufts of hairs. Excisional specimens reveal a sinus tract extending into the dermis and subcutaneous tissue, surrounded by chronic inflammation. Hairs are found in the sinuses in three-quarters of the cases 40 . Small, asymptomatic or slightly tender, openings in the interdigital web spaces of the hands have been observed in barbers, hairdressers, and dog groomers. When these individuals cut hair while wearing sandals, lesions can develop in the web spaces of the feet as well. Penetration of short hairs into the interdigital spaces incites an inflammatory foreign body granuloma. The clinical course is usually self-limited but can be complicated by repeated infections, which may require surgical excision of the involved area 39 . Histologically, a sinus tract lined by epidermis and containing one or several hairs is seen. Hairs extending deeper than the sinus tract incite a foreign body reaction. INJECTABLE SOFT TISSUE FILLERS With the exception of autologous fat, all injectable soft tissue fillers, resorbable or non-resorbable, represent foreign bodies and therefore have the potential to cause foreign body reactions ( Figs. 94.10 & 94.11 ; see Ch. 158 ). Two types of reactions have been reported: non-immunogenic and immunogenic. The former is characterized by localized tissue necrosis, which occurs shortly after implantation, and such reactions are probably the result of local vascular inter- ruption; two-thirds of local necrotic events occur in the glabellar area 41 . Depending upon the particular filler, associated foreign body reactions can range from relatively common (e.g. paraffin) to rare (e.g. hyaluronic acid) 42 . Paraffin and silicone are discussed above and the histopathologic features of inflammatory reactions to various fillers are outlined in Table 94.5 41 . Foreign body reactions usually appear within 1–2 years after injection, and spontaneous resolution occurs in the majority of cases within a year, while the remainder have lesions that wax and wane 43,44 . Hyaluronic Acid Currently, hyaluronic acid is the most commonly utilized injectable soft tissue filler, in part because the incidence of foreign body reactions is much lower (0.4%) than that reported for bovine collagen (3%–4%) 42 . When a reaction does occur, the injected site becomes firm, tender, edematous, and erythematous, and an abscess may form. This reaction responds to intralesional injections of cortico- steroid or hyaluronidase (see Ch. 158 ) 44 , although some patients may be willing to wait for spontaneous resolution which can occur over several months. Bovine Collagen In general, bovine collagen alone has been replaced by other less antigenic soft tissue fillers, especially hyaluronic acid. However, there are fillers in which bovine collagen is combined with polymethyl methacrylate microspheres, e.g. Bellafill ® (formerly Artefill ® ). Despite negative skin testing (which is required prior to treatment), a small proportion of patients injected with bovine collagen still develop a local reaction (see Fig. 94.1 ) 44 . was performed in a beauty salon for cosmetic purposes. DISORDERS OF LANGERHANS CELLS AND MACROPHAGES MISCELLANEOUS Intralesional Corticosteroids Foreign body reactions to intralesional corticosteroids are quite rare despite the widespread use of this treatment modality. Reactions result from failure of the injected material to disperse in the usual manner or from incomplete absorption, leaving a small residuum that evokes a foreign body reaction 45 . Histologically, pools of granular, lightly stained material surrounded by a histiocytic and foreign body granulomatous infiltrate are seen in the dermis. Cellular reactions are absent around sites of recent injections 45 . Sutures Nylon and polypropylene sutures used in contemporary surgery are relatively inert (see Ch. 144 ), but most other materials regularly produce chronic inflammation and granuloma formation (see Fig. 151.19 ). The incubation period varies from weeks 46 to years 47 . The incision site may appear inflamed, red, and edematous. A sinus tract may develop, through which the suture material is extruded. Inflammation persists until the suture material is totally removed. Histologically, granulomatous inflammation of various types is seen surrounding suture material: foreign body, histiocytic, palisading, or a combination thereof (see Fig. 94.2 ) 46,47 . Transepidermal elimination of the suture material occurs 46 . Polyamide “Hair” Implants In patients with androgenetic alopecia in whom autologous hair trans- plantation is not feasible (e.g. inadequate donor sites), polyamide “hair” fibers have been used for synthetic scalp hair restoration. Although some authors have reported complications in only ~1% of patients, foreign body reactions are a real risk ( Fig. 94.12 ) 48 . Polyamide fiber hair restoration is not approved in the US. Mesotherapy Mesotherapy involves placement of a pharmacologic substance into the “mesoderm” (dermis and subcutis). For example, injections of deoxy- cholic acid (Kybella ® ) have been approved for the reduction of submental fat and may lead to a temporary chemical panniculitis. However, non-standardized combinations such as phosphatidylcholine plus a detergent solvent (e.g. deoxycholic acid) are also used for lipolysis. Alexander Nyström and Leena Bruckner-Tuderman Biology of the Extracellular Matrix 95 SECTION 15 ATROPHIES AND DISORDERS OF DERMAL CONNECTIVE TISSUES be compared to alloys, with each having metallurgic properties that differ from each other and those of the pure metals. Individual ECM macromolecules are usually oligomers composed of one or several polypeptides. Intimate contacts between the subunits are formed by coiled-coil structures, such as the collagen triple helix or supercoiled α -helices comprised of three or more polypeptides. In addition, large matrix macromolecules can be regarded as linear sequences of structural modules that are similar in a large variety of proteins 1 . The modules can be recognized by several cellular receptors, but receptor clustering is determined in a tissue-specific manner, and the response may be different in different tissues. Our knowledge of matrix macromolecules has increased dramati- cally due to advances in molecular genetics and proteomics. Numerous molecules have been characterized and their expression, regulation, tissue specificity, and functions discerned 2 . The assembled ECM struc- tures are generally adhesive, enabling the attachment of tissue-specific cells, leukocytes, tumor cells, and even microorganisms ( Fig. 95.1 ). Through integrin-mediated interactions with cells, matrix molecules control cell proliferation, differentiation, and migration, especially during development and regenerative processes. Without contact with the ECM, many cells undergo a form of apoptosis known as anoikis . Furthermore, the ECM can function as a reservoir of information; certain proteoglycans and proteins bind growth factors (e.g. trans- forming growth factor [TGF]- β ), releasing and activating them as needed to control cellular functions 2 . To date, mutations in > 50 different genes encoding ECM molecules have been found to cause heritable disorders in humans and mice. A hallmark of collagens is the presence of hydroxyproline (Hyp) in the Y position of this repeat sequence. Collagens are expressed in all tissues of the human body, and distinct sets of collagens co-polymerize into highly organized suprastructures, e.g., fibrils and filaments, in a tissue-specific manner  Elastin provides tissues with elasticity. Elastin monomers contain repetitive hydrophobic sequences and are highly cross-linked. The cross-links between several individual molecules provide both elasticity and insolubility to elastic fibers, which can be stretched by 100% or more and still return to their original form. The elastic fibers in the dermis contain a microfibrillar component that connects the fibers to surrounding structures INTRODUCTION The different types of extracellular matrix (ECM) represent specifically organized assemblies of the matrix macromolecules listed in Table 95.1 . These macromolecules have characteristic patterns of aggregation into insoluble suprastructures with a high degree of order at successive hierarchic levels 1 . Each of these structures is tissue-specific and adapted to the particular needs of a given tissue. The major constituents are often similar in functionally diverse ECMs. However, various types of less abundant proteins associate with the major ECM components, and differences in their relative composition determine tissue-specific organization of ECM suprastructures. ATROPHIES AND DISORDERS OF DERMAL CONNECTIVE TISSUES STRUCTURE AND FUNCTION OF THE EXTRACELLULAR MATRIX Collagens Collagens play an important role in maintaining the integrity of most tissues. The collagen family includes 28 proteins formally defined as collagens 3 ( Table 95.2 ); they contain 44 distinct polypeptide chains, each encoded by a different gene. At least 15 other proteins have collagen-like domains, e.g. macrophage scavenger receptor 1 and 2, ectodysplasin, pulmonary surfactant proteins. Collagen triple helix All collagens consist of three polypeptide chains, known as α -chains, which are folded into a triple helix. In some collagens, the α -chains are identical (homotrimers), while others contain two or three different α -chains (heterotrimers). In the collagenous repeat of each polypeptide chain, every third amino acid is glycine (Gly). The sequence of an α -chain can be expressed as (Gly-X-Y) n , where X and Y represent other amino acids and n varies according to the length of the repeat. Proline (Pro) and hydroxyproline (Hyp) residues commonly occupy the X and Y positions, respectively, and hydrogen bonds between the hydroxyl groups of Hyp contribute to the stability of the helix. Biology of the Extracellular Matrix collagen (type I) has an uninterrupted Gly-X-Y repeat sequence of almost 1000 amino acid residues; this forms a rigid, rodlike structure with a diameter of 1.5 nm and length of 300 nm. In some collagens, the (Gly-X-Y) n repeats are interrupted by one or more amino acids. The interruptions may be numerous and longer than the (Gly-X-Y) n repeats and they provide the molecule with flexibility, which is important for its specific functions 3 . Biosynthesis of collagens Collagen biosynthesis involves a number of post-translational modifi- cations ( Fig. 95.2 ). Some collagens are first synthesized as procollagens that have propeptide extensions at their N-terminus, C-terminus, or both. The main intracellular steps in collagen biosynthesis include the following: 3-Hyp, and hydroxylysine (Hyl) glucosylgalactosyl-Hyl After the chains have become associated and sufficient Hyp residues have been formed in each chain, a nucleus of the triple helix forms (usually in the C-terminal region), and the triple helix propagates towards the other end of the molecule in a zipper-like fashion 4 . The procollagen molecules are then transported from the endoplasmic reticulum across the Golgi apparatus without leaving the lumen of the Golgi cisternae. During this transport, the triple helices begin to aggregate laterally and form early fibrils ready for secretion 5 . The folding and transport of these large, rigid collagens require special machinery 6,7 . Deficiencies in the proteins that interact with collagens during these intracellular events can lead to phenotypes similar to collagen deficiency disorders 8 . The extracellular steps in biosynthesis include cleavage of the N- and/ or C-terminal propeptides, assembly into suprastructures with other collagens and non-collagenous components, and formation of covalent cross-links. The specific enzymes involved in the biosynthesis of collagens include prolyl-4-hydroxylase and prolyl-3-hydroxylase, which hydroxylate Pro residues to Hyp, and three lysyl hydroxylases, which hydroxylate Lys residues to Hyl. Adapted from Myllyharju J, Biology of the Extracellular Matrix Elastic Fibers The elasticity of many tissues, including the skin, depends upon the structure of elastic fibers, which have variable compositions. A charac- teristic property of these fibers is that they can be stretched by 100% or more and still return to their original form. Their main components are elastin and microfibrils. Elastin Elastin is a highly cross-linked protein 13 . Its monomer, tropoelastin, exists in several tissue-specific splice variants. Ala- and Lys-rich repeats form critical cross-linking domains within a background of hydrophobic amino acid repeats. Lysyl oxidase, the same enzyme that catalyzes collagen cross-linking, catalyzes the formation of desmosine cross-links between elastin molecules, which account for the elasticity and insolubility of the elastic fibers. Elastin makes up ~90% of mature elastic fibers. During fiber assembly, tropoelastin self-assembles and interacts with fibulins 4 and 5, fibrillin 1, and microfibril-associated glycoprotein-1 (MAGP-1). A model for this spatially and temporally regulated process is shown in Fig. 95.5 13 . Microfibrils Microfibrils (10 to 12 nm in diameter) insert into the basement membrane in a perpendicular orientation (classically referred to as “oxytalan fibers”) and extend into the papillary dermis, where they gradually merge with the elastic fibers that form a plexus parallel to the dermal–epidermal junction (classically referred to as “elaunin fibers”). These fibers appear to be continuous with the elastic fibers in the reticular dermis, which contain more abundant elastin. Microfibrils consist mainly of fibrillins 13 but also contain and associate with other large cross-banded fibrils represent dermal mixed fibrils containing collagens I, III, V, other minor collagens, and decorin (a proteoglycan). The cross-banding has a characteristic periodicity of 64 nm. The filamentous network in the background contains microfibrillar and basement membrane components.

Fibrillins 1–3 are large glycoproteins that contain both epidermal growth factor (EGF) and cysteine (Cys) repeats. The EGF repeats bind calcium, which is required for protein stabili- zation. Fibrillin 1 interacts with perlecan in the epidermal basement membrane to attach microfibrils to the dermal–epidermal junction. Fibrillin interactions with heparan sulfate proteoglycans and integrin receptors also contribute to microfibril assembly (see Fig. 95.5 ) 13,14 . In addition to guiding elastic fiber assembly and providing struc- tural support, fibrillins function together with LTBPs to regulate cell signaling 13 . The four members of the LTBP family are high-molecular- weight glycoproteins characterized by EGF-like and 8-Cys repeats, and they all associate with the small latent complex of TGF- β (see below; latent complex) binds to fibrillin-containing microfibrils. Together, they control the bioavailability of TGF- β in the skin and other tissues. LTBPs contain multiple proteinase-sensitive sites, providing the means to solubilize the large latent complex from ECM structures. Another group of signaling molecules that can bind to fibrillins are bone morphoge- netic proteins (BMPs) 13 . BMPs are secreted as cross-linked dimeric complexes that are associated through their prodomains, which interact directly with the N-terminus of fibrillin. Fibrillins and LTBPs, therefore, have important roles in targeting latent, activatable TGF- β and BMPs into different ECMs. Thus, microfibrils serve not only as a force-bearing element and scaffolding for elastin deposition in the dermis, but also as an important repository for signaling molecules in the skin 2,13 . The Extrafibrillar Matrix The dermal fibril networks and cells are embedded in an amorphous extrafibrillar material that binds water and provides the hydrated consis- tency of the skin. Previously, this amorphous material was presumed to be biologically unstructured and inert and was called “ground substance”. This prediction turned out to be incorrect; the extrafibrillar matrix is molecularly and structurally diverse, highly organized, and biologically active. It contains a number of proteoglycans and glyco- proteins, hyaluronic acid, and water. The functions of the extrafibrillar matrix are adapted to the biologic needs of each tissue. Adapted Biology of the Extracellular Matrix Glycosaminoglycans and proteoglycans GAGs are polysaccharides composed of sulfated and acetylated sugars with negative charges that bind large amounts of ions and water. The most prominent and ubiquitous protein-free GAG is hyaluronic acid, a giant polysaccharide composed of thousands of N-acetylglucosamine/ glucuronic acid disaccharides. However, other GAGs bind to proteins via a serine hydroxyl group, forming proteoglycans ( Fig. 95.7 ) 15 . There are four classes of proteoglycans based upon their tissue localization: intracellular, cell-surface, pericellular, and extracellular 15 . Proteoglycans differ remarkably in their protein content as well as the number, type, and length of their GAG side chains ( Table 95.3 ). Four known GAGs can bind proteins to form proteoglycans; they are chondroitin sulfate, dermatan sulfate, keratan sulfate, and heparan sulfate 15 . The correct balance of chondroitin sulfate and dermatan sulfate is necessary for skin function and integrity 16 . Versican, which contains these two GAGs, is an important dermal proteoglycan that can be synthesized by fibroblasts, smooth muscle cells, and epithelial cells. It is associated with the elastic fiber system and forms large complexes with hyaluronic acid, which provide the skin with its tautness (see Fig. 95.7 ). Heparan sulfate chains sequester growth factors (e.g. fibroblast growth factors [FGFs], vascular endothelial growth factors [VEGFs]) and present them to their receptors. Perlecan is a major heparan sulfate- containing proteoglycan found in all basement membranes, including the epidermal basement membrane. Collagen XVIII, a collagen/heparan sulfate hybrid, is also present in epidermal and vascular basement membranes as well as the skin 17 . Syndecans are transmembrane heparan sulfate proteoglycans that control cell adhesion to the ECM and cytoskeletal organization. Syndecans 1, 2, and 4 are expressed in the skin and can be found in keratinocytes, dendritic cells, and fibro- blasts, where they are thought to mediate “outside-in” cell signaling 15 . Glypicans are membrane-anchored heparan sulfate proteoglycans that interact with growth factors and other extracellular proteins in the skin to regulate developmental and regenerative events 18 . Functions of the Extracellular Matrix Structural role of the extracellular matrix In the past, the ECM was simply regarded as a structural scaffold that gave organs their shape and consistency. However, there has been much progress in our understanding of the broad spectrum of ECM supra- structures and their specific functions. Basement membranes are sheets with limited tensile strength but important tissue-specific properties that enable particular cell attachments; they also regulate morpho- genesis, differentiation, and barrier functions. Structural role of the extracellular matrix
text: the past, the ECM was simply regarded as a structural scaffold that gave organs their shape and consistency. However, there has been much progress in our understanding of the broad spectrum of ECM supra- structures and their specific functions. Basement membranes are sheets with limited tensile strength but important tissue-specific properties that enable particular cell attachments; they also regulate morpho- genesis, differentiation, and barrier functions. At the dermal–epidermal junction, specific basement membrane-associated aggregates ensure strong adhesion of the epidermis to the dermis and thus resistance against external shear forces. In the dermis, different ECM networks are embedded in the water-binding extrafibrillar matrix, maintaining the elasticity, resilience, and tautness of the skin. The specific ECM compositions and post-translational modifications determine the elastic properties and stiffness of a given tissue. Adapted ATROPHIES AND DISORDERS OF DERMAL CONNECTIVE TISSUES Regulation of cellular functions In addition to their structural roles, ECMs are biologically active. In vitro studies as well as transgenic and knockout mouse models (see Ch. 3 ) have demonstrated the importance of ECMs as potent regulators of cellular functions during development, regeneration, wound healing, inflam- mation, and tumorigenesis. ECM macromolecules can influence a wide range of cellular processes, including adhesion, migration, cytoskeletal organization, division, differentiation, polarization, and apoptosis. Cells use a variety of receptors, such as integrins and cell surface proteoglycans, to recognize signals from the ECM 2 . The β 1 integrin family represents the most prevalent class of matrix receptors. The α -subunit of the integrin determines the specificity for individual matrix protein ligands, but the affinity and degree of specificity vary. Some integrins recognize only one ligand, while others can bind to several matrix proteins. “Outside” signals from the ECM can have different effects on the cell 24 . For example, they may induce clustering of integrins on the cell surface and lead to the formation of protein complexes between the cytoplasmic domains of the integrins and the cytoskeleton, thereby influencing cell shape. Alternatively, activation of integrins by the ECM can stimulate signal transduction pathways involving focal adhesion kinase (protein tyrosine kinase 2), paxillin, and tensin. ECM–integrin interactions may also induce mitogen-activated protein kinase-mediated regulation of transcription, cell proliferation, and differentiation. Further regulation of ECM–integrin signaling is mediated by divalent cations, phospholipids, and other agents 25 . Integrins also sense and respond to ECM rigidity through mechanisms involving changes in integrin binding dynamics, stretch-activated ion channels, and unfolding of mechanosensitive proteins (e.g. talin, vinculin) in focal adhesions (see Fig. 28.3B ) 24 . These events regulate cell migration and stem cell fate. Growth factors in the TGF- β family are potent regulators of ECM formation, in addition to their immunomodulatory functions and regulatory role in cell growth 2 . They are secreted from cells as latent complexes containing TGF- β and its propeptide latency-associated peptide (LAP). In most cells, LAP is covalently linked to LTBP, forming the large latent complex (see Fig. 95.6 ). Secreted large latent complexes associate covalently with ECM proteins. TGF- β can be released from these complexes by a variety of mechanisms including mechanical forces and matrix-degrading proteinases originating from fibroblasts or inflammatory cells. In addition to LTBPs, several other ECM molecules, including proteoglycans and thrombospondin, can bind and modulate the activity of TGF- β . DISEASES RELATED TO ECM DEFECTS Molecular studies of the genes and proteins involved in ECM disorders have produced a wealth of information regarding the normal biology of the ECM 13,16,23,26,27 . Putative functions for many matrix macromolecules were found or confirmed when mutations in their genes were defined in diseases. For example, the fundamental roles of collagens VII and XVII in dermal–epidermal adhesion became clear when mutations in the corre- sponding genes were discovered in patients with hereditary epidermolysis bullosa (EB) 26 . Inherited ECM diseases with cutaneous manifestations are listed in Table 95.5 , and the molecular mechanisms and patho- physiology of selected conditions are delineated below. Ehlers–Danlos syndrome (EDS), cutis laxa, and pseudoxanthoma elasticum (PXE) are covered in more depth in Chapter 97 , and EB is discussed in Chapter 32 . Ehlers–Danlos syndrome Collagens and tenascin-X The quantitatively major components of the collagen fibrils found in the ECMs of many tissues (e.g. skin, tendon, bone, cartilage) are collagens I, II (absent from skin), and III. Ehlers–Danlos syndrome Collagens and tenascin-X The quantitatively major components of the collagen fibrils found in the ECMs of many tissues (e.g. skin, tendon, bone, cartilage) are collagens I, II (absent from skin), and III. Smaller amounts of minor collagens (e.g. types V, IX, XI, XII, XIV) are expressed in a tissue-specific manner 3 . Mutations in the genes encoding major and minor collagens can result in distinct abnormalities in different organs 3 . For example, defects in COL3A1 , which encodes collagen III, are responsible for the vascular type of EDS 16 , an autosomal dominant condition that presents with thin translucent skin, excessive bruising, and life-threatening arterial, gastrointestinal, and uterine ruptures. Mutations in COL3A1 have also been found in patients whose primary clinical manifestation is arterial aneurysms. Alterations in genes encoding minor fibrillar collagens can also cause severe connective tissue diseases, suggesting pivotal functions for these quantitatively minor components. Collagen V nucleates fibrillogenesis involving collagens I and III; this interaction limits the solubility of macromolecules in fibrils and regulates the geometry of lateral aggre- gation as well as the overall shapes and sizes of the collagen aggregates. Consistent with this concept, the classical type of EDS occasionally results from mutations in COL1A1 (encodes the α 1 -chain of collagen I), whereas mutations in COL5A1 and COL5A2 (encode the α 1 - and α 2 -chains of collagen V) account for ~50% of patients. Patients with classical EDS exhibit variable degrees of skin hyperelasticity and fragility, atrophic scarring, and joint hypermobility ( Fig. 95.8A ). Mutations in the gene encoding tenascin-X, a glycoprotein in the extrafibrillar matrix, can cause a recessive form of EDS with similar clinical findings of hyperextensible skin and joint hypermobility 16 . Biology of the Extracellular Matrix Post-translational modification of collagen Mutations in genes encoding proteins involved in post-translational modification of collagen (see above and Fig. 95.2 ) have been found to underlie other forms of EDS. For example, loss-of-function mutations in the lysyl hydroxylase 1 gene lead to abnormal lysyl hydroxylation and glycosylation of collagens in a subset of patients with the kypho- scoliotic type of EDS, a recessive disease characterized by hyperexten- sible and fragile skin as well as hypermobile joints, scoliosis, and ocular fragility. Failure to cleave the N-propeptide from procollagen I causes the arthrochalasia type of EDS, a dominant disorder that features severe joint hypermobility, including dislocations. text: and glycosylation of collagens in a subset of patients with the kypho- scoliotic type of EDS, a recessive disease characterized by hyperexten- sible and fragile skin as well as hypermobile joints, scoliosis, and ocular fragility. Failure to cleave the N-propeptide from procollagen I causes the arthrochalasia type of EDS, a dominant disorder that features severe joint hypermobility, including dislocations. The persistence of this propeptide on collagen I drastically alters fibrillogenesis, and the fibrils that form are thin and irregular in diameter. Affected individuals typically have a splice-site mutation in COL1A1 or COL1A2 that causes exon skipping and elimination of the cleavage site for ADAMTS-2 (procollagen I N-proteinase) in the pro α 1 (I) or pro α 2 (I) chain. Loss-of- function mutations in ADAMTS2 cause the dermatosparaxis type of EDS ( Fig. 95.8B ); as in the arthrochalasia type, procollagen I N-propeptides persist and sterically disturb polymerization of the collagen fibrils. Dermatosparaxis has a distinct phenotype that includes characteristic facies and fragile, sagging skin with a doughy consistency. Mutations in the zinc finger protein 469 gene ( ZNF469 ) or PR/SET domain 5 ( PRDM5 ), which are involved in transcriptional regulation of fibrillar collagens, result in corneal fragility as well as variable skin hyperexten- sibility and wrinkling 16 . Proteoglycan processing As discussed above, dermal proteoglycans have important roles in collagen fibril organization. Accordingly, mutations in B3GALT6 and B4GALT7 , which encode galactosyltransferases that initiate GAG synthesis, cause a spondylodysplastic type of EDS 16,28.29 . Mutations in B3GAT3 , which encodes a glucuronosyltransferase that catalyzes the formation GAG-protein linkages, can lead to wrinkled acral skin 30 . The musculocontractural type of EDS is caused by mutations in CHST14 and DSE , which encode dermatan-4-sulfotransferase 1 and dermatan sulfate epimerase, respectively 16,31 . Loss of these enzymes’ activity in dermatan sulfate synthesis leads to a reduced dermatan sulfate : chondroitin sulfate ratio, which disrupts decorin function and thereby impairs collagen fibrillogenesis 16 . The skin changes are often accompanied by extracutaneous manifestations, including pulmonary emphysema, bladder diverticula, hernias, and arterial anomalies. Histologically, there is fragmentation or diminution of elastic fibers. Recessive and dominant forms of cutis laxa can result from mutations in multiple genes, including those that encode the elastic fiber compo- nents elastin, fibulin 4, and fibulin 5 32 (see Table 95.5 ). A severe form of cutis laxa associated with extensive pulmonary, gastrointestinal, and urinary abnormalities is caused by mutations in the latent TGF- β binding protein-4 gene ( LTBP4 ), demonstrating the central role of TGF- β signaling in ECM assembly during development 32 . Other inherited disorders are characterized by secondary effects on elastic fiber deposition or degradation 23 . For example, elastic fibers are calcified and fragmented secondary to decreased activity of anti- mineralization proteins in pseudoxanthoma elasticum (see below and Ch. 97 ). In patients with α 1 -antitrypsin deficiency and some forms of acquired atrophoderma, elastic fibers are prematurely degraded due to unregulated elastase activity. Decreased or aberrant deposition of elastic fibers in certain tissues is also characteristic of Marfan syndrome (see below). Marfan syndrome Fibrillin 1 is the major component of microfibrils and therefore has an important structural role in elastic fibers. Fibrillin 1 mutations cause Marfan syndrome, an autosomal dominant disorder with variable connective tissue weakness in the skin as well as skeletal, ocular, and cardiovascular systems 13,23 . Cutaneous manifestations include striae and elastosis perforans serpiginosa. text: Marfan syndrome (see below). Marfan syndrome Fibrillin 1 is the major component of microfibrils and therefore has an important structural role in elastic fibers. Fibrillin 1 mutations cause Marfan syndrome, an autosomal dominant disorder with variable connective tissue weakness in the skin as well as skeletal, ocular, and cardiovascular systems 13,23 . Cutaneous manifestations include striae and elastosis perforans serpiginosa. In addition to structural disturbances in elastic fibers and microfibrils, fibrillin mutations may decrease the sequestration of latent TGF- β complexes (see Fig. 95.6 ), thus rendering them more prone to activation. This leads to unpro- ductive tissue remodeling, abnormal cellular behavior, and loss of ECM integrity. The highly homologous fibrillin 2 exhibits different spatial and temporal expression during development, and the functional relationship between the two molecules is not fully understood. Mutations in the gene encoding fibrillin 2 lead to congenital contractural arachnodactyly, which features skeletal abnormalities in the absence of ocular and cardiovascular features 13 . Loeys–Dietz syndrome Heterozygous mutations in the genes encoding the TGF- β receptors 1/2 or TGF- β 2/3 can cause Loeys–Dietz syndrome, which is characterized by aortic aneurysms, generalized arterial tortuosity, variable craniofacial malformations (e.g. bifid uvula, cleft palate, hypertelorism), skeletal anomalies, and joint laxity. A subset of patients has cutaneous manifes- tations similar to those of the vascular type of EDS, including trans- lucent skin, easy bruising, and atrophic scarring 13,16 . The phenotypic overlap with Marfan syndrome and vascular EDS is not surprising, considering the association between fibrillin and latent TGF- β and the role of TGF- β in regulating collagen expression. Other fibrillin-associated syndromes Genetic mutations that alter the C-terminus of fibrillin 1 cause marfanoid–progeroid–lipodystrophy syndrome , which is characterized by an extreme reduction in subcutaneous fat. Mutations affecting the integrin-binding site of fibrillin 1 lead to abnormal microfibril assembly and cause stiff skin syndrome , which features diffusely thickened skin since birth, limited joint mobility, nodules over the distal interpha- langeal joints, and short stature. In addition, fibrillin 1 deficiency repre- sents a cause of Weill–Marchesani syndrome 13 , characterized by thick skin, short stature, shortened digits, and ectopia lentis. Mutations in ADAMTSL2 , which encodes the extracellular ADAMTS-like protein 2 that interacts with TGF- β and fibrillin 33 , alter TGF- β bioavailability. Mutations in ADAMTSL2 , which encodes the extracellular ADAMTS-like protein 2 that interacts with TGF- β and fibrillin 33 , alter TGF- β bioavailability. This results in geleophysic dysplasia , which presents with thick skin, short stature, and joint contractures. Pseudoxanthoma elasticum PXE is a heritable disorder characterized by cutaneous, vascular, and ocular involvement that results from the accumulation of fragmented and calcified elastic fibers in the dermis, arterial walls, and Bruch’s membrane, respectively (see Ch. 97 ). The skin findings – laxity and yellowish papules and plaques – are the most common and often the earliest manifestation of PXE. Although PXE has traditionally been considered as a prototypic heritable ECM disorder, it is caused by mutations in the gene for the ATP-binding cassette (ABC) subfamily C member 6 (ABCC6) trans- porter, which is primarily expressed in the liver 34 . The absence of functional ABCC6 results in reduced ATP secretion from hepatocytes, which leads to reduced plasma concentrations of inorganic pyrophos- phate (PPi), a physiologic inhibitor of mineralization (see Fig. 97.5 ) 34 . Mutations in the γ -glutamyl carboxylase gene ( GGCX ) can lead to a PXE-like phenotype together with a deficiency in vitamin K-dependent coagulation factors. GGCX catalyzes vitamin K-dependent γ -glutamyl carboxylation, which activates coagulation factors and the matrix gla protein (MGP), an inhibitor of pathologic mineralization. Epidermolysis bullosa EB represents a group of hereditary diseases characterized by mechanical fragility of the skin that results in blister formation 26,35 (see Ch. 32 ). Mutations in the collagen VII gene ( COL7A1 ) cause both dominant and recessive forms of dystrophic EB 36 . Because collagen VII is a component of the anchoring fibrils, cleavage occurs just below the lamina densa in the uppermost dermis; as a result, blisters tend to heal with scarring. Patients with severe forms of recessive dystrophic EB harbor mutations that lead to premature termination codons 36 , and collagen VII and anchoring fibrils are absent. Milder forms of dystrophic EB are associated with missense mutations in one or both copies of COL7A1 and anchoring fibril dysfunction.
