In the absence of p53, the activity of the pro-apoptotic protein Bax is inhibited, thereby impairing apoptosis and promoting cell survival. Apoptosis is an important orderly process, which begins with the activation of orchestrating initiator caspases such as caspase 8 and 9. The latter in turn activate effector caspases, nucleases, and other lytic enzymes, resulting in the ordered degradation of genomic DNA and proteins including cytoskeleton components such as actin and lamins. THE TISSUE PERSPECTIVE Architectures in Cancer Ecosystems Oncogenic signaling alters the physiologic organization of cells in tissues and organs A characteristic pathologic feature of advanced cancer is the disruption of normal tissue and organ architecture. Cancer cells often have increased morphologic heterogeneity, impaired cellular differ- entiation, and the phenotypic plasticity of their lineage progenitors 2 . The surrounding tumor microenvironment is frequently characterized by numerous inflammatory immune cells, newly formed vessels, and altered structure of the extracellular matrix. As similar features are observed in wound healing, cancer is thought to behave like a chronic wound that does not heal 32 . The identification of oncogenic driver mutations which dysregulate intercellular communication networks of ligands, receptors, and signaling mediators that have several functions – determining cell-fate decisions and morphologic patterning during embryogenesis, orchestrating tissue regeneration following injury or stress, and maintaining homeostasis in adult tissues – provides an explanation for this observation 33 . The evolution of cancer cells with increased transcriptional and epigenetic plasticity is critically shaped by reciprocal interactions with each other and with immune cells, endothelial cells, and fibro- blasts within different niches of the tumor microenvironment 34 . The various cell phenotypes and their niches create a dynamic cancer tissue ecosystem that is coordinated by an altered intercellular communi- cation network. Within this ecosystem, malignant and non-malignant cells dynami­cally adapt their phenotypes in response to the changing microenvironmental conditions during cancer progression and in response to therapeutic intervention. This includes the sensing of DNA damage in cancer cells by innate immune cells, as well as the subsequent genetic selection and phenotypic adaptation of cancer cells exposed to cytotoxic T cells that specifically recognize cancer mutations 30,35 . In addition, hypoxia promotes the release of angiogenic factors and initiates neovascularization. Inflammation and hypoxia promote cancer cell plasticity and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transi- tions that activate cellular migration programs and support invasive growth and metastatic spread 34 . Phenotypic Plasticity and Epigenetic Reprogramming Increased cell state heterogeneity and plasticity is a hallmark of progressive tumor growth The skin epithelium continuously self-renews through the activity of a long-lived population of adult stem cells that reside in microenvi- ronmental niches. Adult stem cells undergo asymmetric cell divisions to give rise to transiently proliferating progeny and eventually to terminally differentiated cells that perform skin-specific functions. Keratinocytes, for example, continuously regenerate and eventually undergo programmed cell death to form the stratum corneum. Melanocytes and intraepithelial leukocytes have a longer lifespan and predominantly expand following tissue injury. Physical damage, chemical toxins, and pathogens induce cellular stress and activate stem cell niches in the skin to increase their proliferative output, replace damaged cells, and restore tissue homeostasis. A typical example is the response to sunburning UV irradiation ( Fig. 107.5 ). Importantly, tissue damage repair responses involve a transiently increased plasticity of stem cell states that allows precursor cells to adapt their differentiation pathways 36 . Principles of Cutaneous Tumor Biology Initial proof-of-principle for the ability of T cells to specifically eradicate human cancer was obtained in studies where lymphocytes were isolated from melanoma metastasis tissues, expanded ex vivo and reinfused into patients. The clinical efficacy of monoclonal antibodies targeting the immunoregulatory receptors CTLA-4 and PD-1 (immune checkpoint blockade) on T cells represented a breakthrough for T cell immunother- apies and is currently changing the treatment of many cancer patients 39–41 . DNA damage in cancer cells triggers the cGAS–Sting pathway and alerts the innate immune system 30,31 . This also activates dendritic cells that take up cancer cell fragments and induces their migration to the regional lymph nodes ( Fig. 107.8A ). Here, dendritic cells present tumor antigens to naive T cells and stimulate their expansion and differen- tiation into effector T cells. These cells of the adaptive immune system home into tumor tissues where they can eradicate the malignant cell population 35,39 . The ability of tumor-specific T cells to broadly recognize mutated peptides, which stochastically arise as a conse- quence of genomic alterations in cancer cells, represents a cornerstone of modern tumor immunology. These mutated peptides (termed neoan- tigens ) are presented to T cells in the binding groove of MHC molecules in a similar manner as viral antigens (see Ch. 4 ). This explains why the efficacy of T cell immunotherapies directly correlates with the mutational burden of cancer cells. Tumor-specific T cells also recognize self-antigens derived from normal gene products that are expressed only in specific cell types. Proteins of the MAGE gene family, which are physiologi- cally expressed in embryonic tissues and are restricted to reproductive organs in adults (termed cancer testis antigens ), represent another class of tumor antigens recognized by T cells and are frequently re-expressed in cancer cells due to epigenetic alterations 35,39 . Detailed immunohistopathologic investigations revealed that cancer tissues vary widely with respect to the infiltration of T cells and other immune cells. Recently, clinical and experimental evidence has accumu- lated that oncogenic driver mutations orchestrate the tumor immune landscape. For example, mutations that activate the Wnt signaling pathway or MYC promote evasion of cellular immunity by preventing T cells from entering tumor tissues, a phenomenon called T cell exclusion 42 . However, the interaction between tumor and immune cells is not unidirectional, and immune cells may also secrete cytokines that are conducive to cancer cell survival and proliferation. Today, it is well documented that the anti-tumoral T cell response imposes a critical cell-extrinsic barrier to malignant transformation 43 . Cancer-Promoting Inflammation A growth-promoting inflammatory microenvironment can drive cancer progression Progressively growing cancer cells engage in dynamic reciprocal inter- actions with surrounding immune cells, creating a microenvironment that fosters their survival and proliferation 47 . This is driven in part by cancer cell-intrinsic oncogenic signaling and the secretion of growth- promoting, proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines. In addition, cancer-promoting inflammatory microenvironments can result from repetitive tissue injury due to the action of physical and chemical carcinogens. The potential role of inflammatory cells within cancer tissues in promoting malignant progression was already recognized by Rudolph Virchow in 1863 in his “irritation theory of cancer”. This was experimentally verified using chemical carcinogens and UV irradiation as initiators and inflammatory promotors. Chronic inflammation, both intrinsic and extrinsic to cancer cells, increases the recruitment of myeloid immune cell populations with T cell suppressive phenotypes that normally orchestrate tissue regen- eration. DNA damage responses and genomic instability of cancer cells contribute to a protumorigenic inflammatory response, for example due to leakage of extrachromosomal double-stranded DNA into the cytosol, which activates innate antiviral immune responses via the cGAS–STING pathway. Inducing or Accessing Vasculature Hypoxic environments activate proangiogenic signaling pathways Increased blood supply of oxygen and nutrients is required for continuous tumor growth. The identification of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) as one of the principle molecular regulators of tumor angiogenesis represents a milestone in cancer research 48 . Cancer cells produce VEGF in response to hypoxic conditions that stabilize and activate this hypoxia-inducible factor. Binding of VEGF to its receptor VEGFR2 on endothelial cells initiates the formation of new blood vessels through neoangiogenesis. Mechanistically, this is orches- trated by motile endothelial cells, called tip cells, that break down the surrounding extracellular matrix (ECM) and initiate the growth of new vascular sprouts. This process is tightly regulated by Notch signaling via the secretion of the delta ligand-like 4 (DLL4) by endothelial tip cells (see Fig. 102.7 ). However, newly formed blood vessels in tumors are mostly abnormal, both structurally and functionally. Their architecture is chaotic, tortuous, and leaky due to a lack of normal pericyte coverage, resulting in irregular blood flow, decreased perfusion, and chronic hypoxia. The cross-talk between hypoxic cancer cells and endothelial cells is also criti- cally shaped by proangiogenic and proinflammatory mediators secreted by cells of the immune system in the tumor microenvironment. For example, macrophages and neutrophils can secrete VEGF-A and other proangiogenic factors such as angiopoietin-1 (ANGPT1) and hepatocyte growth factor (HGF). Therapeutic inhibition of proangiogenic signaling has been shown to normalize the tumor vasculature and improve the efficacy of chemo- and immunotherapies. Conversely, effective immunotherapies can contribute to vessel normalization 49 . Activating Invasion and Metastasis Phenotypic plasticity enables cancer cell invasion, migration, and metastasis If cancers are detected early, patients can be cured by surgical excision. This is frequently achieved for cancers in the skin that are immediately visible. However, in some cases cancer cells are able to invade adjacent tissue, enter lymph and blood vessels, spread throughout the body, and colonize distant organs before they are locally resected. Histologically distinct cancer entities differ in their propensity and their patterns of metastatic dissemination. This was already noted in the late 19th century by the English surgeon Stephen Paget who proposed that the organ preference of cancer metastasis might result from favorable interactions between metastatic cancer cells and the unique tissue microenvironments in different organs. This “seed and soil” theory was complemented later to include the impact of mechanical factors such as the anatomy of vascular and lymphatic drainage from the site of a primary tumor. Research over the past several decades has provided insights into cellular and molecular mechanisms that drive cancer metastasis 50–52 . The characterization of cancer cell subpopulations that initiate and sustain the development of metastases represented a key conceptual advance. These rare metastasis-initiating cells display the stem cell-like phenotype and plasticity of their lineage progenitors that helps them to survive the adverse physical and metabolic conditions in the circulation and evade immune cell recognition and destruction 51 . Metastasis-initiating cancer cells undergo reversible epithelial-to- mesenchymal transitions and enter slow-cycling and dormant cell states during the metastatic cascade. The switch of adhesion molecules from epithelial to mesenchymal cell states, most notably from E-cadherin to N-cadherin, is regarded as a critical step in initiating migration and invasion of carcinoma cells. Inflammatory cells in the microenvironment contribute to the disassembly of the extracellular matrix (ECM) and its constituents via enzymes such as matrix metal- loproteinases (MMPs), thereby facilitating invasive growth. Supportive interactions with endothelial cells promote cancer cell migration and proliferation along blood vessel surfaces, increasing the likelihood of intravasation and dissemination through the circulation. Dynamic adaptation of cell adhesion networks protects cancer cells from anoikis, a type of apoptosis-like destruction of cells that have lost their cell- matrix contact. Here, they survive and remain dormant for longer periods of time within perivascular niches, before they grow out as clinically apparent metastases ( Fig. 107.8B ) 51 . Despite impressive advances in our understanding of the biology underlying cancer metastasis, patients with metastatic disease frequently develop resistance to currently available treatments. Progressive growth of disseminated cancer cells remains responsible for the majority of cancer-associated deaths. Current large scale sequencing studies of cancer metastases reveal an increasingly heterogeneous and complex picture of genomic alterations at this late stage of cancer evolution. These studies found that the majority of oncogenic driver mutations occur before metastatic dissemination. However, chromosomal insta- bility and copy-number variations such as whole genome doubling were more frequently observed in metastatic cancer cells from many tumor types 53 . Evidence is accumulating that the unique microenviron- ments in different organs, most notably the metabolic conditions and the immune cell composition that determine therapy responses, also shape the evolution of cancer genomes during metastatic progression. Integrated analyses of the whole cancer ecosystems are required to fully understand metastatic disease as a prerequisite for the development of patient-specific therapeutic strategies. PATHOGENESIS OF KERATINOCYTE CARCINOMAS Keratinocyte carcinomas derive from epidermal keratinocytes and worldwide represent the most common cancer type in fair-skinned populations. The majority of keratinocyte carcinomas are basal cell carcinomas (BCCs), which are locally destructive and only rarely develop metastases. Cutaneous squamous cell carcinomas (cSCCs) are less common, but more likely to metastasize and are responsible for the majority of deaths from keratinocyte carcinomas (see Ch. 108 ). Genomic sequencing of keratinocyte carcinomas has revealed the highest mutational burden of any cancer type, with molecular signa- tures of UV-induced DNA damage. This is consistent with lifelong sun exposure as the most important environmental risk factor 54,55 . Molecular Pathogenesis of Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC) Genetic linkage studies in families with basal cell nevus syndrome (BCNS or Gorlin syndrome; see Ch. 108 ), a rare inherited disorder in which multiple BCCs develop comparatively early in life, provided an initial insight into the specific molecular pathogenesis of BCC – this was beyond the known mutations in TP53 that are present in all keratinocyte carcinomas. These studies identified PTCH1 as a tumor suppressor gene that is inactivated in BCNS patients and whose protein product is an inhibitor of the Hedgehog signaling pathway (see PTCH1 as a frequent event in sporadic BCCs 57 . The Hedgehog signaling pathway was discovered in Drosophila , is highly conserved during evolution, and plays an important role in tissue patterning and cell fate during embryonal development. In the skin, Hedgehog signaling is responsible for the developmental regulation of hair follicles and sebaceous glands. In adult tissues, it is involved in epithelial and neural stem cell maintenance as well as in tissue repair responses. Oncogenic activation of Hedgehog signaling is observed in various types of cancer, including BCC, medulloblastoma, and pancreatic, breast, colon, ovarian, and small cell lung carcinomas. Experimental activation of Hedgehog signaling in epidermal keratino- cytes from genetically engineered mice leads to skin tumors with a BCC phenotype, demonstrating the functional importance of this pathway in vivo 58 . Whole exome sequencing studies confirmed BCCs as the tumor entity with the highest number of mutations and provided a comprehensive picture of the landscape of oncogenic driver mutations in BCC metas- tases ( Fig. 107.9A ). Whole exome sequencing studies confirmed BCCs as the tumor entity with the highest number of mutations and provided a comprehensive picture of the landscape of oncogenic driver mutations in BCC metas- tases ( Fig. 107.9A ). In addition to driver mutations that activate the Hedgehog pathway in 85% of BCCs, these studies identified mutations in target genes of N-Myc as well as the Notch and Hippo-YAP pathways 54 . These findings are thought to provide an explanation for the phenotypic variation of BCCs. Recently, it was shown that in genetically engineered mice, combined experimental activation of the Hedgehog and Notch signaling pathways, together with overexpression of N-Myc, was able to drive progressive and unrestrained growth of BCCs 59 . These observa- tions support a model in which the aggressive growth of BCCs is the result of multiple complementary genetic alterations, consistent with the concept of cancer evolution ( Fig. 107.9B ). Molecular Pathogenesis of Cutaneous Squamous Cell Carcinoma (cSCC) The pathogenesis of cSSC has been studied experimentally for decades in mice using mutagenic chemicals such as dimethylbenzanthrene (DMBA) and UV irradiation in two-stage carcinogenesis models. The identification of oncogenic Hras mutations in cSCCs arising in DMBA-exposed mice represents a milestone in skin cancer biology 1 . Subsequent murine studies demonstrated an important role for loss- of-function mutations in p53 in Ras-driven cSCCs, enabling chromo- somal alterations and genomic instability. Initial studies in a limited number of human cSCCs confirmed recurrent oncogenic driver mutations in HRAS and TP53 . Deeper insights into the molecular pathogenesis of cSCCs and the identification of additional oncogenic drivers had to await the comprehensive characterization of a larger number of cSCCs using next-generation sequencing of whole exomes. In the 1980s, Notch genes were identified and found to orchestrate an ancient cell signaling pathway that is highly conserved within the animal kingdom. Notch signaling plays an important role in cell–cell communication during embryogenesis and is critically required for the development of many tissues and organs including the brain, the heart and vasculature, the hematopoietic system, and the skin. It promotes the self-renewal of stem and progenitor cells, orchestrates cell fate decisions, and regulates cell differentiation in a cell context- dependent manner. Notch signaling is maintained at a low level in adult organisms and is rapidly upregulated during repair responses following tissue injury. The landscape of driver mutations in Importantly, mutations in Notch pathway genes are observed in a wide range of malignancies, most notably in multiple non-cutaneous carcinomas, leukemias, and brain tumors. The oncogenic activity of Notch signaling depends on the cellular context. Initial studies showed that increased Notch signaling is oncogenic in leukemias. In contrast, Notch signaling has tumor suppressor activity in the skin, most likely because it supports keratinocyte differentiation. A recent comprehensive bioinformatics analysis of available genome sequencing data for cSCCs provided a comprehensive overview of the landscape of oncogenic driver mutations, confirming the important role of mutations in Notch pathway genes as the second most frequent group of oncogenic drivers after TP53 and Rb ( Fig. 107.10A ) 55 . Today, sequential acquisition of oncogenic driver mutations in genes that encode proteins in the p53–Rb and Notch pathways, followed by mutations in epigenetic regulators and the acquisition of structural and numerical chromosome alterations, are thought to represent the evolu- tionary trajectory of cSCC development ( Fig. 107.10B,C ). Progressively growing carcinomas acquire chromosomal alterations, aberrantly activate the phenotypic plasticity of their stem and progenitor cells, recruit suppressive T cells that subvert anti-tumoral immunity, and engage with endothelial cells to support metastatic dissemination. CURRENT DEVELOPMENTS AND FUTURE PERSPECTIVES Mapping the Evolution of Cancer Ecosystems in Space and Time Recent advances in single-cell and spatially resolved technologies have enabled analysis of tumor specimens at an unprecedented resolution. The next frontier in cancer research is to use these techniques to further understand the spatial and chronologic complexity of cancer. Current projects such as the NIH Human Biomolecular Atlas Program (HuBMAP) aim to generate references of human tissues by combining (epi-)genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomics analyses with single- cell and spatial resolution 61 . In analogy to the first human reference genome created more than 20 years ago, these frameworks may serve as invaluable tools for understanding the dynamics of tissue development. Similar approaches focusing on cancer rather than healthy tissues are attempting to reconstruct the heterogeneity and complex interactions between cancer cells and their host organisms 62 . Similar approaches focusing on cancer rather than healthy tissues are attempting to reconstruct the heterogeneity and complex interactions between cancer cells and their host organisms 62 . This wealth of infor- mation is already catalyzing the development of novel bioinformatical analysis tools and promoting the convergence of diverse scientific disci- plines with the potential to once again revolutionize our understanding of cancer. The aforementioned projects may have the capability of answering some of the key riddles of cancer in the coming decade: the mechanisms of metastatic spread, the tissue specificity of oncogenic events, the cell(s) of origin of cancer, and the influence of the cancer microenvironment. The Microbiome and Cancer Although the discovery of microbiota influencing tumor development dates back more than 100 years, only recent discoveries have suggested a far deeper relationship between cancer cells and surrounding microbes. Due to the low biomass compared to the tumor cells themselves, and the diverse strains of microbiota colonizing different areas of the bodies and tumor types, the study of cancer-associated microbiota has proven to be challenging. However, recent technological advances have enabled their study, highlighting that microbiota have the capacity to modulate multiple aspects of cancer development, progression, and therapeutic response 63 . As an example, correlations have been observed between specific bacterial strains in the gut and responses to immunotherapy, suggesting that the microbiome profoundly influences host immune responses and thereby therapeutic efficacy. Additionally, metastatic dissemination has been shown to be influenced by intracellular bacteria. As lifestyle Principles of Cutaneous Tumor Biology factors such as diet or smoking modulate the microbiome, these findings open new avenues of patient-centric therapeutic approaches. In the near future, synthetic biology approaches using engineered bacteria as cancer therapeutics may complement the current arsenal of targeted and immune therapies. McMeniman and Peter Wolf Actinic Keratosis, Basal Cell Carcinoma, and Squamous Cell Carcinoma Several years later, Sir Jonathan Hutchinson published a review of 42 cases of BCCs, identifying the tumor as a single entity with many different clinical and histopathologic forms. Krompecher first suggested that a BCC arose from the cells of the basal layer of the epidermis, but there were additional theories regarding the site of origin of this tumor, including from the hair follicle and other adnexal structures. EPIDEMIOLOGY Keratinocyte carcinomas occur worldwide in all races and ethnic- ities. They represent the most common malignancy in the US and are associated with substantial morbidity and a relatively small but significant mortality rate. An estimated 5.5 million NMSCs occurred in ~3.3 million individuals in the US in 2012 2 , with one in five Americans developing skin cancer during their lifetime 3 ( > 95% will be NMSC). In a more recent analysis, the incidence of NMSC was noted to be significantly higher in Americans > 65 years of age, with a rate of 45 individuals with NMSC/1000 persons and a case rate of 75 cases of NMSC/1000 persons 4 . The most important factor related to development of these neoplasms appears to be skin phenotype ( Table 108.1 ) 5–12 , but other factors also play a significant role. As an example, the incidence is about ten times higher in White versus Hispanic men and five times higher in White versus Hispanic women 13 . However, deriving precise data is hampered by the fact that these neoplasms are not routinely included in most state cancer registries and patients with NMSC are often treated in private offices rather than hospitals. The average amount of annual UVR correlates with the incidence of skin cancer. There is also a direct relationship between incidence and latitude, in that the closer individuals are to the equator, the greater their exposure to UVR. In Australia, in 2002, the cumulative risk by age 70 years of having at least one BCC or cSCC was 70% for men and 58% for women. Incidence also increases with age, with a sharp increase in BCCs in men after the age of 60 years. Incidence also increases with age, with a sharp increase in BCCs in men after the age of 60 years. In those under 40 years of age, the majority of NMSC is found in women, but, by age 80, the incidence in men exceeds that in women by a 2–3 : 1 ratio 13 . Actinic keratoses (AKs) are most often found in fair-skinned individuals, but can be seen in all races. AKs are so common that it has been estimated that up to 12% of individuals in the US have them 14 . AKs are also very common in other countries with large fair-skinned populations. For example, in Austria when 4449 outpatients > 30 years of age were screened, an overall AK prevalence of 39% in men and 24% in women was observed, with prevalence increasing with age in both sexes 15 . Over 80% of AKs occur in sites with the most cumulative sun exposure, e.g. the bald scalp, superior helices of the ears, face, dorsal hands, extensor forearms. Risk factors include skin phototypes I and II, significant cumulative sun exposure, a prior history of AKs, increasing age, immunosuppression, and male sex 16 . AKs are also markers for an increased risk of developing invasive cSCC 17 , but the rates of transfor- mation are low and difficult to assess (see below) 18 . The demographics of cSCC are similar to those of AKs, with the majority of SCC occurring on the head, neck, upper extremities 19 , or shins. In light-skinned populations, the degree of UV exposure is related to SCC development, while chronic irritation or injury can play a role in all populations. cSCC is found more frequently in men (M : F = 3 : 1), especially in younger age groups, and the incidence increases significantly after age 60 years 13 . The incidence of cSCC has been rising worldwide in all age groups over the last several decades at an estimated 3%–10% per year, with > 400 000 cases of invasive SCC diagnosed annually in the US 20 . In individuals with fair skin, ~75%–80% of these malignancies are BCCs and up to 25% are SCCs 1 . The incidence of both continues to rise, leading to an increasing burden of disease. In this chapter, cSCC includes SCCs that arise on the lower vermilion lip. HISTORY In 1775, Sir Percivall Pott noted an etiologic relationship between SCC and chimney soot exposure in his short treatise Chirurgical Observations Relative to the Cancer of the Scrotum . During the Industrial Revolution, links to arsenic, coal tar, shale oil, and creosote were also identified. In the late 1800s, Paul Unna noted a connection to UVR, when he described skin cancer development in chronically sun-exposed sites in sailors. Evidence of the basal cell nevus syndrome (BCNS), consisting of jaw cysts, syndactyly and bifid ribs, has been identified in Egyptian mummies almost 4000 years old. In the 1850s, Lebert first used the term “rodent ulcer” to describe untreated BCCs of long duration. In some studies, SCCs located on the ear, lip, and genitalia appear to have a higher risk of death. While melanoma among White individuals is responsible for 90% of skin cancer deaths before 50 years of age, in adults over 85 years of age, the majority of skin cancer deaths are attributable to cSCC 6 . A population-based analysis of CDC data revealed that mortality rates due to NMSC had been decreasing through 2000, were relatively stable until 2010, and then significantly increased by 44% through 2017 22 . Possible explanations included a true increase due to factors such as an aging population and an increase in immunosuppressed patients in addition to changes in cause of death documentation. For the period studied, the NMSC mortality rate was 1.24/100 000 persons/year (0.62, 0.38, and 0.23 for sun-exposed, genital, and perianal sites, respectively). At all three sites, mortality rates due to NMSC increased in White, but not in Black, individuals. BCC is the most common skin cancer in humans, and men generally have higher rates of BCC than do women (1.5–2 : 1) 23 . Over the last 30–40 years, it is estimated that incidence rates have risen between 20% and 80%. In the US, a disproportionate increase has been observed in young women. Similar increases in incidence rates have been noted worldwide, with the incidence doubling in Finland and Switzerland and increasing in Wales by 50% over this time period. Incidence rates for BCC also increase with age, and the median age at diagnosis is 68 years. In 2002, an incidence rate for BCC of 884 per 100 000 per year was observed in Australia. In this geographic location, cSCC typically occurs at half the rate of BCC among men and at about one-third the rate among women. Mortality from BCC is quite rare and occurs primarily in immuno- compromised patients and individuals with BCNS. Cases of metastatic BCC are more likely from tumors with aggressive histopathologic patterns (morpheaform, infiltrating, metatypical, basosquamous). Perineural growth, also referred to as perineural invasion, may be an indicator of aggressive disease 24 . Metastases often involve regional lymph nodes, lungs, bone, and skin. The mean age at the time of death is higher than with cSCC, and the age-adjusted mortality rate for BCC has been estimated at 0.12 per 100 000. Mortality risk is related to increasing age, lighter skin phototypes, and male sex ( > 2 compared with women). PATHOGENESIS See Chapter 107 . For BCCs, intermittent intense episodes of UV exposure and sunburns at any age appear to increase risk, whereas cumulative long-term UV exposure and childhood sunburns increase the risk for developing cSCCs and AKs 25,26 . Sun exposure early in life appears to have a greater influence on subsequent skin cancer risk than at a later age. For example, individuals born in countries with high ambient UV radiation such as Australia have significantly higher incidence rates of BCC and cSCC as compared to those with a similar genetic background (e.g. British, northern Europeans) who migrated to these areas later in life from countries with lower ambient UV radiation 25,27,28 . Indoor tanning usage Multiple studies have demonstrated an increased risk for the devel- opment of BCCs and cSCCs in those who are exposed to artificial sources of UVR. Intentional tanning has been shown to increase the risk of SCC development 29 and Karagas et al. 30 demonstrated that any use of tanning devices was associated with odds ratios of 2.5 for SCC and 1.5 for BCC, even after adjustment for history of sunburns, sunbathing, and sun exposure. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 12 studies (n = 9328 cases of NMSC) fundamentally confirmed these findings 31 . In response, many countries have passed legislation aimed at regulating indoor tanning facilities. Notably, Australia has actually completely banned this commercial industry while some states in the US prohibit minors from indoor tanning 32 . Therapeutic UVR exposure Individuals with psoriasis have been shown to be at increased risk for the development of keratinocyte carcinomas. Whereas long-term follow-up of psoriasis patients who were treated with UVR plus tar (Goeckerman) or narrowband UVB found no increased risk 33 , long-term PUVA therapy was associated with a significant, dose-related risk of cSCC development (adjusted relative risk = 8.6 for an accumulated exposure of between 100 and 337 treatments) 34 . With prolonged PUVA therapy, a slightly increased risk for BCC development was noted as well. In addition to the direct effects of PUVA, PUVA-induced immuno- suppression may also play a role. Ionizing radiation Exposure to ionizing radiation leads to a threefold increased risk for BCC and cSCC 35 . The risk is in proportion to the radiation dose. Larger fractionated doses ( > 12–15 Gy) are thought to be necessary to induce tumor formation, so the risk with a given total dose may be less if a larger number of smaller fractionated doses are given. Most SCCs and BCCs that arise after exposure to ionizing radiation do so after a long latency period of up to several decades, with most tumors appearing ~20 years after the initial exposure. Treatment of tinea capitis with radiation (prior to the discovery of effective systemic antifungal medications) has been linked to the development of multiple BCCs. In a study of 2224 children given X-ray therapy for tinea capitis (compared with a control group of 1380 tinea capitis patients given only topical medications), the relative risk for developing BCC of the head and neck among irradiated White individuals was 3.6 36 . Patients with BCNS are exquisitely sensitive to ionizing radiation and it should be avoided if possible (see below). Occupational risk factors Persons with outdoor occupations have a higher risk of developing skin cancer 37 . Based upon decades-old evidence, airline pilots, who are also exposed to ionizing radiation at flight altitudes, have about twice the risk of developing keratinocyte carcinomas than the general population 38 . Other occupations associated with an increased risk for NMSC include agricultural workers, gardeners, sailors, and locomotive engineers. Chemical exposures Multiple organic chemicals have been associated with an increased risk for the development of keratinocyte carcinomas 39 (see Table 108.2 ). Occupational chemical exposures which can lead to skin cancer most commonly involve pesticides, asphalt, tar, and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, and they typically result in SCC. The skin cancers induced by chemical exposures are usually localized as well as multiple, most often appearing on the arms 40 . Arsenic is a well-defined cause of SCC (see Ch. 88 ). A clue to arsenic exposure is the presence of palmoplantar arsenical keratoses. BCC has also been reported following extensive arsenic exposure. The typical latency period from exposure to tumor development is 20–40 years 41 . Human Papillomavirus Infection Human papillomaviruses (HPV) represent a large group of DNA tumor viruses that infect the epithelia of both skin and mucosae, inducing hyperproliferative lesions, most commonly warts. HPV is associated with anogenital SCCs, particularly in HIV-infected patients. Individuals with the genetic condition epidermodysplasia verruci- formis (EV) are known to have a significantly increased risk of devel- oping SCCs, especially in sun-exposed sites. Infection with the HPV types referred to as EV- or beta-types (see Table 79.1 ) is also observed in the general population, in particular in immunosuppressed solid organ transplant recipients 42 . Because these specific HPV subtypes are thought to act as facilitators for the accumulation of UVR-induced mutations during the development of SCC 43 , a goal is to design thera- peutic HPV vaccines 44 . Immunosuppression Organ transplantation Solid organ transplant recipients have a markedly increased incidence of skin cancer, primarily cSCC. The incidence of BCC in organ transplant recipients is up to 5–10 times greater than in the general population, while the incidence of SCC is 30–250 times greater. Risk factors include skin phototypes I/II, cumulative sun exposure, previous history of skin cancer, age at transplantation, and the degree and the length of immunosuppression. cSCC is a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in transplant recipients 45,46 . The pathogenesis of skin cancer in transplant recipients is multifactorial, involving decreased immunity, direct carcinogenic effects of immunosuppressive medications, and HPV infection in addition to UVR exposure. Transplant recipients are prone to developing numerous lesions and are more likely to suffer local and regional recur- rences and metastases 45 . AKs and SCCs begin to appear with increasing frequency several years after transplantation. Lesions are often multiple and usually develop in sun-exposed areas. cSCCs from transplant recipients frequently contain HPV DNA, but it can be from a range of HPV strains including those that occur in common benign cutaneous warts (HPV types 1 and 2), EV (HPV-5 and others; see above), high-risk oncogenic warts (HPV types 16 and 18), and low-risk oncogenic genital warts (HPV types 6 and 11). Sometimes, several HPV types are detected within a single tumor. More recently, a role for polyomaviruses in the development of cSCCs has been proposed. In one series of renal transplant patients from the US, 5% of the patients died of skin cancer. In another series of heart transplant patients from Australia, 27% died of skin cancer. Two-thirds of these deaths were due to cSCC. Several studies have shown that in renal transplant patients sirolimus, an mTOR inhibitor, reduced the devel- opment of cSCCs when compared to calcineurin inhibitors (e.g. cyclo- sporine, tacrolimus) 47 . However, the impact may be related to the number of previous SCCs 48 . More recently, belatacept, a fusion protein that prevents CD28 activation, was also observed to reduce skin cancer risk in renal transplant recipients 49 . Based upon currently available data, sirolimus and belatacept appear to be preferable in patients with a history of SCCs or strong risk factors. Additional interventions include reduction in immunosuppression, aggressive screening, discontinuing hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ), and instituting acitretin. These tumors can be aggressive and monitoring that incorporates anal cytology is recommended 52 . They develop primarily in individuals with cutaneous photodamage and can appear within weeks of beginning the kinase inhibitor. Fortunately, the combination of a selective BRAF inhibitor with a MEK inhibitor, as is routinely done nowadays, significantly reduces the incidence of side effects of both drugs, including the formation of SCCs and KAs. Voriconazole is also associated with the development of UVR-induced skin cancers, possibly a result of the phototoxic moieties of its metabolites. Genetic Risk Factors Genetic predisposition Phenotypic characteristics such as red hair, light skin, poor ability to tan, and freckling have been identified as risk factors for melanoma as well as NMSC 25 . Pigmentation is a polygenic trait, with polymor- phisms in several genes leading to the variation observed in the human race (see Ch. 65 ). A key gene encodes the human melanocortin-1 receptor (MC1R) which is expressed on the cell surface of melanocytes. Population-based studies in diverse ethnic groups have shown that the coding region of the human MC1R is remarkably polymorphic. In White individuals, there is a strong association between nine common MC1R variant alleles and the red hair/fair skin phenotype, thus placing these individuals at higher risk of photocarcinogenesis 58 . Based upon genome-wide association studies and candidate gene studies (see Ch. 54 ), ~30 and at least 11 susceptibility loci for BCC and cSCC, respectively, have been identified, and they include multiple pigmen- tation loci. A markedly increased incidence of keratinocyte carcinoma and melanoma is observed in these individuals, if they are exposed to sunlight. cSCCs and BCCs appear at an early age (median age, 8 years), and in affected individuals who are < 20 years of age the risk is 4800 times that of the general population. Strict UV avoidance can signifi- cantly decrease skin cancer formation. Oculocutaneous albinism Oculocutaneous albinism encompasses a group of autosomal recessive disorders in which there is a variable degree of pigmentary dilution of the skin, eyes, and hair (see Ch. 66 ). Individual lesions may be papulonodular, pedunculated, pigmented, eroded, ulcerated, or have a combination of these features. The pigmented BCCs are sometimes misdiagnosed clinically as melanocytic nevi (see Fig. 108.20 ). The clinical course of the cutaneous tumors is usually indolent prior to puberty, after which they enlarge and eventually ulcerate, as in the general population. Individuals with BCNS are exquisitely sensitive to ionizing radiation, and hundreds of tumors can develop in children within sites of radiation following radiotherapy for medulloblastoma. Additional cutaneous findings include epidermoid (infundibular) cysts and facial milia. Bazex–Dupré–Christol syndrome and Rombo syndrome Bazex–Dupré–Christol syndrome is a rare condition, consisting of follicular atrophoderma (usually occurring as circumscribed areas on the dorsal aspect of the hands and feet), hypotrichosis, localized hypohi- drosis, milia, epidermoid cysts, and multiple, primarily facial, BCCs. The BCCs develop during the second decade of life and frequently have a trichoepithelioma-like histopathologic appearance. In most families, the inheritance pattern is X-linked dominant and mutations in ACTRT1 have been detected, resulting in aberrant activation of the hedgehog signaling within primary cilia 60 . Sometimes a source of semantic confusion is the completely different Bazex syndrome (acrokeratosis paraneoplastica), in which psoriasiform plaques of the fingers, toes, ears, and nose are often associated with SCC of the upper aerodigestive tract. The so-called Rombo syndrome has many of the features of Bazex– Dupré–Christol syndrome. Patients have an atrophoderma vermic- ulatum-like appearance on the cheeks, with evidence of sweat duct proliferation histologically. In addition, they often have hypotrichosis, blepharitis, peripheral (facial/acral) telangiectatic erythema, milia, trichoepitheliomas, and BCCs. Rothmund–Thomson syndrome (RTS) During the first few months of life, patients develop photodistributed erythema, edema, and vesicles of the cheeks and face (see Ch. 87 ) 61 . Additional cutaneous findings include gradual appearance of poiki- loderma, thinning of scalp hair, and hypoplastic nails. While osteo- sarcoma develops in type II RTS (due to dysfunction of the DNA helicase RecQL4), NMSC can develop in both types. Mutations in ANAPC1 , whose protein product mediates ubiquitination and controls progression through mitosis and G1 of the cell cycle, are responsible for type I RTS. Keratitis–ichthyosis–deafness (KID) syndrome In addition to congenital sensorineural hearing loss, patients present with a transient erythroderma at birth or during infancy followed by discrete plaques of erythrokeratoderma as well as palmoplantar kerato- derma (see Ch. 57 ) 61 . Mutations in genes that encode connexins lead to KID syndrome (see Ch. 58 ); these gap junction proteins are expressed in ectoderm-derived epithelia of the inner ear, cornea, and epidermis. Patients have an increased susceptibility to viral, bacterial, and fungal infections and can develop the follicular occlusion triad, proliferating pilar tumors, and early-onset mucocutaneous SCCs (see Table 57.5 ). Risk of Additional Cancers Individuals who have had a BCC or cSCC are at increased risk for the development of additional BCCs and SCCs 62 , compared to the general population. They are also at increased risk for developing cutaneous melanoma 63 . Based upon epidemiologic studies, persons with a history of BCCs or SCCs may be at increased risk for developing and dying from other (non-skin) cancers 64–66 . Field cancerization In field cancerization, areas of the skin with significant photodamage (e.g. the bald scalp) have multiple clusters of p53-mutated keratino- cytes 67 and they may or may not be clinically apparent. The presence of multiple actinic keratoses points to the diagnosis. Treatment regimens should focus not just on specific tumors but on the entire affected anatomical site (see below). The term “actinic keratosis” is preferred over solar keratosis, partly because the abbreviation SK also stands for seborrheic keratosis. AKs have historically been characterized as being “precancerous” or “premalignant” because the atypical keratinocytes within these lesions are confined to the epidermis. There is no risk of metastasis until these lesions evolve into invasive carcinoma, but AKs are viewed as potential precursors of cSCC. The likelihood of a solitary AK progressing into an invasive cSCC is difficult to predict, with estimates varying widely from 0.1% to 20%. Lesions are frequently clustered in areas of highest cumulative sun exposure, such as the superior helices of the ears, upper forehead, supraorbital ridge, nasal bridge, malar eminences, dorsal hands, extensor forearms, shins, and the bald scalp (see Fig. 108.2C ). Of note, clinically, AKs may spontaneously regress, but then can reappear at the same site. Visual inspection is best performed with simultaneous palpation to detect lesions that may not be readily apparent. This is especially true in individuals with significant background erythema from chronic sun exposure or rosacea. Clinical subtypes of AKs include the classic variant already described, hypertrophic (often hyperkeratotic), pigmented, lichenoid, atrophic, and actinic cheilitis. Hypertrophic (hyperkeratotic) AKs are easily identified on visual inspection as papules and plaques with scale or scale-crust and an erythematous base (see Fig. 108.2D ). The erythematous base often extends beyond the overlying hyperkeratosis. The hyperkeratotic scale can become white or yellow–brown over time. Due to their thickness, patients often find these lesions to be bothersome. Occasionally, a hyper- keratotic AK may develop a cutaneous horn that manifests as a column of thick cornified material that protrudes above the skin. The major entity in the differential diagnosis of a hyperkeratotic AK is a cSCC. Pigmented AKs represent a subtype that often lacks associated erythema and has a hyperpigmented or reticulated appearance ( Fig. 108.3 ). These lesions can at times be difficult to distinguish from reticulated seborrheic keratoses, lentigines, or even the lentigo maligna subtype of cutaneous melanoma. Dermoscopy may be a useful adjunct in these situations (see Ch. 0 ). Clinical clues are the location on sun-exposed skin, background solar changes, and hyperkeratosis that is sometimes appreciable by palpation. In cases in which the diagnosis is questionable, a biopsy is required to exclude the possibility of melanoma. Other variants of SCC in situ include a pigmented variant often seen in individuals with darker skin types and a verrucous form. Invasive cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma Invasive cSCC usually arises within a background of sun-damaged skin, most commonly on the bald scalp, face, neck, extensor forearms, dorsal hands, and shins ( Fig. 108.7A,B ). SCCs are often papulonodular, but can be plaque-like, papillomatous, or even vegetating ( Figs. 108.7C,G and 108.8 ). The degree of scale varies, with some lesions becoming quite hyperkeratotic ( Fig. 108.7E,F ); secondary changes include crusting, erosions, and ulcerations ( Fig. 108.7D,H ). Dermoscopic features are outlined in Chapter 0 . The natural history of cSCCs also varies, from slowly enlarging to rapidly growing with significant tenderness and even pain. Of note, paresthesias, anesthesia, and pain may be signs of perineural invasion. Keratoacanthoma Keratoacanthomas (KAs) are considered by some to be a variant of cSCC and by others to represent benign tumors (i.e. a pseudo­ malignancy). The exact nosology is still uncertain, although there are some data that support its differentiation from “conventional” SCC. Typically, a rapidly enlarging papule evolves into a sharply circum- scribed, crateriform nodule with a keratotic core over a period of a few weeks ( Fig. 108.9A–D ), and then it may resolve slowly over months to leave an atrophic scar. Most lesions occur on the head and neck or in sun-exposed areas of the extremities, with or without symptoms of pain or tenderness. The Ferguson–Smith syndrome is an autosomal dominant condition due to mutations in TGFBR1 which encodes TGF- β receptor type 1. Multiple KAs develop within sun-exposed areas, usually beginning during the third decade of life. Lesions typically regress over weeks to months, but rare examples of metastases have been reported. Verrucous carcinoma Verrucous carcinoma is a rare, well-differentiated variant of SCC which tends to occur in middle-aged and older adults. It is considered a low-grade malignancy with three major subtypes: (1) epithelioma cunic- ulatum (plantar surface of the foot); (2) giant condyloma acuminatum of the genitalia (also known as Buschke–Löwenstein tumor; see Ch. 79 ); and (3) oral florid papillomatosis (oral mucosa). Of note, the “cunicu- latum” refers to the rabbit burrow-like appearance with crevices. Clinically, verrucous carcinomas present as large (sometimes huge), exophytic tumors with a papillomatous or verrucous surface ( Fig. 108.10A,B ). They are commonly associated with HPV infection, and distinguishing between a verrucous carcinoma and a large wart or condyloma acuminatum can be challenging. Gradual penetration of verrucous carcinomas into underlying tissues can result in destruction of subcutis, fascia, and bone. These tumors can arise within scars and amputation stumps ( Fig. 108.10C ) as well as in association with fistulae of osteomyelitis and chronic venous insufficiency. Verrucous carcinomas often recur after attempted removal, but they usually do not metastasize, except for recurrent or irradiated tumors with anaplastic transformation. Some authors consider subungual KAs, proliferating tricholemmal cysts (proliferating pilar tumors), and papillomatosis cutis carcinoides (which favors the shins and dorsal feet) to be subtypes of verrucous carcinoma. Lymphoepithelioma-like carcinoma of the skin Lymphoepithelioma-like carcinoma of the skin (LELCS) is an uncommon neoplasm that shows histopathologic similarities to lymphoepithelioma-like carcinoma (LELC), an undifferentiated nasopharyngeal carcinoma associated with EBV infection. LELCS has the potential for both sweat glandular and follicular differentiation. Clinically, it presents as a dermal papule or nodule arising in the head and neck region. In contrast to LELC, EBV genome integration is not found in LELCS, and metastases are rare. Evidence of HPV infection is also usually absent. LELCS is considered by some to be a variant of cSCC, while others view it as a type of cutaneous adnexal carcinoma. Histologically, LELCSs are localized within the dermis or subcutis, with involvement of the overlying epidermis having been observed in only a few cases. Reflectance confocal microscopy Reflectance confocal microscopy (RCM) is an imaging technique which allows non-invasive horizontal imaging of the epidermis and superficial dermis at almost the same resolution as routine histology. However, RCM (and dermoscopic) features of keratinizing tumors are often difficult to visualize due to the surface scaling which obscures underlying structures. Pathology Actinic keratosis There is partial thickness involvement of the epidermis by atypical keratinocytes with nuclear pleomorphism, especially in the basal layer, as well as disordered maturation. Hyperkeratosis and parakeratosis are constant findings. Acrosyringia and acrotrichia are often uninvolved , resulting in orthokeratosis above the ostia of these structures ( Fig. 108.11A ). In the dermis, actinic elastosis is seen. A minority of dermatopathologists employ a grading system – early AK (grade I), AK involving the lower two-thirds of the epidermis (grade II), full-thickness atypia of the epidermis (grade III; SCC in situ ) – but this classification has not gained widespread acceptance. In addition to atrophic and bowenoid AKs, several other histo- pathologic variants have been described, including acantholytic ( Fig. 108.11B ), hypertrophic (hyperkeratotic), pigmented, and lichenoid. In hypertrophic AKs, marked hyperkeratosis with associated parakeratosis is evident. If pronounced, this can lead to cutaneous horn formation. Pigmented AKs additionally show basilar pigmentation in a pattern similar to a solar lentigo ( Fig. 108.11C ). Keratoacanthoma A keratoacanthoma (KA) typically has a “volcano-like” architecture. The tumor is comprised of well-differentiated keratinocytes with a brightly eosinophilic glassy cytoplasm, surrounding a core filled with cornified material ( Fig. 108.14 ). An inflammatory infiltrate of lymphocytes, and often eosinophils, is usually present. Small intratumoral abscesses of neutrophils are common, and neurotropism may be observed. As the lesion regresses, the dome-shaped architecture flattens and fibrosis develops at the base of the lesion. Cytologic atypia is usually not pronounced in a KA. If hyperchromatic nuclei or abnormal mitoses are prominent, then the diagnosis of an invasive KA-like SCC should be rendered. However, this term should not be applied to every SCC that has a warty appearance. Cytologic atypia is minimal, and the tumor has a pushing border as opposed to an infiltrating invasive edge. Verrucous carcinoma can be associated with HPV infection, and histopathologic distinction from a large wart or condyloma is often difficult and may be impossible if the entire tumor is not available for microscopic examination. The major distinguishing features of a verrucous carcinoma are the massiveness and depth of the lesion, as well as the pronounced irregular architecture. Histopathologic simulators of SCC There are a number of histopathologic simulators of SCC, including seborrheic keratosis, verruca vulgaris, inverted follicular keratosis, prurigo nodularis, hypertrophic lichen planus, hypertrophic lupus erythematosus, and the pseudocarcinomatous hyperplasia that can occur in a range of disorders (e.g. dimorphic fungal infections, healing wounds, tattoos, some non-keratinocyte tumors). Architectural pattern and recognition of cellular and nuclear features of malignancy are critical in establishing a diagnosis. In some cases, only clinical corre- lation allows a distinction between SCC and some of these conditions. Of note, SCC may occur in the setting of a pre-existing benign tumor (e.g. seborrheic keratosis) as well as within chronic pseudoepithelio- matous hyperplasia related to hypertrophic lichen planus or hyper- trophic lupus erythematosus. Atypical squamous proliferation Atypical squamous proliferation (ASP) is a term used to describe the histologic findings found in papulonodules and thick plaques that develop within markedly sun-damaged skin, usually on the shins and following trauma. This term is preferred over keratoacanthoma-like squamous proliferations as they often lack a central keratotic core. Although ASPs are associated with less cytologic atypia than cSCCs 72 , distinction can prove challenging. Immunohistochemical staining for p53 may be helpful with positivity in basal and immediately supra- basal layers in ASP, in contrast to full-thickness positivity in cSCC. BASAL CELL CARCINOMA Clinical Features Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is a tumor that usually arises within sun-damaged skin. However, it may also develop in sites with minimal sun exposure, e.g. inner canthus, retroauricular; rarely BCCs occur on the palms, soles, and mucous membranes. Currently, despite the description of multiple subtypes of BCC, a universally accepted classi- fication scheme is lacking, but a standardization of terminology has recently been proposed 73 . Nonetheless, four major distinctive clinico- pathologic types are commonly recognized, namely, nodular, superficial, morpheaform, and fibroepithelial (also referred to as fibroepithelioma of Pinkus) 74 . Combinations of the latter three types with nodular BCC can occur. While all types of BCC may ulcerate, ulceration is observed more often in the nodular type. Also, variable amounts of melanin may be present within these tumors, even though the majority of BCCs are amelanotic; pigmented BCCs are observed more commonly in those with darker skin phototypes. When one attempts to classify BCCs, a significant confounding factor is the number of different histopathologic patterns that become entwined with clinical subtypes. Examples are cystic, mucinous, micronodular, and basosquamous BCCs. Although these patterns may be seen in all four major clinicopathologic types of BCC, they are observed more frequently in the nodular type. Nodular basal cell carcinoma Nodular BCC is the most common subtype, accounting for ~50% of all BCCs. Lesions typically present as a shiny, pearly papule or nodule with a smooth surface and the presence of arborizing telangiectasias ( Fig. 108.16 ). With time, the tumor can enlarge and ulcerate (rodent ulcer, phagedenic ulcer), but an elevated rolled border usually remains and is a clinical clue to the diagnosis. A variable degree of pigmentation may be seen within the tumor ( Fig. 108.17A–C ). Sites of predilection are the face, especially the cheeks, nose, nasolabial folds, forehead and eyelids, but nodular BCCs may arise in any hair-bearing area of the skin. They rarely occur in non-hair-bearing sites, e.g. oral or genital mucosa, palms and soles. This BCC variant favors the trunk and extremities; less often, it occurs in the head and neck region. Multiple lesions may be present. The growth pattern of superficial BCCs is primarily horizontal, but tumors may occasionally become deeply invasive, with induration, ulceration, and nodule formation. Subclinical lateral spread accounts for the significant recurrence rate of these tumors after routine surgical treatment. The tumor cells have large, relatively uniform nuclei and scant cytoplasm; cellular borders are indistinct and desmo- somes are inapparent. Apoptotic cells are common. The fibromyxoid stroma is intimately associated with the tumor islands, often showing increased cellularity. A characteristic feature of BCC is retraction of the stroma around the tumor islands, creating microscopically visible clefts ( Fig. 108.22B ). Although this latter feature may not be seen in all instances, when present it is useful in differentiating BCCs from histo- pathologic simulators. In nodular BCC , large, round or oval aggregations of basaloid kerati- nocytes extend from the epidermis into the dermis ( Fig. 108.22C ). Overlying ulceration with an associated inflammatory response may be present. Peripheral palisading is usually prominent and peritumoral clefts are often conspicuous in nodular BCC ( Fig. 108.22D ). Centrally, the nuclei lack organization and are more randomly distributed. In larger tumor islands, central areas of necrosis may develop, leading to the formation of cystic spaces. True cystic or nodulocystic BCCs contain mucin pools within the tumor islands ( Fig. 108.22E ). Micronodular BCCs are composed of tumor islands much smaller than those of nodular BCC ( Fig. 108.22F ). The cellular features are similar. Superficial BCCs are characterized by small, superficially located buds of basaloid cells extending no more deeply than the papillary dermis, with or without clefting (see Fig. 108.22A,B ). In a given two-dimen- sional plane of section, there are skip areas along the epidermis, hence the synonym “superficial multifocal BCC”. There is evidence that many of these multifocal buds connect in a net-like pattern, such that most tumors are not truly multifocal. Pigmented BCCs usually have the overall architecture of a nodular BCC. They contain aggregates of melanin, often irregularly distributed, and sometimes an increased number of intratumoral melanocytes ( Fig. 108.22G ). Melanophages are frequently dispersed within the dermis. Morpheaform, sclerosing and infiltrative BCCs share similar histo- pathologic features. A common finding is a pattern of strands and cords of basaloid keratinocytes extending between collagen bundles ( Fig. 108.22H ). These tumor islands may be composed of very few cells and may surround nerves. A peripheral palisaded pattern of tumor cells is absent and stromal retraction (cleft formation) is also frequently not evident. Fibroepithelial BCC (fibroepithelioma of Pinkus) is a variant of BCC characterized by thin anastomosing strands and cords of tumor cells that project downward from the epidermis in a fenestrated pattern and are embedded in a fibrovascular stroma ( Fig. 108.22I ). Both peripheral palisading and peritumoral retraction are less prominent. The differ- ential diagnosis includes eccrine syringofibroadenoma and reticulated seborrheic keratosis. Infundibulocystic BCCs have cords of follicular germs with small infundibular cysts that display differentiation towards hair follicle structures. Although they can be difficult to differentiate from tricho- epitheliomas or other follicular adnexal neoplasms, immunostaining for PHLDA1, a marker of epithelial follicular stem cells, is stronger and more diffuse in trichoepitheliomas 76 . Multiple hereditary infundibulo- cystic BCC syndrome has been associated with a germline mutation in SUFU . Additional histopathologic subtypes of BCC Basosquamous carcinoma Basosquamous carcinoma (metatypical BCC, keratotic BCC) is a tumor that has histopathologic features of both BCC and cSCC ( Fig. 108.22J ). These tumors may behave biologically more like an SCC than a BCC, i.e. they have more aggressive behavior with a greater likelihood of both recurring after treatment and metastasizing. It has been estimated that this variant constitutes 1% of all keratinocyte carcinomas. When metastases occur, they may have the same microscopic appearance as the original tumor or may resemble a poorly differentiated SCC. Micronodular basal cell carcinoma This histopathologic term applies to BCCs in which smaller aggregations of basaloid cells infiltrate the dermis (see Fig.108.22F ). Micronodular BCCs possess a destructive behavior, with subclinical spread and high rates of recurrence. Clinically, they may present as infiltrated macules, papules/nodules, or plaques and are basically indistinguishable from nodular BCCs. A recent consensus project suggested that infiltrating, sclerosing, and micronodular subtypes should be grouped together under the umbrella term “infiltrating BCCs” 73 . Histopathologic simulators of BCC Other basaloid tumors that may simulate BCC include adnexal neoplasms, in particular trichoblastoma ( Table 108.6 ). In contrast to BCC, clefts in trichoblastoma are located within the stroma and not in direct proximity to the basaloid tumor islands. In addition, follicular germs and papillae, simulating rudimentary hair follicles, are commonly found in trichoblastomas. Basaloid induction within dermatofibromas and reactive folliculocentric basaloid proliferation may also simulate BCC histopathologically. TREATMENT Several national and international organizations have established guidelines of care for BCCs and cSCCs. When available, these guide- lines are based upon evidence but are oftentimes developed via expert consensus 77–79 . Evaluation and Risk Assessment Evaluation of a suspected NMSC requires a history, physical exami- nation, and biopsy of the suspicious lesion. The history should assess duration, rate of growth, and any prior therapy, as well as any personal or family history of prior skin cancers. Localized neurologic symptoms, although rare, may suggest the possibility of perineural involvement. Any history of prior radiation therapy to the area should be elicited. Current medical problems (e.g. chronic lymphocytic leukemia), medica- tions (e.g. voriconazole, hydroxyurea), and allergies should be reviewed. Evidence of immunosuppression (e.g. organ transplantation, immuno- suppressive medications, HIV infection) should be determined, and any of the risk factors listed in Table 108.2 identified. Physical examination should include observation and palpation of the tumor to determine exact location and size, and whether it appears to have any connection to underlying structures such as muscle, cartilage, or bone. Nevertheless, a properly performed biopsy is essential to the diagnosis and management of any lesion. Numerous biopsy techniques, including excisional, incisional, shave, saucerization, and punch, may be employed (see Ch. 146 ). For obvious skin cancers, especially in elderly patients, a tissue specimen is sometimes obtained at the same time as definitive therapy. If a superficial process (such as a superficial BCC or SCC in situ ) is suspected, or if shallow therapy (such as curettage and electro- desiccation) is being contemplated, a shave biopsy is usually adequate for establishing a diagnosis. In most other instances, a punch biopsy or deep saucerization that extends to subcutaneous fat is preferred. AKs, on the other hand, are often treated without prior biopsy unless invasive NMSC is suspected; clinical judgment determines which AKs require treatment and which can be left untreated. Actinic Keratosis, Basal Cell Carcinoma, and Squamous Cell Carcinoma Surgical and Destructive Procedures Standard excision Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma Low-risk cSCC should be excised with a surgical margin of 4–6 mm. Standard excision without micrographic assessment of the complete margin (see Fig. 150.1 ) may be considered for select high-risk tumors, but strong caution is advised. US guidelines of care consider available data insufficient for evaluation of standard excision for high-risk tumors 78 . Basal cell carcinoma Surgical excision is the standard treatment for most primary BCCs. In 98% of cases of non-morpheaform BCCs < 2 cm in diameter, 4-mm margins are adequate for removal 79 . However, for facial lesions, simple excision with narrow margins is often not adequate for effective removal. For high-risk BCCs, US guidelines of care recommend Mohs micro- graphic surgery 77 while European guidelines recommend a surgical margin of 5–15 mm (depending on tumor characteristics) when micro- graphic surgery is not available 79 . Curettage alone Barlow et al. 80 reported a 5-year cure rate of 96% when 302 biopsy- proven BCCs were treated by a single investigator with curettage alone. Minimal hypopigmentation and scarring was observed. Some clinicians combine curettage with application of topical agents such as imiquimod postoperatively. Curettage with electrodesiccation Curettage with electrodesiccation is frequently used by dermatologists to treat BCCs. Cure rates as high as 97%–98% have been reported 81 , but careful selection of appropriate lesions (e.g. those without extension into the deep dermis) is necessary. In terminal hair-bearing sites, extension of neoplastic cells down follicular structures could also lead to incom- plete removal. Curettage and electrodesiccation can be used for smaller SCCs in situ and well-differentiated primary SCCs < 1 cm in diameter. Mohs micrographic surgery Mohs micrographic surgery results in superior histopathologic verifi- cation of complete removal of the tumor and allows for maximum conservation of tissue (see Ch. 150 ). Although Mohs micrographic surgery remains cost-effective when compared to either excisions done in a surgical center or hospital operating room or radiation therapy, it is more expensive than in-office standard excision. In one series of BCCs treated with Mohs micrographic surgery, a recurrence rate of only 1% over 5 years was observed. This was superior to all other modalities, including excision (10%), curettage and desiccation (8%), radiation therapy (9%), and cryotherapy (7.5%). However, percentages do vary NEOPLASMS OF THE SKIN among studies, depending in part on the physicians involved and the types of lesions selected for inclusion. Although direct comparison of different studies is difficult, Mohs micrographic surgery clearly has the highest cure rate when all tumor types as well as recurrent tumors are taken into consideration 82 . In one series of recurrent BCCs, Mohs micrographic surgery had a long-term recurrence rate of 5.6%, superior to all other modalities, including excision (17%), radiation therapy (10%), and curettage with electrodesiccation (40%). Radiation therapy Radiation therapy is a therapeutic option for patients with a BCC or cSCC who are not well suited for surgery (see Ch. 139 ) 83,84 . Before choosing this therapy, both function and cosmetic outcome are considered. Advantages include avoidance of an invasive procedure in a patient who may not be able to tolerate surgery or is unwilling to undergo surgery. Disadvantages include lack of margin control, poor cosmesis in some patients, a prolonged course of therapy, and increased risk for future skin cancers. Scars from radiation therapy tend to worsen with time, in contrast to surgical scars, which improve over time. Radiation is often used as an adjuvant modality following treatment of aggressive or high-risk cSCC with surgery, especially when perineural involvement is identified, to reduce local or locoregional recurrence 84a . Verrucous carcinomas, which are well differentiated and rarely metastasize, are usually not treated with radiotherapy, since there is concern that cellular transformation may result in a worse prognosis. Radiotherapy is not well suited for morpheaform BCCs, as they are relatively radioresistant, or for patients with BCNS since X-rays can lead to mutations in the second PTCH allele, with subsequent tumorigenesis. Cryosurgery Cryosurgery is a mainstay of treatment for AKs, but has also been used to treat BCCs and cSCCs (see Ch. 138 ). It has the advantage of being a relatively easy to perform and quick procedure (particularly in the case of AKs) and is advantageous for those patients wishing to avoid invasive surgery. Complications may include hypertrophic scarring and postinflammatory pigmentary changes. A serious potential adverse outcome is recurrent carcinoma that can become extensive because of concealment by the fibrous scar tissue. Photodynamic therapy Photodynamic therapy (PDT) is FDA-approved for the treatment of multiple AKs (see Ch. 135 ). In the European Union and elsewhere, it is also approved for cSCC in situ and BCC. PDT is used primarily for superficial BCCs and occasionally as second-line therapy for nodular BCCs when surgery is not clinically recommended. Guidelines of care address clinical indications, photosensitizer administration, and light exposure specifications 85 . Daylight PDT, which is less painful than classic PDT, can be particularly useful in patients with numerous AKs and field cancerization. In organ transplant recipients, a systematic review found that PDT was the most effective treatment for AKs, when compared to topical imiquimod, ingenol mebutate, diclofenac sodium, and 5-fluoruracil 86 . However, in a randomized trial in immunocom- petent patients, topical 5-fluorouracil was more effective than PDT, topical imiquimod, or topical ingenol mebutate for the treatment of AKs 87 . Laser Laser surgery is an uncommon treatment for BCCs and cSCCs, with limited data in the literature and restriction to low-risk tumors. Non-Surgical Treatments Topical therapies and side effects of FDA-approved topical agents. 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) is used primarily for the treatment of AKs and occasionally for superficial BCCs and selected cSCCs in situ . In a randomized trial in immunocompetent patients, 5-FU was more effective for the treatment of AKs than other standard therapies (see above) 87 . Side effects are usually limited to significant local skin reactions (see Ch. 129 ). Diclofenac sodium , a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID), is also an effective option for the treatment of AKs. However, longer treatment cycles are required. Imiquimod is a Toll-like receptor 7 agonist whose major side effect is a local skin reaction that can include erosions and crusting (see Ch. 129 ). The 5% formulation is FDA-approved for the treatment of superficial BCCs while 2.5%, 3.75%, and 5% formulations are approved for non-hypertrophic AKs on the face and scalp. When compared to surgery in a randomly controlled trial of 501 patients with BCCs, tumor clearance was 82.5% in the imiquimod group versus 98% in the surgery group 88 . For SCC in situ , clearance rates of 73%–88% at 3–6 months have been reported 89 . Tirbanibulin , a drug that inhibits Src kinase signaling and tubulin polymerization, has been recently approved as a 1% ointment for the treatment of AKs. In two phase III trials, complete clearance of lesions after 5 days of application was observed in 44% to 54% of study participants 90 . Topical agents currently under investigation include the hedgehog pathway inhibitor patidegib for the treatment of BCCs 91 . Application of 2% or 4% patidegib gel has shown promising results, especially in patients with BCNS. Additional compounds under development for the treatment of AKs are sinecatechin , which is derived from green tea leaves, and tuvatexib , a hexokinase inhibitor. Combination therapy Combining more than one therapeutic modality has the potential advantage of enhancing the cure rate while minimizing adverse effects and maximizing cosmetic results. Both topical 5-FU cream and 5% imiquimod cream have been used to pretreat BCC sites prior to Mohs micrographic surgery, leading to a decrease in tumor size before surgical removal. Imiquimod cream has also been used, in conjunction with topical 5-FU cream, for the treatment of cSCC in situ in transplant recipients. Excellent cosmetic results have been reported when BCCs were treated with just curettage followed by 6 weeks of topical 5% imiquimod cream. In patients with AKs, combination therapy with calcipotriene (calcipotriol) 0.005% ointment plus 5% 5-FU cream twice daily for four consecutive days led to a response rate of 88% 92 . When PDT was combined with other topical agents (e.g. imiquimod), higher AK clearance rates were observed in comparison to monotherapy 85 ; this approach has also been employed for actinic cheilitis. Chemowraps To treat multiple AKs, especially on the extremities and in the setting of field cancerization, wraps composed of zinc oxide-impregnated gauze can be used to occlude 5-FU cream 93 . In one series of 25 patients with widespread AKs, a response rate of 60% was achieved following weekly 5-FU chemowraps. Monitoring of patients for severe local reactions and systemic toxicity is recommended 94 . Intralesional treatment There are reports describing the effectiveness of directly injecting NMSCs with cytostatic drugs such as methotrexate, bleomycin, and 5-FU, or injecting immunomodulators such as interferon alpha 2b, with response rates of about 80% 95 . Because of a limited level of evidence, the use of intratumoral agents should be considered in selected patients ( Table 108.9 ). Systemic Therapy Treatment of advanced cutaneous SCC Systemic therapy is utilized when tumors are neither surgically resectable nor curable by radiotherapy or when metastases have Actinic Keratosis, Basal Cell Carcinoma, and Squamous Cell Carcinoma developed. Currently, there are no consensus-based recommendations regarding the best treatment for advanced cSCC. Immunotherapy with immune checkpoint inhibitors Response rates of > 40% in advanced cSCCs have been reported with anti-PD-1 antibodies including cemiplimab, pembrolizumab, and nivolumab 96 . For example, cemiplimab led to overall response rates (ORRs) of 44% and 45% for locally advanced cSCC and metastatic cSCC, respectively. As a result, cemiplimab is FDA approved for both indications. In patients who received pembrolizumab, ORRs of 42% and 32% were observed in patients with unresectable cSCC and recurrent or metastatic cSCC, respectively; it is now FDA-approved for the latter group of patients. Of note, in more than one study, patients with PD-L1 + tumors had significantly higher response rates than those with negative tumors 79b , leading to the suggestion that immunohistochemical evaluation of PD-L1 be performed when considering immunotherapy. Inactivating mutations in PTCH1 , PTCH2 , or SUFU or activating mutations in SMO lead to activation of the hedgehog signaling pathway and have been associated with the development of BCCs (see Fig. 107.6 ); mutations in the first three genes can lead to BCNS. The hedgehog pathway inhibitors vismo- degib ( Fig. 108.23 ) and sonidegib are quite effective systemic treat- ments for advanced BCC. Vismodegib was first reported to have antitumor activity in locally advanced or metastatic BCC in 2009 97 . Of the 33 patients treated with vismodegib in the phase I trial, two had a complete response (6%) while 16 had a partial response (48%). There was a reduction in the number of new BCCs as well as the size of existing BCCs. In further studies, individuals with metastatic BCC and locally advanced BCC had ORRs of ~30% and ~40%–45%, respectively. Nearly all patients in these trials reported adverse reactions ( Table 108.10 ), leading to treatment discontinuation in about 30% of study participants. More recently two intermittent vismodegib regimens have been evaluated in patients with multiple BCCs and BCNS; these individual drug modifi- cations (with non-dosing periods) led to equal efficacy but a lower rate of adverse events 98 . Sonidegib , another hedgehog signaling inhibitor (via smoothened antagonism), also demonstrated efficacy in locally advanced and metastatic BCC. Immunotherapy with immune checkpoint inhibitors BCCs contain a high mutational tumor burden due to chronic UV-induced damage to DNA. This leads to an abundance of tumor neoantigens, providing a rationale for the use of immune checkpoint inhibitors, in particular anti-PD-1 antibodies 99 . Pembrolizumab, nivolumab, and cemiplimab have been investigated, and cemiplimab is currently FDA-approved for locally advanced or metastatic BCC in patients previously treated with a hedgehog pathway inhibitor or for whom a hedgehog pathway inhibitor is inappropriate. When cemiplimab was used as second-line therapy for locally advanced BCC (e.g. following development of resistance to hedgehog inhibitors), an ORR of 31% was observed 100 .
