Clinical features The clinical presentation of a mixed tumor is indistinctive. The lesions present as cutaneous papulonodules that can be misconstrued as cysts ( Fig. 111.9 ). Involvement of the head and neck is common and lesions may also develop on the trunk or within axillary or genital skin. Pathology Mixed tumor presents pathologically as a well-circumscribed nodule that resides within the deep reticular dermis or subcutis. Its biphasic morphology includes epithelial structures encompassed by ample varied stroma 22 . There is always a prominent collagenous component to the stroma, but myxoid and adipocytic zones can also be found. Despite its name, stromal hyaline cartilage is found in less than half of all chondroid syringomata. The epithelial component of a mixed tumor displays two primary patterns. Most mixed tumors demonstrate large inter-anastomosing and branching tubules lined by two cell layers – columnar cells with decapitation secretion at the luminal border and cuboidal cells periph- erally; this configuration has been dubbed apocrine mixed tumor 25 ( Fig. 111.10 ). Less commonly, mixed tumors show an epithelial component that includes many small, rounded, cuticulated ducts ( Fig. 111.11 ). Such lesions have been interpreted by some as eccrine. Rather, it seems likely that all mixed tumors are hamartomas of folliculo­sebaceous-apocrine lineage and that the configuration of the epithelial component can vary. The cylindromatosis gene ( CYLD ), whose protein product functions as a tumor suppressor, underlies epithelioma adenoides cysticum. CYLD encodes a deubiquitinating enzyme that impedes the nuclear factor (NF)- κ B and c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) pathways 28 . Specifically, missense mutations lead to amino acid substi- tutions within the ubiquitin (Ub)-specific protease (USP) domain of the CYLD protein in patients with multiple familial trichoepitheliomas. Epithelioma adenoides cysticum can be cosmetically troublesome and is associated with a risk of secondary BCCs and parotid gland neoplasms 29 . Patients can also develop cylindromas and spiradenomas (see Fig. 111.5 ). The molecular features of sporadic trichoepitheliomas are largely unknown, with occasional tumors displaying somatic mutations in PTCH1 (inacti- vating) or CTNNB1 (activating), which have been described primarily in BCCs and pilomatricomas, respectively. Lesions described historically as trichoblastomas were often larger and deeper than simple trichoepitheliomas. Pathology All trichoepitheliomas and trichoblastomas have in common the archi- tectural attributes of a benign neoplasm, namely: relative symmetry, circumscription, and a lack of substantial cytologic atypicality. In addition, all are linked by a prominence of follicular germinative cells with enveloping fibrocytic stroma that varies in degree 27,30 . In classic trichoepithelioma, the fibrocytic stroma is conspicuous and constitutes as much as half of the cellularity of the lesion in a given cross-section. In other lesions that simulate BCC, follicular germinative cells may be arrayed as either small or large nodules with only scant intervening sclerotic stroma. The coarse fibrous stroma typically maintains tightly adherent contact to the lesional follicular germinative cells 30 . This is in distinct contrast to the pattern of BCC, in which clefts between basaloid cells and stromal elements often serve as a diagnostic clue. In classic trichoepithelioma, follicular germinative cells are often disposed as small clusters or as reticulate and cribriform cords ( Fig. 111.13 ). There are usually foci of pronounced bulbar differenti- ation, emulating the follicular bulb and papilla; these structures have been termed papillary mesenchymal bodies 30,31 . Classic trichoepithe- lioma does not typically show follicular germinative differentiation exclusively. There may be tiny collections of mature sebocytes, reflecting concurrent sebaceous differentiation, and (apocrine) ductal differentiation may also be noted. Treatment Trichoblastoma is benign and provokes no imperative for surgical treatment. Multiple facial trichoepitheliomas can be cosmetically disabling and many affected patients desire some type of inter- vention. Longitudinal evaluation for the possibility of secondary BCC is warranted 29 . Because of the number of lesions, conventional excision is not indicated. Other ablative approaches, including laser or electrosurgical destruction, have been employed with some success 36 . Partial responses with topical sirolimus (1% cream; 0.2% gel), topical imiquimod (5% cream), or oral vismodegib, either alone or in combi- nation with CO 2 laser, have been described in case reports or small series 37 . Desmoplastic trichoepithelioma (desmoplastic trichoblastoma) Introduction Originally termed sclerosing epithelial hamartoma , desmoplastic tricho- epithelioma represents a variant of trichoblastoma with exaggerated stromal sclerosis (desmoplasia) 38 . It can easily be misinterpreted as morpheaform BCC by the uninitiated. Clinical features Desmoplastic trichoepithelioma commonly presents as a firm skin- colored to erythematous annular plaque with a central dell. The cheek of a woman represents a stereotypical context 38 . Most examples do not exceed 1 cm in diameter. Nearly all desmoplastic trichoepitheliomas are solitary. Multiplicity is a rarity. Pathology Desmoplastic trichoepitheliomas are composed of cords of basaloid cells, often two cells wide, arrayed interstitially amongst coarsened collagen bundles ( Fig. 111.14 ) 27,38 . The lesions are relatively circum- scribed and are often confined to the upper two-thirds of the reticular dermis, although this is difficult to appreciate in biopsies en parte . Small cystic foci of isthmic or infundibular keratinization may be present, and if these cystic spaces are predominant, the designation trichoadenoma is apt (see below). The cornifying cysts can rupture and elicit a granulo- matous reaction, and small secondary foci of calcification may also be identified 27,38 . Neoplasms and Proliferations with Matrical Differentiation Pilomatricoma (pilomatrixoma, trichomatrioma, calcifying epithelioma) Introduction Pilomatricoma is a benign neoplasm or cyst typified by follicular matrical cornification. It has been demonstrated that activating mutations in CTNNB1 , the gene that encodes β -catenin, are generally present in matrical neoplasms, including pilomatricomas 39 . β -catenin is a component of a key signaling pathway that influences cell differen- tiation and proliferation (see Ch. 55 ). Pilomatricomas also commonly demonstrate trisomy 18 40 . Some patients with multiple familial pilomatricomas have germline missense gain-of-function mutations in PLCD1 . Clinical features Pilomatricoma usually presents as a solitary skin-colored, yellow, or bluish papule or nodule ( Fig. 111.15 ). Rarely, multiple lesions are evident, sometimes in association with myotonic dystrophy, Turner syndrome, Rubinstein–Taybi syndrome, or familial adenomatosis polyposis-related syndromes including Gardner syndrome (when cystic) 41 . Firmness is typical and reflects secondary calcification as well as accompanying fibrosis and granulomatous inflammation. Some lesions are “rock-hard” and plate-like on palpation. An angulated shape can be appreciated by stretching the overlying skin (“tent sign”). Although pilomatricomas may develop on any hair-bearing surface, the majority occur on the head or upper trunk 42 . Most tumors appear during childhood and adolescence, but pilomatricomas may develop at any age and can simulate BCC, clinically or microscopically, especially in later adulthood. In rats and humans, pilomatricomas have been observed in association with vismodegib administration. Courtesy Adnexal Neoplasms Pathology Histopathologically, an early pilomatricoma frequently presents as a cyst with central matrical cornification. The cyst wall consists of basaloid matrical cells that show an abrupt transition to central eosin- ophilic, cornified matrical cells in which barely discernible nuclear outlines remain ( Fig. 111.16 ). Sometimes, pink trichohyalin granules, illustrative of matrical cornification, are identifiable at the transition point. The central anucleate cornified cells are commonly referred to as ghost or shadow cells. In fully developed pilomatricomas, a cystic configuration is commonly lost. Solid collections of basaloid matrical cells and matrical corneocytes are present in varying degrees. The cornified matrical cells elicit considerable fibrosis and a secondary granulo- matous infiltrate, which can become predominant in longstanding lesions. Matrical cells have a proliferative capacity as high as any human tissue and can display numerous cells in mitosis. The desig- nation proliferating pilomatricoma refers to a pilomatricoma with a high mitotic index. At times, such lesions can be misinterpreted as carcinoma 43 , but in contrast to pilomatrical carcinomas, they lack an infiltrative growth pattern and marked tumor necrosis. In late lesions, basaloid matrical cells may be lacking. An involutional pilomatricoma at times can present with only a few shadow cells buried in a larger fibrosing granulomatous reaction. Calcification, ossification, and occasionally transepidermal elimination also ensue in late lesions. By immunohistochemistry, specific nuclear expression of β -catenin is found in the basaloid cells, when they are present. Treatment Pilomatricoma is a benign lesion that is usually treated by simple enucleation. A pilomatricoma may recur after limited excision. If multiple recurrences are observed, complete excision (with negative margins) should be performed to exclude pilomatrical carcinoma. Treatment Pilomatricoma is a benign lesion that is usually treated by simple enucleation. A pilomatricoma may recur after limited excision. If multiple recurrences are observed, complete excision (with negative margins) should be performed to exclude pilomatrical carcinoma. Pilomatrical carcinoma Introduction Pilomatrical (matrical) carcinoma is an uncommon malignancy that exhibits matrical cornification, much like pilomatricoma 44 . Mutations in CTNNB1 (encodes β -catenin) are common in matrical carcinomas 39 . This suggests a partial common pathogenesis for pilomatricoma and matrical carcinoma. Although on a practical basis no clear association exists, there is a theoretical risk for the possibility of matrical carcinoma developing from conventional pilomatricoma. Clinical features Matrical carcinoma is typically a disease of adulthood. Lesions develop on the head and neck, often in the retroauricular area. Although a patho- genic link with ultraviolet irradiation has not been established, many matrical carcinomas develop within severely sun-damaged skin. If a diagnosis of matrical carcinoma is offered in a child or young adult at an age when the diagnosis is improbable, the case should be reassessed for the possibility of pilomatricoma. Pathology Much like pilomatricoma, matrical carcinomas include both basaloid matrical cells and anucleate matrical corneocytes. In contrast to pilomatricoma, the matrical carcinoma cells usually display nuclear pleomorphism. An infiltrative configuration or poor circumscription is usually apparent, especially in an excisional biopsy. Tumor necrosis is commonly present. There may be considerable squamous cornifi- cation as well, and parts of a given lesion may resemble conventional squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). Matrical carcinoma should be distinguished microscopically from BCC with matrical differentiation 45 . The latter entity represents an otherwise conventional BCC in which small foci of matrical cornifi- cation are identifiable. The clinical behavior of this variant is thought to be identical to that of conventional BCC. As in pilomatricomas, nuclear expression of β -catenin is seen in the basaloid cells of matrical carci- nomas, as well as in a relevant proportion of BCCs. Thus, negative staining of basaloid cells points to a BCC. Treatment Matrical carcinoma is a low-grade form of adnexal carcinoma that poses some risk for metastasis, although the risk is believed to be low 44 . The variant desmoplastic tricholemmoma is especially common in this context 49 . Both sporadic and nevus sebaceus-associated tricholemmomas often contain HRAS mutations. Multiple tricholemmomas typically present on facial or genital skin. Multiple tricholemmomas are a common manifestation of Cowden syndrome/PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome (see Ch. 63 & Fig. 111.5 ) 46,50 . Loss of PTEN expression within a tricholemmoma, as assessed by immuno- histochemistry, is suggestive that the patient has Cowden syndrome 52 . Pathology Microscopically, tricholemmomas present as small circumscribed lobular proliferations composed of pallid, glycogen-containing outer root sheath cells. There is often a broad connection to the surface epidermis ( Fig. 111.17 ) 46,48,50 . A papillated surface is common, and there may be verrucous hyperplasia with hypergranulosis, thereby simulating the pattern of a verruca in a superficial biopsy. Squamous eddies are not uncommon. There is a palisade of small, compact basal keratinocytes at the periphery of a lesional lobule, and a flanking thickened basement membrane that is PAS-D (periodic acid Schiff with diastase)-positive is commonly present. Outer root sheath differentiation can also be recog- nized through use of CD34 immunostaining. In desmoplastic tricholemmoma, small central angular clusters of outer root sheath cells are arrayed in an infiltrative pattern with enveloping sclerotic stroma. This creates a configuration that at times simulates carcinoma 49,53 . Most commonly, a desmoplastic focus is accompanied or surrounded by areas of conventional tricholemmoma that serve as the basis for accurate interpretation, but the diagnosis can be deceptive in partial or superficial biopsies. Treatment Tricholemmoma is a benign adnexal neoplasm with limited prolif- erative capacity. After recognition by biopsy, no further treatment is needed unless there is uncertainty regarding the diagnosis. If there is a desire for ablation, cryotherapy, electrosurgical destruction, shave, curettage, or excision may be employed. Tricholemmal (trichilemmal) carcinoma This malignant analogue of tricholemmoma represents an invasive lesion composed in part of glycogen-containing clear cells, similar to cells of the follicular outer sheath. If a thickened, PAS-positive, prominent basement membrane can be identified peripheral to areas of clear cell change, it is probably of considerable diagnostic significance. CD34 immunopositivity may also be of potential diagnostic value. Many of these carcinomas show accompanying keratinization and thus there is considerable overlap with lesions that have been pigeonholed as clear cell SCC. Treatment Tricholemmal carcinoma represents a carcinoma with limited metastatic potential. These lesions are probably best considered equiv- alent to SCC and treated as such. Neoplasms and Proliferations with Superficial Follicular (Infundibular and Isthmic) Differentiation Tumor of follicular infundibulum (infundibuloma; isthmicoma) Introduction This benign lesion is commonly known as tumor of follicular infun- dibulum (TFI) or infundibuloma , but the designation isthmicoma is more apt, as the proliferation primarily shows follicular isthmic differentiation. Clinical features TFI prototypically presents clinically as a subtle macule, thin papule, or plaque 54,55 . Lesions are skin-colored or sometimes slightly hypopigmented and may appear slightly atrophic 54 . Many examples are diagnosed incidentally within skin cancer excision specimens where no known clinical lesion was even identifiable. TFI may occur in multiplicity ( Fig. 111.18A ) and assume a reticulated pattern; patients with this presentation may defy diagnosis for a time because of the subtlety of both the clinical and the microscopic findings 54–56 . Patients with multiple atrophic-appearing TFI may display a clinical pattern reminiscent of disseminated superficial porokera- tosis or multiple actinic keratoses. TFI is rarely present in Cowden syndrome. Pathology TFI consists of a plate-like proliferation of eosinophilic isthmic kerati- nocytes arrayed in reticulate fashion in the superficial dermis, in broad, but intermittent, continuity with both the surface epidermis and extant follicular structures 54 . Most of the constituent keratino- cytes have cytoplasm similar to keratinocytes of the follicular isthmus, follicles in catagen phase, or the cells of an isthmic (pilar) cyst ( Fig. 111.18B ). The keratinocytes are paler than those of the surface epidermis, and often a few scattered dyskeratotic keratinocytes are present. Some lesions will display tricholemmal foci in which pallid keratinocytes or a thickened basement membrane can be found, and occasionally a hybrid of TFI and tricholemmoma may be encountered. Additionally, small buds of follicular germinative cells may jut from the undersurface of a TFI. Rarely, small clusters of sebocytes may be found within TFI 57 . Sebaceous or apocrine ducts have also been documented 56 . Treatment TFI is a benign adnexal proliferation with negligible proliferative capacity. Adnexal Neoplasms Trichoadenoma (trichoadenoma of Nikolowski) Introduction The term trichoadenoma is a misnomer, as there are no adenomas of follicular lineage since the hair follicle is not a structure that exhibits glandular differentiation. Trichoadenoma represents a benign follicular neoplasm with sclerotic stroma that consists largely of small cystic spaces that exhibit infundibular and isthmic differentiation 58 . Clinical features The clinical presentation of trichoadenoma is not distinctive. The neoplasm presents as a skin-colored papule or small plaque. Pathology Trichoadenoma is usually positioned in the superficial dermis. Cornifying cysts with infundibular or isthmic keratinization comprise the bulk of the proliferation ( Fig. 111.19 ) 58 . The sclerotic stroma is often accompanied by thin strands of basaloid cells, similar to the cords observed in desmoplastic trichoepithelioma. Trichoadenoma and desmoplastic trichoepithelioma have many overlapping histopathologic features, and, in their “pure” forms, likely represent opposite poles of the spectrum of the same entity. Treatment Trichoadenoma is a benign adnexal neoplasm with negligible prolif- erative capacity. No further treatment is necessary unless the patient desires removal. This term describes a group of nodular/cystic neoplasms characterized microscopically by abrupt keratinization akin to that of the follicular isthmus or in a follicle in catagen phase 59 . In the past, it was known that PPT could simulate SCC microscopically, but the entity was generally regarded as a benign process, although it was recognized that, occasionally, locally destructive behavior could occur 59 . Recently, this concept has been called into question, and a proposal has been issued that PFCN represents a mix of benign and malignant neoplasms grouped together under one rubric 27 . The proposal further iterates that a benign PFCN should be designated as proliferating follicular-cystic acanthoma (PFCA), while a malignant PFCN should be designated as proliferating follicular-cystic carcinoma (PFCC). As some examples of PFCN share features with carcinoma, including clinical characteristics such as locally destructive behavior, microscopic charac- teristics such as nuclear atypicality, and molecular characteristics such as aberrations in ploidy, this proposal seems diagnostically practical 60,61 . Of note, an activating PIK3CA mutation was detected in a metastatic PFCC 61a . Clinical features PPT presents as a nodule, usually no more than a few centimeters in size, although there have been reports of lesions exceeding 20 cm in diameter. The lesions can develop in men but a female predominance is seen in most series. Roughly 90% of cases arise in the scalp, probably as a reflection of the density of follicles at that locale. The prototypical presentation is as a nodule on the scalp of an elderly woman. The tumors are usually well circumscribed but may be multinodular. Their circumscription is reflected in smooth borders and the fact that lesions generally shell out from adjacent tissues during surgical excision. Pathology PPT consists of a large and/or deep nodule that resides in the dermis or subcutis 59 . Because of its large size, the laboratory commonly receives fragmented specimens. Both solid and cystic patterns are usually evident at low magnification, with cystic areas exhibiting the pattern of an isthmic (pilar) cyst ( Fig. 111.20 ). The constituent keratinocytes are mostly isthmic keratinocytes with dense eosinophilic cytoplasm, and centrally there is an abrupt transition to compact keratin with little intervening granular layer. NEOPLASMS OF THE SKIN The degree of cytologic atypicality varies among lesions and amongst different areas of a given lesion. Commonly, the neoplastic cells contain enlarged vesicular nuclei with prominent nucleoli and some degree of nuclear hyperchromasia; mitotic figures are usually identified, but overt anaplasia is usually not present. Since some examples of PPT represent low-grade forms of carcinoma, tumors with marked cytologic atypi- cality, extensive necrosis, a lack of circumscription, or extraordinary numbers of mitotic figures warrant designation as PFCC 60 . Treatment As noted, some examples of PPT may represent carcinoma. If a lesion has been enucleated in its entirety or near entirety, is circumscribed, and lacks substantial cytologic atypia, it can be interpreted as PFCA and additional surgical therapy is not necessary. If a given lesion lacks circumscription, shows substantial cytologic atypia or necrosis, or has been sampled en parte , then complete excision is warranted, as PFCC remains a concern. text: DIFFERENTIATION Sebaceous gland hyperplasia Introduction Sebaceous gland hyperplasia (SGH) does not represent a true neoplasm. It represents benign enlargement of sebaceous glands. Numerous lesions can develop following systemic administration of immunosup- pressive medications, in particular calcineurin inhibitors. Clinical features SGH is relatively common and presents with one or multiple yellowish, occasionally telangiectatic papules, usually on the central or upper face and sometimes on the upper trunk ( Fig. 111.21 ). Commonly, the clinical lesions display a central dell that corresponds to a central follicular infundibular ostium. Beaded lines represent a unique expression of SGH in which a linear array of hyperplastic sebaceous glands is present in the vicinity of the clavicle or on the neck 62 . Biopsy is occasionally indicated to exclude BCC, but the dermoscopic findings of a crown of blood vessels, rather than arborizing vessels, assist in the diagnosis (see Ch. 0 ). Pathology The sebaceous gland in SGH shows normal morphology, with a thin rim of seboblasts surrounding the remainder of the gland, composed of mature sebocytes. The enlarged sebaceous lobules usually circumferen- tially surround a central infundibulum. Treatment If treatment is desired, lesions can be removed or diminished by shave, light electrosurgical destruction, cryotherapy, or laser ablation 63 . Long-term topical retinoid application may be beneficial. A short course of oral isotretinoin has been utilized for patients with extensive or disfiguring lesions. Commonly, the term sebaceous adenoma has been applied to superficial benign sebaceous neoplasms with a predominance of mature sebocytes, while sebaceous epithelioma and sebaceoma have been applied to sebaceous neoplasms with a predominance of seboblasts. The dated term sebaceous epithelioma is inherently confusing, as the diagnosis has been utilized differently by various authorities. To some, a sebaceous epithelioma represents a low-grade form of sebaceous carcinoma or BCC with sebaceous differentiation. Others have utilized the term to characterize sebaceoma or sebaceous proliferations of uncertain potential. We believe that the designation sebaceous epithe- lioma should be abandoned. Adnexal Neoplasms Clinical features Sebaceous adenomas present clinically as papules or nodules, usually less than a centimeter in diameter, distributed on the head or neck and sometimes on the upper trunk. The lesions are not clinically distinctive except when there is a yellowish color, which is often not apparent. Superficial sebaceous adenomas are usually relatively small and papular, while sebaceomas may present as a deep nodule 64,65 . Multiple sebaceous neoplasms, especially cystic ones, may be a presenting sign of the Muir–Torre syndrome (MTS; see Table 63.5 ), in which patients can also develop multiple keratoacanthomas and visceral carcinomas, especially colonic adenocarcinoma 66,67 . Sebaceous neoplasms with a keratoacanthoma-like pattern point to the diagnosis of MTS (see below). Pathology Conventional sebaceous adenoma is usually captured in continuity with the surface epidermis and is relatively small and circumscribed. The relative proportions of basaloid seboblastic cells and mature sebocytic cells varies, but sebocytes usually predominate. Seboblasts comprise a thin multilayer of cells at the periphery of each lobule. Mitotic figures can be found in seboblasts but are not conspicuous. Necrosis is not typically evident in an adenoma unless the lesion has been traumatized. Significant necrosis, whether of single cells or en masse , raises concern for the possibility of carcinoma. Seboblasts predominate in sebaceoma and sebocytic differentiation may be only focal, yielding a microscopic pattern not unlike a large nodular trichoblastoma ( Fig. 111.22 ). If sebaceous differentiation is only focal, then epithelial membrane antigen (EMA) or adipophilin immunoperoxidase staining can be considered as a diagnostic supplement. EMA labels mature sebocytes in the normal sebaceous gland, while adipophilin labels multivacuolated lipid-containing cells. Use of immunohistochemistry to assess for loss of expression of mismatch repair proteins encoded by MTS-associated genes, e.g. MSH2, MSH6, MLH1, and PMS2, has been reported to be an effective screening technique 68 . However, it should be noted that loss of expression, as detected by immunohistochemistry, does not necessarily reflect underlying germline mutations. Occasionally, mutations can occur in sporadic neoplasms 69 . Additionally, protein expression can sometimes be detected within tumors in patients who actually harbor a germline mutation in the gene encoding that particular protein; this is usually due to the presence of a protein that, despite being dysfunctional, can react with the antibody utilized for the test 68 . For these reasons, assessment for loss of expression of a mismatch repair protein is most helpful as a screening technique for MTS, but, if found, is not fully diagnostic, and confirmatory genetic testing should be considered after assessing risk for MTS (see Table 63.5 ). In the same context, assessment of microsat- ellite instability may also serve as a screening technique. Treatment Once a definite microscopic diagnosis has been achieved, no further treatment is obligatory. It is often difficult to establish the circum- scription of lesions captured in superficial or partial biopsies. Complete excision of such lesions is appropriate to exclude the possibility of BCC with sebaceous differentiation or sebaceous carcinoma. Deeply situated lesions of MTS may be prone to rapid growth. Sebaceous carcinoma Introduction The term sebaceous carcinoma designates an adenocarcinoma with sebaceous differentiation. By historical convention, these carcinomas have been separated into ocular and extraocular types. Originally, periorbital sebaceous carcinomas were thought to hold a graver prognosis, but more recent data suggest that tumors in this location have a similar overall survival rate as sebaceous carcinomas arising elsewhere 70 . Clinical features The clinical presentation of sebaceous carcinoma is not distinctive. Typical clinical lesions include erythematous nodules or plaques that may be ulcerated or crusted and only occasionally display yellowish coloration. More commonly, the lesions display an erythematous or pearly morphology that is indistinguishable from common forms of keratinocyte carcinoma. Early in presentation, ocular lesions are very commonly misdiagnosed as blepharitis or ocular rosacea. Sebaceous carcinomas commonly develop in the periorbital area but also occur elsewhere on the head and neck and less commonly on the trunk. Carcinomas from the trunk often display a nodular pattern, and superficial biopsies from such lesions may be deceptive and can be misinterpreted 70 . Sebaceous carcinoma can occur in patients with Muir–Torre syndrome (MTS), but the identification of a sebaceous carcinoma alone is not sufficient to diagnose the syndrome 66 . However, any unusual sebaceous neoplasm is probably sufficient provocation for consideration of the disease (see Table 63.5 ). Pathology Like many malignancies, sebaceous carcinoma often exhibits asymmetry, a lack of circumscription, and areas with an infiltrative pattern. In nodular sebaceous carcinoma, cells are arrayed as large nests and lobules. In infiltrative sebaceous carcinomas, jagged nests and thin strands are found. Sebaceous carcinoma can involve the surface epidermis or conjunctiva in a pagetoid pattern, especially in ocular lesions 71,72 . This can be confused with Bowen disease or melanoma. The degree of sebaceous differentiation in sebaceous carcinoma varies greatly, as does the degree of nuclear atypicality ( Fig. 111.23 ). The degree of sebaceous differentiation in sebaceous carcinoma varies greatly, as does the degree of nuclear atypicality ( Fig. 111.23 ). Some carcinomas display obvious sebocytic differentiation, while other examples may be largely seboblastic or undifferentiated in appearance. Differentiation from sebaceous adenoma may be difficult, but loss of expression of bcl-2 and p21 as well as higher p53 and Ki-67 expression represent useful immunohistochemical markers that point to sebaceous carcinoma. Recently, it has been shown that TERT promoter mutations are present in a minority of sebaceous carcinomas and absent in sebaceous adenomas 73 . Stains for lipid, such as oil red O or Sudan black, have been utilized in the past as a tool to confirm sebaceous differentiation through labeling of cytoplasmic fat. However, such stains have little routine practical applicability as they require the use of frozen tissue substrate. EMA and adipophilin immunohistochemical staining represent the best supplemental tests for confirmation of sebaceous differentiation. When authentic sebaceous differentiation is present, coarsely vacuolated cytoplasmic positivity can be seen with either stain. Crateriform or cystic sebaceous neoplasms that display a clinical appearance and microscopic architecture reminiscent of keratoacan- thoma are uncommon lesions that probably represent low-grade carci- nomas 66 . Sebaceous neoplasms with a keratoacanthoma-like pattern probably only occur in the context of MTS. eration of both basaloid seboblastic cells and scattered mature sebocytes with coarsely vacuolated cytoplasm (inset). NEOPLASMS OF THE SKIN Treatment Sebaceous carcinoma is an adnexal carcinoma with significant, albeit variable, metastatic potential. The primary treatment remains surgical extirpation, including removal via Mohs micrographic surgery. Although the risk of metastatic disease was formerly believed to be high, particularly for ocular carcinomas, the data contained within many older reports may be skewed by inclusion of carcinomas diagnosed late in their evolution. Extensive disease of the eye has been treated with ocular enucleation, especially when ocular conjunctival involvement was present. The metastatic potential of both superficial sebaceous carcinoma and sebaceous carcinoma with an infiltrative pattern may be limited, although additional study will be necessary to fully establish this as well as the possibility that missense mutations in PCDH15 are associated with metastatic ocular sebaceous carcinoma. NEOPLASMS AND PROLIFERATIONS WITH APOCRINE (OR ECCRINE) DIFFERENTIATION In most textbooks, adnexal neoplasms with glandular and ductular differentiation have been rigorously separated into eccrine and apocrine neoplasms. Commonly, the distinction was based upon enzyme histo- chemistry, an imprecisely applied technique that is no longer available. Discrimination has also been based upon conventional microscopic assessment, a useful but imprecise tool, at least for the distinction of eccrine and apocrine attributes. A few authorities have responded to this difficulty by grouping apocrine and eccrine neoplasms together, in recognition of the fact that it is impos- sible to determine whether a given lesion, such as a given syringoma, is of apocrine or eccrine lineage. In the sections that follow, the traditional categorization as apocrine or eccrine will be maintained, but areas of overlap will be expressly noted. For entities such as syringoma, poroma, and hidradenoma, which can be of either apocrine or eccrine lineage, the presentation will be included in the discussion of apocrine lesions. Benign Neoplasms and Proliferations with Apocrine (or Eccrine) Ductal and Tubular Differentiation Syringoma Introduction Syringoma represents a benign adnexal neoplasm with mostly ductal (syringeal) differentiation. Historically, syringomas have been inter- preted as neoplasms of eccrine lineage 74,75 . The term syringoma can be used to describe neoplasms of either apocrine or eccrine lineage, and it is currently impossible to judge the lineage of any given lesion other than by its context 1,2 . The lesions are removed from women more commonly than men, although it is not clear that this represents treatment bias. There is an increased incidence in Asian populations as well as an associ- ation with Down syndrome. Clear cell syringomas are associated with diabetes mellitus. Syringomas may occur at any site on the body but are prone to occur in the periorbital area, especially the eyelids 77 . Sometimes, lesions involve the upper trunk (favoring the ventral surface) or genital skin 76,78 . Eruptive syringomas most commonly involve the trunk but may involve the extremities, including the palms and soles. Some cases of eruptive syringomas may be familial with autosomal dominant inheritance. Acral syringomas, which are rare, are those that are most clearly of eccrine lineage, as the acini of glabrous (non-hair-bearing) skin are exclusively eccrine 79 . Syringoma-like foci can be found in biopsy specimens of cicatricial alopecias. Although initially thought to represent authentic syringomas and to play a role in pathogenesis 80 , later studies aptly demonstrated that, in fact, these foci represented reactive changes in response to the inflammation and scarring from the cicatricial alopecia. That is, these foci were simply bystanders 81 . Occasionally, syringoma-like changes can also be seen in non-scarring alopecia. The epithelial component of the proliferation is composed of cells with pale or pinkish cytoplasm forming nests and atypical nuclei and ample coarsely vacuolated cytoplasm. Depending upon the exact plane of section, the nests of a syringoma vary in shape, and some nests may assume a morphology that resembles a comma or a tadpole ( Fig. 111.25 ). Typically, half or more of the nests in a given plane of section will show central ductal differentiation. Usually, a syringoma lacks keratinization, although at times super- ficial cornification can be seen. Syringomas also typically lack evidence of follicular differentiation. If either follicular differentiation or keratini- zation is identified, other differential diagnostic possibilities should be strongly considered. The combination of superficial cornification, poor circumscription, and extension into the deep reticular dermis (or subcutis) favors microcystic adnexal carcinoma over syringoma. A lesion with strands of basaloid cells, focal superficial cornification, and focal calci- fication probably represents desmoplastic trichoepithelioma rather than syringoma. If there are only cornifying cysts present and authentic ductal differentiation is lacking, then the most likely diagnosis is trichoadenoma. Treatment Syringoma is a benign adnexal neoplasm with negligible proliferative capacity. After definitive diagnosis, no further surgical intervention is needed unless adnexal carcinoma remains a clinicopathologic consider- ation. Syringomas may be treated with careful application of trichloro- acetic acid, cryotherapy, punch excision or electrosurgical destruction, with variable results. This can be difficult in the common situation in which multiple lesions are present on eyelids. Disseminated lesions can be cosmetically disabling and therapeutically challenging, and laser ablation might be the best choice 82 . Clinical features Poromas usually present as solitary papules, plaques, or nodules ( Fig. 111.26 ) 4 . When sessile vascular plaques surrounded by thin indented moats appear on the palms and soles, an astute dermatologist can strongly suspect the diagnosis. They can appear on any cutaneous surface, where they are less readily identified with specificity. The scalp is another common site, with or without an associated nevus sebaceus 18 . Presumably, poromas arising secondarily within nevus sebaceus represent apocrine poromas. Occasionally, a poroma will be pigmented. Poromas commonly display highly vascularized stroma, and a clinical pattern suggestive of pyogenic granuloma is common, especially in poromas that involve acral skin. Rarely, multiple poromas will develop, either in an acral or in a widespread distribution, a clinical pattern referred to as poromatosis. Poromatosis can occur following chemotherapy and/or radiation therapy. Up to 90% of sporadic poromas contain YAP1 - MAML2 and YAP1- NUTM1 fusion genes that can lead to tumorigenesis presumably via transactivation of the transcription factor TEAD 86 . Less often, WWTR1 - NUTM1 fusions and additional fusions involving NUTM1 are detected. NUT immunohistochemical staining may be used to differentiate poroid neoplasms with NUTM1 fusions from other types of adnexal tumors 86a . Pathology The principal finding in all forms of poroma consists of a circumscribed proliferation of compact cuboidal keratinocytes with small monomor- phous nuclei and scant eosinophilic cytoplasm. Poromas can be wholly intraepidermal, a pattern known historically as hidroacanthoma simplex; can occur in broad continuity with the epidermis (juxta- epidermal poroma; Fig. 111.27 ); or can develop wholly (or nearly so) nests of cells with pale cytoplasm positioned within sclerotic stroma. Some poromas display innumerable foci in which poroid cells form small cuticulated ductal spaces. In other lesions, ducts may be difficult to identify, and a resemblance to seborrheic keratosis may ensue. Poromas may occasionally display tubular (rather than ductal) foci in which a central cuticle is lacking. If such tubular foci are lined by columnar cells with holocrine secretion at the luminal border, a presumptive diagnosis of apocrine poroma can be offered. At times, a poroma may display striking clear cell change. The constituent nuclei in such lesions are small but are surrounded by ample pale cytoplasm. Poromas are an exception to the rule that necrosis en masse is a clue to a malignancy. Curiously, poromas commonly display small collections of cells in coagulation necrosis. In malignant tumors, necrosis is usually a consequence of rapid growth (growth beyond the capacity of perfusion), but this is an unlikely explanation for necrosis in poroma, in which cellular proliferation is low. Hidradenoma Introduction Hidradenoma is a form of benign adnexal neoplasm that is a close relative of poroma but is usually characterized by cells with ample cytoplasm, is never wholly intraepidermal, and does not commonly have a broad-based connection to the epidermis. As has been mentioned, some authorities use the broad designation acrospiroma to refer to both hidradenoma and poroma jointly. Although commonly classified as an eccrine neoplasm, hidradenomas are thought to be of either apocrine or eccrine lineage 74,75 . The majority of hidradenomas show histopatho- logic features suggestive of apocrine lineage 1,89 . In approximately half of hidradenomas, a t(11;19) translocation, resulting in a CRTC1 - MAML2 fusion gene, is present 90,91 . Fusions of CRTC3 - MAML2 or EWSR1 - POU5F1 have also been described. Clinical features Hidradenoma lacks any distinctive clinical attributes. The lesion presents as a solitary dermal or subcutaneous nodule; sometimes, a cystic quality or serous drainage can be detected. Pathology Hidradenomas are mostly dermal neoplasms with a nodular, sharply circumscribed pattern when viewed at low magnification. Some hidrad- enomas may display a juxta-epidermal pattern superficially with multi- focal attachment to the epidermis, much like poroma. Although the stroma of hidradenoma is commonly sclerotic and may contain ectatic vessels, usually the granulation tissue-like quality that typifies the stroma of a poroma is not present. If desmoplastic stroma is conspicuous and exaggerated, the designation desmoplastic hidradenoma is recom- mended. The cells of hidradenoma are large with ample cytoplasm but uniform nuclei, which are generally somewhat larger than the nuclei of poroma. Overt clear cell change (clear cell hidradenoma) is common, as is cystic degeneration (solid-cystic hidradenoma) 92 ( Fig. 111.29 ). Ductal differentiation can be found with scrutiny, although the degree observed may be minimal. Some lesions contain tubules

Benign Neoplasms with Apocrine Differentiation Apocrine adenoma Introduction Any benign neoplasm with apocrine differentiation, including poroma and hidradenoma, could be grouped under the broad roof of this rubric. On a practical basis, only adenomas with conspicuous glandular differentiation are included in this category. Usually, these prolifera- tions exhibit abundant apocrine epithelium and conspicuous decapi- tation secretion, in which part of the cytoplasm pinches off into a lumen. Apocrine adenomas may present with a tubular or papillary microscopic pattern or a combination of the two. Entities within this conglomeration include tubular adenoma, papillary adenoma, syringo- cystadenoma papilliferum , and hidradenoma papilliferum . The latter entity, also known as papillary hidradenoma , is a source of potential semantic confusion with conventional hidradenoma. Papillary hidrad- enoma (hidradenoma papilliferum) is an apocrine adenoma that usually exhibits a pronounced frond-like pattern with apocrine epithelium lining the constituent papillae. In contrast, conventional hidradenoma (acrospiroma) exhibits a mostly solid configuration. Tubular, papillary, or tubulopapillary adenomas with conspicuous apocrine differentiation may develop within the parenchyma or secretory apparatus of the breast. Apocrine adenomas in continuity with the nipple commonly exhibit a tubulopapillary pattern and have been referred to as erosive adenomatosis 95,96 . Adnexal Neoplasms Syringocystadenoma papilliferum presents as a papule or plaque almost exclusively on the head or neck. Syringocystadenomas usually exhibit a crusted surface that may ooze serosanguinous fluid ( Fig. 111.30 ); this is a reflection of the fact that the papillae of a syringocystadenoma are in continuity with the epidermal surface, permitting extrusion of secretory products. Most papillary syringocystadenomas present on the scalp in association with nevus sebaceus (see Fig. 111.7 ) 18,97 . Sporadic forms of syringocystadenoma papilliferum can harbor either BRAF V600E mutations or activating mutations in HRAS (or less often KRAS ), while those that arise within a nevus sebaceus carry the same HRAS mutation as the underlying nevus 17 . Hidradenoma papilliferum usually presents as a smooth dermal or subcutaneous nodule, usually no more than a centimeter in diameter. Most papillary hidradenomas arise on the vulva, but development within skin of the breast, axilla, and inguinal or perianal areas has also been documented 98 . Pathology At low magnification, tubular and papillary adenomas are usually well- circumscribed neoplasms positioned within the dermis, the super- ficial subcutis, or a combination of the two. Adenomas with a tubular pattern are composed mostly of rounded glandular spaces that vary in size and are lined by one or several layers of cuboidal cells with pale cytoplasm and small nuclei. Most spaces have small lumina and some display columnar apocrine cells apically. Papillary adenomas contain conspicuous tufts, with luminal cells that display an apocrine pattern. A combination of tubular and papillary patterns is not uncommon. Papillary syringocystadenoma ( syringocystadenoma papilliferum ) is distinctive for its wide papillary fronds that are in continuity with the surface squamous epithelium ( Fig. 111.31A,B ). Syringocystadenomas are only rarely cystic. The fronds are lined by a bilayer, with basal cuboidal cells and apical columnar apocrine cells, and the cores of fronds virtually always contain a dense infiltrate of lymphocytes and plasma cells ( Fig. 111.31C ). A plasmacytic infiltrate commonly accom- panies neoplasms of apocrine lineage, and thus the mere presence of plasma cells in a given lesion is not sufficient to confirm a diagnosis of syringocystadenoma. At low magnification, papillary hidradenoma ( hidradenoma papil- liferum ) consists of a well-circumscribed nodule within the dermis and usually lacks both a connection to the surface epithelium and the prominent plasmacytic infiltrate of syringocystadenoma papilliferum. Both tubules and papillary fronds are usually present, and broad elongated fronds with delicate fibrous cores are usually identifiable ( Fig. 111.32 ). Both tubules and fronds are usually lined by a bilayer, with basal cuboidal myoepithelial cells and apical apocrine cells, and the apical cells usually display a conspicuous holocrine secretion. At least some of the basal layer cells represent authentic myoepithelial cells with contractile function, and labeling of the myoepithelial layer through immunohistochemical staining for actin filaments can sometimes be of diagnostic value in the distinction from adenocarcinoma, which often lacks a complete myoepithelial layer. Treatment Apocrine adenomas are completely benign lesions. Complete conser- vative excision is curative. Spiradenoma Definition The term spiradenoma connotes a benign adnexal neoplasm that has been historically designated as being of eccrine lineage, although reassessment indicates an apocrine process 1,74,75 . Spiradenoma not uncommonly occurs jointly with cylindroma and both occur jointly with trichoepithelioma/trichoblastoma (see Fig. 111.5 ); the most parsi- monious explanation for this complex juxtaposition is that both spirad- enoma and cylindroma are of folliculosebaceous-apocrine lineage 99 . Both spiradenomas and cylindromas occur jointly with trichoepithe- liomas in the Brooke–Spiegler syndrome that is due to mutations in CYLD , again implying kinship rather than disparate lineage. To date, spiradenoma has never been observed on glabrous (non-hair-bearing) skin. If spiradenoma were truly eccrine, occurrence on the palm or sole would be the rule and not the exception. Clinical features Spiradenoma typically presents as a dermal or subcutaneous papule or nodule in nearly any location; extraordinary lesions may achieve a diameter of several centimeters. Although the nodules may be asymmetrically distributed, each is sharply circumscribed. The nodules are composed of basaloid cells without obvious differentiation, although tubular apocrine foci can be observed on occasion. Upon close scrutiny, individual nodules exhibit a trabecular internal morphology, with compact basophilic cells lining the borders of trabeculae and larger cells with scant pale cytoplasm within their centers ( Fig. 111.33 ). Usually, small lymphocytes are scattered throughout trabecular areas. Some large (giant) spiradenomas develop cystic areas of degeneration or striking vascular ectasia as secondary events. Compact eosinophilic basement membrane material, arrayed either as tiny PAS-positive droplets or as circumferential bands, can occasionally be found within a spiradenoma, although such deposits are more commonplace in cylindroma. Treatment Spiradenoma is a benign adnexal neoplasm. Despite its basaloid appearance, spiradenoma holds negligible proliferative capacity and recur- rence is uncommon after simple enucleation or conservative excision. Cylindroma Introduction The term cylindroma describes a form of benign adnexal neoplasm that is closely related to spiradenoma. Clinical features Cylindromas can present singly or in multiplicity and are not clini- cally distinctive; thus a biopsy is required for diagnosis. Solitary lesions commonly appear on the head and neck, especially the scalp ( Fig. 111.34 ), but they can also develop within skin of the trunk or genitalia. Multiple cylindromas may coalesce and form giant mosaic plaques on the scalp, which has been pejoratively referred to as a turban tumor 100,101 . The recognition of multiple cylindromas should prompt consideration of the Brooke–Spiegler syndrome or multiple cylindroma- tosis (both autosomal dominant conditions), most examples of which are associated with CYLD mutations. An MYB–NFIB gene fusion, similar to that identified in adenoid cystic carcinoma of the breast or the head and neck, has been described in sporadic cylindromas by some, but not all, investigators. Pathology At low magnification, cylindromas consist of sharply circumscribed nodules arrayed within the dermis and/or subcutis. The nodules are composed of nests of basaloid cells in close apposition, arrayed in a complex pattern that has been likened to a jigsaw puzzle. A rim of densely eosinophilic, PAS-positive basement membrane material commonly envelops the individual nests, and droplets of similar compo- sition are often scattered in the centers of small nests ( Fig. 111.35 ). Foci of ductular and apocrine tubular differentiation can sometimes be found but are inconspicuous. Treatment Cylindroma is a benign adnexal proliferation. Despite its basaloid appearance, cylindroma holds negligible proliferative capacity and recurrence is uncommon after complete excision. Adnexal carcinomas can develop de novo or they can arise in association with extant benign adnexal neoplasms. Going forward, correct designations such as porocarcinoma and spiradenocarcinoma should be employed while the oxymoronic designations malignant poroma and malignant spiradenoma should be eschewed 2 . For certain types of adnexal carcinoma, such as spiradenocarcinoma or cylindrocarcinoma, the adenocarcinomas that develop from the benign neoplasm often lack a decisive pattern of differentiation and may only be specifically diagnosable through recognition of a remnant of the residual benign lesion. A spiradenocarcinoma in the absence of detectable spiradenoma will likely only be recognizable as poorly differ- entiated adenocarcinoma. Some forms of adnexal adenocarcinoma, such as porocarcinoma, display distinctive differentiation that is recog- nizable in a de novo lesion or in a carcinoma that developed within an existent tumor. Clinical features In general, the presentation of adnexal adenocarcinomas is not distinctive. Patients who develop adnexal carcinoma within an existent benign neoplasm often relate a history of recent rapid (or explosive) enlargement of a previously stable, longstanding plaque or nodule ( Fig. 111.36 ). Ulceration and bleeding are common associated findings. Adnexal adenocarcinoma presents as a plaque or nodule, and biopsy and microscopy are required for diagnosis. Perhaps the most is known about the presentation of microcystic adnexal carcinoma (MAC), a low-grade form of adnexal carcinoma (also known as sclerosing sweat duct carcinoma ) that has been carefully evaluated in several large series 102 . MAC typically presents in young or middle-aged adults, most commonly in women and occasionally in children, and lesions slowly enlarge over years and are often misdiag- nosed prior to the time of definitive recognition ( Fig. 111.37 ) 102 . The most common location is the lip. Curiously, a left-sided predominance was noted in the largest series from the US, suggesting that UV light exposure (from driving) might be contributory to carcinogenesis, much like common forms of keratinocyte carcinoma. Pathology All forms of adnexal adenocarcinoma share architectural attributes of malignancy, such as asymmetry, lack of circumscription, and an infil- trative configuration. There is considerable variability in the degree of cytologic atypia, and no standard currently exists for the grading of these neoplasms. Some forms of adnexal carcinoma may display overtly anaplastic cytomorphology while other carcinomas, such as MAC or syringomatous carcinoma, display very subtle nuclear atypia. Syringomatous carcinoma refers to a rare form of carcinoma with distal ductal differentiation 103,104 . It may be of either apocrine or eccrine lineage, and generally lineage cannot be discerned microscopically. Syringomatous carcinoma is characterized by poor circumscription and an infiltrative pattern at low magnification and is composed of small nests and tubules of pale cells with central cuticulated ducts. The degree of nuclear atypia is usually modest, and thus a superficial biopsy, which hides the lack of circumscription, can lead to misinterpre- tation as syringoma. To date, syringomatous carcinoma has only been observed as a de novo malignancy. MAC is a close relative of syringomatous carcinoma that is distinctive for its biphasic or multiphasic differentiation. MAC displays a ductal component identical to that of syringomatous carcinoma coupled with follicular and (sometimes) sebaceous differentiation ( Fig. 111.38 ) 102,105,106 . The follicular component of MAC consists most notably of small cystic (microcystic) foci with follicular infundibular and isthmic keratinization, similar to the superficial follicular keratini- zation observed in desmoplastic trichoepithelioma or trichoadenoma. Areas resembling the follicular outer sheath may also be present. Extensive infiltration of the reticular dermis and perineural extension of tumor cells are common findings. Like poroma, porocarcinoma may be of apocrine or eccrine lineage, and it is generally impossible to determine the exact lineage of any given tumor. The degree of cytologic atypia is variable 104,108 , and some examples of porocarcinoma display little cytologic atypia. Thus, close attention must be paid to other attributes of malignancy and small or partial biopsies may defy exact diagnosis. Porocarcinoma is composed of nests of eosinophilic or pallid cuboidal cells that infiltrate the dermis and perhaps subjacent deeper tissues, and ductal differen- tiation is usually conspicuous ( Fig. 111.39 ). Porocarcinoma may display intraepidermal growth, with a pagetoid or nested pattern within the epidermis in some cases 104,108 . The same molecular alterations observed in poromas have been described in porocarcinoma (see above), together with mutations in TP53, RB1, CDKN2A , and HRAS (see Ch. 107 ). Hidradenocarcinoma may develop de novo or in association with an existent hidradenoma. Hidradenocarcinoma may be of apocrine or eccrine lineage. Cases reported in the older literature were notable for the presence of marked clear cell change, much like clear cell hidradenoma. CRTC1 – MAML2 fusion genes (also seen in up to half of hidradenomas) and amplification of ERBB2 have been described. The differential diagnosis includes cutaneous metastases of mucoepi- dermoid carcinoma of the salivary glands. Spiradenocarcinoma and cylindrocarcinoma are usually poorly differentiated carcinomas that develop de novo or more commonly in association with an existent spiradenoma or cylindroma 109,110 . Both are extremely rare and may come to medical attention late in their course, as their evolution within longstanding stable lesions may contribute to a delay in pursuit of care by the patient. In addition to the molecular alter- ations found in their benign counterparts (with the possible exception of MYB–NFIB gene fusions), loss-of-function TP53 mutations and ALPK1 hotspot mutations have been described in spiradenocarcinoma. Adenoid cystic carcinoma is a type of relatively undifferentiated adnexal carcinoma that resembles micronodular BCC but is generally distinctive for the presence of cribriform (net-like) glandular differ- entiation and a paucity of accompanying myxoid stroma. Primary cutaneous adenoid cystic carcinomas have been misinterpreted as metastatic lesions. Although initially postulated to represent a type of eccrine carcinoma, most authorities believe the entity represents a neoplasm of apocrine lineage. Adenoid cystic carcinoma tends to display considerable local invasiveness and most examples remain confined to the skin over years or even decades, but metastasis to lymph nodes and parenchymal organs can also rarely occur 111 . CD117 immunoposi- tivity has been reported in association with adenoid cystic carcinoma and may be of value in providing additional diagnostic support. Fusion genes involving NF1B , most commonly mutually exclusive MYB – NFIB or MYBL1 – NFIB fusions, have been reported. Primary cutaneous cribriform carcinoma is a partially circumscribed tumor composed of interconnected solid aggregations of basophilic epithelial cells perforated by empty round spaces resulting in a sieve- like or cribriform pattern. Intraluminal bridges are typically present. This tumor has some resemblance to adenoid cystic carcinoma and is often in the differential diagnosis of the latter. Primary cutaneous cribriform carcinoma is a partially circumscribed tumor composed of interconnected solid aggregations of basophilic epithelial cells perforated by empty round spaces resulting in a sieve- like or cribriform pattern. Intraluminal bridges are typically present. This tumor has some resemblance to adenoid cystic carcinoma and is often in the differential diagnosis of the latter. The most reliable micro- scopic findings that favor adenoid cystic carcinoma over cribriform carcinoma include a poorly circumscribed pattern of growth, the presence of basophilic mucinous material within lacunae, and a lack of intraluminal bridges. Mucinous carcinoma , another form of adnexal adenocarcinoma, is characterized by small collections of epithelial cells floating in large pools of mucin. The epithelial cells can sometimes assume a cribriform configuration. An associated in situ component is present in some cases. In our view, the relatively recently described entity endocrine mucin- producing sweat gland carcinoma is a variant of mucinous carcinoma rather than a unique entity. Lastly, extramammary Paget disease may represent extension of an underlying apocrine carcinoma and this entity is discussed in detail in Chapter 73 . Secretory carcinoma of the skin is another form of adnexal adenocar- cinoma 111a . It is characterized by a well-circumscribed proliferation of relatively cytologically bland cells configured as nodules. The nodules contain tubular and microcystic spaces with abundant eosinophilic secre- tions. Foci of more solid growth are also seen. Most cases of secretory carcinoma of the skin are associated with an ETV6-NTRK3 fusion gene 111b . Treatment As a generality, the majority of adnexal adenocarcinomas are low-grade forms of carcinoma that are locally invasive but pose a low risk for metastasis. Many adnexal carcinomas that yield metastatic spread are large or were diagnosed late in their evolution. Surgical extirpation, including removal via Mohs micrographic surgery, remains the primary therapeutic modality. Careful microscopic classification is crucial to developing experience with larger groups of histopathologically homoge- neous lesions in order to assess natural history as well as proper medical and surgical care. The clinical morphology of such lesions is not distinctive. Some lesions are alleged to maintain function of the eccrine apparatus. This can manifest clinically as mucinous discharge or localized hyperhidrosis. Microscopically, the judgment as to whether eccrine glands are normal in number or increased can be difficult, especially in a partial biopsy. The absolute number of eccrine units is increased and the constituent units are of increased size in eccrine nevi. The surrounding stroma may be exclusively fibrotic or may include adipocytes. When the stroma also harbors an increase in small vascular channels, the designation eccrine angiomatous hamartoma can also be applied (see Fig. 39.5 ). These lesions are typically congenital and present as papules or plaques on the hands or feet, with digitate hyperkeratosis ( Fig. 111.40 ). The focal hyperkeratosis corresponds to cornoid lamellae that are often situated within acanthotic acrosyringia. Eccrine acini are qualitatively and quantitatively normal in porokeratotic nevi, suggesting that these lesions should not be classified as a form of adnexal nevus. From the standpoint of nosology, these lesions probably fit best on the spectrum of epidermal nevi. Somatic mosaicism for mutations in GJB2 , which encodes connexin 26 (see Ch. 58 ), has been reported in patients with porokeratotic eccrine ostial and dermal duct nevi. Papillary adenoma and adenocarcinoma Introduction The concept of papillary adenoma was originally put forth under the designation aggressive digital papillary adenoma 112–114 . These neoplasms are uncommon and often occur on acral skin of the fingers, toes, palms and soles, a topographic restriction that suggests that many or most are of eccrine lineage. Papillary adenoma was deemed aggressive because the neoplasms were prone to local recurrence if not completely excised, and some lesions were found to erode bone or infiltrate adjacent soft tissue 113 . Some neoplasms first classified as aggressive papillary adenoma have metastasized 114 , and thus it appears this spectrum includes both adenomas and adenocarcinomas. It has also been suggested that all acral papillary lesions represent adenocar- cinomas, but this seems biologically unlikely. Of note, human papillo- mavirus 42 has recently been described as a tumor driver in aggressive digital papillary adenocarcinoma 115 . Clinical features Papillary adenoma/adenocarcinoma presents as a solitary nodular lesion in an adult of any age. Lesions up to several centimeters in diameter have been observed. There is a male predilection. The lesions may be deeply situated and can impinge upon or erode underlying bone. The favored metastatic route appears to be hematogenous, and metastases involving the lung can occur. Pathology Papillary adenocarcinomas are extraordinarily cellular and display a combination of solid and papillary areas; they are occasionally cystic ( Fig. 111.41 ) 113 . A cribriform pattern can sometimes be found. For carcinomas with a largely cribriform or tubular configuration, the designation tubulopapillary carcinoma can be employed. Irrespective of the architecture of the lesion, its constituent cells have hyperchro- matic nuclei and relatively little cytoplasm, and mitotic figures are usually readily identifiable. text: Thomas Wiesner and Raymond L. Barnhill Benign Melanocytic Neoplasms and Melanotic Lesions 112 SECTION 18 NEOPLASMS OF THE SKIN Key features  Small, uniformly pigmented macules in sun-exposed sites  More common in fair-skinned individuals and more noticeable in summer than in winter  Hyperpigmentation of the basal layer of the epidermis without an increase in melanocyte density Epidemiology and Pathogenesis Ephelides are common in fair-skinned individuals, especially those with red hair, and occur more frequently in women. They first appear in early childhood and usually stabilize in number during adulthood, followed by gradual fading. Ephelides result from an increase in sun-induced melanin synthesis and transport of melanosomes from melanocytes to keratinocytes. Frequent sunburns and variants of the melanocortin-1 receptor gene ( MC1R ) play an important role in the development of ephelides (see Fig. 65.13 ) 1 . Clinical Features Ephelides are limited to sun-exposed sites – primarily the face, upper trunk, and dorsal aspects of the arms. Ephelides are well demarcated, uniformly pigmented, oval to irregular-shaped macules that are usually 1 to 3 mm in size. Depending upon the intensity of sun exposure, ephelides vary in color from light to medium brown. In the summer, they are more conspicuous and then fade during the winter. Ephelides are benign with no potential for malignant transformation. However, higher numbers of ephelides correlate with an increased risk of acquired melanocytic nevi and melanoma 2 . Pathology There is hyperpigmentation of the basal layer of the epidermis without an increase in the number of melanocytes. Compared to adjacent uninvolved epidermis, melanocytes in ephelides are larger and have more branching of dendrites and stronger DOPA positivity, indicating increased activity 3 . Differential Diagnosis Ephelides must be distinguished from simple lentigines, solar lentigines, small café-au-lait macules, and junctional nevi. In addition to being confined to sun-exposed skin, the clinical appearance of ephelides varies depending upon the amount of exposure to UVR ( Table 112.1 ). Café-au-lait macules are usually solitary and larger than ephelides. Treatment If ephelides are a cosmetic concern, sun exposure should be minimized and use of sunscreens, hats, and protective clothing recommended. Topical retinoids and hydroquinone may lighten lesions, but it is difficult to achieve an homogeneous clinical effect and potential side effects (e.g. irritation, dyspigmentation) need to be considered. Pigment- specific lasers represent an additional treatment option, but recurrences are common 4 . Chapter Contents Circumscribed Melanotic Lesions . .

text: . . . . . . . 2002 Recurrent Melanocytic Nevus . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 2003 INTRODUCTION Melanocytic nevi are benign melanocytic neoplasms that most commonly develop within the epidermis or dermis. Histologically, there is a proliferation of melanocytes, both in nests and as solitary cells, with the nests defined as aggregates of three or more melanocytes in direct contact. Melanocytic nevi are usually caused by genomic aberrations (oncogenic mutations or translocations) that activate oncogenes and result in a clonal proliferation of affected melanocytes. The non-nevus melanotic lesions discussed in this chapter can also be tan to dark brown or black in color, but in contrast to melanocytic nevi, they have minimal, if any, increase in melanocyte density. In addition, there is no nesting of melanocytes. Their hyperpigmentation is due to an increase in melanin synthesis and its subsequent transfer to keratinocytes. Other benign and malignant tumors (e.g. seborrheic keratoses, keratinocyte carcinomas) that can also be hyperpigmented are discussed in Chapters 108–111 and 115 . CIRCUMSCRIBED MELANOTIC LESIONS EPHELIDES Synonym:  Freckles NEOPLASMS OF THE SKIN CAFÉ-AU-LAIT MACULES Key features  Well-circumscribed, uniformly light to dark brown macules or patches  Usually 2 to 5 cm in diameter (in adults), but can vary from a few mm to > 20 cm in size  Hyperpigmentation of the basal layer of the epidermis without an increase in melanocyte density  Found in 10%–20% of the normal population, but multiple lesions raise the possibility of an underlying genetic disorder Epidemiology Café-au-lait macules (CALMs) may be present at birth, but usually become clinically apparent during the first year of life. The number of CALMs in an individual can vary from one to more than a dozen. Single CALMs are found in 10% to 20% of the normal population, and up to 1% of healthy children have up to three CALMs, especially African- American children 5 . Pathogenesis The hyperpigmentation observed in CALMs is due to an increase in the melanin content within keratinocytes. While the underlying pathogenesis is not fully understood, UVR-independent mediators that stimulate melanin synthesis and transfer are likely involved (see Ch. 65 ). Clinical Features The term café-au-lait refers to the characteristic homogeneous color of CALMs, reminiscent of coffee with milk. Their color varies from light to dark brown and correlates with the individual’s background consti- tutive pigmentation. CALMs are macular and most have an oval shape with a distinct regular border and uniform color (“typical” CALMs; vary from freckle-like lesions ( ≤ 2 mm) to patches that are > 20 cm in diameter ( Fig. 112.1B ). CALMs enlarge proportionately with overall body growth and then remain stable in size during adulthood. A, Courtesy Julie Benign Melanocytic Neoplasms and Melanotic Lesions CALMs are benign lesions that may be located anywhere on the body, with the exception of the mucous membranes. By dermoscopy, a homogeneous brown patch is seen with perifollicular hypopigmen- tation; a faint reticular pattern may also be present. When multiple CALMs are present, the possibility of an underlying genetic disorder needs to be considered ( Table 61.3 ). Compared with neurofibroma- tosis type 1 (NF1), the CALMs of McCune–Albright syndrome are typically fewer in number, larger, have a midline demarcation, and tend to be unilateral. If present, superimposed lentigines (due to widespread “freckling” extending beyond the axillae) can point to NF1-associated CALMs. Pathology Light microscopy shows a normally configured epidermis with a slight increase in melanin within basilar keratinocytes, but no or a minimal increase in melanocyte number. The adnexal epithelium is spared of hyperpigmentation. Melanin macroglobules (large pigment particles resulting from fusion of autophagosomes containing varying numbers of melanosomes) are often seen in NF-associated CALMs 6 , but are also found in normal skin, isolated CALMs, and other pigmented lesions. Differential Diagnosis Hyperpigmented macules or patches that might be confused with CALMs include pigmentary mosaicism (segmental pigmentation disorder, Blaschko-linear hyperpigmentation), early nevus spilus (before the “speckles” have appeared), Becker melanosis (without obvious hypertrichosis), mastocytoma, mosaic (segmental) neurofibro- matosis, and postinflammatory hyperpigmentation. Smaller lesions may resemble lentigines or acquired melanocytic nevi, while larger lesions may be confused with relatively flat congenital melanocytic nevi. Café-noir spots are hyperpigmented patches that have an even darker hue (relative to background skin) than CALMs and are seen in LEOPARD syndrome (Noonan syndrome with multiple lentigines) and Carney complex. Treatment Topical agents (e.g. hydroquinone) and sun protection have no effect on CALMs. The clinical response to pigment-specific laser therapy is difficult to predict (see Ch. 137 ), and recurrence rates are frequent 4 . In addition to recurrence, risks of laser surgery include transient hyperpig- mentation or hypopigmentation, slight scarring, permanent hyperpig- mentation, and incomplete clearance. BECKER MELANOSIS (NEVUS) Synonyms:  Becker’s nevus  Becker’s pigmentary hamartoma  Nevoid melanosis Key features  Unilateral, hyperpigmented, often hypertrichotic patch or slightly elevated plaque  Most commonly on the anterior or posterior chest of male patients  Onset usually during adolescence Epidemiology Becker melanosis occurs in ~1 in 200 individuals, with no racial predilection. This cutaneous hamartoma is usually unilateral and can initially appear as a light brown patch during late childhood to adoles- cence, followed by an increase in thickness, pigmentation, and hair growth. The latter changes are thought to reflect its androgen depen- dence. While Becker melanosis is often reported to be six times more common in males than in females, a more equal sex distribution has been suggested with androgen-dependent changes leading to a higher incidence of its diagnosis in men 7 . Pathogenesis Postzygotic mutations in ACTB , which encodes beta-actin, have been detected in the majority of Becker nevi and in Becker nevus syndrome. There is some evidence that the ACTB mutations may lead to activation of the Hedgehog signaling pathway in these organoid hamartomas 8 . Other investigators observed an increase in androgen receptors in dermal fibroblasts, and an increased sensitivity to androgens has been postulated 9 . This would provide an explanation for the onset of Becker melanosis during or after puberty, as well as its clinical and histologic manifestations,

Normally, Becker melanosis appears as a single lesion, but multiple lesions have occasionally been observed. The diameter ranges from a few centimeters to > 15 cm, and the most common configuration is block-like, although linear patterns have been reported. The hyperpigmentation varies from uniformly tan to dark brown, and while the lesions are well demarcated, the margins are usually irregular. The center of the lesion may show slight thickening and corrugation of the skin. Hypertrichosis usually develops after the hyperpigmentation, and the hairs become coarser and darker with time (see Fig. 112.2B ). Sometimes, the hypertrichosis is subtle and can only be appreciated by comparison with the contralateral side. The hypertri- chosis and pigmentation may not overlap completely. After its initial appearance, Becker melanosis may enlarge slowly for a year or two but then remains stable in size. The color can fade with time, but hypertri- chosis usually persists. After its initial appearance, Becker melanosis may enlarge slowly for a year or two but then remains stable in size. The color can fade with time, but hypertri- chosis usually persists. Normally, Becker melanosis is asymptomatic, but some patients report pruritus. Firmness to palpation may point to an associated smooth muscle hamartoma. In some patients, perifollicular papules may be a sign of coexistent proliferation of the arrector pili muscle. Acneiform lesions strictly limited to the area of hyperpigmentation have also been reported. Becker melanosis is a benign lesion, and malignant transfor- mation has not been reported. In contrast to the hyperplasia of the ectodermal and mesodermal tissues in Becker melanosis, devel- opmental anomalies that are generally hypoplastic in nature have occasionally been associated with Becker melanosis (often referred to as Becker nevus syndrome). These abnormalities include hypoplasia of the ipsilateral breast, areola, nipple and arm, ipsilateral arm short- ening, lumbar spina bifida, thoracic scoliosis, and pectus carinatum, as well as enlargement of the ipsilateral foot. Accessory scrotum and supernumerary nipples have also been reported. In cases of Becker melanosis with associated abnormalities, the male : female ratio is reversed at 2 : 5 (in comparison to the reported 6 : 1 in those without abnormalities) 10 . Pathology There is a variable degree of acanthosis, hyperkeratosis, and sometimes mild papillomatosis. Regular elongation of the rete ridges and hyperplasia of the pilosebaceous unit may be observed. The melanin content of the keratinocytes is increased, whereas the number of melanocytes is normal or only slightly increased, without nesting. Melanophages may be found in the papillary dermis. A concomitant smooth muscle hamartoma is often, but not invariably, present in the dermis. Differential Diagnosis The differential diagnosis primarily includes CALM, congenital melanocytic nevus, plexiform neurofibroma, and congenital smooth muscle hamartoma. The latter hamartoma tends to be smaller in size, but some authors consider Becker melanosis and congenital smooth muscle hamartoma to be two ends of a clinical spectrum (see Ch. 117 ). By dermoscopy, Becker melanosis, as compared to congenital nevi, is less likely to have focal thickening of network lines, globules, or homogeneous diffuse pigmentation. In an occasional patient, histologic evaluation is required to confirm the diagnosis, especially if the lesion is in an unusual location and there is an associated smooth muscle hamartoma. Treatment Patients with Becker melanosis should be examined for possible soft tissue and bone abnormalities (see above). When there are cosmetic concerns, electrolysis, waxing, camouflage makeup, and laser treat- ments represent therapeutic options. The hypertrichosis is often easier to address than the hyperpigmentation via laser therapy (see Ch. 137 ). As with CALMs, incomplete clearance and recurrences are commonly observed 4 . SOLAR LENTIGINES Synonyms:  Lentigo senilis  Liver spot  Old age spot  Senile freckle Key features  Tan to dark brown or black macules, primarily in sun-exposed sites in middle-aged and older adults  Hyperpigmentation of the basal layer of the epidermis, usually in association with elongation of the rete ridges  No or only a slight increase in the number of melanocytes Solar lentigines are common benign lesions resulting from chronic UVR exposure that results in epidermal hyperplasia. These lesions are found in > 90% of the White population older than 60 years of age ( Fig. 112.3 & Fig. P1 ), but are also seen in Asians, especially on the face (see Ch. 87 ). The clinical differential diagnosis includes macular seborrheic keratosis (oftentimes considered on a spectrum with solar lentigo), pigmented actinic keratosis, pigmented Bowen disease, and lentigo maligna as well as benign pigmented lesions such as lentigo simplex, ephelis, small CALM, and junctional melanocytic nevus. Solar lentigines are discussed in detail in Chapter 109 . Sometimes there is an eruptive form called lentigi- nosis, with or without obvious precipitating factors. After melanocyte activation, lentigo simplex represents the most common histology in matrix biopsies of longitudinal melanonychia (see Ch. 71 ). In darkly pigmented individuals, lentigo simplex is the most common histologic pattern for cutaneous pigmented lesions in acral sites. Oral melanotic macules are found primarily in adults over 40 years of age. The most common sites are the vermilion border, followed by the gingiva, the buccal mucosa, and the palate. From 30% to 60% of melanomas within the oral cavity are preceded by melanosis for several months or years. The labial (lip) melanotic macule usually appears between the second and fourth decades of life and has a strong predi- lection for White women. The incidence of lentiginosis or melanosis of the female genital area is probably higher than reported. For example, 15% of 106 females between the ages of 16 and 42 years had genital “nevi”, and in a study of 100 random autopsies, three cases showed melanosis of the genitalia. Most lesions are found on the labia minora, but they can also occur on the labia majora, the vaginal introitus, the cervix, the periurethral area, and the perineum as well as perianally.
