text: 15% of 106 females between the ages of 16 and 42 years had genital “nevi”, and in a study of 100 random autopsies, three cases showed melanosis of the genitalia. Most lesions are found on the labia minora, but they can also occur on the labia majora, the vaginal introitus, the cervix, the periurethral area, and the perineum as well as perianally. In general, lentiginosis and melanosis of the female genitalia are benign conditions; atypia is uncommon and progression to melanoma has rarely been observed 11 . In a study of 10 000 men between 17 and 25 years, 14% were noted to have “pigmented nevi” of the genitalia 12 . It is uncertain what proportion represented penile lentiginosis or melanosis since no clinical descrip- tions or histologic studies were reported. In the literature, the ages of patients with penile lentiginosis or melanosis range from 15 to 75 years. The glans penis, penile shaft, and perianal region are the most common sites of involvement of anogenital lentiginosis in men. The incidence of primary acquired melanosis (PAM) of the conjunctiva is unknown. It is nearly always unilateral and is subdivided into two groups: PAM with no atypia and PAM with atypia. The latter can progress to melanoma. PAM must be distinguished from conjunc- tival nevi (thicker and more circumscribed) and complexion-associated melanosis (bilateral and around the limbus) as well as melanoma. Pathogenesis Hyperpigmentation of the basilar keratinocytes likely arises from an increased production of melanin and the slightly increased number of singly arranged melanocytes. To date, insights into lentigo formation have not been forthcoming despite the discovery of the genetic bases of several syndromes associated with lentiginosis. In contrast to solar lentigines (see Ch. 109 ), somatic activating mutations in FGFR3 or PIK3CA are absent in lentigo simplex 13 . Some penile lesions have been reported to follow injury, irritation, or PUVA therapy; in women, hormonal factors are thought to play a role. Acral lentigines may be influenced by genetic factors since they are frequently found in darkly pigmented individuals. Clinical Features Lentigines simplex are light brown to black, homogeneously pigmented macules. They are well circumscribed and round or oval, have regular borders, and are usually < 5 mm (often < 3 mm) in diameter. These lentigines can occur anywhere on the body, including palmoplantar skin, without any predilection for sun-exposed sites. Multiple lentigines are present at birth or appear during early infancy and may increase in number during childhood. The lesions are generalized, occurring in both sun-exposed and sun-protected sites, including genitalia, palms, and soles. The Carney complex is an autosomal dominant syndrome charac- terized by multiple lentigines and multiple neoplasias, including: myxomas of the skin, heart (atrial), and breast; psammomatous melanotic schwannomas; epithelioid blue nevi of skin and mucosae; growth hormone-producing pituitary adenomas; and testicular Sertoli cell tumors ( Fig. 112.5A ). Components of the Carney complex have been described previously as the NAME (n evi, a trial myxoma, m yxoid neurofibroma, e phelides) and LAMB ( l entigines, a trial myxoma, m ucocutaneous myxoma, b lue nevi) syndromes. The skin lesions have an acrofacial distribution pattern and favor the perioral region (see Fig. 53.31 ). Mucosal lesions may affect the palate, tongue, buccal mucosa, and conjunctivae. The major differential diagnosis is Laugier–Hunziker syndrome in which there are acromucosal lentigines and longitudinal melanonychia, but no consistent internal manifestations ( Fig. 112.6 ). In partial unilateral lentiginosis , also referred to as segmental lentig- inosis, there is unilateral clustering of lentigines, suggesting a devel- opmental abnormality of melanocytes. The onset is often during childhood. There is no background hyperpigmentation (as in nevus spilus) and the lesion can expand in a wavefront-like manner. Patients with facial lesions may have ocular involvement and CALMs may also be present. Partial unilateral lentiginosis may be associated with mosaic (segmental) NF1 (see Table 61.2 ). Pathology Lentigo simplex is characterized by increased melanin in the basal layer and sometimes even in the upper layers of the epidermis and the stratum corneum. The number of melanocytes in the basal layer is slightly increased, but there are no melanocytic nests. Melanophages and a mild inflammatory infiltrate are often present in the superficial dermis. Lesions on mucous membranes, including the lips, show acanthosis with or without elongation of the rete ridges ( Fig. 112.7 ). Slight melano- cytic hyperplasia is usually observed, but may be absent. Hyperkeratosis, telangiectasia, activated fibroblasts, and large dendritic melanocytes have been described in labial melanotic macules. Ultrastructurally, melanin macroglobules have been observed within the melanocytes, as well as in keratinocytes and melanophages. These are not specific for lentigo simplex since they have been described in other pigmented lesions (see above). Differential Diagnosis The differential diagnosis of a solitary lentigo simplex consists primarily of a junctional melanocytic nevus, a flat form of compound melano- cytic nevus, solar lentigo, and ephelis. In some instances, cutaneous melanoma, pigmented spindle cell nevus, and cutaneous intracorneal hemorrhage might enter into the differential diagnosis. Although there is a continuum from simple lentigo to junctional melanocytic nevus, the former is often smaller than the latter and it may not show distorted skin markings when viewed with side-lighting. Microscopically, histologic findings consistent with dermal melanocytosis can be found in the presacral area of 100% of newborns, irrespective of race 14 . Pathogenesis The blue color in dermal melanocytosis is secondary to melanin- producing melanocytes in the middle to lower dermis. Melanocytes appear in the dermis during the 10th week of gestation and then either migrate into the epidermis or undergo cell death, except for melanocytes in the dermis of the scalp, extensor aspects of the distal extremities, and the sacral area. The latter is the most common site for dermal melanocy- tosis. The bluish coloration results from the Tyndall phenomenon: dermal pigmentation appears blue because of decreased reflectance of light in the longer-wavelength region compared with the surrounding skin. Longer wavelengths, such as red, orange and yellow, are not reflected, compared with the shorter wavelengths of blue and violet, which are reflected. Clinical Features The classic location is the sacrococcygeal and lumbar regions and the buttocks, followed by the back. Dermal melanocytosis may consist of a single or multiple patches and usually involves < 5% of the body surface area. The lesions are macular and have a round, oval, or angulated shape. The size varies from a few to more than 20 cm with the color varying from light blue to dark blue to blue–gray. Extrasacral variants tend to be more persistent, and there is overlap between persistent lesions and the entities adult-onset dermal melanocytoses, nevus of Ito, and patch blue nevus. Extensive dermal melanocytosis should raise the possibility of phakomatosis cesioflammea (type II phakomatosis pigmentovascularis [PPV]) and phakomatosis cesiomarmorata (type V PPV; see Table 104.4 ). When CALMs and satellite congenital melano- cytic nevi reside within areas of dermal melanocytosis, a rim that lacks dermal melanocytes may be seen around each lesion ( Fig. 112.8 ). These melanocytes are DOPA-positive and lie parallel to the epidermis between the collagen bundles without disturbing the normal architecture of the skin. Occasionally, persistent dermal melano- cytosis has the histology of a blue nevus with involvement of the subcutis, muscle, and fascia by melanocytes, but lacks thick collagen bundles. Differential Diagnosis The differential diagnosis of dermal melanocytosis includes nevus of Ota, nevus of Ito, and patch blue nevus. The latter has many names in the literature, including dermal melanocyte hamartoma, acquired dermal melanocytosis, and acquired linear dermal melanocytosis; clearly there is overlap with the rare adult-onset dermal melanocytosis. The clinical differential diagnosis may also include venous malforma- tions or deep infantile hemangiomas and a contusion. Although the distinctive clinical presentation of dermal melanocytosis generally allows easy distinction from these entities, there have been reports of the misdiagnosis of child abuse. Treatment Persistent lesions may be treated with cover-up cosmetics or lasers (see nevus of Ota). Benign Melanocytic Neoplasms and Melanotic Lesions Nevus of Ota Epidemiology Nevus of Ota occurs predominantly in individuals with darker skin phototypes, especially in Asians, but has also been described in White individuals 15 . Approximately 80% of all reported cases have been in women; however, this figure may be somewhat skewed as a result of greater cosmetic concerns in women. In Japan, nevus of Ota is seen in ~0.4%–0.8% of all dermatologic patients. The lesion has two peaks of onset: the first (~50%–60% of all cases) is during infancy (before the age of 1 year), with the majority present at birth, and the second (40%–50%) is around puberty. Although rare familial forms of nevus of Ota have been reported, the condition is generally not considered hereditary. Pathogenesis The blue to blue–gray color in nevus of Ota is due to melanin-producing melanocytes in the dermis. The larger concentration of melanocytes in nevus of Ota in comparison to dermal melanocytosis is thought to indicate a hamartoma. Somatic activating mutations in GNA11 or GNAQ were detected in up to 15% of cases of nevus of Ota, as compared to 65%–75% of blue nevi (primarily GNAQ ) and 80%–85% of primary uveal melanomas 16 . In mice, germline mutations in Gnaq lead to an increase in dermal pigmentation. The possibility of a hormonal influence in women has been raised. Clinical features Nevus of Ota is usually characterized by a confluence of individual macules varying from pinhead-sized to several millimeters in diameter ( Fig. 112.9A ). The shape of the individual macules may be round, oval, or serrated, whereas the overall appearance is that of an irregu- larly demarcated and often mottled patch. The overall size varies from a few centimeters to extensive unilateral and occasionally bilateral involvement. The color varies from shades of brown to gray, blue, black, and purple. The overall size varies from a few centimeters to extensive unilateral and occasionally bilateral involvement. The color varies from shades of brown to gray, blue, black, and purple. Nevus of Ota is usually unilateral and favors the distribution of the first two branches of the trigeminal nerve. The most common sites of involvement are the periorbital area, temple, forehead, malar area, earlobe, pre- and retroauricular regions, nose, and conjunctivae. In approximately two-thirds of patients, the ipsilateral sclera is involved. Rarely, nevus of Ota affects the cornea, iris, fundus oculi, retrobulbar fat, periosteum, retina, and optic nerve. Iris mammillations and glaucoma (~10% of patients) 17 have been reported, but vision is usually not impaired. Other frequent sites of involvement include the tympanum (55%), nasal mucosa (30%), pharynx (25%), and palate (20%). Occasionally, the external auditory canal, mandibular area, lips, neck, and thorax are involved. In 5% to 15% of patients, the lesion is bilateral. Nevus of Ota may extend over time and persists for life. Variations in color intensity have been described, especially in association with periods of hormonal flux such as menstruation, puberty, or menopause. Melanomas arising within nevi of Ota are unusual, with uveal melanomas estimated at 1 in 400 in White individuals and even less often in Asians. Cutaneous melanomas are rare, but typically have presented as new subcutaneous nodules, although other tumors such as atypical cellular blue nevi have also been described 18 . In addition to the uveal tract, primary melanomas of the orbit, chiasma, and meninges have been observed in association with nevus of Ota, as it is one of the entities that can have associated neuromelanosis and meningeal melanocytomas. Of note, BAP1 mutations have been detected in cases that progressed to melanoma, pointing to a role in malignant transformation. Pathology The non-infiltrated areas in nevus of Ota show pigmented, elongated, and dendritic melanocytes scattered between the collagen bundles ( Fig. 112.9B ). In comparison to dermal melanocytosis, the cells are more numerous and located within the upper third of the reticular dermis. Occasionally, cells are found also in the papillary dermis and deep in the subcutaneous fat. Hyperpigmentation of the basal epidermis and an increase in basilar melanocytes may occur. Differential diagnosis The differential diagnosis of nevus of Ota includes dermal melano- cytosis (Mongolian spot), adult-onset dermal melanocytosis, blue nevus (patch or plaque), melasma, partial unilateral lentiginosis (when it involves the face), a nevus spilus that develops blue nevi, venous malformations, and ecchymoses. Dermal melanocytosis differs from nevus of Ota and other dermal melanocytoses due to its location in the lumbosacral region and its spontaneous regression during childhood. Treatment Nevus of Ota and nevus of Ota-like macules have been treated success- fully by Q-switched ruby, alexandrite, and Nd:YAG lasers 4,19 . Although malignant changes are rare in patients with nevus of Ota, patients with eye involvement should be followed more carefully by an ophthalmol- ogist, since the majority of associated melanomas are ocular in origin and some patients develop glaucoma. Suspicious lesions, especially a new subcutaneous nodule, should be biopsied. Any complaint of neuro- logic symptoms requires further investigation. Acquired nevus of Ota-like macules (Hori nevus) are characterized by bilateral, grouped, blue–gray to gray–brown macules of the zygomatic area. Less often, similar lesions are on the forehead, upper outer eyelids, and nose. This entity has been reported primarily in Chinese or Japanese women ranging from 20 to 70 years of age. In contrast to nevus of Ota, the eye and oronasal mucosa are not involved. It is often misdiagnosed as melasma, but the distinction is important as nevus of Ota-like macules can be successfully treated with laser surgery, similar to nevus of Ota. Patch blue nevus overlaps with the rare disorder adult-onset dermal melanocytosis and presents as a diffusely gray–blue area that may have superimposed darker macules. The age of onset and sites of involvement vary, with some lesions having a linear distribution. MELANOCYTIC NEVI The term “nevus” is used to describe a hamartoma (e.g. epidermal nevus, sebaceous nevus) or a proliferation of melanocytes. Melanocytic nevi are defined histologically by nests of melanocytes, with a nest representing an aggregate of three or more melanocytes in direct contact. Melanocytic nevi are usually caused by genomic aberrations (mutations, translocations) that activate oncogenes, resulting in a clonal proliferation of melanocytes ( Table 112.3 ). Genetic syndromes in which patients develop numerous melanocytic nevi are summarized in Table 112.4 . In general, congenital blue nevi are unusual, with most blue nevi arising during childhood or adolescence and up to a quarter first appearing in middle-aged adults. However, ~25% of cellular blue nevi are congenital, and they are more common in women (female : male ratio = 2 : 1). Pathogenesis Blue nevi are benign tumors of dermal melanocytes 20 . During the second half of gestation, dermal melanocytes disappear, but some residual melanin-producing cells remain in the dermis of the scalp, sacral region, and dorsal aspect of the distal extremities. These are the sites where blue nevi most commonly occur. The blue coloration is the result of the Tyndall phenomenon (see above). Blue nevi frequently contain somatic activating mutations in GNAQ (50–60%) or GNA11 (7–15%); less commonly there are mutations in CYSLTR2 (~3%), NRAS (~3%), or BRAF (~1%) and GRM1 fusions (see Clinical Features Common blue nevi are well-circumscribed, dome-shaped papules that are blue, blue–gray, or blue–black in color ( Fig. 112.10A–D ) 15 . They are usually 0.5 to 1.0 cm in diameter, rarely larger. These nevi may occur anywhere, but about 50% are found on the dorsal aspect of the hands and feet, with other common sites the face and scalp. Blue nevi have also been observed in the oral and genital mucosae, cervix, prostate, spermatic cord, and lymph nodes. Over time, hypopigmentation may develop within the center of blue nevi, and an “achromic” variant has been described. Usually, blue nevi are solitary, but they may be multiple, agminated, or arise within a nevus spilus or plaque blue nevus. Concentric, target- like lesions (target blue nevi) have also been described. Dermoscopically, a blue nevus is characterized by homogeneous blue–gray to blue–black pigmentation (see Ch. 0 ). Their surface is often smooth but sometimes irregular. The most common sites are the buttocks, sacrococcygeal area, and scalp, followed by the face and feet. The foci, found either in the marginal sinuses or in the capsule, are usually small and discrete. They may result from passive transport or represent arrested migration from the neural crest. This type of nodal involvement (“benign metas- tasis”) has been described in a minority of the reported cases of cellular blue nevi. Benign Melanocytic Neoplasms and Melanotic Lesions Pathology Common blue nevi are composed of elongated, often slightly wavy melanocytes with long, branching dendrites ( Fig. 112.10E,F ). The melanocytes, with their long axes parallel to the epidermis, lie grouped or in bundles in the upper and mid dermis. Occasionally, they extend into the subcutaneous tissue or approach the epidermis but do not alter it. Most melanocytes are filled with fine melanin granules that obscure their nuclei and extend into their dendrites. Variable numbers of melanin-laden macrophages are also present. The amount of collagen is usually increased, giving the lesion a fibrotic or sclerotic appearance. In the hypopigmented variant, melanin content is minimal centrally 20 . Cellular blue nevi are well-circumscribed, nodular dermal tumors that are larger in diameter and have a higher cellular density than common blue nevi. Most often, well-defined nests of fusiform to ovoid melano- cytes are surrounded by collagen and numerous melanophages (see with the majority of pigment residing in melanophages. Aggregates of spindle cells may be arranged in intersecting bundles extending in various directions, a disposition resembling the storiform pattern of a neurofibroma. In cellular blue nevi, penetration of rounded, well-defined cellular islands into the subcutaneous tissue is frequently noted. Some of the cells may appear atypical, with nuclear pleomor- phism accompanied by multinucleated giant cells, rare mitoses, and inflammatory infiltrates. Lastly, while there are classic histopatho- logic differences between common and cellular blue nevi, overlapping features are seen in some lesions 20 . Atypical cellular blue nevi demonstrate one or more of the following features compared to conventional cellular blue nevi: larger size ( > 1–2 cm), asymmetry, ulceration, infiltrating features, cytologic atypia, mitoses, and necrosis 22 . Such lesions have been associated with lymph node metastases and evolution to frank melanoma. GENETIC SYNDROMES ASSOCIATED WITH NUMEROUS ACQUIRED MELANOCYTIC NEVI Familial atypical mole and melanoma

NEOPLASMS OF THE SKIN Melanoma arising from blue nevus (MBN) refers to a melanoma arising within a pre-existing blue nevus, nearly always the cellular type. Classically, a rapidly growing, large ( > 2 cm) nodule arises on the scalp (followed by the face and trunk) in an adult who is usually > 45 years of age. MBNs are often aggressive, with frequent metastasis to regional lymph nodes and the liver. In addition to the GNAQ or GNA11 mutations in blue nevi, MBN often show additional genomic aberra- tions in BAP1 or SF3B1 23 . Differential Diagnosis The clinical differential diagnosis of a common blue nevus includes traumatic tattoo, vascular lesions including venous lake and angioker- atoma, combined nevus, sclerosing hemangioma, primary or metastatic melanoma, pigmented spindle cell nevus, atypical nevus, pigmented dermatofibroma,

Differential Diagnosis The clinical differential diagnosis of a common blue nevus includes traumatic tattoo, vascular lesions including venous lake and angioker- atoma, combined nevus, sclerosing hemangioma, primary or metastatic melanoma, pigmented spindle cell nevus, atypical nevus, pigmented dermatofibroma, papular pigmented basal cell carcinoma, and glomus tumor. Cellular blue nevi also need to be distinguished from nevus of Ota, when on the face, as well as cutaneous neurocristic hamartoma, a complex proliferation of nevus cells, Schwann cells, and pigmented dendritic and spindled cells. Histologically, an atypical cellular blue nevus needs to be distinguished from MBN. Occasionally, a cutaneous melanoma metastasis may resemble a blue nevus. Treatment Blue nevi that are < 1 cm in diameter, clinically stable, located in a typical anatomic site, and have no atypical features do not require removal. Histologic evaluation should be considered for lesions that appear de novo , are multinodular or plaque-like, or have undergone change. Atypical cellular blue nevi should be resected completely in order to prevent recurrence and because of the risk for malignant trans- formation or metastases. The approach to typical cellular blue nevi varies, but if observation is difficult (e.g. lesions on the scalp), excision can be considered. PIGMENTED EPITHELIOID MELANOCYTOMA Synonyms:  Epithelioid blue nevus  PRKAR1A-inactivated melanocytoma  Animal-type melanoma Key features  Rare tumor that usually presents as a slowly growing pigmented papulonodule  Characterized by inactivation of PRKAR1A Epidemiology and Pathogenesis The term pigmented epithelioid melanocytoma (PEM) encompasses tumors previously referred to as epithelioid blue nevus and “animal- type”, “melanophagic”, or “pigment synthesizing” melanoma. PEMs are rare tumors that occur in both sexes with diverse ethnic backgrounds. The majority of PEMs have a loss of PRKAR1A immuno- reactivity or inactivating mutations in PRKAR1A . The latter lead to activation of protein kinase A catalytic subunits (PRKACA, PRKABA) and induce melanocyte proliferation, differentiation, and pigmentation. Inactivation of PRKAR1A is usually combined with kinase fusions or mutations in genes (e.g. BRAF , NRAS , NF1 , CYSLTR2, GNAQ , GNA11 ) involved in other melanocytic tumors (see Table 112.3 ) 24 . Clinical Features and Pathology PEM presents as a slowly growing pigmented papule or nodule. It usually arises in the second or third decade, with the extremities being the most common site. Although PEMs were first described as a feature of Carney complex (see Table 112.2 ), they also may occur sporadi- cally 25,26 . Histologically, a PEM is composed of pigmented epithelioid melanocytes with large vesicular nuclei. These cells are often admixed with heavily pigmented spindled and dendritic melanocytes as well as melanophages. Cytologic atypia and dermal mitoses may be present. PEMs frequently metastasize to regional lymph nodes but rarely spread extranodally and are almost never fatal. The clinical appearance of a PEM is similar to a cellular blue nevus. Histologically, it needs to be differentiated from primary or metastatic melanoma as well as tumoral melanosis due to complete or almost complete regression of melanoma. COMMON ACQUIRED MELANOCYTIC NEVI Synonyms:  Nevocellular nevus  “Mole” Key features  A junctional nevus is a brown to black macule with melanocytic complexes at the dermoepidermal junction  An intradermal nevus is a skin-colored to light pink or brown papule with complexes of melanocytes in the dermis  A compound nevus is a brown papule with combined histologic features of junctional and intradermal nevi Epidemiology The prevalence of melanocytic nevi depends on age, ethnicity, genetic, and environmental factors. In early childhood, only a few nevi are present, but their number then increases and reaches a peak in the third decade of life; thereafter, nevi disappear with age 27 . There is a period of particularly rapid development of nevi at puberty. A study in Scotland noted that, in the first decade of life, girls had an average of three nevi and boys two nevi. For the peak age interval of 20 to 29 years, women and men had mean nevus counts of 33 and 22, respectively. In the seventh decade of life, women had a mean of 6 nevi and men 4 nevi, reflecting a progressive decline. A

Benign Melanocytic Neoplasms and Melanotic Lesions White individuals generally have greater numbers of nevi than populations with more darkly pigmented skin, e.g. African-Americans and Asians. In White individuals, the number of nevi is highest in those with skin phototype II. Additionally, melanocytic nevi (includes lentigines) on the palms and soles, nail beds, and conjunctivae are more prevalent in Africans and Asians. The mean acral “nevus” count for Africans in Uganda was 11, versus 2 to 8 for African-Americans. Genetic factors also play a role in the prevalence of nevi: increased numbers of nevi have been shown to cluster in families, especially those with familial melanoma. Although an autosomal dominant mode of inheritance has been postulated for clinically atypical nevi in hereditary melanoma families, the pattern of inheritance may be more complex. Environmental factors such as sun exposure influence the development of melanocytic nevi as exemplified by the nevus counts of the outer versus inner arm or the back versus buttocks. However, genetic factors seem to directly determine an individual’s potential for developing melanocytic nevi, and the final expression of this potential is influenced by solar exposure. In addition, individuals appear to inherit different propensities for nevogenesis 27 , e.g. there is a higher correlation of nevus counts in monozygotic twins (r = 0.94) as compared to dizygotic twins (r = 0.60) 28 . Pathogenesis The majority of melanocytic nevi arise from an activation of oncogenes that allows a clonal proliferation of affected melanocytes. In common acquired nevi, the initiating oncogenic event is usually an activating mutation in BRAF (80%) or NRAS (5%). Factors leading to the onset of melanocytic nevi are poorly

In common acquired nevi, the initiating oncogenic event is usually an activating mutation in BRAF (80%) or NRAS (5%). Factors leading to the onset of melanocytic nevi are poorly understood but include the genetic influ- ences alluded to earlier and environmental agents, principally UV exposure ( Table 112.5 ). In genome-wide association studies (GWAS), a correlation was found between the number of melanocytic nevi and certain single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) located near the MTAP , PLA2G6 , IRF4 , and KITLG genes. Clinical Features Melanocytic nevi are well-circumscribed, round to ovoid lesions, generally measuring from 2 to 6 mm in diameter. In general, they are symmetric and have a homogeneous appearance. While some common nevi may display slight asymmetry, the borders are usually regular and well-defined. Junctional nevi are macular lesions with a uniform, medium-to-dark brown color and slight accentuation of skin markings visible with side-lighting ( Fig. 112.12A ). The dermoscopic features of a junctional nevus include a uniform pigment network thinning out towards the periphery (see Table 0.15 ) ( Fig. P2 ). Compound nevi show variable degrees of elevation and in general somewhat lighter shades of brown than do junctional nevi ( Fig. 112.12C ). Dermoscopically, compound nevi are characterized by a globular architecture with multiple round to ovoid globules sometimes forming a cobblestone pattern (see Table 0.15 ). Intradermal nevi are usually more elevated and show lighter shades of brown or even skin-colored tones compared to compound nevi ( Fig. 112.12E ). These nevi can also be pink in color. The dermoscopic features of an intradermal nevus predominantly consist of focal globules or globular-like structures. In addition, pale to whitish structureless areas and fine linear or comma vessels may be present ( Fig. P3 ). In addition to clinical and dermoscopic overlap amongst all three types of nevi, intradermal nevi (and to a lesser degree compound nevi) may be papillomatous with pseudo-horn cysts. Nevi, especially acquired “congenital-appearing” nevi, contain hairs that are coarse and dark compared to those in the surrounding skin. Melanocytic nevi associated with epidermolysis bullosa Distinctive melanocytic nevi termed “epidermolysis bullosa (EB) nevi” or “EB nevi” may develop at the sites of antecedent bullae or erosions primarily in patients with forms of EB that are recessively inherited (see Ch. 32 ) 29 . These nevi can have a strikingly large size (up to 3 cm) as well as asymmetry, border irregularity, dark color, and satellitosis. Their development may be related to repetitive disruption of the basement membrane zone with the promotion of proliferation or dispersion of melanocytes into the blister cavity with their subsequent proliferation in its floor. Although there are no reports of cutaneous melanoma devel- oping at the sites of EB nevi, melanoma can occasionally arise within the setting of EB; thus longitudinal observation is warranted. Melanocytic nevi associated with lichen sclerosus Occasionally, melanocytic nevi develop within areas of genital lichen sclerosus 30 . The lesions are often dark brown to black in color, irregular in outline, and can measure ≥ 6 mm. As a result, the possibility of melanoma is frequently considered clinically, and histologic distinction is not always easy. Differential Diagnosis The differential diagnosis of melanocytic nevi includes the full spectrum of pigmented and skin-colored lesions (see Ch. 0 ). Raised nevi, poten- tially confused with seborrheic keratoses, are less likely to have a verrucoid surface and pseudo-horn cysts and do not have a cerebriform surface when examined by dermoscopy. Both neurofibromas and fibroepi- thelial polyps may be indistinguishable from skin-colored or slightly pigmented, pedunculated intradermal nevi. Their incidence peaks in the third and fourth decades of life. They are more common in individuals with darker skin phototypes. As in common acquired nevi, acral nevi have mutations in BRAF or NRAS in a mutually exclusive pattern. Clinical Features Acral nevi are usually macular or only slightly elevated. They may display a uniform brown or dark brown color, but often have linear stria- tions. The characteristic dermoscopic features of acral nevi are due to the unique anatomy of acral skin. Both the palms and soles have parallel ridges (mountains) and furrows (valleys), with the intraepidermal eccrine ducts passing through the ridges ( Fig. 112.14 ). In acral nevi, the nests of nevus cells are situated around the furrows. The three major dermo- scopic patterns seen in acral nevi are the parallel furrow ( Fig. 112.15 ), the lattice-like ( Fig. P4 ), and the fibrillar pattern ( Table 112.6 ) 33 . Generally, the color is homogeneous and the margins are well defined. The surface topography may be smooth or, in some instances, verrucous. Relatively flat, polypoid, and pedunculated morphologies have also been described. Occasional lesions may have erosions and scale-crust while others may be firm due to sclerosis and resemble dermatofibromas (i.e. desmoplastic) 36 . Telangiectasia is a frequent finding. For highly atypical or histologically ambiguous variants, a margin of ~1 cm is recommended. It is also advisable that patients with atypical lesions have periodic evaluations every 6 to 12 months. Sentinel lymph node biopsy, although controversial, may be considered on a case-by-case basis for clearly atypical lesions with a Breslow depth ≥ 1 mm. However, there is mounting evidence that sentinel lymph node involvement by Spitz tumors is not necessarily analogous to conven- tional metastatic melanoma 38 , as almost all of the cases studied to date have not shown progression of disease beyond the sentinel lymph nodes. Whole-genome sequencing followed by targeted therapy has also been employed. In a patient with unresectable “agminated” Spitz nevi and GOPC-ROS1 fusion, the oral tyrosine kinase inhibitor crizotinib led to improvement. Agminated (grouped) Spitz nevi are characterized by varying numbers of individual, raised nevi occurring in a localized or segmental distri- bution and arising in otherwise clinically normal skin ( Fig. 112.17 ). Some confusion has arisen in the literature as lesions arising within a CALM-like tan background have been referred to as agminated Spitz nevi; however, these lesions would be better termed Spitz nevi within a nevus spilus (speckled lentiginous nevus). Spindle and epithelioid cell proliferations can also develop within large/giant congenital nevi. Atypical Spitz tumor (Spitz melanocytoma) refers to a melanocytic neoplasm that morphologically and genetically lies between Spitz nevus and Spitz melanoma. Spitz melanoma are rare lesions and the diagnosis is best established by integrating clinical, histologic, and molecular criteria (see Ch. 113 ) 39 . Compared to atypical Spitz tumors, Spitz melanomas exhibit even greater asymmetry, poor circumscription, and higher degrees of nuclear atypia with numerous mitoses. Pathology Spitz nevi are usually symmetric, sharply circumscribed, and composed of large epithelioid and/or spindled melanocytes. The melanocytes usually extend from the epidermis into the reticular dermis in an inverted-wedge configuration. The closely apposed nests of cells within a uniformly hyperplastic epidermis often contribute to a so-called “raining-down” appearance ( Fig. 112.18 ). Both mononuclear and multi- nucleated giant epithelioid cells are frequently observed. These cells extend into the dermis as nests, fascicles, or single cells. In general, there is orderly infiltration of the dermal collagen by melanocytic complexes with so-called maturation, i.e. gradual diminution of nuclear and cellular sizes as well as the size of nests. The individual cells usually have abundant cytoplasm that stains slightly bluish or pink and nuclei with open chromatin patterns. Rather uniform nucleoli are usually also noted. Intraepidermal eosinophilic globules (Kamino bodies) are commonly found in Spitz nevi, but may occasionally be encountered in other melanocytic tumors including cutaneous melanoma. Kamino bodies represent altered components of the basement membrane, including collagen types IV and VII. In Spitz nevi, some histopathologic patterns are associated with particular genetic features. text: atypical process, possibly cutaneous melanoma. Pathology Pigmented spindle cell nevi display a well-circumscribed and orderly appearance ( Fig. 112.19 ). Lesions are usually only slightly raised with nevus cells confined to the epidermis, although they may involve the papillary dermis. The lesion is well circumscribed and is typified by fascicles of uniform, slender spindle cells that are closely aggregated ( Fig. 112.19 , inset). The cells usually contain fine, granular melanin and their nuclei have delicate chromatin and small inconspicuous nucleoli. There may be clefting around the intraepidermal fascicles. Numerous melanophages are usually present in the papillary dermis. Upward migration of nevus cells throughout the epidermis is sometimes noted, but usually these cells are confined to the lower half of the epidermis. Atypical variants exhibit prominent single-cell hyperplasia extending peripherally along the basal layer of the epidermis and in a pagetoid pattern throughout the epidermis. Cytologic atypia may also be present to a varying degree in these atypical variants. Differential Diagnosis The clinical differential diagnosis of pigmented spindle cell nevi includes early melanoma, atypical nevus, blue nevus, angiokeratoma, and pigmented basal cell carcinoma. In general, the borders of pigmented spindle cell nevi are regular and well-defined. The color is also homoge- neous in most instances. However, atypical forms of pigmented spindle cell nevi may have irregular borders and variation in color. Although spindle cell nevi have a characteristic dermoscopic pattern, histopath- ologic examination is required for diagnosis. It must be emphasized, however, that the clinicopathologic presentation of typical pigmented spindle cell nevi is distinctive. Its history is that of a recently developed or changing, small, well-circumscribed, black lesion on the thigh of a young woman (usually in her 20 s). These lesions are often conspicuous because of the dearth of pigmented lesions elsewhere on the body. Treatment The proper treatment of pigmented spindle cell nevi is complete excision with clear margins. The reason for this recommendation is to prevent recurrence, since the pathology of recurring lesions may be alarming and difficult to distinguish from melanoma. For pigmented spindle cell nevi with atypical features, wider surgical margins are advised. For example, we advocate resection margins of 5 to 10 mm for markedly atypical forms of pigmented spindle cell nevus because histopatho- logic distinction from melanoma may be exceedingly difficult. Periodic follow-up, i.e. every 6 to 12 months, is also strongly advised for patients with atypical variants of pigmented spindle cell nevus.

WNT-ACTIVATED DEEP PENETRATING/ PLEXIFORM NEVUS Synonyms:  Deep penetrating nevus/melanocytoma  Plexiform spindle cell nevus/melanocytoma Key features  Well-circumscribed, symmetric, darkly pigmented papule measuring 5–10 mm in diameter  Due to concomitant activation of the WNT signaling pathway (typically due to a CTNNB1 mutation) and the MAPK pathway (typically due to a BRAF mutation)  Histologically characterized by spindled and/or epithelioid melano- cytes extending into the deep reticular dermis and arranged in a wedge-shaped or plexiform pattern Epidemiology and Pathogenesis WNT-activated deep penetrating/plexiform nevi are rare tumors that occur in all age groups, with a mean age of 30 years and a slight predom- inance in women 43 . Most lesions arise from common acquired nevi due to an additional mutation that activates the WNT signaling pathway. In more than 90% of cases, these mutations affect a critical domain of CTNNB1 , which encodes β -catenin. In rare cases, this pathway is activated by loss-of-function mutations in APC . The additional MAPK pathway activation is due to mutations in BRAF or rarely mutations in MAP2K1 or HRAS , or BRAF fusions. WNT pathway activation leads to an increase in pigmentation, cell volume, and nuclear cyclin D1 levels, thereby altering the phenotype of a BRAF -mutated common acquired nevus into a WNT-activated deep penetrating/plexiform nevus 44 . Clinical Features These nevi occur most commonly in the head and neck region, followed by the extremities and trunk. They are typically symmetric, well-­circumscribed, darkly pigmented papules with a diameter that is < 10 mm 45 . Pathology WNT-activated deep penetrating/plexiform nevi are predominantly dermal melanocytic neoplasms. In most lesions, a junctional component and variably large areas of a conventional nevus are present, i.e. the histopathologic features of a “combined” nevus. Nests of enlarged epithelioid to spindle-shaped pigmented melanocytes are admixed with melanophages. In most lesions, a junctional component and variably large areas of a conventional nevus are present, i.e. the histopathologic features of a “combined” nevus. Nests of enlarged epithelioid to spindle-shaped pigmented melanocytes are admixed with melanophages. The deep penetrating subtype is often wedge-shaped with bulbous extension into the deep reticular dermis or subcutis, with melanocytes extending along adnexal and neurovascular structures. In the plexiform spindle cell subtype , the melanocytes are located more superficially and are arranged in a fascicular-plexiform pattern. By immunohistochemistry, nuclear positivity for β -catenin or LEF1, which is also involved in WNT signaling, may help establish the diagnosis (cytoplasmic positivity is not specific) 45 . Differential Diagnosis The clinical differential diagnosis includes melanoma and other types of melanocytic nevi, especially blue nevi, combined nevi, pigmented Spitz nevi, and pigmented epithelioid melanocytomas. However, the funda- mental diagnostic issue is histologic differentiation from melanoma. Compared to melanomas, these nevi usually occur in younger patients, are smaller, have a regular, symmetric, and plexiform architecture, predominantly junctional melanocytic proliferation that is characterized by well-defined margins, symmetry, and an overall plate-like configuration. Several nests have a vertical configuration and some may show “perforation” of the epidermis. Inset: the melanocytes are spindle-shaped and heavily pigmented. NEOPLASMS OF THE SKIN and display monomorphous cells with low-grade atypia and a mitotic rate of ≤ 2 mitoses/mm 2,45 . True bona fide melanomas derived from a WNT-activated deep penetrating/plexiform melanocytoma appear to be extremely rare. Treatment These nevi usually exhibit a benign clinical behavior. However, atypical lesions may spread to regional lymph nodes and eventually have an unfavorable clinical outcome 43 . Consequently, some authors recommend complete excision, whereas others reserve this recommen- dation for lesions with clinically or histologically atypical features. In the case of partial biopsies, patient age, size of the lesion, and clinical and histopathologic features can be considered, but it is important to note that histopathologic differentiation from melanoma may be very difficult or even impossible when the entire lesion is not examined. BAP1-INACTIVATED MELANOCYTIC NEVUS Synonyms:  BAP1-inactivated melanocytic tumor  BAP1-inactivated melanocytoma  BAPoma  Melanocytic BAP1-mutated atypical intra- dermal tumor (MBAIT)  Wiesner nevus Key features  Skin-colored to reddish-brown, dome-shaped, 5–10 mm papule  Caused by a bi-allelic inactivation of the BAP1 tumor suppressor gene, usually in combination with a BRAF mutation  Histologically characterized by an epithelioid cell morphology Epidemiology and Pathogenesis BAP1-inactivated melanocytic nevi are rare tumors, but their exact preva- lence is unknown. They can occur sporadically or in association with the BAP1 tumor predisposition syndrome (BAP1-TPDS), which is a rare autosomal dominant tumor syndrome due to germline BAP1 mutations 46 . These nevi usually arise from a bi-allelic inactivation of BAP1 in a conventional nevus, which usually has a BRAF mutation, or less commonly a NRAS mutation or RAF1 fusion. The BAP1 inactivation results in an epithelioid cell morphology of the clonally expanding melanocytes 47 . In sporadic tumors, bi-allelic BAP1 inactivation often occurs through a loss-of-function mutation in one BAP1 allele and a chromosomal deletion in the remaining wild-type BAP1 allele. In patients with BAP1-TPDS, bi-allelic BAP1 loss is due to inactivation of the remaining wild-type BAP1 allele. Clinical Features BAP1-inactivated melanocytic nevi can occur anywhere on the skin, but are more commonly observed in chronically sun-exposed sites. They usually present as inconspicuous, skin-colored to reddish-brown, dome-shaped papules measuring 5–10 mm in diameter ( Fig. 112.20 ). Some lesions have small brown areas at their periphery, representing remnants of a conventional nevus. By dermoscopy, they usually appear as: (1) structureless pink-to-tan lesions, sometimes with irregular eccentric dots/globules or peripheral vessels; (2) a network with raised structureless pink-to-tan areas; or (3) a globular pattern 48 . Solitary BAP1-inactivated melanocytic nevi occur sporadically and are usually not associated with an increased cancer risk. In contrast, multiple BAP1-inactivated melanocytic nevi are associated with the BAP1-TPDS. Genetic testing for BAP1 germline mutations should be considered in patients with multiple such nevi or with a family history of BAP1-TPDS-associated cancers, most commonly uveal or cutaneous melanoma, mesothelioma, and renal cell carcinoma 46 . Pathology BAP1-inactivated melanocytic nevi are predominantly intradermal melanocytic proliferations with occasional junctional involvement. The majority have remnants of an adjacent conventional nevus (e.g. small nevoid cells) plus larger epithelioid cells ( Fig. 112.21A–C ), i.e. features of a “combined” nevus. The minority have no remnants of a conven- tional nevus. The characteristic cells are large, epithelioid melanocytes with well- defined cytoplasmic borders, large amounts of eosinophilic cytoplasm, and vesicular nuclei with prominent nucleoli. The BAP1-inactivated melanocytes reside within the dermis and are typically not pigmented. They can show varying degrees of nuclear size, including nuclear pleomorphism with dispersed chromatin patterns and prominent nucleoli. The mitotic activity is low, and tumor-infiltrating lympho- cytes are frequently present. In the epithelioid cells, bi-allelic BAP1 inactivation typically leads to complete loss of nuclear BAP1 expression by immunohistochemistry, and this is a good surrogate for demonstration of BAP1 inactivation at a molecular level. In combined cases, BAP1 immunoreactivity is retained within the nevoid compartment ( Fig. 112.21D ) 49 . Differential Diagnosis The differential diagnosis includes intradermal nevi, neurofibromas, and fibroepithelial polyps. However, the notable diagnostic issue is the histologic differentiation from spitzoid lesions and melanoma. In some cases with spitzoid cytomorphology, BAP1-inactivated melano- cytic nevi may resemble a Spitz nevus; however, Kamino bodies are absent and typically there is a lack of the wedge-shaped silhouette of Spitz nevi as well as lack of expression of BAP1. Combined BAP1-inactivated melanocytic nevi may be confused with melanoma arising in a nevus. Helpful clues are recognition of the typical epithe- lioid melanocytes and loss of BAP1 expression by immunohisto- chemistry in the absence of malignant features. However, because BAP1-inactivated melanoma, sometimes in association with a pre-existing melanocytic nevus, may occasionally be observed, BAP1 inactivation per se is not a criterion for benignity. Treatment BAP1-inactivated melanocytic nevi typically have an indolent clinical course 50 . However, the increased incidence of BAP1-inactivated cutaneous melanomas in patients with multiple BAP1-inactivated melanocytic nevi indicates an increased risk of progression to melanoma. Epidemiology Estimates of the incidence of atypical melanocytic nevi cover a wide range, as would be expected given the lack of consensus regarding definitions. Most estimates are in the 10% range for the general population but up to 40% in patients with melanoma. Atypical melano- cytic nevi may be single or multiple. In the general population, atypical nevi may arise in a “sporadic” fashion, i.e. without a history of familial melanoma, versus in the context of a family history of atypical moles and/or melanoma. In both clinical settings, there is agreement that these nevi indicate some increase in melanoma risk. Sporadic atypical melanocytic nevi may occur at any time, while persons with a family history of atypical melanocytic nevi and/or melanoma usually manifest their atypical lesions by the end of the second decade. In contrast to common acquired nevi that tend to appear in increasing numbers around puberty, atypical melanocytic nevi may appear, even in an eruptive fashion, as late as the sixth decade. Histologic contiguity of atypical melanocytic nevi to melanomas was frequently observed in several studies 60 , but the development of melanoma in association with an individual atypical melanocytic nevus in the sporadic setting seems to be an uncommon event and not more frequent than the development of melanoma in other types of melanocytic nevi. One study estimated that the annual transformation rate of any single melanocytic nevus into melanoma ranged from ≤ 1 in 200 000 ( ≤ 0.0005%) to ≤ 1 in 33 000 ( ≤ 0.003%) 60a . Clinical Features Atypical nevi occupy an intermediate position on a continuum with common nevi at one end and cutaneous melanoma at the other end, and, as a result, they overlap with both. No single feature is diagnostic of atypical melanocytic nevi; rather, a constellation of clinical and dermo- scopic findings is required for their recognition ( Figs. 112.22 & see Fig. P9 ). Some authors recommend the following criteria: a macular component plus at least three of the following features: size > 5 mm, color varie- gation, ill-defined border, uneven peripheral contour, and erythema 61 . By definition, these lesions have a flat component representing junctional proliferation, and there is often a central raised portion that represents a dermal component resulting in the resemblance to a “fried egg” or a “head with shoulders”. The more clinical abnormalities present, the greater the likelihood that the lesion will prove to be histologically atypical. Benign Melanocytic Neoplasms and Melanotic Lesions The overwhelming majority of atypical melanocytic nevi are clini- cally stable. However, there is evidence that some lesions eventuate in cutaneous melanoma. Progressive abnormalities in DNA content, cytogenetic alterations, and increased expression of melanocyte- associated antigens by immunohistochemistry have been correlated with progressive degrees of histologic atypia 60 . Although findings suggest a progression of atypical melanocytic nevi toward melanoma, atypical melanocytic nevi are not inevitable precursors to melanoma, and their presence can be viewed as a phenotypic marker of “an entire skin at risk”. Pathology Prototypic atypical melanocytic nevi are characterized by several archi- tectural features. Compared to ordinary nevi, these nevi are often larger (commonly > 5 mm in diameter), poorly circumscribed, slightly asymmetric, relatively flat (especially at the periphery of the lesion), and often show heterogeneity. In atypical melanocytic nevi, the junctional component frequently extends beyond the dermal component (the “shoulder” phenomenon). Of particular importance is architectural disorder of the intraepi- dermal component, which occurs in two patterns that are often present simultaneously to a varying degree ( Fig. 112.24 ). The first is lentig- inous melanocytic proliferation that is almost always associated with elongated epidermal rete ridges. In general, the basilar melanocytes are concentrated in the lowermost portions of the rete ridges, and the frequency of basilar melanocytes varies greatly, e.g. from one melanocyte per one to two keratinocytes to the melanocytes replacing the basilar keratinocytes and resulting in a confluent, clustered, or multilayered cellular appearance. The second pattern consists of melanocytic nests that are irregularly disposed along and between the rete ridges, as compared to ordinary nevi. These nests vary in size and shape, are often elongated, commonly have their long axes oriented along the dermal–epidermal junction, and contain variable numbers of cells. Colliding nests of melanocytes frequently fuse or “bridge”. Discohesion of cells within these nests is also common; this feature contrasts with the cohesive appearance of junctional nests of melanocytes in ordinary nevi. Atypical nevi often have a higher density of melanocytes in the intraepidermal component than do ordinary nevi. Atypical melanocytic nevi often exhibit cytologic atypia. The latter is discontinuous and variable, from only a small percentage of melanocytes demonstrating nuclear atypia to most cells being atypical. Cytologic atypia often correlates with the degree of architectural abnormality. Pleomorphism

The latter is discontinuous and variable, from only a small percentage of melanocytes demonstrating nuclear atypia to most cells being atypical. Cytologic atypia often correlates with the degree of architectural abnormality. Pleomorphism of the nuclei (i.e. variation in size, shape, and staining properties) is the most characteristic attribute of the nuclear changes in atypical melanocytic nevi. However, nuclear enlargement and hyper- chromatism also occur. The cells are frequently typified by a perinuclear clear space resulting from cytoplasmic shrinkage, which is an artifact of tissue processing. Criteria for grading the degree of cytologic atypia and even architectural abnormality have been proposed, but there is neither consensus regarding using a grading system nor how to define different grades of atypia. The dermal component of atypical melanocytic nevi may be composed of typical nevus cells, as in any acquired nevus, or of cells that may exhibit atypia. In addition to the abnormal architectural disorder and cytologic atypia, atypical melanocytic nevi usually exhibit changes related to host response. Two forms of collagenous change occur in the papillary dermis and a mixture of the two patterns is not uncommon. The most common pattern, termed concentric fibrosis , is a condensation of collagen around the epidermal rete. A less common pattern, termed lamellar fibroplasia , consists of finely layered or laminated collagen beneath the rete tips with fibroblasts arranged in a linear array along the laminated collagen fibers. Both patterns can also be observed in melanoma. Lymphocytic infil- trates, usually distributed in a perivascular fashion and less commonly in a band-like pattern, are also frequently observed. Finally, atypical melanocytic nevi usually have prominent vascularity throughout the papillary dermis, which is due to dilation and hypertrophy of existing vascular channels, rather than angiogenesis. Although atypical melanocytic nevi can clinically resemble melanoma, many of these lesions fall into one of the benign dermoscopic melanocytic patterns (see Fig. P9 ). Features employed to evaluate a melanocytic nevus include colors, symmetry, and organization. Benign melanocytic lesions tend to have few colors and are symmetric with regard to the distribution of colors and struc- tures. When these structures are symmetrically distributed and there are fewer than three colors (light brown, dark brown, and black) noted, they create a pattern seen in many benign lesions. The most common benign patterns are reticular, globular, and homogeneous (see Fig. 0.37 ). In addition, there are the subset patterns of reticular–homogeneous, reticular–globular, and globular–homogeneous (see Fig. P9 ) 62 . Finally, another subset of atypical melanocytic nevi is characterized by uncertain melanocytic dermoscopic patterns. Just as the clinical and histologic features of atypical melanocytic nevi are a continuum, so too are the features with dermoscopy. These lesions should either be excised or serially monitored. The histopathological differential diagnosis of atypical (dysplastic) melanocytic nevi from melanoma may be very difficult and may be influenced by the threshold of a given dermatopathologist for the diagnosis of early melanoma. For example, some cases classified as “dysplastic nevus with severe architectural and morphologic atypia” in one center may be diagnosed as “melanoma in situ ” by another. Immunohistochemical stains may be helpful, and strong positivity for PRAME ( pr eferential expressed a ntigen of me lanoma) in the majority of neoplastic cells is a strong criterion for the histopathologic diagnosis of melanoma. In addition, atypical nevi located on chronic sun-damaged skin and/or the face should be judged with caution, as the likelihood of melanoma is significant in these settings. Treatment As within any area of medicine, the physician is first obliged to do no harm. Such an approach is particularly important in patients with atypical melanocytic nevi with avoidance of overly aggressive proce- dures, surgery, and follow-up. Common sense should prevail at all times and consideration should be given to whether the intervention has an impact on potentially reducing melanoma mortality. Treatment depends upon several factors including: (1) whether the patient presents with one or a few nevi versus numerous nevi; (2) whether the patient has a personal history of melanoma; and (3) whether there exists a familial setting of atypical melanocytic nevi and/or melanoma. The risk of melanoma is probably continuous and increases with the number of nevi, clinical atypia of nevi, and personal and familial occurrence of atypical nevi and melanoma. Regardless of the risk group, any pigmented lesion suspicious for melanoma and any significantly changing lesion should, in the authors’ opinion, be excised completely with free margins. Some authors have advocated “deep” shave excision (saucerization) for superficial lesions, which is acceptable as long as the lesion is removed entirely, including its base. As opposed to partial punch biopsy, which should be discouraged, the latter allows for assessment of the overall architecture of the lesion and leads to less sampling error. A helpful rule of thumb in following patients with many atypical melanocytic nevi is to search for lesions that clearly stand out as different from the patient’s other (baseline) nevi (“ugly duckling”); such lesions should be examined carefully. It should be kept in mind that new nevi will continue to develop and nevi may enlarge and change with time, especially in young individuals. One must use common sense in assessing this normal evolution of nevi and not be overly aggressive in removing such nevi. An acceptable practice is to follow such patients on a regular schedule with a total body skin examination plus dermoscopy, baseline photography, and/or digital dermoscopy, as preferred by the clinician. Computerized assessment and comparison of clinical photographs is increasingly being employed. The frequency of follow-up examinations is individualized and is based on the previously mentioned risk factors, i.e. numbers and clinical atypia of nevi, lesion stability, and personal and family history of melanoma. For any melanocytic lesion, it is important to know if the lesion has been adequately sampled and if the lesion was considered to be clini- cally atypical. If lesions are “severely” atypical, re-excision is recom- mended because of frequent overlap with, and difficult distinction from, melanoma in situ . For atypical melanocytic nevi with lesser degrees of atypia, the answer regarding whether to re-excise is controversial. In general, if lesions are “mildly” atypical, no re-excision is recommended, as long as no significant residuum of the nevus is clinically apparent. If lesions are “moderately” atypical, the decision to re-excise is particularly difficult. Studies show that dermatologists tend to re-excise moderately atypical lesions if a biopsy margin is positive 63 . Despite this propensity for re-excision, available data do not necessarily support re-excision of moderately atypical nevi. Independent retrospective studies examining the utility of re-excision of moderately atypical nevi conclude that re-excision of these nevi rarely results in a change in diagnosis 64 . In a study of 1809 mildly and moderately atypical nevi, 765 were found to have positive margins and of these 495 underwent re-excision. Of the 495 re-excisions, only a single case resulted in a clinically significant change 65 . Therefore, the current data may not support a blanket recommendation to re-excise all moderately atypical nevi even if there are positive margins. Unfortunately, the discussion of whether or not to re-excise dysplastic nevi is greatly confounded by the lack of a uniform grading system amongst pathologists. Often this leaves dermatologists erring on the side of caution when it comes to this clinical decision. Therefore, even when no residual lesion is clinically obvious, re-excision might be considered, depending upon a number of factors: the initial degree of concern clinically, the size of the nevus (versus the size of the biopsy), the color (more inclined with amelanotic lesions as assessing residuum is more difficult), the site (easy or difficult to visualize by the patient), the patient’s ability and interest in following the site, and the patient’s prior personal and family history of melanoma. In general, follow-up of patients with multiple atypical nevi, especially in the context of a personal or family history of melanoma, should be every 3 to 12 months, depending on the clinical situation. One should consider documentation of nevi by body charts and clinical photography as judged appropriate, with periodic updating. Individual photographs of the most atypical or difficult-to-follow nevi are particularly helpful. Additional tools such as dermoscopy and/or digital imaging devices may be useful diagnostic aids. Finally, individuals presenting with atypical melanocytic nevi should have a family history taken for the presence of atypical melanocytic nevi and/or melanoma. First-degree blood relatives should be examined both for documentation and to assess and poten- tially diminish their own risks of developing melanoma. Lesions indistinguishable from congenital nevi may appear up to 2 years after birth and are therefore referred to as tardive congenital nevus . Finally, histopathologic features of congenital nevi may be observed in melanocytic tumors acquired during childhood or adolescence, with dermatopatholo- gists often referring to them as melanocytic nevi with a congenital pattern. Benign Melanocytic Neoplasms and Melanotic Lesions Some congenital melanocytic nevi may be just a few millimeters in size and appear clinically indistinguishable from common acquired nevi. In general, congenital melanocytic nevi are classified as small ( < 1.5 cm), intermediate- or medium-sized (1.5 to 20 cm), large ( > 20 to 40 cm), and giant ( > 40 cm), based upon their size in adults 68 . Given the eventual size, a congenital nevus ≥ 9 cm on the scalp or ≥ 6 cm on the trunk in a newborn is assigned to the large/giant category; with extensive involvement (e.g. the entire trunk), assignment to the giant category is self-evident. Patients with ≥ 3 small or medium-sized congenital melanocytic nevi or a giant congenital melanocytic nevus may have associated neurocu- taneous melanosis (see below). Epidemiology The prevalence of congenital melanocytic nevi varies widely depending on the study, ranging from 0.5% to 30% 67 , but in our experience occur in ~1% of newborns. Most lesions are 3 to 4 cm in diameter. Large/ giant congenital nevi are rare, with an estimated incidence of 0.005% (1 in 20 000). Patients with large/giant nevi often have multiple smaller (satellite) nevi, with greater numbers correlating with an increased risk of neurocutaneous melanosis (see below). Familial aggregation of congenital nevi has occasionally been reported. Pathogenesis The majority of congenital melanocytic nevi have oncogenic NRAS mutations. BRAF mutations are detected in up to 7% of cases while KRAS mutations and kinase fusions are rare 69 . Individual melano- cytes begin to appear in fetal skin before 40 days’ gestation. Given the observation of congenital divided nevi of the eyelid and the fact that the eyelids open during the sixth month of gestation, it appears that congenital melanocytic nevi can develop prior to the sixth month of gestation. Patients with a large/giant congenital nevus and/or multiple satellite lesions should be thought of as having a systemic disease ( Fig. 112.25 ), as nevus cells can be found in sites beyond the skin and central nervous system (CNS), such as the retroperitoneum. They may or may not have associated hypertrichosis ( Fig. 112.26 ), and perifollicular hypo- or hyperpigmentation may be seen. Some congenital melanocytic nevi have rugose or pebbly surfaces (see Fig. 112.26A,B ). Lesions that are initially minimally

Clinical Features Small and medium-sized congenital nevi are usually round or oval, fairly symmetric, slightly raised, and tan in color ( Fig. P6 ). They may or may not have associated hypertrichosis ( Fig. 112.26 ), and perifollicular hypo- or hyperpigmentation may be seen. Some congenital melanocytic nevi have rugose or pebbly surfaces (see Fig. 112.26A,B ). Lesions that are initially minimally elevated often become thicker and darker in color and may develop a verrucous appearance. After an initial darkening during the first year of life, some congenital melanocytic nevi may become lighter in color with aging, including satellite lesions. In addition, congenital nevi can develop the halo phenomenon (see below), and occasionally, congenital nevi completely regress, even without forming a halo. As hamartomas, congenital nevi can exhibit asymmetry and color variation, develop papules and nodules (e.g. proliferative nodules), and change over time (see Fig. 112.26 ); however, histologic examination of any concerning areas is recommended ( Table 112.10 ). Areas within congenital nevi can also undergo neuroti- zation and develop compressible, boggy plaques or nodules ( Fig. 112.27 ). The dermoscopic structures seen in congenital nevi include the following: globules, diffuse background pigmentation (structureless), milia-like cysts, hypertrichosis, hyphae-like structures, and perifollicular pigment changes. The most common dermoscopic patterns are reticular, globular, reticular–globular (see Fig. P6 ), diffuse brown pigmentation, and multicomponent. The multicomponent pattern is often difficult to distinguish from melanoma and requires either monitoring or biopsy. Varying numbers of satellite lesions often accompany large/giant congenital melanocytic nevi (see Fig. 112.25B ). Such lesions typically resemble small or medium-sized congenital melanocytic nevi. Of note, some patients present with multiple medium-sized congenital nevi in the absence of a large congenital nevus (see Fig. 112.25A ), and these individuals are at greatest risk for neurocutaneous melanosis (up to 70% in one study). Neurocutaneous melanosis (melanocytosis) In neurocutaneous melanosis, there can be diffuse involvement of the leptomeninges that cover the brain and/or the spinal cord. In addition, intraparenchymal melanosis or solid tumors within the brain paren- chyma may be observed. The melanocytes can be benign or malignant and can result in obstruction (with hydrocephalus) or a mass effect. In addition, a variety of intracranial and intraspinal anomalies (e.g. Dandy–Walker malformation, extensive arachnoid cysts) can be seen in association with neurocutaneous melanosis 66,67 . A

Benign Melanocytic Neoplasms and Melanotic Lesions As noted previously, neurocutaneous melanosis occurs primarily in patients with ≥ 3 small or medium-sized congenital melanocytic nevi or a giant congenital melanocytic nevus with satellitosis. In one series of 33 patients with neurocutaneous melanosis associated with giant congenital melanocytic nevi, all nevi had a posterior axial location (involving the head, neck, back, and/or buttocks); 31 of 33 patients had satellite nevi. In another study, 80% had posterior axis involvement and 55% had more than 20 satellite nevi. Of note, neurocutaneous melanosis can also be seen in patients with nevus of Ota and phakoma- tosis pigmentovascularis. Melanoma arising in congenital nevi Although all sizes of congenital melanocytic nevi may be associated with melanoma, historical estimates of melanoma risk have been exaggerated because of referral and selection bias and misdiagnosis. The risk of melanoma increases with the size of the nevus, with most studies reporting an incidence rate of melanoma in small/medium congenital melanocytic nevi of < 1%. For example, a prospective study of 230 medium-sized congenital melanocytic nevi in 227 patients, followed on average for 6.7 years, failed to document the development of a single case of melanoma. Similarly, in a longitudinal cohort study of 265 patients with medium-sized congenital melanocytic nevi, none developed melanoma. On the other hand, several studies have noted substantial melanoma risk linked to large or giant congenital melanocytic nevi. In a prospective study of 92 patients with large/giant congenital melanocytic nevi, three patients developed melanoma in extracuta- neous sites

Similarly, in a longitudinal cohort study of 265 patients with medium-sized congenital melanocytic nevi, none developed melanoma. On the other hand, several studies have noted substantial melanoma risk linked to large or giant congenital melanocytic nevi. In a prospective study of 92 patients with large/giant congenital melanocytic nevi, three patients developed melanoma in extracuta- neous sites (brain, CNS, retroperitoneum) during follow-up averaging 5.4 years. The authors calculated the cumulative 5-year life-table risk for melanoma to be 4.5% and the standardized morbidity ratio to be 239, leading to the recommendation for continuous surveillance 71 . A comprehensive review of 14 studies that examined the development of melanoma in patients with congenital melanocytic nevi reported an overall risk of melanoma of 0.7% (in those with congenital melano- cytic nevi of all types), with a risk of 2.5% and 3.1% in large and giant nevi, respectively 72 . When a cutaneous melanoma develops in a relatively small congenital melanocytic nevus, it appears most commonly at the dermal–epidermal junction in a pattern similar to that of other conventional melanomas. However, cutaneous melanomas arising in larger congenital melano- cytic nevi can develop within the dermis, subcutaneous fat, or even deeper, as a distinct nodule 73 . Rarely, other malignant tumors may arise in these lesions, including rhabdomyosarcomas, malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors, fibrosarcomas, leiomyosarcomas, osteogenic sarcomas, and liposarcomas. Leptomeningeal melanomas can arise in patients with neurocuta- neous melanosis and most commonly involve the frontal and temporal lobes. As expected, these melanomas have a poor prognosis. Abnormalities associated with congenital nevi Patients with large/giant congenital nevi can also have urinary tract anomalies, obstruction of orifices by the nevus (e.g. perianal), and infil- tration of lymph nodes and the mother’s placenta by nevus cells. Pathology In contrast to common acquired nevi, which are confined to the papillary and upper reticular dermis, congenital nevi may have infiltration of the lower reticular dermis, subcutaneous fat, fascia, and even deeper ( Fig. 112.29 ). It is characteristic to observe melanocytes in a single- cell array throughout the middle or lower reticular dermis and even extending into the septa of the subcutis. Melanocytes often surround (cuffing) and/or infiltrate blood vessels, adnexal structures such as hair follicles, sebaceous glands and sweat glands, and cutaneous muscles and nerves. There

Melanocytes often surround (cuffing) and/or infiltrate blood vessels, adnexal structures such as hair follicles, sebaceous glands and sweat glands, and cutaneous muscles and nerves. There is often maturation and diminished cellularity with increasing depth within the dermis. Uncommonly, congenital melanocytic nevi may show striking neural differentiation suggesting a peripheral nerve sheath tumor such as a neurofibroma or schwannoma. Structures resembling Meissner corpuscles, Verocay bodies, or neuroid tubules may be observed. In some patients, nodular proliferations can arise within congenital nevi (“proliferating nodules”), particularly those that are medium-sized, large, or giant. These nodules can be very difficult to distinguish from melanoma arising in a congenital nevus, both clinically and histo- pathologically. Proliferating nodules usually arise during the first few years of life or are present at birth. They tend to blend well with the remaining nevus and have only slight atypia and occasional mitoses. When analyzed by array comparative genomic hybridization (aCGH), proliferating nodules contain gains and losses of entire chromosomes, in contrast to melanomas that contain several gains and losses, but only of portions of chromosomes. Differential Diagnosis The differential diagnosis of small congenital nevi includes congenital smooth muscle hamartoma, neurofibroma, atypical nevus, and melanoma. For medium-sized congenital nevi, an additional entity to consider is Becker melanosis, including those with an associated smooth muscle hamartoma. Large/giant congenital melanocytic nevi are occasionally misdiagnosed as plexiform neurofibromas, as the latter can have both hyperpigmentation and hypertrichosis. Of course, the possibility of melanoma exists for any clinically atypical area (e.g. darkening, nodularity) within a congenital nevus. The differ- ences between melanoma and a proliferating nodule are outlined in the Pathology section. Treatment The treatment of congenital melanocytic nevi is primarily related to two factors: their cosmetically disfiguring appearance and their increased risk for progression to melanoma. The decision to remove a congenital nevus is individualized and based on melanoma risk, age, anatomic location (especially proximity to vital structures), presence or absence of neurocutaneous melanosis, anticipated cosmetic outcome, and complexity of removal. In the absence of a cosmetic concern, the routine excision of uniform-appearing small and medium-sized congenital nevi no longer seems justified due to the low melanoma risk. An acceptable alternative to surgical excision is baseline photography, education, and yearly examination. The treatment of large/giant congenital nevi is more problematic, since melanoma risk is present from birth. In the past, dermabrasion was sometimes performed, resulting in a more lightly pigmented and less elevated congenital nevus. Repeat curettage performed in the first few weeks of life (when there is a cleavage plane in the upper dermis) has led to similar results. Scarring and prolonged healing in the case of large lesions are the drawbacks. Lasers (e.g. Q-switched ruby, Q-switched alexandrite) have also been used to treat congenital nevi, but recurrence of pigmentation is an issue as is persistence of nevus cells 74 . In theory, these secondary genomic alterations contribute to the development of the nevi. Halo nevi generally develop in individuals under the age of 20 years, with a mean age at presentation of ~15 years. There is no sex predilection, but patients who develop halo nevi have a higher number of melanocytic nevi. Approximately 20% of individuals with halo nevi have vitiligo and their nevi are less often associated with atypical features 77 . The inflammatory infiltrate usually consists predominantly of T cells, especially cytotoxic CD8 + T cells 78 . Although the basis for nevus cell destruction in halo nevi is poorly understood, both humoral and cellular immunologic factors have been implicated. Clinical Features Halo nevi are most commonly observed in teenagers and young adults, and they are often initially noted in the summer. This is likely because tanning leads to greater contrast with the halo. The trunk is the most common location and 25%–50% of affected individuals have two or more halo nevi. Numerous eruptive halo nevi is a rare phenomenon. In older adults, a distinction is made between persistent halo nevi versus new-onset halo nevi (see below). Halo nevi are characterized by a central melanocytic nevus component that may be relatively flat or raised and dark brown to pink in color. The nevus may exhibit surface scale or crusting. Surrounding the central nevus is a well-circumscribed annulus of hypo- or depigmented skin ( Fig. 112.31A,B ). Erythema occasionally precedes the development of the depigmented halo, which is thought to appear over a period of weeks to months. In typical halo nevi, the central nevus often measures 3–6 mm in diameter, has smooth and well-defined borders, and has a homogeneous color (stage I). By dermoscopy, globular and/or homoge- neous patterns that typify benign nevi in children and young adults are usually observed 80 . The white halo is often symmetric with a uniform width that may vary from a few millimeters up to several centimeters (uncommon), but it can be asymmetric ( Fig. 112.31C ). A Wood’s lamp can enhance or discern the halo and allow for assessment of the number of halo nevi. Dermoscopically, the halo is white and structureless ( Fig. P7 ). The development of circumscribed poliosis involving scalp hairs, eyebrows, or eyelashes can be a clue to the presence of a halo nevus in these locations. Complete repigmentation of the skin is seen in the majority of patients, but the process may take years to decades (stage IV). Rarely, the central nevus persists and the halo repigments. In most patients, halo nevi occur as an isolated phenomenon in the setting of multiple melanocytic nevi. However, a relationship to vitiligo, melanoma, and atypical nevi has been well documented. Multiple halo nevi may be a sign of an ocular or cutaneous melanoma elsewhere, especially in older adults whose lesions are of recent onset. Occasionally, halo nevi appear following immunotherapy for melanoma or adminis- tration of other medications, e.g. imatinib, tocilizumab. Pathology The halo nevus may be junctional, compound, or dermal. In the fully evolved stages, the central nevus is associated with a well-circum- scribed, dense infiltrate of lymphocytes and histiocytes, which occupies the papillary dermis and penetrates the nests of nevus cells. The lymphohistiocytic infiltrate can be so prominent that the nevus cells are difficult to distinguish from surrounding cells without special stains. Degenerating nevus cells can sometimes be identified in this zone. Differential Diagnosis Common acquired melanocytic nevi with halo phenomenon must be distinguished from: (1) other melanocytic proliferations with halos, such as congenital melanocytic nevi, atypical nevi, blue nevi, Spitz nevi, primary melanomas, or melanoma metastases; and (2) non-melano- cytic lesions with halos, such as dermatofibromas, seborrheic keratoses, flat warts, mollusca contagiosa, basal cell carcinomas, lichen planus, psoriasis, or sarcoidosis.
