Pathology KHE is characterized by ill-defined, frequently coalescing nodules composed of fascicles of moderately plump spindled endothelial cells with eosinophilic to clear cytoplasm and bland nuclei that form elongated, slit-like lumina containing erythrocytes, reminiscent of Kaposi sarcoma ( Fig. 114.22A ). The spindle cells often encompass nests of more epithelioid endothelial cells and pericytes that are surrounding platelet-rich microthrombi (which can be highlighted by CD61 immunostaining). At the margin of the lesion, the spindle cells may infiltrate into the surrounding adipose tissue and between collagen bundles, or they may be encased by desmoplastic stroma. The spindle cells are strongly immunoreactive for the pan-endothelial marker CD31, the blood vascular marker CD34, and the lymphatic endothelial markers podoplanin ( Fig. 114.22B ), LYVE-1, VEGFR-3, and Prox1 50 . Mitotic activity is variable, but generally low. Focally, lobules of small, rounded capillaries lined by flat endothelia merge with the spindled areas. Extravasated erythrocytes and hemosiderin granules are typically present, and tumor cells may contain intracytoplasmic erythrocyte fragments and hyaline globules. Often there is a prominent component of dilated vessels with a lymphatic morphology that intermingles with the tumor lobules, but these vessels are often most obvious within the marginal soft tissues. Residual KHE, i.e. remaining after successful medical treatment, represents a dormant, often sclerotic, version of the original disease process. Differential diagnosis In addition to tufted angioma, the differential diagnosis includes infantile hemangioma, congenital hemangiomas (e.g. rapidly involuting [RICH], non-involuting [NICH]), and Kaposi sarcoma. Infantile hemangiomas, unlike KHE, express an unusual and complex endothelial phenotype shared only by placental capillaries, most commonly manifested by immunohistochemical staining for GLUT1 26,27 . Infantile heman- giomas also lack both fascicles of spindle cells and foci with a mixed lymphatic–blood vascular phenotype. Tufted angioma is thought to be a milder, more superficial form of KHE that is distinguished by a relative scarcity of endothelial spindling and an absence of pericyte-rich epithe- lioid nodules. Kaposi sarcoma, which is rare in children (outside of Africa), lacks the lobularity of KHE, characteristically contains plasma cell infiltrates, and is positive for HHV-8. Treatment Tufted angiomas and KHEs that are localized and superficial can be cured by wide local excision. Two patients in this original series had lymph node metastases, and one of them later developed distant metas- tases and died. Subsequently reported cases have behaved in a benign fashion, although follow-up for some has been limited 100 . Based on the prominent presence of lymphatic vessels, the tentative potential for malignant or borderline clinical behavior, and the defining presence of papillary intravascular proliferation, the currently favored designation for this tumor is papillary intralymphatic angioendothelioma (PILA) 100 ; this term has also been adopted by the WHO 71 . Because of their shared hobnail endothelial morphology and similar biologic behavior, Weiss and Goldblum 4 have suggested that the term hobnail hemangioen- dothelioma be used to embrace both PILA and retiform hemangioen- dothelioma. However, the lack of convincing evidence of lymphatic differentiation in the latter has seriously undermined any potential relatedness of these two entities 101 . Epidemiology Compilations of reported cases have shown no clear sex predilection, with ~75% of patients being children and the remainder primarily young adults.

Epidemiology Compilations of reported cases have shown no clear sex predilection, with ~75% of patients being children and the remainder primarily young adults. Tumors may be present at birth. A more recent series of 12 patients in which the mean age was 30 years suggests a wider age range 100 . Clinical features These tumors most commonly originate within the soft tissues of an extremity and rarely other sites such as bone or spleen. Lesions can present as either enlarging, diffuse, firm swellings of skin and subcu- taneous tissue or as soft intradermal plaques; sometimes there is also a pink or blue discoloration of the skin. The size range is wide (up to 40 cm) 100 . A number of cases appear to have arisen within pre-existing lymphatic malformations. The WHO currently classifies PILA as an intermediate (rarely metastasizing) vascular tumor 71 , and in the 2014 ISSVA classification scheme 72 it is considered a locally aggressive or borderline tumor. Lesional vessels are variable in size. Very rarely, there is a complex admixture of the features of RHE with a variety of other distinct vascular patterns, especially epithelioid changes reminiscent of epithe- lioid hemangioendothelioma, resulting in CHE 103,104 . Epidemiology RHE and CHE occur most commonly in young adults, although the age range is wide. There is no clear sex predilection. Pathogenesis As noted in the previous section, use of the term hobnail hemangio- endothelioma (not to be confused with hobnail “hemangioma”) to encompass both PILA and RHE has been proposed 4 . However, increas- ingly convincing evidence that RHE endothelial cells, unlike those of PILA, usually do not express lymphatic markers has weakened this proposal. In an RHE from an apparently immunocompetent patient, HHV-8 sequences were detected 105 . More recently, 5/13 (38%) of RHEs and 3/11 (27%) of CHEs arising within soft tissue were found to have rearrangements of YAP1 , with five (including all three CHEs) having a YAP1 – MAML2 fusion. Such findings support the inclusion of RHE and CHE within a morphologic spectrum 106 . Additional reported gene fusions in neuroendocrine CHEs are PTBP1 – MAML2 and EPC1 – PCH2 106,107 . Clinical features The clinical appearance of both RHE and CHE is not specific and the vascular nature may not be suspected clinically. RHE typically presents as a solitary, slow-growing, reddish blue plaque, exophytic mass or dermal/subcutaneous nodule, most commonly on the extremities. Most CHEs also appear on the distal extremities, typically appearing as a nodular mass or ill-defined swelling. Rarely, these tumors occur in viscera. In the original series of RHEs, nearly 60% recurred locally, and 1 of 14 patients followed longitudinally developed lymph node involvement 16 . To date, there have been no RHE-related deaths. Following surgical excisions, there may be multiple recurrences of CHEs, with the potential for lymph node metastasis. Pathology RHE is one of a small group of vascular anomalies characterized by endothelial cells with a so-called hobnail appearance; this group also includes targetoid hemosiderotic lymphatic malformation and PILA. Overall, there is a diffuse infiltration of the reticular dermis and/or subcutis by an arborizing network of elongated, thin-walled vessels forming a pattern reminiscent of normal rete testis. The margins are ill-defined. Higher magnification of the lesional vessels reveals a lining of bland endothelial cells with prominent apical nuclei that protrude into the lumina in a hobnail or “matchstick” fashion. Mitotic figures are rare, and cytologic atypia is minimal, or rarely, mild. Solid foci of spindle cells expressing endothelial markers are often present, as are occasional intravascular papillae. Unless the tumor arises within the background of a vascular malformation, cavernous lymphatic-like vessels are absent as are the prominent intravascular proliferations characteristic of PILA. The endothelial cells of RHE consistently express pan-endothelial markers such as CD31 and ERG, but usually do not express lymphatic markers such as podoplanin, VEGFR3, and Prox1 101 . CHEs are infiltrative tumors that by definition must be composed of at least two morphologically distinct vascular tumor patterns, most commonly resembling RHE and epithelioid hemangioendothelioma, but occasionally resembling spindle cell hemangioma, angiosarcoma, or vascular/lymphatic malformations 103 . CHEs consistently express CD31 and ERG and variably express podoplanin 103 . Pathology The architecture of dermal PMHE ranges from loosely fascicular to focally plexiform or storiform, with infiltrative borders. There are sheets, nests, and short intersecting fascicles of plump spindled cells with ample eosinophilic cytoplasm and vesicular nuclei with prominent nucleoli within the mid and deep reticular dermis, often with extension along connective tissue septa into the subcutis 110 . Focally, clusters of more epithelioid, rounded cells with slightly atypical vesicular nuclei and rhabdomyoblast-like appearance may be present. The epidermis can be normal or hyperplastic. There is consistent coexpression of endothelial markers and cytokeratins, including expression by most tumor cells of CD31, ERG, FLI-1, and cytokeratin AE1/AE3 110 . In nearly all cases, there is diffuse nuclear FOSB expression. Differential diagnosis The histologic differential diagnosis of PMHE includes epithelioid sarcoma, epithelioid hemangioendothelioma, and epithelioid angio- sarcoma 110 . Unlike PMHE, epithelioid sarcoma shows moderate cytologic atypia and is EMA + , CD34 + , INI-1 − , and CD31 − . Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma has epithelioid cells with prominent cytoplasmic vacuolization, myxohyaline stroma, CD34 positivity, and character- istic WWTR1 – CAMTA1 fusions. Epithelioid angiosarcoma has marked cytologic atypia, frequent mitotic figures, and positivity for CD34. Diffuse nuclear FOSB immunostaining points to the diagnosis of PMHE 111 . Treatment Treatment options include simple surgical excision, amputation (multi- focal disease), chemotherapy 112 , and radiotherapy. Partial responses to everolimus 113 and sirolimus 114 have been reported. This disease entity became known as Kaposi sarcoma and historically has been considered a chronic, protracted disease primarily affecting elderly men, generally Jewish (Ashkenazi) or of Mediterranean/Eastern European descent. Despite occasional reports regarding its occurrence in organ transplant recipients and its endemic form in Africa, KS received little attention until it became epidemic among men who have sex with men and was recognized as a sign of acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). A new human herpesvirus (HHV-8), also referred to as KS-associated herpesvirus, was recognized as the probable inductive agent of all clinical variants of KS. The mechanisms that control the clinical variability of KS are likely to involve a number of interrelated factors modulated by the patient’s immune status and have yet to be fully defined. Pathogenesis Immunohistochemical and ultrastructural studies have firmly estab- lished the endothelial nature of KS, but it remains controversial whether this endothelial phenotype is vascular, lymphatic, or perhaps a composite of both. Moreover, many, if not most cells forming the substance of a plaque or nodule of KS are spindled cells distinctly unlike normal endothelial cells in morphology, although expressing pan-endothelial markers like CD31. These spindled cells also coexpress markers of blood vascular differentiation (CD34) and lymphatic differ- entiation (VEGFR-3 102,115 , podoplanin 116 , LYVE-1 117 ). A seminal discovery was that, in vitro , Kaposi sarcoma herpesvirus (taxonomical name HHV-8) can infect both lymphatic and blood vascular endothelial cells and induce transcriptional reprogramming, leading to expression of lymphangiogenic molecules in infected blood vascular endothelial cells 118 and a more blood vascular profile in infected lymphatic endothelial cells 119 . This potentially explains the mixed lymphatic/ blood vascular phenotype of KS, but also emphasizes the difficulty in precisely assigning endothelial cell derivation based solely on marker studies 120 . HHV-8 can also induce aberrant expression of mesenchymal markers in endothelial cells (endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition) via Notch- dependent signaling 121 . This may provide an explanation for why poorly differentiated KS endothelial cells express mesenchymal and macro- phage as well as endothelial markers 122 . Of note, there is also evidence that HHV-8 may cause a mesenchymal-to-endothelial transition, transforming mesenchymal stem cells into KS endothelial cells 123 . The relative contributions of these transitions in cellular differentiation to the pathogenesis of KS remain unclear. Vascular Neoplasms and Neoplastic-Like Proliferations It also remains unclear whether KS is essentially hyperplastic or neoplastic in nature, or both. While some studies employing X-chromosome inactivation (methylation) patterns have supported singular, presumably disseminated, clones 124 , others utilizing the same methodology in examining sets of multiple lesions from single patients have found either oligoclonal composition within a given lesion or dissimilar, presumably independently developing, clones 125 . Despite these lingering uncertainties about both endothelial phenotype transi- tions and clonality, it is noteworthy how much compelling molecular, clinical, and epidemiological evidence has accumulated to confirm that infection with HHV-8 causes, or at least strongly influences, the devel- opment of KS 126 . This virus is known to be present in most patients with all clinical types of KS, and seroreactivity to HHV-8 is not present to a significant degree in the normal population. The HHV-8 genome, when detected in the blood of HIV-positive men, strongly predicts their subsequent development of KS. HHV-8 contains homologs of cellular genes that can stimulate cell proliferation, inflammation, and angiogenesis and perhaps inhibit apoptosis 127 . In vitro , HHV-8 enhances the proliferation of primary endothelial cells or extends their life span, while not producing complete oncogenic transformation 128 . The host immune response and cytokines (particularly fibroblast growth factor) released by the virally infected cells may further support tumor growth in an autocrine and paracrine manner 129–131 . The role of inflammation in KS is supported by the observation that in patients with AIDS, pre-existing KS can get worse, at least transiently, in the setting of the immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS; see Ch. 78 ) 132 . Clinical features Classic KS typically presents as slowly growing, pink to red–violet macules on the distal lower extremities that may coalesce to form large plaques ( Fig. 114.24 ), or develop into nodules or polypoid tumors. Initially unilateral lesions progress to a more widely disseminated multi- focal pattern. Early lesions may regress, while others evolve, leading to lesions in different stages at the same time. Patients with longstanding KS may have lesions in the mouth and gastrointestinal tract that are usually asymptomatic as well as lymphedema. African endemic KS can be classified into four subgroups: nodular, florid, infiltrative, and lymphadenopathic. The nodular variant resembles classic KS in course and appearance, whereas the florid and infiltrative types are more biologically aggressive. The lymph- adenopathic type is notably different in several regards: it predomi- nantly affects children, the primary tumors involve the lymph nodes (although skin and mucosal lesions may also be present), and its course is fulminant and fatal. KS due to iatrogenic immunosuppression (transplantation-associated KS) is generally clinically similar to classic KS. It may resolve completely upon removal of immunosuppressive therapy. The patch stage is characterized by a superficial dermal proliferation of small, angulated vessels lined by inconspicuous endothelial cells, suggestive of lymphatics. These delicate but “jagged” vessels tend to separate collagen bundles and are accompanied by a sparse infiltrate of lymphocytes and plasma cells as well as small numbers of spindle cells expressing endothelial markers. In the more advanced plaque stage, the vascular proliferation extends to include the deeper dermis and may involve the subcutis ( Fig. 114.26 ). The spindled endothelial cell population also expands among the ramifying small vessels. In the nodular phase, there is replacement of dermal collagen by these spindled endothelial cells. Pleomorphism and significant numbers of mitotic figures are absent. The spindle cells form intersecting fascicles and are separated by characteristic slit-like spaces containing erythro- cytes ( Fig. 114.27 ). The resulting sieve-like pattern of vascular spaces is highly characteristic of KS. Intracellular and extracellular hyaline globules are thought to represent degenerated erythrocytes 4 . The tumor nodules are often rimmed by ectatic or crescentic vessels, hemosiderin deposits, lymphocytes and plasma cells, and may be compartmentalized by fibrous bands. Some tumors contain prominent ectatic meshworks of vessels and have been referred to as “lymphangioma-like” KS. Tumors with a frankly sarcomatous appearance, nuclear pleomorphism, and brisk mitotic activity may occur either as a late stage within previ- ously indolent lesions or as an initial presentation, with the latter most commonly observed in African endemic cases. Demonstration of expression of the latency-associated nuclear antigen (LANA-1) of HHV-8 has proved to be a highly sensitive and specific marker of KS and other HHV-8-associated disorders such as multicentric Castleman disease and primary effusion lymphoma in both HIV-positive and HIV-negative patients (see Fig. 114.27 , left inset) 134,135 . Immunohistochemical detection of this antigen in vascular tumors is more diagnostically useful than detection of the HHV-8 genome by PCR since a few non-KS vascular tumors in both immuno- compromised and immunocompetent patients have been found to be positive for HHV-8 by PCR, but not for LANA-1 by immunohisto- chemical staining, presumably due to detection of HHV-8 within blood cells circulating through the tumors 134 . Histologically, patch stage KS must be distin- guished from stasis changes, well-differentiated angiosarcoma, and benign vascular proliferations and tumors; positivity for LANA-1 points to the diagnosis of KS. Histologically, the most important differential diagnostic consid- erations in nodular stage KS are KHE, spindle cell hemangioma, and moderately differentiated angiosarcoma, all of which are negative for LANA-1 of HHV-8. Although KS and spindle cell hemangioma are both characterized by proliferations of spindle cells, KS lacks the cavernous spaces of the latter. KHE is almost exclusively a disease of infancy and childhood and is distinguished from KS by a strongly lobular archi- tecture and lack of plasma cell infiltrates. Angiosarcoma is charac- terized by endothelial atypia and mitotic activity, both absent in KS. Late-stage KS may both clinically and histologically resemble pseudo- Kaposi sarcoma, i.e. acroangiodermatitis of Mali that is related to chronic venous insufficiency and Stewart–Bluefarb syndrome that can be associated with an arteriovenous malformation. These reactive, hyperplastic entities differ from KS in that the hyperplasia can be seen to derive from pre-existing vasculature and staining for HHV-8 is negative. Late-stage KS lesions can also be confused histologically with a number of non-vascular spindle cell sarcomas such as fibrosarcoma and leiomyosarcoma. In these cases, demonstration of CD31 immuno- reactivity helps confirm the vascular differentiation of KS. Other entities that can mimic KS clinically but which can be easily distinguished on the basis of histologic features include cutaneous metastases, leukemia or lymphoma cutis, venous and lymphatic malfor- mations, and the cutaneous manifestations of polyarteritis nodosa and erythema elevatum diutinum. Cryotherapy must usually be sufficiently vigorous to cause epidermal ulceration, and the resulting scar seems to replace the vascular proliferation of KS. Extensive, multi- focal disease often requires systemic treatment (see below). Radiation therapy is an option for multifocal, but relatively localized, cutaneous KS. Reported regimens include single-dose radiation (8 to 12 Gy) delivered to an extended field and total skin electron beam therapy (4 Gy fractions weekly) for 6 to 8 weeks (see Ch. 139 ). Radiation therapy also plays a role in the treatment of localized oral KS, but may have a briefer effect in AIDS-related KS than in classic KS 138 . Rapidly progressive KS (defined by development of 10 or more new cutaneous lesions per month), pulmonary KS, symptomatic visceral involvement, and significant lymphedema are indications for systemic chemotherapy. Liposomal anthracyclines, paclitaxel, and vinblastine are used singly or in combination; less often vincristine, gemcitabine, vinorelbine, etoposide, and/or bleomycin are administered 139,140 . High-dose interferon- α is sometimes employed, but its use is frequently limited by side effects 141 . Immunomodulatory drugs (IMiDs) that inhibit growth of blood vessels such as pomalidomide have also been used successfully for cutaneous and oral KS. Additional potential therapies include sirolimus (see below) and tyrosine kinase inhibitors (e.g. pazopanib). As noted previously, flares of KS can occur as a manifestation of IRIS (see Ch. 78 ), but this does not necessarily translate into a poor prognosis. Organ transplant patients with KS pose a particular therapeutic challenge, that of balancing the risk of graft rejection with the benefit of improvement in KS. In addition to reduction of immunosup- pression 142 , substitution of sirolimus for cyclosporine can also lead to clinical improvement of KS. In 15 renal transplant recipients, this substitution led to resolution of all of the KS lesions in all of the patients, both clinically (by 3 months) and histologically (by 6 months). The authors observed neither episodes of rejection nor changes in kidney graft function 143 . This observation has been independently corroborated by additional studies, albeit not always with equally impressive response rates 144 . It is not yet clear if the beneficial effect of sirolimus reflects lessened immunosuppression or possibly a more direct antitumor effect related to inhibition of HHV-8-induced effects (e.g. PI3K and AKT phosphorylation) 120 . Organ transplant patients with KS also respond to conventional local and systemic therapies used in other forms of KS. The original description of epithelioid hemangioendothelioma (EHE) incorporated this definition as these tumors can give rise to metastases but their biologic behavior may be relatively indolent 145 . The WHO and ISSVA have recently reclassified EHE as a malignant, rather than intermediate or borderline, vascular tumor. Only angiosarcoma shares that designation (see Table 114.1 ) 71,72 , although EHE is clearly associated with a better prognosis than classic angiosarcoma. Epidemiology EHE typically arises in adults, but in a younger age group than angio- sarcoma 146 . Occurrence in preadolescent children is exceedingly rare. Unlike angiosarcoma, women appear to be affected slightly more frequently than men. Pathogenesis EHE is a clonal neoplastic proliferation of endothelial cells. Most classical cases have a t(1;3)(p36.3;q25) translocation which generates a WWTR1–CAMTA1 fusion protein that is likely an early causative event in oncogenesis 147–149 . WWTR1 (3q25) encodes a transcriptional coactivator 150 while CAMTA1 (1p36) encodes a calmodulin-binding transcription activator 151,152 . There is a WWTR1–CAMTA1 fusion- negative subset of EHE that arises primarily in young adults; compared to classic EHE, more well-developed vascular structures and voluminous eosinophilic cytoplasm are present 153 . This subset contains an alter- native gene fusion, YAP1-TFE3 153 . To date, the WWTR1–CAMTA1 and YAP1–TFE3 fusions have not yet been detected in other neoplasms, in particular the morphologic mimics of EHE such as epithelioid angiosarcoma, epithelioid sarcoma- like hemangioendothelioma, and epithelioid hemangioma. However, it is not yet certain that these fusions are unique to EHE 147,148 . Notably, both the WWTR1–CAMTA1 and YAP1–TFE3 gene fusions are reliably detected by FISH and/or RT-PCR 154 . Clinical features Most tumors present as a slightly painful mass within deep soft tissues, but lesions can develop in the skin, viscera, or bone and are multifocal in up to 50% of patients 155 . Skin involvement is usually associated with an underlying soft tissue or bone tumor, but purely cutaneous examples do occur 145 , primarily on the extremities. Skin tumors can be multi- nodular, and they need to be distinguished from cutaneous metastasis from a visceral primary tumor 156 . Skin tumors can be multi- nodular, and they need to be distinguished from cutaneous metastasis from a visceral primary tumor 156 . Some cases are closely associated with or arise from a vessel, usually a vein. Occlusion of that vessel may lead to secondary symptoms (e.g. edema, thrombophlebitis). Overall, ~30% of patients develop metastases within the regional lymph nodes, lung, liver, or bone, and < 50% of patients with metas- tases have died of their disease. One study of 30 patients suggested that dermal tumors may have a better prognosis than more deeply seated lesions 145 . Pathology Similar to its more common counterparts involving soft tissue and bone, cutaneous EHE has an infiltrative growth pattern of epithelioid tumor cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm that form poorly canalized nests and cords within a distinctive myxohyaline stroma ( Fig. 114.28 ). An important clue to their endothelial origin is the presence of small cords and nests of endothelial cells forming small intracytoplasmic vacuoles as a sign of primitive vascular differentiation. An angiocentric growth pattern may be present, but is less commonly observed in cutaneous tumors. Unlike epithelioid heman- gioma, inflammation is sparse. Mitotic rate is variable and only weakly correlates with clinical outcome 145 . The tumor cells of EHE are positive for endothelial markers such as ERG, CD31, and CD34 and may also be positive for podoplanin, LYVE-1, and Prox1 (at least focally), suggesting lymphatic or mixed lymphatic–blood vascular differentiation 157,158 . Electron microscopy shows that EHE cells, unlike normal endothelial cells, contain abundant cytoplasmic intermediate filaments 159 . These filaments can cause immunopositivity for cytokeratins and/or smooth muscle antigen, leading to misdiagnosis 146 . Differential diagnosis The differential diagnosis is broad and includes epithelioid sarcoma, metastatic signet ring adenocarcinoma, melanoma, and epithelioid angiosarcoma. An essential criterion for diagnosis of EHE is immuno- histochemical evidence of endothelial differentiation 145 . Treatment Appropriate therapy involves wide local excision without adjuvant chemotherapy or radiotherapy, given the typically low-grade nature of these tumors. Regional lymph nodes should also be evaluated since these represent a common site for metastases. Anecdotally, stabilization of disease has been observed with interferon, celecoxib, and thalidomide 150 . Updated clinical practice guidelines were published in 2021 160 . Epidemiology Angiosarcomas are unusual neoplasms that occur more often in White men and develop primarily in middle-aged or older adults, with the highest incidence in individuals > 70 years of age 161 . Those rare examples that occur during childhood or adolescence are more likely to arise in or around viscera (especially the heart or pericardium) 162 or in association with other disease states 163 , including chronic or congenital lymphedema, chronic radiodermatitis, and immunosuppression. Pathogenesis Angiosarcomas are clonal proliferations of malignantly transformed cells expressing endothelial differentiation. When compared with other sarcomas, distinct upregulation of vascular-specific receptor tyrosine kinase genes, including TIE1 , KDR , FLT1 and TEK , has been observed in angiosarcomas 164 . Furthermore, high-level MYC amplifi- cation (chromosome 8q24) is consistently seen in radiation-induced and lymphedema-associated angiosarcomas 165,166 . MYC amplification leads to upregulation of the miR-17-92 cluster, which downregulates thrombospondin-1, a potent inhibitor of angiogenesis 167 . The WWTR1 – CAMTA1 gene fusion typically seen in EHE has not been detected in angiosarcomas, including epithelioid angiosarcomas 148 . Mechanisms underlying the association between chronic lymphedema and angio- sarcoma remain uncertain. Theories include induction of neoplastic change by unknown carcinogens in accumulated lymphatic fluid and the idea that areas with chronic lymphedema are “immunologically privileged sites” due to loss of afferent lymphatic connections. Radiotherapy has been shown to be an independent risk factor for angiosarcoma development, best exemplified in breast cancer patients (see below). Environmental chemical exposures linked to angiosarcoma, particularly of the liver, include vinyl chloride, thorium dioxide, arsenic, radium, and anabolic steroids 168 . Lastly, neither HHV-8 infection nor cumulative sun exposure appears to be associated with angiosarcoma. Approximately 70% of these tumors occur in patients over 40 years of age, with the highest incidence in those > 70 years of age. About 50% involve the head and neck ( Fig. 114.29 ). More advanced lesions are violaceous nodules that bleed easily and may ulcerate. The area of involvement spreads centrifugally, eventually covering large portions of the head and neck. The prognosis is invariably poor, with a less than 15% survival over a 5-year period 161 . More than 90% of all angio- sarcomas associated with lymphedema arise after mastectomy and lymph node dissection (Stewart–Treves syndrome). In these cases, the inner aspect of the upper arm is the most common site of involvement. Other forms of chronic lymphedema are associated with angiosarcoma, including congenital, filarial, traumatic, and idiopathic. The duration of lymphedema prior to appearance of angiosarcoma ranges from 5 to 25 years. Even though the incidence is very low ( < 0.05% in a recent survey of breast cancer patients) 169 , the greater use of breast-sparing surgery paired with irradiation has translated into an increase in post-irradi- ation sarcomas. The latter arise within breast parenchyma and overlying skin, with an average post-treatment interval of 6 years. Post-irradiation angiosarcomas appear as infiltrative plaques or nodules in or near the area of irradiated tissue and share the poor prognosis of all forms of angiosarcoma ( Fig. 114.30 ). Angiosarcomas of skin and soft tissue have also been reported in association with benign and malignant nerve sheath tumors 170 , defunctionalized arteriovenous shunts in renal transplant patients 171 , long-term exposure to various foreign materials 172 , xeroderma pigmen- tosum 173 , and bilateral retinoblastoma 174 . MRI, which shows a nonspecific decreased or variable signal intensity in T1 images, an increased signal in T2 images, and enhancement with gadolinium, is more useful than CT in accurately delineating the extent of local disease, including involvement of neurovascular structures and joints. It is also the imaging modality of choice for evaluating tumor response to preoperative radiation or chemotherapy. Pathology Angiosarcomas involving the skin, although highly variable in degree of endothelial differentiation both between and within individual tumors, do not vary in histology as a class; the latter includes those of the “usual type” not associated with lymphedema, those associated with chronic lymphedema, and those associated with chronic radioder- matitis. Well-differentiated areas display an anastomosing network of sinusoidal vessels, often bloodless, lined by a single layer of endothelial cells of slight to moderate nuclear atypia. These exhibit a highly infil- trative pattern, splitting apart collagen bundles and groups of adipose cells. In less well-differentiated areas, the endothelial cells with more pronounced nuclear pleomorphism and mitotic activity pile up and form papillary projections ( Fig. 114.31 ). In poorly differentiated areas, luminal formation may be non-apparent and mitotic activity may be high, mimicking other high-grade sarcomas, carcinoma, or melanoma. Hemorrhage and blood-filled cavities may be present. Most angiosarcomas stain positively for CD31, CD34, ERG, c-MYC, and Fli-1 175–177 , with CD31 and ERG generally considered the most useful markers. These so-called “epithelioid angiosarcomas” consist of large, rounded cells with prominent eosinophilic nucleoli in which the only morphologic evidence of vascular differentiation may be the presence of occasional intracytoplasmic vacuoles. Cytokeratin positivity is present in about one-third of epithelioid angiosarcomas 180,181 , making distinction from carcinoma problematic. Fortunately, this distinction can be accom- plished by demonstration of coexistent CD31 and/or ERG expression. The proportion of purely epithelioid cutaneous angiosarcomas appears to be higher among pediatric cases (90%) compared to adult cases (30%) 182 . Differential diagnosis Early recognition and histologic diagnosis are crucial in the treatment of angiosarcoma. In sites of previous radiation, it can be difficult to distin- guish angiosarcomas from atypical vascular lesions. Well-differentiated angiosarcomas, which display only slight cytologic atypia despite their high-grade biologic behavior, may also closely resemble micro- cystic lymphatic malformation. Other vascular neoplasms that must be distinguished from angiosarcoma histologically include PILA, RHE, epithelioid hemangioendothelioma, and KHE/tufted angioma. Intravascular proliferation of atypical endothelial cells is not a feature of KS and HHV-8 is negative in angiosarcoma. Nuclear staining for c-MYC can be useful for distinguishing angiosarcoma (positive in the majority of cases) from its mimickers (negative). Distinguishing post- radiation atypical vascular lesions of the skin from radiation-induced angiosarcoma of the breast can sometimes be challenging ( Table 114.4 ). Treatment Surgical excision with wide margins is indicated. Even with negative margins by histologic examination, the recurrence rate and chance of metastatic disease are high. This may in part reflect the tendency for multifocality. Systemic therapies are limited and include taxanes ( + / − radiotherapy) and anthracyclines 183,184 . There are also isolated reports of the successful use of IMiDs, targeted therapies (e.g. pazopanib), and immune checkpoint inhibitors. Radiotherapy alone may be palliative, but does not improve survival. Current evidence supports division of these tumors into two major disparate categories: (1) the glomus tumor proper, a cellular lesion that tends to be well circumscribed, solitary, and subungual; and (2) the glomuvenous malformation (GVM), a frequently multifocal lesion, traditionally termed a “glomangioma”, that most commonly presents in infants or children and histologically resembles a venous malformation in which lesional vessels are rimmed by glomus cells. Epidemiology Solitary glomus tumors can occur at any age, but are most common in young adults. Although these tumors in general show no sex predi- lection, subungual lesions are more common in women. GVMs are less common (accounting for 10%–20% of all glomus cell lesions) and typically present in children without sex predilection; many are evident at birth. Pathogenesis The

Epidemiology Solitary glomus tumors can occur at any age, but are most common in young adults. Although these tumors in general show no sex predi- lection, subungual lesions are more common in women. GVMs are less common (accounting for 10%–20% of all glomus cell lesions) and typically present in children without sex predilection; many are evident at birth. Pathogenesis The fact that the most common site of occurrence of glomus tumors (the subungual region of the finger) corresponds to one of the densest areas of distribution of the normal glomus body suggests that many glomus tumors represent neoplastic proliferations originating from pre-existing normal glomus cell populations. However, the occasional occurrence of glomus tumors at sites where normal glomus bodies may not be found, including bone, gastrointestinal tract, trachea, and nerve, suggests that some glomus tumors may arise from pluripotent mesen- chymal cells or even ordinary smooth muscle cells. Despite the shared presence of benign glomus cells, glomus tumors and GVMs differ widely in clinical and histopathologic features and are likely unrelated in pathogenesis. The resemblance to venous malforma- tions plus the early presentation of GVMs strongly supports their now widely accepted malformative etiology as well as abandonment of the traditional term glomangioma . Familial GVM is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion, with patients tending to have multiple lesions that continue to appear later in life, sometimes in response to trauma 186 . At least 40 different germline mutations in GLMN , which resides on chromosome 1p22.1 and encodes glomulin, have been detected; glomulin may function as an immunophilin ligand 187–190 . In one study, the most common GLMN mutation was present in ~45% of families 191 . The frequent multi- focality, incomplete but high (~90%) penetrance, and delayed devel- opment in familial GVM suggest a paradominant inheritance pattern in which somatic mutations likely serve as “second hits”. Interestingly, in a recent study of 28 cases of familial GVM, second hits were identified in 16 lesions. Although these included a few intragenic mutations and deletions as well as one interstitial deletion containing GLMN , the majority of identified mutations represented acquired uniparental isodisomy, with a breakpoint region near the centromere at 1p13.1– 1p12. It is assumed that somatic mutations within or affecting GLMN are the likely cause of sporadic GVMs. Knock-out mouse studies have shown that glomulin is essential for the viability and appropriate development of the embryonic vasculature during vascular remodeling 193 . In embryonic and adult mice, glomulin is expressed primarily in vascular smooth muscle cells 194 . Clinical features The glomus tumor is a benign lesion that usually presents in young adults (20–40 years of age) as a small ( < 2 cm), blue–red papule or nodule in the deep dermis or subcutis of the distal upper or lower extremities. They are tender to touch, and may be associated with severe paroxysmal pain in response to temperature changes and pressure. The hand, especially the nail beds and palm, is most commonly affected ( Fig. 114.33 ), but cutaneous lesions can also occur at other sites. Unusual extracutaneous glomus tumors have been reported in the gastrointestinal tract, bone, mediastinum, trachea, mesentery, cervix, and vagina. Extremely rare instances of malignant transformation within glomus tumors, with documented metastasis, have been described 195 . They are generally asymptomatic lesions that vary widely in appearance, from multiple, soft, red to blue nodules that may be widely distributed or confluent to multifocal, pink to deep blue plaque-like lesions ( Figs. 114.35 & 114.36 ); occasionally, single punctate lesions are seen. Although they clinically resemble venous malformations, GVMs differ in appearance from the latter in a number of aspects 196 : they tend to be more nodular or cobblestone-like in appearance, more blue and less compressible, and they do not swell with exercise or dependency. Lesions typically thicken and become more blue in color with time. Although less painful than the glomus tumor, GVMs may be tender to palpation, and bouts of pain may occur in association with menstruation and pregnancy. All reported cases have behaved in a benign fashion. Pathology The common glomus tumor is a generally well-circumscribed prolif- eration of solid sheets and clusters of uniform glomus cells focally clustering around a variable number of capillary-sized, endothelium- lined vessels ( Fig. 114.37 ). The stroma can be myxoid or hyalinized and may contain numerous small nerve twigs. A dense fibrous pseudo- capsule may be present. The glomus cells are distinctive in their uniformly rounded or polygonal shape, centrally placed and rounded nuclei, and pale eosinophilic cytoplasm. PAS staining reveals basement membrane material around individual tumor cells. Mitotic figures may be present, but are normally configured. In that glomus cells represent modified smooth muscle cells with myofilaments, there is consistent expression of vimentin and muscle actin isoforms, and variably reported expression of desmin. Examples demonstrating gradual transition from rounded glomus cells to elongated, well-differentiated smooth muscle cells have been termed glomangiomyomas 197 . Although the great majority of glomus tumors display no significant cytologic atypia, some have atypical or frankly malignant features. It is likely that many cases of the so-called blue rubber bleb nevus syndrome, a familial disorder characterized by multiple venous malformations, actually represent examples of multiple GVMs. Treatment Solitary glomus tumors can be treated successfully by local surgical excision. Other options include electrodesiccation and sclerotherapy. GVMs are less amenable to surgery than are common glomus tumors, due to their more extensive and multifocal nature. In a series of large facial “glomangiomas” 196 , MRI was the best modality for definition of the extent of the lesions and their relationship to other anatomic structures. In this same series, surgical resection reduced the area of discoloration and improved facial contour, while sclerotherapy was less effective than for venous malformations 196 . Laser surgery employing CO 2 , KTP, Nd:YAG, and pulsed dye lasers may also be helpful. In a retrospective study of 17 patients with GVMs who were treated with dual wavelength pulsed dye–Nd:YAG laser therapy, a reduction of at least 60% was observed 196 . Residual lesions following subtotal resec- tions may slowly re-expand 196 . Epidemiology Infantile hemangiopericytomas are uncommon tumors that typically appear in the first year of life and are usually congenital. There is a male predominance by ~2 : 1. Examples in older children have occasionally been reported. Pathogenesis The frequent zonal pattern of myofibroblastic differentiation in infantile hemangiopericytomas has led to the proposal that infantile hemangio- pericytoma and infantile myofibromatosis may lie upon a continuous spectrum of myofibroblastic lesions 199 . In addition, a family of adult tumors with perivascular myoid differentiation has been described that overlaps histologically with infantile myofibromatosis and includes two newer entities, termed glomangiopericytoma and myopericytoma . Granter et al. 200 , in support of similar observations by Requena and colleagues 201 , have proposed that this widening spectrum of tumors and their distinctive cellular components might be better explained by derivation from a pluripotent periendothelial cell capable of differenti- ating along smooth muscle, pericytic, and glomus cell lines, rather than from myofibroblasts. Clinical features Infantile hemangiopericytomas are nodules that primarily occur in the subcutaneous and dermal tissues of the head and neck. Congenital examples may be alarming in size at birth or grow rapidly thereafter. Multicentric cases have been reported and have in some instances been misinterpreted as examples of distant metastasis. Although benign behavior appears to be the rule, large tumors may be problematic if they hemorrhage or threaten vital structures. Lesions in the tongue and in deeply seated sites, such as the mediastinum and abdomen, have been reported. Rare multisystemic forms in neonates may be lethal. Local recurrence after excision is common, although spontaneous tumor regression has also been documented. Pathology Infantile-type hemangiopericytomas, unlike the adult type, are usually dermal or subcutaneous in location and are often multilobulated. They typically show a biphasic growth pattern in which primitive hemangio- pericytomatous areas resembling the adult tumors (short spindle cells arranged around thin-walled, branching vessels) blend with less cellular areas containing plump myofibroblast-like cells set within a collagenous matrix. Focal necrosis and significant mitotic activity may be present, but are not indicative of poor prognosis. Differential diagnosis Infantile hemangiopericytomas demonstrate nonspecific clinical and radiologic features and require histologic examination for definitive diagnosis. They may be confused clinically with an infantile heman- gioma due to rapid postnatal growth, and large congenital lesions may suggest a rapidly involuting congenital hemangioma or infantile fibro- sarcoma. Further diagnostic considerations include infantile myofibro- matosis and subcutaneous pyogenic granuloma. Treatment Conservative treatment following establishment of the diagnosis via histologic examination is generally recommended given the potential for spontaneous regression. Complete surgical resection is a reasonable option in some cases, although there appears to be a conflicting tendency of these tumors to both locally recur and spontaneously regress. NEUROMAS Key features Traumatic neuroma  Develops at the site of previous trauma  Skin-colored papule or nodule that is often painful or sensitive  Circumscribed histologically, but not encapsulated  Regenerative proliferation of axons and Schwann cells within fibrous scar tissue Solitary circumscribed neuroma  Formerly known as “palisaded encapsulated neuroma”  Solitary papule or nodule, usually on the face of adults  Circumscribed histologically; partially or completely encapsulated  Compactly arranged fascicles of spindle cells with only vague palisading of nuclei Introduction Neuromas are proliferations of neural tissue in which the ratio of axons to Schwann cells is only slightly less than the normal 1 : 1 ratio. There are two major subtypes: traumatic (or amputation) neuroma and solitary circumscribed neuroma (SCN). Traumatic neuromas are complex regenerative proliferations of nerve fibers that follow injury. SCN, formerly known as palisaded encapsulated neuroma, is a benign peripheral nerve sheath tumor whose development is not preceded by apparent tissue injury. History The current view of traumatic neuroma was introduced by Huber and Lewis based on the concept of Wallerian degeneration. SCN was described by Reed and co-workers in 1972 4 . Epidemiology Traumatic neuromas are relatively uncommon but can occur at any age and in either sex. They are more prevalent in professions with a high probability of physical injuries. SCN develops spontaneously and gradually without obvious preceding trauma. These tumors appear during adulthood (mean age, 45 years), and there is no sex predispo- sition or association with known tumor predisposition syndromes 2–4 . Pathogenesis The term “neuroma” refers to a benign nerve sheath tumor charac- terized by a relatively balanced proliferation of Schwann cells and axons, resulting in an axon to Schwann cell ratio close to the normal 1 : 1 ratio 5 . As a result, their clinical relevance was poorly understood. Clinically, cutaneous neural tumors often look alike and most of them are benign. However, their correct diagnosis can be helpful in recognizing important clinical syndromes and this can contribute to better patient management 1 . CLASSIFICATION, TERMINOLOGY, AND HISTOGENESIS Cutaneous neural tumors can be classified into two major groups: those derived from peripheral nerves and those derived from ectopic or heterotopic neural tissue ( Table 115.1 ). The former group were classi- cally subdivided into true nerve sheath neoplasms and hamartomatous tumors, although this classification may be specious due to evidence that most hamartomas are driven by clonal expansion of a neoplastic cell population 2,3 . Cutaneous neural tumors tend to differentiate toward one or more elements of the nervous system; as a result, they recapitulate to varying degrees the morphogenesis of normal peripheral nerves. Therefore, knowledge of the organization of the normal peripheral nerve ( Fig. 115.1 ) is crucial to understanding the histogenesis of cutaneous neural tumors 2 . The basic element of a peripheral nerve is the nerve fiber, which is composed of an axon and its surrounding Schwann cell layer. A peripheral nerve can be compared to a conventional telephone cable, in which each axon and its surrounding Schwann cell layer correspond to a telephone wire and its insulation, respectively. Nerve fibers are bundled within nerve fascicles by the perineurium, a sheath composed of specialized perineurial cells (see Fig. 115.1 ). Inside the nerve fascicle, the space between individual nerve fibers is referred to as the endoneurium. The bundles of nerve fascicles are further encased in a supportive fibrous sheath called the epineurium. To a variable extent, this architectural arrangement is recognizable in many cutaneous neural neoplasms. The most important constituent cells are the Schwann cell, the perineurial cell, and the various nonspecific mesenchymal cells, such as fibroblasts and mast cells. These cells are capable of proliferation and malignant transformation. Other elements of

These cells are capable of proliferation and malignant transformation. Other elements of the peripheral nerve, which are cell parts or products (i.e. axons and myelin, respectively), cannot duplicate. Schwann cells are derived from the neural crest and perineurial cells appear to be modified fibroblasts of mesodermal origin. This difference in histogenesis is also reflected in the distinct antigenic expression of these cells. Schwann cells express S100 protein NEOPLASMS OF THE SKIN Traumatic neuromas represent exuberant proliferations of nerve fibers that develop in response to an extrinsic nerve injury. Ideally, a severed nerve is reestablished via an orderly growth of axons and proliferating Schwann cells from the proximal to the distal end of the nerve 6 . If the two nerve ends are not maintained in close apposition, the reparative process fails, resulting in a tangle of irregularly proliferating proximal nerve fascicles embedded within scar tissue. In SCN there is a coupled proliferation of Schwann cells and axons within the confinement of the perineurium. Its exact pathomechanism remains to be determined. Although a reactive process following minor tissue injury (e.g. facial acne) has been postulated, no definite traumatic origin has been demonstrated 2 . Clinical Features Traumatic neuromas are usually solitary, skin-colored or reddish purple, firm papules or nodules at sites of wounds, surgical scars, and amputations 7,8 ( Fig. 115.2 ). On the lower extremities, they may be multiple 7 . Early lesions are asymptomatic, but after a few months they gradually become painful, frequently with a lancinating character. Variable tingling and itching can be associated with the pain. In neonates and young infants, similar lesions may be located on the lateral surface of a normal digit, most commonly the ulnar side of the fifth digit. Such tumors, also referred to as “rudimentary supernu- merary digits”, have traditionally been regarded as traumatic neuromas secondary to amputation of supernumerary digits in utero 9 (see of a pre-existing supernumerary digit, leading some authors to propose that these lesions may represent true congenital malformations. SCNs present as asymptomatic, rubbery to firm, skin-colored to pink papules or nodules ranging in diameter from 2 to 6 mm 4 . Approximately 90% are located on the face, primarily around the nose, but they also occur on the cheek, chin, lips, and oral mucosa 10 . The remaining 10% occur elsewhere, including the trunk and extremities. In MEN2B, also referred to as multiple mucosal neuroma syndrome or MEN type 3, numerous soft, skin- or mucosa-colored papules and nodules appear on the eyelid margins, mucosal lips, tongue, and conjunctivae, as well as the nasal and laryngeal mucosae (see Fig. 63.2 ). Additional findings include pheochromocytomas, medullary carcinoma of the thyroid, gastrointestinal ganglioneuromatosis, rare perinasal cutaneous neuromas, and palpable foci of dermal hyperneury (see Table 63.2 ). Multiple mucocutaneous neuromas with a predilection for the face and distal extremities may also be a manifestation of the PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome (see Tables 63.3 & 63.4 ). Pathology Traumatic neuromas are usually well-circumscribed nodules located at any level of the dermis or the subcutis. They are encased by a fibrous sheath, although the distal end can be poorly defined. The constituent cells are Schwann cells and accompanying perineurial cells with spindle-shaped nuclei and cytoplasm. Special stains show several axons in an irregular, haphazard pattern 1,2 . SCNs present as well-circumscribed, ovoid or round nodules within the mid dermis, although some lesions may extend into the subcutis; occasionally, there is a multinodular, plexiform growth pattern. The tumor appears at least partially encapsulated by a thin connective tissue sheath composed of perineurial cells 10 ( Fig. 115.4 ). The parenchyma consists of interwoven fascicles of spindled cells. Fascicles are compactly and relatively uniformly arranged, occasionally separated by clefts. The stroma is relatively monomorphous, and in contrast to traumatic neuromas, there is no evidence of inflammation, granulation tissue, or scarring 5 . Neural and Neuroendocrine Neoplasms (Other than Neurofibromatosis) The nuclei of the spindle-shaped tumor cells are elongated and wavy with tapered ends and an evenly basophilic chromatin pattern. Occasionally, a parallel arrangement of the nuclei is present, but distinct palisading or Verocay body formation is unusual 11–13 . No appreciable nuclear pleomorphism or mitotic activity is observed. In contrast to schwannomas, abundant axons throughout the tumor nodules may be highlighted via special stains 11 ( Fig. 115.5 ). Mucosal neuromas in MEN2B consist of non-encapsulated, tortuous proliferations of nerve bundles with a prominent perineurium, while dermal hyperneury is characterized by an increased number of enlarged and haphazardly arranged dermal nerves. Epithelial sheath neuroma represents a more recently described entity in which there is hyper- plasia of mature nerve fascicles within the dermis (akin to dermal hyperneury), but each fascicle is surrounded by an aberrant sheath of squamous epithelium instead of normal perineurium; these features must be distinguished from perineural invasion by malignant tumors 14 . Differential Diagnosis The diagnosis of traumatic neuroma is usually suspected by the history of a painful or symptomatic papulonodule at a site of injury and is confirmed by pathologic examination. Clinically, SCNs may resemble a BCC, adnexal tumor, intradermal melanocytic nevus, or neurofi- broma (see Table 115.2 ). The diagnosis usually depends upon histologic examination (see Table 115.3 ). Treatment Surgical excision of traumatic neuromas is recommended, with an attempt to reposition the proximal nerve stump into a scar-free area 7 . SCNs are easily excised, and some can even be enucleated from the surrounding dermis or subcutaneous tissue 4 . There is no sex or racial predilection. Approximately 90% of schwannomas are solitary and occur sporadi- cally 2 . Multiple schwannomas can be a manifestation of neurofibroma- tosis type 2 (NF2) or schwannomatosis, with both disorders having a mosaic (segmental) form. Patients with NF2, an autosomal dominant disorder, can develop meningiomas and bilateral vestibular schwan- nomas (“acoustic neuromas”) (see Table 61.5 ) 2,16–19 . The latter tumors are unusual in schwannomatosis which is sporadic in the majority of patients (see below). Psammomatous melanotic schwannoma (also more recently referred to as “malignant melanotic schwannian tumor”) is a variant that typically arises from spinal and autonomic nerves 20 . This tumor may occur sporadically as well as in the setting of Carney complex (see Ch. 112 ). Primary cutaneous psammomatous melanotic schwannomas are exceedingly rare and appear to have a more indolent behavior than extracutaneous counterparts. Pathogenesis Because a schwannoma is a neoplastic proliferation of periaxonal or endoneurial Schwann cells, it develops as an encapsulated mass within the confines of the perineurium. Pathogenesis Because a schwannoma is a neoplastic proliferation of periaxonal or endoneurial Schwann cells, it develops as an encapsulated mass within the confines of the perineurium. Normal nerve fascicles are passively displaced to the periphery, with the bulk of the tumor appearing devoid of other normal peripheral nerve components 2 . Only after careful dissection can the attached nerve trunk be demonstrated. Loss of expression of merlin, the oncosuppressor protein encoded by NF2 21,22 , leads to the development of schwannomas. Somatic inacti- vating mutations in NF2 occur in 50%–75% of sporadic schwannomas, while germline inactivating mutations lead to NF2. Both inherited and sporadic (~40% of patients) schwannomatosis are associated with germline mutations in either SMARCB1 or LZTR1 , coupled with somatic biallelic inactivation of NF2 in each tumor 17–19 . The devel- opment of psammomatous melanotic schwannomas, either sporadi- cally or in association with Carney complex, is related to inactivation of PRKAR1A . Clinical Features Schwannomas present as solitary, soft, skin-colored to pink or yellow, smooth-surfaced, dermal or subcutaneous papulonodules ( Fig. 115.6 ). In general, their diameter ranges between 0.5 and 3 cm 23 . They are most commonly found on the flexor aspect of extremities along a larger nerve trunk, followed by the head and neck region 24 . Tumors are usually asymptomatic, but occasionally pain and tenderness occur, in particular if forceful movements place the attached nerve under tension. Motor disturbances and paresthesias are extremely rare 25 . Pathology Schwannomas are well-circumscribed, nodular or ovoid tumors composed of differentiated Schwann cells. They are located in the deep dermis or subcutis and are almost always encapsulated. The tumors are composed of hypercellular (also called Antoni A-type tissue) and hypocellular (Antoni B-type tissue) areas 2 . Within areas of Antoni A-type tissue, there is proliferation of spindle cells with indistinct cytoplasmic contours and uniform nuclei 26 . Nuclear palisading is a typical finding and palisaded nuclei arranged in double rows can result in characteristic “Verocay bodies” 2,3 ( Fig. 115.7 ). Mitotic figures are absent or rare. Antoni B-type tissue areas have characteristic large, irregularly spaced vessels with thickened fibrotic walls, as well as variable degrees of

Within areas of Antoni A-type tissue, there is proliferation of spindle cells with indistinct cytoplasmic contours and uniform nuclei 26 . Nuclear palisading is a typical finding and palisaded nuclei arranged in double rows can result in characteristic “Verocay bodies” 2,3 ( Fig. 115.7 ). Mitotic figures are absent or rare. Antoni B-type tissue areas have characteristic large, irregularly spaced vessels with thickened fibrotic walls, as well as variable degrees of edematous, mucinous, cystic, xanthomatous, and fibrotic changes within the hypocellular stroma. Such degenerative changes, which are often associated with some degree of cytologic atypia, are the predominant feature in so-called ancient schwannomas . These latter tumors should not be confused with cellular schwannomas , a histologic subtype composed largely of Antoni A-type tissue but lacking Verocay bodies, that rarely occur in the skin 27 . Axons are sparse in schwannomas and may be best detected at the tumor’s periphery in proximity to nerve attachments 28 . Additional less common subtypes of schwannomas include plexiform, epithelioid (frequently associated with loss of SMARCB1 expression), and microcystic/reticular schwannomas 29–31 . In psammomatous melanotic schwannoma, a mixture of spindled and epithelioid cells that resembles syncytial tissue is seen. The cells have variable pleomorphism and nuclear atypia, and focal areas may demonstrate typical neural organization, i.e. nuclear palisading and whorl formation. Melanin deposition is often heavy, obscuring cytologic details. Psammomatous structures, consisting of eosinophilic laminated and whorled structures with variable calcification, are a frequent and characteristic finding. The cells stain positively for S100 protein and SOX10 and in psammomatous melanotic schwannomas also stain positively for Melan-A, HMB-45, and tyrosinase 32 . NEUROFIBROMA Key features Solitary type  Skin-colored to tan–violet papule or nodule  May be pedunculated or have the “buttonhole” sign  Predilection for the trunk and head  Spindle cell proliferation with variable mixture of the components of the peripheral nerve, including residual axons  Fibrosis and mucinous changes are common Plexiform type  Pathognomonic of NF1  Large, occasionally pigmented, bag-like mass  Favors the trunk and proximal extremities  The plexiform variant has similar cytologic constituents as the solitary or sporadic type, but carries a risk of malignant transformation Introduction Neurofibromas are benign nerve sheath tumors composed of a complex proliferation of neuromesenchymal cells (Schwann cells, perineurial cells, fibroblasts, and mast cells), along with residual interspersed axons 2 . Cutaneous neurofibromas are common, especially as solitary lesions. The presence of multiple neurofibromas raises the possibility of one of the several types of neurofibromatosis, including the mosaic form (see Ch. 61 ). Plexiform neurofibromas are pathognomonic of NF1. History Neurofibromas were originally described as fibrous tumors by von Recklinghausen. A neuroectodermal origin was suggested by Verocay and eventually confirmed by immunohistochemical and ultrastructural studies. Epidemiology Localized cutaneous neurofibromas are the most common peripheral nerve sheath tumors, and have neither age nor sex preference. Diffuse and plexiform neurofibromas are considered to be of congenital origin. Pathogenesis Neurofibromas differ from schwannomas in that several cell types are involved in their histogenesis. Regardless of the histologic subtype of neurofibromas (e.g. localized cutaneous, diffuse, plexiform), the basic process is proliferation of the entire “neuromesenchyme”, which includes Schwann cells, perineurial cells, endoneurial fibroblasts, and mast cells 2 . Axons are easily found in neurofibromas, although the axon to Schwann cell ratio is significantly lower than the normal 1 : 1 ratio. Within a neurofibroma, only a subpopulation of Schwann cells is neoplastic, carrying a clonal biallelic inactivation of NF1 . Nullizygosity ( NF1 − / − ) of Schwann cells is a prerequisite, but is not sufficient, for neurofibroma formation; the latter may require the promoting effect of

Within a neurofibroma, only a subpopulation of Schwann cells is neoplastic, carrying a clonal biallelic inactivation of NF1 . Nullizygosity ( NF1 − / − ) of Schwann cells is a prerequisite, but is not sufficient, for neurofibroma formation; the latter may require the promoting effect of a NF1 + / − microenvironment, in particular NF1 -haploinsufficient mast cells 33 (see Fig. 61.2 ). The pathogenesis of sporadic cutaneous neurofi- bromas remains unclear, as most of them show retained expression of neurofibromin 34 . Clinical Features Clinically, localized cutaneous neurofibromas present as asymp- tomatic, skin-colored, soft or rubbery papulonodules. They range in size from 0.2 to 2 cm and may become pedunculated 2 . These tumors grow slowly and the “buttonhole” sign is often present 2 , i.e. the tumor is easily invaginated. Approximately 10% of patients develop multiple localized cutaneous neurofibromas, with some of these patients having one of the several types of neurofibromatosis (see Ch. 61 ). Additional clinicopathologic subtypes of neurofibroma include diffuse, intraneural, and plexiform variants. The diffuse subtype may present as indurated or soft nodules and plaques, while the intraneural variant presents as solitary fusiform masses. Except for plexiform neurofibromas, these subtypes rarely undergo malignant change. Plexiform neurofibromas are especially important because they are considered pathognomonic of NF1 and carry a significant risk of trans- formation into malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors (MPNSTs) 2 . These neurofibromas affect large segments of a nerve, distorting it into a “bag of worms”, and present as baggy or pedunculated subcutaneous masses that can feel rope-like on palpation and are frequently hyperpig- mented ( Fig. 115.8 ). Involvement of an entire extremity leads to elephan- tiasis neuromatosa. Recognition and correct patient management is crucial in these cases, especially in subtle forms of NF1, where the other cutaneous stigmata may not be obvious. The exact incidence of malignant transformation is not known but it is estimated to occur in 2%–30% of NF1 patients, depending on disease severity in the population studied 2 . Pathology Neurofibromas are poor- to well-circumscribed, nodular or oblong tumors that can be located anywhere within the dermis and subcutis 2,3 . Even when localized grossly, they lack a capsule and tend to infiltrate surrounding soft tissues. The common localized cutaneous variant usually has its center in the superficial dermis, creating a dome-shaped or polypoid elevation of its surface ( Fig. 115.9 ). The tumor is composed of a fine fibrillary lattice of haphazardly arranged slender spindle cells 35 , and the stroma can be variably vascular, fibrotic, edematous or myxomatous. In addition to Schwann cells and perineurial cells, plump fibroblasts and mast cells are present. Vague palisading of nuclei may occur, occasionally with true Verocay body formation, and can be regarded as hybrid neurofibroma/schwannoma tumors 2,35 . Mitotic figures are absent or rare. By utilizing special stains, rare scattered axons may be demonstrated, as in all other variants. The diffuse variant lacks a well-defined growth pattern as it infiltrates the dermis and subcutis; characteristically, Meissner body-like struc- tures may be observed in the deeper parts of these tumors. Intraneural neurofibromas are well-circumscribed masses along a peripheral nerve, being encapsulated by perineurium or epineurium 2 . The neoplastic tissue progressively expands within the nerve branch then extends into the surrounding soft tissue, resulting in the frequent combination of intraneural and diffuse extraneural growth patterns. MPNSTs may develop from pre-existing plexiform neurofibromas via deletions of the CDKN2A / CDKN2B locus. text: MPNSTs may develop from pre-existing plexiform neurofibromas via deletions of the CDKN2A / CDKN2B locus. While cytological atypia alone in neurofibromas is not worrisome (“ancient neurofibromas”), malignant transformation is heralded by an intermediate histopathologic step (so-called “atypical neurofibromatous neoplasm of uncertain biologic potential” [ANNUBP]), which is defined by a variable combination of nuclear atypia, increased cellularity, and increased mitotic activity 36 . Differential Diagnosis The clinical differential diagnosis of a solitary neurofibroma includes an intradermal melanocytic nevus, schwannoma, soft fibroma, and fibrolipoma (see Table 115.2 ). The majority of solitary or sporadic neurofibromas have similar clinical and histologic features to the multiple papular neurofibromas seen in patients with NF1. Plexiform neurofibromas with overlying hyperpigmentation and hypertrichosis can resemble congenital melanocytic nevi. As the latter can undergo neurotization and may be accompanied by satellite lesions, exami- nation of the patient for Lisch nodules, axillary freckling, and café-au- lait macules is essential. Histologically, a plexiform neurofibroma must be differentiated from other plexiform tumors, including plexiform schwannoma, plexiform SCN, and desmoplastic melanoma. Treatment Neurofibromas are usually treated by simple excision. The evaluation and management of plexiform neurofibromas and neurofibromatosis is discussed in Chapter 61 . Pathology Nerve sheath myxoma is a well-defined, lobular or plexiform neoplasm that is usually located in the reticular dermis ( Fig. 115.12 ). It often appears encapsulated by a compression of the surrounding fibrous tissue 39 . There is a hypocellular myxoid stroma with rare scattered spindled, stellate, or dendritic cells. The cells usually have scant pale cytoplasm with indis- tinct cytoplasmic contours and hyperchromatic, ovoid, or angulated nuclei 39,41 . Nucleoli are small and mitotic figures are rare or absent. On occasion, multinucleated giant cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm can be identified. Histochemically, the myxoid stroma stains strongly positive for acidic mucopolysaccharides (see Ch. 46 ) 39 . In a minority of cases, scattered neurofilament-positive axons may be detected 41 . The tumor cells are positive for S100 protein, SOX10, and collagen type IV and the capsule has a weak and discontinuous expression of epithelial membrane antigen (EMA) and other perineurial markers 2,41 . Cellular neurothekeomas are composed of ill-defined multilobular masses or fascicles in the reticular dermis 40 ( Fig. 115.13 ). In some cases, the growth pattern can be frankly infiltrative or dissecting without any hint of a residual capsule, and there may be involvement of the super- ficial subcutis 42,43 . Cytologically, the predominant cell types are epithe- lioid or polygonal cells with ample eosinophilic cytoplasm and round nuclei with an open chromatin pattern 40,43 . Many cells have prominent nucleoli. Less often, the constituent cells are spindle-shaped with hyper- chromatic nuclei, resembling those observed in nerve sheath myxomas. Mitotic figures are often present but are usually normal morphologi- cally. Rare cases with increased mitotic figures and cytologic atypia have been reported 43 . The stroma can be markedly fibrotic or even hyalinized. There is no detectable connection with peripheral nerves. The tumor does not have a consistent immunohistochemical profile, with the nonspecific marker NKI/C3 expressed in essentially all cases. Expression of PGP9.5 (neuron-specific peptide), microphthalmia transcription factor (MITF; see Ch. 65 ), and smooth muscle actin may be observed in individual cases. Importantly, expression of

The exceedingly rare “cutaneous non-neural granular cell tumor” is a morphologically indis- tinguishable neoplasm that lacks expression of S100 protein or SOX10 and has frequent ALK (anaplastic lymphoma kinase gene) rearrange- ments 46 . Occasionally, granular cell change may occur in a variety of unrelated neoplasms as a secondary phenomenon (see below) 47 . History This tumor was originally thought by Abrikossoff, who used the term “granular cell myoblastoma”, to be derived from muscle 48 . Feyrter first suggested a neural origin. Epidemiology Granular cell tumor is a relatively rare tumor that occurs primarily in adults (age 30–50 years) and favors men and African-Americans. Up to 10% of patients have multiple lesions, and ~70% of tumors are located in the head and neck region, including 25% on the tongue 2 . Other common locations are the breast (5%–15%) and proximal extremities. Visceral lesions may develop in the gastrointestinal and upper respi- ratory tracts. Pathogenesis The neural origin of granular cell tumor has been a subject of debate, but immunohistochemical and ultrastructural studies have clearly proven its schwannian differentiation. Granular cells express S100 protein, SOX10, and CD57 (a neuronally expressed adhesion molecule), like Schwann cells 49–51 . Loss-of-function mutations in the V-ATPase accessory genes ATP6AP1 (60%) and ATP6AP2 (10%) have been detected in the majority of cutaneous and extracutaneous neural granular cell tumors, irrespective of anatomic site and biological behavior 52,53 . How inactivation of these membrane proton pumps leads to accumulation of lysosomes and tumorigenesis requires further investigation. Multiple cutaneous granular cell tumors can be seen in patients with RASopathies such as NF1, Noonan syndrome, and Noonan syndrome with multiple lentigines (LEOPARD syndrome), thus implying a role of the RAS/MAPK pathway in their pathogenesis 54 (see Fig. 55.4 ). Clinical Features A granular cell tumor presents as an asymptomatic or occasionally tender or pruritic, skin-colored to brownish-red, firm dermal or subcutaneous papulonodule, ranging in diameter from 0.5 to 3 cm. Occasionally, the surface will be ulcerated or verrucous. Granular cell tumors are slowly growing and in general have a benign behavior. Rarely, malignant behavior is observed (local infiltration or metastasis), more often when the tumor arises from a visceral or deep location. Malignant granular tumors may develop de novo or via malignant transformation of a pre-existing benign lesion 55 . Pathology The dermis contains a poorly circumscribed nodule composed of polygonal, pale-staining cells that may infiltrate into the adjacent subcutis. The cells have abundant, granular, faintly eosinophilic cytoplasm with round, dark nuclei ( Fig.

Pathology The dermis contains a poorly circumscribed nodule composed of polygonal, pale-staining cells that may infiltrate into the adjacent subcutis. The cells have abundant, granular, faintly eosinophilic cytoplasm with round, dark nuclei ( Fig. 115.14 ) 56 . Characteristic larger cytoplasmic granules are called pustulo-ovoid bodies. With the PAS reaction, the granules are positive, but they are diastase-resistant. Occasionally, a perineurial growth pattern is present; however, the tumor is devoid of axons. Increased numbers of mast cells are present in some lesions, and the overlying epidermis is frequently hyper- plastic. Rarely, a plexiform growth pattern has been described 56 . Histopathologic criteria predictive of aggressive behavior are not well established, but may include necrosis, increased mitotic rate, spindling of the cells, high nuclear : cytoplasmic ratio, vesicular nuclei, and nuclear pleomorphism 2,55,57 . True (neural) granular cell tumors express S100 protein, SOX10, PGP9.5 (neuron-specific peptide), and nerve growth factor receptor. The cells may stain positively for CD68 and NKI/C3, but are negative for the lineage-restricted histiocytic marker CD163 as well as melanocytic differentiation markers Melan-A and HMB-45. There may be diffuse nuclear reactivity for MITF and TFE3, posing a diagnostic challenge with TFE3 -rearranged tumors and PEComas 58,59 . Differential Diagnosis The clinical differential diagnosis of lingual lesions includes an irritation fibroma, verruca, and squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). Elsewhere, this tumor may resemble a dermatofibroma, regressing verruca, or adnexal neoplasm (see Table 115.2 ). Granular cell tumors can induce consid- erable pseudoepitheliomatous (pseudocarcinomatous) hyperplasia of the overlying epithelium, and superficial biopsy samples have been mistaken for SCC, especially on the tongue 60 . A variety of epithelial and mesenchymal neoplasms can show granular cell change, including BCCs, leiomyomas, dermatofibromas, and leiomyosarcomas 47 . Treatment The treatment is complete excision. If incompletely excised, this tumor has a high local recurrence rate, due to the plexiform or perineurial growth pattern. This is because any cellular component of the peripheral nerve can give rise to these tumors, including perineurial or endoneurial fibroblasts (rather than Schwann cells) 61,62 . MPNST is primarily a tumor of deep soft tissues and rarely involves the skin. Despite its rarity, MPNST has clinical relevance for dermatologists because this malignancy develops within 2%–30% of plexiform neurofibromas, which are associated with NF1 63 (see Ch. 61 ). A definitive diagnosis requires histologic examination, usually in conjunction with immunohistochemistry and molecular biologic analysis. Histologically, in the most common form, there is a proliferation of atypical spindle cells, often arranged in a “herringbone” pattern. There is variable cytologic atypia, numerous abnormal mitotic figures, and areas of necrosis and hemor- rhage ( Fig. 115.16 ) 61,62 . Staining for S100 protein and SOX10, if positive, is only patchy or focal 51 . Regardless of the clinical setting (sporadic, NF1-associated, or radiotherapy-associated), MPNSTs show frequent and concurrent loss-of-function mutations in NF1 , CDKN2A / CDKN2B , and the polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2)-related genes EED or SUZ12 63 . Complete loss of PRC2 activity and an associated lack of immunohistochemical expression of the epigenetic marker H3K27me3 (trimethylation of lysine 27 on histone H3 which represses transcription) are observed in > 80% of high-grade MPNSTs and may represent a useful tool for its differen- tiation from other soft tissue sarcomas 64 . NEOPLASMS OF THE SKIN Introduction Merkel cell carcinoma (MCC) is an aggressive cutaneous carcinoma that shares ultrastructural and immunohistochemical features with other neuroendocrine tumors. Although rare, the incidence of MCC is rapidly increasing along with the aging population. These tumors display nonspecific clinical features and highly aggressive behavior. Early recognition and adequate therapy are therefore critical. History This tumor was originally described by Toker and given the name “trabecular carcinoma” based on its lattice-like and infiltrative growth pattern 65 . Subsequently, the neuroendocrine nature of this tumor was recognized. Similarities to the normal Merkel cell of the skin led to its name 66 . Epidemiology The male : female ratio is 1.5 : 1 and its incidence increases strikingly with age, e.g. MCC is 10 000 times more likely to arise in an 80-year-old individual than in a 20-year-old 67 . Other risk factors include lightly pigmented skin, extensive sun exposure, and chronic immunosuppression (e.g. organ transplantation recipients, hematologic malignancies) 68 . Pathogenesis The cells of MCC and the normal Merkel cell, a touch-sensing cell located in the basal layer of the epidermis, share several features. However, the MCC’s cell of origin is unclear and it appears unlikely that normal Merkel cells give rise to this carcinoma 66 . This tumor is also referred to as “primary neuroendocrine carcinoma of the skin”, a term that is often used in pathology reports. In 2008, a landmark discovery revealed the association of MCC with a novel polyomavirus, now referred to as Merkel cell polyomavirus (MCPyV) 69 . In humans, this polyomavirus is ubiquitous as it can be readily detected within the
