This tumor is also referred to as “primary neuroendocrine carcinoma of the skin”, a term that is often used in pathology reports. In 2008, a landmark discovery revealed the association of MCC with a novel polyomavirus, now referred to as Merkel cell polyomavirus (MCPyV) 69 . In humans, this polyomavirus is ubiquitous as it can be readily detected within the normal skin of most healthy people where it exists in an episomal form. Very rarely, a clonal integration event leads to critical portions of the virus being spliced into a human chromosome, ultimately resulting in MCC. Of note, the integration event must be accompanied by mutation(s) that lead to truncation of the large T antigen and inactivation of its helicase domain. If not inactivated, the helicase domain would initiate DNA replication at the integration site which would then lead to cell death. Inhibition of viral oncoproteins in polyomavirus-infected tumor cells results in a cessation of proliferation, suggesting that ongoing viral protein expression is required for MCCs 70 . In the US, ~80% of MCCs are driven by this polyomavirus 71 , while the remaining 20% are virus-negative. The latter tumors arise in chroni- cally sun-damaged skin and contain very high numbers of UV-signature mutations 72 . Interestingly, only about 40% of MCCs in Australia are virus-induced, with the majority related to ultraviolet exposure. In contrast, in Asian countries, where people have more pigmented skin, 90% of MCCs are virus-driven. Clinical Features This cutaneous carcinoma can develop at any site, but favors the head and neck region, followed by the extremities and the buttocks. It usually presents as a pink–red to violaceous, firm, dome-shaped, solitary nodule that has grown rapidly ( Fig. 115.17 ) 67 . Ulceration can occur. Overall, the behavior is that of an aggressive tumor, with significant risk of local, regional, and/or distant recurrence and metastasis. In an analysis of 9387 cases of MCC, 65% of patients presented with local disease whereas 26% and 8% presented with nodal or distant metastases, respectively 73 . Tumor diameter at the time of diagnosis influences prognosis, with lesions > 2 cm (but without invasion of fascia) having a 40% overall survival at five years (compared to 55% for tumors ≤ 2 cm; Table 115.6 ) 73 . Occasionally, paraneoplastic syndromes, similar to those seen with other neuroendocrine carcinomas, occur in patients with MCC. These include malignancy-associated hyponatremia and Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome. Pathology The tumor appears as a poorly defined dermal mass, often infiltrating the subcutaneous fat, fascia, and even muscle. While it may show various growth patterns, a sheet-like growth pattern is seen most commonly, followed by nested and trabecular patterns ( Fig. 115.18A ) 74 . Characteristically, the edge of the tumor shows a trabecular infiltrating pattern 65 . The tumor is composed of monotonously uniform, small, round to oval cells that are about two to three times larger than mature lymphocytes 65,66 . Their cytoplasm is scant and faintly amphophilic. The nuclei of these cells are ovoid with a finely dispersed chromatin pattern and distinct nuclear membranes ( Fig. 115.18B ). Nucleoli are usually not prominent, but mitotic figures are abundant. Extensive areas of necrosis, individual cell necrosis, and characteristic crush or drying artifacts are common 74 . Intralymphatic involvement by tumor cells is not uncommon, sometimes distant from the main tumor mass. In some cases, single neoplastic cells or tiny aggregates are present at the edge of the biopsy specimen, rendering evaluation of the surgical margin difficult without the aid of immunohistochemistry (see below). Various types of differentiation have been described in MCC, including rosette-like structures resembling Homer Wright rosettes of neuroblastoma, epidermotropic involvement with pagetoid spread, and eccrine and squamoid differentiation 75,76 . Immunohistochemically, there is a characteristic perinuclear globule upon staining for low-molecular-weight cytokeratins (CK) such as CK20, CK5/6, and CK7 ( Fig. 115.18C ). This corresponds to the ultrastructural distribution of paranuclear whorls of intermediate filaments 74,75 . In addition, there is positive staining for various neuroendocrine markers, including chromogranin, synaptophysin, somatostatin, calcitonin, and vasoactive intestinal peptide 75 . These peptides are associated with ultrastruc- turally demonstrable, membrane-bound, dense-core secretory granules. The tumor also expresses neuron-specific enolase and occasionally neural filaments, CD56, and CD99; however, immunostaining for S100 protein is characteristically negative 75 . Likewise, a negative reaction for thyroid transcription factor 1 (TTF-1) helps to differen- tiate MCC from cutaneous metastases of other small cell carcinomas (pulmonary and extrapulmonary); the latter are characteristically positive for this marker 75 . Recognition of MCPyV, which can be detected by immunohistochemical (e.g. T antigen) and molecular biologic methods 77 , provides an additional tool for diagnosis; however, false-positive PCR results are possible given the ubiquitous nature of the virus. For prognostication, increased p63 expression may portend clinically aggressive behavior, but to date has not altered prognosis based upon stage ( Table 115.6 ) 78 . Negativity for MCPyV may associated with a somewhat poorer prognosis, whereas ALK-positive MCC (which is usually accompanied by MCPyV positivity) appears to have a less aggressive behavior 72,79 . A dataset for the reporting of MCCs has recently been proposed 79a . Histologically, there is a broad spectrum of small, round, blue cell tumors of diverse histo- genesis that can be confused with MCC 75 . These include metastatic neuroendocrine carcinoma of the lung (small cell or oat cell carcinoma), poorly differentiated eccrine carcinoma, lymphoma, metastatic neuro- blastoma, primary peripheral primitive neuroectodermal tumor, Ewing sarcoma, melanoma, and poorly differentiated SCC 74,75 . Treatment For newly diagnosed locoregional MCC, surgery remains the principal initial therapy. Excision of the primary tumor plus sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) are recommended for most patients ( Fig. 115.19 ), with these procedures also providing prognostic information 80–82 . SLNB positivity at the time of the initial MCC diagnosis is estimated to be 35% 83 . Age > 65 years, immunosuppression, primary tumor on the trunk, and larger tumor size are associated with higher rates of SLN positivity 83,84 . However, even tumors ≤ 5 mm are associated with a positive SLNB in ~15% of patients 83 . Surgery is often followed by radiation therapy to the primary site and in some patients, the draining lymph node basin (see Fig. 115.19 ). The management of MCC often requires a multidisciplinary approach with involvement of surgeons, medical and radiation oncologists, and dermatologists. Updated guidelines are readily available 85 and Fig. 115.19 provides a current algorithm for evaluation and treatment 86–93 . Prior to the advent of immunotherapy, cytotoxic chemotherapy was the primary option for advanced stage disease, but responses were not durable 94 . Several clinical trials, in which anti-PD-1 and anti-PD-L1 antibodies demonstrated significantly improved progression-free survival and overall survival compared to historical data for conventional chemotherapy 90–93,93a , led to FDA approval of avelumab, pembrolizumab, and retifanlimab. These antibodies are now considered first-line therapies for advanced MCC 85 . However, primary or acquired resistance to immunotherapy remains a major challenge, ultimately affecting > 50% of treated patients 90–93,93b . Careful surveillance is important because MCC recurs in up to 40% of patients 95 and effective treatments are now available.

A baseline deter- mination (within a few months of initial therapy) of the presence or absence of circulating antibodies against the Merkel virus oncoprotein is recommended 96 . In seropositive patients, antibody titers correlate with tumor burden and represent a sensitive and specific assay that can be followed longitudinally 96,97 . However, ~50% of patients do not produce these antibodies 96,97 and surveillance via imaging is required in these seronegative patients. The latter group may have an ~40% higher risk of recurrence compared to seropositive patients of the same stage. Over 80% of recurrences of MCC arise within the first 3 years after diagnosis 95 . There is a web-based recurrence risk calculator ( merkelcell. org/recur ) that factors in stage as well as the disease-free interval since treatment, immune status, sex, age, and location of the primary site. This calculator provides an accurate assessment of a patient’s ongoing risk of recurrence and assists in planning frequency of surveillance testing. Pathogenesis Nasal glial heterotopia (NGH) is the result of embryologic displacement of brain tissue, usually along the cranial closure lines and without apparent communication with underlying structures (see Figs. 64.1 & 64.8 ) 98 . It has Neural and Neuroendocrine Neoplasms (Other than Neurofibromatosis) a predilection for the perinasal area; therefore, it is commonly referred to as a nasal “glioma”. As this is not a true neoplasm, the term is misleading 99 . Clinical features NGHs are firm, smooth-surfaced, skin-colored to red–violet papulonodules that may have obvious telangiectasias and range in size from 1 to 3 cm. Approximately 60% are located on the bridge of the nose ( Fig. 115.20 ), with the remainder usually located intranasally or in both locations 99,100 . Pathology In a NGH, an ill-defined, non-encapsulated neuropil-like mass is seen within the dermis and subcutis. The neuropil-like tissue is composed of nests and strands of pale-staining, finely vacuolated or fibrillary matrix in which various types of astrocytes can be found 98 . Gemistocytic astro- cytes, with polygonal, eosinophilic cytoplasm and eccentric nuclei, as well as multinucleated giant cells, are relatively common. Mature neurons are present in variable numbers 99 . Occasionally, residual meningoendothelial cells, ependymal cells, choroid plexus-like struc- tures, and pigmented cells can be identified 100 . No mitotic activity or aggressive growth pattern has been described. Differential diagnosis Clinically, the lesion must be differentiated from other facial midline lesions (see Ch. 64 ) 99,101 as well as an infantile hemangioma, dermoid cyst, and nasal polyp (see Table 64.1 ). Treatment Most cutaneous neural malformations can be effectively treated by excision. Epidemiology Meningeal heterotopias are rare lesions, usually apparent at or shortly after birth 103 . Pathogenesis Rudimentary meningoceles are thought to result from herniation of the meningeal lining into the skin and subcutaneous tissues during embry- ologic development, usually with no residual communication with the CNS (see Fig. 64.8 ) 104 . Although these lesions are sometimes classified as type I cutaneous meningiomas 103 , considering their non-neoplastic nature, they are better classified as rudimentary meningoceles 104 . Clinical features Rudimentary meningoceles most commonly present on the scalp of neonates and infants at the sites of cranial closure (see Fig. 64.1 ). Less often they occur on the forehead (midline) or overlie the spine. Skin-colored papules or nodules on the scalp are often associated with alopecia and/or the “hair collar” sign 105 . Pathology A rudimentary meningocele is an ill-defined mass of cavernous, pseudo- vascular spaces embedded in a markedly collagenous stroma 104,106 . The spaces may be lined by elongated meningoendothelial cells charac- terized by eosinophilic cytoplasm, round or ovoid nuclei, and a fine chromatin pattern. Similar cells dissect or wrap around collagen fibers, producing “collagen bodies”. No significant cytologic atypia or mitotic activity is present. Focal calcification and psammoma bodies (eosino- philic laminated and whorled structures with variable calcification) may occur. Meningothelial cells consistently express vimentin and EMA, whereas immunoexpression of S100 protein is variable. Type II and type III meningiomas are in the histologic differential diagnosis. They usually develop on the scalp of adults, either along the course of a cranial nerve (type II) or as a cutaneous “metastasis” or direct extension of a primary meningioma of the arachnoid lining (type III) 103,105,107 . Within the deep dermis or subcutis, there is a multinodular mass, often with an infiltrative growth pattern 108–110 . The cells may show a variable degree of differentiation, and in the most common form, the spindle cells have a concentric, whorl-like arrangement 108 ; psammoma bodies are often present 108–110 . Mitotic figures are rare in type II and variably increased in type III. Clinically, these nodular tumors may have associated alopecia and can resemble an epidermoid or pilar cyst, adnexal tumor, or cutaneous metastasis. They may occur in the setting of neurofibromatosis (types I and II) 111 . Lastly, the deeper portions of rudimentary meningoceles may have an infiltrative growth pattern with pseudovascular spaces, with a resemblance to angiosarcoma. Treatment As with nasal glial heterotopia, imaging studies are required prior to biopsy or excision. The latter is performed primarily by neurosurgeons. They display a wide spectrum of clinicopathologic features based on their relative degree of differen- tiation, ranging from very primitive neuroectodermal tumors to more mature forms such as neuroblastomas. History The concept of neuroectodermal tumors was introduced by Stout in 1918. Since then, different terms have been used for tumors with cytologically similar features, reflecting the controversy regarding this entity. Dehner performed a comprehensive review of the nosology of this diverse group of lesions, suggesting the term “primitive neuroec- todermal tumors” (PNET) 112 . This concept was then further expanded following the recognition that PNET and extraosseous Ewing sarcoma can have similar immunohistochemical and chromosomal abnormal- ities (e.g. translocations involving EWSR1 ), and therefore nowadays they are considered within the same neoplastic spectrum 113 . Epidemiology Neuroblastoma is the third most commonly observed childhood malig- nancy, and cutaneous metastases are frequent 3 . Most neuroblastomas develop as sporadic tumors, although familial cases have been reported. Primary cutaneous PNETs are tumors of adulthood (mean age, 40 years) and are exceedingly rare 3 . Cutaneous ganglioneuroma has a predilection for the trunk. Pathogenesis PNETs of the skin either represent metastases from a PNET of the adrenals and/or ganglionic chain (traditionally designated as neuroblas- tomas) or develop de novo from heterotopic neural crest cells 2 . In the latter case, they are referred to as peripheral PNETs or as peripheral neuroblastomas. ALK is implicated in the tumorigenesis of many familial and some sporadic cases of neuroblastoma. In addition, DNA ploidy and specific genetic abnormalities, such as MYCN oncogene amplification or aberrations of chromosomes 11q or 1p, influence prognosis 114 . Cutaneous ganglioneuroma is best regarded as resulting from abnormal migration and differentiation of neural crest cells. These nodules may blanch upon stroking and develop an erythematous halo 115,116 . Serum and urine catechol- amine levels are typically elevated. Neural and Neuroendocrine Neoplasms (Other than Neurofibromatosis) Clinical Features In children, the cutaneous metastases of neuroblastoma often manifest as multiple, blue to purple, dermal papules or nodules that resemble the “blueberry muffin” lesions seen with congenital infections or hemato- logic disorders 4 (see Ch. 121 ). These nodules may blanch upon stroking and develop an erythematous halo 115,116 . Serum and urine catechol- amine levels are typically elevated. In children, complete spontaneous regression has been described in stage IV-S neuroblastoma, including cutaneous metastases 117 . In adults, PNETs are rapidly growing dermal or subcutaneous nodules that favor the trunk or head. Ulceration is common. These highly aggressive neoplasms have an almost invariably fatal outcome. Pathology In metastatic neuroblastoma, an ill-defined or infiltrative mass is present in the dermis and/or the subcutis. However, when smaller and more superficial, deposits are more defined. The tumor mass is composed of atypical, small, dark cells with scant cytoplasm 2,112 . The cells have larger nuclei than mature lymphocytes (with a coarse chromatin pattern) and they form irregular nests, cords, or poorly cohesive sheets. Rosette formation, by concentrically arranged tumor cells in double or multiple circles, is common. The center of the rosettes contains converging fine fibrillary material characteristic of Homer Wright-type rosettes 2 ( Fig. 115.21 ). Mitotic activity is high, and abnormal mitoses are abundant. Extensive areas of necrosis and hemorrhage are common. As the tumor differentiates, the relative proportion of neuroblastoma components decreases, and the ganglioneuromatous elements increase. Eventually, the tumor may show features indistinguishable from a ganglioneuroma 117 . Cutaneous ganglioneuromas are characterized by mature ganglion cells immersed in a Schwann cell-rich stroma. Lesions consisting of only ganglion cells may also occur and are referred to as “ganglion cell choristomas”. Ganglion cells are round-to-polygonal with vesicular nuclei and abundant pale cytoplasm; the latter contains Nissl granules which may be highlighted by a toluidine blue stain. Immunohistochemically, the cells of neuroblastomas and ganglio- neuromas react variably with neural and neuroendocrine markers, depending on their state of differentiation. These markers include neuron-specific enolase, S100 protein, neurofilaments, synaptophysin, chromogranin, and CD99 (see Ch. 0 ) 114 . Primary cutaneous PNETs have similar histopathologic features to those of the classic neuroblastoma, but ganglionic or neuromatous differenti- ation is not characteristic. These two tumors also share major immuno- histochemical features. However, MIC-2(013) is commonly expressed by PNETs, but not by neuroblastomas, facilitating their

These markers include neuron-specific enolase, S100 protein, neurofilaments, synaptophysin, chromogranin, and CD99 (see Ch. 0 ) 114 . Primary cutaneous PNETs have similar histopathologic features to those of the classic neuroblastoma, but ganglionic or neuromatous differenti- ation is not characteristic. These two tumors also share major immuno- histochemical features. However, MIC-2(013) is commonly expressed by PNETs, but not by neuroblastomas, facilitating their distinction 114,117–120 . Differential Diagnosis In children, the clinical differential diagnosis includes other types of cutaneous metastasis, extramedullary hematopoiesis, and mastocytosis, whereas in adults it includes adnexal tumors, lymphoma, and soft tissue sarcomas. Histologically, both metastatic neuroblastoma and primary cutaneous PNET must be differentiated from other small, round, blue cell tumors that form rosettes and may involve the skin 120,121 (see discussion in MCC section). Cutaneous ganglioneuroma must be distinguished from cutaneous metastases of neuroblastoma, with age of onset and other clinical history required for distinction. Treatment The effective treatment of neuroblastoma requires an interdisci- plinary team that includes oncologists, surgeons, and radiation therapists. The overall prognosis of localized tumor involvement has improved with combined surgical excision, multiagent chemotherapy, differentiating agents (e.g. 13-cis-retinoic acid), immunotherapy (e.g. dinutuximab), hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, and radio- pharmaceuticals 114 . Important prognostic factors include the age, stage, histologic differentiation, specific genetic abnormalities (e.g. MYCN oncogene amplification, 11q aberration), and response to initial chemotherapy 2 . Kutzner Fibroblastic, Myofibroblastic, and “Fibrohistiocytic” Proliferations and Neoplasms of the Skin SKIN TAGS Synonyms:  Acrochordons  Fibroepithelial polyps Clinical Features Skin tags are very common, presenting as soft, skin-colored to slightly hyperpigmented, pedunculated papules that favor the neck, axilla, and groin ( Fig. 116.1 ). Skin tags are usually asymptomatic but can become painful secondary to irritation or infarction. Epidemiology Men and women are equally affected, and close to 50% of all individuals have at least one skin tag 1 . Although skin tags were once thought to be associated with colonic polyps, more recent studies have not confirmed this relationship 2 . Skin tags have also been reported as a cutaneous marker for diabetes mellitus 3 . Pathology Histologically, skin tags are polypoid with loose to dense collagenous stroma and thin-walled blood vessels. In Birt–Hogg–Dubé syndrome and Cowden syndrome, patients can have typical skin tags, but sometimes the “skin tags” represent fibro- folliculomas, trichodiscomas or perifollicular fibromas versus sclerotic fibromas, respectively 4 . Treatment Unless irritated or infarcted, skin tags are more of a cosmetic issue than a clinical concern and can be removed by scissor excision. CUTANEOUS ANGIOFIBROMA Synonyms:  Fibrous papule  Pearly penile papule  Ungual fibroma (Koenen tumor)  Fibrous papule of the nose Cutaneous angiofibroma is a descriptive term for a group of lesions with different clinical presentations and implications, but similar histologic findings. Clinical Features Fibrous papules are solitary, dome-shaped and shiny, skin-colored to reddish papules located on the face of adults, most commonly on the nose ( Fig. 116.2 ) 5 . Clinically, they can mimic small intradermal melanocytic nevi, basal cell carcinomas (BCCs), or adnexal tumors. By dermoscopy, a white color is often seen. Pearly penile papules are pearly, white, dome-shaped, closely aggre- gated small papules located on the glans penis, commonly in a multi- layered and circumferential manner on the corona ( Fig. 116.3 ). They are found in up to 30% of young postpubertal adults and are more common in uncircumcised men 6 . They can be mistaken for condy- lomata acuminata or hypertrophied sebaceous glands. Pathology All angiofibromas are dome-shaped lesions composed of a dermal proliferation of plump or stellate fibroblasts in a collagenous stroma with an increase in the number of thin-walled, dilated blood vessels ( Fig. 116.4 ). The collagen fibers can be arranged in a concentric fashion around hair follicles and blood vessels (a variant known as perifollicular fibroma). Elastic fibers are decreased in number. Some fibroblasts can be multinucleated. Granular and clear-cell variants have been described. DERMATOFIBROMA Synonyms:  Benign fibrous histiocytoma (preferred terminology in soft tissue pathology)  Fibroma simplex  Sclerosing hemangioma  Nodular subepidermal fibrosis  Histiocytoma  Dermal dendrocytoma Clinical Features Dermatofibromas occur primarily in adults and often develop on the lower extremities. They are firm, minimally elevated to dome-shaped papules that are usually < 1 cm in diameter, but occasionally are > 2 cm. The lesions are commonly hyperpigmented ( Fig. 116.5 ). On palpation, they may seem attached to the subcutaneous tissue; pinching the lesion gently usually results in apparent downward movement of the tumor, also known as the “dimple sign”. By dermoscopy, a central white scar-like patch or white network surrounded by a delicate pigment network is most commonly observed (see Ch. 0 ). Although some dermatofibromas are thought to arise at sites of trauma or arthropod bites, their precise etiology is unknown. Multiple eruptive dermatofibromas have been observed in patients with autoimmune disorders (e.g. lupus erythematosus) and atopic derma- titis and in the setting of immunosuppression (e.g. HIV infection) 8 . Clinically, dermatofibromas can be confused with cysts or melanocytic nevi, especially those with fibrosis. In the case of larger lesions, the possibility of dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (DFSP), which is less well defined and multilobed, may be considered. Pathology Dermatofibromas are characterized by a nodular dermal prolifer- ation, predominantly composed of spindle-shaped fibroblasts and myofibroblasts arranged as short intersecting fascicles ( Fig. 116.6 ). pedunculated. papule. of the glans penis. NEOPLASMS OF THE SKIN The fibroblasts and myofibroblasts have plump oval nuclei with small nucleoli and mitoses may be present. An admixture of these cells with mono- or multinucleated histiocytes with vacuolated (xanthomatous) cytoplasm can be seen, hence the synonym benign fibrous histio- cytoma. “Keloidal” collagen bundles, which are refractile with polarized light, are seen at the periphery ( Fig. 116.7 ); the presence of peripheral “entrapped” collagen bundles is considered a classic hallmark of derma- tofibroma. Hemorrhage into a dermatofibroma explains the common finding of hemosiderin. The overlying epidermis is usually hyperplastic. Sometimes there are aggregates of basaloid cells with follicular differentiation emanating from the epidermis (follicular and basaloid “induction”). This finding may be confused with a superficial BCC. There are, however, a few reported cases of true BCCs evolving within longstanding dermatofibromas 9 . Histologic variants of dermatofibroma are listed in Table 116.1 . Positive immunohistochemical reactions for vimentin, factor XIIIa 10–12 , muscle-specific actin and CD68, as well as a negative reaction for CD34 (in the center of the lesion), support the diagnosis of derma- tofibroma. Evolving cellular dermatofibromas may stain strongly for α -smooth muscle actin (SMA). The histologic differential diagnosis includes keloid, scar, connective tissue nevus, dermatomyofibroma, DFSP (CD34-positive), and nodular Kaposi sarcoma (HHV8-positive, ERG-positive). Of note, dermatofibromas may show CD34 positivity at the periphery while the center is usually CD34-negative, in contrast to DFSP which is homogeneously CD34-positive. Whether dermatofibromas are reactive or neoplastic has been an area of controversy for a long time. The detection of clonality in a subset of fibrous histiocytomas in addition to a large size, mitotic activity, and/or high recurrence rate in some dermatofibromas and the very rare metastatic potential suggest that fibrous histiocytoma is a tumor rather than a reactive inflammatory process 13–17 . ACRAL FIBROMYXOMA Synonyms:  Superficial acral fibromyxoma  Digital fibromyxoma Clinical Features Acral fibromyxoma is a rare tumor of acral sites first described in 2001 23 . There is a 2 : 1 male : female ratio, with a broad range for age of onset 24–27 . The tumor presents as a slowly enlarging, often painful mass, with an average size of 1–2 cm. It usually develops on the toes or fingers, with two-thirds of tumors occurring close to or involving the nail bed 24–26 ; 3% of tumors invade adjacent bone 24,27 . Less common sites include the palm or heel 28 . The clinical differential diagnosis includes primarily ungual fibroma and verruca. Pathology Acral fibromyxomas are located within the dermis with extension into the subcutis. There are non-encapsulated, poorly circumscribed masses composed of spindled to stellate cells arranged in a vague storiform or loosely fascicular growth pattern ( Fig. 116.11 ). The stroma is myxoid to fibromyxoid with prominent blood vessels and frequent mast cells. Most tumors have alternating areas of fibrous and myxoid stroma 24 . Minimal cellular atypia is common, and occasionally scattered larger cells with so-called “degenerative change” are present 24 . Mitotic figures are rare. Significant pleomorphism, neural/perineural infiltration, and necrosis are not seen. In cases involving the nail bed, there is often papillary hyperplasia of the nail bed epithelium 28 . The majority of these tumors stain strongly for CD34 with occasional expression of epithelial membrane antigen (EMA) and SMA; expression of CD99, CD10 25 , nestin, and desmin has also been reported (see Ch. 0 ) 24,28 . By immunohistochemistry, the majority of cases demon- strate loss of retinoblastoma 1 (RB1) expression due to deletion of RB1 29 ( Table 116.3 ). The histologic differential diagnosis includes cellular digital fibroma, myxoid neurofibroma, superficial angiomyxoma, and DFSP. Treatment These tumors follow a benign course, with ~25% recurring after complete excision 24 . Neither malignant transformation nor metastasis has been reported 24 . Positivity for CD34 may result in the misdiagnosis of early DFSP. PLEOMORPHIC FIBROMA OF THE SKIN Clinical Features This unusual variant of a fibroma was described by Kamino et al. 32 in 1989. Pleomorphic fibromas of the skin usually present in adults, with a slight preponderance in women. They favor the extremities and appear as asymptomatic, solitary, skin-colored, dome-shaped or polypoid papules which measure from a few millimeters to nearly 2 cm in diameter. Clinically, they resemble skin tags, neurofibromas, or intradermal melanocytic nevi but are firmer to palpation. Treatment is simple excision, and to date there have been no reports of recurrence. Pathology Pleomorphic fibromas are polypoid or dome-shaped, well-circumscribed dermal lesions characterized by low cellularity with a predominance of thick collagen bundles in a haphazard array. There are scattered spindled cells and irregularly shaped multinucleated cells with scanty cytoplasm, indistinct cellular borders, and large pleomorphic and hyper- chromatic nuclei ( Fig. 116.13 ). Some of the multinucleated cells have multilobed nuclei. Mitotic figures are rare. The spindle-shaped cells and the irregularly shaped, multinucleated cells are positive for vimentin and CD34 33 , and the spindle-shaped cells react positively for muscle-specific actin. The differential diagnosis includes dermatofibroma with atypical cells, atypical fibroxanthoma, and neurofibroma with atypical cells. DERMATOMYOFIBROMA This tumor was described as plaque-like dermal fibromatosis in 1991 by Hügel 36 and as dermatomyofibroma by Kamino et al. 37 . It is a benign fibroblastic/myofibroblastic dermal neoplasm 38 . Clinical Features Dermatomyofibromas most commonly occur in young women and favor the shoulder area, axilla, upper arm, and neck. Occasionally, these tumors arise during childhood. They are asymptomatic, well-circum- scribed, oval or annular, skin-colored to red–brown plaques that have a smooth surface and measure 1–2 cm in diameter. Pathology Dermatomyofibromas are well-circumscribed plaques involving the reticular dermis and the upper portion of the subcutaneous septae; they are composed of well-defined, long fascicles of spindle-shaped cells parallel to the skin surface ( Fig. 116.16 ). The cells have a very uniform appearance, with elongated nuclei having rounded or pointed ends and one or two small nucleoli. There is no evidence of nuclear atypia, and mitoses are rare. The cells are separated by thin collagen fibers and elastic fibers are preserved. The fascicles, spindle-shaped cells, collagen fibers, and elastic fibers may have a wavy appearance. The adnexal structures are spared. With Verhoeff–van Gieson stain, the elastic fibers appear slightly increased in number. The spindle-shaped cells react positively for vimentin and are variably positive for muscle-specific actin; staining for desmin, factor XIIIa, and CD34 is negative. These results support a fibroblastic/ myofibroblastic differentiation rather than smooth muscle differenti- ation 36–38 . The histologic differential diagnosis includes dermatofibroma, DFSP, myofibroma, smooth muscle tumors, fibrous hamartoma of infancy, fibromatoses, and fibroblastic connective tissue nevus. Treatment The treatment is simple excision. Recurrence is uncommon even when marginally or incompletely excised 38 . TENOSYNOVIAL GIANT CELL TUMOR (LOCALIZED TYPE) Synonyms:  Giant cell tumor of tendon sheath  Localized nodular tenosynovitis Clinical Features This tumor usually presents as a firm nodule on the hand or finger ( Fig. 116.17 ), but can also occur on the toes and other periarticular sites. It is typically slowly growing and fixed to subcutaneous structures without attachment to the overlying skin, except on the distal fingers and toes. Although usually asymptomatic, there can be pain, numbness, or stiffness of the affected digit. Localized tenosynovial giant cell tumor is the most common tumor of the hand and can present at any age, but usually appears in adults 30 to 50 years of age and is more common in women than in men

FIBROMA OF TENDON SHEATH Synonym:  Tenosynovial fibroma Clinical Features This benign tumor presents as a small subcutaneous nodule. It is most frequently found on the hands and feet, with the most common site of involvement being the thumb. While usually asymptomatic, there can be limitation in the range of motion of involved joints 43 . This fibroma usually presents in those 20 to 50 years of age. Men develop these tumors three times more often than women. The clinical differential diagnosis includes localized type of tenosynovial giant cell tumor, neuroma, ganglion cyst, rheumatoid nodule, and subcutaneous granuloma annulare. Pathology The tumor has a well-circumscribed lobular appearance and is attached to a tendon sheath. It is composed of dense hyalinized collagen with scattered spindle-shaped fibroblasts/myofibroblasts and stromal clefts. There are characteristic elongated slit-like vessels as well as occasional giant cells and foci of myxoid change. Tumor cells stain focally for α -smooth muscle actin. In some cellular variants, USP6 rearrange- ments similar to those in nodular fasciitis have been reported, raising the question if such variants represent tenosynovial nodular fasciitis 44 . A linear arrangement occasionally occurs. These nevi may represent hamartomas rather than neoplasms. Clini­ cally and histologically, they may be subtle and even resemble normal skin. Several variants have been described, based upon the dominant tissue component present, and they are listed above, along with their synonyms. The shagreen patch of tuberous sclerosis most commonly presents as a pebbly plaque with a “pigskin” appearance on the lower back (see Ch. 61 ). In the Buschke–Ollendorf syndrome, multiple skin-colored or slightly yellowish papules are seen and are referred to as derma- tofibrosis lenticularis disseminata. This syndrome is due to loss-of- function mutations in LEMD 3 which then lead to loss of antagonism of the TGF- β and bone morphogenic protein signaling pathways 54 . The disorder is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern and the papules begin at an early age. In radiograms, a characteristic stippled appearance to the bone is seen, called osteopoikilosis ( Fig. 116.21 ). This abnor- mality is asymptomatic. Connective tissue nevus is the sole category A criterion for Proteus syndrome. The nevi occur most commonly on the plantar surface and acquire a cerebriform appearance, but can be seen elsewhere (e.g. hands, abdomen; see Fig. 104.10 ). Courtesy NEOPLASMS OF THE SKIN Pathology There is usually a poorly demarcated area of increased dermal collagen bundles without an apparent increase in fibroblasts. Those lesions with a prominent collagen component are designated as collagenomas . A variant with increased elastic fibers has been called elastoma . Many of the cutaneous lesions in Buschke–Ollendorf syndrome tend to have increased elastic fibers, but some appear to be primarily collagenous. Mucinous connective tissue nevi are characterized by increased mucin deposition within the dermis. Fibroblastic connective tissue nevus is a recently delineated variant that presents as a solitary, slowly growing, asymptomatic, firm plaque or nodule. It has a smooth surface and is tan–white to light brown in color. These nevi most commonly occur on the trunk and in the head and neck region of children, with involvement of the deep dermis and superficial subcutis 55 . There is an intra- dermal proliferation of bland CD34 + fibroblastic/myofibroblastic cells arranged in short-intersecting fascicles. It must be distinguished from CD34 + plaque-like dermal fibroma (medallion-like dermal dendrocyte hamartoma; see eTable 116.1 ), DFSP, and dermatomyofibroma. Differential Diagnosis Although the differential diagnosis includes fibromatoses, fibrous hamartoma of infancy, infantile myofibromatosis, and dermatofi- bromas, clinicopathologic correlation usually establishes the diagnosis fairly easily. INCLUSION BODY FIBROMATOSIS Synonyms:  Infantile digital fibroma  Recurring digital fibrous tumor of childhood Clinical Features Inclusion body fibromatosis commonly presents as multiple, firm, smooth, skin-colored, dome-shaped nodules on the dorsolateral aspects of the fingers and toes ( Fig. 116.22 ). They can be up to several centi- meters in diameter and tend to spare the thumb and great toe. Almost all cases occur in infants under 1 year of age. Rare adult cases of a histologically similar tumor have been reported at extradigital sites 56 . Multiple lesions may be seen in patients with terminal osseous dysplasia with pigmentary defects.

The multicentric form without visceral involvement (and the solitary form) typically undergo spontaneous regression but can recur, whereas the visceral form is associated with a mortality rate of up to 75%. Solitary myofibromas represent the third and the most common form of infantile myofibromatosis (~75% of cases). They exist on a spectrum with myopericytomas , may also develop in older children or adults, and have a good prognosis (see below) 60 . Pathology In the 5th edition of the WHO classification of soft tissue and bone tumors, myofibromas are categorized within the group of pericytic/ perivascular tumors. These tumors are composed of circumscribed nodules with a biphasic appearance. Areas of plump spindle-shaped myofibroblasts with abundant cytoplasm, arranged in fascicles within a collagenous stroma, blend with more cellular areas composed of smaller, rounder cells having less cytoplasm and an associated stag-horn pattern of dilated branching blood vessels. Mitotic figures, necrosis, intravas- cular growth, and stromal hyalinization can be present. Immunohistochemically, the spindle and rounded cells are positive for vimentin and SMA, with negative staining for desmin, as is seen in myofibroblasts. The histologic differential diagnosis includes infantile hemangiopericytoma, which some authors suggest exists on a continuum with myofibromatosis (see Ch. 114 ). Treatment Patients with only soft tissue and bony involvement have a good prognosis, as the tumors regress spontaneously within months via massive apoptosis 65 . Those with visceral involvement have a high mortality rate within the first 4 months owing to the compromise of vital organ function (e.g. cardiopulmonary failure). However, if patients survive beyond this period to when the tumors begin to regress, the prognosis is much improved. Because the tumors tend to regress, debulking surgery is recommended only for symptomatic lesions. Targeted tyrosine kinase inhibitors (e.g. imatinib) and combination chemotherapy have been used in severe cases 59 . It presents as a solitary, firm, deep dermal nodule and is often diagnosed clinically as a dermatofibroma, cyst, or angioleiomyoma. Multicentric variants are rare. Pathology These perivascular tumors possess a broad morphologic spectrum: at one end is a myoid nodular proliferation resembling an angioleiomyoma and at the other end is a hemangiopericytoma-like, richly vascularized, biphasic tumor with both myoid basophilic spindle cell nodules and richly vascu- larized myopericytic sheets. A highly characteristic finding is the “spinning off” of the outer vessel wall of small myopericytic cells. Myopericytomas may have degenerative changes including symplastic nuclear atypia, hyalinization, and cystic changes. The term myopericytomatosis has been introduced for an apparently benign variant of myopericytoma characterized by innumerable, discrete microscopic myopericytomatous nodules that typically diffusely involve superficial soft tissue in adults. When PDGFRB alterations are present, tyrosine kinase inhibitors represent a potential therapeutic strategy, if needed 61,70 . CALCIFYING APONEUROTIC FIBROMA Synonyms:  Juvenile aponeurotic fibroma  Calcifying fibroma  Cartilage analogue of fibromatosis Clinical Features This is a very rare entity that presents as a solitary, slowly growing, asymptomatic, firm subcutaneous nodule that is usually fixed to under- lying structures. It occurs primarily on the hands, and sometimes on the feet. A characteristic radiologic finding is the presence of stippled calcifications. Most cases occur in young children and adolescents, and boys are affected more frequently than girls 71 . Pathology The tumor is poorly circumscribed with an infiltrating border. It is composed of sheets of spindled and epithelioid fibroblasts with parallel nuclei in a collagenous stroma. The biphasic pattern of plump epithe- lioid cells in conjunction with slender spindle cells can be striking. Most cases have a myofibroblastic immunophenotype with expression of α -smooth muscle actin. In addition, there are characteristic islands of calcifications surrounded by palisaded epithelioid fibroblasts ( Fig. 116.25 ). In older lesions, these areas of calcification can undergo chondroid and osseous metaplasia. FN1 - EGF gene fusions have been reported in these tumors and can facilitate diagnosis in unusual cases 72 . myofibromatosis. Multiple firm violaceous papulonodules on the scalp. text: INFANCY Synonym:  Subdermal fibromatous tumor of infancy Clinical Features This tumor typically presents as a solitary, painless, skin-colored subcu- taneous nodule. It favors the axilla, shoulder, and upper arm, although it can appear in other sites such as the groin 73,74 . There is a variable rate of growth, and a fibrous hamartoma can become quite large. Fixation to underlying structures may be observed. Occasionally, hyperhidrosis and hypertrichosis are present 75 . Most of these tumors appear within the first year of life, but some are congenital. Boys are affected three times as often as girls 73,76 . Fibrous hamartomas may mimic other subcutaneous malignancies of infancy such as rhabdomyosarcoma and cutaneous metastases (e.g. neuro- blastoma, leukemia) as well as other fibromatoses and subcutaneous fat necrosis. Pathology This tumor is not well circumscribed, and it is composed of three distinctive elements in variable proportions: (1) a proliferation of spindle-shaped, α -smooth muscle actin-positive myofibroblasts arranged as broad fascicles within a collagenous stroma; (2) nests and aggregates of smaller, round to plump, spindle-shaped, immature mesenchymal cells within a myxoid matrix (primitive-appearing cells can express CD34); and (3) mature adipocytes ( Fig. 116.26 ). Hyalinized zones with cracking artifact, mimicking giant cell fibroblastoma, are frequently observed 77 . Treatment Fibrous hamartoma of infancy is benign and the usual treatment is local excision, with recurrence being fairly uncommon 76 . If left untreated, the tumor continues to grow and stabilizes in size by mid-childhood. In rare cases, the presence of “sarcomatous” areas provides evidence that these are complex neoplasms rather than hamartomas 77 . Pathology The tumor develops at the dermal/subcutaneous junction and appears as an infiltrative mass that may invade muscle. It is composed of small nodules of histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells surrounded by fascicles of spindled cells in variable proportions. These spindle cells express SMA. Mitotic figures and mild nuclear pleomorphism may be seen as well as lymphovascular invasion. NEOPLASMS OF THE SKIN ATYPICAL FIBROXANTHOMA Clinical Features This tumor usually presents as a rapidly growing, exophytic, dome- shaped nodule that measures from 1 to 2 cm in diameter ( Fig. 116.30 ). Secondary changes include serosanguineous crusts and ulceration 89 . In the 5th edition of the WHO classification of soft tissue and bone tumors, atypical fibroxanthoma (AFX) is defined as a dermal-based mesenchymal neoplasm of uncertain differentiation that develops within photodamaged skin. It is viewed as existing on a disease spectrum with pleomorphic dermal sarcoma. However, when strict diagnostic criteria are applied, AFX generally behaves in a benign fashion 90–92 . Pathology This dermal-based tumor is well circumscribed and commonly ulcerated, and it usually has a collarette of hyperplastic epithelium. The neoplasm is confined to the dermis, with minimal to no infil- tration of the subcutaneous fat; extensive infiltration of fatty tissue actually excludes the diagnosis of AFX. The tumor can push both adnexal ­structures and abnormal elastic fibers (solar elastosis) to the bottom of the lesion. AFX is composed of atypical spindle-shaped cells with moderate amounts of cytoplasm and large atypical cells with abundant pale- staining vacuolated cytoplasm. The cells have large pleomorphic and hyperchromatic nuclei and some of them are multinucleated ( Fig. 116.31A ). Several morphologic variants of AFX exist – spindle-cell non-pleomorphic, clear cell, pigmented, myxoid, osteoclast-like giant cell-rich, keloidal, and granular cell ( Fig. 116.31B–D ) 93–98 . DERMATOFIBROSARCOMA PROTUBERANS Clinical Features Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (DFSP) is a locally aggressive sarcoma of intermediate malignancy that favors young to middle-aged adults. Lesions that are present at birth or with an onset during childhood have also been reported. DFSP occurs on the trunk in 50%–60% of patients, the proximal extremities in 20%–30%, and the head and neck in 10%–15%. There is a predilection for the shoulder or pelvic region. Initially, a slowly growing, asymptomatic, skin-colored, indurated plaque is seen that eventually develops violaceous to red–brown nodules measuring from one to several centimeters in diameter ( Fig. 116.32 ) 100 . On palpation, the lesion is firm and attached to the subcutaneous tissue. There are reports of accelerated growth during pregnancy 101 . The early plaque stage may be misdiagnosed as a benign tumor and incompletely excised. Moreover, superficial samples may not yield diagnostic material. Congenital and childhood-onset DFSP may have an atrophic appearance and/or hypopigmented to blue–red color, with the latter potentially leading to misdiagnosis as a vascular malfor- mation or tumor. Multiple DFSPs have been observed in children with adenosine deaminase-deficient severe combined immunodeficiency 102 . Pathology Early plaque lesions are characterized by a flat surface and low cellularity and are comprised of slender spindle-shaped cells arranged as long fascicles parallel to the skin surface. The cells are scattered between thin collagen fibers and infiltrate thick collagen bundles which appear cellular and wavy. Nuclear atypia is minimal and mitotic figures are rare. Adnexal structures are infiltrated and obliterated. The spindle cells infiltrate into the subcuta- neous tissue, very often in a multilayered pattern ( Fig. 116.33A ) 103 . In the nodular stage, the tumor becomes more cellular, with the cells arranged as short fascicles in a “storiform” arrangement ( Fig. 116.33B ). The cells infiltrate the subcutaneous tissue in a “honeycomb” pattern. Nuclei are hyperchromatic, and mitotic figures are easily identified. The nodules may develop myxomatous areas, characterized by more rounded to stellate cells in a highly vascular myxomatous stroma. For the nodular stage, it includes deep dermatofibroma extending to the subcutaneous tissue, fibrosarcoma, and malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor. The clini- copathologic criteria for CD34 + plaque-like dermal fibroma (medallion- like dermal dendrocyte hamartoma) and superficial, mostly dermal DFSP overlap. In a recent systematic review of relevant studies (2002–2017) in which imatinib was administered for metastatic or locally advanced DFSP, there was a complete response, partial response, or stable disease in 5%, 55%, and 28% of patients, respectively 116 . Either dosage (400 or 800 mg/day) led to similar results. Tumor progression occurred in 9% of patients, with severe adverse side effects in 15% 116 . Fibroblastic, Myofibroblastic, and “Fibrohistiocytic” Proliferations and Neoplasms of the Skin FIBROSARCOMA Clinical Features Previously, the term “fibrosarcoma” encompassed a heterogeneous group of high-grade and low-grade soft tissue tumors. Nowadays, specific tumor entities within the group of fibroblastic and myofibroblastic soft tissue sarcomas can be identified via molecular diagnostics ( Table 116.4 ) 121 . Classic fibrosarcomas usually affect middle-aged adults. The most common location is the lower extremities, followed by the upper extremities, trunk, and head and neck region. This is a neoplasm predominantly of the deep soft tissues, with secondary involvement of the overlying subcutis and skin. Fibrosarcoma is a slowly growing tumor that measures from 1 to 10 cm in diameter and is usually diagnosed when it becomes a palpable painful nodule or plaque 123 . They may appear in old burn scars and in areas of prior irradiation 124 . Pathology The tumor is composed of a proliferation of atypical spindle-shaped cells arranged as intersecting fascicles in a “herringbone” pattern ( Fig. 116.35 ). There are thin collagen bundles between the cells which have scanty cytoplasm and elongated hyperchromatic nuclei. Mitotic figures are easily identified and myxomatous foci may be present. A sclerosing epithelioid variant that simulates an infiltrating carcinoma has been described 125 . High-grade fibrosarcomas are characterized by increased cellularity with more atypical nuclei, a higher mitotic rate, foci of necrosis, and a less distinct “herringbone” pattern. Treatment The traditional treatment for fibrosarcoma is wide excision. When wide free margins cannot be achieved, adjuvant radiation therapy and amputation are additional options. In high-grade fibrosarcomas, neoad- juvant or adjuvant systemic chemotherapy is given. Hematogenous metastases to the lung, and less often to the bones, develop in patients with high-grade or poorly differentiated fibrosarcomas. The overall 5-year survival rate is ~40% 123 . In tumors with NTRK fusions, targeted therapy with pan-tropomyosin receptor kinase (TRK) inhibitors (e.g. larotrectinib, entrectinib) has shown encouraging results 126,127 . EPITHELIOID SARCOMA Synonyms/variants:  Classic or conventional – distal type  Proximal – large-cell type Clinical Features In the 5th edition of the WHO classification of soft tissue and bone tumors, epithelioid sarcomas are classified within the tumor group with uncertain differentiation. Two clinicopathologic subtypes of epithelioid sarcoma are recognized: (1) the conventional or classic (“distal”) form , characterized by its proclivity for acral sites and a pseudogranulo- matous growth pattern; and (2) the proximal-type (“large-cell”) variant that usually arises more proximally or on the trunk and is composed of nests and sheets of large epithelioid cells 90,128 . Classic epithelioid sarcomas present as a slow-growing, firm, subcutaneous nodule of the distal extremities, usually the hands and fingers. There may be associated ulceration if the tumor involves the dermis. Advanced metastatic disease can present as a linear arrangement of widely spaced, ulcerated nodules extending from distal to proximal sites on affected extremities, with intervening tumor-free skin. If there is involvement of a large nerve, associated pain, paresthesias, and muscle wasting can occur 129 . The majority of patients are between 20 and 40 years of age, and men are affected twice as often as women. Hand and finger lesions may resemble the localized type of tenosynovial giant cell tumor (giant cell tumor of tendon sheath), fibroma of tendon sheath, nodular fasciitis, subcutaneous granuloma annulare, rheumatoid nodule, or ganglion cyst. Penile lesions can mimic Peyronie disease 129 . Pathology In classic “distal” epithelioid sarcoma , there is a nodular proliferation of spindle-shaped to round or epithelioid/polygonal cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and small uniform nuclei without prominent nucleoli ( Fig. 116.36A ). Epithelioid tumor cells are usually seen centrally, with a gradual transition to a spindle cell morphology towards the periphery 128 . When present, cytoplasmic vacuoles may mimic vascular tumors. Within larger tumor nodules, zones of central necrosis surrounded by palisaded tumor cells can be seen as well as a mixed chronic inflammatory cell infiltrate. Proximal-type epithelioid sarcoma has a multinodular, sheet-like growth pattern and is composed of large epithelioid (carcinoma-like) cells that have enlarged vesicular nuclei with prominent nucleoli and abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm. Within larger tumor nodules, zones of central necrosis surrounded by palisaded tumor cells can be seen as well as a mixed chronic inflammatory cell infiltrate. Proximal-type epithelioid sarcoma has a multinodular, sheet-like growth pattern and is composed of large epithelioid (carcinoma-like) cells that have enlarged vesicular nuclei with prominent nucleoli and abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm. A rhabdoid morphology is more commonly observed in this variant. While necrosis can be seen, a pseudogranulo- matous morphology is more typical of the classic form (see above). Both subtypes of epithelioid sarcoma demonstrate an infiltrative growth pattern and these tumors are frequently associated with fascia, periosteum, tendons, and nerves. The tumor cells are typically positive for keratins, EMA, and CD34 while negative for S100, HMB45, and CD31. ERG expression has been reported in up to two-thirds of tumors. Epithelioid sarcomas have distinct genetic alterations of 22q11–12, including mutations, deletions, and other alterations of the tumor suppressor gene SMARCB1/INI1 (see Table 116.3 ) 90 . Therefore, loss of INI1 expression by immunohistochemistry is characteristic of both conventional and proximal-type epithelioid sarcoma 130 ( Fig. 116.36B ). Treatment Both subtypes typically demonstrate an infiltrating growth pattern along tendons, nerves and fascia, with skip lesions commonly observed in classic “distal” epithelioid sarcomas. Although earlier therapeutic approaches involved radical surgery, including amputation, there has been a movement toward more conservative surgery with adjuvant radiation therapy 131 . Epithelioid sarcoma, especially the proximal (“large-cell”) type, is an aggressive tumor with a high local recurrence rate. For all epithe- lioid sarcoma variants, 5- and 10-year overall survival rates are 60%–80% and 40%–60%, respectively 90,129,132 . Metastases develop in 40%–50% of patients, usually after repeated recurrences, and frequently involve the lung and regional lymph nodes. For metastatic or locally advanced epithelioid sarcoma with INI1 loss, tazemetostat, an oral inhibitor of the methyltransferase enzyme EZH2, improved disease outcome 133 . text: SECTION 18 NEOPLASMS OF THE SKIN Steven Kaddu Smooth Muscle, Adipose, and Cartilage Neoplasms TUMORS OF SMOOTH MUSCLE Leiomyoma Synonyms:  Superficial leiomyoma  Leiomyoma cutis  Superficial benign smooth muscle tumor Key features  Three distinct variants: piloleiomyoma, genital leiomyoma, and angioleiomyoma  A solitary or multiple clustered (piloleiomyomas) papules or nodules in an adult  Piloleiomyomas and angioleiomyomas may be painful  Multiple piloleiomyomas may be a manifestation of hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer (Reed syndrome)  Smooth muscle cells (myocytes) are fusiform cells with centrally located, cigar-shaped nuclei Introduction Superficial (cutaneous) leiomyomas represent benign smooth muscle tumors that can arise from: (1) arrector pili muscles; (2) the dartoic, vulvar, or mammary smooth muscles; or (3) the muscles enveloping dermal blood vessels. Thus, they are subclassified into piloleiomyomas (solitary or multiple), leiomyomas of the external genitalia, and angioleio- myomas. Some authors categorize vulvar and scrotal leiomyomas separately, based upon distinctive clinical and histologic features 1 . History In an early review article, Arthur Purdy Stout 2 cites an 1854 publi- cation of Rudolf Virchow as the first case report of multiple leiomyomas involving the skin near the areola in a 32-year-old man. Epidemiology Cutaneous leiomyomas are relatively uncommon neoplasms, but their exact incidence is not known 3 . Angioleiomyomas appear to be more common than piloleiomyomas 4 , with genital leiomyomas being the least common variant. Pathogenesis The exact pathogenesis of superficial leiomyomas has yet to be deter- mined. Piloleiomyomas are thought to arise from the smooth muscle cells within the arrector pili muscle of the folliculosebaceous unit. Leiomyomas of the external genitalia are probably derived from the network of smooth muscles in the external genitalia (e.g. scrotum, vulva) and areolae. Angioleiomyomas are believed to originate from the smooth muscle within the walls of arteries and veins. However, there is a morphologic spectrum that encompasses angioleiomyoma and myopericytoma. Angioleiomyomas may exhibit cytogenetic abnor- malities including monosomy of chromosome 13 and loss of 6p, 21q, and 13q, as well as NOTCH2 rearrangement. Multiple piloleiomyomas may occur sporadically or they may be inherited in an autosomal dominant manner (with variable penetrance) as a component of hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer (HLRCC), also referred to as Reed syndrome, in which patients have multiple cutaneous leiomyomas and uterine leiomyomatosis as well as renal cell cancer 5,6 ( Table 117.2 ). Affected individuals are heterozygous for germline loss-of-function mutations in the

Multiple piloleiomyomas may occur sporadically or they may be inherited in an autosomal dominant manner (with variable penetrance) as a component of hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer (HLRCC), also referred to as Reed syndrome, in which patients have multiple cutaneous leiomyomas and uterine leiomyomatosis as well as renal cell cancer 5,6 ( Table 117.2 ). Affected individuals are heterozygous for germline loss-of-function mutations in the fumarate hydratase gene INTRODUCTION Smooth muscle, adipose, and cartilage neoplasms arising in the skin and subcutis comprise a wide spectrum of benign and malignant neoplasms that show myocyte, adipocyte, and chondrocyte differentiation, respec- tively. Tumors of fat, especially lipomas, occur most commonly. These neoplasms often present as solitary lesions with significant overlap in clinical appearance. In addition, the clinical differential diagnosis can be rather broad ( Fig. 117.1 ). As with other cutaneous tumors, multiple lesions raise the possibility of an inherited disease (e.g. hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer). In this group of neoplasms, the histopathologic diagnosis is estab- lished primarily on the basis of characteristic morphologic features, including architecture and cytomorphology, as well as identification of the predominant direction and level of differentiation ( Fig. 117.2 ). Determination of whether a tumor is benign or malignant also requires assessment of features such as circumscription and if atypia and increased mitotic activity are present. Great care is necessary when applying traditional morphologic criteria for malignancy to cutaneous mesenchymal neoplasms because some clinically less aggressive tumors may exhibit prominent atypical features. In other words, aggressive behavior is not always predictable based solely on morphologic findings. For several of these neoplasms, immunohistochemical studies provide helpful diagnostic information ( Table 117.1 ). Cytogenetic analysis and molecular studies are increasingly being used for diagnosis and classifi- cation of many soft tissue tumors as there can be relatively histiotype- specific molecular features (see below). A number of tumor-related and patient-related factors may influence the choice of treatment, including tumor type and size, anatomic location, patient’s life expectancy, presence of comorbidities, and cosmetic concerns. For the majority of solitary, benign, or relatively non-aggressive malignant neoplasms, excisional surgery with clear margins is the treatment of choice. However, removal of a benign tumor is often done at the patient’s request rather than for medical reasons. text: A number of tumor-related and patient-related factors may influence the choice of treatment, including tumor type and size, anatomic location, patient’s life expectancy, presence of comorbidities, and cosmetic concerns. For the majority of solitary, benign, or relatively non-aggressive malignant neoplasms, excisional surgery with clear margins is the treatment of choice. However, removal of a benign tumor is often done at the patient’s request rather than for medical reasons. Other modalities, e.g. cryotherapy, laser ablation (multiple leiomyomas), liposuction (large lipomas), may be preferable in certain patients. For more aggressive malignant tumors, the therapeutic goal is complete eradication, via either wide local excision or Mohs micro- graphic surgery, while trying to preserve normal function and avoiding mutilating surgery. As expected, the most significant predictor of recur- rences is surgical margin status. In some dermal sarcomas, extension into the subcutis represents a negative prognostic factor. Although the molecular basis of HLRCC is known, how this translates into smooth muscle tumors is not understood. Multifocal subcutaneous leiomyomas arising in the setting of immunodeficiency, including HIV infection, may be associated with Epstein–Barr virus infection. Clinical features Piloleiomyomas can be solitary or multiple, and in an occasional patient may even number in the hundreds. They present as firm, reddish- brown to skin-colored papules or nodules. Solitary piloleiomyomas develop primarily during adulthood and there is an approximately equal sex distribution 7 ; rare congenital or pediatric cases have been reported. When multiple, the distribution pattern is most often clustered ( Fig. 117.3 ), linear, or along the lines of Blaschko, but widespread lesions are observed occasionally. Most piloleiomyomas measure 1–2 cm in diameter, and they usually develop on the extremities and trunk (especially the shoulder), with solitary lesions favoring the limbs and multiple lesions the trunk 7 . Piloleiomyomas are often associated with spontaneous or induced pain, e.g. following cold exposure, but the explanation is still unclear 7 . Genital leiomyomas are most often solitary and painless. They can develop on the vulva, penis, scrotum, nipple, or areola and usually measure less than 2 cm in diameter. Occasionally, lesions are pedunculated. Angioleiomyomas most commonly present as a solitary, firm subcu- taneous nodule on the lower extremity. They often develop in women during the fourth to sixth decades of life 4 . Approximately 50% of angioleiomyomas are painful. Pathology Piloleiomyomas are typically centered within the reticular dermis,

Occasionally, lesions are pedunculated. Angioleiomyomas most commonly present as a solitary, firm subcu- taneous nodule on the lower extremity. They often develop in women during the fourth to sixth decades of life 4 . Approximately 50% of angioleiomyomas are painful. Pathology Piloleiomyomas are typically centered within the reticular dermis, with focal extension into the subcutaneous fat in some cases. They are composed of interlacing fascicles of relatively bland smooth muscle cells (myocytes), which peripherally tend to ramify between surrounding dermal collagen bundles ( Fig. 117.4 ); often there is a close relationship to hair follicles 4 . Occasionally, the overlying epidermis is hyperplastic. Smooth muscle cells have abundant brightly eosinophilic cytoplasm and blunt-ended, cigar-shaped nuclei. Mitotic figures are rare. In the presence of bland cytology, one or two morphologically normal mitotic figures per 10 high-power fields may be seen, which does not signify aggressive behavior. In leiomyomas, smooth muscle differentiation is usually obvious in H&E-stained sections, but sometimes special stains for smooth muscle cells are utilized. Tumor cells consistently stain positively for both smooth muscle actin (SMA) and desmin, with other useful markers listed in Table 117.1 . In HLRCC, there is often negative immunohisto- chemical staining for fumarate hydratase in the cutaneous leiomyomas (in one series, 83% sensitivity/75% specificity 9 ). Intracellular accumu- lation of S-(2-succino)-cysteine in uterine leiomyomas may suggest fumarate hydratase aberration but this is not specific for HLRCC 10 . In contrast to uterine leiomyomas, cutaneous leiomyomas do not express receptors for estrogen or progesterone 11 . Genital leiomyomas of the scrotum or vulva tend to be larger and better circumscribed than piloleiomyomas. Scrotal leiomyomas are usually homogeneous spindle cell tumors, while vulvar lesions may demonstrate an epithelioid cytology, myxoid changes, and/or hyalin- ization 1 . Leiomyomas of the nipple closely resemble piloleiomyomas. Angioleiomyomas are usually well-circumscribed tumors centered within the superficial subcutis ( Fig. 117.5 ). They are composed of bland smooth muscle cells compactly arranged into bundles and whorls around thick-walled vascular channels 4 . Degenerative changes including hyalinization, focal thrombosis, myxoid changes, dystrophic calcifi- cation, pyknotic nuclear atypia, and fat foci may be present. Tumors composed of a proliferation of blood vessels, smooth muscle cells, and adipose tissue are termed angiomyolipomas or angiolipoleiomyomas. Differential diagnosis For single lesions, the clinical appearance is nonspecific and the differ- ential diagnosis includes a wide range of entities that can present as solitary dermal nodules, including dermatofibromas. When a lesion is painful or there is a clustering of multiple red–brown papulonodules, the diagnosis may be strongly suspected prior to biopsy. Histopathologically, leiomyomas need to

text: AND RENAL CELL CANCER (REED SYNDROME) Genetic aspects • Autosomal dominant • Mutations in the gene on chromosome 1q42.3-43 that encodes fumarate hydratase, an enzyme in the mitochondrial Krebs cycle Clinical features • Cutaneous leiomyomas: multiple painful, grouped, skin-colored to red–brown papules appear during the second to fourth decades • Uterine leiomyomas: > 90% of affected women; menorrhagia and pelvic pressure or pain • Renal cell carcinoma: 10%–15% of patients with syndrome; most commonly type 2 papillary renal cell carcinomas that are often early-onset and aggressive (metastases in > 50% of patients); less often tubulo-papillary or collecting duct carcinomas Screening of individuals with multiple cutaneous leiomyomas • Abdominal and pelvic ultrasound (or CT scan) • Complete history and physical examination, including pelvic examination in women • Immunohistochemistry of cutaneous leiomyomas: (1) negative staining for fumarate hydratase (in one series, 83% sensitivity and 75% specificity was found 9 ); and (2) intracellular accumulation of S-(2-succino)-cysteine • Genetic testing for heterozygous pathogenic variant in the fumarate hydratase gene ( FH ; 70%–90% detected by sequence analysis) • If pathogenic FH variant not detected, can measure fumarate hydratase activity (will be ≤ 60%) Patients with confirmed syndrome • Complete history and physical examination yearly, including pelvic examination in women • Yearly abdominal MRI (if baseline or follow-up scan normal) • If renal lesion detected, then CT scan and renal ultrasound performed; PET-CT scan can be done • Complete physical examination (including pelvic examination in women) of first-degree family members and other family members as indicated; abdominal and pelvic ultrasound as indicated Establishing diagnosis: heterozygous pathogenic variant in FH (rarely not detected). Clinical criteria: major criterion is multiple cutaneous leiomyomas (at least 1 confirmed histologically); minor criteria are: (1) severely symptomatic uterine leiomyomas before age 40; (2) type 2 papillary renal cell carcinoma before age 40; and (3) first-degree relative who meets one of these aforementioned criteria. Diagnosis is strongly suspected if major criterion met or ≥ 2 minor criteria present. PET, positron emission tomography. Smooth Muscle, Adipose, and Cartilage Neoplasms Treatment Simple excision is usually curative for solitary or limited tumors. For those tumors that are not amenable to surgery because of their number or location, treatment with gabapentin, medications that reduce smooth muscle contraction (e.g. nifedipine, nitroglycerin, doxazosin), cryotherapy, or CO 2 laser ablation may provide relief from pain 12,13 . Leiomyosarcoma Synonyms:  Atypical intradermal smooth muscle neoplasm  Piloleiomyosarcoma  Superficial leiomyosarcoma  Superficial malignant smooth muscle tumor Key features  Malignant smooth muscle neoplasm  Occurs primarily in adults > 50 years of age  Most commonly located on the extremities, in particular the lower leg  Dermal leiomyosarcomas are typically cured by simple excision and rarely metastasize; subcutaneous leiomyosarcomas require wide excision and have a 25%–40% risk of metastasis Introduction For management and prognostic reasons, it is important to differentiate between “superficial leiomyosarcomas” that are limited to the dermis and lesions that primarily arise in or extensively involve the subcutis. The former have a favorable prognosis and can recur, but very rarely metastasize. Subcutaneous leiomyosarcomas, in contrast, metastasize in ~25%–40% of cases 14,15 . To emphasize this distinction, the term atypical intradermal smooth muscle neoplasm has been suggested for dermal lesions (rather than leiomyosarcoma). Epidemiology Cutaneous and subcutaneous leiomyosarcomas are rare neoplasms, comprising only 4%–6.5% of soft tissue sarcomas 16,17 . Pathogenesis Dermal leiomyosarcomas are thought to arise from either arrector pili or genital smooth muscles. Subcutaneous leiomyosarcomas probably originate from vascular smooth muscle. Predispositions include Li– Fraumeni syndrome due to TP53 mutations, retinoblastoma (RB) inactivation due to RB1 or CDKN2A (p14 ARF ) mutations or deletions (see Fig. 107.4 ), and Epstein–Barr viral infection in the setting of immunosuppression. Anecdotal reports describe a rare association with trauma and radiation 17,18 . Clinical features Cutaneous and subcutaneous leiomyosarcomas classically present as a solitary, firm, skin-colored to red–brown nodule or plaque. Dermal location for multiple piloleiomyomas. Leiomyosarcomas favor the extremities, in particular the lower leg of older adults ( Fig. 117.6 ) 4,19,20 . There is a slight male prepon- derance 4 . Patients with multiple tumors should be evaluated to exclude the possibility of metastases due to a primary retroperitoneal or visceral leiomyosarcoma. Pathology The histopathologic features of leiomyosarcomas span a morphologic continuum that, at the well-differentiated end, demonstrates an overlap with leiomyomas, while poorly differentiated lesions closely resemble atypical fibroxanthomas or “malignant fibrous histiocytomas” 21 . Leiomyosarcomas of moderate differentiation are comprised of cells that cytologically resemble normal smooth muscle cells. However, compared to leiomyomas, malignant smooth muscle tumors are more cellular, exhibit cytologic atypia, and contain easily identifiable mitotic figures ( Fig. 117.7 ). At least focally, the spindle cells are arranged in fascicles. Cytologically, poorly differentiated leiomyosarcomas may resemble myofibroblastic or fibrohistiocytic tumors. Notably, the degree of differentiation may vary within a single tumor. Rarely, the cells have an epithelioid appearance 22 . A definitive diagnosis of leiomyosarcoma often requires adjuvant special stains and/or immunohistochemical studies to support the cell lineage. Leiomyosarcomas consistently stain positive for SMA and desmin. Of the two markers, SMA is more sensitive and desmin is somewhat more specific; additional useful markers are listed in Table 117.1 . By definition, dermal leiomyosarcomas (atypical intradermal smooth muscle neoplasms) are superficial malignant neoplasms with at least 90% of the tumor confined to the dermis 23 . They are usually poorly circumscribed and are composed of spindle cells; the latter are focally arranged in fascicles that infiltrate between adjacent collagen bundles. In comparison, subcutaneous leiomyosarcomas tend to be better circum- scribed and may be surrounded by a pseudocapsule of compressed tissue. In comparison, subcutaneous leiomyosarcomas tend to be better circum- scribed and may be surrounded by a pseudocapsule of compressed tissue. Differential diagnosis Because the clinical features are not unique, the differential diagnosis includes a number of tumors that can present as solitary plaques, e.g. dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans, or firm nodules (see Fig. 117.1 ). The histopathologic differential diagnosis usually raises two problems: the differentiation of leiomyosarcoma from leiomyoma and its delin- eation from other spindle cell neoplasms. Traditionally, the number of mitotic figures is used as the most reliable diagnostic criterion when trying to predict clinical behavior. In the presence of cytologic atypia, a mitotic rate of one or more mitotic figures per high-power field is generally considered to be indicative of malignancy 16 . It is important to remember, however, that the prognosis of leiomyosarcomas appears to depend more on the depth of involvement (dermal vs subcuta- neous), and the extent of mitotic activity is probably more important in subcutaneous lesions. Necrosis and angiolymphatic invasion are generally not useful in predicting prognosis for patients with dermal and ­subcutaneous leiomyosarcomas. The distinction of leiomyosarcoma from other dermal spindle cell neoplasms nearly always requires immunophenotyping. This is best approached by using a panel of antibodies that examine the neoplasm for its line of differentiation ( Table 117.3 ). A standard panel consists of antibodies to SMA, desmin, cytokeratin, S100 protein, and CD68. Leiomyosarcoma will usually be SMA-positive and desmin-positive, but negative for keratin, S100 protein, and CD68. Treatment Wide excision with meticulous examination of all surgical margins is crucial in order to prevent recurrence. Recurrent tumors tend to infil- trate more deeply, and they are often less well differentiated. In addition, they are more difficult to treat and carry a higher risk of metastasis. Several authors have reported successful treatment with Mohs micro- graphic surgery 17 , allowing for complete margin control. As noted previously, some authors have even suggested using the term “atypical intradermal smooth muscle neoplasm” rather than leiomyosarcoma 24 . Subcutaneous leiomyosarcomas metastasize in 25%–40% of patients. The risk of metastasis appears to be related to size, as metastasis is unlikely in tumors < 5 cm in diameter. Metastatic spread occurs hematogenously to the lung and, less often, other visceral organs, or via the lymphatics to regional lymph nodes 18,23 . Smooth Muscle Hamartoma Key features  Congenital or acquired skin-colored to hyperpigmented plaque on the trunk or proximal extremities  Commonly exhibit follicular prominence and/or hypertrichosis  Clinical and histopathologic overlap with Becker melanosis (nevus) Introduction Hamartoma is derived from the Greek word hamartia , which means “fault”, “defect”, or “flaw”, and oma (tumor). Hamartomas are defined as lesions that are: (1) most commonly present at birth, but can also be acquired; and (2) are composed of aberrant mature or nearly mature structures. The term hamartoma is synonymous with “nevus”, for example, nevus sebaceus, apocrine nevus, eccrine nevus. A smooth muscle hamartoma may be congenital or acquired and may be associated with Becker melanosis (nevus). History The first description of a smooth muscle hamartoma is attributed to Stokes in 1923 25 . Epidemiology The estimated incidence ranges from 1 : 1000 to 1 : 27 000 live births. Clinical features Smooth muscle hamartomas not associated with Becker melanosis (nevus) present as firm, skin-colored or hyperpigmented plaques, most commonly located on the trunk, buttocks, or proximal extrem- ities ( Fig. 117.8 ). Differential diagnosis Clinically and histologically, smooth muscle hamartomas demonstrate overlap with Becker melanosis, and the two lesions possibly represent a spectrum of phenotypic expression of the same process. Leiomyomas usually present as papulonodules rather than plaques. Histologically, the smooth muscle fibers in a piloleiomyoma aggregate to form dermal tumors with irregular margins, but they are not haphazardly scattered throughout the dermis as in a smooth muscle hamartoma. Treatment Therapy may be indicated for cosmetic reasons. A small lesion may be amenable to excision. Treatment of Becker melanosis with lasers that target melanin (e.g. Q-switched ruby laser) lead to modest, if any, improvement 27 . Photoepilation of pigmented hairs via laser therapy is usually more successful (see Ch. 137 ). TUMORS OF FAT Lipoma Key features  Common benign tumor of mature fat  Asymptomatic, soft to rubbery, subcutaneous nodule arising at any site but rare on the hands and feet  Multiple lipomas are seen in familial multiple lipomatosis, Madelung disease, adiposis dolorosa, Gardner syndrome, PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome, and Proteus syndrome Introduction (Ordinary) lipomas are benign tumors composed of mature adipo- cytes. They are among the most common neoplasms in humans, and they represent the most common mesenchymal neoplasm 28 . Lipomas are often solitary, but 5%–10% of patients have multiple lipomas, usually in the setting of a lipomatosis or less often a multisystem syndrome. Epidemiology Lipomas develop at any age, but they usually become clinically apparent between the fourth and sixth decades of life. Most studies report the incidence of lipomas to be slightly higher in men than in women 28 . Pathogenesis Little is known about the pathogenesis of lipomas. Of note, the incidence of lipomas is increased in overweight individuals, diabetics, and patients with elevated serum cholesterol 28 . In familial multiple lipomatosis, there is clearly a genetic component. In approximately two-thirds of patients, clonal chromosomal aberrations are present ( Table 117.4 ).
