Epidemiology LG is a rare disease of adults, usually presenting in the fifth to sixth decade of life. The male-to-female ratio is approximately 2 : 1. The disease can affect children, most commonly in the setting of immuno- deficiency syndromes 28,29,62 . Pathogenesis The pathogenesis of LG is often related to EBV infection, occasionally in combination with immunosuppression. Factors associated with LG include use of immunosuppressive medications (e.g. azathioprine, methotrexate, imatinib), HIV infection, Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome, X-linked lymphoproliferative syndrome, and additional lymphopro- liferative disorders 28,29 . In the WHO classification of hematopoietic tumors, LG is categorized as an angiocentric/angiodestructive lympho- proliferative disease with variable histological grades 28,29 . Clinical features Patients with LG present with symptoms related to pulmonary involvement, such as cough, dyspnea, and chest pain. Constitutional symptoms include fever, weight loss, malaise, arthralgias, and myalgias. Cutaneous lesions develop in 25%–50% of patients and usually present as nodules or ulcerated plaques ( Fig. 121.12 ). Rarely, LG may present as a maculopapular exanthem. The kidney, brain, and gastrointes- tinal tract may be affected. In contrast to angioimmunoblastic T cell lymphoma, the lymph nodes and spleen are rarely involved. Pathology In LG, there are three histopathologic grades: (1) grade 1 – polymor- phous lymphoid infiltrate without cytologic atypia, along with a few large cells, and few cells are positive for EBV-encoded RNA 1 (EBER-1) and latent membrane protein via in situ hybridization and immuno- histochemistry, respectively; (2) grade 2 – polymorphous inflammatory background with scattered large cells and more abundant EBER-1 + cells; and (3) grade 3 – sheets of large B cells and numerous EBER-1 + cells predominate over the inflammatory background. The amount of necrosis increases with the grade and angiocentricity/angiodestruction is consistently present. Granulomatous changes are often present. The neoplastic cells stain positively for CD20 and CD79a, and in most high- grade lesions there is a monoclonal rearrangement of the J H genes 9,28,29 . McNiff Cutaneous Metastases 122 SECTION 18 NEOPLASMS OF THE SKIN EPIDEMIOLOGY Depending upon the series, cutaneous metastases occur in 1% to 10% of patients with metastatic disease (to any organ) 1 . Although uncommon, their recognition is important because they can be the first sign of metastatic disease and, as a result, have profound prognostic implications. The proportion of patients with metastatic disease who have cutaneous metastases depends upon the particular malignancy, e.g. the highest incidence is in individuals with metastatic melanoma, where up to 45% of patients can develop skin metastases ( Table 122.1 ) 1 . Sex-specific cancer rates also influence the frequency of the various types of cutaneous metastases. In women, skin metastases are most often due to breast carcinoma (70%) and melanoma (12%), followed by carcinomas originating from the ovary, head and neck, and lung 1 . In men with skin metastases, the most common underlying malignancies are melanoma (32%), followed by carcinomas of the head and neck (16%), lung (12%), and colon (11%). The overall prevalence of a cancer is also an important determinant. For instance, although skin metastases develop in only 2.5% of patients with metastatic lung cancer, they account for 12% of all cutaneous metas- tases in men due to the high prevalence of lung cancer 1 ( Fig. 122.2 ). The skin is not a particularly common site for metastatic spread, and because the clinical appearance of cutaneous metastases can mimic more common disorders, e.g. epidermoid cysts (inflamed and non-inflamed; Fig. 122.1 ), lipomas, cellulitis, there may be a delay in diagnosis. An understanding of the clinical spectrum as well as advances in histological assessment of skin metastases is vital to estab- lishing the correct diagnosis. It is generally accepted that certain cancers tend to metastasize to distinct tissues. The mechanism by which they choose their final desti- nation is related to hemostatic forces and surface protein expression patterns. When tumor emboli lodge in the first vascular bed they encounter, adhesion molecule interactions (e.g. integrins) facilitate extravasation and account for the commonly noted involvement of regional nodal basins. Yet, certain cancers have an affinity for specific tissues that are not anatomically convenient, such as prostate cancer spreading to bone and ocular melanoma metastasizing to the liver 3 . CLINICAL FEATURES The clinical characteristics of cutaneous metastasis can provide important clues. When a patient with a known history of cancer presents with an extremely firm and rapidly growing erythematous nodule or an eruption of multiple skin nodules in close proximity to the primary tumor ( Table 122.2 ), the diagnosis of cutaneous metastasis is relatively straightforward. However, the skin lesions may grow more slowly, and while metastases typically appear within several years of the diagnosis of the primary malignancy, they can present decades later. The color of cutaneous metastases varies, from skin-colored to pink–red to blue–black, with the latter most commonly observed in metastatic melanoma ( Fig. 122.3 ). In general, dermal and subcuta- neous metastases are firmer on palpation than lipomas or epidermoid and tricholemmal (pilar) cysts. Cutaneous metastases can arise from hematogenous or lymphatic spread as well as direct extension. Similarly, the age of the patient plays a role, with rhabdomyosarcoma and neuroblastoma responsible for the majority of cutaneous metas- tases seen in children 2,3 . Cutaneous metastases develop an average of 36 months (range, 1 to 177 months) after the initial diagnosis of the primary malignancy 2,4 . Unfortunately, the vast majority (~95%) of patients with cutaneous metastases have advanced, stage III or IV disease. Rarely, cutaneous metastases can be the presenting sign of an internal malignancy ( < 1% of all new cancer diagnoses). PATHOGENESIS In 1889, Dr Stephen Paget espoused the “seed and soil” hypothesis as the paradigm of metastatic disease – a malignancy must develop the capability to dissociate from its native environment, survive during transit, and then propagate in a new milieu. This process includes detachment, intravasation, circulation, stasis, extravasation, and finally proliferation 5,6 . It is estimated that ≤ 0.01% of tumor cells shed into the vasculature form metastatic foci at distant sites 7 . The ability of a malignancy to acquire metastatic potential is thought to occur via one of two mechanisms 8 . In the clonal expansion or linear progression model, selective growth advantages are acquired during the course of tumor development. Over time, subpopulations of cells acquire genetic characteristics that enable them to dissociate and then propagate in distant tissues. In this model, metastatic foci have similar phenotypes and genotypes to the original tumor. An example of lymphatic spread is in-transit metastases of melanoma while direct extension is most commonly observed with breast carcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck. There are additional examples of anatomic localization, including the predilection of gastrointestinal malignancies to metastasize to the periumbilical region, referred to as a Sister Mary Joseph nodule ( Fig. 122.4 ). Occasionally, implantation of tumor occurs at the time of a surgical procedure, e.g. chest tube placement for a malignant pleural effusion due to lung cancer. Although the distribution of cutaneous metastases is usually more random in the case of hematogenous spread, the scalp can be a preferred site for some malignancies, e.g. renal cell carcinoma. Of all the carcinomas that metastasize to the skin, breast cancer may be the one with the widest range of clinical presentations ( Table 122.3 ), varying from papulonodules to patches of erythema mimicking erysipelas (inflammatory carcinoma) to woody induration with a peau d’orange appearance ( Fig. 122.5 ). The latter is often referred to as “ en cuirasse ” due to its clinical resemblance to the leather armor of a soldier ( cuirassier ) 1 . In addition, intravascular metastases can lead to erythem- atous papules that may resemble vascular proliferations, including the angiosarcomas that can follow breast irradiation (see Ch. 114 ). Less common presentations include the dermatitis-like appearance of Paget disease, both mammary and extramammary (see Table 122.3 ). Metastases of renal cell carcinoma can resemble pyogenic granulomas, including a tendency to bleed (see Fig. 122.3B ). Rarely, intravascular metastases lead to a reticulated vascular pattern that is reflective of a vaso-occlusive process or the cutaneous metastases assume an unusual distribution pattern, e.g. zosteriform. In addition to metastases from solid organs, leukemias and systemic lymphomas can also involve the skin (see Chs. 119–121 ). PATHOLOGY Adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), and melanoma represent the three major categories of cutaneous metastases ( Table 122.4 ). In broad terms, these metastatic tumors generally lack an epidermal connection or involvement, are situated in the dermis or subcutis, and are composed of nodules, nests, or cords of atypical cells with mitoses ( Table 122.5 ). However, it is important to note that occasionally there are primary “dermal” nodular melanomas 9 , and primary cutaneous spindle cell SCCs often lack a prominent epidermal component. When there is intra- vascular involvement, this may be confused with benign entities such as intralymphatic histiocytosis ( Fig. 122.9 ). Complete evaluation of a cutaneous metastasis often requires the use of a panel of histochemical stains ( Fig. 122.10 ; see Table 122.4 ) 12 . While such stains are not a substitute for a detailed history and physical examination plus diagnostic imaging and biopsy of the primary tumor 12 , the resulting information does provide direction and may circumvent the need for a more invasive biopsy of another tissue. In order to distinguish between a primary cutaneous tumor (usually an adnexal carcinoma) and a cutaneous metastasis (especially of adenocarcinoma), immunostains, in particular p40/p63, CK5/6 and D2–40 (podoplanin), can prove helpful 13–15 . Primary cutaneous tumors are typically positive for some or all these markers and metastases lack staining. Important exceptions are p63-positivity in some metastatic adenocarcinomas (breast, urothelial, and lung) and an absence of p63 staining in some primary cutaneous adnexal carcinomas. In the case of cutaneous metastases from adenocarcinomas, various combinations of CK7 and CK20 expression can provide useful information (see Fig. 122.10 ) 15 . This panel is also employed to evaluate extramammary Paget disease, in which CK20 positivity points to a secondary form of the disease that is originating from a visceral malignancy (see Fig. 73.16 ). NEOPLASMS OF THE SKIN Certain organ-restricted markers may also be useful including: CD10, RCC, and PAX8 (positive in renal and ovarian tumors); thyroid-specific transcription factor-1 (TTF-1) (thyroid, lung; see Fig. 122.2 ); thyro- globulin (thyroid); prostate specific antigen (PSA) and NKX3.1 (prostate); CDX2, CDH17, and SATB2 (gastrointestinal); Hep Par1 and arginase-1 (hepatocellular carcinoma); and CD56 and insulinoma-associated protein 1 (INSM1) (neuroendocrine) (see Table 122.4 ). In cutaneous metastases of SCC, staining for pankeratins and EMA may be positive, but this infor- mation is not helpful in determining the site of the primary SCC. In addition to the histologic examination of conventional skin biopsies, cutaneous metastases can be sampled via fine-needle aspiration cytology 16 . TREATMENT AND PROGNOSIS Typically, cutaneous metastases are a harbinger of late-stage or progressive disease and as such portend a poor prognosis. The average survival time following the initial diagnosis of cutaneous metastasis is 7.5 months 17 and half of patients expire within the first 6 months 18 . Whether the patient has a known or unknown primary malignancy, the development of cutaneous metastases calls for a multidisciplinary approach, including medical and surgical oncologists, radiation oncolo- gists, and mental health care providers when appropriate. Localized treatment of cutaneous metastases can be undertaken for functional, palliative, or cosmetic indications.

Descriptive Studies Many of the studies currently being done in dermatology are descriptive. These include case reports and case series. A case report is a detailed description of an individual patient’s demographics, clinical presen- tation, diagnosis, treatment, and disease course. A case series reports on some aspect(s) of a disease, diagnostic procedure, or treatment in a group of patients with common characteristics 20 . Case reports and series are useful for determining the manifestations of rare condi- tions, reporting the preliminary outcomes of experimental therapies, and generating hypotheses for larger studies. A major limitation of case series is the lack of a control group ( Table 123.4 ) 20,21 , although previous data (e.g. on the prevalence of risk factors in the general population) can sometimes be utilized for comparison. An example of a valuable case series is the description of scalp involvement in patients with dermatomyositis by Kasteler and Callen 22 . THE PUBLIC HEALTH IMPORTANCE OF DERMATOLOGY Skin conditions are a major cause of morbidity worldwide. Based on analysis of global burden of disease data 4 , skin diseases accounted for over 41 million disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) lost in 2013 and ranked as the fourth most common cause of non-fatal disease burden ( Table 123.1 ). In the US, dermatology accounts for 4% of all outpatient visits, representing the third most common subspecialty ambulatory visit (after ophthalmology and orthopedics). In addition, ~5%–8% of primary care and 4% of emergency department visits are primarily for dermatologic conditions, with the most common outpatient diagnoses including eczema, skin infections, benign neoplasms, acne, psoriasis, and skin cancer 5–7 . Notably, in 2010, the symptom of itch accounted for 1% of all outpatient visits in the US 8 . Not only are dermatologic conditions common, but some are rising in incidence. For example, the incidence of melanoma increased by ~3% per year in the US from 1981 to 2005, and then at a lower rate of ~1% per year from 2005 to 2019 9 ; these increases have included all tumor thickness groups, although mortality has overall been stable, with improvement more recently, especially in women and younger diagnosis facilitated by knowledge of epidemiology. Using Epidemiology to Identify the Cause of Disease Case–control, cohort, and cross-sectional studies are often performed to help elucidate the etiology and risk factors of a disease (see Table 123.4 ). These methods involve studying a disease of interest (e.g. cutaneous SCC) and an exposure that is suspected of being a risk factor for the disease (e.g. ultraviolet [UV] radiation), so that the study participants can be categorized as having the disease or not and as being exposed to the potential risk factor or not ( Table 123.5 ). Case–control study A case–control study identifies a group of individuals with a disease, as well as a comparison group without the disease from the same population. The study design retrospectively evaluates the level of exposure in the disease group (cases), as compared to that in the group without disease (controls). To ensure that those with disease and without are comparable, both types of participants should be sampled from a single population and data collected in the same way for each group 23 . In addition, cases and controls should be matched on possible confounding factors; for example, if there is a 60-year-old female case, then a 60-year-old female control from the same general population would be selected. A confounder is an extraneous variable that is associated with both the exposure and the disease being studied; it could therefore account for a part or all of the relationship between the exposure and disease. Although the confounder may be a contributing factor to the disease, it is not caused by the exposure and thus is not along the “causal pathway” between the exposure and disease 1,2 ( Fig. 123.2 ). Age and sex are examples of possible confounders. These and other character- istics that may be associated with both the exposure and the disease should also be recorded and placed in the statistical model. If an association remains after accounting for confounders, it is more likely to be a true one. In a case–control study, one can calculate the odds of having had the exposure among those with disease (a/c), as compared to the odds of having

In a case–control study, one can calculate the odds of having had the exposure among those with disease (a/c), as compared to the odds of having had the exposure among those without disease (b/d) (see an odds ratio (OR), which equals (a/c)/(b/d) or ad/bc. An OR = 1 denotes a null association, whereas an OR statistically significantly greater or less than 1 indicates a positive or negative association, respectively. An OR is different from a relative risk (RR), the rate of disease among those exposed divided by that among those unexposed, (a/a + b)/(c/c + d) (see Cohort study section below). While the RR cannot be directly calcu- lated from a case–control study, the OR approximates the RR when the disease is rare. One of the major advantages of a case–control study is that it can yield information on a disease with many possible predictors, yet use only a limited number of participants. Therefore, it is well-suited for the investigation of rare conditions. Also, these studies are relatively inexpensive and time-efficient. One of the disadvantages of a case– control study is that it is not clear if the exposure preceded the disease, so causality cannot be established. In addition, this type of study has several potential biases. Sampling bias can occur when cases and controls are collected separately and may not be comparable. Because of the retrospective ascertainment of exposure, recall bias can occur; for example, those with disease may recall the exposure with greater detail because they have been contemplating the potential causes of their condition. Of note, a case–control study does not yield information on the incidence or prevalence of a disease. An example of a case–control study is that by Picard et al. 24 , which examined the association between psoriasis (here the “exposure”) and coronary artery disease. At the end of the study, one can calculate the rate of cutaneous SCC among those with high-dose UV exposure (a/a + b) and compare it to the rate of SCC among those without high-dose UV exposure (c/c + d). Therefore, a cohort study compares the incidence of disease between those exposed and not exposed to particular risk factor(s). This is usually expressed in terms of a RR (see definition above). Similar to an OR, a RR of 1 repre- sents a null association, whereas a RR statistically significantly greater or less than 1 indicates a positive or negative association, respectively. A cohort study can be done prospectively, allowing for more control over measuring outcomes (preferred particularly for fatal diseases), or retro- spectively, which is less expensive and requires less time. One of the advantages of a cohort study is that it can determine the incidence of a disease, which is the number of new cases divided by the total number of people at risk in a particular population (e.g. partici- pants in the study) over a specified time period (e.g. length of study) 1 . It also gives information on the natural history of a disease, since it captures data from the time of disease onset. Another advantage is that a cohort study establishes temporality, as the exposure precedes the outcome, and therefore allows for causal inference between the exposure and disease. The disadvantages are that a cohort study often requires a large sample size and is less feasible for rare outcomes. A cohort study by Zhang et al. 25 looked at the association between tanning bed use and development of skin cancers.

Another advantage is that a cohort study establishes temporality, as the exposure precedes the outcome, and therefore allows for causal inference between the exposure and disease. The disadvantages are that a cohort study often requires a large sample size and is less feasible for rare outcomes. A cohort study by Zhang et al. 25 looked at the association between tanning bed use and development of skin cancers. Their study population included > 70 000 female nurses who were followed between 1989 and 2009. After adjusting for possible confounders (e.g. age, skin type, sun exposure, UV index at place of residence), they found that for an incremental increase of 4 sessions/year in mean use of tanning beds prior to age 35 years, the RR of developing BCC was 1.15 (95% CI, 1.11 to 1.19). Thus, the use of tanning beds a mean of 4 or 8 times per year resulted in a ~15% or ~30% higher risk of BCC, respectively, compared to not using tanning beds. This demonstrates a “dose response” effect, i.e. women who used tanning beds more often had a higher skin cancer risk. Furthermore, the authors noted that women exposed to tanning beds in their teenage or college years were at higher risk than those exposed later in life. Effect modification or interaction occurs when the association between the exposure and disease varies across levels of a variable (e.g. age; Fig. 123.4 ). Therefore, the exposure and effect modifier have an interdependent role in their effect on the disease. When this happens, the association between exposure and disease should be displayed at various levels or strata of the effect modifier 1,2 . Cross-sectional study A cross-sectional study is similar to a cohort study, except that the initial population does not need to be free of the disease of interest and both the exposure and disease are measured at a single time point, without a follow-up period. It yields information on the prevalence of disease, which is the number of affected individuals divided by the number of people in the population at risk (e.g. total number of study participants), at a given time. It allows one to study the association between exposure and disease, but it does not provide information about which preceded the other. It allows one to study the association between exposure and disease, but it does not provide information about which preceded the other. Cross-sectional study results are often expressed in terms of ORs or relative prevalence , which compares the prevalence rate of a disease among those exposed to that among the unexposed. While mathematically it is represented by (a/a + b)/(c/c + d) (see Table 123.5 ), here a/a + b and c/c + d are prevalence rates, rather than incidence rates, as in a cohort study. The advantages of a cross-sectional study are that it is relatively fast, inexpensive, and does not require follow-up. It is the only epidemio- logic study that gives the prevalence of a disease, exposure, or other risk factor. One of its weaknesses is that it does not demonstrate temporality, and so it cannot establish a causal relationship between the exposure and disease. Also, it is not practical for rare diseases or rare exposures, which would require a very large study population. An example of a cross-sectional study is one by Love et al. 26 , which used a national database representative of the non-institutionalized civilian US population, the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey. It found that the prevalence of metabolic syndrome was 40% among psoriasis cases, compared to 23% among controls. After adjusting for age, sex, race/ethnicity, smoking status, and C-reactive protein levels, the OR for the association between psoriasis and metabolic syndrome was 1.96 (95% CI 1.01–3.77). Therefore, patients with psoriasis had a 1.96 times or 96% greater odds of having metabolic syndrome, as compared to those without psoriasis. Participants can be blinded to their group, as can the observers (double- blinded). The participants are followed for a given period of time, during which disease outcomes and safety are measured. In a randomized controlled trial (RCT), participants are randomized to receive the intervention versus a placebo or an alternative therapy. Participants can be blinded to their group, as can the observers (double- blinded). The participants are followed for a given period of time, during which disease outcomes and safety are measured. Table 123.6 presents the four phases for testing of new drug therapies. Intention-to-treat analysis is then performed, which classifies participants into the inter- vention group that they were assigned through randomization, rather than the actual intervention that they received; variation can arise if participants crossed over into the other intervention group because of non-compliance, side effects, or other reasons. This preserves the randomization of the study design. However, an analysis taking into account the actual intervention received is done as well, for comparison. The outcome measures for a RCT vary according to the outcome of interest (e.g. relative risk, percentile improvement comparison across groups, prognosis measures; Table 123.7 ). The concept of statistical significance is applied to assess whether the differences in outcome occurred by chance or likely represent a true effect of the intervention. The major advantage of a controlled trial is its ability to demonstrate causality ( Table 123.8 ). Randomization can eliminate confounding effects and blinding can eliminate bias. The disadvantages are that controlled trials are relatively expensive, can expose participants to potential harm, and answer a narrow clinical question. Generally, participants in clinical trials should be easy to recruit as well as reasonably likely to benefit and unlikely to be harmed from the inter- vention; participants with a high level of adherence to the treatment and follow-up plan are also desirable. The design of the intervention should balance efficacy and safety, with interim monitoring during the trial to ensure that participants are not exposed to a harmful intervention, denied a beneficial intervention, or continued in a trial that cannot answer the question it was intended to answer. Whenever possible, trials should include comparison with placebo. When comparing active treatments in an equivalence or superiority trial, comparison with the gold-standard treatment for the patient population being studied can maximize the relevance to clinical practice. A well-designed blinded RCT is thought of as the gold standard for study design 21 (see Table 123.4 ). An example of an RCT is assessment of the efficacy and safety of etanercept in children and adolescents with moderate to severe plaque psoriasis by Paller et al. 27 . It involved randomizing 211 pediatric patients (4 to 17 years of age) with psoriasis to a double-blinded trial of once- weekly subcutaneous injections of etanercept or placebo, for 12 weeks. The primary endpoint was ≥ 75% improvement from baseline in the psoriasis area and severity index (PASI 75). The patients randomized to receive etanercept were significantly more likely to achieve a PASI 75 (57%) than those receiving placebo (11%) (P < 0.001). The authors were able to conclude that etanercept significantly reduced disease severity in children and adolescents with moderate to severe plaque psoriasis. Systematic Reviews A systematic review identifies completed studies that address a specific research question and then aggregates and statistically analyzes the results across studies, to arrive at a conclusion about a body of research 1 . Although traditionally applied to RCTs, systematic reviews can also draw data from observational studies. A systematic review should have a written protocol addressing the research question it seeks to answer, utilize comprehensive and unbiased methods for identifying studies, and clearly describe the statistical aspects of the review, i.e. meta-analysis. It should also include a summary estimate of effect plus CI based on the findings of all eligible studies (see Fig. 123.3 ). In addition, it should have an assessment of heterogeneity across the studies used, to indicate the degree of variability in the findings in different studies. It should address publication bias by taking into account unpublished studies, as positive studies are more likely to get published. It also usually includes subgroup analyses based on additional measures done by some or all of the studies that are supplemental to the main research question. If any of the design decisions were questionable or arbitrary, analyses should be done to assess how sensitive the findings of the meta-analysis are to decisions taken in designing particular studies or inclusion of certain studies. Here, the less sensitive the study the better. The characteristics and the findings of individual studies should be displayed clearly in tables and figures to allow the reader to visualize the data and not rely solely on the conclusions of the meta-analysis 2,23 . The advantage of a systematic review is that it enables the integration of the results of multiple studies, allowing for greater power. However, a systematic review is only as valuable as the quality of the studies upon which it is based. Caution must be exercised in interpreting systematic reviews, with recognition that they may not take into account unpublished studies, the quality of all of the studies may not be equal, studies may not be comparable (e.g. different outcome measures), and adjusting for biases can be a formidable task. In addition, having a single estimate of risk based on those from several studies may give a false sense of certainty regarding the magnitude of the risk 2,23 . A systematic review of RCTs that have homogeneous results gets the highest ranking of all study types 21 (see Table 123.4 ), but the level of evidence is considerably lower for systematic reviews limited by the factors discussed above. The Cochrane Skin Group, which stems from the larger Cochrane Collaboration Group that reviews a variety of healthcare studies, is dedicated to the production of systematic reviews on dermatologic topics 28 . An example of a systematic review is that by Wehner et al. 16 , which utilized available studies to summarize the effects of indoor tanning on risk of BCC and cutaneous SCC. The authors searched large databases (e.g. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science) and extracted data from the 12 studies (all observational) that met their inclusion criteria, with assessment of methodologic quality, heterogeneity, and publication bias through established methods. They found summary RRs of 1.29 (95% CI, 1.08–1.53) for BCC and 1.67 (95% CI, 1.29–2.17) for SCC in individuals who reported ever using a tanning bed compared to those who never used tanning beds 16 . By applying these summary RRs to the prevalence of indoor tanning in the US, they calculated the population attributable risk fraction of indoor tanning to be 8.2% for SCC and 3.7% for BCC. GENETIC EPIDEMIOLOGY When considering the etiology of a disease, it is important to account for genetic susceptibility as well as environmental factors. Because of advances in molecular and genetic techniques, epidemiologic studies have expanded to include use of biologic samples. Upon completion of the Human Genome Project in 2003 and the International HapMap Project in 2005, researchers were able to use a technique known as the genome-wide association study (GWAS). This method examines the association between disease and single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), markers for groups of DNA variation inherited together in blocks (haplotypes). Findings from these studies can be used to inves- tigate the molecular pathways of disease. One can look for associa- tions in a hypothesis-driven or non-hypothesis-driven manner. A study by Petukhova et al. 29 illustrates the use of GWAS techniques to explore the pathogenesis of alopecia areata (AA). Using genetic samples from 1054 cases and 3278 controls, they identified 139 SNPs significantly associated with AA (P ≤ 5 × 10 − 7 ). They found an associ- ation between these SNPs and the genomic regions containing several genes that control the activation of T cells and cytokine production. HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH The field of health services research applies techniques of epidemio- logic investigation to assess the association between health services provided in the community and disease outcomes. Outcomes for this kind of research include traditional endpoints such as mortality and morbidity, as well as others such as usage and access, patient satisfaction, quality of life, and disability measures. In addition to the efficacy of an intervention in an ideal, controlled environment, it is important to assess effectiveness in real life situations (e.g. with factors that decrease adherence; Table 123.9 ) and efficiency (e.g. cost : benefit ratio). HEALTH POLICY IMPLICATIONS OF RESEARCH The ultimate goal of medical research is to benefit patients. The appro- priate application of research findings to healthcare policy and practice is a critical component of medical advances. The international “choosing wisely” campaign is a physician-led, patient-focused initiative with the goal of utilizing evidence-based medicine to improve quality of care and reduce the unnecessary and potentially harmful use of tests, proce- dures, and treatments. Patient-centered communication and shared decision-making have also been highlighted as top priorities in cancer care. For example, overdiagnosis of asymptomatic BCCs in patients near the end of life may lead to anxiety and intensive treatments with harms that outweigh the benefits, whereas an individualized approach that incorporates the patient’s input and overall prognosis can optimize their overall well-being 30 . Quality-of-Life Measures Quality of life (QOL) has been defined by the World Health Organization (WHO) as “the individuals’ perception of their position in life, in the context of the cultural and value systems in which they live and in relation to their goals, expectations, standards, and concerns”. QOL is an important outcome measure for dermatologic conditions because, while many conditions are not fatal, they can cause significant morbidity leading to decreased QOL. Patients may place different weights on various QOL measures depending on their personal values, background, and education. Therefore, development of a QOL measure that is valid can be challenging. The most commonly used QOL instrument in dermatology is the Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI), which has been employed for numerous conditions. It is a self-administered, 10-item questionnaire about patients’ perceptions of the impact of their skin disease over the last week 31 . The DLQI has been validated for dermatology patients aged ≥ 16 years, with good-to- excellent internal consistency, high test–retest reliability, and results that correlate with those of other QOL instruments (although less so for mental and emotional aspects) 32 . Another commonly used, validated dermatologic QOL instrument is Skindex, which is available in 29- and 16-item versions with separate scores for symptoms, emotions, and functioning 33,34 . IMPORTANT CONCEPTS WHEN DESIGNING AND REVIEWING A STUDY Research Question and Design There are important concepts to consider when planning research or interpreting published literature. These concepts apply to both obser- vational studies and clinical trials ( Table 123.10 ). First, it is important to be aware of the study design needed to best answer the research question of interest. Furthermore, one must recognize the questions that a particular study design can and cannot answer; for example, a case–control study cannot determine causality. Methods When considering study methodology, it is important to recognize the importance of a control group and to understand random (due to chance) and systematic errors that may affect the study. Systematic errors are due to bias, “sources of variation that distort the study findings in one direction” 23 . The opposite of systematic errors is validity. Several types of bias that can occur in epidemiologic studies are described in Table 123.11 . Some studies are particularly prone to certain types of bias. For example, retrospective studies are especially susceptible to recall bias, a type of information bias (see section on Case–control study). An effort should be made in the study design to decrease systematic errors. The baseline patient characteristics, exposures, other risk factors, and disease characteristics should be measured reliably and accurately ( Fig. 123.5 ). Information on validity (accuracy) is often expressed using sensitivity and specificity or predictive values. Sensitivity represents the likelihood of testing positive for someone who has the disease (a/a + c) ( Table 123.12 ). Specificity is the likelihood of testing negative for someone who does not have the disease (d/b + d). The positive predictive value is the likelihood of having the disease when testing positive (a/a + b). The negative predictive value is the likelihood of not having the disease when testing negative (d/c + d). Predictive values depend on the prevalence of a disease – the higher the prevalence, the higher the positive predictive value and the lower the negative predictive value. Statistical methods should include adjustments for potential confounders including when examining the association between exposure and disease (see Fig. 123.2 ). If not adjusted for, confounders may lead to a false association between an exposure and a disease. When analyzing disease outcome, it is also important to test for effect modifi- cation of the exposure by other study variables suspected of playing an interdependent role with the exposure (see Fig. 123.4 ). If there is a significant effect modification variable for an association, then the association measure should be presented for different levels of the effect modification variable. Results In analyzing results, it is important to assess whether baseline charac- teristics significantly differ across both exposure and outcome groups. If this occurs, such potential confounders need to be placed in the statistical model addressing the association between the exposure and disease so that they may be adjusted for. Next, the correct outcome measure must be reported for a given study design, e.g. OR for a case–control study. Statistical significance is typically demonstrated by a P value ≤ 0.05 and/ or by a 95% CI that does not include 1 within the interval for measures that represent a ratio (zero for measures that represent a difference). A 95% CI that shows significance indicates that there is 95% confidence that the association is not due to chance alone (see Fig. 123.3 ). Whether the study was sufficiently powered to detect a statistically significant difference should also be determined. Power is affected by the number of participants. When planning a study,

Conclusions In drawing conclusions about the results, the factors that support causality for the association in question should be determined (see whether the association makes biological and clinical sense. If it does not make sense, a type I error may have occurred, where a statisti- cally significant association is found when one does not truly exist (false positive). The more statistical tests that are performed for a study, the more likely a statistically significant association will be found based on chance alone. In studies utilizing large databases where many compar- isons are made, the false discovery rate increases and statistical methods (e.g. the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure) should be used to adjust P values in order to mitigate the risk of type I errors 35 . Alternatively, if an association is not found when one would be expected, a type II error may have occurred, where no statistical significance is found when one truly exists (false negative). This can be caused by a study not having enough power. The conclusions that can be drawn given the type of study design must be recognized, taking into account the strengths and limitations, including potential biases. In extrapolating the results, the generaliz- ability of the study must also be considered. This pertains to how appli- cable the results are to the greater population and groups that did not participate in the study. It should also be noted if a trial was industry- sponsored. Lastly, it is important to consider the implications of the study on current clinical practices and the direction of future research. Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) and the Consolidated Standards for Reporting Trials (CONSORT) There is a need to ensure appropriate reporting of findings from dermatologic studies. Langan et al. 36 found that dermatologic papers infrequently reported sample size calculations, missing data, losses to follow-up, and statistical methods. Ubriani et al. 37 noted that in 2004–2005 only 20%–49% of articles published in three prominent dermatology journals reported the design of their study in the title or abstract of the paper. In order to improve the quality of reporting of observational studies in medical research, criteria for reporting have been suggested in the form of the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE)

Ubriani et al. 37 noted that in 2004–2005 only 20%–49% of articles published in three prominent dermatology journals reported the design of their study in the title or abstract of the paper. In order to improve the quality of reporting of observational studies in medical research, criteria for reporting have been suggested in the form of the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) checklist. Items critical for inclusion include the design of the study in the title or abstract and an informative summary of what was done in the abstract. The methods section should describe: (1) eligibility criteria, sources, and selection methods for participants; (2) methods of follow-up, matching criteria (if applicable), and numbers of exposed/unexposed individuals; (3) all outcomes, exposures, predictors, potential confounders, and effect modifiers, as well as diagnostic criteria; (4) all statistical methods (including those dealing with confounding), examination of subgroups and interactions, how missing data and losses to follow-up were addressed, and any sensitivity analysis 38 . The Consolidated Standards for Reporting Trials (CONSORT) statement is a similar initiative for improving the quality of reporting for RCTs. This 25-item checklist emphasizes reporting how the trial was designed, analyzed, and interpreted. It also includes a flow diagram that displays the progress of all participants through the trial 39 . OPPORTUNITIES FOR RESEARCH IN DERMATO-EPIDEMIOLOGY While each of the study types discussed above provides valuable infor- mation, there is a relative paucity of studies that include a control group or a large study population in dermatologic research. Considering the high prevalence of many skin conditions and the rising incidence of diseases such as melanoma, the field of dermatology is likely to play a bigger role in public health research in the future. Therefore, it is important for dermatologists to understand epidemiologic and clinical research techniques, and to advocate for the inclusion of dermatology- related questions in local, state, and national surveys, allowing for larger epidemiologic studies to be conducted. Associations of dermatologic conditions with comorbid diseases have become increasingly well characterized, and the implications of skin disease treatment on population health are now being explored. For example, patients with psoriasis have an increased risk of metabolic syndrome, myocardial infarction, and stroke; studies are now evalu- ating the effect of psoriasis treatment on coronary artery disease and other cardiovascular risk markers 40

For most of the skin surface in humans, the stratum corneum is typically comprised of about 20 corneocyte cell layers, which differ in their thickness, packing of keratin filaments, filaggrin content and number of corneodesmosomes, depending on body site 8 . Corneocytes are reinforced by a highly resilient sheath of multiple proteins, cross-linked into the CE, while the cell interior is packed with keratin filaments embedded in a matrix composed primarily of filaggrin and its breakdown products. Some of these breakdown products serve as “natural moisturizing factor” while others have antimicrobial properties 11 . At the stratum granulosum–stratum corneum interface, lamellar body contents are secreted, fused end-to-end, and progressively elongated into lamellar membrane sheets 12,13 , a sequence requiring the action of a battery of lipolytic “processing” enzymes (see below) ( Fig. 124.2 ). Glucosylceramide-based bilayers with cubic-like symmetry are organized within the extracellular spaces into ceramide-based lamellar membranes that surround the corneocytes 14 (lipid processing). Variations in the number of lamellar membranes (which determines lipid weight %), membrane substructure, and/or lipid composition provide the structural and biochemical basis for site-related variations in permeability 15 . The volume of the extracellular lipid-enriched matrix of the stratum corneum includes the structures that limit transdermal delivery of hydrophilic drugs as well as the so-called stratum corneum “reservoir” 16 . Within this reservoir, lipid-soluble drugs (e.g. topical corticosteroids) can accumulate and be slowly released. Of note, its volume can vary dramatically. For example, at baseline, these domains account for ~10% of stratum corneum volume, but with hydration or the inspis- sation of topical agents, they can account for up to 50% of stratum corneum volume. Ceramides account for ~50% of the total stratum corneum lipid mass and are crucial for the lamellar organization of the stratum corneum barrier 17 . Of the nine ceramide species, acylceramides or ceramides 1, 4, and 7 (which contain ω -hydroxy-linked essential fatty acids in an ester linkage) are epidermis-unique compounds, known to be important for barrier function 12 . Keratinocytes also synthesize triglycerides, with the final step in the pathway catalyzed by diacylglycerol transferase (DGAT). Lipases and acyltransferases then break down the triglyc- erides, thereby releasing fatty acids that serve as building blocks for ceramides and acylceramides. The latter are both essential for lamellar bilayer and CLE formation. Free fatty acids , which consist predominantly of very-long-chain, saturated species with ≥ 18 carbon atoms, and cholesterol each account for 10%–15% of stratum corneum lipids. A subset of fatty acids contains linoleic acid thus providing an explanation for the abnormal extra- cellular matrix observed in essential fatty acid deficiency. Cholesterol promotes the intermixing of different lipid species and regulates its “phase” behavior 18 . A decrease in the concentration of any of these critical lipid species alters their molar ratio within lamellar membranes which then compromises barrier integrity and function. STRUCTURAL BASIS FOR THE PERMEABILITY BARRIER The skin provides the largest interface between the human body and the external environment 1,2 . Therefore, one of its most important functions is to prevent ingress of potentially harmful exogenous substances (outside-in barrier). However, because desiccation is incompatible with life (inside-out barrier requirement), the skin must also prevent excessive loss of water and other bodily constituents 3 . Tight junctions not only play an important role in directly blocking passage of some molecules – they also direct epidermal differentiation and formation of the lipid barrier 4,5 . Tight junctions not only play an important role in directly blocking passage of some molecules – they also direct epidermal differentiation and formation of the lipid barrier 4,5 . Of note, the tight junction barrier develops before the lipid barrier, both in a fetal rat model and in human epidermal equivalents (HEE), with tight junction expression receding as the lipid barrier develops 6 . The skin’s remarkable barrier properties are sustained in large part by epidermal homeostasis 1,2 , which insures that the generation of corneocytes and lipids is optimized in order to support this function 7 . The corneocytes within the stratum corneum are composed primarily of keratin filaments encased in a cornified envelope (CE), and they have been likened to “bricks”. Corneocytes are further surrounded by a cornified lipid envelope (CLE) and an extracellular milieu of lipids organized as multiple lamellar bilayers, analogous to “mortar” ( Fig. 124.1 ) 8 . At the stratum granulosum–stratum corneum interface, keratino- cytes contain abundant filament aggregating protein (filaggrin), which also plays a role in barrier function. Filaggrin has a predominance of arginine over lysine residues and is found within liquid-like kerato- hyalin condensates. As a result of their phase separation- and pH-driven assembly and disassembly during keratinocyte terminal differentiation, these membrane-less structures become osmotically active amino acids. The latter undergo deamination regulated by changes in environmental humidity 9 . As they differentiate, keratinocytes accumulate lipid-containing lamellar bodies, i.e. tubuloreticular structures, whose secreted contents play a key role in the formation of the stratum corneum (see Fig. 124.1 ). These extracellular structured lipids will comprise ~10% of the volume of the stratum corneum 10 . They prevent excessive loss of body water and likewise block entry of exogenous compounds, including most topically applied drugs (except for those that are lipid-soluble and of low molecular weight). In a vectorial process, keratinocytes differentiate while moving outward from the basal to the outer epidermal layer, forming lipid-enriched lamellar bodies and tight junctions within the granular layer. The skin barrier is intimately linked with the innate immune system, e. g. antimicrobial peptide production, Langerhans cell activation. The stratum corneum barrier is a unique two-compartment system, analogous to a brick wall. Whereas lipids are sequestered extracellularly within the stratum corneum, the corneocytes are lipid- depleted but protein-enriched. Although epidermal lipid synthesis is both highly active and largely autonomous from systemic influences, it can be regulated by external influences, i.e. changes in the status of the permeability barrier 19 . Acute perturbations of the permeability barrier by environmental factors stimulate a charac- teristic recovery sequence that leads to restoration of normal function over about 72 hours in young skin (the cutaneous stress test) 20 . This metabolic sequence includes a rapid increase in cholesterol, free fatty acid, glucosylceramide, and ceramide synthesis that is restricted to the underlying epidermis; this is attributable to a prior increase in mRNA and enzyme activity/mass for each of the key synthetic enzymes ( Fig. 124.3 ). Synthesis of each of these key lipids is required for normal barrier homeo- stasis, particularly in the context of barrier repair 12,19 . Lamellar Body Secretion The unique two-compartment organization of the stratum corneum is attributable to the secretion of lamellar body-derived lipids and co-localized hydrolases at the stratum granulosum–stratum corneum interface 12 . Under basal conditions, lamellar body secretion is slow, but sufficient to provide for barrier integrity. Following acute barrier disruption, calcium is lost from the outer epidermis and much of the preformed pool of lamellar bodies in the outermost cells of the stratum granulosum is quickly secreted 20–22 . Calcium (Ca 2 + ) is an important regulator of lamellar body secretion, with the normally high levels of Ca 2 + within the stratum granulosum restricting lamellar body secretion to low, maintenance levels 23,23a . CUTANEOUS DISEASES AND BARRIER DYSFUNCTION Abnormalities of the skin barrier are observed in both common and rare skin diseases. Causes of barrier dysfunction include (but are not limited to): mechanical trauma, exposure to detergents or solvents, seborrhea, prolonged water exposure, ultraviolet radiation, infection, inflammatory dermatoses, certain drugs, and genetic mutations and polymorphisms. Low humidity downregulates barrier competence while cold tempera- tures impair permeability barrier homeostasis 38 . Many disorders of cornification, including the ichthyoses, are due to pathogenic variants in genes that encode key components of the skin barrier, such as keratin and enzymes involved in extracellular lipid synthesis, among others 39 . Mutations and genetic polymorphisms in barrier-related genes also contribute to the pathogenesis of more common skin diseases, e.g. filaggrin in atopic dermatitis (see Ch. 12 ) 40,41 or cornified envelope proteins LCE3B and LCE3C in psoriasis 42 . Aging skin also displays barrier abnormalities and increased susceptibility to xerotic eczema and pruritus due to age-associated declines in CE proteins and stratum corneum lipid content as well as elevated skin surface pH 43,44 . Barrier dysfunction induces a wide range of cellular responses in epidermal keratinocytes. Beyond controlling barrier recovery, they also affect epidermal proliferation (important in wound healing) and inflam- mation (outside-in link between barrier and inflammation) 45 . The latter is characterized by the production and release of epidermal cytokines involved in both innate immunity (e.g. TNF, IL-1 α ) and leukocyte recruitment and activation (e.g. IL-17, IL-22). When epidermal inflam- mation occurs on a large scale, it can have a local as well as a systemic impact via circulating cytokines 46,47 . This may explain in part the associ- ation between skin diseases with barrier dysfunction and disorders such as cardiovascular disease 46 . In addition, phospholipid hydrolysis, catalyzed by one or more secretory phospholipases (e.g. sPLA 2 ), generates a family of nonessential free fatty acids, which are also required for barrier homeostasis 25 . Sphingomyelin hydrolysis by acidic sphingomyelinase generates two of the nine ceramides required for normal barrier homeostasis (see Fig. 124.2 ). Sphingomyelinase is upregulated during epidermal injury, during which ceramide generation contributes to barrier recovery 26 as well as inflam- mation via its role as a second messenger in TNF receptor signaling 27 . The resultant epidermal disease represents an example of outside-in pathogenesis. Finally, cholesterol sulfate is desulfated during passage from the inner to the outer stratum corneum 28 . Both cholesterol sulfate and its processing enzyme, steroid sulfatase, are concentrated in membrane domains of the stratum corneum. In addition to lipid precursors and lipolytic enzymes, lamellar bodies contain proteases and antiproteases that orchestrate the orderly digestion of corneodesmosomes, allowing corneocyte shedding or desquamation . By controlling the thickness of the stratum corneum, the rate of desquamation has a major impact on the barrier properties of skin. For example, while stratum corneum from palmoplantar skin is more permeable than in other sites, it is much thicker and therefore has a longer lag time for the penetration of topically applied drugs 1 . When stratum corneum permeability is increased in the setting of skin diseases such as psoriasis 29 and inherited ichthyoses 30 , associated scale (due to abnormal desquamation and a thickened stratum corneum) provides partial compensation by mitigating barrier dysfunction. Lamellar bodies also deliver antimicrobial peptides, including human β -defensin 2 and LL-37 (the carboxy-terminal fragment of human cathe- licidin). In addition, corneocyte-derived peptide fragments 31 , sebaceous gland-derived fatty acids, and free long-chain bases derived from ceramides exhibit antimicrobial activity 32 . Antimicrobial peptide levels and permeability barrier function are interdependent 33 . For example, topical agents that improve the skin barrier simultaneously enhance antimicrobial peptide production 34 . Emerging evidence supports a crosstalk between host immune effectors and cutaneous microorganism communities, i.e. the skin microbiome 35 . The first mechanism is relatively well characterized 48 , with structural defects in the stratum corneum a rather straightforward explanation for impaired barrier function. The second mechanism typically involves a pronounced disorganization of stratum corneum lipid lamellae, as for example in psoriasis 47 . Psoriatic scale contains immature CEs 49,50 and CLEs (as assessed by covalently bound lipid composition) that make them fragile and less hydro- phobic 51 than normal corneocytes, which could explain the failure to properly organize extracellular lipids into barrier-providing mature lipid lamellae. There are also changes in the composition of the extra- cellular lipids in some inflammatory skin diseases, particularly in the chain length of ceramides and fatty acids 52 , which correlate with alterations in the lateral packing of lipid membranes and increased permeability. How inflammation induces these changes is an area of active investigation since the role of several inflammatory cytokines (e.g. IL-1, TNF) on epidermal homeostasis and barrier function remains unclear 53 . Finally, psychological stress disrupts permea- bility barrier homeostasis, impairs stratum corneum cohesion 54 , and compromises epidermal innate immunity by increasing endogenous glucocorticoids 55,56 . TREATMENT OF SKIN BARRIER DYSFUNCTION Therapies for barrier dysfunction are still limited. Semi-occlusive emollients, especially petrolatum 57 , reduce transepidermal water loss, although less effectively than native stratum corneum lipids 58 . Impermeable and vapor- permeable dressings can provide nearly complete occlusion and are as effective as potent topical corticosteroids in the treatment of psoriasis 59 , but are normally limited to small treatment areas. Moreover, these treat- ments are no substitute for the stratum corneum as a microbial barrier – they are applied on top of (superficial to) the microbiome, thereby providing an underlying moist environment that facilitates microbial growth and enhanced penetration. Targeted therapy of barrier dysfunction must address the underlying cause. While inflammation can be treated with anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory drugs, a new class of therapeutic agents that addresses defects in lipid metabolism is emerging. For example, porokeratosis and CHILD syndrome, both resulting from defects in cholesterol synthesis, have been reported to improve following appli- cation of cholesterol plus lovastatin (the latter blocks accumulation of pathogenic lipid precursors) 62,63 . Ceramide-based, triple-lipid mixtures are employed to address defective barrier function. Increasing knowledge about the pathophysiology of skin barrier-driven diseases should offer major opportunities for novel therapies. REFERENCES Skin Barrier and Transdermal and Topical Drug Delivery PARAMETERS AFFECTING SKIN PERMEABILITY The skin is an attractive site for drug delivery, whether for topical delivery to locally treat cutaneous conditions or for transdermal delivery into the systemic circulation via absorption through the skin for other indications 64,65 . However, normal skin provides a significant barrier to drug absorption, whereas diseased skin can provide a lesser or greater barrier, depending on its associated epidermal changes 66 . While the most straightforward method of circumventing the stratum corneum barrier is an intradermal needle injection (e.g. the Mantoux technique) 67 , this is often not practical for patients to perform on a routine basis. Understanding the parameters that affect the permeability of this barrier is essential for achieving successful drug therapy via the skin without intradermal or subcutaneous injections. While local cutaneous effects are generally achieved by dissolving or suspending the drug in a vehicle that is applied topically as a semi-solid formulation (e.g. cream or ointment) 68 , administration of systemic therapy via the skin is typically accomplished through the use of a patch. Drug Concentration The driving force for percutaneous absorption is the concentration of soluble drug in the vehicle. Many older topical drug products were marketed with the expectation that higher concentrations were more potent. Although true for some products such as tretinoin gels and creams (0.01%–0.1%), in which the drug is completely solubilized at all concentrations, for others it is not the case. Partition Coefficient In general, topically applied drugs are poorly absorbed because only a small fraction partitions into the stratum corneum. Most of the drug remains on the skin surface, subject to loss from a multitude of factors (exfoliation, sweating, wash-off, rub-off, adsorption onto clothing, and chemical or photochemical degradation). Even 10–12 hours following application, a drug that has not been lost by exfoliation or rub-off remains largely on the skin surface, and it is easily removed by a simple soap and water wash 73 . In the case of patches worn for several days, as much as half of the original amount of drug may still be present in the patch when it is removed, and this can pose a safety hazard upon disposal, especially with potentially dangerous drugs such as fentanyl 74 . A number of physical and chemical factors can improve partitioning. Hydration of the skin due to occlusion, either from a topical formulation or a patch, expands the reservoir volume available to drugs within the stratum corneum; this can increase absorption by as much as five- to ten-fold 75 . Common excipients such as ethanol and propylene glycol can also alter barrier structure so as to increase partitioning 76 . In addition, many excipients have good solvent properties and, as a result, positively affect C v as well as K m . The use of high concentrations of propylene glycol to maximize bioavailability has become pervasive among the super- and high-potency corticosteroids, but at a price. STRATEGIES TO ENHANCE TRANSDERMAL DRUG DELIVERY Despite the significant permeability barrier of the stratum corneum, drug delivery via the skin is a very attractive option and is widely employed for both local and systemic therapy ( Table 124.4 ; Fig. 124.7 ) 64,65 . Topical treatment of cutaneous disorders obviously targets the site of disease, thereby minimizing adverse side effects elsewhere within the body. Delivery of systemic therapies via the skin avoids degradation of the medication within the gastrointestinal tract and from first-pass metabolism by the liver, both of which are associated with oral admin- istration of drugs, in addition to evading the pain and safety issues associated with injections. Transdermal delivery of drugs, especially via long-acting patches, enables infrequent dosing and maintenance of steady-state drug levels. Many dermatologic medications can be applied topically to the skin because the required dosage is often exceedingly small and therefore they can be effective even in the setting of highly inefficient absorption. In addition, a number of skin disorders are associated with compro- mised barrier function, which leads to an enhanced drug uptake in sites of involvement 79 . In contrast, systemic drug delivery via the skin typically requires administration of larger doses through normal skin. As a result, at the time of writing, fewer than two dozen drugs have been FDA-approved for transdermal administration. Chemical Enhancement Chemical enhancers include compounds that interact with the lipid matrix of the stratum corneum to alter its nanostructure and thereby increase permeability 64,65,76 . The major advantages of chemical enhancers are that they are typically low cost, can be incorporated into a conven- tional patch or topical formulation, and do not require the complexity of a battery-powered device. The primary disadvantage of chemical enhancers is that they are often associated with skin irritation or toxicity when present at high concentrations and with long exposure times 77 . Following 24–48 hours of occlusion, corneocytes swell, the intercellular spaces become distended, and the lacunar network becomes dilated. Distention of lacunae is thought to eventually lead to connections within an otherwise discontinuous system, creating “pores” in the stratum corneum interstices through which polar and non-polar substances can penetrate more readily. Finally, liposomes and nanoparticles represent additional “chemical” methods frequently employed to enhance delivery into the skin, especially in the case of cosmetics and moisturizers 86 . While intact liposomes typically do not penetrate the stratum corneum 87 , they can be used to increase effective drug solubility in a vehicle ( C v ) and facilitate partitioning into the skin ( K m ). When nanoparticles contain drugs, this can result in an increase in drug concentrations on the skin surface, thereby increasing drug delivery into the skin, and, in some cases, nanoparticles enable slow release of drugs over time 88 . methods to increase drug delivery via the skin, many of which require the use of devices and some of which hold the promise to significantly expand the spectrum of drugs that can be administered transdermally to include water-soluble molecules and macromolecules 89,90 . Stripping is a simple technique used in research protocols to remove stratum corneum by sequential application of adhesive tape or cyanoac- rylate glue 91 . Tape stripping removes both corneocytes and extracellular lipids, thereby reducing the elongated path length that drugs otherwise need to traverse, and it mechanically disrupts lamellar bilayers, even in the retained lower stratum corneum layers. Barrier disruption of human skin requires multiple strippings, which can lead to inflam- mation. More strippings are required to disrupt the barrier in subjects with skin phototypes V and VI (darkly pigmented) than with phototypes I and II (lightly pigmented) 92 . Iontophoresis and electroporation represent electrically assisted, physical approaches to enhance delivery of drugs/macromolecules across the stratum corneum 93 . Iontophoresis uses low currents applied for minutes to hours from an externally placed electrode (with the same charge as the drug) in order to drive these molecules across the stratum corneum, primarily by electrophoresis 94 . As the rate of drug delivery is generally proportional to the applied current, iontophoresis offers an opportunity for programmable drug delivery, especially with the more recent development of miniaturized microprocessor systems. Clinically, iontophoresis has been employed to deliver: fentanyl and lidocaine for pain relief 95 , pilocarpine to induce sweating (as a diagnostic test) 96 , tap water to treat hyperhidrosis 97 , and sumatriptan for migraine relief. Reverse iontophoresis has been used to extract glucose from the skin as a means of monitoring glucose levels in diabetic patients 98 . Electroporation (electropermeabilization) utilizes very short (micro- second to millisecond) and relatively high voltage (~100 V) electrical pulses to induce structural rearrangement of stratum corneum lipids, leading to pore formation 99,100 . Although currently at the research stage with regard to transdermal delivery, electroporation is being used to drive chemotherapeutic agents into superficial skin tumors by applying surface or penetrating electrodes 101 . While ultrasound is widely and safely employed in both medical diagnostics and physical therapy, this technology can also be used to enhance transdermal delivery. This enables delivery of much larger molecules with much greater fluxes into the skin. With thermal ablation , microsecond- to millisecond-long pulses of heat are applied utilizing electrical filaments, radiofrequency electrodes, or lasers which lead to micropores in the stratum corneum 105,106 . With thermal ablation , microsecond- to millisecond-long pulses of heat are applied utilizing electrical filaments, radiofrequency electrodes, or lasers which lead to micropores in the stratum corneum 105,106 . Because the pulses are so short, there is not enough time for heat to propagate deeply into the tissue, thereby localizing the ablation to the epidermis and minimizing pain; these latter effects have been demonstrated in clinical trials. An at least partial removal of the stratum corneum and an increase in skin permeability can be accomplished via sandpaper abrasion and microdermabrasion 107,108 . Fractional photothermolysis has also been used to create micron-scale holes in the skin ( Chs. 136 & 137 ), as a means of enhancing delivery of several topical agents, including lidocaine, 5-aminolevulinic acid, and 5-fluorouracil 109 . Finally, microneedles represent another micron-scale approach to drug delivery via the skin and this technique has received significant attention in recent years 110 . Microneedles typically measure 0.2–1 mm in length; they can be solid or hollow and are manufactured by micro- fabrication tools adapted from those developed for the microelectronics industry. In clinical trials, solid microneedles have been used to punch microscopic holes into the skin prior to the application of drug-loaded patches such as those containing naltrexone 111 . Drug-coated solid microneedles, designed to undergo dissolution upon insertion into the skin, have also been tested, and the efficacy of zolmitriptan delivered in this manner for the treatment of migraine headaches has been demonstrated 112 . Fully water-soluble microneedles that encapsulate pharmaceutical compounds have also been developed, in particular for simplified vaccinations via patches that generate no sharps waste ( Fig. 124.10 ) 113 . Microneedle technology has gained widespread use in the field of cosmetic dermatology. Initially, microneedles in a roller format were used to produce microinjuries to the skin in order to induce collagen formation and reduce the appearance of wrinkles 114 . More recently, water-soluble microneedles composed of hyaluronic acid have been employed for at-home delivery of dermal filler. Various microneedle designs have also been used to administer bioactive agents into the skin with claimed beneficial properties. Hollow microneedles have been designed to enable simple and reliable intradermal injections. Cortisone and hydrocortisone have fairly significant mineralocorticoid potency, whereas prednisone and prednisolone have slight mineralocorticoid effects. A drug that has no mineralocorticoid activity, such as methylprednisolone, would be most appropriate in situations where mineralocorticoid effects must be avoided 4 . Plasma half-lives of the various systemic glucocorticoids vary from about 1 to 5 hours, as seen in Table 125.1 . However, the plasma half-life is a poor indicator of the duration of action (biologic activity) of each drug. Duration of biologic effect is best assessed by the period of suppression of ACTH secretion from the pituitary gland after the admin- istration of a single dose of a particular glucocorticoid. As indicated in intermediate-acting agents for 24–36 hours, and long-acting agents for more than 48 hours. Duration of biologic activity is a critical factor in choosing a glucocorticoid for alternate-day therapy. Intermediate-acting agents should be used for this purpose, with long-acting agents avoided because there would be no period for recovery of the hypothalamic– pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis (see below) 4 . Absorption and Distribution Oral glucocorticoids are absorbed in the jejunum, with peak plasma levels occurring 30–90 minutes after intake. Administration of these drugs with food may delay absorption but does not decrease the amount absorbed. Once glucocorticoids reach the plasma, the primary carrier protein is corticosteroid-binding globulin (CBG), also known as transcortin. Most endogenous cortisol is bound to CBG, and low doses of exogenous gluco- corticoids are primarily bound by this high-affinity, but low-capacity, carrier system. With higher glucocorticoid doses, some binding also occurs to albumin in a low-affinity fashion, but with a greater capacity because of the larger amount of albumin in plasma. The avidity with which exogenous glucocorticoids bind to these two carrier proteins is less than that of endogenous cortisol. As exogenous glucocorticoids fill CBG binding sites, an increase in low-affinity binding to albumin leads to a greater fraction of free (unbound) glucocorticoid. This free fraction is biologically active, entering cells and mediating glucocor- ticoid effects 5 . Disorders that result in decreased binding proteins in the plasma, such as hepatic or renal disease, increase the free fraction of exogenous glucocorticoids and thereby augment the therapeutic effects and toxicities of these drugs. In 1951, Sulzberger and colleagues 2 first reported the use of systemic cortisone and adreno- corticotropic hormone (ACTH) as therapies for inflammatory skin diseases. One year later, Sulzberger and Witten successfully treated eczematous eruptions with topical hydrocortisone. A novel method of high-dose glucocorticoid therapy was introduced to dermatology in 1982 by Johnson and Lazarus 3 , who used pulse intravenous therapy for pyoderma gangrenosum. During the past 40 years, a variety of other anti-inflammatory/immunomodulatory drugs have been developed, allowing for a “steroid-sparing” effect and minimization of risks from long-term therapy with systemic glucocorticoids. MEDICAL THERAPY The Hypothalamic–Pituitary–Adrenal (HPA) Axis A working knowledge of the normal function of the HPA axis is required to understand glucocorticoid physiology. The hypothalamus produces corticotropin-releasing hormone, which is released in small pulses into the pituitary circulation. The anterior pituitary responds to corticotropin- releasing hormone with synthesis of ACTH and its subsequent pulsatile secretion into the peripheral circulation. ACTH is the hormone that stimulates the middle layer of the adrenal cortex to generate and release cortisol. Under basal conditions, the adrenals produce ~20–30 mg of cortisol (equivalent to 5–7.5 mg of prednisone) per day in an adult, but this may increase up to 10-fold under times of maximal stress. ACTH also has some role in stimulating adrenal androgen production, but it is not significantly involved in the production of the major mineralocor- ticoid, aldosterone. The major mineralocorticoid control mechanisms are the renin–angiotensin system and serum potassium levels. There are three main control mechanisms for endogenous cortisol secretion 6 . ACTH also has some role in stimulating adrenal androgen production, but it is not significantly involved in the production of the major mineralocor- ticoid, aldosterone. The major mineralocorticoid control mechanisms are the renin–angiotensin system and serum potassium levels. There are three main control mechanisms for endogenous cortisol secretion 6 . The first is a negative feedback effect by plasma cortisol, which inhibits the secretion of corticotropin-releasing hormone and ACTH by the hypothalamus and pituitary, respectively. The second method of regulation is the pulsatile secretion of ACTH, which is based on a circadian cycle, with increasing pulses beginning several hours after the onset of sleep and reaching a maximum shortly before waking. From these ACTH pulses, the peak release of cortisol in a typical sleep cycle is at about 6–8 a.m. With other sleep cycles, the circadian pattern will adjust so that peak cortisol levels occur just prior to waking. The third form of control of endogenous cortisol production comes from neural effects on the HPA axis in response to various emotional or physical stresses. These neural stimuli include catecholamine production from the brainstem, corticotropin-releasing hormone from sites other than the hypothalamus, and vasopressin. Molecular Mechanisms As depicted in Fig. 125.2 , the glucocorticoid free (unbound) fraction enters cells and exerts its effects by binding to a cytoplasmic glucocor- ticoid receptor, which is within a protein complex that includes heat shock proteins 5 . Binding of glucocorticoids to this receptor leads to their translocation into the nucleus and eventual release from the protein complex. In the nucleus, the glucocorticoid receptor forms a dimer that binds to glucocorticoid response elements in the promoter region of certain genes (see Fig. 125.2 ). Approximately 10–100 genes in each cell are regulated directly by glucocorticoids 7 . This binding affects the rate of transcription, inducing or (less often) repressing specific messenger RNA production and protein synthesis. The glucocorticoid receptor also interacts with other transcription factors that have a central role in the inflammatory response as well as their coactivator molecules, such as cAMP response element binding protein (CREB)-binding protein. Nuclear factor- κ B (NF- κ B) is an important transcription factor that induces the expression of many genes that play a significant role in chronic inflammation, encoding various cytokines, adhesion molecules, inflammatory enzymes, and growth factors. The glucocorticoid receptor also interacts with other transcription factors that have a central role in the inflammatory response as well as their coactivator molecules, such as cAMP response element binding protein (CREB)-binding protein. Nuclear factor- κ B (NF- κ B) is an important transcription factor that induces the expression of many genes that play a significant role in chronic inflammation, encoding various cytokines, adhesion molecules, inflammatory enzymes, and growth factors. By indirectly and directly inhibiting NF- κ B, the gluco- corticoid receptor can dramatically reduce the inflammatory process (see Fig. 125.2 ) 5 . The glucocorticoid receptor also has an inhibitory effect on activator protein 1 (AP-1), a heterodimeric transcription factor composed of proteins such as c-jun, c-fos, and activating transcription factor; this likewise controls expression of growth factor and cytokine genes. The key cytokines and other proinflammatory molecules that are inhibited by glucocorticoids and the effects of these drugs on inflam- matory cells are summarized in Table 125.2 8,9 .
