Photodynamic Therapy thin AKs more readily than hypertrophic AKs 34 . D-PDT with either mALA or ALA nanoemulsion gel have been used successfully to treat AKs 35 . Actinic cheilitis represents a useful potential PDT application since alternative treatment approaches such as surgical vermilionectomy or laser vaporization are more complicated and have associated morbidities 36 . Basal cell carcinomas (BCCs) Superficial BCCs respond well to PDT, with an expected primary clearance rate of 92%–97% at 12 weeks and 9% recurrence rate at 12 months ( Fig. 135.6 ) 37,38 . Although less effective than surgery, PDT has the advantage of improved cosmetic outcome over both surgery and cryotherapy. Longer term follow-up with a two-session protocol found that the 5-year response rate for imiquimod (80%) was superior to either 5-fluorouracil (70%) or PDT (63%) for clearance of superficial BCCs 39 . More than one session of PDT is recommended to treat a given BCC and two separate illuminations per treatment session (fractionation) increases the long-term clearance rate 16 . Nodular BCCs do not appear to be as well suited to PDT in that lower and variable response rates of 35%–90% have been observed 40 . This type of BCC is best treated surgically when possible. Similarly, difficult- to-treat BCCs (e.g. high risk areas of the face, recurrent, sclerosing type) are probably best treated by Mohs micrographic surgery because of the importance of achieving deep margin control. Multiple superficial BCCs arising in the context of cancer-prone genodermatoses such as basal cell nevus syndrome are a good indication for PDT since multiple lesions can be treated during one session and multiple surgeries thereby minimized 41 . D-PDT has also been studied for the treatment of superficial and nodular BCCs, with ~75% of lesions treated with two sessions having a complete response at 12 months 42 . Because daylight activation of photo- sensitizers may be due predominantly to the superficially penetrating blue wavelengths within natural outdoor light 13 ,

such as basal cell nevus syndrome are a good indication for PDT since multiple lesions can be treated during one session and multiple surgeries thereby minimized 41 . D-PDT has also been studied for the treatment of superficial and nodular BCCs, with ~75% of lesions treated with two sessions having a complete response at 12 months 42 . Because daylight activation of photo- sensitizers may be due predominantly to the superficially penetrating blue wavelengths within natural outdoor light 13 , it is not yet known if daylight is a sufficiently effective light source for treating BCCs. Squamous cell carcinomas (SCCs) Bowen disease is confined, by definition, to atypical keratinocytes that span the entire epidermis, and is thus eminently within the therapeutic range of PDT. Many PDT experts consider Bowen disease to be an ideal application since PDT can be used to treat multiple lesions as well as large, extensive plaques. A PDT clearance rate for Bowen disease of ~90% can be achieved with a 2-year sustained clearance rate of ~70% 43 . For clearance of Bowen disease, PDT outperforms topical 5-fluorouracil, imiquimod, and cryotherapy 44,45 . Bowen disease of the anogenital region and lower extremity can also be an appropriate target for PDT. In the case of lower extremity Bowen disease, a single session of ablative fractional laser-assisted PDT demonstrated superior long-term efficacy compared to two standard mALA sessions, with a 5-year clearance rate of 85% 46 . In this setting, the fractional laser is not used for photosensi- tizer activation, but rather for treatment site preparation prior to topical drug application (see Ch. 136 ). PDT is not recommended for recurrent Bowen disease or microinvasive or invasive SCC 43 . PDT photochemoprevention of AKs and keratinocyte carcinomas PDT is an effective intervention for managing field cancerization beyond just clearing visible AKs. There is increasing evidence that skin sites treated with topical PDT may develop new lesions at a slower rate, raising the possibility of a photodynamic prevention effect 47 . Photochemoprevention with PDT may prove especially beneficial in reducing the incidence of AKs and SCCs in solid organ transplant recip- ients, particularly when periodic “maintenance” PDT is performed 48 . Although PDT is a potential treatment that would allow anatomic preservation, variable success has been reported; the absence of conclusive evidence precludes its recommendation as first-line therapy. Other neoplasms Because activated and malignant T cells can be selectively sensitized by exogenous ALA, PDT has been used to treat the mycosis fungoides form of cutaneous T cell lymphoma 49 . Patch- or plaque-stage lesions may be more responsive than tumor-stage mycosis fungoides. While PDT’s historical roots in dermatology lie in its initial use during the 1970s to treat intracutaneous metastases 1 , it is now widely accepted that PDT is far more appropriate for treating superficial carcinomas rather than advanced disease. Non-Oncologic PDT Applications Acneiform disorders Not only did early studies demonstrate that exogenous ALA could induce PpIX formation within the skin, they also noted the prefer- ential accumulation of active photosensitizer and selective phototox- icity within the pilosebaceous unit. In addition, singlet oxygen exerts antibacterial and anti-inflammatory effects. These effects, in addition to antibiotic resistance and the challenges surrounding the use of oral isotretinoin, have provided an impetus to developing PDT regimens for acne. A reduction in inflammatory acne lesions of 60%–70% was reported with both ALA and mALA PDT, with the two photosensitizers producing similar effects. These effects, in addition to antibiotic resistance and the challenges surrounding the use of oral isotretinoin, have provided an impetus to developing PDT regimens for acne. A reduction in inflammatory acne lesions of 60%–70% was reported with both ALA and mALA PDT, with the two photosensitizers producing similar effects. Use of higher red light fluences and longer incubation times are associated with longer remission, but also with more pain and local reactions 50 ( Fig. 135.7 ). Currently, there is no consensus as to the optimum PDT parameters for treating acne. It should be noted that Cutibacterium (formerly Propionibacterium ) acnes produces cutaneous porphyrins, which can be readily demon- strated with Wood’s lamp examination of any sebaceous-dense area, including normal skin. Exposure to high-intensity blue light alone, in the absence of any exogenous PDT prodrug, can lead to clinical improvement of inflammatory acne lesions. PDT has also been used to treat other acneiform disorders. It was superior to topical 1% clindamycin for the treatment of perioral derma- titis in a small split-face trial 51 . Rosacea and hidradenitis suppurativa represent other diseases for which PDT was reported as being useful 52,53 . In patients with rosacea, ALA-PDT reduced papulopustular lesions as well as flushing, pruritus, burning, and prickling sensations. Photoaging When used to treat AKs and keratinocyte carcinomas, PDT is thought to produce cosmetically favorable results, including improvement of sun-damaged skin. Well-designed trials directly comparing PDT to non-PDT treatments in which photoaging is the primary focus are sparse relative to the extent that this treatment approach is promoted and used in clinical practice (see Fig. 135.5 ). A randomized trial of repetitive D-PDT to prevent AKs found a significant reduction in fine lines, pigmentation, skin roughness, and erythema 54 . Optimal PDT parameters for treatment of photoaging have not yet been determined. Histologically, PDT appears to increase collagen deposition and decrease elastosis 55 . Cutaneous infections There are several mechanisms by which PDT can treat infectious diseases. Singlet oxygen may directly destroy microbes or it may activate host immunologic reactions against the microorganisms. In addition, PDT can induce necrosis of infected tissue, for example, in the treatment of verrucae or condylomata. Conditions that have been shown, in controlled trials, to improve with PDT include verrucae vulgares 56 , condylomata acuminata 57 , and leishmaniasis 58 . The emergence of

text: and decrease elastosis 55 . Cutaneous infections There are several mechanisms by which PDT can treat infectious diseases. Singlet oxygen may directly destroy microbes or it may activate host immunologic reactions against the microorganisms. In addition, PDT can induce necrosis of infected tissue, for example, in the treatment of verrucae or condylomata. Conditions that have been shown, in controlled trials, to improve with PDT include verrucae vulgares 56 , condylomata acuminata 57 , and leishmaniasis 58 . The emergence of ­drug-resistant bacteria plus the need for better antibiotic stewardship have also motivated investigations into employing PDT for bacterial skin infections and colonized chronic leg ulcers 59 . In addition, PDT has been used on superficial fungal infections such as tinea pedis and onychomycosis. Vascular anomalies Systemic photosensitizers are biodistributed via the peripheral circu- lation and it stands to reason that intravascular drug activation with light would be useful in inducing the involution of abnormal vascular structures. Vascular malformations such as port-wine birthmarks have been shown to respond to systemic PDT with results that appear to be at least equivalent to those achieved with conventional pulsed dye laser therapy 60 . Experience with this technique is largely from China, where hematoporphyrin-type preparations are used systemically. Topical ALA/pulsed dye laser-activated PDT has also been described 61 , taking advantage of combined photodynamic and photothermal effects. ADVERSE EFFECTS AND COMPLICATIONS OF PDT Neither PDT photosensitizers nor artificial visible light ordinarily possess significant inherent toxicity, and the adverse effects related to PDT are largely an extension of the photochemical and photobiologic reactions that are generated by reactive oxygen moieties. Interestingly, erythropoietic protoporphyria and X-linked dominant protoporphyria could be considered possible toxicity models for ALA and its congeners since they result in constitutive overaccumulation of PpIX. Photosensitivity With topical PDT, photosensitivity manifests as varying degrees of local erythema, edema, and/or blistering of any exposed site, with subjective symptoms of pain or a burning sensation. Conventional chemical sunscreens, even those with a high sun protection factor, are not useful in managing local photosensitivity since the action spectrum extends throughout the visible spectrum, which is not blocked by these sunscreens. Pain The incubation period, which follows application of the topical photo- sensitizer, is generally uneventful, but within seconds to minutes of illumination of the skin with artificial light, patients will often experience a range and series of unpleasant sensations at the site of light exposure. Inflammation At the end of the light exposure, the treated site will usually exhibit an immediate wheal and flare reaction. Over the next 24–48 hours, localized phototoxicity may manifest as edema, induration, urticaria, purpura, pustules, and blistering, along with exudation and crusting ( Fig. 135.8 ). Depending on the indication and the PDT drug–light dose, frank tissue necrosis may supervene accompanied by erosions and ulceration. Local reactions can evolve over the ensuing 1–4 weeks and any wounds will heal by second intention. For the treatment of AKs, cutaneous application of mALA for 30 minutes (rather than the recommended 3 hours) and/or pretreatment with superpotent topical corticosteroids led to reduced cutaneous inflammation but equivalent efficacy 65 . D-PDT typically generates local reactions that are milder and of shorter duration. Photosensitizer Allergy Multiple case reports have documented contact hypersensitivity to mALA. In a controlled trial, contact sensitization to mALA was observed in as many as 35% of patients who had previously undergone five or more mALA-based PDT sessions; only 1.7% of the control subjects who had not previously undergone PDT demonstrated sensitization 66 . Rare, Unusual or Controversial Reactions Exceptionally, PDT has been reported to precipitate herpes simplex reactivation 67 , facial nerve palsy, hypertensive crisis, alopecia, localized bullous pemphigoid, pityriasis rubra pilaris, erosive pustular derma- tosis of the scalp, and transient memory impairment. Cases of kerati- nocyte carcinomas recurring with more aggressive histology 68 , arising de novo 69 , or progressing within PDT fields have been reported; melanomas have also been reported following PDT, but the significance of these findings is difficult to interpret in the absence of control data. PRACTICE AND TECHNIQUES The practical administration of PDT requires attention to a number of details during the preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative stages (see Table 135.5 ). Although the commercial PDT systems for derma- tology come with officially recommended and approved protocols, the practice of PDT is not uncommonly off-label, both in terms of indications and specific procedural steps guided by the individual practi- tioner’s experience and empiric preferences. One round of topical drug plus light (administered as a single exposure or as multiple fractionated exposures) can be considered a single PDT session. A “course” or “cycle” of PDT may involve one or more individual PDT sessions separated by a set time interval. What should not be underestimated is the time and staffing necessary to provide appropriate patient counseling and education as well as intraoperative support and supervision during the light exposure phase. Consensus recommendations and guidelines from various expert groups and dermatologic societies have been published to guide the use of PDT 13,70,71 . FUTURE DIRECTIONS Controlled trials and cumulative clinical experience continue to redefine the spectrum of PDT applications. On the horizon are new photosensi- tizers and novel ways of delivering ALA. Knowledge gained from D-PDT, including less associated pain, has led to investigations in which low irradiance LED sources are used instead of conventional light sources. Advances in PDT have been accompanied by progress in imaging techniques such as confocal reflectance microscopy. Combination of the two in the future could lead to noninvasive diagnosis and delineation of cutaneous carcinomas as well as treatment and long-term evaluation. text: PHYSICAL TREATMENT MODALITIES SECTION 20 Fernanda H. Sakamoto, Mathew M. Avram and R. Rox Anderson Lasers and Other Energy-Based Technologies – Principles and Skin Interactions INTRODUCTION The last century took us from Einstein’s insight into the quantum nature of light, to the invention of the ruby laser in 1960, to the wide spectrum of lasers available today. In particular, the principle of selective photo- thermolysis guided the development of pulsed lasers that target specific skin structures such as blood vessels, melanosomes, tattoo ink, and hair follicles. Flashlamps, also called intense pulsed light (IPL) sources, can mimic these lasers to some extent. In contrast, fractional photo- thermolysis uses thousands of microscopic zones of thermal injury to stimulate skin remodeling. Additional energy-based technologies include focused ultrasound, radiofrequency electric current, pulsed electromagnetic field therapy, and controlled skin cooling. The field of energy-based treatments is dynamic, and a steady source of innovation. LASERS LASER is an acronym for l ight a mplification by s timulated e mission of r adiation. It is a physical process that can be explained by Einstein’s principles of electromagnetic radiation 1 . The quantum unit of electro- magnetic energy is a photon, and stimulated emission occurs when one photon stimulates an excited atom to emit a second, identical photon. The idea of lasers was envisioned by Charles Townes and colleagues 2 , and in 1960 the first laser, utilizing a flashlamp-excited ruby crystal, was introduced 3 . Soon thereafter, Leon Goldman 4 initiated dermato- logic applications of laser technology. All lasers have four essential components ( Fig. 136.1 ): (1) a gas, liquid, or solid medium that can be excited to generate light ( Table 136.1 ); (2) a source of “pump” energy for exciting the medium; (3) mirrors at the end(s) which form an optical cavity that favors the amplification process; and (4) a delivery system. Light is amplified as it travels back and forth between the laser’s mirrors thereby generating a very high intensity laser beam. Laser light has several properties that are different from other light sources. Monochromaticity refers to emission of a well-defined wavelength, rather than a band of wavelengths. Coherence describes light waves that travel in phase, both in time and space, similar to a column of soldiers marching in step. Collimation refers to a very parallel beam of light. Coherence and collimation allow lasers to be focused to very small spot sizes (see Fig. 136.1 ). Lasers may emit a continuous beam or pulses of light, with nearly all dermatologic lasers currently in use emitting pulsed light. Q-switched lasers produce short pulses at very high peak power. “Q” refers to a quality factor for light traveling across the laser cavity, which can be changed suddenly, i.e. “switched”, to produce a short, intense burst of light. Dermatologic Q-switched lasers are designed to produce pulses of ~1–100 nanoseconds, with fluence (the energy delivered per unit area) typically in the 2–10 J/cm 2 range. These short, high-power pulses are particularly useful for selective removal of tattoos and pigmented lesions while limiting thermal damage to surrounding tissues 5 . The repetition rate for pulsed lasers is expressed in hertz (Hz). Of note, some lasers emit a rapid train of low-energy pulses that behave surgically like continuous-wave lasers and are called quasicontinuous. SKIN OPTICS At the skin surface, 4%–7% of light of all wavelengths is reflected because of the change in refractive index between air ( n = 0) and stratum corneum ( n = 1.45) 6 . This is termed Fresnel reflectance because it follows Fresnel’s equations relating reflectance to the angle of incidence, plane of polarization, and refractive index 7 . The remaining 93%–96% of incident light enters the skin, where it is scattered and/or absorbed ( Fig. 136.2 ). The four primary skin chromophores are water, lipids, hemoglobin, and melanin ( Fig. 136.3 ). Chromophores exhibit characteristic bands of absorption at certain wavelengths. It is this fact that allows for the delin- eation of specific targets for different laser wavelengths. While melanin absorbs broadly across the visible and ultraviolet (UV) spectrum, oxyhemo­globin and reduced hemoglobin in blood exhibit strong bands in the UV, blue, green, and yellow regions. Water and lipids have strong absorption in the infrared (IR) region ( Fig. 136.4 ). Optical properties of the epidermis and dermis are different. In pigmented epidermis, melanin absorption is usually the dominant process over the majority of the optical spectrum (200–1000 nm) (see Fig. 136.3 ). In the dermis, there is strong, wavelength-dependent scattering by collagen fibers, which attenuates penetration of light. This scattering varies inversely with wavelength. In general, between 280 and 1300 nm, the depth of penetration increases with wavelength ( Fig. 136.5 ). Beyond 1300 nm, penetration decreases due to the absorption of light by water. The most deeply penetrating wavelengths are 650–1200 nm, while the least penetrating wavelengths are within the UV and IR regions. Physical treatment modalities THERMAL INTERACTIONS Most laser interactions involve heat. As temperature is raised, essential macromolecules are denatured including proteins, DNA, RNA, and cell membranes, leading to loss of function. Thermal coagulation yields cell necrosis and, if widespread, a burn. Laser skin surgery requires precise control over the placement and amount of heat-induced injury. Most human cells can easily withstand temperatures up to 40°C. Cellular survival is dependent upon both exposure time and temper- ature. In most organisms, exposure to sub-lethal heat induces a cellular reaction termed the heat shock response. Normal protein synthesis is replaced by synthesis of proteins called heat shock proteins; the latter confer some resistance to thermal injury 8 . Laser-induced thermal injury is well described by an Arrhenius model 9 – the rate of denatur- ation is exponentially related to temperature. Thus, accumulation of denatured material rises exponentially with temperature and propor- tionally with time 10 . Near a critical temperature (which is different for different tissues), rapid coagulation occurs; this is what accounts for the well-defined histologic boundaries of dermal coagulation in laser and other burn injuries. In the dermis, type I collagen plays a primary role in thermal coagulation, whereas elastin is extremely thermally stable and can survive boiling without apparent injury. Fibrillar type I dermal collagen has a sharp melting and shrinkage transition at 60–70°C. At or above this temperature range, scarring becomes more likely. SELECTIVE PHOTOTHERMOLYSIS The concept of selective photothermolysis 14 first arose to guide the design of a laser for treating pediatric port-wine birthmarks. Selective, localized heating (with focal destruction of “target” structures) is achieved by a combination of selective light absorption and a pulse duration shorter than or approximately equal to the TRT of the targets . Choice of wavelength(s) must correspond to absorption by chromo- phores within the skin targets. The wavelength must also penetrate to the anatomic depth of the skin targets. The TRT of a target is proportional to the square of its size ( Table 136.2 ). Thus, for a given material and shape, an object half the size will cool in one-quarter of the time. For most tissue structures, TRT (in seconds) is approximately equal to the square of the target dimension (in millimeters). Shape also affects TRT, and for a given thickness, planes cool faster than spheres. In general, the optimal pulse duration for selective photothermolysis is approximately equal to the TRT. Selective photothermolysis typically utilizes pulsed (rather than continuous) sources 15 . Blood vessels encompass a wide range of TRTs, including capillaries (tens of microseconds), large venules of adult port-wine birthmarks (up to tens of milliseconds), and telangiectasias and leg veins (hundreds of milliseconds). Small, pigmented targets (e.g. melanosomes within melanocytes in a nevus of Ota, tattoo ink particles within fibroblasts) are best treated with short (sub-microsecond) pulses, while larger pigmented targets (e.g. hair follicles) have longer TRTs and are best treated with longer (millisecond) pulses 16 . The potential for targeting intracellular particles and structures is increasing as lasers with even shorter pulses, e.g. picosecond (10 − 12 second) or femtosecond (10 − 15 second), are becoming available for medical use. At the extremely high intensity of femtosecond lasers, molecules can simultaneously absorb more than one photon, which opens the door to very precise sub-surface tissue cutting without thermal damage, as well as UV-like photochemistry triggered deep within the tissue. Femtosecond lasers are already in use for precise cornea surgery. PHOTOMECHANICAL EFFECTS Pulsed lasers can also cause mechanical effects 17 . Sudden heating induces thermal expansion with consequent acoustic and/or shock waves that can rupture or increase permeability of cell membranes. Cavitation, the violent formation and collapse of steam bubbles, may also occur. Examples of mechanical injury are purpura due to vessel rupture from pulsed dye lasers emitting pulses less than ~10 milliseconds 18 , and tattoo ink particle fracture from lasers emitting picosecond pulses. A number of parameters control laser–tissue effects, including wavelength, fluence, irradiance, spot size, and pulse duration ( Table 136.3 ). With smaller spot sizes, scattering leads to a greater loss of photons from the beam as it penetrates the skin, as compared to larger spot sizes. Epidermal damage can be minimized through the use of skin cooling, which is especially important with darkly pigmented skin. All cooling methods extract heat at the skin surface via a cooling agent (gas, liquid, or solid). For dynamic cryogen spray cooling, a very cold liquid fluoro- carbon is sprayed onto the skin. Solid contact cooling typically consists of a cold sapphire window held against the skin, through which laser or IPL energy is delivered. Cold air or cold gels can also be used for skin cooling. The terms precooling, parallel cooling, and postcooling refer to cooling before, during, and after the laser exposure, respectively 19 . For pulse durations shorter than ~5 milliseconds (e.g. from many pulsed dye and all Q-switched lasers), there is not enough time for parallel cooling to extract much heat, but precooling provides some protection. For short-pulsed lasers, cryogen spray cooling represents the most aggressive and effective form of precooling. Parallel cooling is effective for pulses longer than ~5 milliseconds. APPLICATIONS OF LASER PRINCIPLES Currently available medical lasers are outlined in Table 136.4 and their applications are discussed in Chapter 137 . Ablative (Vaporizing) Skin Resurfacing The ablative lasers are far-IR CO 2 (10 600 nm) or erbium (Er:YAG: 2940 nm) devices which emit wavelengths strongly absorbed by water. Pulsed and/or scanned focused beams are used to precisely vaporize super- ficial tissue, causing a “plume” of material leaving the skin. Most of the heat is removed during vaporization, but a thin layer of residual thermal damage remains that is useful for hemostasis. Laser resurfacing is very useful for treating photoaging, scars, and lesions such as epidermal nevi and seborrheic keratoses. Resurfacing removes the old epidermis and stimulates contraction and remodeling of the dermis for many months after treatment. Being a controlled partial-thickness burn, meticulous technique and wound care are important in order to avoid infection and other complications. Scarring, transient hyperpigmentation, delayed- onset permanent hypopigmentation, prolonged erythema, and bacterial, viral, and fungal infections have been reported after laser resurfacing 20 . Yellow, flashlamp-pumped pulsed dye lasers (PDLs) that emit 0.45 to 40 millisecond pulses of 585–600 nm light are therefore frequently used to treat microvascular lesions; 532 nm green lasers and some IPLs represent alternatives. Most port-wine birthmarks require six or more treatments in order to achieve stable improvement, and only a minority can be fully removed. Treatment is more effective before 6 months of age, and resistance may be due in part to vessels deeper than 1.5 mm (see Fig. 136.5 ). When the pulse duration exceeds ~20 milliseconds, there is little or no immediate purpura because cavitation and vessel rupture are avoided. It should be noted, however, that even when no immediate post-treatment purpura is observed, delayed purpura can still occur due to a phase of vasculitis several days after treatment 22 . Potassium titanyl phosphate (KTP) lasers, with a wavelength of 532 nm and variable pulse durations in the millisecond domain, are also used to treat vascular lesions. In general, there is less resultant purpura than with PDLs (see Fig. 137.2 ). When combined with parallel skin cooling windows, these lasers can be very versatile. Filtered xenon flashlamps, which emit a wide range of wavelengths, serve as sources of IPL. Compared with most vascular lasers, IPL is less selective and less powerful but is still useful for selective photo- thermolysis of telangiectasias and poikiloderma. IPL sources typically deliver a large, uniform, rectangular exposure spot. For removal of lentigines, the telangiectasias of rosacea and poikiloderma of Civatte, or dark terminal hairs in fair-skinned individuals, IPL provides a good alternative to lasers. However, for treatment of entities that require very short pulses, e.g. tattoos or nevus of Ota, IPL should not be used. Interactions During Treatment of Pigmented Lesions and Tattoos Melanosomes are melanin-containing organelles that range from ~0.3–1 micron in size, and they can act as a primary target for selective photothermolysis of pigmented lesions 23 . Melanin has a broad absorption spectrum (see Fig. 136.3 ), which lends itself to possible targeting by a wide range of lasers 24 . Choice of treatment wavelength is based on avoiding absorption by other chromophores and on matching the depth of light penetration to the depth of the lesion. In general, red and near-IR lasers are the most selective and penetrating devices for pigment cell targeting. The TRT of melanosomes is about 70–250 nanoseconds 14 , making Q-switched lasers an excellent choice for targeting melanosomes. When the fluence threshold for melanosome disruption is reached, the melanin-containing cell dies, and Q-switched lasers are able to selectively target individual pigmented cells. Of note, different laser wavelengths are needed for different ink colors (see Table 136.4 ). Picosecond (10 − 12 sec) laser pulses have long been known to be more effective than nanosecond pulses for pulverizing tattoo ink particles 26 and are now commercially available 27 . With shorter pulse durations, photoacoustic effects may be greater and photothermal effects reduced, providing a possible explanation for less inflammation and less postinflammatory hyperpigmentation. Q-switched ruby and alexandrite lasers are very useful for epidermal and dermal pigmented lesions (e.g. lentigines, nevus of Ota) as well as for black and green tattoos (see Ch. 137 ). Café-au-lait macules and melano- cytic nevi may respond to treatment with Q-switched ruby lasers (or, for nevi, long-pulsed ruby lasers that target nests of melanocytes), but recur- rences are common and residual dermal melanocytes remain in laser- treated nevi 28,29 . Laser treatment of congenital melanocytic nevi is usually considered when surgical options are limited. However, laser removal of acquired melanocytic nevi is quite controversial given the potential risk for partial removal of a subtle early melanoma. Of note, postinflammatory hyperpigmentation and melasma respond poorly to laser treatment 30 . The Q-switched Nd:YAG laser emits at 1064 nm, with typical pulse durations of 10 nanoseconds. Its primary use is in the treatment of black tattoos and dermal melanocytoses such as nevus of Ota in highly pigmented skin. Interactions During Hair Removal Permanent reduction of pigmented hairs is currently the most popular medical laser procedure. By damaging stem cells in the outer root sheath and/or dermal papilla, high-energy, millisecond-domain pulses at wavelengths in the red to near-IR region of the spectrum are highly effective. Ruby , alexandrite , diode , and Nd:YAG lasers are all used for this purpose, and IPL sources are also effective. However, due to the paucity of melanin, none of these devices work well for blonde or white hair. Since light must first travel through the pigmented epidermis to reach hair follicles, skin cooling is essential for safe permanent reduction of hair in individuals with darkly pigmented skin. The primary mechanism for temporary hair loss is induction of catagen, which can occur at low fluences whereas higher fluences produce enough follicular injury to cause permanent miniaturization or degeneration of terminal hair follicles. Low-energy IPL devices and an 810 nm diode laser source intended for home use are also available 31 . For unknown reasons, paradoxical hypertrichosis due to stimulation of a vellus-to-terminal hair transition can occur after laser or IPL treatments, particularly on the face of Mediterranean women. Non-Ablative Skin Rejuvenation Non-ablative facial rejuvenation for the treatment of fine lines and non-dynamic rhytides uses mid-IR lasers (e.g. 1320 nm Nd:YAG, 1450 nm diode, 1540 nm erbium:glass) whose wavelengths are weakly absorbed by water. These lasers work via thermal effects on the dermis, presumably stimulating a wound healing response. Responses to non-ablative rejuvenation are usually gradual and subtle, and well- controlled studies are lacking. Fractional Photothermolysis Fractional photothermolysis (FP) represents a treatment strategy in which numerous small zones of thermal injury are created ( Fig. 136.6 ), stimulating turnover and remodeling of both the epidermis and dermis 32 . Non-ablative FP uses focused, mid-IR, laser microbeams to create a pixelated pattern of microscopic columns of thermal damage, called microthermal treatment zones (MTZs). Typically, ~1

Fractional Photothermolysis Fractional photothermolysis (FP) represents a treatment strategy in which numerous small zones of thermal injury are created ( Fig. 136.6 ), stimulating turnover and remodeling of both the epidermis and dermis 32 . Non-ablative FP uses focused, mid-IR, laser microbeams to create a pixelated pattern of microscopic columns of thermal damage, called microthermal treatment zones (MTZs). Typically, ~1 million MTZs are placed per full-face treatment. Density (percentage of skin treated) and depth of thermal damage are separately controlled. The energy delivered per MTZ accurately controls the depth of treatment which is typically up to ~2 mm, i.e. well into the reticular dermis. In general, the depth of thermal damage should correlate with the depth of skin pathology being treated, e.g. a greater depth for hypertrophic scars than for atrophic scars 33 . Tissue spared around each MTZ initiates rapid repair and stimu- lates remodeling. Desquamation of the epidermal portion of each MTZ removes some basal layer pigment and a small amount of papillary dermal debris. Non-ablative FP has been reported to improve several skin conditions including scars, fine rhytides, telangiectasias, derma- toheliosis, and poikiloderma. There are a myriad of commercially available non-ablative, as well as ablative, FP devices (see Ch. 137 ). Ablative FP uses carbon dioxide or erbium (Er:YAG) lasers to vaporize many small vertical channels that can extend deeply into the skin. Because remodeling is provided by tissue between the columns of ablation, the depth of ablation can be far deeper than with traditional ablative resurfacing procedures. Care must be taken to avoid scarring, especially in areas where thin skin has limited adnexal structures such as the infraorbital and neck regions. By creating deep channels into the dermis, ablative FP is also an effective mechanism for enhancing topical drug delivery (see below) 34–37 . Clinical applications of fractional lasers include treatment of photo- aging, striae distensae, poikiloderma, and scars. Ablative FP has been shown to significantly improve the elasticity and appearance of hyper- trophic traumatic or burn scars 38–40 . The mechanisms by which micro- scale burns within the narrow, deep, FP-induced laser wounds lead to improvement of scars from thermal burns remain largely unknown. Physical treatment modalities Laser-Induced Optical Breakdown (Plasma Formation) The term plasma is used to describe matter where electrons are stripped away from atoms and molecules, producing free electrons and ions. Natural examples of plasma include lightning, the sun, and a candle flame. The high intensity of a focused, pulsed laser can cause plasma formation. Laser-induced plasmas are commonly used for intraocular surgery, but cutaneous applications have recently been introduced. For example, as a treatment for epidermal pigmented lesions or photoaging, a lens array can be used to focus a picosecond pulsed laser so that it can induce optical breakdown within the epidermis 41,42 . Interactions During Laser Targeting of Lipids and Sebaceous Glands Lipids absorb near-infrared wavelengths around 915, 1210, 1726, and 2300 nm 43,44 . Despite the depth of subcutaneous fat and sebaceous glands, controlled skin cooling allows selective photothermolysis of these lipid-rich structures 44 . That is, by extracting heat at the skin surface, deeply penetrating wavelengths absorbed by lipids can be used to selectively heat sebaceous glands or subcutaneous fat. Despite the depth of subcutaneous fat and sebaceous glands, controlled skin cooling allows selective photothermolysis of these lipid-rich structures 44 . That is, by extracting heat at the skin surface, deeply penetrating wavelengths absorbed by lipids can be used to selectively heat sebaceous glands or subcutaneous fat. Recently, 1726 nm laser devices have been approved to treat mild to severe acne in the US and Europe, with a reported clearance of 40–80% of inflammatory acne for up to 2 years, depending on the device. Alternatively, for skin structures that lack specific natural chromo- phores, use of exogenous nanoparticles or microparticles can allow “customized” targeting. For example, in order to target sebaceous follicles, gold microparticles tailored to absorb near-infrared wavelengths have been introduced for acne treatment 45–47 . These particles absorb light very strongly by creating surface plasmon resonance; the latter occurs when the frequency of incoming light matches the frequency for electric currents to resonate in the particle. The particles are forcefully massaged into sebaceous follicles before laser treatment. Laser-Based Diagnostics Laser technology has been instrumental in the development of biological microscopy and tissue imaging. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) uses near-IR, low-coherence light for high-resolution cross-sectional imaging of body tissues. OCT is now a standard procedure in ophthal- mology and is employed in high-resolution coronary artery imaging. Its use in dermatology is rapidly emerging. Laser confocal microscopy captures light scattered or emitted from a thin plane “section” inside skin and can be used to delineate tumor margins. Reflectance confocal microscopy is able to view the skin in vivo with histology-like resolution down to a depth of ~0.3 mm, whereas OCT is capable of imaging the skin to a depth of ~2 mm. Because histochemical stains are not used, both confocal microscopy and OCT of skin tumors reveal useful diagnostic features that are different from those of conventional histopathology. While confocal microscopy is limited to imaging small areas, OCT generally does not have that limitation. The field of in vivo microscopy continues to rapidly advance. NON-LASER ENERGY SOURCES Flashlamps (Intense Pulsed Light) Filtered xenon flashlamps, also referred to as intense pulsed light (IPL) sources, are used for non-ablative skin rejuvenation, pigmented hair removal, and the treatment of vascular and pigmented lesions. By utilizing filters, different wavelength bands can be chosen, which are delivered in millisecond-domain pulses. Compared with lasers, IPL devices are generally less target-selective, as they emit a wider range of wavelengths and are unable to deliver the very short pulses needed for selective photothermolysis of very small targets such as tattoo ink particles or the melanin-containing cells of nevus of Ota. Attempts to remove tattoos with IPL are inappropriate (despite advertising or FDA approvals to the contrary), as this often leads to burns and/or scarring. In a side-by-side comparative study, IPL was inferior to the PDL for the treatment of port-wine birthmarks. Despite limitations, IPL devices are very versatile and can successfully treat epidermal pigmented lesions, poikiloderma, and telangiectasias. Of note, moderate irradiances at wavelengths absorbed by cytochromes have long been reported to modulate metabolism in mammals. The FDA mandate to balance risks and benefits is such that devices posing no known risk are sometimes cleared for sale with little or no evidence of efficacy, and many sources sold for PBM do not have specific indications. The FDA has cleared low-power red lasers and/or LEDs (continuous, mW power, 630–800 nm wavelength) for treatment of carpal tunnel syndrome and for stimulating hair growth in patients with androgenetic alopecia, based on evidence from clinical trials 50,51 . Although the latter have shown a statistically significant increase in terminal hair counts relative to placebo, the clinical significance remains to be determined, and the combination of PBM with medical or surgical treatments for hair loss remains largely untested. Nonetheless, scien- tific and clinical evidence has been mounting in support of PBM having bona fide photobio­logic effects mediated via mitochondrial activity. Mitochondrial signaling pathways affected by light include those that are redox-sensitive, ATP- and cyclic AMP-dependent, and/or regulated by nitric oxide 52 . Radiofrequency Radiofrequency (RF) describes a rapidly alternating electric current that locally heats tissue, based on both local current density and electrical impedance of the tissue. The energy deposited at a certain site is propor- tional to the local tissue impedance multiplied by the square of the local current density. As the name implies, RF generators operate at frequencies similar to radio bands. The current is delivered from one or more electrodes held in contact or close proximity to the skin. The number of treatment electrodes defines an RF device as monopolar, bipolar, or multipolar. In monopolar RF devices, one pole is located on the treatment handpiece, while the other (if present at all) is a large “passive” electrode placed remotely on the patient’s body ( Fig. 136.7A ). In monopolar RF devices, one pole is located on the treatment handpiece, while the other (if present at all) is a large “passive” electrode placed remotely on the patient’s body ( Fig. 136.7A ). Bipolar and multipolar RF devices have multiple active electrodes that are held against the skin, and current flows between them ( Fig. 136.7B ). Because electrode size and spacing have a strong influence, the pattern and depth of heating can be adjusted to some extent. Invasive RF needles are also available, which produce a fractional pattern of deep thermal injury. Unlike most lasers and IPL sources, there is little or no intrinsic selec- tivity to the deposition of energy from an RF source. The single relevant exception is lipid-rich tissue such as subcutaneous fat, which has substantially higher electrical impedance due to its lower water content. A large RF electrode configured to deliver a current path through subcu- taneous fat could, in theory, preferentially heat fibrous septae. This is because the septae carry a higher current density than the fat lobules which surround them. Following large-electrode, monopolar or bipolar RF, cellulite improvement has been described by several authors, but the apparent improvement in appearance does not correspond to fat destruction 53 . While many monopolar and bipolar RF devices have been described for skin “tightening” as well as removal of cellulite or fat, the quality of clinical study-based evidence is generally poor. The RF devices intended for “tightening” are designed to produce partial denaturation of type I collagen, which occurs at temperatures above ~60°C and leads to some immediate tissue contraction and subsequent new collagen synthesis 54 . Because improper electrode contact with skin is a common cause of injury (e.g. burns), some devices have integrated skin cooling systems and/or sensors that monitor proper electrode–skin contact. At high frequencies, RF can also be transmitted across a dielectric (insulating) material, similar to radio transmissions through air. RF transmission to the skin from an emitting electrode is called capacitive coupling. At the high frequencies utilized with capacitive coupling, a combination of induced current and rotational oscillations in water molecules produces tissue heating 55 . High-Intensity Focused Electromagnetic (HIFEM) In HIFEM treatments, there is application of low-frequency magnetic field pulses (3–30 Hz) using a non-contact device. The magnetic pulses induce electric currents in tissue that can stimulate action potentials, producing muscle contraction 61 . This therapeutic modality has been used for decades in sports medicine, and nowadays dermatologists are also offering HIFEM treatments for muscle toning and body contouring. Intense exercise or induced muscle contraction can reduce intramus- cular fat, but (despite claims) reduction of subcutaneous fat via HIFEM treatments has not yet been proven 62 . Nano-Pulse Stimulation (NPS) NPS consists of applying high-voltage, nanosecond electrical pulses that are delivered by parallel rows of microneedles inserted into tissue. The electrical pulses porate cellular and organelle membranes, leading to increased intracellular calcium, disruption of ATP production, and consequent cell apoptosis 63,64 . NPS has been investigated for the treatment of seborrheic keratoses 65 , sebaceous hyperplasia 66 , and viral warts 67 , but the potential for causing useful selective and/or sublethal cellular responses remains unclear. Physical treatment modalities Ultrasound High-frequency acoustic waves are routinely used for diagnostic medical imaging, at frequencies from ~20 kHz to 10 MHz. Ultrasound is an oscillating pressure (stress) wave that propagates at the speed of sound 68,69 , with minimal scattering in soft tissues. This minimal scattering allows the ultrasound waves to be focused deeply within most soft tissues. Intensity is concentrated near the focal point, to the extent that tissue damage can occur by one or more of three mechanisms – heating, cavitation, or shock waves. Heating is favored at high ultra- sound frequencies while cavitation (a rapidly expanding gas bubble) is favored at low ultrasound frequencies; shock waves are high pressure, supersonic pressure waves that can be very destructive. Therapeutically, focused ultrasound can be used to destroy targets, such as renal calculi by shock waves, tumors by heating, and thrombi by cavitation, in addition to dermatologic applications. The attenuation (absorption) of ultrasound is greater at higher frequencies, and different materials have different attenuation coefficients 69 . Focused, pulsed ultrasound devices capable of locally destroying subcutaneous abdominal fat have been FDA-cleared for waist circum- ference reduction (see Ch. 156 ). In addition, a non-invasive, focused ultrasound device, operating at MHz frequencies, has been FDA-cleared for brow lifts. This device focuses millisecond-domain pulses at the level of the deep dermis and/or superficial fascia, up to a depth of ~4.5 mm ( Fig. 136.8 ). A small focal zone of thermal damage is produced with each pulse, sufficient to achieve tissue contraction at the focus. The treatment transducer is also used for imaging, in order to verify positioning and treatment at the proper tissue plane. This represented the first combined diagnostic and therapeutic ultrasound device for dermatologic use. Because lipids crystallize at temperatures well above the freezing point of tissue water, lipid-rich cells, including adipocytes and sebocytes, suffer stress and undergo apoptosis (see Ch. 156 ). Following deep cooling, cold panniculitis occurs (see Ch. 100 ) 70 , eventuating in selective loss of subcutaneous fat tissue 71,72 .

Because lipids crystallize at temperatures well above the freezing point of tissue water, lipid-rich cells, including adipocytes and sebocytes, suffer stress and undergo apoptosis (see Ch. 156 ). Following deep cooling, cold panniculitis occurs (see Ch. 100 ) 70 , eventuating in selective loss of subcutaneous fat tissue 71,72 . Prolonged hypoesthesia is a common side effect when cryolipolysis is employed to remove unwanted subcutaneous fat; the proposed underlying mechanism is damage to the lipid-rich myelin sheaths that surround cutaneous sensory nerves. However, this effect has recently been recog- nized as a potential treatment for cutaneous pain and pruritus 73 . FUTURE DIRECTIONS In vivo optical image-guided laser surgery for cutaneous malignancies would be a welcome advance 74 . Currently, dermatologists use histology- guided Mohs micrographic surgery, primarily for the removal of non-life- threatening tumors. Development of a rapid, image-guided version of Mohs micrographic surgery would represent a valuable and improved approach. Use of Raman spectroscopy to detect inelastic light scattering from molecular vibration modes can provide a “fingerprint” image of a desired molecule, thus allowing precise in vivo analysis of the skin 75,76 . It may even be possible to manipulate immunologic responses, e.g. inducing tolerance, preventing inflammation; experimentally, lasers have been used to enhance the immune response to vaccines by increasing antigen-presenting cells 77 . An injectable version of cryolipolysis has been developed that utilizes ice slurries, similar in concept to a physiologic daiquiri. Injected ice slurry has been shown to produce neural selective cryoneurolysis 78 and fat reduction 79 . The same innovation may be useful as a treatment for sleep apnea 80 . A potential improvement in fractional lasers would be the ability to guide the laser microbeam based on skin imaging. For example, the precise texture of the skin could potentially be rewritten by image- guided laser ablation, similar in principle to the precise laser surgery performed to correct refractive power of the cornea. Fractional lasers can destroy or remove nearly half of the tissue of the skin, followed by rapid healing without a scar, a capability unmatched by any classical surgical tool. Fractional lasers can destroy or remove nearly half of the tissue of the skin, followed by rapid healing without a scar, a capability unmatched by any classical surgical tool. However, it is clearly the microscale pattern of injury – not the laser per se – that underlies the skin’s tolerance to fractional laser treatment. As a result, the general concept of fractional photothermolysis has spawned various other techniques. For example, in patients with photo- aging, mechanical removal of full-thickness micro-columns of skin tissue via coring needles has recently been shown to produce similar esthetic results as fractional laser treatment, again with rapid and scar-free healing. Recently, a micro-coring device was FDA-approved for the treatment of lower face photoaging and laxity. Fractional coring needles can also be used to obtain full-thickness skin tissue for grafting, and recently such needle harvesting has been shown to greatly reduce donor site morbidity 81–84 . Lasers and energy-based technologies will forever be an innovative, changing, and integral part of dermatology. text: SECTION 20 PHYSICAL TREATMENT MODALITIES Christopher B. Zachary, Kristen M. Kelly and Erica G. Baugh Lasers and Other Energy-Based Therapies Pulsed Dye Laser The pulsed dye laser (PDL) is considered to be the laser of choice for the treatment of various cutaneous vascular lesions, especially facial telangiec­ tasias, port-wine birthmarks (PWBs), superficial hemangiomas, poikilo­ derma of Civatte, and erythematotelangiectatic rosacea 2 . Hypertrophic and keloidal scars, psoriasis, and warts are also amenable to treatment with PDL. While the initial PDL systems emitted 577 nm yellow light, slightly longer wavelength PDL devices (585 or 595 nm) were subsequently adopted to allow deeper tissue penetration of up to 1.2 mm. The choice of appropriate PDL parameters affects tissue response, in terms of both efficacy and appearance. Short pulse durations (0.45–3 millisecond [ms]) cause a purpuric reaction related to intravascular coagulation or vessel leakage ( Fig. 137.2C,D ). While very effective for telangiectasias, the bruised appearance is not cosmetically acceptable to many patients. Although slightly less effective, longer pulse durations (6–10 ms) with multiple passes or “pulse stacking”, consisting of appli­ cation of a rapid succession of pulses to a particular location with cooling to achieve “purpura-free” treatments, is quite effective and less noticeable. Epidermal protection during laser treatments, including those with PDL, is critical. Cooling helps to reduce blistering, crusting, and subse­ quent dyspigmentation, i.e. hypo- and hyperpigmentation. The most common cooling strategies are contact cooling, forced cold air, and cryogen spray. The Syneron-Candela PDL systems incorporate cryogen spray cooling (Dynamic Cooling Device™) which is deployed immedi­ ately before the light pulse, while Cynosure systems use forced cold air. In addition to protecting the epidermis from non-selective thermal damage, cooling allows for the use of higher fluences, with improved efficacy. KTP Laser (Frequency-Doubled Nd:YAG Laser) KTP 532 nm laser light is produced by passing 1064 nm light from an Nd:YAG (neodymium–yttrium–aluminum–garnet) laser through a potassium titanyl phosphate (KTP) crystal, which effectively halves the wavelength and doubles the frequency. Since this wavelength closely corresponds to the first absorption peak of hemoglobin at 542 nm, the KTP laser can be used to effectively treat some vascular lesions (e.g. telangiectasias) in a purpura-free manner ( Fig. 137.2A,B ). In addition, this laser is a popular device for the removal of lentigines and other epidermal pigmented lesions. While this laser is best employed in patients with skin phototypes I–III, it can used in darker skin photo­

In addition, this laser is a popular device for the removal of lentigines and other epidermal pigmented lesions. While this laser is best employed in patients with skin phototypes I–III, it can used in darker skin photo­ types (IV–VI) for unique applications, such as dermatosis papulosa nigra. Nd:YAG Laser The deeply penetrating Nd:YAG 1064 nm laser has significantly less hemoglobin absorption than the wavelengths of the PDL or KTP lasers. However, its absorption by melanin is also very limited. The latter property theoretically enhances the safety profile of the 1064 nm laser in patients with darker phototypes. This laser can be used to treat deeper vascular lesions and spider veins up to 3 mm diameter 3 . Because of its poor coefficient of absorption by hemoglobin, much higher fluences are required to produce transmural heating of blood vessels. As a conse­ quence of the higher fluences and longer pulse widths, this wavelength has a narrow window of safety, with a significant potential for volumetric heating and collateral damage; in addition, it tends to be quite painful. Cooling is critical for epidermal protection and pain control, as well as to reduce the risk of scarring from nonspecific thermal injury. Nd:YAG lasers should be used with extra caution when treating vascular lesions. INTRODUCTION This chapter considers laser and light applications for both medical and aesthetic purposes as related to the skin. Anderson and Parrish developed the concept of selective photothermolysis 1 whereby laser energy could be used for targeted destruction of skin components (see Ch. 136 ). Their 1983 treatise continues to support our understanding of laser–tissue interactions and still drives new therapeutic applica­ tions of lasers in dermatology. Given the multiplicity of lasers available ( Fig. 137.1 ), the laser surgeon must understand the capabilities and limitations of each device so that the appropriate system can be selected and the parameters tailored to treat the intended target. Safe and effective laser therapy is achieved when the operator understands the nature of the target, its location within the skin, and the potential collateral damage. Other energy-based devices, such as those that utilize radiofrequency waves, intense focused ultrasound, or microwaves,

TYPES OF LASERS AND INTENSE PULSED LIGHT The earliest lasers used by dermatologists were applied to vascular lesions and consisted of continuous or quasi-continuous wave lasers, which emitted a constant beam of light. These included argon (488, 514 nm), argon pumped tunable dye (488–638 nm), copper vapor and copper bromide (511 nm, 578 nm), potassium titanyl phosphate (KTP, 532 nm), and krypton (568 nm) lasers. Although these lasers had wavelengths that corresponded to the hemoglobin absorption spectrum, the nature of their continuous beams generally induced nonspecific thermal damage to surrounding structures, leading to scarring and dyschromia. The root of the problem, a mismatch between the laser pulse duration and the thermal relaxation time of the target tissue (see Ch. 136 ), was effectively resolved once it was understood that laser pulse duration should approximately match the thermal relaxation time of the targeted tissue. Sophisticated filtering and pulsing systems prevent unwanted wavelengths from damaging the skin, thus making this device more selective and quite versatile. Integrated skin cooling is a useful feature present in some devices, and it can be employed to provide epidermal protection, while at the same time allowing greater fluences to reach deeper targets. IPL systems can be used to treat a number of conditions, including rosacea, PWBs, hemangiomas, poikiloderma of Civatte and lentigines, as well as provide overall photorejuvenation. Cold ultrasound gel or aloe vera gel should be applied both to protect the epidermis from excessive heat and to reduce the difference in refractive indexes between air and skin, thereby allowing better penetration and absorption of light. In addition, the gel enhances gliding of the handpiece from one location to the next. Despite these measures, thermal injury to the epidermis can still occur, leading to blistering, scarring, and permanent pigmentary altera­ tions. This is generally operator-dependent, with a greater risk when treating patients with a tan or darker skin phototypes ( Fig. 137.3 ). IPL is most commonly used for patients with phototypes I–III with chronic photodamage or for hair removal. For treatment of patients with more darkly pigmented skin, longer wavelength filters or lower fluences plus longer pulse widths can be used ( Fig. 137.4 ). Filters can also be used for other specific indications, e.g. treatment of vascular lesions. Based upon the energy absorbed per volumetric unit, the minimum fluence necessary for the CO 2 laser to produce tissue ablation has been calculated to be 5 J/cm 2 . Below this fluence, tissue is not vaporized, rather it is coagulated. However, both vaporization and coagulation are useful in the treatment of skin disease, and these wavelengths can be manipulated to achieve an appropriate balance of the two. When using these resurfacing lasers,

Based upon the energy absorbed per volumetric unit, the minimum fluence necessary for the CO 2 laser to produce tissue ablation has been calculated to be 5 J/cm 2 . Below this fluence, tissue is not vaporized, rather it is coagulated. However, both vaporization and coagulation are useful in the treatment of skin disease, and these wavelengths can be manipulated to achieve an appropriate balance of the two. When using these resurfacing lasers, the photothermal coagulative effect is responsible for hemostasis, collagen rejuvenation, skin tightening, and, by extension, many of the complications such as scarring that can be seen with these devices. To achieve selective photothermolysis of the skin with the CO 2 laser, it has been suggested that the ideal pulse duration is ≤ 1 ms. The development of high-powered, short-pulsed CO 2 lasers (as compared to their continuous wave predecessors) has allowed for more selective control of tissue vaporization and thermal injury. The first pass of the high-energy, short-pulsed CO 2 laser induces localized tissue vapor­ ization with surrounding coagulation/desiccation. Since this residual carbonized tissue acts as a heat sink, subsequent CO 2 laser pulses tend to vaporize less and heat more, causing non-selective damage. Thus, second and subsequent passes should only be applied after removal of the desiccated “charred” material at the surface of the skin 4,5 . The Er:YAG laser emits light at 2940 nm, with water affinity being nearly 15 times greater than that of the CO 2 laser. This allows the Er:YAG laser to vaporize tissue more efficiently, leaving only a small residue of coagulated tissue. As a consequence of the limited photo­ thermal effects, hemostasis and collagen contraction are significantly reduced with Er:YAG lasers. Sub-ablative coagulation settings, achieved by lengthening the laser pulse duration, have been incorporated into newer modulated Er:YAG laser systems (e.g. Sciton ® ), inducing more hemostasis and resulting in better tissue contraction. While pure Er:YAG lasers demonstrated only modest tissue tightening as compared to CO 2 lasers, modulated Er:YAG systems have produced comparable resurfacing results 5 . It is critical that the laser surgeon be constantly aware of the depth of vaporization. The fully ablative CO 2 and long-pulsed Er:YAG lasers remain the gold standard for photorejuvenation, wrinkle reduction, and skin tightening. To date, nothing can beat the results obtained by an experienced laser surgeon using one of these lasers. Specifically, even

It is critical that the laser surgeon be constantly aware of the depth of vaporization. The fully ablative CO 2 and long-pulsed Er:YAG lasers remain the gold standard for photorejuvenation, wrinkle reduction, and skin tightening. To date, nothing can beat the results obtained by an experienced laser surgeon using one of these lasers. Specifically, even deep, coarse and fixed perioral and periorbital rhytides can be significantly diminished or eliminated ( Fig. 137.5 ) 4 . Redundant skin is tightened by thermal coagulation, collagen contraction, and associated fibroplasia. However, this dramatic improvement comes at the expense of slow healing. A split-face study of Er:YAG and CO 2 laser resurfacing demonstrated this duality; the side treated with the CO 2 laser had 63% improvement with 7.7 days of crusting, compared to the Er:YAG laser-treated side which had 48% improvement with an average of 3.4 days of crusting 6 . In general, more significant clinical improvement has gone hand in hand with more thermal damage, leading to more discomfort, more extensive wound care, and longer healing times. Additional side effects include persistent erythema for 3 + months, risk of scarring, a 15% chance of delayed-onset permanent hypopigmentation, and a line of demarcation between treated and untreated areas. All patients with actinic bronzing will note an improvement or lightening of their skin pigmentation in the treated areas. To avoid any demarcation lines in these regions, it is prudent to treat entire anatomic areas. This is partic­ ularly true for skin phototypes I and II. Skin phototypes IV–VI tend not to have actinic bronzing and hence focal or geographic areas can be treated. Treatment of acne scarring is a common indication for ablative lasers. Elevated or distensible acne scars are most amenable to resurfacing, compared to icepick and non-distensible scars, which are often resistant 7 . Focal ablation has been effectively used for resurfacing benign epidermal tumors and proliferations such as seborrheic keratoses, epidermal nevi, and verrucae; actinic keratoses and actinic cheilitis can also be signifi­ cantly improved 8 . Lasers and Other Energy-Based Therapies Among the most significant risks with ablative resurfacing is infection, whether by bacteria, viruses, or fungi. Specifically, and especially if the treated region involves perioral skin or adjacent areas, antiviral medica­ tions (e.g. valacyclovir, famciclovir) should be initiated prophylactically the day prior to, or at least the morning of, the procedure and continued for 15 days. This is true even in the absence of prior herpetic infection so as to prevent the possibility of a generalized herpetic infection in the denuded skin. Antibiotic coverage, especially against staphylococci, may be prudent, but is much debated. Antifungal prophylaxis with fluconazole (a single-dose 200 mg tablet) given during the early postop­ erative period has been demonstrated to prevent candidal infection and may promote re-epithelialization. FRACTIONATED LASERS Traditional laser resurfacing yielded impressive facial photorejuvena­tion and significant tissue tightening. However, these outcomes were often at the cost of delayed healing, persistent redness and swelling, infection, unpredictable pigmentary changes (hypo- or hyperpigmentation), and scarring. In 2004, fractionated photothermolysis (FP) was introduced ( Table 137.1 ). The development of fractionated lasers has changed the way laser surgeons practice. One can be aggressive in terms of depth and density, and yet relatively safe in terms of patient downtime, postop­ erative recovery, and complications. In contrast to traditional lasers where the spot size of the device defined the smallest treatment unit on the skin, hundreds of controlled microscopic zones of coagulative or ablative injury are delivered to the skin with each scan or stamp of the fractional device 9 . In contrast to traditional lasers where the spot size of the device defined the smallest treatment unit on the skin, hundreds of controlled microscopic zones of coagulative or ablative injury are delivered to the skin with each scan or stamp of the fractional device 9 . These areas of microscopic thermal injury are defined as microscopic treatment zones (MTZs; also referred to as microthermal zones). While MTZs appear to be minute dots on the skin, they actually represent exact columns or cylinders of epidermal and dermal thermal damage (see Fig. 136.6 ) 10 . MTZs are deliberate and calibrated such that the resultant depth, width, and density are defined. Each microdot or cylinder of damage is surrounded by normal unaffected skin, which acts as a reservoir for healing and enables these micro-wounds to resolve quickly with minimal discomfort ( Fig. 137.7 ). Histologically, the healing wounds appear as microscopic epidermal necrotic debris (MENDs); the latter are composed of fragmented and damaged skin components, including epidermis, dermis, melanin, and elastin 11 . The laser handpiece employs a scanning system allowing for uniform deposition of MTZs. The second-generation system (Fraxel ® DUAL) includes both 1550 nm and 1927 nm wavelengths. This is a major development as it increases the versatility of this device. The 1550 nm wavelength allows for adjustment of the MTZ energies up to 70 mJ with a depth of injury down to 1500 microns and treatment densities of 5%–50% (Video 137.1). The depth of these MTZs is an operator-dependent parameter and can be adjusted to match the thickness of skin or entity being treated. The very nature of fractional photothermolysis (FP) allows for the safe application of incredibly high fluences to narrow tissue columns, which if applied to confluent areas would certainly cause delayed healing and tissue scarring. New indications and applications for this novel technology continue to evolve and include patients with chronic photodamage, skin laxity, rhytides, striae, and multiple types of scarring, including acne, hypopig­ mented, traumatic, and surgical scars ( Fig. 137.8 ). One of the first clinical applications of FP was treatment of facial melasma. While initial studies were promising with near-complete clearance of melasma after a few treatments, this early exuberance has been tempered by a more considered and lengthy assessment of response, with the tendency of melasma to recur. The first commer­ cially available system was the Fraxel re:pair laser, originally manufac­ tured by Reliant Technologies. Lasers and Other Energy-Based Therapies The fractional devices, both ablative and non-ablative, have been used for traditional resurfacing indications such as improvement of rhytides and acne scarring ( Fig. 137.9 ). Initial studies utilizing re:store ® for the treatment of periorbital rhytides showed mild improvement in 12% of patients, noticeable improvement in 30%, and moderate to significant improvement in 54% after one to four treatments 13 . Settings for pulse energy and treatment density should be tailored for the individual patient. Collective experience has also shown that fine to moderate rhytides respond more favorably than do deeper rhytides, and less dramatic improvement should be expected compared to fully ablative resurfacing 14 . When used for acne scarring, fractional deep dermal ablation (FDDA™) treatment has demonstrated significant efficacy. In a study of 30 patients with moderate to severe acne scarring who underwent one to three treatments 15 , mild to moderate overall improvement was noted with energies ranging from 20 to 100 mJ and densities of 600–1600 MTZ/cm 2 . A fractionated ablative depth of 1.5 mm or greater will likely induce optimal outcomes when treating acne scarring. A fractionated ablative depth of 1.5 mm or greater will likely induce optimal outcomes when treating acne scarring. The concept that a high density of fractional injury always provides better outcomes has recently been challenged, with some evidence that a low-to-medium density is as good or better. Although some patients may initially view multiple treatments as inconvenient, the benefits of rapid skin healing (within 5–7 days) and remarkably little postoperative discomfort compared to traditional laser resurfacing are distinct advan­ tages (see Fig. 137.7 ). Ablative FP offers the opportunity for relatively safe treatment of anatomic regions that were notoriously difficult to rejuvenate with conventional ablative resurfacing. Areas such as the neck and upper chest can now be more easily treated, albeit at reduced energy and density. Another advantage of fractionated systems is the ability to safely treat all skin phototypes, including patients with darkly pigmented skin ( Fig. 137.10 ). Evidence that fractionated laser therapies induce neocollagenesis is supported histologically. Increased expression of collagen remodel­ing markers such as heat shock proteins (47, 70 and 72), collagen III, proliferating cell nuclear antigen, and α -smooth muscle actin have been demonstrated within treatment areas 16,17 . In addition to inducing neocollagenesis, ablative fractionated systems induce volumetric tissue reduction and dermal plumping 17,18 . Taken collectively, the vapor­ ization volume of millions of tiny-diameter cylinders of skin adds up. A standard aggressive fractionated CO 2 laser treatment can remove 5–7 cm 3 from the skin of the face 19 . The original hope was that this volumetric tissue reduction would result in impressive skin tightening. In practice, every one of these tiny holes is actually repaired with new collagen and elastin, leading to improvement in color, texture and tone, but with less skin tightening than anticipated. However, periodic treat­ ments will improve skin laxity and could possibly prevent or delay the need for future facelift procedures. Fractionated lasers represent a major therapeutic advance in the treatment of surgical, traumatic, and burn scars. PHYSICAL TREATMENT MODALITIES improvement in overall appearance, texture, mobility, and symptoms such as pain and itch has been well described 20 . The traditional approach was to allow scars to mature for 1–2 years prior to any intervention, but this has been demonstrated to be incorrect. Early intervention, even at the time of suture removal, can hasten healing and reduce ultimate disfigurement. A combination approach consisting of PDL, fractionated lasers (ablative or non-ablative), and/or radiofreqency microneedling ( ± intralesional corticosteroids or 5-­fluorouracil) is likely to improve the appearance of scars 21 (see below). Fractionated Laser Assisted Drug Delivery Significant advances have been made in fractionated laser assisted drug delivery by disrupting the barrier function of the stratum corneum 22 . Both ablative and non-ablative lasers can dramatically increase the uptake of any topical agent. Understanding the relation of depth of fractionated ablation, the associated collar of spongy coagulation inside each channel, the density of laser channels, and the hydrophilic/ lipophilic nature of the topical medications are all important. The MTZs function as channels through which even large-sized molecules may be delivered to essentially any depth within the skin. Studies have been conducted utilizing a diverse array of therapeutic agents including anesthetics, chemotherapeutic drugs, corticosteroids, and stem cells 23,24 . Fractionated delivery of topical aminolevulinic acid (ALA) for photodynamic therapy (PDT) in areas such as the extremities can dramatically improve drug absorption and efficacy. TREATMENT OF CHRONIC PHOTODAMAGE While we are blessed by the sun in terms of “the good outside”, chronic sun exposure wreaks havoc with our skin, inducing lentigines, telan­ giectasias, rhytides, and cutaneous carcinomas. Although successful laser treatment of lentigines and telangiectasias is possible based upon specific wavelengths (see above), there is a less well understood improvement that comes from nonspecific heating of the dermis, which induces the production of new collagen and elastin. It has been said that twice yearly treatments with IPL could maintain a youthful appearance. In a study of 135 patients with poikiloderma of Civatte, IPL treatment of the neck and/or upper chest led to > 75% clearance of telangiectasias and hyperpigmentation after a mean of three treatments 25 . While the emitted light is broad, IPL filters allow for more targeted treatments. It has been postulated that the shorter wavelengths are responsible for the improvement in pigmentation and telangiec­ tasias, while the longer wavelengths are responsible for collagen remod­ eling via thermal effects on tissue water 26 . However, many wavelengths are absorbed by dermal water and their impact is likely the cause of improved appearance, particularly

While the ablative lasers can produce dramatic improvement in skin laxity and photodamage, their short-term side effects of discomfort, oozing, edema, persistent erythema, and extended healing time, plus the potential risks for infection, scarring, and delayed-onset hypopig­ mentation have led to a shift toward non-ablative laser therapies. “Subsurface remodeling” secondary to dermal wound healing responses can be seen in patients treated by IPL, PDL, and a number of other lasers. The long-pulsed PDL can be used with a multiple-pass technique for photorejuvenation. It is worthy to note that both the 585 nm and 595 nm PDLs have received FDA clearance for treatment of periocular wrinkling. While collagen remodeling has been demonstrated histologi­ cally, clinical improvement of wrinkles is variable and modest. In addition to specifically improving pigmentation, KTP and Nd:YAG lasers have also been shown to cause a 20%–40% improvement in texture and a 20%–30% improvement in rhytides 27 . Lastly, laser surgeons must appreciate the science behind the energy delivery, rather than base assumptions on exaggerated claims by device manufacturers. No one laser or wavelength meets all of the objectives required for skin rejuvenation. Lasers and Other Energy-Based Therapies The most commonly used devices for the treatment of vascular lesions include IPL and the 532 nm KTP, 595 nm PDL, and 1064 nm Nd:YAG lasers. Other systems such as the 755 nm alexandrite and the 800 nm and 940 nm diode lasers also play an important role in the treatment of vascular lesions ( Table 137.2 ). Clinical improvement is best achieved by photothermal vascular damage 28 . As the pulse width approximates or slightly exceeds the thermal relaxation time of the target vessel, photothermal damage results. This induces intravascular thrombosis or vessel rupture and subsequent collagenous fibrosis of the blood vessel wall and adjacent tissues 28 . These changes result in vessel disappearance or an immediate purpuric reaction (see Fig. 137.2D ). Given the unwanted cosmetic appearance of the latter, which can last for 2 weeks, longer pulse widths ( > 6 ms) are often used, as they produce gentler heating of the target vessel and avoid bruising altogether. However, some degree of intravascular thrombosis may be a prerequisite for clinical improvement and resolution of vascular lesions, as is the case in port-wine birthmarks (PWBs). Port-Wine Birthmarks (PWBs) One of the first clinical applications of laser therapy was treatment of congenital vascular lesions, namely PWBs. PWBs are capillary malfor­ mations that involve primarily the mid to superficial dermis; they occur in 0.3%–0.5% of newborns and initially present as pink to red patches. These vascular anomalies are cosmetically and psychologi­ cally problematic and are frequently located on the face. When PWBs are bilateral and/or involve the “forehead area”, there is a higher risk of Sturge–Weber syndrome 29 , with somatic activating mutations in GNAQ found in both Sturge–Weber syndrome and non-syndromic PWBs 30 (see Ch. 104 ). PWBs located on the extremities may be a sign of Klippel–Trenaunay or Parkes Weber syndrome, with associated tissue hypertrophy and additional vascular malformations (venous, lymphatic, arteriovenous) present. An early treatment of PWBs utilized the continuous wave argon laser (488 and 514 nm). Despite the wavelength’s relative specificity for its vascular target, this laser caused marked scarring in up to a third of patients due to nonspecific thermal injury. The latter occurred because the pulse duration of ~200 ms dramatically exceeded the thermal relax­ ation time of the PWB vessels (~1–10 ms) 31 . A therapeutic paradigm shift then occurred based upon the concept of selective photother­ molysis, leading to the development of the PDL which was specifically designed to treat PWBs. While the early PDLs emitted a 577 nm wavelength, the current PDL systems deliver 585 and 595 nm wavelengths, allowing targeted delivery of laser energy deeper into the skin with increased efficacy. These longer wavelengths are less well absorbed by hemoglobin, but they penetrate slightly deeper into the skin 32 .
