Lasers and Other Energy-Based Therapies While 70% of PWBs will have good or very good improvement following treatment ( Fig. 137.11 ), a minority ( < 10%) will have very modest or no improvement. The degree of PWB clearance is dependent on several factors including the size of the lesion and its anatomic location 35 . For example, centrally located facial lesions (i.e. medial cheeks, upper lip, and nose) tend to be more treatment-resistant as compared to lesions located in the periorbital region or on the forehead, lateral cheeks, or chin. Likewise, PWBs on distal extremities are more treatment-resistant and require a more aggressive approach. Although a remarkable response can be obtained after one laser treatment, treatment of PWBs typically requires multiple (10 or more) sessions. Given that PWBs are composed of various-sized blood vessels, each with its own requisite treatment parameters, the PDL may prove inade­ quate in eliminating the entire capillary malformation. A poor response may be related to poor laser penetration, a mismatch of parameters to vessel size, inadequate vascular heating, or scarce or poor chromophore uptake 36 . Given the limitations of the PDL, resistant components of PWBs can be treated with the alexandrite laser or IPL.

Infantile Hemangiomas Representing the most common tumor of infancy, hemangiomas have a predilection for the head and neck region (60%), followed by the trunk and the extremities. They are present in 1%–2% of neonates and there is a higher incidence in premature infants. These tumors classically grow rapidly within the first few weeks of life. Infantile hemangiomas may have both superficial and deep components, with the superficial portions appearing red and the deeper components appearing blue. They can be categorized as focal or segmental (see Ch. 103 ). Their natural maturation involves a proliferative phase, a static phase, and an involutional phase. Although hemangiomas can regress leaving the affected skin with normal texture and color, many heal with hyper- or hypopigmentation and atrophy or fibrofatty change (see Fig. 103.9 ). Treatment of infantile hemangiomas, if any, should be tailored to the specific lesion, with consideration of its location, size, proliferative rate, and whether it is likely to produce a functional or anatomic deficit. Currently, oral β -blockers, most commonly propranolol, are a mainstay of therapy for infantile hemangiomas that threaten vital functions, are potentially disfiguring, or have severe ulceration 37 . Other thera­ peutic options include monitoring, topical timolol (for thin lesions), corticosteroids (topical, intralesional or systemic), laser therapy, and less often surgical excision. Although the role of laser therapy in the treatment of infantile hemangiomas is still controversial 38 , in some studies PDL has been shown to slow progression, decrease time to involution, and promote healing of ulcerated lesions 39 . A retrospective study of 90 patients with infantile hemangiomas treated with PDL demonstrated a significant improvement in color and decrease in thickness in 81% and 64% of patients, respectively 40 . A retrospective study of 90 patients with infantile hemangiomas treated with PDL demonstrated a significant improvement in color and decrease in thickness in 81% and 64% of patients, respectively 40 . Combining systemic β -blockers with laser therapy may lead to a more rapid response and enhanced resolution; for example, in one retrospective study of infants with segmental facial hemangiomas treated concurrently or sequentially (propranolol followed by PDL), there was more complete clearance over a shorter time period following concurrent or sequential therapy (3 and 6 months, respec­ tively) compared to propranolol alone (almost 10 months) 41 . Ulceration, scarring, and pigmentary changes can occur if the epidermis is not adequately protected via cooling or if excessive energies are employed. Telangiectasias Patients frequently present with facial telangiectasias and they are often associated with chronic photodamage and rosacea. Telangiectasias can also occur on the face and elsewhere in the setting of liver disease, autoimmune connective tissue diseases, surgical scars, and the overuse of topical corticosteroids. Facial telangiectasias are typically located on the nose, cheeks and chin; they measure 0.1–1.0 mm in diameter and are commonly treated with PDL, KTP laser, or IPL. When the PDL is used with short pulse durations, significant clearance can be achieved, albeit with significant bruising (see Fig. 137.2D ). Clearance of facial vessels can be achieved with non-purpuric energy fluences or treat­ ments that employ energy fluences ranging from 6 to 8.5 J/cm 2 with longer pulse durations (6–20 ms) and 7–12 mm spot sizes. At these settings, multiple passes and/or cautious pulse-stacking techniques (see above) are typically employed to improve efficacy. Multiple treatment sessions may be required. These techniques can also benefit patients with recurring flushing and central facial erythema ( Fig. 137.12 ). Treatment of telangiectasias with the KTP laser induces little or no bruising compared to the PDL (see Fig. 137.2 ), but edema can occur. However, to compensate for the diminished absorption of 1064 nm light by hemoglobin (nearly 10-fold less compared with 595 nm light), an increased fluence is required, making vigorous cooling necessary both for epidermal protection and to reduce patient discomfort. Finally, IPL is commonly employed for purpura-free treatment of facial telangiectasias utilizing a 550 or 560 nm cut-off filter. The treatment endpoint for telangiectasias is vessel spasm or change in the vessel color to a duskier appearance. Options include IPL, PDL, and KTP laser; newer devices such as the fractionated ablative and non-ablative lasers can also be used. When there is insufficient overlap of adjacent PDL pulses, a persistent “honeycomb-like” appearance may occur, with circles of improvement in color, texture, and tone surrounded by a network of relatively untreated skin ( Fig. 137.13 ). This mottled look can require multiple treatments to eradicate. Since IPL can favorably improve both dyspigmentation and telangiec­ tasias, this system is perhaps more ideally suited to treat poikiloderma of Civatte. Several studies have reported 50%–75% improvement in both the vascular component and the actinic dyspigmentation, with a low side-effect profile 25 . The pertinent short-term side effects are transient erythema and intentional darkening of lentigines, which all disappear in about a week. Although “footprinting” is possible with IPL, it is far less common than with PDL, given the larger size of the crystal IPL handpiece. Additionally, use of a multiple-pass technique applied in different orien­ tations tends to minimize this unintended “footprint” consequence. Whether as a consequence of age, hormonal or genetic factors, or from trauma to the vessel wall, venous valvular incompetence produces increased hydrostatic pressure and ultimately vessel dilation (see Fig. 105.2 ). Whereas facial telangiectasias are generally superficial, small in caliber, and have normal hydrostatic pressures, leg veins are larger in diameter, thicker in caliber, and are situated more deeply within the skin. Additionally, as in any treatment site, there is heterogeneity in the size, color, and caliber of ectasias. These properties make treatment of leg veins even more challenging. Sclerotherapy is the first-line therapy for telangiectasias of the lower extremities (see Ch. 155 ). Laser treatment represents a viable option in a minority of patients such as those with needle phobias, telangiectatic matting 43 , or a history of adverse reactions to sclerosing agents (see Table 137.2 ). The PDL and KTP lasers can be used to treat small-caliber, pink and red blood vessels which are too fine to cannulate with sclerotherapy needles, e.g. the telangiectatic matting that can be a consequence of prior sclerotherapy. Given that leg veins are heterogeneous in their color, size, caliber and depth, and that many result from venous valvular incompetence, duplex ultrasonography can assist in determining the most appro­ priate treatment strategy. Combination therapy using endovenous lasers, ambulatory phlebectomy, and sclerotherapy may represent the best approach for long-term, successful treatment of lower extremity ectasias (see Ch. 155 ). Synergistic improvement may be achieved when these treatments are used in combination. Pyogenic Granulomas Pyogenic granulomas (PGs) are idiopathic, abruptly appearing, vascular neoplasms that tend to grow rapidly and bleed easily. Over half of these lesions recur after electrocoagulation, presumably because such desiccative treatments fail to ablate the deeper vascular compo­ nents 44 . Both the argon and CO 2 lasers have been used to treat these neoplasms. More specific targeting of the vascular nature of PGs has been attempted with the PDL, whether used directly on the lesion or in combination with glass slide diascopy to blanch out superficial compo­ nents. Higher success rates may be achieved with antecedent removal of the papular component (by shave or electrodesiccation techniques) prior to PDL targeting of the more deeply situated vessels. While shave removal followed by desiccation is still the first-line treatment for most patients, less scarring is noted with the PDL, when used either with modest energy fluences (1.5 ms pulses) without cooling or multiple stacked pulses (5–10 ms) with cooling . Venous Lakes and Cherry Angiomas Venous lakes are commonly seen on the lips or ears as gray–blue to purple compressible papulonodules representing dilated venules within the superficial dermis. These lesions are brought to the attention of dermatologists because of cosmetic concerns or a history of periodic bleeding. Traditionally, electrocoagulation has been used, but scarring and recurrence are common. IPL and PDL can be used but often light penetration is not deep enough. Longer wavelength devices including alexandrite laser or Nd:YAG laser may improve resolution. Cherry angiomas, which vary in color from bright red to purple, are also benign lesions of cosmetic concern (see Ch. 114 ). Optimal treatment is by PDL or KTP lasers, although some clinicians still use more traditional technology such as electrocoagulation. Verrucae Verruca vulgaris is caused by the human papillomavirus, which induces epidermal hyperplasia and neovascularization in affected skin. The use of lasers is said to be based on the principle of targeting their vascular component, which is evident histologically as dilated blood vessels within the dermal papillae. Use of the PDL has been shown to induce intravascular thrombosis and vessel wall necrosis in patients with verrucae 45 . However, the nonspecific heat effect from lasers is likely the main mechanism underlying wart clearance with laser therapy. “Laserthermia” of warts, particularly with the Nd:YAG laser, has produced clearance in 75% of patients 46 . Most notably, scarring and onychodystrophy can result from treatment of periungual verrucae with such ablative laser therapies 48 . A notable lack of bleeding and scarring makes the PDL laser a favorable choice. Given the limited penetration of the PDL, hyper­ keratotic portions of the wart are first pared down. If bleeding occurs, hemostasis should be achieved, being careful to avoid application of flammable topical agents to the treatment area. Then, the lesions are treated until a dusky gray color is seen. However, rather high fluences are utilized, making this treatment quite painful, especially on the fingers. Depending upon the pain tolerance of the patient, digital nerve blocks may be needed. This procedure can be repeated every 2–4 weeks until clinical resolution. While laser therapy for verrucae is not exclusively beneficial, it does supplement the dermatologist’s armamentarium in the treatment of these recalcitrant lesions. Pain Considerations PDL treatment can be associated with significant discomfort and has been typically described as a “hot rubber band” snapping on the skin. Whereas this procedure is generally well tolerated by adults, children may require anesthesia. When local anesthesia is chosen (most often for localized lesions), agents that blanch the vasculature and decrease the hemoglobin target need to be avoided. In addition, topical anesthetics should not be applied to ulcerated lesions and dosing recommenda­ tions need to be followed (see Tables 143.4 & 143.5 ). Larger vascular anomalies in children may require injected local or general anesthesia. KTP laser therapy is associated with fleeting stinging as the laser is applied onto the skin. TREATMENT OF MELANIN-CONTAINING LESIONS Ephelides and Lentigines Since melanin has a broad absorption spectrum (see Fig. 136.3 ), many lasers can be used to treat melanin-containing lesions. At the lower end of the therapeutic window, the penetration of green lasers is limited to the superficial papillary dermis. These lasers are best utilized for epidermal pigmented lesions. Thus, the frequency-doubled Nd:YAG (532 nm) laser, either Q-switched or normal mode, effectively treats lentigines and ephelides in most skin phototypes with limited recur­ rence 49 . Of note, in patients with a history of systemic gold therapy, Q-switched lasers will likely induce permanent darkening of the skin; such exposure needs to be determined prior to treatment. Additional lasers, e.g. the 800 nm diode, as well as IPL can also be used to treat epidermal pigmented lesions ( Table 137.3 ). While the PDL is most commonly used for vascular lesions, 595 nm light is also well absorbed by melanin and can be used to treat pigmented lesions. By incorpo­ rating compression, the vascular component of the skin is blanched out and melanin-containing lesions can be targeted. In general, the Q-switched ruby and alexandrite lasers are more effective when treating more deeply situated pigmented lesions (e.g. nevus of Ota), as these wavelengths have an increased depth of penetration. PHYSICAL TREATMENT MODALITIES Benign Melanocytic Nevi Laser removal of acquired and congenital nevi is controversial since no specimen is available for tissue diagnosis and margin assessment. Furthermore, the future biologic behavior of laser-resistant cells and the effect (if any) of laser thermal injury on these cells is unknown. Patients with atypical pigmented lesions should be examined carefully and regularly, preferably with total body imaging. Laser treatment of melanocytic lesions should only be considered for clinically banal lesions in patients with no personal or family history of melanoma. Both acquired and congenital melanocytic nevi have been treated with Q-switched ruby, alexandrite, and Nd:YAG lasers 51 . The 694 and 755 nm devices can improve the appearance of acquired junctional melanocytic nevi without scarring. In general, smaller and thinner lesions are typically more treatment-sensitive. While congenital nevi can be lightened, complete eradication is much more difficult and recur­ rence is common. Laser therapy decreases the number of pigmented nevus cells in the papillary dermis, but is unlikely to affect deeper seated, non-pigmented cells that are closely associated with adnexal structures. This has been demonstrated histologically as persistent nests of nevus cells in the mid papillary and deeper dermis at depths of 0.16–0.44 mm. Deeper components of these nevi located within muscle or under fascia will also remain unaffected by laser surgery. The normal mode (non-Q-switched), long-pulsed ruby and alexandrite lasers have also been used to treat acquired nevi. Clinicians should remember that early cutaneous melanoma can have a subtle clinical appearance and they should have a low threshold for biopsy. Café-au-Lait Macules and Nevus Spilus Café-au-lait macules (CALM) are tan–brown patches, which histo­ logically correspond to hypermelanosis of the basal melanocytes and keratinocytes. While these lesions can be seen in genodermatoses such as neurofibromatosis and McCune–Albright syndrome (see Ch. 61 ), they are typically isolated benign lesions. Cosmetic improvement can be achieved with the Q-switched ruby, alexandrite, and KTP lasers. However, CALM can be resistant to laser therapy, and they are prone to a high rate of recurrence. Use of the long-pulsed alexandrite laser has been reported to have a lower incidence of recurrence 52 . Nevus spilus consists of multiple lentigines and/or melanocytic nevi superimposed on a background CALM. Although the treatment of these lesions is very similar to that of CALM, these are typically more resistant and require multiple sessions. They may respond to normal- mode laser wavelengths or IPL. Rarely, malignant transformation has been described in nevus spilus, and thus caution is advised when treating with laser or light therapy. Nevus of Ito Clinically, nevus of Ota and nevus of Ito appear as blue–gray patches and histologically, spindled pigment-producing melanocytes are present in the papillary dermis. These entities differ only in their anatomic location. Nevus of Ota involves the face (primarily V1/V2 distribution), while nevus of Ito corresponds to the distribution of the posterior supraclavicular and lateral brachial nerves. Both have been success­ fully treated with Q-switched ruby, alexandrite, and Nd:YAG lasers 53 . Generally, high energy fluences are required, with multiple treatments spaced at least 6 weeks apart. A drawback of the Q-switched ruby laser is the tendency for hypopigmentation, which is a consequence of increased absorption by normal epidermal melanin. Hypopigmentation is observed less often with Q-switched alexandrite lasers (755 nm), which also achieve deeper penetration into the dermis. Near-infrared lasers, namely the Q-switched Nd:YAG (1064 nm), have even deeper penetration into the skin but are less well absorbed by melanin. Although these characteristics appear to negate each other, they allow for safer use in patients with darker skin and also allow for clearance of more deeply seated pigment. When in a sacral location, circumscribed dermal melanocytosis (Mongolian spot) spontaneously lightens in 95% of individuals by age 10 years. More persistent extra- sacral lesions can be treated with Q-switched lasers. Blue nevi share some histologic features with nevi of Ota and Ito but are well-circumscribed gray–blue to blue–black papules (common) and plaques (cellular). As such, laser treatment of these lesions is similar to that of nevi of Ota and Ito. While blue nevi are clinically benign, rare malignant transformation has been reported in cellular blue nevi. In addition, the clinical differential diagnosis of blue nevi may include cutaneous melanoma and thus dermoscopy can provide useful information. Becker Melanosis (Nevus) Becker melanosis is a hamartoma that typically presents during childhood or early adolescence as light to dark-brown patches or plaques on the shoulder, upper back, or lateral arm (see Ch. 112 ). It is associated with variable amounts of hypertrichosis as well as a smooth muscle hamartoma. Because melanin is located in both the epidermis and the dermal follicular matrix, treatment of Becker melanosis may require targeting both of these components. The basal layer melanin component requires nanosecond range pulse durations, and successful lightening has been accomplished with Q-switched ruby and alexandrite lasers 57 . In contrast, the follicular melanin responds more favorably to the ms pulse durations that characterize photoepilation systems. While these simplistic distinctions allow for methodical treatment, Becker melanosis is typically somewhat resistant to therapy. Often,

Postinflammatory Hyperpigmentation and Drug-Induced Discoloration Postinflammatory hyperpigmentation (PIH) is a common side effect of many dermatologic procedures, both medical and cosmetic. For patients with darker skin phototypes, PIH should be anticipated and a treatment plan promptly initiated. Common topical therapies include corticosteroids, retinoids, and bleaching creams. A newer treatment strategy is the use of fractionated photothermolysis with a low density and low to moderate energy. The fine columns (referred to as micro­ thermal or microablative zones; see below) can be generated at a desired depth, allowing for drug delivery and increased penetration of thera­ peutic topical agents into the skin. For treatment-resistant patients, Q-switched ruby, alexandrite, and Nd:YAG lasers have been used to expedite resolution of PIH. However, since PIH can be caused by these devices, circumspection is appropriate. As opposed to PIH, which is due to excess melanin, discoloration that results from sclerotherapy is a consequence of vessel destruction, erythrocyte extravasation, and interstitial hemosiderin deposition. The Q-switched ruby laser has been used successfully to treat this common sequela from sclerotherapy, with a reported 92% improvement rate 58 , but the success rate is quite variable. Drug-induced hyperpigmentation or discoloration represents deposition of drug metabolites, iron, melanin, or a combination of these components in the dermis and/or epidermis (see Table 67.5 ). The resultant color depends on the initiating medication and can range from blue–gray or brown to yellow or red. Use of Q-switched ruby, alexandrite, and 1064 nm Nd:YAG lasers has led to improvement of minocycline-, amiodarone-, imipramine- and silver (argyria)-induced hyperpigmentation or discoloration. HAIR REMOVAL Hair removal is one of the most commonly performed laser procedures. According to the American Society for Dermatologic Surgery, there were 385 000 laser hair removal procedures completed in 2018 alone 59 . While the distribution, density, and color of hair is related to sex and genetic background, the acceptability and desirability of hair are often related to societal and cultural norms. Markedly excessive hair can be a marker for an underlying endocrinopathy or a medication side effect and a possible etiology should be investigated prior to photoepilation (see Ch. 70 ). While most patients who undergo photoepilation have the cosmetic objective of decreasing unwanted hair, there are several medical applications of laser hair removal, such as treatment of pseudo­ folliculitis barbae or folliculitis decalvans. Although the patient’s ultimate desire may be to achieve total hairlessness in an anatomic region, complete eradication of hair is often an unattainable objective. Realistic expectations are key and the laser surgeon should clearly and specifically communicate these objectives to the patient. For some patients with particularly coarse, dense unwanted hair, a successful outcome might be a transition to finer, lighter hair. Potential side effects should be reviewed, including pigmentary changes (hyper- or hypopigmentation), erythema, edema, discomfort, and very rarely, scarring. Photoepilation is based on selectively delivering energy to both pigmented and non-pigmented structures within the hair follicle. Thermal energy delivered to the melanin-rich hair shaft and hair bulb matrix will destroy surrounding follicle structures while minimizing non-selective injury to the surrounding tissues. Often, non-pigmented structures near the follicle are targeted, such as the follicular stem cells that line the outer root sheath and actually reside quite far from the pigmented hair shaft (see Ch. 68 ) 60 . Three mechanisms have been proposed to explain hair follicle destruction. These include: (1) photo­ thermal injury to the follicle via direct heating of the follicle; (2) photo­ mechanical injury by induction of shock waves and violent cavitation; and (3) photochemical injury by production of toxic intermediaries such as singlet oxygen or free radicals 61 . Heat-induced change of the follicular structures and immediate surrounding tissues can result in transient growth arrest via induction of catagen or

These include: (1) photo­ thermal injury to the follicle via direct heating of the follicle; (2) photo­ mechanical injury by induction of shock waves and violent cavitation; and (3) photochemical injury by production of toxic intermediaries such as singlet oxygen or free radicals 61 . Heat-induced change of the follicular structures and immediate surrounding tissues can result in transient growth arrest via induction of catagen or permanent hair removal via follicular fibrosis. Although the absorption of melanin corresponds to wavelengths from 400 to 1200 nm, the best lasers for photoepilation have wavelengths of 600 to 1100 nm, a range where there is more selective absorption by melanin and the light penetrates relatively deeply into the skin. Given this relatively broad therapeutic spectrum, many laser systems have been utilized, including the ruby (694 nm), alexandrite (755 nm), diode (800–810 nm), and Nd:YAG (1064 nm) lasers, in addition to a variety of IPL systems with different cut-off filters. The optimal wavelength is probably in the ruby laser range (694 nm), but longer pulsing beyond 3 to 4 ms is problematic, which has led to the utilization of alternative wavelengths. However, the safety and efficacy of laser hair removal is dependent on the operator’s sophisticated knowledge regarding the practical application of laser–tissue interactions and the principles of selective photothermolysis. From a practical perspective, this entails accurate selection of the laser system, the optimal pulse duration, and the appropriate fluence to achieve hair removal while protecting the epidermis and minimizing non-selective dermal heat injury. Inappropriate selection can result in permanent scarring and dyspigmentation. Selection of the appropriate pulse duration is critical for effective photo­ epilation. As the thermal relaxation time of a hair follicle is ~10–30 ms, the pulse duration should be adjusted to match these parameters. However, extension of the pulse duration beyond the thermal relax­ ation time of the follicular unit promotes delivery of thermal damage to the surrounding non-pigmented stem cells and should induce more consistent follicular destruction 60 . Coarser, thicker, and darker hairs may have relatively longer thermal relaxation times compared to thinner, finer hairs 61 . The ideal patient for hair removal is one with lighter skin (phototypes I–III) and dark brown to black hair ( Fig. 137.14 ). PHYSICAL TREATMENT MODALITIES In general, higher energy fluences achieve greater hair reduction. However, since overzealous energy fluences might induce excessive collateral heat, a conservative selection of parameters is recommended. Typical danger zones are the chin and lip (where there is a greater density of hair follicles) as well as pigmented genital or inguinal skin. Energy fluence can be titrated up, if necessary, with each treatment as hair becomes less dense but tissue endpoints should be carefully monitored to avoid adverse effects. Parameters are not interchangeable between devices, even those with the same laser or IPL wavelength. It is incumbent on the operator to know how to operate each system that he or she employs. Laser hair removal in patients with darker skin can be more problematic as epidermal melanin competes with the follicular target. For patients with skin phototypes IV–VI, the long-pulsed Nd:YAG laser is generally regarded as the safest system. However, the most common criticism of the long-pulsed Nd:YAG laser is the associated pain. Appropriate cooling of the epidermis is critical with hair removal devices. Cooling can be applied immediately prior to (pre-cooling), during (parallel cooling), or after laser pulsing (post-cooling). Aside from protecting the epidermis from excessive heat, contact cooling handpieces allow compression of the skin and facilitate delivery of more laser energy to the targeted hair follicles. Although commercial laser and IPL companies might argue otherwise, no system is inherently superior for photoepilation. In general, lighter skin phototypes (I–III) respond better to treatment with the 755 nm alexandrite or the 800 nm diode laser, while darker skin phototypes (IV– VI) respond better to treatment with the 1064 nm Nd:YAG laser. Most studies have shown comparable efficacy rates when sufficient energy fluence is used and multiple treatments are performed. Regardless of the laser or IPL system utilized, serial treatments are required for significant, long-term hair reduction. Paradoxical hypertrichosis following the use of hair removal devices is a well-documented side effect of photoepilation. This has generally been described in patients with Mediterranean, Hispanic or Asian backgrounds, skin phototypes III or IV, and dark lanugo hair. Of note, it can occur with any of the laser or IPL hair removal systems. Initial reports suggested that affected patients should be evaluated for hyper­ androgenemia, but paradoxical hypertrichosis occurs more commonly than does hyperandrogenemia 64 . The largest retrospective analysis to date of 750 patients found that the overall incidence of paradoxical hypertrichosis was 4.5% (although it is likely higher), and the hyper­ trichosis occurred most often on the face and neck of patients with skin phototypes III and IV. These authors postulated that the hair induction occurred at the borders of the treated areas, perhaps because of sub-therapeutic energy fluences during laser therapy and local inflammatory responses following photoepilation 65 . While paradoxical hypertrichosis can be difficult to treat, in one author’s experience (CBZ), treatment with the nanosecond Q-switched Nd:YAG (1064 nm) laser can provide at least temporary improvement. It has been suggested that application of ice to the perimeter of the treatment area and use of the highest tolerated energy fluence may minimize this side effect. Proper pre-treatment preparation of the skin prior to photoepilation allows for optimal treatment results. Failure to recognize the need to avoid treating suntanned skin has resulted in numerous burns, scars, and permanent pigmentary changes. In severe cases this may result in dermal necrosis and marked scarring. For traumatic scars characterized primarily by erythema, vascular lasers are used to target oxyhemoglobin within the scar’s microvascu­ lature 69 . PDL at low fluence settings and short pulse width is most commonly used, with treatments every 1 or 2 months until goals are reached 20 . If multiple devices are to be used during a scar treatment session, it is important to treat the erythematous element first, to avoid erythema or blood created by the other procedures being targeted by the vascular laser 69 . In patients with skin phototypes I–IV, PDL can be especially effective in improving the quality and cosmetic appearance of surgical scars when instituted early, i.e. from the day of suture removal 69 . Scar texture and dyspigmentation can be addressed with fractional laser resurfacing. For hypertrophic and contracted scars, ablative fractional lasers are the most effective treatment, as they induce robust tissue remodeling and improvement in symptoms and cosmesis can be seen within days to weeks 20 . Burn scars are most effectively treated with at least three rounds of the ablative fractional CO 2 laser at 4- to 6-week intervals 70 ; low densities are recommended 71 . Hypertrophic or keloidal surgical scars respond well to intralesional injections of triamcinolone acetonide ± 5-fluorouracil after ablative fractional resur­ facing 69 . Since atrophic scars reflect collagen destruction, both ablative and non-ablative fractional lasers are employed as they induce neocol­ lagenesis and remodeling within atrophic areas. Similar results are observed, but non-ablative fractional lasers are better tolerated 20 and safer in skin phototypes IV–VI 71 . Fractional laser resurfacing may begin once the scar has stable epidermal coverage, with a minimum interval of 1 to 3 months between treatments until the desired improvement or a therapeutic plateau is reached 20 . Because darker skin phototypes are more susceptible to PIH with high-density non-ablative fractional resurfacing, lower densities are preferable. TREATMENT OF STRIAE DISTENSAE Striae distensae are common after pregnancy, growth spurts in adoles­ cence, or rapid weight gain. Histologically, there is thinning of the epidermis and atrophy of the dermis. In their early inflammatory stages, they often appear pink to purple in color and are called striae rubrae. The latter mature and take on a more pallid color and then are termed striae albae (see Ch. 99 ). Although treatment of striae is not medically necessary, many patients seek cosmetic improvement. Several lasers, including PDL, 308 nm excimer, fully ablative, ablative fractional, non-ablative fractional (1450/1550 nm), and Q-switched or low-fluence, long- pulsed Nd:YAG (1064 nm) lasers, as well as IPL, have been used with varying degrees of success with regard to the color and texture of striae 73 . More targeted studies have correlated clinical improvement with increased elastin remodeling or formation. Fractionated photo­ thermolysis has been shown to improve atrophic scars 4 , and in a pilot study of striae in patients with skin phototypes IV–VI, epidermal thickening and remodeling of collagen and elastin fibers was observed after 1550 nm fractionated photothermolysis 74 . In spite of some wistful reports, the results of striae treatment with lasers have been quite disappointing. TREATMENT OF CELLULITE The treatment of cellulite is covered in Chapter 156

TREATMENT OF TATTOOS A tattoo represents the presence of exogenous pigmented material in the skin. Although the most common purpose for tattooing is artistic and cosmetic, it has also been utilized in the medical field, in particular as radiation port markers. Additionally, tattoo pigment composed of lead, carbon, asphalt, gunpowder, or coal can be introduced explosively or traumatically. Once embedded, the exogenous pigment is taken up predominantly by dermal macrophages. These pigment particles measure from 2 to 400 nm, but generally average ~40 nm in diameter. Tattoo removal is a common patient request. Prior to advancements in laser technology, removal was frequently associated with disfig­ uring scarring. With the evolution of the Q-switched nanosecond and picosecond lasers, pigment eradication can now be more safely achieved, with less scarring and/or pigmentary changes. Q-switched lasers are characterized by having extremely short pulses, which induce photomechanical and photoacoustic laser–tissue inter­ actions. The immediate local exponential increase in temperature to 200–300°C causes dramatic expansion of organelles such as lysosomes within macrophages, followed by their equally catastrophic contraction/ collapse, leading to cavitation of the tattoo-bearing macrophages. The exceptionally short pulse duration limits the thermal damage to just the macrophage. Clinically, the laser tissue reaction is seen as immediate epidermal whitening, which is essentially nitrogen vapor within the epidermis and immediately adjacent to the tattoo pigment particles in the dermis ( Fig. 137.15 ). Mechanical damage results in cell membrane rupture and the release of exogenous pigment into the extracellular space. Some of this released pigment departs the skin and drains via the lymphatics to local lymph nodes, while the remainder is simply re-phagocytosed. In addition, there is fragmentation of tattoo ink particles and this changes their optical properties and/or allows easier reuptake by macrophages followed by removal from the site. More difficult to remove are yellow and orange pigments, as these are not well absorbed by currently commercially available Q-switched laser light. Despite all the advances in laser therapy, total eradication of tattoos can prove frustratingly difficult. Amateur tattoos often incorporate blue–black pigments that are carbon-based, such as India ink. Given that these tattoos have only a few colors and lower ink density, coupled with the observation that they may be placed at variable depths (primarily superficially) in the skin, amateur tattoos are relatively easy to remove. Professional tattoo artists incorporate a wider spectrum of colors and deposit the pigments within the deep papillary and superficial reticular dermis. Hence, removal can be problematic, even with the best devices. Complications of tattoo removal include both hyper- and hypopig­ mentation. While hypopigmentation can be observed with the ruby and alexandrite lasers, hyperpigmentation commonly occurs in patients with more darkly pigmented skin. It has often been said that Q-switched lasers remove tattoo pigment without scarring. While this is often true, there can be significant textural changes after multiple treatments with high energy fluence devices. Additionally, inflammatory reactions to tattoo ink have been reported, including eczematous, granulomatous, and lichenoid reactions. When systemic reactions occur after laser treatment, they are the consequence of mobilized antigens. Paradoxical darkening of skin-colored tattoo ink is a common phenomenon following treatment with any of the Q-switched lasers. This unfortunate event happens immediately after a single laser pulse and is caused by a shift from an oxidized state to a reduced state in the tattoo pigment. This was classically reported as darkening of red “lip liner” to dark brown or black pigment as the ferric oxide tattoo was reduced to ferrous oxide ( Fig. 137.17 ). Similar color changes can be seen in tattoos with titanium dioxide, a common agent used to lighten tattoo pigments; when a Q-switched laser is applied to titanium, it can change from white to blue–black. Although this problematic side effect can be improved via continued treatment with any of the Q-switched lasers, a test spot is wise with such tattoos, particularly on the face. TREATMENT OF PSORIASIS AND VITILIGO Psoriasis affects nearly 2% of the US population and often commits patients to a lifetime of treatment. The range of therapies includes topical corticosteroids and vitamin D 3 analogues, systemic retinoids, methotrexate, phototherapy, and targeted immunomodulators (“biologic agents”; see Ch. 8 ). Despite the variety of treatment options available, some psoriatic plaques are recalcitrant. Application of laser therapy may represent a novel approach to resistant lesions, particularly those in “problem areas” such as the scalp and intertriginous zones. The most commonly used laser for psoriasis is the 308 nm XeCl excimer laser. As a localized narrowband UVB therapy, the excimer laser has been demonstrated to clear psoriatic plaques by impeding epidermal cell proliferation and perhaps inducing localized immunosuppression. Compared to conventional UVB phototherapy, treatment with the excimer laser cleared psoriatic plaques two times faster and with lower cumulative UVB doses 79 . Additionally, PDL has been used to treat psoriasis by targeting the underlying abnormal vasculature. While both systems are beneficial, the excimer laser has been shown to yield more favorable improvement 80 . The excimer laser has also been shown to produce impressive improvement of vitiliginous skin when used as adjuvant therapy, especially when combined with topical tacrolimus 81 . Lastly, the excimer laser has been used to repigment, at least temporarily, some of the patients who developed delayed-onset permanent hypopigmentation following standard CO 2 or Er:YAG laser resurfacing procedures. PHYSICAL TREATMENT MODALITIES persistent erythema or delayed hypopigmentation that are seen with traditional resurfacing have been reported only rarely with fractionated lasers. Additionally, lines of demarcation are easily avoided by feath­ ering the transitional skin between treated and untreated regions with near-minimal fluence and density settings. Because only minute areas of damage are induced and the skin heals rapidly, fractionated ablative systems offer an unparalleled safety margin as compared to traditional ablative lasers. However, infection is still the most significant complication and can lead to permanent scarring. It is advised that all patients begin oral antiviral therapy the day prior to, or the morning of, the procedure. They should also have easy access to postoperative skin evaluations, especially if fever, pain, angular erythema, or pustular discharge is noted. Use of oral antibiotics and antifungal agents can be decided on a case-by-case basis. Although scarring is an infrequent event, recent case reports have alerted laser surgeons to be cautious in “underprivileged” areas such as the neck and chest which are relatively devoid of adnexal struc­ tures 83 . Whereas skin on the cheek with its thicker dermis and abundant sebaceous glands can tolerate high energies and up to 70% ablation for certain indications, more modest energy and significantly less ablation density should be employed on thinner, finer, and less privileged areas. Another noteworthy consideration for minimizing the risk of scarring is avoidance of immediate and direct scanned overlap of treatment areas. Use of a non-overlapping technique allows the treated skin suffi­ cient time to cool before the application of the subsequent pass. This prevents bulk heating, a likely cause of scarring when it has occurred with fractional laser therapy. Patients with a prior history of melasma or other pigmentary disorders might be pretreated with topical hydro­ quinone prior to the procedure. RADIOFREQUENCY AND ULTRASOUND Skin Tightening Monopolar radiofrequency (RF) energy generates dermal heat in a manner which is directly related to tissue impedance. The first commercially available monopolar RF device was ThermaCool TC™ (Thermage ® ) which delivered high-frequency RF energy to the skin via a thin, coupling electrode handpiece with active cooling. In vivo studies demonstrated that RF energy produced collagen contraction after disrupting hydrogen bonds within the collagen triple-helix structure 84 . After RF tissue tightening received FDA clearance for periorbital rhytide reduction in 2002, it was more widely used on the face and neck for improvement of skin laxity. A split-face study demonstrated average brow elevation of 2–4 mm, superior palpebral crease elevation of 1.9 mm, and reduction of jowl surface area by 22% 84 . Although other early studies reported similar conclusions, results in clinical practice were far more variable and unpredictable, and the treatments were associated with significant patient discomfort 85 . Aside from transient erythema and edema, irregular depressions (“mattress-top” irregularities) were seen, which were attributed to excessive treatment (outside the recommended parameters) causing localized fat atrophy. New algorithms and devices were developed, which increased both the reproducibility of the results and patient comfort. They included the use of: (1) lower energies over a larger tip in a multiple-pass technique 13 ; (2) a transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation

and unpredictable, and the treatments were associated with significant patient discomfort 85 . Aside from transient erythema and edema, irregular depressions (“mattress-top” irregularities) were seen, which were attributed to excessive treatment (outside the recommended parameters) causing localized fat atrophy. New algorithms and devices were developed, which increased both the reproducibility of the results and patient comfort. They included the use of: (1) lower energies over a larger tip in a multiple-pass technique 13 ; (2) a transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS)-like interruption of RF energy interspersed with hot/cold skin stimulation; (3) vibration (acting on the gate theory of pain); (4) a modulated RF profile; and (5) more distributive electrodes. In 2017, RF technology received FDA clearance for non-invasive smoothing of skin on the face, around the eyes, and body. Bipolar RF devices create localized heat by conducting current between the two electrodes on the skin surface (see Fig. 136.7 ). Studies purport to have shown a 25%–50% improvement in wrinkles, skin smoothness, and texture 13 . There are reasons to believe that the bipolar devices are not as efficient as monopolar devices in their ability to tighten tissue or create new collagen. Ultrasound (US) has emerged as a recognized technique for non-invasive tissue tightening. The primary mechanism is the absorption of either very brief focused or much longer diffuse acoustic energy. US is colorblind and thus can be used on all skin phototypes. Ultherapy™ (Merz) utilizes high intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) and has been cleared by the FDA for improvement in the appearance of the face, neck, and décolletage. Depth-specific transducers induce ms pulses of focal injury within the skin without damage to the epidermis. Use of a prototype device led to significant skin tightening, with a 1 mm eyebrow lift in > 75% of treated subjects 86 . In cadaveric skin, damage was noted at a depth of 4.2 mm, including damage to the superficial muscular aponeurotic system (SMAS) 87 . This targeted approach was met with significant enthusiasm, and a number of investigators have observed good clinical improvement. However, some clinicians still remain highly skeptical about the long-term benefits. Side effects include focal bruising and pain, reported by 25% and ≤ 55% of patients, respectively. SofWave ™ (SofWave Medical Ltd) provides more diffuse US with mid-dermal heating to 60–70°C, maximally targeting a depth of 1.5 mm for 5 seconds without damage to the underlying structures including bone, nerves,

87 . This targeted approach was met with significant enthusiasm, and a number of investigators have observed good clinical improvement. However, some clinicians still remain highly skeptical about the long-term benefits. Side effects include focal bruising and pain, reported by 25% and ≤ 55% of patients, respectively. SofWave ™ (SofWave Medical Ltd) provides more diffuse US with mid-dermal heating to 60–70°C, maximally targeting a depth of 1.5 mm for 5 seconds without damage to the underlying structures including bone, nerves, fat, and blood vessels. This device has no disposables, no moving parts, and no optics. The parallel delivery of more diffuse ultrasound beams, integrated cooling, and a large contact area allow for less discomfort and faster treatments. Patients should understand that these devices are no replacement for surgical skin tightening and may take multiple treatments to achieve the desired outcome. Radiofrequency Microneedling Devices Radiofrequency (RF) microneedling devices have made major inroads into traditional methods for skin rejuvenation. A plethora of such devices have been FDA cleared and are used for rejuvenation, “tightening”, and improvement in scarring. Some are monopolar, while others are bipolar; electrodes are either insulated or non-insulated (see Table 137.1 ). The original device, Profound ® RF (Candela), was shown to induce new collagen and elastin within the mid dermis, leading to improvement in facial and extrafacial skin laxity. However, the procedure is quite uncomfortable, requiring topical anesthetic, nerve blocks, and possibly nitrous oxide and parenteral pain control. In general, RF microneedling is performed 4–6 times at one-month intervals using only topical anesthesia. The needle density and length are sufficient to provide both superficial and deep controlled thermal injury (see Table 137.1 ). MICROWAVES In the electromagnetic spectrum, microwaves lie between infrared light and radio waves. Microwaves can heat substances via a process called dielectric heating. The latter occurs when energy causes a rotation of dipole molecules. Because it is an ion, water has a high dipole moment whereas fat has a low dipole moment. As a result, there is less absorption in the subcutaneous layer and selectivity for the dermis. Furthermore, application of concurrent cooling protects the upper dermis and selec­ tively heats the deeper dermis. Dielectric heating by microwaves was found to induce both eccrine and apocrine sweat gland thermolysis with relative selectivity. This discovery led to the first commercially available therapeutic microwave device – miraDry ® (Miramar Labs). Studies have shown that 90% of patients had at least a 50% reduction in sweating, and ~80% maintained this reduction at 12 months 88 . All subjects experienced transient swelling, discomfort, and/or numbness within the treatment area, with a few patients noting longer-lasting side effects including altered sensation in or around the treatment site, papulonodules in the axillae, and hair loss 89 . Lasers and Other Energy-Based Therapies HOME-BASED LASERS The notion that home-based laser and light devices might someday replace office-based treatments has not caused many physicians to lose sleep. In practice, however, there are some devices that can efficiently remove hair, reduce the signs of photodamage, induce a degree of skin tightening, and improve acne. That said, there is an even larger number of devices that are totally ineffective. In general, those devices that are effective and designed by highly skilled engineers are rather expensive, while the ineffective devices are relatively cheap and therefore appealing to the consumer. Potential economic rewards have driven some companies to manufacture devices which are so ineffective that they are awarded FDA clearance by virtue of their safety alone. Although little peer-reviewed literature is available, one well-controlled, office-based study demonstrated that nearly all of the patients were able to correctly administer their own treatments. Additionally, the observed side effects of hyper- and hypopigmentation, crusting, and blistering were transient and had resolved by the conclusion of the study 90 . EMERGING TECHNOLOGIES To prevent and control acne via sebaceous gland suppression, gold- coated silica microparticles can be excited with commonly available lasers at a low energy fluence 91 . Localized damage can be achieved with minimal injury to surrounding structures. Sebacia Microparticles (Sebacia, Inc.) is the first such commercially available product. In addition, when sebum was compared to water, a wavelength of 1726 nm was found to have a small but significant absorption differential. Use of a “sebum laser” led to focal damage of sebaceous glands with sparing of surrounding structures and was reported to prevent and treat acne. Nano-Pulse Stimulation™ (NPS™) technology (Pulse Biosciences, Inc.) utilizes non-thermal energy and has a unique mechanism of action that targets only cellular morphology while sparing the non-cellular stroma ( Fig. 137.18 ) 92,93 . Ultrafast (nanosecond) electrical energy pulses are delivered via microneedle arrays. In clinical trials, NPS has been used to treat common warts, seborrheic keratoses, sebaceous hyperplasia, and superficial basal cell carcinomas, with a reportedly low incidence of hyper- or hypopigmentation and rarely scarring. Regulated cell death has also been observed in malignant tumor-bearing animals as has a secondary immune response that leads to rejection of re-intro­ duced malignant cells of the same lineage 94 . Laser engineers are very insightful and they can provide us with semi-intelligent laser, light, and other energy systems that can more precisely target the correct structures and induce appropriate healing responses. The mechanisms of injury in cryosurgery can be attributed to both direct and indirect effects ( Table 138.1 ). Such events are the result of fast freezing followed by slow thawing, i.e. a freeze–thaw cycle. Repeated freeze–thaw cycles increase the destructive effects of cryosurgery. The material interposed between the cryogen and the lesion to be treated is also a determinant of the speed of freezing. Air is a poor conductor of cold such that the greater the distance between the skin lesion and the source of the cryogen, the lesser the freezing. Water is a better conductor than air (e.g. a presoaked verruca freezes faster), and ice is better than water as in the intra- and extracellular ice crystals present after the first freeze–thaw cycle. Finally, metal is an excellent conductor explaining the deep and fast freezing of tissue that results from frozen metal probes placed in direct contact with the skin 3 . Different cells and tissues have different sensitivities to cold. The lethal temperature for melanocytes is around − 4°C, while that for keratinocytes is − 35°C. Keratinocyte cancer cells require around − 50°C, sarcoma cells − 60°C, and vascular endothelium − 15°C to − 40°C. Of note, cartilage and bone are quite resistant to freezing. Cryoimmunology Cryoimmunology is the study of the innate and humoral immune responses to antigens derived from frozen skin lesions. Development of newer immunologic assays has made it possible to measure such responses, which can be either immunostimulatory or immuno­suppressive 4 . One major difference between conventional excisional surgery and cryosurgery is that the latter leaves the tumor “ in situ ”. At the center of the frozen lesion, there will be necrosis due to direct cellular damage (see Table 138.1 ), leading to release of tumor-specific antigens capable of stimulating an immune response. Once the innate immune system is activated, antigen-presenting cells (APCs) engulf tumor fragments and present processed antigens to T cells, initiating both T and B cell immune responses (see Ch. 4 ). At the periphery, the temperatures are higher and therefore sublethal, with the cells undergoing apoptosis rather than necrosis. This leads to “silent cell death” associated with minimal inflammation (see Table 138.1 ) 4 . The

These include agents that augment ice injury (e.g. glycine), inducers of apoptosis (e.g. topical 5-fluorouracil) 6 , and immunomodu- lators (e.g. topical imiquimod). However, further studies are needed to better understand the under- lying mechanisms of cryoimmunology, define the ideal parameters for tumor destruction, and determine the precise interactions between cryosurgery and potential adjuvants. With the advent of potent cryogens, selective destruction of tissue became possible. James M. Arnott is credited with first describing the use of controlled freezing in the 1800s to destroy tumors 1 . Liquefied oxygen and carbon monoxide preceded the introduction of liquid nitrogen (LN) by Carl von Linde. By 1898, James Dewar had developed a flask that permitted storage and transportation of LN thereby rendering LN accessible to physicians. In 1899, Archibald Campbell White reported on the successful treatment of multiple benign and malignant skin conditions with liquefied air applied via an adapted bottle; the latter could be considered the prototype of modern hand-held units. Herman V. Allington then described how LN-saturated cotton swabs could be used to treat various skin conditions. In 1961, the neurosurgeon Irving S. Cooper, together with Arnold Lee, developed the first cryosurgical probe. Increased use of LN for medical purposes followed the design of safe portable hand-held units. PRINCIPLES OF CRYOSURGERY AND CRYOBIOLOGY Cryosurgery is defined as a surgical procedure that utilizes very low temperatures to destroy living tissue. The term cryotherapy should be reserved for when living tissue is exposed to cold in order to induce physiological changes but not tissue destruction. Cryobiology repre- sents the study of the effects of low temperatures on living tissues. Heat transfers from hot to cold 2 , and the larger the temperature difference between a cryogen and its target tissue, the faster the heat transfer. The ideal cryogen has the lowest possible temperature and is capable of producing the parameters necessary to destroy both benign and malignant cells; for the latter, the tissue temperature needs to be below − 50°C. Because a double freeze–thaw cycle is more destructive, it is the recommended cryosurgical procedure for skin cancer. Except for very small lesions, local anesthesia is administered. In addition, since keratin is a poor conductor of cold, removal of excess keratin via curettage or paring will assist in reaching the correct freezing temper- ature at the base of the tumor, thus improving effectiveness 21 . The most commonly used techniques are open (spray) and closed (contact, probe); the closed technique is preferred as it leads to deeper and faster freezing (see Table 138.2 ). However, it is important to use a probe that corresponds to the size and shape of the tumor to assure complete apposition. Palliative Treatment Cryosurgery has long been used for palliative (compassionate) treatment of skin cancer ( Table 138.6 ) 29 . Detailed discussion with the patient and/ or family/caretakers should be undertaken before instituting palliative treatment. The goal is to reduce pain, bleeding, infection, tissue destruction, foul smell, and/or tumoral masses that cause personal and social rejection. Palliative cryosurgery can improve quality of life in individuals with inoperable tumors or in those who reject conventional therapies or are poor surgical candidates due to underlying medical conditions. Large tumoral masses can be treated by either: (1) the segmental technique; or (2) the fractional technique. In the segmental technique, the tumor is divided by imaginary lines into portions. Each segment is treated independently, allowing the freezing fronts to overlap. The aim is to avoid excessive freezing in the center of the tumor prior to the freeze front reaching the periphery. In the fractional technique, the center of the tumor is treated and then allowed to heal 30 . The latter is especially true for the lower extremities. The expected course and postoperative care are outlined in Table 138.7 . Degree of edema will be determined by the depth of the freeze as well as the anatomic location, e.g. cryosurgery of eyelid lesions often leads to more edema (even with light freezing) than does a deep freeze on the arm. Patients with cold sensitivity can also develop more edema after cryosurgery. For lesions that develop a large bulla, the fluid is often drained to decrease pressure and possibly hasten healing; the blister roof is usually left intact to serve as a biologic dressing although the recommen- dation of some cryosurgeons is to remove it, especially for verrucae to minimize risk of reimplantation. A gauze dressing can be placed if there is significant oozing and application of a bland topical ointment such as petrolatum enhances second intention healing. Eschars due to cryone- crosis, a later event when deep freezing is performed, should be debrided to facilitate healing. When X-rays (often referred to as photons) are absorbed by biological matter, an electron may be ejected from an atom with the local release of large amounts of energy resulting in DNA damage. Rapidly dividing cells, i.e. malignant cells, are more susceptible to lethal injury and mitotic death. Although normal adjacent tissues maintain mechanisms for repair following sublethal damage, there are limitations as to the dose of ionizing radiation normal tissue can tolerate, beyond which late reactions arise (see below). A therapeutic ratio is achieved when radiation is delivered in small divided doses (fractions), which allows time for repair of sublethal DNA damage in normal tissues without compromising tumor destruction. Treatment Machines In the modern era of radiation oncology, high-energy megavoltage (MV) photons (6–25 MV) are generated by a linear accelerator (LINAC) located within a heavily shielded concrete bunker. One of the advantages of megavoltage radiotherapy is its ability to treat deep-seated internal malignancies with relative skin sparing. However, in general, when treating cutaneous lesions, deep beam penetration and skin sparing are not desirable. Less penetrating modalities that avoid skin sparing, such as low-energy kilovoltage (kV) photons (50–300 kVp) supplied by a superficial/orthovoltage machine, superficial brachytherapy or electron beam therapy, are preferred modalities for cutaneous lesions. With these therapies, tissue penetration is measured in millimeters to centimeters and there is less normal tissue exposure. Radiotherapy modalities are summarized in Table 139.1 . Terminology The International Unit of radiotherapy is a Gray (Gy) 3 . One Gy is equiv- alent to 100 cGy or 100 rads (in the older terminology). A fraction of radiotherapy refers to the dose delivered in one treatment. Treatments are typically delivered on a daily (Monday to Friday) basis. The daily outpatient treatments are only minutes in duration and treatment regimens usually consist of 10 to 30 weekday visits. Radiotherapy Doses Typical fractionation protocols for small SCCs and BCCs consist of 40 Gy in 10 (4 Gy) fractions or 50 Gy in 20 (2.5 Gy) fractions. Hypofractionation refers to the delivery of larger doses per fraction (4–7 Gy); typically a lower total dose is then delivered based upon the biological effective dose (BED; Table 139.2 ). The latter is calculated based upon a 2 Gy per fraction equivalent that is required to eradicate a tumor

Hypofractionation refers to the delivery of larger doses per fraction (4–7 Gy); typically a lower total dose is then delivered based upon the biological effective dose (BED; Table 139.2 ). The latter is calculated based upon a 2 Gy per fraction equivalent that is required to eradicate a tumor 4 . This calculation provides an explanation for commonly prescribed schedules: 45 Gy in 15 (3 Gy) fractions, 40 Gy in 10 (4 Gy) fractions, and 35 Gy in 5 (7 Gy) fractions. For BCCs and SCCs, there is not a marked dose–response such that local control is similar whether a patient receives 40 Gy in 10 fractions (47 Gy BED) or 50 Gy in 20 fractions (52 Gy BED). When the tumors are larger or more infiltrative, better local control is achieved with a BED of around 60 Gy. However, late effects increase as the total dose and dose per fraction increase and it is these late effects that will impact cosmesis and late tissue damage (e.g. fibrosis, atrophy, ulceration due to necrosis). It is also used to treat less common, but potentially aggressive, cutaneous malignancies and, occasionally, benign diseases. The former include Merkel cell carcinoma, Kaposi sarcoma (AIDS- and non-AIDS-related), angiosarcoma, adnexal carcinoma, lymphoma, and lentigo maligna. While the majority of skin cancers are amenable to excision or other treatment modalities (e.g. electrodesiccation and curettage) which are often more cost-effective, there are clinical settings where radiotherapy is favored. For example, definitive radiotherapy is often recommended when the outcome (functional and/or cosmetic) is likely to be better with radiotherapy than with surgery, especially in the situation where the clinician is constrained by the site or size of the tumor. Likewise, elderly patients with advanced lesions for whom complex surgery is best avoided are also excellent candidates for radiotherapy. The qualities and “hardness” of superficial/orthovoltage photon beams are determined by the placement of filters within the radiation beam 5 . “Half value layer” (HVL) is an important concept in radiation physics and it refers to the thickness of an absorbent filter (often copper [Cu] or aluminum [Al]) that is required to reduce the beam intensity by 50%. These filters serve to remove the softer photon component and improve the penetration quality of the beam. The following are two examples of the influence of filters: a typical 100 kVp superficial photon beam with an HVL of 7 mm of Al delivers 100% of a prescribed dose to the surface, 85% at 5 mm, and 70% at 10 mm whereas a 250 kVp ortho- voltage beam with an HVL of 2.5 mm of Cu delivers 95% of prescribed dose at 5 mm and 90% at 10 mm. In summary, different photon beam energies will have unique HVLs that result in varied beam qualities and dose penetration. Superficial radiotherapy Office-based superficial radiotherapy was once the standard modality by which dermatologists treated skin cancer 6 . Typical machines delivered photons of 30–150 kVp with a depth dose suitable for most patients with cutaneous malignancies < 5 mm in depth 7 . Over time, the high cost of radiotherapy machines and increased enthusiasm and training in dermatologic surgery led to a significant decline in office-based radio- therapy. More recently, introduction of superficial radiation therapy (SRT) machines has led to renewed interest in office-based radiotherapy for BCCs and cutaneous SCCs. Some clinicians estimate tumor thickness and then choose an appropriate beam energy and HVL that will achieve 90%–95% of the prescribed dose at the depth of the tumor. An important consideration when delivering orthovoltage radio- therapy is the generation of a photoelectric effect due to a higher energy range when compared to low-energy photons. A consequence of this photoelectric effect is the delivery of a higher dose of radiation to under- lying bone or cartilage. The latter does not occur with electrons (see below) or low-energy photons (see above). As a result, some clinicians use this as a justification for the use of electrons when treating lesions near bone or cartilage, although supportive clinical data are limited. Low-energy electrons (6–8 MeV [megaelectron volts]) offer an alternative to low-energy photons when treating cutaneous tumors, but the former do have some disadvantages 8 . For example, electron beams are relatively skin-sparing ( Fig. 139.1 ), and, as a result, a tissue equivalent bolus needs to be placed on the skin surface ( Fig. 139.2 ). Also, utilizing electron beams for small treatment fields ( < 4 cm 2 ) may result in tumor underdosing at the deepest extent of the tumor. Brachytherapy Radioisotope brachytherapy Radioisotope brachytherapy represents radiotherapy that is delivered by the direct application of a radioactive source near or inside involved tissues. Most centers utilize a high dose-rate (HDR) system that delivers more than 12 Gy/hr, with Ir-192 being the most commonly used isotope. Treatments are delivered by the placement of surface applicators onto the skin at the site of the tumor. The radioactive source is often delivered to the applicators via a remotely controlled machine in a dedicated shielded HDR suite. Applicator selection varies depending on the location and surface contours of the target area, e.g. conical surface applicators for flat surfaces, flexible mesh style “flap” applicators for molding onto curved surfaces. When treating deeper tumors, interstitial catheters may be surgically placed within the target tissue. The dose “fall-off” is steep with brachytherapy, providing an excellent opportunity to spare adjacent normal tissue which is not easily achieved with photon- or electron-based treatments. Per American Brachytherapy Society (ABS) consensus guidelines, HDR skin brachytherapy represents a standard of care option for appropriately selected patients with kerati- nocyte carcinomas 9 . Because HDR delivery systems require Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) oversight, special shielded vaults, and careful security and safety protocols, radioisotope brachytherapy is performed by a radiation oncologist in a controlled setting. The currently available systems operate in the 50–70 kVp energy range, require little shielding, and are considered more portable. Electronic brachytherapy systems are not subject to NRC oversight, but may need to adhere to local regulations 10 . Similar to radioisotope brachytherapy, a steep dose fall-off allows for sparing of adjacent organs and tissues. However, there are some concerns as to tissue dose calculations as well as the potential for different radiobio- logical effectiveness due to the photons’ low energy. Therefore, consensus guidelines for calculating tissue dosages are yet to be finalized 10,11 . As with radioisotope brachytherapy, suitable lesions need to be super- ficial ( < 3–4 mm in depth) and well-defined. While data are emerging regarding the safety and efficacy of electronic brachytherapy for the treatment of keratinocyte carcinomas, given the lack of both long-term follow-up and a consensus regarding dosimetric properties of this modality, the ABS does not advise its use outside of prospective or registry trials 10 . In situations where reconstruction with grafts or flaps is required, improved cosmesis may result from radiotherapy 12 . Disadvantages of Radiotherapy Radiotherapy does have its disadvantages; in particular, most patients require a protracted course of treatment compared to what is often a simple outpatient excision. Patients should also be informed that because of the risk of serious late effects such as soft tissue and cartilage necrosis, a second course of definitive radiotherapy cannot be delivered to the same site. In addition, the reduced “quality” of irradiated skin may make subsequent surgery difficult if the tumor recurs or persists following radiation therapy. Over time, irradiated skin may also develop dyspigmentation, telangiectasias, and a shiny appearance. Lastly, individuals with xeroderma pigmentosum or basal cell nevus syndrome should not be irradiated owing to their marked predisposition for devel- oping multiple and recurrent skin cancers, often at a young age. Tumors that have deeply invaded cartilage or bone often do better with a combination of excision plus adjuvant radiotherapy, although definitive radiotherapy still remains an option. Radiotherapy of lesions located on the foot, anterior lower leg, or dorsum of the hand, although not contraindicated, should be avoided if possible; lesions in such sites are best treated with excision. Unfortunately, radiotherapy to poorly vascularized tissue is often associated with poor healing, thus irradi- ation of skin cancers arising in sites of chronic ulceration, trauma, or thermal burns should be avoided, if possible. In addition, patients with systemic sclerosis and other causes of cutaneous fibrosis may experience severe fibrotic reactions following radiotherapy. Radiotherapy has a very small (~1 in 1000) risk of causing a radiation-induced in-field malignancy (often soft tissue/bone sarcoma) 10–15 or more years after exposure. However, these data were obtained from studies involving many different malignancies treated by various techniques and dosing schedules. RADIOTHERAPY OF BENIGN SKIN DISORDERS Background The role of radiotherapy in treating benign cutaneous disorders has markedly diminished over the past several decades. It is no longer ethical to offer radiotherapy as a treatment for acne, warts, hirsutism, or tinea capitis. The role of radiotherapy in treating inflammatory skin conditions (e.g. dermatitis, psoriasis, lichen planus) is historical due to efficacious alternative treatments (e.g. corticosteroids, phototherapy, systemic immunomodulators), and the risk of exposing patients to ionizing radiation. Superficial radiotherapy has occasionally been used to treat recalcitrant Hailey-Hailey disease. Keloids Recurrent keloids, often refractory to re-excision and intralesional corticosteroid injections, can have significant cosmetic, functional, and psychologic sequelae for patients. The addition of low-dose (12–20 Gy) adjuvant radiotherapy delivered in three to five fractions, beginning within 24–48 hours following surgery, can markedly and safely reduce the incidence of recurrence 13 . A recent dose-response study involving 250 keloids concluded that 20 Gy delivered in 5 fractions was the optimal postoperative regimen, when balancing relapse rate (2%) against adverse effects 14 . A common site for keloids is the earlobe and patients can be treated with low-energy photons plus lead shielding of surrounding tissues. Young patients with keloids of the lower anterior neck (in close proximity to the thyroid gland) should not be irradiated. RADIOTHERAPY OF IN SITU CUTANEOUS MALIGNANCIES Squamous Cell Carcinoma In Situ (Bowen Disease) Radiotherapy can be used, albeit infrequently, to treat SCC in situ . The malignancy is limited to the epidermis and its appendages, arises more commonly in sun-exposed sites, and usually presents as a slowly growing, scaly, erythematous plaque. A biopsy is important to exclude the possibility of eczema or psoriasis. Only a small minority ( < 5%) become invasive SCCs, although this may be higher (10%–30%) in genital lesions such as erythroplasia of Queyrat. Patients are treated with 40–50 Gy in 10–20 fractions using superficial low-energy photons (110–150 kVp), with reported local five-year cure rates of 98%–100% 15 . Patients with widespread actinic keratoses have been treated with radiotherapy under special circumstances. Given that other very effective therapies are readily available (see Ch. 108 ), radiotherapy should not be considered a first-line treatment modality. Lentigo Maligna Lentigo maligna (melanoma in situ arising within photodamaged skin) often presents as a longstanding and large-sized hyperpigmented patch on the face of elderly patients (see Ch. 113 ). The size and location often preclude simple excision, and radiotherapy remains a well-established, evidenced-based option with excellent five-year cure rates of 90%–95% 16 ( Fig. 139.3 ). Reported doses range from 35 to 100 Gy administered in 5–10 fractions, i.e. large doses per fraction. However, dose fractionation schedules of 40–50 Gy in 10–20 fractions would also be efficacious 17 . Field margins of 1–1.5 cm are recommended, demarcated by Wood’s lamp examination or confocal microscopy (if available), and treating to a depth of at least 5 mm. A B maligna (melanoma in situ ). PHYSICAL TREATMENT MODALITIES RADIOTHERAPY OF INVASIVE CARCINOMAS, SARCOMAS, AND LYMPHOMAS Basal Cell Carcinoma Definitive radiotherapy BCCs – in particular primary tumors < 2 cm in diameter – can be treated with a number of therapeutic modalities. However, there is a paucity of randomized controlled trials comparing these different modalities. In a Cochrane Review focusing on BCCs, the authors analyzed the published results of seven different treatment categories 18 . Although they suggested the need for further research, surgery and radiotherapy appeared to be the two most efficacious modalities, with surgery probably leading to the lowest recurrence rates 18 . Of note, Mohs micro- graphic surgery is said to result in some of the highest long-term cure rates 19 . While local control rates (90%–95%) for either excision or radio- therapy are probably similar, management decisions are often based on other factors ( Table 139.3 ). For example, radiotherapy would be favored in an elderly patient with a BCC located on the nasal tip or nasal alae ( Fig. 139.4 ). In the locations outlined in Table 139.3 , excision followed by primary closure is often difficult to accomplish and grafts or flaps are frequently required if surgical excision is chosen ( Fig. 139.5 ). In addition, achieving negative deep margins via excision may be difficult in these locations. Although larger lesions ( > 20 mm) can still be eradi- cated via definitive radiotherapy (see below), with increasing size and depth of invasion, local control rates decrease. Therefore, surgery combined with adjuvant radiotherapy is often recommended to try to achieve better local control. Superficial BCCs that involve large areas are also treated with radio- therapy ( Fig. 139.6 ), although alternatives such as photodynamic therapy, electrodesiccation and curettage, and topical imiquimod are reasonable options. It is important to note that tumors can take many weeks to completely regress after radiotherapy and, therefore, early re-biopsy is not recommended. Squamous Cell Carcinoma Definitive radiotherapy The approach to treating patients with cutaneous SCC is influenced by the small risk ( < 5%) 22 of metastatic spread to regional lymph nodes and the need to achieve local control. Of note, some patients can be considered as having high-risk SCC when certain unfavorable features are present; these include recurrent tumor, diameter > 2 cm, thickness > 2 mm, invasion beyond fat, high-grade (i.e. poorly differentiated) histology, perineural invasion, ear or non-hair-bearing lip as the primary site, and immunosuppressed host. These SCCs have a greater risk of developing recurrence and metastatic nodal disease 23 . In general, high-risk patients should have lesions excised with wider margins and be followed closely for at least 5 years 24 . However, depending upon the circumstances, some patients are treated with definitive (or adjuvant) radiotherapy. Definitive radiotherapy of cutaneous SCC is an excellent treatment option, especially in the clinical settings outlined in patients from having extensive surgery. In addition, for sites such as the lower lip, radiotherapy can result in excellent maintenance of function (even with more extensive tumors; Fig. 139.7 ), as well as cure rates comparable to surgery (see section on lip SCC) 25 . To date, there is no consensus as to which high-risk patients should be offered elective treatment (e.g. surgical, radiotherapy) of regional lymph nodes. Future sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) studies may help resolve this issue. The currently recommended margins for the surgical excision of SCC are 4–6 mm, with wider margins for high-risk tumors 27 . For the latter, Mohs micrographic surgery or wide local excision under general anesthesia may be utilized. In a study of cutaneous SCCs, 95% of tumors < 2 cm in diameter had negative margins if excised with a 4 mm margin as did 95% of tumors > 2 cm when excised with a 6 mm margin 28 . It is generally not appropriate to merely observe an incompletely excised SCC. Recurrent SCCs are associated with a lower control rate and a higher incidence of regional metastases, when compared to previously untreated SCCs 29 . Adjuvant (postoperative) radiotherapy Adjuvant radiotherapy is an option when excision of an SCC is incom- plete and re-excision is not advisable. In addition, it is considered when there are high-risk features such as perineural invasion, an immuno- compromised host, and an anatomic site that has a high risk of recur- rence. Special clinical situations are outlined below. Keratoacanthomas A keratoacanthoma (KA) typically presents as a rapidly enlarging papulonodule with a central keratin plug. Difficulty often arises in distinguishing these tumors histologically from well-differentiated SCCs, and many authorities consider most KAs to be a well-differ- entiated variant of SCC. Although KAs can regress spontaneously, a significant number become large and unsightly with destruction of underlying tissue. If surgery is not considered, radiotherapy consisting of 25 Gy in 5 fractions can lead to durable regression. If the diagnosis of KA versus well-differentiated SCC is uncertain, a dose fractionation schedule appropriate for an SCC should be prescribed.
