COMPRESSION IN SCLEROTHERAPY AND VENOUS DISEASE Graduated compression has many benefits in patients with venous disease including providing symptomatic relief, hastening venous ulcer healing, and minimizing the risk of venous ulcer recurrence 13,14 . By reducing the diameter of veins, compression therapy increases flow velocity and decreases the chance of thrombus formation. Following sclerotherapy (which is essentially a controlled thrombophlebitic reaction), compression reduces the diameter of the resulting throm- bosis of the treated vein, which minimizes the inflammatory reaction, thereby decreasing the extent and incidence of post-treatment hyper- pigmentation, recanalization of the vein, and telangiectatic matting. Compression also increases the contact between the sclerosant and the endothelial lining of the vessel wall, potentiating pan-vessel obliteration. There are three main types of graduated compression: graduated elastic compression stockings or bandages, inelastic compression garments or bandages, and pneumatic compression pumps 15 . Compression bandages are not recommended, as they are difficult to apply in a graduated manner and hold their compression for only a few hours after application. Most sclerotherapy patients wear thigh-high or pantyhose stockings. In addition, most manufacturers now offer so-called “fashion hose” which approximate 18 mmHg pressure and are sheer, leading to greater patient compliance. In a multicenter study performed by Weiss et al. 17 , 20–30 mmHg graduated compression stockings were shown to increase sclerotherapeutic efficacy and diminish post-treatment hyperpigmen- tation. At least 3 days of compression were necessary to produce this positive effect and 3 weeks of daytime wear was found to be the optimal time required for maximal effect 17 . We recommend that all patients wear graduated compression stockings for 1 week (“24/7”) after the procedure. It is important for the patient to wear the stockings 24 hours a day, even while in the shower and when sleeping. If one removes the stockings in the shower, the superficial veins dilate. If one removes the stockings at night, the super- ficial system also dilates. Because stockings are worn around-the-clock for the first week, it is recommended that all patients wear thigh-high stockings, as these are more hygienic and easier to use than pantyhose, which extend up to the waist. SCLEROSING SOLUTIONS The optimal sclerosing agent is one that induces pan-endothelial destruction or removal 18 . Thrombosis alone will not obliterate vessels because intact endothelium contains tissue plasminogen activator that can dissolve thrombi, leading to recanalization. The ideal sclerosing agent should possess no systemic toxicity and produce local endothelial destruction that fully extends to the adventitia with minimal thrombus formation 19 . The resultant vascular destruction induces an inflammatory reaction which leads to fibrosis and eventual obliteration of the vessel. There are several important points to remember when choosing a particular sclerosing solution and determining the appropriate sclerosant concentration ( Table 155.4 ) 20 : 1. If the sclerosant is too weak, insufficient endothelial damage will occur, leading to thrombosis secondary to varicose vessel wall damage. However, there will be no fibrosis and recanalization of the vessel occurs. 2. Too strong a solution may lead to uncontrolled destruction of vascular endothelium as well as additional vessel wall layers, which may eventuate in hyperpigmentation, neoangiogenesis (telangiec- tatic matting), and ulceration secondary to sclerosant extravasation. Excessive inflammation can also develop, leading to painful super- ficial thrombophlebitis. 3. Choose the minimal sclerosant concentration (MSC) that will cause irreversible damage to the cellular wall of the abnormal vessel. Sclerosing agents are classified into three groups based upon the mechanism whereby they cause injury to the endothelium ( Table 155.5 ): 1. Hyperosmotic agents – the osmotic agents include hypertonic saline, hypertonic saline–dextrose, and non-chromated glycerin. Their primary mechanism of action involves endothelial cell damage via dehydration ( Fig. 155.8A ). 2. Chemical irritants – the chemical irritants include chromated glycerin (glycerin plus potassium chromate) and polyiodide iodide. It is also important to have a working knowledge of the complication profile of each sclerosing solution (see Table 155.5 ). For example, hyper- tonic saline, an osmotic sclerosant, is associated with burning and cramping on injection and an increased incidence of ulcerative necrosis secondary to extravasation. Sodium tetradecyl sulfate and polidocanol have been associated with a low incidence of allergic reactions, ranging from urticaria to anaphy- laxis ( < 0.01%). However, with increasing usage, it is now thought that the risk of type I (i.e. immediate hypersensitivity) reactions is actually extremely low. In fact, after over 35 years of use in over 100 000 patients, the authors have never seen an allergic reaction except for one case of urticaria. Hyperpigmentation has been reported in 5%–30% of patients treated with all sclerosing solutions except glycerin, which has a < 1% incidence of pigmentation. In the authors’ experience, the incidence of hyperpigmentation is related more to the concentration of the sclerosing agent as well as patient skin type, vessel type, and other vascular fragility factors 24–26 . Creating foaming detergent solutions by mixing them with air or CO 2 (typically in a mixture of 1 ml of solution with 4 ml of air or CO 2 ) has been found to increase the potency of the sclerosing solution twofold while decreasing its adverse effect profile fourfold. Foam displaces blood and remains for an extended time in the target vessel. This makes the sclerosing solution more efficient, so that it may be utilized at lower concentrations. The use of CO 2 rather than room air allows the gas– sclerosant bubbles to break down faster, minimizing the possibility of gas embolization into the arterial circulation via a patent foramen ovale. Of note, the detergent moiety in the foam is broken down within seconds and/or within centimeters of its injection. As a result, the foam bubbles that reach the heart are purely air with no toxicity, similar to the release of air bubbles after a SCUBA dive. TECHNIQUES FOR TREATING TELANGIECTASIAS AND RETICULAR VEINS The treatment of telangiectasias and reticular veins is most commonly performed for cosmetic improvement, but up to 50% of these patients also report a variety of symptoms from dull aching legs to throbbing pain over the telangiectasia 27,28 . Telangiectasias are best defined as nearly flat, red to blue vessels 0.1–1 mm in diameter ( Table 155.6 ). Venulectasias are blue- to violet-colored vessels, sometimes distended above the skin surface and most often 1–2 mm in diameter. Reticular veins have a cyanotic blue to blue–green hue and are visually 2–4 mm in diameter. When a complex of reticular veins is located on the lateral thigh, it is felt to be a vestige of embryonal development known as the lateral subdermal plexus 29,30 . The treatment of telangiectasias and reticular veins is undertaken only after all sources of reflux have been addressed, as it is important to treat proximal sites of reflux first and to treat larger vessels before smaller veins. Alone or in combination with laser or intense pulsed light technology, sclerotherapy of small-diameter vessels is the most common challenge faced by the dermatologic surgeon who performs sclerotherapy. Direct puncture without aspiration. This technique relies on the feeling associated with perforating the vein wall. Although it is slightly more precarious for beginners, this technique can be mastered with time. 3. Air bolus variant ( Fig. 155.9A ). Injection of < 0.5 ml of air prior to introduction of the sclerosant will displace blood in the vein. Once intravascular access is confirmed, the sclerosant can be safely injected. Air inadvertently introduced into the tissues is not as damaging as the sclerosant might be. Too strong of a push may lead to truncal distention and rupture. The persistence of varicose veins after treatment is usually due to recanalization of the intramural thrombus that develops, and the empty vein technique may reduce the amount of thrombus. Other advantages of this technique are that an empty vein has minimal volume and therefore the endothelium is exposed to a concentration of sclerosant similar to that injected. Also, a smaller volume of sclerosant is necessary to ensure contact with the endothelial surface and lower concentrations of sclerosant may be employed since there is less blood in the vein to dilute the solution 36 . Foamed sclerosing agents, discussed later, displace blood from veins, thereby automatically resulting in the empty vein technique and enhanced efficacy. Injection Technique Injection is performed utilizing one or more of the previously described techniques. The needle may be bent at an angle of 30°. Hand traction is used by either the dermatologic surgeon or an assistant to keep the skin taut ( Fig. 155.9B ). Large vessels are injected before smaller vessels, i.e. injection of the reticular veins feeding smaller telangiectasias or venules may eradicate the latter, minimizing side effects such as hyperpigmentation. Areas of vascular arborization ( Fig. 155.10 ) should be treated before single discrete linear vessels are cannulated 37 . The utilization of alcohol in swabbing the skin prior to injection will decrease the index of refraction of light and thus make the vessels more visible at the skin surface. In addition, cross-polarized light can be used to enhance vessel visualization by eliminating reflection of light from the skin surface. The resulting microfoam produces endothelial destruction with a very low polidocanol concentration of 1% in a 1 : 7 ratio of liquid : gas phases. The cohesive microfoam fills the vein lumen leading to circumferential contact and displacement of blood resulting in more efficient vein sclerosis. POSTSCLEROTHERAPY COMPRESSION Cotton-roll pads or foam pads may be applied along the entire course of the treated vessels and held in place by a compression garment. Graduated compression stockings that are class I (20–30 mmHg) or preferably class II (30–40 mmHg) are suggested for all patients following sclerotherapy of telangiectasias and reticular veins 17 . Patients should be instructed to walk for 30 minutes after each treatment session in order to minimize thromboembolic events as well as to decrease the diameter of the superficial veins. The optimal duration of compression was shown in a more recent study to be a minimum of 3 weeks of daytime wear, although 3 days of daytime compression led to better results than did no compression 17 . After large-vein sclerotherapy, we recommend 7 days of uninterrupted compression (24/7), during which the patient may bathe or shower by either placing a large plastic bag over the compression bandage or stocking or just allowing the stocking to get wet and then drying it with a hairdryer. After the first 7 days, the compression pads or cotton rolls are discarded and patients are permitted to remove the stocking, as needed, for bathing and sleeping. Ambulation is begun immedi- ately post-treatment. COMPLICATIONS There are three major considerations when anticipating and managing complications of sclerotherapy ( Table 155.7 ). The first is that fastidious technique will minimize the incidence of side effects. Second is an appropriate understanding of maneuvers that may be instituted if something is thought to have gone wrong. Finally, an appreciation of the management options available for adverse sequelae can minimize the intensity of complications when they occur 47 . Ulceration Cutaneous necrosis may occur with any sclerosing agent (although the authors have never seen this with glycerin). It may be the result of extravasation of a sclerosing agent into the perivascular tissues, which is especially common with the use of hypertonic saline, non-foamed sodium tetradecyl sulfate, or polidocanol that is > 1% in concentration; injection into a dermal arteriole or an arteriovenous anastomosis; reactive vasospasm of such a vessel; or excessive cutaneous pressure created by compression techniques 57 . If there is extravasation of hypertonic saline into the perivascular tissue, infiltration of the area with normal saline may dilute the sclerosant. A hemorrhagic bulla may form at the site within 12–24 hours and later progress to an ulcer. If a porcelain-white area appears within the skin immediately after injection, this indicates arteriole injection or spasm. To reduce the likelihood of ulceration, the physician may rub a small amount of 2% nitroglycerin ointment into the area until a reactive hyperemia is seen. Since most ulcerations are less than 4 mm in diameter, second intention healing usually results in an acceptable scar. Larger ulcerations may be excised (as early as possible) and closed for faster healing and a smaller scar. Application of topical silicone gel (e.g. Stratacel ® [Stratpharma]) may reduce the pain associated with the ulcer and speed the rate of healing 58 . Systemic Allergic Reaction True allergic reactions following sclerotherapy treatments are extremely rare. Delayed hypersensitivity reactions, which may be urticarial or morbilliform in nature, can occur from 8 to 16 hours after treatment. Type I immediate reactions, varying from urticaria to bronchospasm to anaphylaxis eventuating in cardiovascular collapse, have been rarely reported. Intrinsically, only hypertonic saline has no potential to act as an allergen. However, the presence of additives such as benzoate or lidocaine may lead to the development of hypersensitivity reactions. Arterial Injection The most feared complication in sclerotherapy is inadvertent injection into an artery. Arterial injection of a sclerosing agent produces a sludge embolus that obstructs small arteries as well as the microcirculation. The most common location for an arterial injection to occur is the popliteal fossa, when attempting to inject the SSV. After an intra-arterial injection, the patient usually notes immediate pain, but not always. COSMETIC SURGERY A dusky cyanotic hue and pallor in the distribution of the injected artery usually occurs within a few minutes to several hours. Arterial pulsations of the posterior tibial or dorsalis pedis arteries are usually not affected. Sloughing of superficial tissues may result in significant scarring or may even require amputation 60 . Arterial injection is a true sclerotherapy emergency. Immediate intervention has been advocated but has never been proven to affect outcome. Procaine (1%), administered via periarterial infiltration, forms a complex with sodium tetradecyl sulfate, rendering it inactive; however, procaine is not effective for polidocanol. Cooling of the limb to minimize tissue anoxia, followed by immediate heparinization for 7–10 days and administration of intravenous dextran (10%, 500 mg daily) for 3 days is recommended. Thrombolysis and the utilization of long-term vasodi- lator therapy (e.g. calcium channel blockers) should be considered. Nerve damage may occur secondary to direct injection of sclerosant or as a result of perivascular inflammation around nerve sheaths. The saphenous and sural veins of the inner leg and foot are high-risk sites and special care should be taken when injecting these locations. Superficial thrombophlebitis develops 1–3 weeks after injection, presenting as a tender erythematous induration of the injected vein. This complication is observed less often if compression is maintained for an adequate period of time following sclerotherapy. When superficial thrombophlebitis occurs, the thrombus should be evacuated and adequate compression, frequent ambulation, and aspirin or an NSAID instituted. The concomitant presence of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) must be considered 47 , and a search for underlying causes for thrombophlebitis other than the sclerotherapy, such as an internal malignancy, may be warranted. AMBULATORY PHLEBECTOMY Ambulatory phlebectomy is an in-office surgical procedure designed for the complete removal of diseased venous segments by means of hook avulsion of the targeted vessel. It was developed in the 1950s by the Swiss dermatologist Robert Mueller 62 . All superficial veins, except for the groin termination of the GSV, may be easily avulsed utilizing this technique. Large veins – in particular, well-demarcated branches of the GSV, SSV or perforators – can be avulsed through microstab incisions 62,63 . Because of potential shift of the vein up to 1 to 2 cm when moving from an upright vertical to a transverse horizontal position, the patient is then asked to lie in the operative position and confirmation of venous position by transepidermal illumination (Veinlite ® [TransLite LLC] or Venoscope ® II [Venoscope LLC]) with separate marking over the veins is performed. This double-marking technique has been found to be helpful in determining positional shift 65,66 ( Fig. 155.14 ). Anesthesia and Intraoperative Materials for Ambulatory Phlebectomy Tumescent anesthesia has several advantages when performing ambulatory phlebectomy. These include: (1) rapid anesthesia of an extensive segment of diseased vein; (2) compression of the vein, allowing it to be removed through a 2–3 mm incision; and (3) easier location of the vein owing to the temporary swelling and firmness of the soft tissues which press the vein against the skin. In addition, tumescent anesthesia reduces blood loss, diminishes bruising, eliminates multiple needle sticks, and produces greater postoperative comfort. Most commonly, tumescent anesthesia comprised of 0.05% lidocaine with 1 : 1 000 00 epinephrine is employed (see Table 156.3 ) 67,68 . Instrumentation for ambulatory phlebectomy should include several varied hook devices, which come in small, medium, and large diameters (sizes 2 to 4) from various manufacturers. The ideal hook should have a comfortable grip to prevent fatigue and a sharp harpoon to catch the adventitia of the vein 62,69 ( Fig. 155.15 ). Ambulatory Phlebectomy Technique Microincisions measuring from 1 to 3 mm in length and parallel to the long axis of the extremity are made with an 18- or 16-gauge hypodermic needle or a #11 blade. The microincisions are made vertically and should follow the relaxed skin tension lines. The interval between incisions varies between 3 and 5 cm according to the type of vein being removed. The vein is then exteriorized utilizing the phlebectomy hook. A gentle rotation or rolling motion of the clamp in the same and/or opposite direction pulls and frees the vein from its secondary connective tissue sheath. The process is repeated at 3–5 cm intervals along the entire length of the marked vein, until the entire diseased vein has been removed or adequate interruption has been made 70,71 . Ambitious “hooking” in the ankle and foot region should be avoided in order to eliminate complications such as swelling, hematoma, and lymphatic and nerve damage. Phlebectomy in the pretibial area should also be performed very carefully because many lymphatic vessels are normally located in this area. Phlebectomy in the popliteal area should be particularly gentle since the skin of the back of the knee is very soft and microincisions are very easily enlarged by overzealous “hooking”. Postoperative Considerations for Ambulatory Phlebectomy Postoperatively, the area is cleansed and antibiotic ointment applied to the puncture sites. The leg is then wrapped, first with cotton gauze and then with an elastic compression dressing extending from the dorsum of the foot to the groin. This dressing helps to promote hemostasis, reduces swelling of the foot and leg, and speeds wound healing. The bandage is removed in 24 hours and a class II (30–40 mmHg) graduated compression stocking is then worn continuously for 1 week (24/7) and after that during waking hours for 2–4 weeks. Walking while the patient is still in the office is encouraged to help mold the pressure wrap and to uncover any persistent bleeding. This allows the patient to quickly return to a normal gait, thus generating normal function of the calf muscle pump and minimizing potential thromboembolic complications. Complications of Ambulatory Phlebectomy Ambulatory phlebectomy satisfactorily removes varicosities of different sizes and results in a series of micro-scars that are cosmetically pleasing to the patient and dermatologic surgeon. The entire procedure can be performed under local tumescent anesthesia on an ambulatory basis 72,73 . Complications may be divided according to the system that has been affected ( Table 155.9 ). The most common complication is the development of a lymphocele, which presents as a firm subcutaneous nodule. Simple aspiration of yellow–clear lymphatic fluid with a 22-gauge needle should be performed every week, with immediate compression over the drained area. Resolution typically occurs after two to three drainage sessions. TARGETING THE SAPHENOFEMORAL JUNCTION (SFJ) Whereas saphenofemoral ligation and stripping was previously the only reliable method to address SFJ incompetence, this surgical procedure has gradually been replaced due to the development of a variety of minimally invasive procedures. Foremost amongst these are endovenous laser ablation and endovenous radiofrequency ablation; when compared to conventional surgery, they are equally or more efficacious with lower complication profiles 74 . Additional techniques, e.g. endovenous steam ablation, catheter-directed or ultrasound-guided foam sclerotherapy, mechanochemical endovenous ablation, are also available as are new products, e.g. polidocanol 1% foam (Varithena ® ), cyanoacrylate adhesive (VenaSeal™ [Medtronic]). Endovenous Laser Ablation (EVLA) In endovenous laser ablation (EVLA), the mechanism of action varies depending upon the wavelength of the laser ( Table 155.10 ). Those wavelengths that primarily target tissue water (e.g. 1320 nm Nd:YAG laser) have proven to be superior to those that primarily target hemoglobin (810–1064 nm) 75,76 . Endovenous Radiofrequency Closure (Ablation) An endovenous catheter-based approach is employed in which a specially designed, insulated electrode that is 7 cm in length delivers radiofrequency (RF) energy-induced heat directly to the vein wall (ClosureFast™ catheter [Medtronic]; Fig. 155.18 ). The endovenous electrode is held in place while energy heats it to a temperature of 120°C. The elevated temperature remains localized to a narrow rim around the active electrode. Proper use of the RF device does require close, stable contact between the active electrode and the vessel wall and the procedure requires tumescent anesthesia to allow contact of the vein wall with the central 7 cm metal core. By strictly controlling the temperature, boiling, vaporization and carbonization of the tissue are avoided. Twenty years of clinical experience suggest that RF endovenous closure, like EVLA, is highly effective at occluding saphenous veins and abolishing reflux. Of note, it is associated with a rapid reduction in lower extremity pain, fatigue, aching, and CEAP clinical class. General anesthesia is the most significant risk factor for developing DVT and the failure to use tumescent local anesthesia is the major risk factor for developing skin burns. In our clinical practices, tumescent anesthesia is always employed and no skin injuries or thrombi have been observed to date. Combination with Ambulatory Phlebectomy Based upon our experience in over 2000 patients, the combination of endovenous ablation techniques with ambulatory phlebectomy can be very effective in eliminating saphenous reflux along with varicose tribu- taries. Indeed, the two procedures may even provide a synergistic effect as single isolated phlebectomies have shown benefit in reducing GSV incompetence 77 . As outlined above, following double-marking of the varicose veins, the area surrounding the GSV and distal tributaries that are to be treated is infiltrated with tumescent anesthesia. Usually 20 cm inferior to the SFJ (mid medial thigh), the GSV can be accessed through a 2–3 mm incision. The GSV is then treated with the endovenous ablation technique (RF or laser) and the varicose tributaries are removed via standard ambulatory phlebectomy technique. A ligature is placed on the exposed portion of the GSV. At the conclusion of surgery, the entire leg is wrapped in a short stretch compression bandage over copious padding that has been placed on the sites where the varicose veins were removed via phlebectomy. The tiny incisions are not sutured as these open 2–3 mm incisions allow for drainage of the anesthetic solution over the next 24 hours. This helps to minimize swelling and bruising. The patient is seen the next day, the compression bandage is removed, and the leg is examined Phlebology and Treatment of Leg Veins for hematoma formation or other adverse sequelae. All other adverse effects are extremely rare. For a complete discussion, see reference 78 . Comparative Clinical Trials Multiple randomized clinical trials have now established the equivalent efficacy of endovenous laser ablation and endovenous RF closure when each is compared to conventional surgery 28,74,79 . The cost effectiveness of these two minimally invasive procedures also appears to be compa- rable to surgery 80 with superior complication profiles 81 . As a result, endovenous laser and RF ablation have increasingly become first-line therapies 82,83 . Other Endovenous Procedures for the Treatment of Saphenofemoral Junction Incompetence Ultrasound-guided foam sclerotherapy (UGFS) is a technique whereby the GSV is sclerosed with a foaming agent such as sodium tetradecyl sulfate or polidocanol utilizing ultrasonography for guidance. This procedure can be effective at abolishing SFJ incompetence and improving clinical outcome in patients with venous disease 84–86 . When compared to conventional surgery, UGFS has been equally efficacious in amelio- rating reflux, but multiple treatment sessions may be required 74,85 . Endovenous thermal ablation with steam is a more recently introduced technique that has been utilized to achieve both radiologic and clinical improvement of SFJ incompetence 87 . Initial reports have suggested that it is not inferior to EVLA 88 . Several novel techniques have been developed for closure of the GSV that do not require tumescent anesthesia. Injection of polidocanol endovenous microfoam 1% (Varithena ® ; see above section for details) has led to improvement in both clinical symptomatology due to SFJ incompetence as well as aesthetic appearance 89 . Similarly, a proprietary cyanoacrylate adhesive (VenaSeal™) has been developed for permanent closure of incompetent superficial

CONCLUSIONS Sclerotherapy, ambulatory phlebectomy, and endovenous vein ablation techniques are excellent treatments for both cosmetic and symptomatic venous disease 91 . Although they all require some additional training and knowledge of superficial venous anatomy and physiology, remarkable medical and cosmetic improvements in the sensation and appearance of legs can be achieved. Thus, the dermatologic surgeon now can treat all forms of varicose and telangiectatic leg veins from the largest to the smallest. Coleman III Body Contouring: Liposuction and Non-invasive Modalities 156 SECTION 22 COSMETIC SURGERY CONSULTATION As with any other medical or surgical consultation, a pertinent review of past medical history, medications, and allergies is essential. The review of systems should be comprehensive enough to exclude any underlying abnormalities which would preclude or modify treatments 4 . Social and psychiatric histories may reveal details which would make the patient an inappropriate candidate for cosmetic treatments. The physical examination for body contouring should be performed with the patient completely unclothed in the body areas of concern to them. The patient should be examined standing up so that the full effects of gravity are apparent. Physical examination consists of both observation and palpation to reveal the thickness and firmness of underlying fatty tissue. The physician should look for asymmetries, scars, hernias, musculoskeletal abnormalities, dimples, skin laxity, and overlying cutaneous lesions. During this examination, it is important to point out any of these features that may affect results. This will add to the patient’s understanding about what may or may not be able to be achieved through body contouring procedures. It is important to accurately describe individual body parts in words that the patient will understand. A diagram of typical anatomic sites may prove helpful (see Fig. 156.6 ). Also, it is important to remember that patients have a different vantage point; photography and/or full-length mirrors may be helpful during the consultation to ensure their understanding. A frank discussion about the patient’s goals should also be had; many patients have unrealistic expectations with regard to body contouring procedures. Patients should also appreciate the pros and cons of the currently available options for body contouring. Patients undergoing non-invasive treatments must understand that results are inferior to tumescent liposuction and that multiple treatments will likely be required. Patients undergoing liposuction procedures must recognize the surgical risks as well as the need for external compression garments. The presence of obesity and/or poor muscle tone are warning signs that the patient may not be an appropriate candidate. Generally, obese patients do not make good candidates for body contouring procedures. These patients may have underlying disorders that place them at higher procedural risk; also, due to their excess weight, these procedures will often create minimal, if any, improvement. Occasionally, patients, mostly male, present with a large amount of visceral fat. Palpation of the abdominal

Generally, obese patients do not make good candidates for body contouring procedures. These patients may have underlying disorders that place them at higher procedural risk; also, due to their excess weight, these procedures will often create minimal, if any, improvement. Occasionally, patients, mostly male, present with a large amount of visceral fat. Palpation of the abdominal tissues reveals a firm underlying musculature with very little fat on the pinch test. These patients are not only poor candidates for body contouring procedures but are also at increased risk for cardiovascular disease. It is important to recommend consultation with a primary care physician and appropriate nutritional experts. LIPOSUCTION Indications and Contraindications Tumescent liposuction is indicated for improving localized adiposities. Certain areas of subcutaneous fat are often not fully responsive to diet and exercise alone, and there are no exercises capable of spot reduction of adiposity. Most liposuction patients complain that the troublesome areas of fat excess “run in the family”. Furthermore, areas of excess subcuta- neous fat can be resistant to caloric restriction or exercise. Tumescent liposuction is able to specifically target these localized areas of excess subcutaneous fat as a complement to, not a replacement for, diet and exercise. INTRODUCTION AND BACKGROUND Liposuction is an effective method for surgically improving localized areas of excess subcutaneous fat. Liposuction has undergone many changes since initial reports in the late 1970s 1–3 . Modern liposuction is performed using dilute local anesthesia, via the tumescent technique, together with small cannulas connected to a vacuum aspirator. When performed correctly using the tumescent techniques, liposuction can be safely performed in an office setting with very few complications. Substantial amounts of fat can be aspirated with minimal blood loss and excellent aesthetic results. Patient selection remains paramount in achieving good results. Liposuction is currently among the most common invasive cosmetic procedures performed in the US. However, recent survey data have shown a decrease in the number of liposuctions being performed. This is likely due to the increased availability of non-invasive technologies that are currently approved by the FDA for the treatment of localized adiposity. These technologies generally have fewer side effects than tumescent liposuction but deliver more modest results. When choosing between liposuction and non-invasive treatments, it is important that patients have realistic expectations.

text: Non-invasive Modalities In general, operating on over 10% of the body increases liposuction risks. Guidelines of care published by dermatologic organizations recommend fat extractions of less than 4500–5000 ml 5,6 . This volume should be considered as an uppermost limit; beyond this, profound fluid shifts may occur, resulting in cardiovascular compromise. Many experienced liposuction surgeons rarely, if ever, remove anywhere near 5000 ml in a single session. Larger extractions also necessitate larger infiltrations of local anesthetics. When the tumescent technique is employed, guidelines of care recommend not exceeding a lidocaine dose of 55 mg/kg 7–10 . In slender patients, this should probably be adjusted down to 45 mg/kg. These dose limits also restrict the number of areas that can be treated during a single liposuction procedure. If, in the physician’s judgment, it is risky to treat all of the areas that concern the patient, serial liposuction should be recommended. These separate surgeries can be spaced days or months apart, according to the patient’s preference. Non-cosmetic indications for liposuction include pseudogyneco- mastia and aspiration of lipomas 11–13 ( Table 156.1 ). Liposuction can be effective for debulking larger tumors with a minimal scar. It can also be used as an alternative for treating axillary hyperhidrosis by destroying eccrine and apocrine glands ( Fig. 156.7 ) 13 . Contraindications are outlined in Table 156.2 . The Preoperative Visit A carefully planned preoperative visit is usually scheduled two or more weeks prior to the actual date of the surgery. Generally, a complete blood count and a complete metabolic profile are obtained; a prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time may be indicated based on history. Some physicians also perform a urinalysis and tests for infec- tious diseases such as viral hepatitis and HIV. Detailed pre- and postoperative instructions should be provided to the patient during this visit. Description of Techniques Tumescent anesthesia The technique of using tumescent local anesthesia for liposuction was developed by the dermatologist Dr Jeffrey Klein. In 1987, Klein published his technique for the infiltration of a dilute solution of lidocaine with epinephrine (adrenaline) into fat, allowing for liposuction to be performed under local anesthesia 7 . Due to significantly reduced bleeding, the previous common complications of seroma and hematoma became uncommon 14 . Bruising was also minimized. The procedure has proven to be remarkably safe. Klein demonstrated that dilute concentrations of lidocaine with epinephrine are not absorbed into the circulation to the same degree as higher 1%–2% concentrations of lidocaine, even when the total doses are equal. He confirmed that using only dilute solutions of lidocaine with epinephrine safely allowed lidocaine dosages of up to 35 mg/kg body weight 8 . This advance allowed larger amounts of fat to be removed with only local anesthesia. A typical tumescent anesthetic formulation is shown in Table 156.3 . Dilute solutions of lidocaine with epinephrine provide safe local anesthesia with excellent vasoconstriction. Sodium bicarbonate is added to adjust the solution to a more physiologic pH. The combi- nation of a dilute solution of lidocaine with the vasoconstrictive effect of epinephrine ensures minimal systemic absorption of lidocaine 15 . The tumescent technique provides a number of advantages ( Table 156.4 ). Local anesthesia persists for up to 24 hours after tumescent liposuction, reducing the need for postoperative analgesia 16 . The extensive vasoconstriction produced by dilute epinephrine reduces the volume of whole blood for each liter of pure fat removed by liposuction to less than 12 ml 14,16 . With rapid postoperative recovery, patients can return to their normal lives quickly. Improved aesthetic results are also seen with tumescent liposuction because smaller cannulas can be used, reducing irregularities of the skin 17 . Surgeons performing tumescent anesthesia should understand the symptoms of lidocaine toxicity and potential treatments (see Ch. 143 ). Prilocaine has been used in Europe for tumescent anesthesia instead of lidocaine 25 . LIPOSUCTION INSTRUMENTATION The basic instruments required for liposuction are suction cannulas, tubing, and an aspirator 26 . Liposuction can be performed using many different types of cannulas and aspirators. The number of holes arranged along the shaft of the cannula is probably unimportant, although two or more holes increase the flow of fat through the instrument. The most important parameter for choosing cannulas is size: the smallest possible cannula should be employed. Smaller-diameter cannulas ( ≤ 3 mm) create smaller tunnels through the fat and achieve smoother results ( Fig. 156.9 ). In addition, smaller-diameter cannulas penetrate the fat more easily and create less tissue trauma. Longer cannulas allow the surgeon to work from fewer skin insertion sites, leaving fewer scars, while shorter cannulas are easier to control as they pass through subcutaneous tissue. The tiny incisions required for insertion of 3 mm cannulas leave nearly invisible scars in most patients, but can be an issue if the patient has a tendency towards keloid formation or hyperpigmentation. Liposuction is based on the technique of criss-crossing tunnels (from multiple insertion sites) through the subcutaneous tissue. Each area to be suctioned should be tunneled from at least two different direc- tions, but often three or four are more effective. Multiple small tunnels ultimately provide the smoothest contraction of the overlying skin and the most thorough removal of fat. Subsequent contraction of the fatty layer occurs much like a wet sponge contracting into a dry one ( Fig. 156.10 ). The liposuction aspirate should be yellow or slightly blood-tinged ( Fig. 156.11 ). Cosmetic surgery Ultrasonic probes pass through the tissue like a “hot knife through butter” and do not provide the usual tactile feedback from tissue resis- tance that manual cannulas do. This makes it difficult for the surgeon to determine in exactly what level of the fat the cannula is located and increases the possibility of intra-abdominal perforation or “end hits” to the opposing dermis. These devices should only be used by experienced surgeons and may be advantageous for skin tightening or if there is excessive fibrous tissue, e.g. gynecomastia. Power-assisted These instruments feature a motorized cannula, which moves in a back and forth or swirling motion ( Fig. 156.12 ). The short, motorized strokes vary according to the instrument and allow the surgeon to precisely sculpt small areas of excess fat. Powered liposuction instru- ments also allow easier penetration of fat, when compared to manual cannulas, but retain some feel of tissue resistance 29 . Studies have shown that powered liposuction increases the fat aspirated (per minute) by 30% or more 29 . There have been no significant compli- cations reported with the use of this approach, although some early users described an increase in seromas. Powered instruments create a larger tunnel than a manual instrument of the same diameter; this should be taken into account when choosing the appropriate size cannula. Laser-assisted Laser-assisted devices are designed to transmit infrared laser energy, via a fiber, subcutaneously during liposuction in order to generate heat. Early iterations of these devices had very low power and showed very little difference compared to manual liposuction 30 . Diode and Nd:YAG laser liposuction devices are available from several manufacturers in a variety of wavelengths. Newer devices have higher power and longer wavelengths that are more selective for fat, potentially increasing their efficacy. Benefits include emulsification of fat to make aspiration easier, decreased blood loss 31 , and potential for increased skin tightening. The laser fibers can cause burns if used incorrectly, although

Laser liposuction does take more time to perform and increases costs. Skin tightening seems to be the main purported advantage to these devices. Although this has been difficult to quantify, studies using subcutaneous laser alone have shown significant improvement in skin laxity 32 . However, manual liposuction alone also produces significant tightening and external energy-based tightening devices may provide the same effect. Radiofrequency-assisted Several newer devices have employed subcutaneous radiofrequency technology in order to try to increase skin tightening. Some of these devices use monopolar radiofrequency while others use bipolar technology. The purported advantage over laser- and ultrasound-assisted liposuction is better control of the heat produced. Radiofrequency- assisted liposuction has been shown to be safe, but when compared to manual liposuction, enhanced skin contraction is still unproven and a direct comparison trial will be difficult. However, several studies have shown that there is potential for this technology to aid in skin contraction 33 . Water-assisted These devices employ powerful streams of water directed into the fat layer to create tunnels to facilitate fat removal. Proponents of this approach claim that this reduces the volume of tumescent fluid required. This makes very little sense since the anesthetic effect of the fluid takes several minutes to take effect, long after the tunnel has already been bored by the water jet. There may be potential benefits with this technology when performing fat transplantation as the fat cells may be better preserved than through physical avulsion, but this remains speculative. In patients with more laxity or fibrous tissue, there may be some advantage. LIPOSUCTION VARIATIONS Guidelines of care published by dermatologic organizations recommend that liposuction be performed as a solo procedure and not combined with other techniques 5,6 . However, there are cases in which liposuction is employed as a fundamental part of a combined surgical procedure. For instance, in rhytidectomy, liposuction of the neck and pre-tunneling of the cheeks are often performed prior to flap dissection and advancement. In patients in whom the neck alone is to be treated, liposuction may be combined with submental resection and platysmal plication, with each surgical component contributing to the final result. External light-based and radiofrequency devices may also be combined with neck liposuction to improve skin contraction. In other anatomic sites, skin excision may be combined with liposuction. Where there is a significant abdominal panniculus, a supra- pubic incision may be used to remove excess skin in conjunction with liposuction of the rest of the abdomen. However, in most patients with a moderate panniculus, this may be unnecessary because of the signif- icant skin retraction that occurs after liposuction of the lower abdomen. The advantage of liposuction over standard excisional surgery is that the former leads to a much smaller scar. As with any adiposity, the lipoma is tunneled in a criss-cross direction until flat. Subsequent healing and fibrosis usually flattens the remaining lipoma further, resulting in a normal contour. It is difficult to suction smaller lipomas and these are best removed through direct puncture excision. However, lipomas the size of a golf ball or larger are excellent candi- dates for liposuction. Since the entire lesion is not surgically removed, lipomas treated in this fashion may be more likely to recur; the patient should be made aware of this possibility. Liposuction should be reserved for lesions that are in cosmetically sensitive areas or those of a size which would necessitate a larger incision. POSTOPERATIVE CARE Following liposuction, patients are usually quite comfortable during the initial postoperative period. It is important to remind patients, well before the procedure takes place, that they are going to have signif- icant drainage for the first day following liposuction surgery. Barrier protection is recommended for car seats, furniture, and bed linens during this period. The patient’s insertion sites may be coated with petrolatum or antibiotic ointment prior to application of absorbent materials. Modern absorbent pads are capable of absorbing significant amounts of drainage from the insertion sites thereby decreasing the need for patients to change pads. Most individuals will experience continued drainage for 24–48 hours following liposuction. Patients are advised to take their first shower with the absorbent bandages and the tape in place, as the shower assists in the removal of the tape. Following the application of sufficient amount and layers of absorbent pads, a compression garment or a compression bandage is fitted. Numerous styles of postoperative liposuction compression garments are available. Postoperative compression minimizes bruising and aids in drainage. Numerous styles of postoperative liposuction compression garments are available. Postoperative compression minimizes bruising and aids in drainage. Gravitational drainage minimizes postoperative edema. It is important to use firm compression immediately following tumescent liposuction 34 . Compression assists patients in feeling more secure and decreases pain by restricting movement of the treated tissue. Many patients actually enjoy the comfort and feel of a compression garment due to the soreness sometimes associated with movement in the immediate postoperative period. Patients with pre-existing laxity or large amounts of fat removal may benefit from a longer period of compression. Infections have occasionally been reported with liposuction and oral antibiotics may provide prophylaxis against more serious infections. Of note, lidocaine is bactericidal 35 . This may explain, in part, the relatively few infections seen with tumescent liposuction. Careful local wound care and cleanliness are essential in producing a good liposuction outcome. Most patients can return to work within 48 hours following their liposuction. It is important to ask the patients to ambulate regularly beginning the day after surgery. This movement encourages drainage as well as remodeling of the subcutaneous tissue. Movement has the additional benefit of increasing lymphatic drainage through inter- mittent pumping action of skeletal muscles. Light exercise may begin 24–48 hours after surgery, but patients should be advised to start at 25% of their normal routine. Generally, patients are back to normal exercise routines after the first postoperative week. All patients are given a set of written postoperative liposuction instructions including important phone numbers should the patient need to contact the physician. These postoperative instructions remind the patient that swelling and firmness beneath the skin and a reduced sensation in the skin are common. This will usually resolve over the first 3 to 4 weeks after the surgery. COMPLICATIONS OF LIPOSUCTION Complications of liposuction must be differentiated from common sequelae. After liposuction, it is common to have prolonged swelling, areas of numbness, bruising, and red incisions. Infections, hematomas, and seromas are rare complications that require medical attention but can usually be resolved rapidly. Serious complications of liposuction are closely linked to the type of sedation employed. There have been a number of deaths from liposuction in patients who had moderate or deep sedation 18,19,36 . The authors are not aware of any deaths from liposuction in patients who underwent the procedure with true tumescent local anesthesia 37 . Deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism postoperatively are surgical complications generally associated with non-ambulatory patients and prolonged procedures under general anesthesia. An advantage of the tumescent local anesthetic technique is that patients are ambulatory immediately after surgery, thus minimizing the risk of this potential problem. Patients who are obese and inactive are more at risk for the development of this complication; this should be taken into consideration during the preoperative evaluation. Abdominal perforation is one of the leading causes of liposuction death 38 . This is exclusively a complication of liposuction under general anesthesia 20 . Deeply sedated patients have decreased muscle tone and are unable to alert the physician to the pain of penetration of the liposuction cannula. Occult abdominal hernias may contribute to this complication. The treating physician should be aware of any abdominal scars and palpate for

General anesthesia also increases risks of respiratory failure and cardiac death 22 . Besides the direct effect of systemic anesthesia, fluid overload may contribute to these problems. Anesthesiologists who are not accustomed to working with patients who have been infiltrated with tumescent anesthetic fluids may inadvertently overhydrate the patient with additional intra- venous fluids. A significant amount of the saline infused subcutaneously is absorbed systemically, automatically correcting for surgical fluid losses. Compounding this problem is the discovery that intravenous fluid bags are typically overfilled by at least 10%, leading to further errors in calculating fluid replacement in liposuction 39 . The keys to avoiding complications in liposuction lie in proper patient selection, appropriate patient evaluation, realistic patient expectations, monitoring according to the degree of sedation, good surgical technique, avoidance of excessive fat removal or overzealous additional simulta- neous procedures, and adequate postoperative care. NON-INVASIVE BODY CONTOURING Liposuction is now a mature procedure and most patients obtain predictable results 40,41 . However, as with all cosmetic procedures, there is a general trend toward trying to accomplish similar results with less invasive techniques. Several non-invasive modalities are currently approved for the treatment of localized subcutaneous fat ( Table 156.6 ). Some of these treatments, such as injection lipolysis, have been in existence for many years, but recently have garnered more interest; other technologies, such as external ultrasonic devices, external cryo­lipolysis, external radiofrequency, and low-level light treatments, are relative newcomers to the field. Cosmetic surgery Injection Lipolysis Mesotherapy, which was originally developed in the 1950s, has re-emerged as a treatment for localized adiposities. Most commonly, this technique involves the subcutaneous injection of a formulation containing phosphatidylcholine plus a detergent solvent that leads to the dissolution of fat cells 42 . Most commonly, this technique involves the subcutaneous injection of a formulation containing phosphatidylcholine plus a detergent solvent that leads to the dissolution of fat cells 42 . More recent work has shown that the detergent solvent, usually deoxycholic acid, is more likely the active ingredient in this solution 43 . Deoxycholic acid works by causing adipocytolysis, leading to a decrease in fat volume via contraction and remodeling. In 2015, deoxycholic acid was approved by the FDA for the reduction of moderate to severe submental fullness. The injections consist of small aliquots (0.1–0.2 ml) placed ~1 cm apart from each other 44 . Treatment volume used varies depending on the amount of adiposity present. Most patients will require several treatments, at least one month apart, for best results. Of note, many physicians are length- ening the time between sessions to allow post-treatment edema to subside more completely prior to the next set of injections. Full results are not apparent until 12 weeks post-therapy ( Fig. 156.13 ). Post-treatment sequelae include edema, ecchymoses, decreased sensation, and hair loss. For most patients, edema is self-limited but in some instances, persistent edema may occur necessitating treatment with intralesional triamcinolone acetonide or anti-inflammatory medications. Post-treatment edema tends to lessen with subsequent deoxycholic acid injections. There have been several reports of off-label use of deoxycholic acid, including for jowls, pre- and post-axillary bra fat, suprapatellar fat pads, and small truncal adiposities 45,46 . The therapeutic efficacy of deoxy- cholic acid injections is limited to smaller adiposities. Its use for larger areas has not been established and would not be clinically or financially feasible. Low Level Light Therapy (LLLT) An external 635 nm diode laser (Zerona™; Erchonia) is FDA-cleared for fat reduction around the waist. Theoretically, this device reduces the size of subcutaneous fat by induction of a photochemical reaction which creates small pores in the adipocyte cell membrane 47 . However, early reports of the results of these treatments had only short follow-up times and no weight control. In addition, several studies have shown that the minimal results produced seem to abate over time, with long-term results still in question as well. High-Intensity Focused Ultrasound High-frequency ultrasound, HIFU (LipoSonix™; Innovations Medical), relies upon ultrasound-induced thermal destruction of adipocytes. This device is based on technology currently employed in the treatment of malignant tumors, in particular prostate cancer. The ultrasound has a focal depth of 1.3 cm and creates tissue temperatures up to about 70°C. The thermal destruction of adipocytes at this depth leads to tissue contraction and reduction of adiposities over an 8- to 12-week period 48 . The FDA cleared this technology for non-invasive waist circumference reduction in 2011 and reduction in waist circumference from a single treatment has been reported to be about 2–3 cm. Patients complain of discomfort during the treatments which can be moderate to severe in some. The most common sequelae from HIFU include post-procedural pain, numbness, edema, and ecchymoses. Non-thermal Focused Ultrasound Non-thermal, external ultrasound (UltraShape Power ® ; Candela™) produces targeted cavitation of fat cells without producing significant heating; this allows the device to achieve lipolysis without creating damage to blood vessels and nerves 49,50 . Disruption of the adipocytes leads to release of fatty acids. The device has been cleared by the FDA for abdominal circumference reduction. Treatments are performed every 2 weeks; generally, 3 treatments are recommended. During treatment, patients experience minimal if any discomfort. The focal depth of the ultrasound is 1.5 cm and care should be taken over bony prominences to avoid reflection of the waves. Post-procedural sequelae are rare and are likely related to technique. Blistering can result from inadequate contact with the device or treatment over a bony area. Patients may resume all activities immediately after treatments and generally have no pain, edema, or bruising. Patients are advised to avoid excessive fat consumption during the first 2 days post- procedure. Treatment results appear gradually with improvement over a 6- to 8-week period. After 3 treatments, an average reduction in waist circumference of 3–5 cm has been reported ( Fig. 156.14 ). Radiofrequency Radiofrequency devices utilize an oscillating electrical field to create heat in target tissues; lower frequencies are able to penetrate more deeply. Several radiofrequency devices are available for multiple aesthetic uses. Devices can be monopolar or unipolar (1 electrode), bipolar, or multi- polar. For fat reduction, results with radiofrequency devices have been mixed with some newer devices reportedly more successful. A selective, contactless radiofrequency device (Vanquish Me™; BTL Aesthetics) uses focused field radiofrequency to target adiposities. A prospective trial showed a 4.93 cm reduction in abdominal circum- ference after 4 weekly treatments; however, 3 patients showed no reduction at all 54 . Use of a vacuum-assisted bipolar device that utilizes software to maintain constant temperature control (Evolve ® ; Inmode) led to a 2.7 cm decrease in abdominal circumference after 6 weekly treatments 55 . Currently, this device combines non-vacuum bipolar heads with suction-assisted heads in order to treat more superficial adiposity and skin laxity. CELLULITE Cellulite is a common problem for most women with variable presen- tations. It can present as dimples, rippling of the skin, and/or super- ficial adiposities. The morphology of cellulite stems from superficial fat deposits, skin laxity, and perpendicular dermal bands which lead to dimpling. For years, treatment options have been less than satisfying in their durability and effectiveness. However, more recently introduced technologies have shown promise for providing durable improvement in the appearance of cellulite ( Table 156.7 ). External Devices There are several commercially available external treatments that attempt to improve cellulite. Most of them are minimally, if at all, effective in providing long-term improvement. text: External Devices There are several commercially available external treatments that attempt to improve cellulite. Most of them are minimally, if at all, effective in providing long-term improvement. For example, body wraps and massages can temporarily improve the appearance of cellulite, but there is no durable improvement. Most of the devices employed for the external treatment of cellulite rely on radiofrequency-induced heat to tighten skin and reduce superficial adiposity. Because these devices only address two of the three causes of cellulite – laxity and superficial adiposity – their effectiveness is limited. They require numerous treatment sessions to produce any improvement and results tend to not be durable. Rapid Acoustic Pulse™ technology, which utilizes high intensity, high frequency, ultrashort acoustic wave pulses, is said to be capable of disrupting fascial connections, rendering the dimpling less evident. However, the results may not be durable beyond the treatment period. Subdermal Devices Since cellulite is created by subdermal bands and adiposity, these devices target the subdermal plane. This approach is minimally invasive and generally performed with tumescent anesthesia. The first device that incorporated subdermal treatment of cellulite was the 1440 nm side-firing laser (Cellulaze ® ; Cynosure). Its laser fibers are designed to refract the beam into two perpen- dicular beams which allow for treatment in two directions. One beam treats skin laxity and superficial adiposity while the second helps to cut the cellulite bands. Although results have been mixed, some authors have reported very good results that were durable ( Fig. 156.17 ) 56 . Other subdermal technologies such as radiofrequency devices can be used in patients with cellulite; however, they address the laxity and superficial adiposity without cutting the dermal bands. Subcision Manual subcision of cellulite dimples has long been effective in some physicians’ hands. When performed by those experienced in this technique, durable results have been observed. Vacuum-assisted subcision Since manual subcision can be technically challenging and time- consuming, attempts have been made to enhance effectiveness and reproducibility. With a vacuum-assisted subcision device (cellfina ® ; Merz Aesthetics), the vacuum secures and elevates the tissue with the dimple, allowing for insertion of an oscillating blade into the correct tissue plane to release the dermal bands 57 . This leads to more exact targeting of the dermal bands and more rapid treatments. Results have been reported as very durable, lasting up to several years. As these vacuum-assisted devices only target dermal bands, they work best for dimpled cellulite and are not very effective in patients with laxity or rippled cellulite. Fat Transfer and Fillers For severe dimpling of cellulite, subcision of dimples alone may not be sufficient. Placement of fat or fillers can help to further smooth these lesions. Based upon their collagen stimulatory properties, fillers such as calcium hydroxylapatite and poly- l -lactic acid microspheres are also being used to treat cellulite 58 . They are injected in a dilute fashion in order to improve skin laxity. Collagenase Injectable collagenase (Qwo ® ; Endo Pharmaceuticals) is the most recent addition to the therapeutic armamentarium for cellulite, and it has shown some promise in clinical trials 59 . In order to release dimpling, the collagenase is injected into dermal bands. There is no need for anesthesia and serial injections are performed every 3 to 4 weeks per current protocols. However, the latter may undergo further revisions. Based upon early results, improvement may be durable (up to at least 2 years). CONCLUSION Technology is constantly providing physicians with new ways to minimize localized adiposities. Regardless of what instrumentation is used, it is likely that in the future liposuction will remain one of the most popular and predictable cosmetic procedures. As more non-invasive treatments become available, it is important to recognize the pros and cons of each of these devices. No matter which type of treatment is performed, the single most important aspect in choosing a therapy is patient selection. text: COSMETIC SURGERY SECTION 22 Marc R. Avram and Nicole E. Rogers Hair Restoration follicle. In mice, combining bulge cells with neonatal dermal cells can give rise to a hair follicle as well as the sebaceous gland and epidermis 1 . Within the hair follicle, stem cells give rise to secondary germ cells with each hair cycle; the latter cells represent a progenitor population that is responsible for the production of the hair shaft during anagen (but undergoes apoptosis at the end of anagen) 2 . In a study that compared bald scalp with hair-bearing scalp in men, the stem cell population was maintained in the bald scalp but there was a marked reduction in progenitor cells, suggesting that study of this second population of cells could provide further insight into male pattern hair loss 3 . In gene expression arrays, increased expression of the gene that encodes prostaglandin D2 synthetase was observed in bald scalp as compared to haired scalp in men with AGA 4 ; the latter enzyme converts prostaglandin H2 (PGH2) to PGD2. Balding scalp was also found to have increased levels of PGD2, and PGD2 was shown to inhibit hair growth in explants of human hair follicles. This inhibition of hair growth by PGD2 required interactions with one of its receptors, pointing to a potential therapeutic target. Population studies have pointed to a polygenic inheritance pattern, with both maternal and paternal genetic influences. Of the associated genes identified to date, the androgen receptor gene ( AR ), present on the long arm of the X chromosome (Xq11–12), has been identified as a major determinant of hair loss in men (AGA2) 5–7 . Within exon 1 of AR is the AR -CAG polymorphism, which refers to the number of repeat sequences of cytosine–adenine–guanine (CAG) present, with the normal range of CAG repeats being 10–40. The number of CAG repeats appears to inversely correlate with the degree of androgen sensitivity. Men with fewer CAG repeats have an increased risk of developing AGA and a higher cellular sensitivity to androgens; they also demonstrate a greater response to finasteride treatment 8 . In contrast, men with > 40 repeats appear to be protected and have androgen insensitivity 9 . Variants in AR may influence hair loss in women as well 10 . Other implicated genes include EDA2R , which encodes the ectodysplasin A2 receptor and is also found on the X chromosome (see Ch. 63 ) 12 , as well as genes located at 20p11 (AGA3) 13 and 3q26 (AGA1) 14 . As more insight is gained into the interplay of these genes, it may be possible to diagnose AGA at an early age and predict who may benefit from therapy. Of note, it is important for patients to realize that while a family history of AGA provides useful information, it does not predict the rate and extent of hair loss in a particular individual. Clinical Features The diagnosis of AGA is usually straightforward, especially in men. This is based upon the characteristic pattern, the miniaturization of hairs, and the lack of clinical inflammation or scalp symptoms (see Ch. 69 ). Occasionally, an unusual presentation requires clinicopathologic corre- lation, and if there is evidence of perifollicular erythema, the possibility of a scarring (cicatricial) alopecia needs to be excluded 15 . In women, patterned alopecia may first become clinically apparent as a result of a superimposed telogen effluvium, perhaps following a febrile illness or birth of a child. These patients require an evaluation for telogen effluvium as outlined in Table 69.4 and possible hyperandrogenemia (e.g. serum free testosterone, DHEA-S), especially in the setting of hirsutism and/ or recalcitrant acne vulgaris or any signs of virilization. The framing preserves a youthful facial appearance by shortening the face and returning the viewer’s focus to the center of the face. While hair is one of the few physical characteristics we can easily control, the inability to correct hair loss can lead to concerns regarding appearance and psychological stress. In the case of androgenetic alopecia, some individuals accept hair thinning as an unavoidable aging phenomenon, whereas others actively seek medical and/or surgical treatment options. HISTORICAL PERSPECTIVE The first hair transplantation procedure for male pattern hair loss was successfully performed in the 1950s, using large punch autografts. Alternative techniques such as hair-bearing flaps and scalp reductions were also performed in an effort to redistribute hair or reduce the size of bald scalp. However, because of unsightly large “plugs”, unnatural orientation of hair, and obvious scars revealed by continued hair loss, these techniques were largely abandoned in favor of follicular unit grafts. The latter are placed into small “recipient” sites (0.5–1 mm in diameter) produced by a blade or needle. Follicular unit grafts can be obtained either manually or mechanically. Treatment (Other Than Transplant Surgery) Medical therapies Topical minoxidil as a 5% solution is FDA-approved for men 16 whereas the 2% solution and 5% foam are approved for both women and men. In general, the therapeutic effects are modest, but it may prove beneficial as an adjunct to hair transplantation 17 . Topical minoxidil can be helpful during the postoperative period to enhance and hasten growth of trans- planted hairs. Minoxidil has multiple known mechanisms of action, but its effect on hair follicles is generally attributed to its vasodilatory or angiogenic properties and perhaps its effect on potassium channels 18 . COSMETIC SURGERY Increased proliferation of dermal papilla cells 19 , an increase in hair caliber, a decrease in the rate of apoptosis of cells in the germinative pool, and more time spent in the anagen phase have all been observed 20 . A possible explanation for the variability in therapeutic responses amongst individuals is differing levels of sulfotransferase activity (which catalyzes minoxidil sulfate) within their hair follicles. There is evidence that aspirin may inhibit this sulfotransferase activity 21 . There has been growing interest in the use of low-dose oral minoxidil for AGA in both men and women 22 . Doses vary from 0.625 to 2.5 mg once or twice daily, with lower doses in women and lower doses initially. Multiple studies have demonstrated safety and efficacy in the treatment of male and female pattern hair loss. Side effects of minoxidil include unwanted hypertrichosis of the cheeks or forehead, headache, ankle edema, and for topical prepara- tions, allergic or irritant contact dermatitis. With regard to the latter, propylene glycol in the vehicle is often the culprit and it has been removed from the 5% foam product (Rogaine ® ). Facial hypertrichosis is more commonly observed with oral minoxidil and the risk may be greater in those with a genetic propensity for dark facial hair. Fetal hypertrichosis has also been reported and so use of minoxidil is discouraged in pregnant or breastfeeding women. Lastly, reported cardiovascular side effects from oral minoxidil (uncommon with low doses) include hypotension, tachycardia, and pericarditis. Finasteride inhibits type II 5 α -reductase, which converts testosterone to DHT and is present in hair follicles (see Fig. 69.10 ). Oral finasteride (1 mg daily) is FDA-approved for men with AGA. In a randomized trial of 1553 men given either finasteride 1 mg or placebo for 1 year (with a blinded extension for a second year), significantly greater hair counts in the balding vertex were observed in those receiving finasteride 23 . Five-year results from the same study demonstrated that hair growth peaked at 1–2 years, but hair counts still remained well above baseline for 90% of patients 24 . Although finasteride was FDA-approved for stimulating the growth of vertex hairs, it also stimulates regrowth of frontal scalp hairs 25 . Its use in combination with hair transplantation has yielded statistically greater hair counts 48 weeks after surgery in comparison to the control/placebo group 26 . There is also some evidence that finasteride may work better in men with higher levels of DHT (such as those in their mid-twenties) 27 . Patients are advised to allow at least 6 months before expecting to see a therapeutic effect. If they discontinue the finasteride, the AGA will return to its pre-treatment appearance. Because finasteride is metabo- lized extensively in the liver, it should be used with caution in patients who have known liver disease 28 . Finasteride also artificially lowers the serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level by ~50% 29 . Therefore, both the primary care physician and the patient need to be made aware of this effect. Although early data from prostate cancer trials suggested that finasteride might increase the histologic grade (i.e. severity) of prostate cancer, 30 subsequent analyses suggested a detection bias 31 .

Overall, the drug is well tolerated. Side effects that occur in < 2% of men taking finasteride include decreased libido, erectile dysfunction and ejaculation disorder, compared with their occurrence in 1% of the placebo group. Rarer side effects include gynecomastia, breast tenderness, and depression 32 . In a double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicenter trial in young men, no changes in spermatogenesis or semen production were observed 33 . However, there have been two reports of severe azoospermia leading to impaired fertility 34 . While the authors feel comfortable prescribing finasteride for men who are planning to have children, it should be discontinued if there are fertility issues, before embarking upon more invasive infertility treatments. Sexual dysfunction, even after discontinu- ation of finasteride, has been reported, but with selection bias, recall bias, and lack of control for confounding factors 35 . Prolonged libido effects in conjunction with other findings such as brain fog and depression have been collectively coined “post-finasteride syndrome”; Merck has updated its packaging to reflect this possibility but the diagnosis remains controversial and poorly understood. Most recently, the FDA added suicidal ideation and behavior to the package insert despite the lack of reasonable evidence of a causal link. Patients who are reluctant to take oral finasteride may benefit from a compounded (off-label) formulation of topical finasteride 36 . We encourage surgical candidates to stabilize their hair loss by taking finasteride, or another medical therapy, for 6 to 12 months prior to hair transplantation. Most men benefit from combination therapy ( Fig. 157.4 ). Patients who report sexual dysfunction side effects should discontinue oral finasteride and, after an interval of 1–2 weeks, try every second- or third-day dosing. Dutasteride differs slightly from finasteride in that it blocks both type I and type II 5 α -reductase isoenzymes. Platelet-rich plasma Platelet rich plasma (PRP) has emerged as an appealing therapy for hair loss given its autologous nature. It was first described in conjunction with hair surgery to increase growth of transplanted follicles 47 . This technique involves obtaining 10–40 ml of the patient’s blood followed by centrifugation in order to achieve a platelet-rich concentration that is 4–7 × baseline. Activated platelets have been shown to release platelet-derived growth factor, epidermal growth factor, transforming growth factor, and vascular endothelial growth factor 48 . The PRP is then injected into areas of alopecia, either alone or in combination with adjuvants such as calcium chloride or calcium gluconate. Numerous proprietary PRP “kits” have been developed for dental, orthopedic, and now dermatologic applications. HAIR TRANSPLANTATION Hair transplantation is a procedure performed in an outpatient setting under local anesthesia. It is based on the theory of donor dominance, i.e. terminal hair from the unaffected posterior scalp will continue its growth pattern even when transplanted to the balding frontal scalp 54 . Unfortunately, until the 1990s, hair transplants often had an unnatural appearance due to unsightly and obvious “plugs”, sometimes likened to a “Barbie-doll” appearance. Over the past two decades, there has been a revolutionary movement away from 3–4 mm grafts containing 15–30 hair follicles to grafts containing groupings of one to four hair follicles, referred to as individual follicular units ( Fig. 157.5 ). This has resulted in the trans- planted hair having a more natural appearance ( Figs. 157.6 & 157.7 ). Candidate Selection As with all surgical procedures, the preoperative consultation is key to the success of the procedure. The consultation establishes whether the patient is an appropriate candidate for hair transplantation, both from a medical and a psychological perspective. In addition, it allows for an assessment of areas of greatest concern and whether the patient has realistic expectations of what a hair transplant can achieve. A complete medical, surgical, and hair loss history is obtained, including previous hair transplants and scalp surgeries as well as scar formation. The etiology of the hair loss is determined, primarily via physical examination of the scalp. Occasionally, additional sites need to be examined and/or clinicopathologic correlation is required. The stage of patterned hair loss also needs to be established (see Figs. 157.2 & 157.3 ). All medications, prescription, over-the-counter and herbal, are reviewed with regard to their effects on hair growth and hemostasis (see Chs. 21 & 133 ). The basic criteria for assessing the appropriateness of a candidate for hair transplantation are outlined in Table 157.1 . In particular, the density of donor hair in the occipital scalp and the caliber of the hair need to be appraised, as both have an impact on the perceived density of the transplant ( Table 157.2 ). Obviously, greater donor density and more grafts to transplant as well as thicker hairs rather than fine hairs lead to a fuller-appearing transplant. Key Concepts Both men and women should be made aware that AGA represents an ongoing process, i.e. it will progress despite undergoing hair transplan- tation. Medications (e.g. oral finasteride, minoxidil) or PRP and LLLT can help to maximize hair density from a transplant by minimizing ongoing hair loss. However, in planning for the transplant procedure, the surgeon should always assume that in the future these medica- tions may be discontinued (see Table 157.2 ). Also, the progressive nature of AGA means that additional hair transplants may be required. The physician should therefore emphasize before the procedure how ongoing hair loss will affect the density and cosmetic appearance of the transplant as well as how this influences the placement of the grafts so as to assure a long-term natural appearance. Rotation of duties can also prove helpful. Donor Region The amount of available donor hair is the primary limiting factor in hair transplantation. In general, there are 65–85 follicular groupings/ cm 2 in the occipital donor scalp 55 . If there are < 40 follicular units/ cm 2 , the patient is considered a poor candidate (see Table 157.1 ). The mid-occipital scalp between the upper and lower occipital protuber- ances is the recommended donor site, given its density of hair and the ability to camouflage the donor scar due to the lack of involvement by AGA. If the harvesting is done too superiorly on the occiput, progressive AGA may reveal the surgical sites. Of note, donor density does not correlate with the extent of current or future hair loss in the frontal scalp or vertex. Harvesting of donor hair is performed via two different techniques: (1) elliptical donor harvesting; and (2) FUE ( Table 157.3 ). FIVE BASIC CRITERIA FOR ASSESSING CANDIDATES FOR HAIR TRANSPLANTATION Age Patients over the age of 25 years are preferable. While patients younger than 25 years of age often seek consultation, there is a hesitancy to operate. Follicular grafts Hair naturally grows in groupings of 1–4 hair follicles, referred to as follicular units (see Fig. 157.5 ) 57 . During the 1960s to 1990s, 3–4 mm grafts that contained multiple follicular units were employed, leading to an unnatural appearance with obvious bundles of hair. Nowadays, each graft contains one follicular grouping with 1–4 hair follicles. Thus, these grafts mimic the normal grouping of scalp hairs and create a natural appearance. When an ellipse is harvested, surgical teams carefully separate 500–2000 follicular units from the donor strip over 1–3 hours (see Fig. 157.9 ). Cutting instruments vary but include #11 and #15 blades as well as #10 prep blades. Good lighting, comfortable chairs, and well- designed instruments are prerequisites for producing follicular units with minimal follicular transection. Most surgeons believe microscopic dissection or magnification reduces transection of follicles during the separation process ( Fig. 157.12 ). It is important to create intact, minimally traumatized follicular units and place the transplanted hair into the recipient sites as efficiently and quickly as possible. As soon as the follicular unit grafts are separated from the donor ellipse, they must be put into a holding solution until they are placed into the recipient sites. It is also an option for patients who have significant tension or extensive scarring from previous elliptical donor harvesting.
